Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Abhidhammāvatāro

The Abhidhammāvatāra

Ganthārambhakathā

Introduction to the Text

1.

1.

Anantakaruṇāpaññaṃ[P 0.0001][M 0.0001][V 0.0001], tathāgatamanuttaraṃ;

Vanditvā sirasā buddhaṃ, dhammaṃ sādhugaṇampi ca.

Having bowed my head to the Buddha—the unsurpassed Tathāgata of boundless compassion and wisdom—and also to the Dhamma and the community of the virtuous;

2.

2.

Paṇḍukambalanāmāya, silāyātulavikkamo;

Nisinno devarājassa, vimale sītale tale.

Who, of unequalled prowess, was seated on the spotless, cool surface of the Paṇḍukambala stone of the king of gods;

3.

3.

Yaṃ devadevo devānaṃ, devadevehi pūjito;

Desesi devalokasmiṃ, dhammaṃ devapurakkhato.

That Dhamma which the God of gods—worshipped by the foremost gods and honored by the gods—taught in the world of the gods;

4.

4.

Tatthāhaṃ [V 0.0002] pāṭavatthāya, bhikkhūnaṃ piṭakuttame;

Abhidhammāvatārantu, madhuraṃ mativaḍḍhanaṃ.

Therefore, for the proficiency of the bhikkhus in the supreme Piṭaka, I shall expound the Abhidhammāvatāra, which is sweet and enhances wisdom;

5.

5.

Tāḷaṃ mohakavāṭassa, vighāṭanamanuttaraṃ;

Bhikkhūnaṃ pavisantānaṃ, abhidhammamahāpuraṃ.

An unsurpassed key for unlatching the door of delusion for the bhikkhus entering the great city of Abhidhamma;

6.

6.

Suduttaraṃ tarantānaṃ, abhidhammamahodadhiṃ;

Suduttaraṃ tarantānaṃ, taraṃva makarākaraṃ.

A raft for those crossing the great ocean of Abhidhamma, which is very difficult to cross, like an ocean teeming with sea-monsters;

7.

7.

Ābhidhammikabhikkhūnaṃ, hatthasāramanuttaraṃ;

Pavakkhāmi samāsena, taṃ suṇātha samāhitā.

I shall explain in brief this unsurpassed handbook for the bhikkhus who are masters of Abhidhamma. Listen to it with concentrated minds.

1. Paṭhamo paricchedo

1. The First Chapter

Cittaniddeso

Exposition of Consciousness

8.

8.

Cittaṃ [M 0.0002] cetasikaṃ rūpaṃ, nibbānanti niruttaro;

Catudhā desayī dhamme, catusaccappakāsano.

The Unsurpassed One, the proclaimer of the Four Truths, taught the ultimate realities as fourfold: consciousness, mental factors, matter, and Nibbāna.

Tattha cittanti visayavijānanaṃ cittaṃ, tassa pana ko vacanattho? Vuccate – sabbasaṅgāhakavasena pana cintetīti cittaṃ, attasantānaṃ vā cinotītipi cittaṃ.

Therein, consciousness (citta) is that which cognizes an object. But what is its verbal meaning? It is said: In a comprehensive sense, it is called ‘citta’ because it thinks (cinteti); or it is also ‘citta’ because it accumulates (cinoti) in its own continuum.

9.

9.

Vicittakaraṇā [P 0.0002] cittaṃ, attano cittatāya vā;

Paññattiyampi viññāṇe, vicitte cittakammake;

Cittasammuti daṭṭhabbā, viññāṇe idha viññunā.

It is ‘citta’ because it produces what is variegated, or because of its own variegated nature. Even in the variegated work of a painter, the term ‘citta’ is used as a designation. Here, this convention ‘citta’ should be understood by the wise one as referring to consciousness.

Taṃ pana sārammaṇato ekavidhaṃ, savipākāvipākato duvidhaṃ. Tattha savipākaṃ nāma kusalākusalaṃ, avipākaṃ abyākataṃ. Kusalākusalābyākatajātibhedato tividhaṃ.

That (consciousness), however, is of one kind in that it has an object. It is of two kinds as that which produces a result and that which does not. Therein, the wholesome and unwholesome are what produce a result; the indeterminate is what does not produce a result. It is of three kinds by the distinction of its nature as wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.

Tattha [V 0.0003] kusalanti panetassa ko vacanattho?

Therein, what is the verbal meaning of this word ‘kusala’?

10.

10.

Kucchitānaṃ salanato, kusānaṃ lavanena vā;

Kusena lātabbattā vā, kusalanti pavuccati.

It is called ‘kusala’ from its destroying (salana) what is reprehensible (kucchita); or from its cutting off (lavana) what is bad (kusa); or because it is to be attained (lātabba) by wisdom (kusa).

11.

11.

Cheke kusalasaddoyaṃ, ārogye anavajjake;

Diṭṭho iṭṭhavipākepi, anavajjādike idha.

This word ‘kusala’ is seen used in the senses of skillful, healthy, and blameless. It is also seen in the sense of having a desirable result. Here, in the Abhidhamma context, it has the meaning of blameless and so forth.

Tasmā anavajjaiṭṭhavipākalakkhaṇaṃ kusalaṃ, akusalaviddhaṃsanarasaṃ, vodānapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Vajjapaṭipakkhattā anavajjalakkhaṇaṃ vā kusalaṃ, vodānabhāvarasaṃ, iṭṭhavipākapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, yonisomanasikārapadaṭṭhānaṃ. Sāvajjāniṭṭhavipākalakkhaṇamakusalaṃ. Tadubhayaviparītalakkhaṇamabyākataṃ, avipākārahaṃ vā.

Therefore, the wholesome has the characteristic of being blameless and having a desirable result, the function of destroying the unwholesome, and purity as its manifestation. Alternatively, the wholesome has the characteristic of being blameless because it is opposed to what is faulty, the function of bringing about purity, a desirable result as its manifestation, and wise attention as its proximate cause. The unwholesome has the characteristic of being faulty and having an undesirable result. The indeterminate has characteristics opposite to both of those, or is incapable of producing a result.

Tattha [M 0.0003] kusalacittaṃ ekavīsatividhaṃ hoti, tadidaṃ bhūmito catubbidhaṃ hoti – kāmāvacaraṃ, rūpāvacaraṃ, arūpāvacaraṃ, lokuttarañceti.

Therein, wholesome consciousness is of twenty-one kinds. This is fourfold according to the plane: sense-sphere, fine-material sphere, immaterial sphere, and supramundane.

Tattha kāmāvacarakusalacittaṃ bhūmito ekavidhaṃ, savatthukāvatthukabhedato duvidhaṃ, hīnamajjhimapaṇītabhedato tividhaṃ, somanassupekkhāñāṇappayogabhedato aṭṭhavidhaṃ hoti. Seyyathidaṃ – somanassasahagataṃ ñāṇasampayuttaṃ asaṅkhārikamekaṃ, sasaṅkhārikamekaṃ, somanassasahagataṃ ñāṇavippayuttaṃ asaṅkhārikamekaṃ, sasaṅkhārikamekaṃ, upekkhāsahagataṃ ñāṇasampayuttaṃ asaṅkhārikamekaṃ, sasaṅkhārikamekaṃ, upekkhāsahagataṃ ñāṇavippayuttaṃ asaṅkhārikamekaṃ, sasaṅkhārikamekanti idaṃ aṭṭhavidhampi kāmāvacarakusalacittaṃ nāma.

Therein, sense-sphere wholesome consciousness is of one kind by plane; of two kinds by the distinction of being with or without a physical basis; of three kinds by the distinction of being inferior, middling, or superior; and of eight kinds by the distinctions of feeling, association with knowledge, and prompting. These are as follows: (1) one consciousness, unprompted, accompanied by joy, associated with knowledge; (2) one consciousness, prompted, accompanied by joy, associated with knowledge; (3) one consciousness, unprompted, accompanied by joy, dissociated from knowledge; (4) one consciousness, prompted, accompanied by joy, dissociated from knowledge; (5) one consciousness, unprompted, accompanied by equanimity, associated with knowledge; (6) one consciousness, prompted, accompanied by equanimity, associated with knowledge; (7) one consciousness, unprompted, accompanied by equanimity, dissociated from knowledge; (8) one consciousness, prompted, accompanied by equanimity, dissociated from knowledge. This is what is called the eightfold sense-sphere wholesome consciousness.

12.

12.

Uddānato duve kāmā, klesavatthuvasā pana;

Kileso chandarāgova, vatthu tebhūmavaṭṭakaṃ.

In summary, there are two kinds of desire (kāma): desire as defilement (kilesakāma) and desire as object (vatthukāma). The defilement-desire is sensual craving; the object-desire is the round of existence in the three planes.

13.

13.

Kilesakāmo [P 0.0003] kāmeti, vatthu kāmīyatīti ca;

Sijjhati duvidhopesa, kāmo vo kārakadvaye.

The defilement-desire desires, and the object-desire is desired; thus this desire is established as twofold in respect of these two grammatical functions (active and passive).

14.

14.

Yasmiṃ [V 0.0004] pana padese so, kāmoyaṃ duvidhopi ca;

Sampattīnaṃ vasenāva-caratīti ca so pana.

And in whatever region this twofold desire moves about, it does so by the power of the favorable conditions found there.

15.

15.

Padeso catupāyānaṃ, channaṃ devānameva ca;

Manussānaṃ vaseneva, ekādasavidho pana.

That region is elevenfold: the four states of woe, the human realm, and the six heavens of the sense sphere.

16.

16.

Kāmovacaratītettha, kāmāvacarasaññito;

Assābhilakkhitattā hi, sasatthāvacaro viya.

Because desire roams about in it, it is designated ‘sense-sphere’ (kāmāvacara). Indeed, as it is characterized by gratification, it is like a traveler with provisions.

17.

17.

Svāyaṃ rūpabhavo rūpaṃ, evaṃ kāmoti saññito;

Uttarassa padasseva, lopaṃ katvā udīrito.

Just as the fine-material world (rūpabhava) is designated ‘rūpa,’ so too is the desire world (kāmabhava) designated ‘kāma,’ spoken with the elision of the latter word.

18.

18.

Tasmiṃ [M 0.0004] kāme idaṃ cittaṃ, sadāvacaratīti ca;

Kāmāvacaramiccevaṃ, kathitaṃ kāmaghātinā.

And because this consciousness always roams about in that desire realm, it is thus called ‘sense-sphere consciousness’ by the Slayer of Desire.

19.

19.

Paṭisandhiṃ bhave kāme, avacārayatīti vā;

Kāmāvacaramiccevaṃ, pariyāpannanti tatra vā.

Or, because it causes rebirth-linking to occur in the desire-realm existence, it is called ‘sense-sphere’; or because it is included therein.

20.

20.

Idaṃ aṭṭhavidhaṃ cittaṃ, kāmāvacarasaññitaṃ;

Dasapuññakriyavatthu-vaseneva pavattati.

This eightfold consciousness, designated as sense-sphere, arises by way of the ten bases of meritorious action.

21.

21.

Dānaṃ sīlaṃ bhāvanā pattidānaṃ,

Veyyāvaccaṃ desanā cānumodo;

Diṭṭhijjuttaṃ saṃsuticcāpacāyo,

Ñeyyo evaṃ puññavatthuppabhedo.

Giving, virtue, mental development, transference of merit, service, teaching, rejoicing in others’ merit, straightening of views, listening to the Dhamma, and reverence—thus the classification of the bases of meritorious action should be known.

22.

22.

Gacchanti saṅgahaṃ dāne, pattidānānumodanā;

Tathā sīlamaye puññe, veyyāvaccāpacāyanā.

Transference of merit and rejoicing in others’ merit are included under giving; likewise, service and reverence are included under the merit of virtue.

23.

23.

Desanā savanaṃ diṭṭhi-ujukā bhāvanāmaye;

Puna tīṇeva sambhonti, dasa puññakriyāpi ca.

Teaching, listening, and straightening of views are included under the merit of mental development. Thus the ten meritorious actions are comprised within these three.

24.

24.

Sabbānussatipuññañca, pasaṃsā saraṇattayaṃ;

Yanti diṭṭhijukammasmiṃ, saṅgahaṃ natthi saṃsayo.

All meritorious recollections, praise, and taking the Three Refuges are, without a doubt, included in the act of straightening one’s views.

25.

25.

Purimā [V 0.0005] muñcanā ceva, parā tissopi cetanā;

Hoti dānamayaṃ puññaṃ, evaṃ sesesu dīpaye.

The prior volition of relinquishing and the subsequent associated volitions constitute the merit of giving. This should be applied accordingly to the other cases.

Idāni assa panaṭṭhavidhassāpi kāmāvacarakusalacittassa ayamuppattikkamo veditabbo. Yadā hi yo deyyadhammappaṭiggāhakādisampattiṃ, aññaṃ vā somanassahetuṃ āgamma haṭṭhapahaṭṭho “atthi dinna”nti ādinayappavattaṃ sammādiṭṭhiṃ purakkhatvā parehi anussāhito dānādīni puññāni karoti, tadāssa somanassasahagataṃ ñāṇasampayuttaṃ [P 0.0004] asaṅkhārikaṃ [M 0.0005] paṭhamaṃ mahākusalacittaṃ uppajjati. Yadā pana vuttanayeneva haṭṭhapahaṭṭho sammādiṭṭhiṃ purakkhatvā parehi ussāhito karoti, tadāssa tameva cittaṃ sasaṅkhārikaṃ hoti. Imasmiṃ panatthe saṅkhāroti attano vā parassa vā pavattassa pubbappayogassādhivacanaṃ. Yadā pana ñātijanassa paṭipattidassanena jātaparicayā bālakā bhikkhū disvā somanassajātā sahasā yaṃ kiñci hatthagataṃ dadanti vā vandanti vā, tadā tesaṃ tatiyacittamuppajjati. Yadā pana te “detha vandatha, ayye”ti vadanti, evaṃ ñātijanena ussāhitā hutvā hatthagataṃ dadanti vā vandanti vā, tadā tesaṃ catutthacittamuppajjati. Yadā pana deyyadhammappaṭiggāhakādīnaṃ asampattiṃ vā aññesaṃ vā somanassahetūnaṃ abhāvaṃ āgamma catūsupi vikappesu somanassarahitā honti, tadā sesāni cattāri upekkhāsahagatāni uppajjanti. Evaṃ somanassupekkhāñāṇappayogabhedato aṭṭhavidhaṃ kāmāvacarakusalacittaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Now the order of arising of these eight types of sense-sphere wholesome consciousness should be understood. When a person, delighted and overjoyed on account of suitable conditions such as the gift and the recipient, or some other cause for joy, performs meritorious deeds such as giving, preceded by right view such as the conviction ‘There is fruit in giving,’ and does so without being prompted by others, then the first great wholesome consciousness arises in him: unprompted, accompanied by joy, and associated with knowledge. But when, in the same way, being delighted and overjoyed and preceded by right view, he performs the deed having been prompted by others, then that same consciousness becomes prompted. In this context, ‘prompting’ (saṅkhāra) is a term for the prior instigation undertaken by oneself or by another. When, however, children who have become familiar with such acts by seeing their relatives do them, feel joy on seeing bhikkhus and spontaneously give whatever they have in hand or pay homage, then the third consciousness arises in them (unprompted, with joy, without knowledge). But when, having been prompted by their relatives saying, ‘Give, dear ones, pay homage,’ they give what is in their hands or pay homage, then the fourth consciousness arises in them (prompted, with joy, without knowledge). When, on account of the unsuitability of the gift or recipient, or the absence of other causes for joy, they are devoid of joy in all four of these cases, then the remaining four types of consciousness, which are accompanied by equanimity, arise. Thus the eight types of sense-sphere wholesome consciousness should be understood as distinguished by feeling (joy or equanimity), association with knowledge, and prompting.

26.

26.

Dasapuññakriyādīnaṃ, vasena ca bahūnipi;

Etāni pana cittāni, bhavantīti pakāsaye.

It should be declared that these consciousnesses arise in many ways, by means of the ten meritorious actions and so forth.

27.

27.

Sattarasa sahassāni, dve satāni asīti ca;

Kāmāvacarapuññāni, bhavantīti viniddise.

It should be pointed out that there are seventeen thousand, two hundred and eighty types of sense-sphere wholesome consciousness.

Taṃ pana yathānurūpaṃ kāmāvacarasugatiyaṃ bhavabhogasampattiṃ abhinipphādeti.

That consciousness, according to its nature, produces the fortune of existence and enjoyments in the happy destinations of the sense sphere.

Itaresu pana rūpāvacarakusalacittaṃ savatthukato ekavidhaṃ, dvīsu bhavesu uppajjanato duvidhaṃ, hīnamajjhimapaṇītabhedato tividhaṃ, paṭipadādibhedato catubbidhaṃ, jhānaṅgayogabhedato pañcavidhaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ – kāmacchandabyāpādathinamiddhauddhaccakukkuccavicikicchāvippahīnaṃ vitakkavicārapītisukhacittekaggatāsampayuttaṃ [V 0.0006] paṭhamaṃ, vitakkavippahīnaṃ vicārapītisukhacittekaggatāsampayuttaṃ [M 0.0006] dutiyaṃ, vitakkavicāravippahīnaṃ pītisukhacittekaggatāsampayuttaṃ tatiyaṃ, vitakkavicārapītivippahīnaṃ sukhacittekaggatāsampayuttaṃ catutthaṃ, vitakkavicārapītisukhavippahīnaṃ upekkhācittekaggatāsampayuttaṃ pañcamanti idaṃ pañcavidhaṃ [P 0.0005] rūpāvacarakusalacittaṃ nāma.

As to the others, the wholesome consciousness of the fine-material sphere is of one kind in that it has a physical basis; of two kinds in that it arises in two planes of existence; of three kinds by the distinction of inferior, middling, and superior; of four kinds by the distinction of the modes of practice; and of five kinds by the distinction of the combination of jhāna factors. These are as follows: (1) The first, associated with initial application, sustained application, zest, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind, having abandoned sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt. (2) The second, associated with sustained application, zest, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind, having abandoned initial application. (3) The third, associated with zest, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind, having abandoned initial and sustained application. (4) The fourth, associated with happiness and one-pointedness of mind, having abandoned initial application, sustained application, and zest. (5) The fifth, associated with equanimity and one-pointedness of mind, having abandoned initial application, sustained application, zest, and happiness. This is what is called the fivefold wholesome consciousness of the fine-material sphere.

Taṃ pana yathāsambhavaṃ pathavīkasiṇādīsu ārammaṇesu pavattivasena anekavidhaṃ hoti. Sabbaṃ panetaṃ rūpāvacarabhāvanāpuññavasappavattaṃ yathānurūpaṃ rūpāvacarūpapattinipphādakaṃ hoti. Evaṃ tāva rūpāvacarakusalaṃ veditabbaṃ.

This consciousness becomes manifold by way of its occurrence with such objects as the earth kasiṇa and so on. All this, proceeding by the power of the merit of fine-material sphere development, appropriately produces rebirth in the fine-material sphere. Thus, for now, the fine-material sphere wholesome consciousness should be understood.

Sesesu pana dvīsu arūpāvacarakusalacittaṃ tāva upekkhāvedanāyogabhedato ekavidhaṃ, savatthukāvatthukabhedato duvidhaṃ, hīnamajjhimapaṇītabhedato tividhaṃ, ārammaṇabhedato catubbidhaṃ. Kasiṇugghāṭimākāsaṃ, tattha pavattaviññāṇaṃ, tassa apagamo, ākiñcaññāyatananti idamassa catubbidhamārammaṇaṃ. Yathāpaṭipāṭiyā etassārammaṇassa bhedato catubbidhaṃ hoti. Seyyathidaṃ – sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamā paṭighasaññānaṃ atthaṅgamā nānattasaññānaṃ amanasikārā ākāsānañcāyatanasaññāsahagataṃ, viññāṇañcāyatanasaññāsahagataṃ, ākiñcaññāyatanasaññāsahagataṃ, nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasaññāsahagatanti idaṃ catubbidhaṃ arūpāvacarakusalacittaṃ nāma. Sabbaṃ panetaṃ arūpāvacarabhāvanāpuññavasappavattaṃ yathānurūpaṃ arūpūpapattinipphādakaṃ hoti. Evaṃ arūpāvacarakusalacittaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Moreover, among the remaining two, the wholesome consciousness pertaining to the formless sphere is, firstly, of one kind by its association with the feeling of equanimity. It is of two kinds by the distinction of having a physical basis and being without one. It is of three kinds by the distinction of being inferior, middling, and superior. It is of four kinds by the distinction of its objects. The concept of infinite space, the consciousness of the base of infinite space, the absence of that consciousness, and the base of nothingness: these are its fourfold objects. According to their order, it is fourfold by the distinction of these objects: consciousness accompanied by the perception of the base of infinite space; consciousness accompanied by the perception of the base of infinite consciousness; consciousness accompanied by the perception of the base of nothingness; and consciousness accompanied by the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. This is called the fourfold wholesome consciousness pertaining to the formless sphere. All this arises by the power of merit from the development of formless-sphere meditation, and it produces rebirth in a corresponding formless realm. Thus the wholesome consciousness pertaining to the formless sphere should be understood.

Itaraṃ pana lokuttarakusalacittaṃ nibbānārammaṇato ekavidhaṃ, niyatāniyatavatthukabhedato duvidhaṃ, tīhi vimokkhamukhehi pattabbato tividhaṃ, catumaggayogabhedato catubbidhaṃ[M 0.0007]. Seyyathidaṃ – sakkāyadiṭṭhivicikicchāsīlabbataparāmāsasaññojanappahānakaraṃ sotāpattimaggacittaṃ, rāgadosamohānaṃ tanuttakaraṃ sakadāgāmimaggacittaṃ, kāmarāgabyāpādānaṃ niravasesappahānakaraṃ anāgāmimaggacittaṃ, rūparāgaarūparāgamānauddhaccaavijjāpahānakaraṃ arahattamaggacittanti idaṃ catubbidhaṃ lokuttarakusalacittaṃ nāma. Ekekaṃ panettha jhānaṅgayogabhedato pañcavidhaṃ hoti, tasmā vīsatividhaṃ hoti. Sabbaṃ panetaṃ lokuttarabhāvanāpuññavasappavattaṃ maggānurūpaphalappavattiyā cattāro ariyapuggale abhinipphādeti. Evaṃ lokuttarakusalaṃ veditabbaṃ.

The other, the supramundane wholesome consciousness, is of one kind by taking Nibbāna as its object; of two kinds by the distinction between having a determinate and an indeterminate basis; of three kinds by being attainable through the three doors to liberation; and of four kinds by the division into the four paths. Namely: the path consciousness of stream-entry, which abandons the fetters of identity view, doubt, and clinging to rules and observances; the path consciousness of once-returning, which attenuates greed, hatred, and delusion; the path consciousness of non-returning, which completely abandons sensual desire and ill will; the path consciousness of arahantship, which abandons attachment to form, attachment to the formless, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance—this is called the fourfold supramundane wholesome consciousness. Each of these, moreover, becomes fivefold by the distinction of jhānic factors, thus making twenty kinds in total. All of this arises from the power of merit of supramundane development and brings about the four noble individuals through the occurrence of the fruition that corresponds to the path. Thus the supramundane wholesome should be understood.

28.

28.

Kāme [P 0.0006][V 0.0007] aṭṭheva rūpe ca, pañca cattārirūpisu;

Cattārānuttarānevaṃ, kusalānekavīsati.

In the sense sphere, eight; in the form sphere, five; in the formless sphere, four; four are supramundane—thus the wholesome are twenty-one.

29.

29.

Kusalākusalāpagatena satā,

Kusale kusalena ca yaṃ kusalaṃ;

Catubhūmigataṃ muninā vasinā,

Lapitaṃ lapitaṃ sakalampi mayā.

Whatever wholesome teaching pertaining to the four planes was spoken by the Sage, the Master—who is mindful, who has gone beyond wholesome and unwholesome, and who is skillful in what is wholesome—all that was spoken has now been uttered by me.

Akusalaṃ pana bhūmito ekavidhaṃ kāmāvacarameva, niyatāniyatavatthuvasena ca ekahetukaduhetukavasena ca paṭisandhijanakājanakavasena ca duvidhaṃ, tīhi vedanāhi yogato ca lobhamūlaṃ dosamūlaṃ mohamūlanti mūlato ca tividhaṃ hoti. Tattha lobhamūlaṃ pana somanassupekkhādiṭṭhippayogabhedato aṭṭhavidhaṃ hoti. Seyyathidaṃ – somanassasahagataṃ diṭṭhigatasampayuttaṃ asaṅkhārikamekaṃ, sasaṅkhārikamekaṃ, somanassasahagataṃ diṭṭhigatavippayuttaṃ asaṅkhārikamekaṃ, sasaṅkhārikamekaṃ, upekkhāsahagataṃ diṭṭhigatasampayuttaṃ asaṅkhārikamekaṃ, sasaṅkhārikamekaṃ, upekkhāsahagataṃ diṭṭhigatavippayuttaṃ asaṅkhārikamekaṃ, sasaṅkhārikamekanti.

The unwholesome, however, is of one kind by plane, being only of the sense sphere. It is twofold by way of having a determinate or indeterminate basis, by way of being rooted in one or two roots, and by way of being rebirth-producing or non-rebirth-producing. It is threefold by its connection with the three feelings, and also threefold by its root, namely, rooted in greed, rooted in hatred, and rooted in delusion. Herein, that which is rooted in greed is eightfold by the distinctions of being associated with joy or equanimity, connected with or disconnected from wrong view, and unprompted or prompted. That is to say: one accompanied by joy, connected with wrong view, unprompted; one accompanied by joy, connected with wrong view, prompted; one accompanied by joy, disconnected from wrong view, unprompted; one accompanied by joy, disconnected from wrong view, prompted; one accompanied by equanimity, connected with wrong view, unprompted; one accompanied by equanimity, connected with wrong view, prompted; one accompanied by equanimity, disconnected from wrong view, unprompted; and one accompanied by equanimity, disconnected from wrong view, prompted.

Yadā [M 0.0008] hi “natthi kāmesu ādīnavo”tiādinā nayena micchādiṭṭhiṃ purakkhatvā kevalaṃ haṭṭhatuṭṭho kāme vā paribhuñjati, diṭṭhamaṅgalādīni vā sārato pacceti sabhāvatikkheneva anussāhitena cittena, tadāssa paṭhamaṃ akusalacittaṃ uppajjati. Yadā pana mandena samussāhitena, tadā dutiyaṃ. Yadā micchādiṭṭhiṃ apurakkhatvā kevalaṃ haṭṭhatuṭṭho methunaṃ dhammaṃ vā paribhuñjati, parasampattiṃ vā abhijjhāyati, parassa bhaṇḍaṃ vā harati sabhāvatikkheneva anussāhitena cittena, tadā tatiyaṃ. Yadā mandena samussāhitena, tadā catutthaṃ uppajjati. Yadā pana kāmānaṃ vā asampattiṃ āgamma aññesaṃ vā somanassahetūnaṃ abhāvena catūsupi vikappesu somanassarahitā honti, tadā sesāni cattāri upekkhāsahagatāni uppajjantīti. Evaṃ somanassupekkhādiṭṭhippayogabhedato aṭṭhavidhaṃ lobhamūlaṃ veditabbaṃ.

For when one, giving precedence to wrong view with the reasoning, 'There is no danger in sensual pleasures,' etc., merely enjoys sensual pleasures, elated and delighted, or regards auspicious sights and other superstitions as essential, with a naturally keen and unprompted mind, then the first unwholesome consciousness arises in him. But when this occurs with a sluggish and prompted mind, then the second arises. When, without giving precedence to wrong view, one merely enjoys sexual intercourse, elated and delighted, or covets another's property, or steals another's belongings, with a naturally keen and unprompted mind, then the third arises. When this occurs with a sluggish and prompted mind, then the fourth arises. But when, due to the non-attainment of sensual pleasures or the absence of other causes for joy, one is devoid of joy in all four cases, then the remaining four accompanied by equanimity arise. Thus the eightfold greed-rooted consciousness should be understood by its distinctions regarding joy, equanimity, connection with view, and prompting.

Dosamūlaṃ pana ekantasavatthukato ekavidhaṃ, asaṅkhārasasaṅkhārabhedato duvidhaṃ domanassasahagataṃ paṭighasampayuttaṃ asaṅkhāraṃ, sasaṅkhāranti. Assa pana pāṇātipātādīsu tikkhamandappavattikāle uppatti veditabbā.

That which is rooted in hatred, however, is of one kind in that it is exclusively with a physical basis. It is of two kinds by the distinction of being unprompted and prompted: one accompanied by displeasure, associated with aversion, and unprompted; and one that is prompted. Its arising should be understood to occur at the time of keen or sluggish activity in such acts as killing living beings.

Mohamūlampi [P 0.0007][V 0.0008] vicikicchuddhaccayogato duvidhaṃ hoti upekkhāsahagataṃ vicikicchāsampayuttaṃ, upekkhāsahagataṃ uddhaccasampayuttanti. Tassa asanniṭṭhānavikkhepakālesu pavatti veditabbāti.

That which is rooted in delusion is also twofold by its association with doubt and restlessness: one accompanied by equanimity and associated with doubt, and one accompanied by equanimity and associated with restlessness. Its occurrence should be understood to be at times of indecision and distraction.

Evaṃ tāva dvādasavidhaṃ akusalacittaṃ veditabbaṃ, sabbaṃ panetaṃ yathānurūpaṃ apāyesu upapattiyā, sugatiyampi dukkhavisesassa abhinipphādakaṃ hoti.

Thus, these twelve kinds of unwholesome consciousness should be understood. All of this, according to its nature, leads to rebirth in the woeful states; and even in a happy destination, it is productive of particular kinds of suffering.

30.

30.

Lobhamūlavasenaṭṭha, dosamūlavasā duve;

Mohamūlavasena dve, evaṃ dvādasadhā siyuṃ.

By way of being rooted in greed, eight; by way of being rooted in hatred, two; by way of being rooted in delusion, two; thus they are twelvefold.

31.

31.

Pāpāpāpesvapāpena[M 0.0009], yaṃ vuttaṃ pāpamānasaṃ;

Pāpāpāpappahīnena, taṃ mayā samudāhaṭaṃ.

That evil mind which was taught by the One who is without evil in regard to evil and non-evil, by the One who has abandoned both evil and non-evil—that has been fully expounded by me.

Itaraṃ pana abyākatamavipākārahato ekavidhaṃ hoti, jātibhedato duvidhaṃ vipākacittaṃ kiriyacittanti. Tattha vipākacittaṃ bhūmibhedato catubbidhaṃ kāmāvacaraṃ rūpāvacaraṃ arūpāvacaraṃ lokuttaranti. Tattha kāmāvacaraṃ duvidhaṃ kusalavipākaṃ akusalavipākanti. Kusalavipākaṃ duvidhaṃ sahetukamahetukañceti.

The other, the indeterminate, is of one kind in that it does not produce a result. By distinction of class, it is twofold: resultant consciousness and functional consciousness. Therein, resultant consciousness is fourfold by distinction of plane: sense-sphere, form-sphere, formless-sphere, and supramundane. Therein, sense-sphere resultant consciousness is twofold: wholesome-resultant and unwholesome-resultant. Wholesome-resultant, in turn, is twofold: with roots and without roots.

Tattha sahetukavipākacittaṃ sakakusalaṃ viya somanassupekkhāñāṇappayogabhedato aṭṭhavidhaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ – somanassasahagataṃ ñāṇasampayuttaṃ asaṅkhāraṃ, sasaṅkhāraṃ, somanassasahagataṃ ñāṇavippayuttaṃ asaṅkhāraṃ, sasaṅkhāraṃ, upekkhāsahagataṃ ñāṇasampayuttaṃ asaṅkhāraṃ, sasaṅkhāraṃ, upekkhāsahagataṃ ñāṇavippayuttaṃ asaṅkhāraṃ, sasaṅkhāranti idaṃ aṭṭhavidhaṃ sahetukavipākaṃ nāma.

Herein, the resultant consciousness with roots, like its corresponding wholesome consciousness, is eightfold by the distinctions of being associated with joy or equanimity, being associated with knowledge, and being unprompted or prompted. Namely: one accompanied by joy, associated with knowledge, and unprompted; one that is prompted; one accompanied by joy, dissociated from knowledge, and unprompted; one that is prompted; one accompanied by equanimity, associated with knowledge, and unprompted; one that is prompted; one accompanied by equanimity, dissociated from knowledge, and unprompted; and one that is prompted. These eight are called the resultant consciousness with roots.

Yathā panassa kusalaṃ dānādivasena chasu ārammaṇesu pavattati, na idaṃ tathā. Idaṃ hi paṭisandhibhavaṅgacutitadārammaṇavasena parittadhammapariyāpannesuyeva chasu ārammaṇesu pavattati. Sampayuttadhammānañca visese asatipi ādāsatalādīsu mukhanimittaṃ viya nirussāhaṃ vipākaṃ, mukhaṃ viya saussāhaṃ kusalanti veditabbaṃ. Imesaṃ pana vipaccanaṭṭhānaṃ veditabbaṃ. Imāni hi paṭisandhibhavaṅgacutitadārammaṇāni hutvā vipaccanti.

However, this does not occur in the same way as one's wholesome consciousness, which occurs in relation to the six objects by way of giving, etc. For this resultant consciousness occurs only in relation to the six objects included among limited phenomena, by way of functioning as rebirth-linking, life-continuum, death, and registration. And although there is no difference in the associated mental states, the resultant should be understood as effortless, like the reflection of a face in a mirror, while the wholesome should be understood as effortful, like the face itself. Moreover, the occasions of their ripening should be understood, for these ripen by functioning as rebirth-linking, life-continuum, death, and registration.

32.

32.

Kāmāvacaradevānaṃ[V 0.0009], manussānaṃ ime pana;

Duhetukatihetūnaṃ, bhavanti paṭisandhiyo.

For the sense-sphere gods and for humans with two or three roots, these become their rebirth-linking consciousnesses.

33.

33.

Tato pavattiyaṃ hutvā, bhavaṅgaṃ yāvatāyukaṃ;

Balavārammaṇe hutvā, tadārammaṇameva ca.

Then, during the course of life, it becomes the life-continuum for the full lifespan; and when a strong object is present, it also becomes the registration-consciousness.

34.

34.

Tato [P 0.0008][M 0.0010] maraṇakālasmiṃ, cuti hutvā pavattare;

Evaṃ catūsu ṭhānesu, vipaccantīti niddise.

Then at the time of death, they occur, having become the death-consciousness. Thus it is shown that they ripen in four instances.

35.

35.

Sabhūmikusaleheva, mahāpākā samā vinā;

Kammadvārañca kammañca, puññānaṃ kriyavatthukaṃ.

The great resultants are similar to the wholesome states of their own plane, except with regard to the doors of action, the action itself, and the basis for meritorious deeds.

36.

36.

Aviññattijanattā hi, avipākasabhāvato;

Appavattanato ceva, pākā puññehi no samā.

Results are not the same as meritorious deeds because they do not produce intimation, because they are of a nature that produces no further result, and because they do not actively occur.

37.

37.

Parittārammaṇattā hi, tesamekantato pana;

Karuṇāmuditā tesu, na jāyanti kadācipi.

Because their object is exclusively limited, compassion and sympathetic joy never arise in them.

38.

38.

Tathā viratiyo tisso, na panetesu jāyare;

Pañca sikkhāpadā vuttā, kusalāti hi satthunā.

Similarly, the three abstinences do not arise in these, for the training precepts have been declared 'wholesome' by the Teacher.

39.

39.

Tathādhipatinopettha, na santīti viniddise;

Chandādīni dhuraṃ katvā, anuppajjanato pana.

Similarly, it should be pointed out that dominants are not present in them, because they do not arise by taking desire and so on as the driving force.

40.

40.

Asaṅkhārasasaṅkhāra-vidhānaṃ pana puññato;

Ñeyyaṃ paccayato ceva, vipākesu ca viññunā.

The distinction between unprompted and prompted in the case of resultants should be understood by the wise from the corresponding meritorious deed and from its conditions.

41.

41.

Hīnādīnaṃ vipākattā, puññānaṃ puññavādinā;

Hīnādayo bhavantīti, vipākā paridīpitā.

It has been explained by the Teacher of merit that resultants are inferior, medium, or superior because they are the results of meritorious deeds that are inferior, medium, or superior.

42.

42.

Idaṃ aṭṭhavidhaṃ cittaṃ, ekantena savatthukaṃ;

Jāyate kāmalokasmiṃ, na panaññattha jāyate.

This eightfold consciousness is exclusively with a physical basis; it arises in the sense-sphere world and does not arise elsewhere.

Evaṃ tāva sahetukavipākacittaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Thus the resultant consciousness with roots should be understood.

Ahetukavipākacittaṃ [V 0.0010] pana alobhādihetuvirahitaṃ upekkhāsahagataṃ cakkhuviññāṇaṃ, upekkhāsahagataṃ sotaviññāṇaṃ, upekkhāsahagataṃ ghānaviññāṇaṃ, upekkhāsahagataṃ jivhāviññāṇaṃ, sukhasahagataṃ kāyaviññāṇaṃ, upekkhāsahagataṃ ahetukamanodhātusampaṭicchanaṃ, somanassasahagataṃ ahetukamanoviññāṇadhātusantīraṇaṃ[M 0.0011], upekkhāsahagataṃ ahetukamanoviññāṇadhātusantīraṇanti idaṃ pana aṭṭhavidhaṃ ahetukavipākacittaṃ nāma.

Rootless resultant consciousness, however, being devoid of roots such as non-greed, is eightfold thus: eye-consciousness accompanied by equanimity, ear-consciousness accompanied by equanimity, nose-consciousness accompanied by equanimity, tongue-consciousness accompanied by equanimity, body-consciousness accompanied by pleasure, rootless receiving mind-element accompanied by equanimity, rootless investigating mind-consciousness-element accompanied by joy, and rootless investigating mind-consciousness-element accompanied by equanimity. This is called the eightfold rootless resultant consciousness.

Idaṃ pana aṭṭhavidhaṃ niyatavatthukato ekavidhaṃ, niyatāniyatārammaṇato duvidhaṃ. Tattha viññāṇapañcakaṃ niyatārammaṇaṃ, sesattayaṃ aniyatārammaṇaṃ. Sukhasomanassupekkhāvedanāyogato tividhaṃ. Tattha sukhasahagataṃ kāyaviññāṇaṃ, dviṭṭhānikaṃ santīraṇaṃ somanassupekkhāyuttaṃ, sesamupekkhāyuttanti.

This eightfold consciousness, however, is of one kind with respect to having a fixed base, and twofold with respect to having a fixed or unfixed object. Among them, the pentad of sense-consciousnesses has a fixed object, while the remaining three have an unfixed object. With regard to association with feeling, it is threefold. Among them, body-consciousness is associated with pleasure, the twofold investigating consciousness is associated with joy and equanimity, and the rest are associated with equanimity.

Diṭṭhārammaṇasutārammaṇamutārammaṇadiṭṭhasutamutārammaṇadiṭṭha-sutamutaviññātārammaṇavasena pañcavidhaṃ. Tattha diṭṭhārammaṇaṃ cakkhuviññāṇaṃ, sutārammaṇaṃ [P 0.0009] sotaviññāṇaṃ, mutārammaṇaṃ ghānajivhākāyaviññāṇattayaṃ, diṭṭhasutamutārammaṇaṃ manodhātusampaṭicchanaṃ, diṭṭhasutamutaviññātārammaṇaṃ sesamanoviññāṇadhātudvayanti.

It is fivefold by way of its object: having a seen object, a heard object, a sensed object, a seen-heard-sensed object, and a seen-heard-sensed-cognized object. Therein, eye-consciousness has a seen object; ear-consciousness has a heard object; the triad of nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness has a sensed object; the receiving mind-element has a seen, heard, or sensed object; and the remaining two mind-consciousness-elements have a seen, heard, sensed, or cognized object.

Vatthuto chabbidhaṃ. Kathaṃ? Cakkhuviññāṇassa cakkhumeva vatthu, tathā sotaghānajivhākāyaviññāṇānaṃ sotaghānajivhākāyavatthu, avasesattayassa hadayavatthumevāti.

With respect to base, it is sixfold. How so? For eye-consciousness, the eye itself is the base. Similarly, for ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness, the ear, nose, tongue, and body are their bases. For the remaining three, the heart-base alone is their base.

Ārammaṇato sattavidhaṃ hoti. Kathaṃ? Rūpārammaṇameva cakkhuviññāṇaṃ, tathā saddagandharasaphoṭṭhabbārammaṇāni paṭipāṭiyā sotaghānajivhākāyaviññāṇāni, rūpādipañcārammaṇā manodhātu, sesamanoviññāṇadhātudvayaṃ chaḷārammaṇanti.

With respect to object, it is sevenfold. How so? Eye-consciousness has only a visible form as its object. Similarly, ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness have, respectively, sound, odor, taste, and tangible objects as their objects. The mind-element has the five sense objects beginning with visible form. The remaining two mind-consciousness-elements have all six objects.

Taṃ sabbaṃ pana ahetukavipākacittaṃ kiccato aṭṭhavidhaṃ hoti. Kathaṃ? Dassanakiccaṃ cakkhuviññāṇaṃ, savanaghāyanasāyanaphusanasampaṭicchanasantīraṇatadārammaṇakiccāni avasesāni.

All that rootless resultant consciousness, however, is eightfold with respect to function. How so? Eye-consciousness has the function of seeing; the remaining ones have the functions of hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, receiving, investigating, and registering.

Tattha [M 0.0012] cakkhuto pavattaṃ viññāṇaṃ, cakkhumhi sannissitaṃ viññāṇanti vā cakkhuviññāṇaṃ, tathā sotaviññāṇādīni. Tattha cakkhusannissitarūpavijānanalakkhaṇaṃ cakkhuviññāṇaṃ[V 0.0011], rūpamattārammaṇarasaṃ, rūpābhimukhabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, rūpārammaṇāya kiriyāmanodhātuyā apagamapadaṭṭhānaṃ. Tathā sotaghānajivhākāyaviññāṇāni sotādisannissitasaddādivijānanalakkhaṇāni, saddādimattārammaṇarasāni, saddādīsu abhimukhabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānāni, saddādiārammaṇānaṃ kiriyāmanodhātūnaṃ apagamapadaṭṭhānāni. Manodhātusampaṭicchanaṃ pana cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ anantarā rūpādivijānanalakkhaṇaṃ, rūpādisampaṭicchanarasaṃ, tathābhāvapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ apagamapadaṭṭhānaṃ.

Herein, 'eye-consciousness' is the consciousness that proceeds from the eye, or the consciousness that is dependent on the eye; similarly for ear-consciousness and so on. Therein, eye-consciousness has the characteristic of cognizing a visible form dependent on the eye; its function is to have just a visible form as its object; it is manifested as the state of facing a visible form; and its proximate cause is the cessation of the functional mind-element that has a visible form as its object. Similarly, ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness have the characteristic of cognizing sound, etc., dependent on the ear, etc.; their function is to have just sound, etc., as their objects; they are manifested as the state of facing sound, etc.; and their proximate cause is the cessation of the functional mind-elements that have sound, etc., as their objects. The receiving mind-element, however, has the characteristic of cognizing a visible form, etc., immediately after eye-consciousness, etc.; its function is to receive a visible form, etc.; it is manifested as being in such a state; and its proximate cause is the cessation of eye-consciousness, etc.

Sesā pana dve ahetukamanoviññāṇadhātuyo chaḷārammaṇavijānanalakkhaṇā, santīraṇādirasā, tathābhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā, hadayavatthupadaṭṭhānāti veditabbā. Tattha paṭhamā ekantamiṭṭhārammaṇe pavattisabbhāvato somanassayuttāva hutvā pañcadvāre santīraṇakiccaṃ sādhayamānā pañcasu dvāresu ṭhatvā vipaccati, chasu pana dvāresu balavārammaṇe tadārammaṇaṃ hutvā vipaccati. Dutiyā [P 0.0010] pana iṭṭhamajjhattārammaṇe pavattisabbhāvato upekkhāsahagatā hutvā santīraṇatadārammaṇapaṭisandhibhavaṅgacutivasena pavattanato pañcasu ṭhānesu vipaccati. Kathaṃ? Manussaloke tāva jaccandhajaccabadhirajaccajaḷajaccummattakapaṇḍakaubhatobyañjananapuṃsakādīnaṃ paṭisandhiggahaṇakāle paṭisandhi hutvā vipaccati. Paṭisandhiyā vītivattāya pavattiyaṃ yāvatāyukaṃ bhavaṅgaṃ hutvā vipaccati. Iṭṭhamajjhatte pañcārammaṇavīthiyā santīraṇaṃ hutvā, balavārammaṇe chadvāre tadārammaṇaṃ hutvā, maraṇakāle cuti hutvāti imesu pana pañcasu ṭhānesu vipaccatīti. Evaṃ tāva ahetukavipākacittāni veditabbāni.

The remaining two rootless mind-consciousness-elements, however, should be understood as having the characteristic of cognizing the six objects, having the function of investigating and so on, being manifested as being in such a state, and having the heart-base as their proximate cause. Therein, the first, since it arises exclusively in relation to a desirable object, is always accompanied by joy. Performing the function of investigating in the five sense-doors, it ripens by occurring in the five doors. However, in the six doors, when the object is strong, it ripens by becoming registering consciousness. The second, however, since it arises in relation to a desirable or neutral object, is accompanied by equanimity. As it proceeds by way of investigating, registering, rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and death, it ripens in five instances. How so? In the human world, at the time of taking rebirth, it ripens by becoming the rebirth-linking consciousness for those born blind, born deaf, born mute, born mentally deficient, born insane, for pandakas, hermaphrodites, eunuchs, and so on. After rebirth-linking has passed, for as long as life lasts, it ripens by becoming the life-continuum. In a five-door process with a desirable or neutral object, it ripens by becoming investigating consciousness; with a strong object in the six doors, it ripens by becoming registering consciousness; and at the time of death, it ripens by becoming the death consciousness. Thus it ripens in these five instances. In this way, for now, the rootless resultant consciousnesses are to be understood.

43.

43.

Kāmāvacarapuññassa[M 0.0013], vipākā honti soḷasa;

Taṃ tihetukapuññassa, vasena paridīpaye.

Of sense-sphere merit, / The results are sixteenfold; / This I shall explain / By way of merit with three roots.

Idāni rūpāvacaravipākacittāni vuccanti. Tāni niyatavatthukato ekavidhāni, jhānaṅgayogabhedato pañcavidhāni. Kathaṃ? Vitakkavicārapītisukhacittekaggatāsampayuttaṃ paṭhamaṃ, vicārapītisukhacittekaggatāsampayuttaṃ dutiyaṃ, pītisukhacittekaggatāsampayuttaṃ tatiyaṃ, sukhacittekaggatāsampayuttaṃ catutthaṃ, upekkhācittekaggatāsampayuttaṃ pañcamanti imāni pañcapi rūpāvacaravipākacittāni upapattiyaṃ paṭisandhibhavaṅgacutivasena pavattanti.

Now the fine-material sphere resultant consciousnesses are spoken of. They are of one kind with respect to having a fixed base, and fivefold with respect to the different combinations of jhāna factors. How so? The first is associated with initial application, sustained application, rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind; the second, with sustained application, rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind; the third, with rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind; the fourth, with happiness and one-pointedness of mind; the fifth, with equanimity and one-pointedness of mind. These five fine-material sphere resultant consciousnesses proceed by way of rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and death at the time of rebirth.

Idāni [V 0.0012] arūpāvacaravipākacittāni vuccanti. Tāni sakakusalāni viya ārammaṇabhedato catubbidhāni honti. Kathaṃ? Ākāsānañcāyatanasaññāsahagataṃ, viññāṇañcāyatanasaññāsahagataṃ, ākiñcaññāyatanasaññāsahagataṃ, nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasaññāsahagatanti imāni cattāri arūpāvacaravipākacittāni.

Now the immaterial-sphere resultant consciousnesses are spoken of. Like their own wholesome counterparts, they are fourfold with respect to the difference in their object. How so? Consciousness accompanied by the perception of the base of infinite space; consciousness accompanied by the perception of the base of infinite consciousness; consciousness accompanied by the perception of the base of nothingness; and consciousness accompanied by the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—these are the four immaterial-sphere resultant consciousnesses.

44.

44.

Kusalānugataṃ katvā, bhājitaṃ kiṃ mahaggataṃ;

Kāmāvacarapuññaṃva, nāsamānaphalaṃ yato.

Why is the sublime resultant explained / Following upon the wholesome? / Because, unlike sense-sphere merit, / Its fruit is not dissimilar.

45.

45.

Attano kusaleheva, samānaṃ sabbathā idaṃ;

Gajādīnaṃ yathā chāyā, gajādisadisā tathā.

This is in every way similar / To its own wholesome counterpart; / Just as the shadow of an elephant / Is similar to the elephant itself.

46.

46.

Kāmāvacarapuññaṃva, nāparāpariyavedanaṃ;

Jhānā aparihīnassa, sattassa bhavagāmino.

Unlike sense-sphere merit, it is not / A fruit experienced at a later time / For a being bound for a new existence / Who has not fallen away from jhāna.

47.

47.

Kusalānantaraṃyeva[P 0.0011], phalaṃ uppajjatīti ca;

Ñāpanatthaṃ panetassa, kusalānugataṃ kataṃ.

And to make known that the fruit / Arises immediately after the wholesome, / For this reason it was explained / Following upon the wholesome.

48.

48.

Paṭippadākkamo ceva, hīnādīnañca bhedato;

Jhānāgamanato cettha, veditabbo vibhāvinā.

The order of the path of practice, / And the distinction of inferior and so on, / And how the jhānas are attained— / This the wise should understand.

49.

49.

Abhāvodhipatīnañca[M 0.0014], ayameva visesako;

Sesaṃ sabbaṃ ca sesena, kusalena samaṃ mataṃ. –

And the absence of predominating factors / Is the only distinction here; / All the rest is held to be the same / As the corresponding wholesome state.

Evaṃ rūpāvacarārūpāvacaravipākā veditabbā.

Thus are the fine-material sphere and immaterial-sphere resultants to be understood.

Idāni lokuttaravipākacittāni honti. Tāni catumaggayuttacittaphalattā catubbidhāni honti. Kathaṃ? Sotāpattimaggaphalacittaṃ, sakadāgāmimaggaphalacittaṃ, anāgāmimaggaphalacittaṃ, arahattamaggaphalacittanti. Evaṃ panettha ekekaṃ jhānaṅgayogabhedato pañcavidhaṃ, puna maggavīthiphalasamāpattivasena pavattito duvidhaṃ. Evaṃ lokuttarakusalavipākacittāni veditabbāni.

Now there are the supramundane resultant consciousnesses. They are fourfold, being the fruit of the consciousnesses of the four paths. How so? The fruition-consciousness of the path of stream-entry, the fruition-consciousness of the path of once-returning, the fruition-consciousness of the path of non-returning, and the fruition-consciousness of the path of arahantship. Herein, each of these is fivefold with respect to the different combinations of jhāna factors; and again, twofold as they proceed by way of the path process and by way of the fruition attainment. Thus are the resultant consciousnesses of the supramundane wholesome to be understood.

50.

50.

Suññataṃ [V 0.0013] animittanti, tathāpaṇihitantipi;

Etāni tīṇi nāmāni, maggassānantare phale.

Emptiness, the signless, / And also the uninclined— / These three are names for the fruit / Immediately following the path.

51.

51.

Labbhanti parabhāgasmiṃ, vaḷañjanaphalesu na;

Vipassanāvaseneva, tāni nāmāni labbhare.

These names are not obtained for the other part, the path, / Nor for the fruits for ordinary use; / By the power of insight alone / Are these names acquired.

52.

52.

Honti sādhipatīneva, lokuttaraphalāni tu;

Vipākedhipatī natthi, ṭhapetvā tu anāsave.

The supramundane fruits, however, / Are indeed accompanied by predominance; / But in the resultant there is no predominance, / Except in the case of the taintless.

53.

53.

Attano maggabhāvena, maggo “maggo”ti vuccati;

Phalaṃ maggamupādāya, maggo nāmāti vuccati. –

Because of its own nature as a path, / The path is called 'path'; / The fruit, arising from the path, / Is also called by the name 'path'.

Evaṃ lokuttaravipākā veditabbā.

Thus are the supramundane resultants to be understood.

Idāni sattākusalavipākāni vuccanti. Akusalavipākaṃ upekkhāsahagataṃ cakkhuviññāṇaṃ, upekkhāsahagataṃ sotaviññāṇaṃ, upekkhāsahagataṃ ghānaviññāṇaṃ, upekkhāsahagataṃ jivhāviññāṇaṃ, dukkhasahagataṃ kāyaviññāṇaṃ, upekkhāsahagataṃ ahetukamanodhātusampaṭicchanaṃ, upekkhāsahagataṃ ahetukamanoviññāṇadhātusantīraṇanti imāni satta akusalavipākacittāni.

Now the seven unwholesome-resultant states are spoken of. Unwholesome-resultant eye-consciousness accompanied by equanimity, unwholesome-resultant ear-consciousness accompanied by equanimity, unwholesome-resultant nose-consciousness accompanied by equanimity, unwholesome-resultant tongue-consciousness accompanied by equanimity, body-consciousness accompanied by pain, rootless receiving mind-element accompanied by equanimity, and rootless investigating mind-consciousness-element accompanied by equanimity—these are the seven unwholesome-resultant consciousnesses.

Ettha [M 0.0015] pana upekkhāsahagatāhetukamanoviññāṇadhātu ekādasavidhenāpi akusalacittena kamme āyūhite kammakammanimittagatinimittesu aññataraṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā catūsu apāyesu paṭisandhi hutvā vipaccati, paṭisandhiyā vītivattāya [P 0.0012] dutiyacittavāraṃ tato paṭṭhāya yāvatāyukaṃ bhavaṅgaṃ hutvā, aniṭṭhamajjhattārammaṇāya pañcaviññāṇavīthiyā santīraṇaṃ hutvā, balavārammaṇe chasu dvāresu tadārammaṇaṃ hutvā, maraṇakāle cuti hutvā vipaccati. Evaṃ pañcasu ṭhānesu vipaccati. Kevalaṃ hi tāni kusalavipākāhetukacittāni kusalakammapaccayāni, imāni akusalakammapaccayāni. Ayamimesaṃ, tesañca viseso.

Here, when kamma has been accumulated by the eleven kinds of unwholesome consciousness, the rootless mind-consciousness-element accompanied by equanimity takes as its object one of the following—kamma, the sign of kamma, or the sign of destiny—and ripens by becoming rebirth-linking in the four planes of misery. After the rebirth-linking has passed, from the second thought-moment onwards for as long as life lasts, it functions as the life-continuum; in a five-door cognitive process with an undesirable or neutral object, it functions as investigating consciousness; with a strong object at the six doors, it functions as registering consciousness; and at the time of death, it functions as the death consciousness. Thus it ripens in five instances. For those wholesome rootless resultant consciousnesses are conditioned by wholesome kamma, while these are conditioned by unwholesome kamma. This is the difference between them.

54.

54.

Aniṭṭhāniṭṭhamajjhattagocare vattare ime;

Sukhādittayayuttā te, dukkhupekkhāyutā ime.

Those occur with objects desirable or neutral, these with objects undesirable or neutral; those are endowed with the triad of feelings beginning with pleasure, these with pain and equanimity.

Evaṃ [V 0.0014] kāmāvacarakusalavipākasahetukamaṭṭhavidhaṃ, ahetukamaṭṭhavidhaṃ, jhānaṅgayogabhedato rūpāvacaravipākaṃ pañcavidhaṃ, ārammaṇabhedato arūpāvacaravipākaṃ catubbidhaṃ, maggasampayuttacittaphalabhedato lokuttaravipākaṃ catubbidhaṃ, cakkhuviññāṇādibhedato akusalavipākaṃ sattavidhanti chattiṃsavidhaṃ vipākacittaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Thus, resultant consciousness should be understood as thirty-sixfold: eightfold sense-sphere wholesome resultant with roots; eightfold sense-sphere rootless resultant; fivefold form-sphere resultant by distinction of jhāna factors; fourfold formless-sphere resultant by distinction of objects; fourfold supramundane resultant as the fruits of the four path consciousnesses; and sevenfold unwholesome resultant by distinction of eye-consciousness and so on.

55.

55.

Evaṃ chattiṃsadhā pākaṃ, pākasāsanapūjito;

Savipākāvipākesu, kusalo sugatobravi.

Thus the Well-Gone One—honored for his teaching on resultants and skilled in what has a resultant and what is without one—spoke of the thirty-sixfold resultant.

Kiriyābyākatacittaṃ pana avipākato ekavidhaṃ, parittamahaggatato duvidhaṃ, kāmāvacararūpāvacaraarūpāvacarabhūmibhedato tividhaṃ. Tattha kāmāvacaraṃ duvidhaṃ sahetukamahetukanti. Tattha sahetukaṃ ekavidhaṃ arahato eva uppajjanato. Somanassupekkhāñāṇappayogabhedato kāmāvacarakusalaṃ viya aṭṭhavidhaṃ hoti. Seyyathidaṃ – somanassasahagataṃ ñāṇasampayuttaṃ asaṅkhārikaṃ, sasaṅkhārikaṃ, somanassasahagataṃ [M 0.0016] ñāṇavippayuttaṃ asaṅkhārikaṃ, sasaṅkhārikaṃ, upekkhāsahagataṃ ñāṇasampayuttaṃ asaṅkhārikaṃ, sasaṅkhārikaṃ, upekkhāsahagataṃ ñāṇavippayuttaṃ asaṅkhārikaṃ, sasaṅkhārikanti imāni aṭṭha sahetukakiriyacittāni. Etāni pana yathānurūpaṃ dānādivasena khīṇāsavānaṃyeva pavattanti. Evaṃ sahetukakiriyacittāni veditabbāni.

Functional consciousness, however, is of one kind as non-resultant; twofold as limited and exalted; and threefold according to the planes: sense-sphere, form-sphere, and formless-sphere. Herein, sense-sphere functional consciousness is twofold: with roots and without roots. Among these, the one with roots is of one kind, arising only in an Arahant. According to the distinctions of joy, equanimity, knowledge, and prompting, it is eightfold like the sense-sphere wholesome consciousness. Namely: 1. Accompanied by joy, associated with knowledge, unprompted. 2. Accompanied by joy, associated with knowledge, prompted. 3. Accompanied by joy, dissociated from knowledge, unprompted. 4. Accompanied by joy, dissociated from knowledge, prompted. 5. Accompanied by equanimity, associated with knowledge, unprompted. 6. Accompanied by equanimity, associated with knowledge, prompted. 7. Accompanied by equanimity, dissociated from knowledge, unprompted. 8. Accompanied by equanimity, dissociated from knowledge, prompted. These are the eight functional consciousnesses with roots. These, according to suitability, occur only in Arahants, by way of giving, etc. Thus the functional consciousnesses with roots should be understood.

Ahetukakiriyacittaṃ pana tividhaṃ kiriyāhetukamanodhātuupekkhāsahagatāvajjanacittaṃ, kiriyāhetukamanoviññāṇadhātusomanassasahagataṃ hasituppādacittaṃ, kiriyāhetukamanoviññāṇadhātuupekkhāsahagataṃ voṭṭhabbanacittanti[P 0.0013].

Rootless functional consciousness is threefold: the functional rootless mind-element accompanied by equanimity, which is five-door-adverting consciousness; the functional rootless mind-consciousness-element accompanied by joy, which is smile-producing consciousness; and the functional rootless mind-consciousness-element accompanied by equanimity, which is determining consciousness.

Tattha kiriyāhetukamanodhātu upekkhāsahagatā hadayavatthuṃ nissāya cakkhudvāre iṭṭhaiṭṭhamajjhattaaniṭṭhaaniṭṭhamajjhattesu rūpārammaṇesu yena kenaci pasāde ghaṭṭite taṃ taṃ ārammaṇaṃ gahetvā āvajjanavasena cakkhuviññāṇassa purecārī hutvā bhavaṅgaṃ āvaṭṭayamānā uppajjati. Sotadvārādīsupi eseva nayo. Itarā pana dve ahetukamanoviññāṇadhātuyo sādhāraṇāsādhāraṇāti duvidhā honti. Tattha asādhāraṇā pana kiriyāhetukamanoviññāṇadhātu somanassasahagatā khīṇāsavasseva chasu dvāresu chasu anuḷāresu ārammaṇesu hasituppādakiccā niyatavatthukā uppajjati. Sādhāraṇā pana ahetukamanoviññāṇadhātu upekkhāsahagatā chaḷārammaṇavijānanalakkhaṇā[V 0.0015], tathābhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā, sā tīsu bhavesu sabbesaṃ sacittakasattānaṃ sādhāraṇā, na kassaci pana sacittakassa na uppajjati nāma. Uppajjamānā panāyaṃ pañcadvāramanodvāresu voṭṭhabbanāvajjanakiccā uppajjati. Cha asādhāraṇañāṇānipi etāya gahitārammaṇameva gaṇhanti. Sabbārammaṇagahaṇasamatthatāya [M 0.0017] sabbaññutaññāṇagatikāti veditabbā. Imāni tīṇi ahetukakiriyacittāni.

Here, the functional rootless mind-element accompanied by equanimity, dependent on the heart-base, arises at the eye-door when a visual object—whether desirable, desirable-neutral, undesirable, or undesirable-neutral—has struck any sense faculty. Taking up that object by way of adverting, it arises as a precursor to eye-consciousness, turning the life-continuum. The same method applies to the ear-door and so on. The other two rootless mind-consciousness-elements are twofold: common and uncommon. Of these, the uncommon one, the functional rootless mind-consciousness-element accompanied by joy, arises only for an Arahant at the six doors with regard to six sublime objects, performing the function of producing a smile; it has a fixed physical basis. The common one, the rootless mind-consciousness-element accompanied by equanimity, has the characteristic of cognizing the six objects and its manifestation is in being such. It is common to all beings with consciousness in the three planes of existence; indeed, there is no being with consciousness for whom it does not arise. When it arises, it performs the function of determining at the five doors and adverting at the mind-door. The six uncommon knowledges also take only the object taken by this. Because it is capable of grasping all objects, it should be understood as the access to the knowledge of omniscience. These are the three rootless functional consciousnesses.

Idha ṭhatvā hasanacittāni pariggaṇhitabbāni. Terasa hasanacittāni. Kusalato catūhi somanassasahagatehi, akusalato catūhīti imehi aṭṭhahi cittehi puthujjanā hasanti, sekhā pana kusalato catūhi, akusalato dvīhi diṭṭhigatavippayuttasomanassasahagatehīti chahi hasanti, khīṇāsavā kiriyato pañcahi somanassasahagatehi hasantīti.

Here, the smile-producing consciousnesses should be enumerated. There are thirteen smile-producing consciousnesses. Worldlings smile with eight consciousnesses: four wholesome ones accompanied by joy and four unwholesome ones. Trainees smile with six: four wholesome ones and two unwholesome ones accompanied by joy and dissociated from wrong view. Those whose cankers are destroyed smile with five functional consciousnesses accompanied by joy.

56.

56.

Somanassayutānaṭṭha, kusalākusalāni ca;

Kriyato pana pañcevaṃ, hāsacittāni terasa.

Eight wholesome and unwholesome consciousnesses are connected with joy, and five are functional; thus there are thirteen smile-producing consciousnesses.

57.

57.

Puthujjanā hasantettha, cittehi pana aṭṭhahi;

Chahi sekhā asekhā ca, hasanti pana pañcahi.

Here, worldlings smile with eight consciousnesses; trainees smile with six, and non-trainees with five.

Idāni rūpāvacarakiriyacittāni honti. Vitakkavicārapītisukhacittekaggatāsampayuttaṃ paṭhamaṃ, vicārapītisukhacittekaggatāsampayuttaṃ dutiyaṃ, pītisukhacittekaggatāsampayuttaṃ tatiyaṃ, sukhacittekaggatāsampayuttaṃ catutthaṃ, upekkhācittekaggatāsampayuttaṃ pañcamanti imāni pañca rūpāvacarakiriyacittāni.

Now there are the form-sphere functional consciousnesses. The first is accompanied by initial application, sustained application, rapture, pleasure, and one-pointedness; the second, by sustained application, rapture, pleasure, and one-pointedness; the third, by rapture, pleasure, and one-pointedness; the fourth, by pleasure and one-pointedness; the fifth, by equanimity and one-pointedness. These are the five form-sphere functional consciousnesses.

Idāni [P 0.0014] arūpāvacarakiriyacittāni vuccanti. Ākāsānañcāyatanasaññāsahagataṃ, viññāṇañcāyatanasaññāsahagataṃ, ākiñcaññāyatanasaññāsahagataṃ, nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasaññāsahagatanti imāni cattāri arūpāvacarakiriyacittāni. Imāni pana rūpārūpakiriyacittāni sakasakabhūmikusalasadisāni. Kevalaṃ panetāni kiriyacittāni khīṇāsavānaṃyeva uppajjanti, kusalāni pana sekhaputhujjanānaṃ. Imāni ca khīṇāsavānaṃ bhāvanākāravasappavattāni, tāni pana sekhaputhujjanānaṃ bhāvanāpuññavasappavattānīti ayameva imesaṃ, tesañca viseso.

Now the formless-sphere functional consciousnesses are spoken of: functional consciousness of the base of infinite space; functional consciousness of the base of infinite consciousness; functional consciousness of the base of nothingness; and functional consciousness of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. These are the four formless-sphere functional consciousnesses. These form and formless functional consciousnesses are similar to the wholesome consciousnesses of their respective planes. However, these functional consciousnesses arise only for those whose cankers are destroyed, while the wholesome ones arise for trainees and worldlings. For those whose cankers are destroyed, these arise by way of the mode of development; for trainees and worldlings, those arise by way of the merit of development. This is the difference between them.

58.

58.

Yā [M 0.0018][V 0.0016] puthujjanakālasmiṃ, abhinibbattitā pana;

Rūpārūpasamāpatti, sā khīṇāsavabhikkhuno.

Those form and formless attainments that were produced when one was a worldling are also for the monk whose cankers are destroyed.

59.

59.

Yāva khīṇāsavo bhikkhu, na samāpajjateva naṃ;

Tāva tā kusalā eva, samāpannā sace kriyā.

As long as the monk with cankers destroyed does not enter that attainment, so long are those attainments wholesome. But if he has entered it, they are functional.

Evaṃ somanassādibhedato kāmāvacarasahetukakiriyacittamaṭṭhavidhaṃ, manodhātumanoviññāṇadhātudvayabhedato ahetukaṃ tividhaṃ, jhānaṅgayogabhedato rūpāvacaraṃ pañcavidhaṃ, ārammaṇabhedato arūpāvacaraṃ catubbidhaṃ, evaṃ bhūmivasena vīsatividhaṃ kiriyacittaṃ veditabbanti.

Thus, the functional consciousness with roots pertaining to the sense-sphere, classified by joy and so on, is eightfold; the rootless, classified by the distinction between the mind-element and the two mind-consciousness-elements, is threefold; the form-sphere, classified by the combination of jhāna factors, is fivefold; the formless-sphere, classified by their objects, is fourfold. Thus, functional consciousness should be understood as twentyfold by way of plane.

60.

60.

Ekādasavidhaṃ kāme, rūpe pañca arūpisu;

Cattārīti ca sabbāni, kriyācittāni vīsati.

Eleven in the sense-sphere, five in the form-sphere, and four in the formless; thus, all functional consciousnesses are twenty.

61.

61.

Lokuttarakriyacittaṃ, pana kasmā na vijjati;

Ekacittakkhaṇattā hi, maggassāti na vijjati.

But why is there no supramundane functional consciousness? Because the path lasts for a single thought-moment, it is not found.

62.

62.

Kriyākriyāpattivibhāgadesako,

Kriyākriyaṃ cittamavoca yaṃ jino;

Hitāhitānaṃ sakriyākriyārato,

Kriyākriyaṃ tantu mayā samīritaṃ.

The Jina, who teaches the distinction between the functional and the non-functional, declared that consciousness is both functional and non-functional. Devoted to the functional and non-functional in terms of what is beneficial and harmful, I have now set forth this doctrine of the functional and non-functional.

Ettāvatā ekavīsatividhaṃ kusalaṃ, dvādasavidhaṃ akusalaṃ chattiṃsavidhaṃ vipākaṃ, vīsatividhaṃ kiriyacittanti ādimhi nikkhittaṃ cittaṃ ekūnanavutippabhedena vidhinā pakāsitaṃ hotīti.

Thus, the consciousness initially classified as twenty-one kinds of wholesome consciousness, twelve kinds of unwholesome consciousness, thirty-six kinds of resultant consciousness, and twenty kinds of functional consciousness has been explained in detail according to the method, making a total of eighty-nine kinds.

63.

63.

Ekavīsati [P 0.0015] puññāni, dvādasākusalāni ca;

Chattiṃseva vipākāni, kriyacittāni vīsati.

Twenty-one are the wholesome consciousnesses, and twelve the unwh wholesome; thirty-six are the resultants, and twenty the functional consciousnesses.

64.

64.

Ekūnanavuti sabbe, cittuppādā mahesinā;

Aṭṭha lokuttare katvā, niddiṭṭhā hi samāsato.

All eighty-nine arisings of consciousness, including the eight supramundane ones, have been briefly pointed out by the Great Sage.

65.

65.

Piṭake [M 0.0019][V 0.0017] abhidhammasmiṃ, ye bhikkhū pāṭavatthino;

Tehāyaṃ uggahetabbo, cintetabbo punappunaṃ.

Those monks who are versed in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka should learn this and reflect upon it again and again.

66.

66.

Abhidhammāvatārena, abhidhammamahodadhiṃ;

Ye taranti imaṃ lokaṃ, parañceva taranti teti.

Those who, by means of the Abhidhammāvatāra, cross the great ocean of Abhidhamma, cross over this world and the next as well.

Iti abhidhammāvatāre cittaniddeso nāma

Thus ends the exposition of consciousness in the Abhidhammāvatāra.

Paṭhamo paricchedo.

The First Chapter.

2. Dutiyo paricchedo

2. The Second Chapter.

Cetasikaniddeso

Exposition of Mental Factors.

67.

67.

Cittānantaramuddiṭṭhā[P 0.0016], ye ca cetasikā mayā;

Tesaṃ dāni karissāmi, vibhājanamito paraṃ.

I shall now make a detailed classification of those mental factors that were pointed out by me immediately after consciousness.

Tattha cittasampayuttā, citte bhavā vā cetasikā. Tepi cittaṃ viya sārammaṇato ekavidhā, savipākāvipākato duvidhā, kusalākusalābyākatabhedato tividhā, kāmāvacarādibhedato catubbidhā.

Herein, mental factors are those associated with consciousness or those that arise in consciousness. They too, like consciousness, are of one kind in that they have an object; of two kinds, as resultant and non-resultant; of three kinds, by way of the division into wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate; and of four kinds, by way of the division into sense-sphere, and so on.

Tattha kāmāvacaracittasampayuttā kāmāvacarā. Tesu kāmāvacarapaṭhamamahākusalacittasampayuttā tāva niyatā sarūpena āgatā ekūnatiṃsa dhammā honti. Seyyathidaṃ – phasso vedanā saññā cetanā vitakko vicāro pīti cittekaggatā saddhā sati vīriyaṃ paññā jīvitindriyaṃ alobho adoso hirī ottappaṃ kāyappassaddhi cittappassaddhi kāyalahutā cittalahutā kāyamudutā cittamudutā kāyakammaññatā cittakammaññatā kāyapāguññatā cittapāguññatā kāyujukatā cittujukatāti. Puna chando, adhimokkho, tatramajjhattatā, manasikāro cāti cattāro niyatayevāpanakā honti. Imehi catūhi tettiṃsa honti[M 0.0020]. Puna karuṇā muditā kāyaduccaritavirati [V 0.0018] vacīduccaritavirati micchājīvavirati ceti ime pañca aniyatā. Ime pana kadāci uppajjanti.

Herein, the mental factors associated with sense-sphere consciousness are sense-sphere mental factors. Among them, to begin with, there are twenty-nine states that are associated with the first great wholesome sense-sphere consciousness as a fixed set. They are: contact, feeling, perception, volition, initial application, sustained application, zest, one-pointedness of mind, faith, mindfulness, energy, wisdom, the life faculty, non-greed, non-hatred, moral shame, moral dread, tranquility of body, tranquility of mind, lightness of body, lightness of mind, malleability of body, malleability of mind, wieldiness of body, wieldiness of mind, proficiency of body, proficiency of mind, rectitude of body, and rectitude of mind. Furthermore, zeal, decision, specific neutrality, and attention are four particular factors. With these four, they become thirty-three. Additionally, compassion, appreciative joy, abstinence from bodily misconduct, abstinence from verbal misconduct, and abstinence from wrong livelihood are five variable factors. These, however, arise only occasionally.

Imesu pana karuṇāmuditāvasena bhāvanākāle karuṇāpubbabhāgo vā muditāpubbabhāgo vā etā uppajjanti, na panekato uppajjanti. Yadā pana iminā cittena micchākammantādīhi viramati, tadā sammākammantādīni paripūrenti, ekā virati uppajjati, karuṇāmuditāhi saha, aññamaññena ca na uppajjanti. Tasmā etesu ekena saha catuttiṃseva dhammā honti.

Among these variable factors, at the time of developing compassion and appreciative joy, either compassion or appreciative joy arises, but they do not arise together. When, with this consciousness, one abstains from wrong bodily action and so on, then right bodily action and so on are fulfilled, and one abstinence arises. The abstinences do not arise together with compassion and appreciative joy, nor with one another. Therefore, with one of these five, there are exactly thirty-four states in total.

68.

68.

Ādinā [P 0.0017] puññacittena, tettiṃsa niyatā matā;

Karuṇāmuditekena, catuttiṃsa bhavanti te.

With the first wholesome consciousness, thirty-three are considered fixed; with one from the group including compassion and appreciative joy, they become thirty-four.

69.

69.

Kasmā panettha mettā ca, upekkhā ca na uddhaṭā;

Yevāpanakadhammesu, dhammarājena satthunā.

Why here were loving-kindness and equanimity not included by the Teacher, the King of Dhamma, among the particular factors?

70.

70.

Abyāpādena mettāpi, tatramajjhattatāya ca;

Upekkhā gahitā yasmā, tasmā na gahitā ubho.

Since loving-kindness is included in non-hatred, and equanimity in specific neutrality, therefore both are not included separately.

71.

71.

Kasmā yevāpanā dhammā, buddhenādiccabandhunā;

Sarūpeneva sabbete, pāḷiyaṃ na ca uddhaṭā.

Why were all these particular factors not mentioned individually in the Pāḷi by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun?

72.

72.

Yasmā aniyatā keci, yasmā rāsiṃ bhajanti na;

Yasmā ca dubbalā keci, tasmā vuttā na pāḷiyaṃ.

Because some are variable, because they do not form a group, and because some are weak—therefore they were not mentioned in the Pāḷi.

73.

73.

Chandādhimokkhamuditā manasi ca kāro,

Majjhattatā ca karuṇā viratittayaṃ ca;

Puññesu tena niyatāniyatā ca sabbe,

Yevāpanā munivarena na ceva vuttā.

Zeal, decision, appreciative joy, attention, specific neutrality, compassion, and the three abstinences—all these particulars are either fixed or variable in wholesome states; therefore they were not mentioned by the Great Sage.

74.

74.

Kasmā panettha phassova, paṭhamaṃ samudīrito;

Paṭhamābhinipātattā, cittassārammaṇe kira.

Why here is contact mentioned first? Because, it is said, of its being the first impact of consciousness on the object.

75.

75.

Phusitvā [M 0.0021][V 0.0019] pana phassena, vedanāya ca vedaye;

Sañjānāti ca saññāya, cetanāya ca cetaye.

Having contacted with contact, one feels with feeling, perceives with perception, and wills with volition.

76.

76.

Balavapaccayattā ca, sahajātānameva hi;

Phassova paṭhamaṃ vutto, tasmā idha mahesinā.

And because it is a strong condition for its co-nascent states, contact is therefore mentioned first here by the Great Sage.

77.

77.

Akāraṇamidaṃ sabbaṃ, cittānaṃ tu saheva ca;

Ekuppādādibhāvena, cittajānaṃ pavattito.

All this is without a temporal cause, for mind-born phenomena occur simultaneously with consciousness, possessing the characteristic of arising together, and so on.

78.

78.

Ayaṃ tu paṭhamuppanno, ayaṃ pacchāti natthidaṃ;

Balavapaccayattepi, kāraṇañca na dissati.

There is no such thing as 'this arose first, this later.' Even in the case of a strong condition, a cause for this is not seen.

79.

79.

Desanākkamato ceva, paṭhamaṃ samudīrito;

Iccevaṃ pana viññeyyaṃ, viññunā na visesato.

It is mentioned first simply due to the order of the teaching. Thus it should be understood by the wise one, without making a special distinction.

80.

80.

Na ca pariyesitabboyaṃ, tasmā pubbāparakkamo;

Vacanatthalakkhaṇādīhi, dhammā eva vijānatā.

Therefore, this sequence of prior and posterior should not be investigated by one who understands the states through their verbal expression, meaning, characteristic, and so on.

Yasmā pana ime dhammā vacanatthalakkhaṇādīhi vuccamānā pākaṭā honti suviññeyyāva, tasmā tesaṃ vacanatthalakkhaṇādīni pavakkhāmi. Seyyathidaṃ – phusatīti phasso. Svāyaṃ phusanalakkhaṇo, saṅghaṭṭanaraso, sannipātapaccupaṭṭhāno, phalaṭṭhena vedanāpaccupaṭṭhāno vā, āpāthagatavisayapadaṭṭhāno. Ayaṃ hi arūpadhammopi samāno ārammaṇesu phusanākāreneva [P 0.0018] pavattati, so dvinnaṃ meṇḍānaṃ sannipāto viya daṭṭhabbo.

But since these states, when explained by way of their verbal expression, meaning, characteristic, and so on, become evident and easily understood, I will therefore explain their verbal expression, meaning, characteristic, and so on. As follows: 'It touches,' thus it is contact. It has the characteristic of touching, the function of impacting, and the manifestation of confluence, or alternatively, of feeling as its result. Its proximate cause is the object that has come into range. For this, although an immaterial state, occurs in the manner of touching an object; it should be seen as like the collision of two rams.

Sundaraṃ manoti sumano, sumanassa bhāvo somanassaṃ, somanassameva vedanā somanassavedanā. Sā vedayitalakkhaṇā, iṭṭhākārānubhavanarasā rājā viya subhojanarasaṃ, cetasikaassādapaccupaṭṭhānā, passaddhipadaṭṭhānā.

'The mind is beautiful,' thus one is 'glad-minded' (sumano); the state of being glad-minded is joy (somanassa); joy itself as a feeling is joyful feeling. It has the characteristic of experiencing, the function of enjoying the desirable aspect of an object, like a king enjoying the taste of delicious food, the manifestation of mental delight, and tranquility as its proximate cause.

Nīlādibhedaṃ [M 0.0022] ārammaṇaṃ sañjānātīti saññā. Sā sañjānanalakkhaṇā, paccābhiññāṇakaraṇarasā vaḍḍhakissa abhiññāṇakaraṇamiva, yathāgahitanimittavasena abhinivesakaraṇapaccupaṭṭhānā, yathopaṭṭhitavisayapadaṭṭhānā.

'It perceives an object with its distinctions, such as blue,' thus it is perception. It has the characteristic of perceiving, and its function is to make a sign for recognizing again, like a carpenter making a mark on wood. Its manifestation is interpreting by means of the sign as apprehended, and its proximate cause is the object as it has appeared.

Cetayatīti [V 0.0020] cetanā. Saddhiṃ attanā sampayuttadhamme ārammaṇe abhisandahatīti attho. Sā cetayitalakkhaṇā, āyūhanarasā, saṃvidahanapaccupaṭṭhānā sakakiccaparakiccasādhakā jeṭṭhasissamahāvaḍḍhakiādayo viya.

'It wills,' thus it is volition (cetanā). The meaning is that it organizes its associated states on the object. It has the characteristic of willing, the function of accumulating (kamma), and the manifestation of coordinating, like a senior pupil or a master carpenter, etc., who accomplishes their own tasks and those of others.

Vitakketīti vitakko. Vitakkanaṃ vā vitakko. Svāyaṃ ārammaṇe cittassa abhiniropanalakkhaṇo, āhananapariyāhananaraso, ārammaṇe cittassa ānayanapaccupaṭṭhāno.

'It applies,' thus it is initial application (vitakka). Or, the applying is initial application. It has the characteristic of directing the mind onto the object; its function is to strike at and thresh the object; and its manifestation is the leading of the mind to the object.

Ārammaṇe tena cittaṃ vicaratīti vicāro. Vicaraṇaṃ vā vicāro. Anusañcaraṇanti vuttaṃ hoti. Svāyaṃ ārammaṇānumajjanalakkhaṇo, tattha sahajātānuyojanaraso, cittassa anupabandhapaccupaṭṭhāno.

'The mind moves about on the object by means of it,' thus it is sustained application (vicāra). Or, the moving about is sustained application. This means 'continued traversing.' It has the characteristic of repeatedly stroking the object, the function of yoking its co-nascent states to that object, and the manifestation of the mind's continuous binding to the object.

Pinayatīti pīti. Sā sampiyāyanalakkhaṇā, kāyacittapīṇanarasā, pharaṇarasā vā, odagyapaccupaṭṭhānā.

'It gladdens,' thus it is zest (pīti). It has the characteristic of endearing. Its function is to refresh the mental body and consciousness, or to suffuse them. Its manifestation is elation.

Cittassa ekaggabhāvo cittekaggatā. Samādhissetaṃ nāmaṃ. So avisāralakkhaṇo, avikkhepalakkhaṇo vā, sahajātānaṃ sampiṇḍanaraso nhāniyacuṇṇānaṃ udakaṃ viya, upasamapaccupaṭṭhāno, visesato sukhapadaṭṭhāno.

The state of one-pointedness of the mind is one-pointedness of mind. This is a name for concentration. It has the characteristic of non-diffusion, or non-distraction. Its function is to consolidate the co-nascent states, like water for bath powder. It manifests as tranquility, and its proximate cause is happiness.

Saddahanti etāya, sayaṃ vā saddahati, saddahanamattameva vā esāti saddhā. Sā panesā saddahanalakkhaṇā, pasādanarasā udakappasādakamaṇi viya, akālusiyapaccupaṭṭhānā, saddheyyavatthupadaṭṭhānā.

'One has faith by means of it,' or 'one has faith,' or 'it is simply the act of having faith'—thus it is faith (saddhā). It has the characteristic of faith. Its function is to clarify, like a water-clearing gem. It manifests as non-turbidity, and its proximate cause is an object of faith.

Saranti [M 0.0023] etāya, sayaṃ vā sarati, saraṇamattameva vā esāti sati. Sā apilāpanalakkhaṇā, asammosarasā, ārakkhapaccupaṭṭhānā, thirasaññāpadaṭṭhānā.

'One remembers by means of it,' or 'one remembers,' or 'it is simply the act of remembering'—thus it is mindfulness (sati). It has the characteristic of not drifting. Its function is non-forgetfulness. It manifests as guarding, and its proximate cause is firm perception.

Vīrabhāvo [P 0.0019] vīriyaṃ. Vīrānaṃ vā kammaṃ vīriyaṃ. Taṃ panetaṃ ussāhanalakkhaṇaṃ, sahajātānaṃ upatthambhanarasaṃ, asaṃsīdanabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, saṃvegapadaṭṭhānaṃ.

The state of a hero is energy. Or, the work of heroes is energy. It has the characteristic of exertion, the function of supporting its co-nascent states, the manifestation of non-collapse, and a sense of urgency as its proximate cause.

Pajānātīti [V 0.0021] paññā. Sā panesā vijānanalakkhaṇā, visayobhāsanarasā padīpo viya, asammohapaccupaṭṭhānā araññagatasudesako viya.

'One understands thoroughly,' thus it is wisdom (paññā). It has the characteristic of discernment. Its function is to illuminate the object, like a lamp. It manifests as non-delusion, like a good guide for one who has gone into a forest.

Jīvanti tena taṃsampayuttadhammāti jīvitaṃ. Taṃ pana attanā avinibbhuttānaṃ dhammānaṃ anupālanalakkhaṇaṃ, tesaṃ pavattanarasaṃ, tesaṃyeva ṭhapanapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, yāpayitabbadhammapadaṭṭhānaṃ. Santepi ca tesaṃ anupālanalakkhaṇādimhi vidhāne atthikkhaṇeyeva taṃ te dhamme anupāleti udakaṃ viya uppalādīni, yathāsakaṃ paccayuppannepi ca dhamme anupāleti dhāti viya kumāraṃ, sayaṃpavattitadhammasambandheneva pavattati niyāmako viya, na bhaṅgato uddhaṃ pavattayati attano ca pavattayitabbānañca abhāvā, na bhaṅgakkhaṇe ṭhapeti sayaṃ bhijjamānattā khīyamāno viya vattisnehova padīpasikhanti.

'The states associated with it live by means of it,' thus it is the life faculty. It has the characteristic of maintaining the states inseparable from itself, the function of making them occur, the manifestation of establishing them, and its proximate cause is the states that are to be maintained. Even when these states are present with their characteristic of maintenance, etc., it maintains them only at the moment of their presence, like water maintaining lotuses. It maintains states that have arisen from their respective conditions, like a wet-nurse maintaining a child. It proceeds only in connection with the states it has set in motion, like a regulator. It does not make them proceed beyond the moment of dissolution, because of the absence of both itself and the states to be made to proceed. It does not establish them at the moment of dissolution, because it is itself breaking up, like the wick and oil of a lamp flame as they are being consumed.

Na lubbhanti tena, sayaṃ vā na lubbhati, alubbhanamattameva vā tanti alobho. So ārammaṇe cittassa alaggabhāvalakkhaṇo kamaladale jalabindu viya, apariggaharaso muttabhikkhu viya, anallīnabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāno asucimhi patitapuriso viya.

'One is not greedy by means of it,' or 'one is not greedy,' or 'it is simply the state of non-greed'—thus it is non-greed. It has the characteristic of the mind's non-adherence to an object, like a drop of water on a lotus leaf. Its function is non-appropriation, like a liberated bhikkhu. It manifests as a state of non-cleaving, like a man who has fallen into filth.

Na dussanti tena, sayaṃ vā na dussati, adussanamattameva vā tanti adoso. So acaṇḍikkalakkhaṇo, avirodhalakkhaṇo vā anukūlamitto viya, āghātavinayanaraso, pariḷāhavinayanaraso [M 0.0024] vā candanaṃ viya, sommabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāno puṇṇacando viya.

'One is not hateful by means of it,' or 'one is not hateful,' or 'it is simply the state of non-hatred'—thus it is non-hatred (adosa). It has the characteristic of non-fierceness, or non-opposition like an agreeable friend. Its function is the removal of vexation, or the removal of feverish passion like sandalwood. It manifests as gentleness, like the full moon.

Kāyaduccaritādīhi hirīyatīti hirī. Lajjāyetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tehiyeva ottappatīti ottappaṃ. Pāpato ubbegassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tattha pāpato jigucchanalakkhaṇā hirī, ottāsalakkhaṇaṃ ottappaṃ. Ubhopi pāpānaṃ akaraṇarasā, pāpato saṅkocanapaccupaṭṭhānā, attagāravaparagāravapadaṭṭhānā. Ime dhammā lokapālāti daṭṭhabbā.
