One is ashamed of bodily misconduct, etc.—this is moral shame (hirī). This is a term for shame. One is afraid of those same things—this is moral dread (ottappa). This is a term for dread of evil. Herein, moral shame has the characteristic of disgust for evil, and moral dread has the characteristic of fear of it. Both have the function of not doing evil. They are manifested as shrinking away from evil. Their proximate causes are self-respect and respect for others. These states should be seen as the guardians of the world.

Kāyapassambhanaṃ kāyapassaddhi. Cittapassambhanaṃ cittapassaddhi. Kāyoti cettha vedanādayo tayo khandhā. Ubhopi panetā ekato hutvā kāyacittadarathavūpasamalakkhaṇā[P 0.0020], kāyacittadarathanimmadanarasā, kāyacittānaṃ aparipphandanasītibhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā, kāyacittapadaṭṭhānā, kāyacittānaṃ avūpasamatāuddhaccādikilesappaṭipakkhabhūtāti veditabbā.

The calming of the body is bodily tranquility; the calming of the mind is mental tranquility. Here, 'body' refers to the three aggregates beginning with feeling. Both of these, taken together, have the characteristic of stilling the distress of body and mind; the function of crushing the distress of body and mind; the manifestation of non-agitation and coolness of body and mind; with body and mind as their proximate cause. They should be understood as being opposed to such defilements as restlessness, which are due to the non-stilling of body and mind.

Kāyalahubhāvo [V 0.0022] kāyalahutā. Cittalahubhāvo cittalahutā. Kāyacittānaṃ garubhāvavūpasamalakkhaṇā, kāyacittagarubhāvanimmadanarasā, kāyacittānaṃ adandhatāpaccupaṭṭhānā, kāyacittapadaṭṭhānā, kāyacittānaṃ garubhāvakarathinamiddhādikilesappaṭipakkhabhūtāti veditabbā.

The lightness of the body is bodily lightness; the lightness of the mind is mental lightness. They have the characteristic of the subsiding of the heaviness of body and mind; the function of crushing the heaviness of body and mind; the manifestation of non-sluggishness of body and mind; with body and mind as their proximate cause. They should be understood as being opposed to such defilements as sloth and torpor, which cause the heaviness of body and mind.

Kāyamudubhāvo kāyamudutā. Cittamudubhāvo cittamudutā. Kāyacittānaṃ thaddhabhāvavūpasamalakkhaṇā, kāyacittānaṃ thaddhabhāvanimmadanarasā, appaṭighātapaccupaṭṭhānā, kāyacittapadaṭṭhānā, kāyacittānaṃ thaddhabhāvakaradiṭṭhimānādikilesappaṭipakkhabhūtāti veditabbā.

The malleability of the body is bodily malleability; the malleability of the mind is mental malleability. They have the characteristic of the subsiding of rigidity of body and mind; the function of crushing the rigidity of body and mind; the manifestation of non-resistance; with body and mind as their proximate cause. They should be understood as being opposed to such defilements as wrong view and conceit, which cause the rigidity of body and mind.

Kāyakammaññabhāvo kāyakammaññatā. Cittakammaññabhāvo cittakammaññatā. Kāyacittānaṃ akammaññabhāvavūpasamalakkhaṇā, kāyacittānaṃ akammaññabhāvanimmadanarasā, kāyacittānaṃ ārammaṇakaraṇasampattipaccupaṭṭhānā, kāyacittapadaṭṭhānaṃ, kāyacittānaṃ [M 0.0025] akammaññabhāvakaraavasesanīvaraṇādikilesappaṭipakkhabhūtāti veditabbā.

The wieldiness of the body is bodily wieldiness; the wieldiness of the mind is mental wieldiness. They have the characteristic of the subsiding of the unwieldiness of body and mind; the function of crushing the unwieldiness of body and mind; the manifestation of success in grasping an object; with body and mind as their proximate cause. They should be understood as being opposed to the remaining hindrances and other defilements that cause the unwieldiness of body and mind.

Kāyapāguññabhāvo kāyapāguññatā. Cittapāguññabhāvo cittapāguññatā. Kāyacittānaṃ agelaññabhāvalakkhaṇā, kāyacittānaṃ gelaññanimmadanarasā, nirādīnavapaccupaṭṭhānā, kāyacittapadaṭṭhānā, kāyacittānaṃ gelaññabhāvakaraassaddhādikilesappaṭipakkhabhūtāti daṭṭhabbā.

The proficiency of the body is bodily proficiency; the proficiency of the mind is mental proficiency. They have the characteristic of non-sickness of body and mind; the function of crushing the sickness of body and mind; the manifestation of blamelessness; with body and mind as their proximate cause. They should be seen as being opposed to such defilements as lack of faith, which cause sickness of body and mind.

Kāyassa ujukabhāvo kāyujukatā. Cittassa ujukabhāvo cittujukatā. Kāyacittānaṃ akuṭilabhāvalakkhaṇā, kāyacittānaṃ ajjavalakkhaṇā vā, kāyacittānaṃ kuṭilabhāvanimmadanarasā, ajimhatāpaccupaṭṭhānā, kāyacittapadaṭṭhānā, kāyacittānaṃ kuṭilabhāvakaramāyāsāṭheyyādikilesappaṭipakkhabhūtāti daṭṭhabbā.

The rectitude of the body is bodily rectitude; the rectitude of the mind is mental rectitude. They have the characteristic of non-crookedness of body and mind, or the characteristic of uprightness of body and mind; the function of crushing the crookedness of body and mind; the manifestation of non-deviousness; with body and mind as their proximate cause. They should be seen as being opposed to such defilements as deceit and craftiness, which cause the crookedness of body and mind.

Chandoti kattukamyatāyetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tasmā so kattukamyatālakkhaṇo chando, ārammaṇapariyesanaraso, ārammaṇena atthikatāpaccupaṭṭhāno, tadevassa padaṭṭhāno.

Desire (chanda) is a term for the wish to act. Therefore, that desire has the wish to act as its characteristic, searching for an object as its function, and need for the object as its manifestation. That itself is its proximate cause.

Adhimuccanaṃ [P 0.0021] adhimokkho. So sanniṭṭhānalakkhaṇo, asaṃsappanaraso, nicchayapaccupaṭṭhāno, sanniṭṭheyyadhammapadaṭṭhāno, ārammaṇe niccalabhāvena indakhīlo viya daṭṭhabbo.

Resolution (adhimokkha) is the act of deciding. It has the characteristic of conviction, the function of not vacillating, and the manifestation of certainty. Its proximate cause is a thing to be decided upon. It should be regarded as being like a pillar because of its immovable nature in regard to the object.

Tesu [V 0.0023] tesu dhammesu majjhattabhāvo tatramajjhattatā. Sā cittacetasikānaṃ samavāhitalakkhaṇā, ūnādhikatānivāraṇarasā, pakkhapātupacchedanarasā vā, majjhattabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā.

Equanimity (tatramajjhattatā) is a state of neutrality towards those various things. It has the characteristic of conveying consciousness and mental factors evenly; its function is to prevent deficiency and excess, or to cut off partiality. It is manifested as a state of neutrality.

Kiriyā kāro, manasmiṃ kāro manasikāro. Purimamanato visadisaṃ manaṃ karotīti ca manasikāro.

Doing (kāro) is action (kiriyā); doing in the mind (manasi kāro) is attention (manasikāro). And it is attention because it makes the mind different from the preceding mind.

Svāyaṃ [M 0.0026] ārammaṇapaṭipādako, vīthipaṭipādako, javanapaṭipādakoti tippakāro. Tattha ārammaṇapaṭipādako manasmiṃ kāro manasikāro. So sāraṇalakkhaṇo, sampayuttānaṃ ārammaṇe saṃyojanaraso, ārammaṇābhimukhabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāno, ārammaṇapadaṭṭhāno, saṅkhārakkhandhapariyāpanno ārammaṇapaṭipādakattena sampayuttānaṃ sārathī viya daṭṭhabbo. Vīthipaṭipādakoti pañcadvārāvajjanassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ, javanapaṭipādakoti manodvārāvajjanassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ, na te idha adhippetā.

This attention is of three kinds: object-generative, process-generative, and impulsion-generative. Herein, the object-generative is attention (manasikāro), doing in the mind. It has the characteristic of directing, the function of yoking the associated states to the object, and the manifestation of facing the object. Its proximate cause is the object. Included in the aggregate of formations, it should be seen as being like a charioteer for the associated states because it generates the object. 'Process-generative' is a term for five-door adverting, and 'impulsion-generative' is a term for mind-door adverting; these are not intended here.

Karuṇāti paradukkhe sati sādhūnaṃ hadayakampanaṃ karotīti karuṇā, kināti vināseti vā paradukkhanti karuṇā. Sā paradukkhāpanayanākārappavattilakkhaṇā, paradukkhāsahanarasā, avihiṃsāpaccupaṭṭhānā, dukkhābhibhūtānaṃ anāthabhāvadassanapadaṭṭhānā.

When there is suffering in others, it makes the hearts of good people tremble, thus it is compassion (karuṇā); or, it assails and destroys the suffering of others, thus it is compassion. It has the characteristic of proceeding in the mode of removing the suffering of others; the function of being unable to endure the suffering of others; the manifestation of non-harming. Its proximate cause is seeing the helplessness of those overcome by suffering.

Modanti tāya, sayaṃ vā modatīti muditā. Sā pamodanalakkhaṇā, anissāyanarasā, arativighātapaccupaṭṭhānā, sattānaṃ sampattidassanapadaṭṭhānā. Keci pana mettupekkhāyopi aniyate icchanti, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ. Atthato hi adoso eva mettā, tatramajjhattupekkhāyeva upekkhāti.

They rejoice with it, or one rejoices oneself, thus it is appreciative joy (muditā). It has the characteristic of gladdening, the function of being unenvious, and the manifestation of dispelling discontent. Its proximate cause is seeing the success of beings. Some, however, hold that it is not distinct from loving-kindness and equanimity, but this should not be accepted. For in meaning, loving-kindness is simply non-aversion, and equanimity is simply neutrality (tatramajjhattatā).

Kāyaduccaritato virati kāyaduccaritavirati. Eseva nayo sesesupi dvīsu. Lakkhaṇādito pana etā tissopi viratiyo kāyaduccaritādivatthūnaṃ avītikkamalakkhaṇā, kāyaduccaritādivatthuto saṅkocanarasā, akiriyapaccupaṭṭhānā, saddhāhiriottappaappicchatādiguṇapadaṭṭhānā. Keci pana imāsu ekekaṃ niyataṃ viratiṃ icchanti. Evaṃ kāmāvacarapaṭhamamahākusalacittena ime tettiṃsa vā catuttiṃsa vā dhammā sampayogaṃ gacchantīti veditabbā.

Abstinence from bodily misconduct is abstinence from bodily misconduct. The same method applies to the other two. As to their characteristics, etc., these three abstinences have the characteristic of non-transgression regarding the objects of bodily misconduct, etc.; the function of shrinking away from the objects of bodily misconduct, etc.; the manifestation of non-doing; and as their proximate cause, such qualities as faith, moral shame, moral dread, and fewness of wishes. Some, however, hold that each of these is a definite abstinence. Thus it should be understood that these thirty-three or thirty-four states enter into association with the first great wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere.

Yathā [M 0.0027][P 0.0022][V 0.0024] ca paṭhamena, evaṃ dutiyacittenāpi. Sasaṅkhārabhāvamattameva hi ettha viseso. Puna tatiyena ñāṇavippayogato ṭhapetvā amohaṃ avasesā dvattiṃsa vā tettiṃsa vā veditabbā. Tathā catutthenāpi sasaṅkhārabhāvamattameva viseso, paṭhame vuttesu pana ṭhapetvā pītiṃ avasesā pañcamena sampayogaṃ gacchanti. Somanassaṭṭhāne cettha upekkhāvedanā paviṭṭhā. Sā pana iṭṭhāniṭṭhaviparītānubhavanalakkhaṇā, pakkhapātupacchedanarasā. Yathā ca pañcamena, evaṃ chaṭṭhenāpi. Sasaṅkhāramattameva hoti viseso. Sattamena pana ṭhapetvā paññaṃ avasesā ekatiṃsa vā dvattiṃsa vā dhammā honti, tathā aṭṭhamenāpi. Sasaṅkhāramattameva viseso. Evaṃ tāva kāmāvacarakusalacetasikā veditabbā.

As with the first consciousness, so it is with the second. The only difference here is the fact of its being prompted. Again, with the third, since it is dissociated from knowledge, setting aside non-delusion, the remaining thirty-two or thirty-three should be understood. Similarly with the fourth, the only difference is the fact of its being prompted. But of those mentioned in connection with the first, setting aside joy, the remainder enter into association with the fifth. Here, neutral feeling has entered in place of gladness. This feeling has the characteristic of experiencing an object in a neutral manner and the function of cutting off partiality. As with the fifth, so it is with the sixth; the only difference is the fact of its being prompted. With the seventh, setting aside wisdom, the remaining thirty-one or thirty-two states are present; and similarly with the eighth, where the only difference is the fact of its being prompted. Thus the mental factors of wholesome sense-sphere consciousness should be understood.

81.

81.

Upekkhāyuttacittesu, na dukkhasukhapītiyo;

Jāyanteva visuṃ pañca, karuṇāmuditādayo.

In consciousnesses accompanied by equanimity, neither pain, pleasure, nor joy arise; and the five—compassion, appreciative joy, and so on—arise only separately.

Avasesesu pana rūpāvacaracittasampayuttā rūpāvacarā, tattha paṭhamacittasampayuttā tāva kāmāvacarapaṭhamacitte vuttesu ṭhapetvā viratittayaṃ avasesā veditabbā. Viratiyo pana kāmāvacarakusalalokuttaresveva uppajjanti, na aññesu. Dutiyena vitakkavajjā dvattiṃsa vā tettiṃsa vā. Tatiyena vicāravajjā ekatiṃsa vā dvattiṃsa vā. Catutthena tato pītivajjā tiṃsa vā ekatiṃsa vā. Pañcamena tato karuṇāmuditāvajjā tiṃsa honti, somanassaṭṭhāne upekkhā paviṭṭhā. Evaṃ rūpāvacarakusalacetasikā veditabbā.

As for the remaining, the mental factors associated with form-sphere consciousness are form-sphere factors. Therein, as to those associated with the first consciousness, the remainder should be understood after setting aside the three abstinences mentioned in connection with the first sense-sphere consciousness. The abstinences, however, arise only in wholesome sense-sphere and supramundane consciousnesses, not in others. With the second, excluding initial application, there are thirty-two or thirty-three. With the third, excluding sustained application, there are thirty-one or thirty-two. With the fourth, excluding joy, there are thirty or thirty-one. With the fifth, excluding compassion and appreciative joy, there are thirty, and equanimity has entered in place of gladness. Thus the wholesome form-sphere mental factors should be understood.

Arūpāvacaracittasampayuttā arūpāvacarā, te pana rūpāvacarapañcame vuttanayena veditabbā. Arūpāvacarabhāvovettha viseso.

The mental factors associated with formless-sphere consciousness are formless-sphere factors. They should be understood according to the method stated for the fifth form-sphere consciousness. The only difference here is their being of the formless sphere.

Lokuttaracittasampayuttā [M 0.0028] lokuttarā, te pana paṭhamajjhānike maggacitte paṭhamarūpāvacaracitte vuttanayena dutiyajjhānikādibhedepi maggacitte dutiyarūpāvacaracittādīsu vuttanayeneva veditabbā. Karuṇāmuditānamabhāvo ca niyataviratibhāvo ca lokuttarabhāvo cettha viseso. Evaṃ tāva kusalacittasampayuttacetasikā veditabbā.

The mental factors associated with supramundane consciousness are supramundane factors. They should be understood, in the case of the path consciousness of the first jhana, according to the method stated for the first form-sphere consciousness; and in the case of the path consciousness with its divisions of the second jhana and so on, according to the method stated for the second form-sphere consciousness and so on. The differences here are the absence of compassion and appreciative joy, the fact that the abstinences are definite, and their supramundane nature. Thus the mental factors associated with wholesome consciousness should be understood.

Akusalā pana cetasikā bhūmito ekavidhā kāmāvacarāyeva, tesu lobhamūlapaṭhamākusalacittasampayuttā [V 0.0025] tāva niyatā sarūpenāgatā pannarasa, yevāpanakā niyatā cattāroti [P 0.0023] ekūnavīsati honti. Aniyatā cha yevāpanakāti sabbe pañcavīsati honti. Seyyathidaṃ – phasso somanassavedanā saññā cetanā vitakko vicāro pīti cittassekaggatā vīriyaṃ jīvitaṃ ahirikaṃ anottappaṃ lobho moho micchādiṭṭhīti ime sarūpenāgatā pannarasa, chando adhimokkho uddhaccaṃ manasikāroti ime cattāro niyatayevāpanakā, ime pana paṭipāṭiyā dasasu cittesu niyatā honti, māno issā macchariyaṃ kukkuccaṃ thinamiddhanti ime chayeva aniyatayevāpanakā.

Unwholesome mental factors, however, are of one plane only, that of the sense sphere. Among them, associated with the first unwholesome consciousness rooted in greed, fifteen arise invariably as such, and four are invariable particulars; thus there are nineteen. Six are variable particulars, making twenty-five in all. These are: contact, pleasant feeling, perception, volition, initial application, sustained application, zest, one-pointedness of mind, energy, life faculty, shamelessness, fearlessness of wrongdoing, greed, delusion, and wrong view—these fifteen arise invariably as such. Intention, decision, restlessness, and attention—these four are the invariable particulars; these, in sequence, are invariable in ten types of consciousness. Conceit, envy, avarice, worry, sloth, and torpor—these six are the variable particulars.

82.

82.

Evaṃ yevāpanā sabbe, niyatāniyatā dasa;

Niddiṭṭhā pāpacittesu, hatapāpena tādinā.

Thus all the particulars, the ten invariable and variable ones, have been pointed out in the sinful types of consciousness by the Such One who has destroyed evil.

Tattha phassoti akusalacittasahajāto phasso. Esa nayo sesesupi. Na hirīyatīti ahiriko, ahirikassa bhāvo ahirikaṃ. Kāyaduccaritādīhi ottappatīti ottappaṃ, na ottappaṃ anottappaṃ. Tattha kāyaduccaritādīhi ajigucchanalakkhaṇaṃ, alajjālakkhaṇaṃ vā ahirikaṃ, anottappaṃ teheva asārajjanalakkhaṇaṃ, anuttāsalakkhaṇaṃ vā.

Herein, 'contact' is the contact that arises together with unwholesome consciousness. This method applies to the others as well. One is not ashamed, thus 'shameless' (ahiriko); the state of being shameless is 'shamelessness' (ahirikaṃ). One has fear of wrongdoing regarding bodily misconduct, etc., thus 'fear of wrongdoing' (ottappaṃ); its absence is 'fearlessness of wrongdoing' (anottappaṃ). Herein, shamelessness has the characteristic of non-detestation of bodily misconduct, etc., or the characteristic of lack of shame. Fearlessness of wrongdoing has the characteristic of not shrinking back from these very things, or the characteristic of lack of dread.

Lubbhanti [M 0.0029] tena, sayaṃ vā lubbhati, lubbhanamattameva vā tanti lobho. So ārammaṇagahaṇalakkhaṇo makkaṭālepo viya, abhisaṅgaraso tattakapāle pakkhittamaṃsapesi viya, apariccāgapaccupaṭṭhāno telañjanarāgo viya, saṃyojaniyesu dhammesu assādadassanapadaṭṭhāno.

One is greedy for it, or one is oneself greedy, or it is merely the act of being greedy, thus it is 'greed.' It has the characteristic of grasping an object, like a monkey-trap of pitch. Its function is sticking, like a piece of meat put on a hot pan. It is manifested as non-abandonment, like the stain of lamp-soot. Its proximate cause is seeing gratification in things that are fetters.

Muyhanti tena, sayaṃ vā muyhati, muyhanamattameva vā tanti moho. So cittassa andhabhāvalakkhaṇo, aññāṇalakkhaṇo vā, asampaṭivedharaso, ārammaṇasabhāvacchādanaraso vā, andhakārapaccupaṭṭhāno, ayonisomanasikārapadaṭṭhāno.

One is deluded by it, or one is oneself deluded, or it is merely the state of being deluded, thus it is 'delusion.' It has the characteristic of mental blindness, or the characteristic of ignorance. Its function is non-penetration, or to conceal the intrinsic nature of the object. It is manifested as darkness. Its proximate cause is unwise attention.

Micchā passanti tāya, sayaṃ vā micchā passati, micchādassanamattameva vā esāti micchādiṭṭhi. Sā ayonisoabhinivesalakkhaṇā, parāmāsarasā, micchābhinivesapaccupaṭṭhānā, ariyānaṃ adassanakāmatādipadaṭṭhānā.

One sees wrongly by means of it, or one oneself sees wrongly, or it is merely the act of seeing wrongly, thus it is 'wrong view.' It has the characteristic of unwise adherence, its function is misapprehending, it is manifested as wrong conviction, and its proximate cause is not wishing to see the noble ones, etc.

Uddhatabhāvo [V 0.0026] uddhaccaṃ. Taṃ avūpasamalakkhaṇaṃ vātābhighātacalajalaṃ viya, anavaṭṭhānarasaṃ vātābhighātacaladhajapaṭākā viya, bhantattapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ pāsāṇābhighātasamuddhatabhasmaṃ viya, ayonisomanasikārapadaṭṭhānaṃ.

The state of being agitated is restlessness. It has the characteristic of disquiet, like water agitated by the wind. Its function is unsteadiness, like a banner fluttering from the wind's impact. It is manifested as turmoil, like ashes scattered by the striking of a stone. Its proximate cause is unwise attention.

Maññatīti [P 0.0024] māno. So uṇṇatilakkhaṇo, sampaggahaṇaraso, ketukamyatāpaccupaṭṭhāno, diṭṭhivippayuttalobhapadaṭṭhāno.

One conceives, thus it is conceit. It has the characteristic of haughtiness, its function is self-exaltation, it is manifested as wishing for renown, and its proximate cause is greed dissociated from wrong view.

Issatīti issā. Sā parasampattīnaṃ usūyanalakkhaṇā, tattheva anabhiratirasā, tato vimukhabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā, parasampattipadaṭṭhānā.

One is envious, thus it is envy. It has the characteristic of resenting others' success, its function is being dissatisfied with that, it is manifested as turning away from it, and its proximate cause is others' success.

Maccharabhāvo macchariyaṃ. Taṃ attano sampattīnaṃ niguhaṇalakkhaṇaṃ, tāsaṃyeva parehi sādhāraṇabhāvaakkhamanarasaṃ, saṅkocanapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, attasampattipadaṭṭhānaṃ.

The state of being avaricious is avarice. It has the characteristic of concealing one's own attainments, its function is being unable to bear their being shared with others, it is manifested as shrinking, and its proximate cause is one's own attainments.

Kucchitaṃ [M 0.0030] kataṃ kukataṃ, tassa bhāvo kukkuccaṃ. Taṃ pacchānutāpalakkhaṇaṃ, katākatānusocanarasaṃ, vippaṭisārapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, katākatapadaṭṭhānaṃ.

Badly done is a misdeed; the state of that is worry. It has the characteristic of subsequent regret, its function is to sorrow over what has been done and what has not been done, it is manifested as remorse, and its proximate cause is what has been done and what has not been done.

Thinatā thinaṃ. Middhatā middhaṃ. Anussāhanasaṃsīdanatā, asattivighāto cāti attho. Thinañca middhañca thinamiddhaṃ. Tattha thinaṃ anussāhanalakkhaṇaṃ, vīriyavinodanarasaṃ, saṃsīdanabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Middhaṃ akammaññatālakkhaṇaṃ, onahanarasaṃ, līnatāpaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, ubhayampi ayonisomanasikārapadaṭṭhānaṃ. Sesā kusale vuttanayena veditabbā.

The state of being sluggish is sloth. The state of being drowsy is torpor. The meaning is lack of striving, sinking down, and impairment of application. Sloth and torpor are sloth-and-torpor. Herein, sloth has the characteristic of lack of striving, its function is to dispel energy, and it is manifested as a sinking state. Torpor has the characteristic of unwieldiness, its function is to envelop, and it is manifested as sluggishness. The proximate cause of both is unwise attention. The remaining factors should be understood by the method stated for the wholesome.

Ettha pana vitakkavīriyasamādhīnaṃ micchāsaṅkappamicchāvāyāmamicchāsamādhayo visesakā. Iti ime ekūnavīsati cetasikā paṭhamākusalacittena sampayogaṃ gacchantīti veditabbā. Yathā ca paṭhamena, evaṃ dutiyenāpi. Sasaṅkhārabhāvo cettha thinamiddhassa niyatabhāvo ca viseso. Tatiyena paṭhame vuttesu ṭhapetvā diṭṭhiṃ sesā aṭṭhārasa veditabbā. Māno panettha aniyato hoti, diṭṭhiyā saha na uppajjatīti. Catutthena dutiye vuttesu ṭhapetvā diṭṭhiṃ avasesā veditabbā. Etthāpi ca māno aniyato hoti. Pañcamena paṭhame vuttesu ṭhapetvā pītiṃ avasesā sampayogaṃ gacchantīti. Somanassaṭṭhāne panettha upekkhā paviṭṭhā. Chaṭṭhenāpi pañcame vuttasadisā eva. Sasaṅkhāratā[V 0.0027], thinamiddhassa niyatabhāvo ca viseso. Sattamena pañcame vuttesu ṭhapetvā diṭṭhiṃ avasesā veditabbā. Māno panettha aniyato. Aṭṭhamena chaṭṭhe vuttesu ṭhapetvā diṭṭhiṃ avasesā veditabbā. Etthāpi māno [P 0.0025] aniyato hoti. Evaṃ lobhamūlacetasikā veditabbā.

Here, however, wrong intention, wrong effort, and wrong concentration are the specific names for initial application, energy, and concentration. Thus, it should be understood that these nineteen mental factors become associated with the first unwholesome citta. As with the first, so too with the second. Here, the distinction is its prompted nature and the invariable presence of sloth and torpor. With the third, excluding wrong view from those stated for the first, the remaining eighteen should be understood. Herein, conceit is variable, for it does not arise together with wrong view. With the fourth, excluding wrong view from those stated for the second, the remaining should be understood. Here too, conceit is variable. With the fifth, excluding zest from those stated for the first, the remaining become associated. Herein, equanimity has entered in place of pleasant feeling. With the sixth, it is just like what was stated for the fifth. The distinctions are its prompted nature and the invariable presence of sloth and torpor. With the seventh, excluding wrong view from those stated for the fifth, the remaining should be understood. Herein, conceit is variable. With the eighth, excluding wrong view from those stated for the sixth, the remaining should be understood. Here too, conceit is variable. Thus the mental factors rooted in greed should be understood.

Domanassasahagatesu paṭighasampayuttesu dosamūlesu dvīsu paṭhamena asaṅkhārikena sampayuttā niyatā sarūpenāgatā [M 0.0031] terasa. Seyyathidaṃ – phasso domanassavedanā saññā cetanā cittekaggatā vitakko vicāro vīriyaṃ jīvitaṃ ahirikaṃ anottappaṃ doso moho ceti ime terasa dhammā chandādīhi catūhi niyatayevāpanakehi sattarasa honti issāmacchariyakukkuccesu aniyatesu tīsu ekena saha aṭṭhārasa honti, etepi tayo na ekato uppajjanti.

In the two cittas rooted in aversion, which are accompanied by displeasure and associated with repugnance, thirteen factors arise invariably as such in association with the first, the unprompted one. These are: contact, painful feeling, perception, volition, one-pointedness of mind, initial application, sustained application, energy, life faculty, shamelessness, lack of moral dread, aversion, and delusion. These thirteen factors, along with the four invariable particulars—intention, etc.—become seventeen. With one of the three variable factors—envy, avarice, and worry—they become eighteen. These three, however, do not arise together.

Tattha duṭṭhu manoti dumano, dumanassa bhāvo domanassaṃ, domanassavedanāyetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tena sahagataṃ domanassasahagataṃ. Taṃ aniṭṭhārammaṇānubhavanalakkhaṇaṃ, aniṭṭhākārasambhogarasaṃ, cetasikābādhapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, ekanteneva hadayavatthupadaṭṭhānaṃ.

Herein, 'a corrupt mind' means a 'displeased mind'; the state of a displeased mind is 'displeasure,' which is a term for painful feeling. 'Accompanied by displeasure' is that which is accompanied by it. It has the characteristic of experiencing an undesirable object, its function is to consume the undesirable aspect, it is manifested as mental affliction, and its proximate cause is exclusively the heart-base.

Dussanti tena, sayaṃ vā dussati, dussanamattameva vā tanti doso. So caṇḍikkalakkhaṇo pahatāsīviso viya, visappanaraso visanipāto viya, attano nissayadahanaraso vā dāvaggi viya, dussanapaccupaṭṭhāno laddhokāso viya sapatto, āghātavatthupadaṭṭhāno. Avasesā heṭṭhā vuttappakārāva. Iti ime sattarasa vā aṭṭhārasa vā navamena sampayogaṃ gacchantīti veditabbā. Yathā ca navamena, evaṃ dasamenāpi. Sasaṅkhāratā, panettha thinamiddhasambhavo ca viseso.

One is corrupted by it, or one is oneself corrupted, or it is merely the act of corruption, thus it is aversion. It has the characteristic of ferocity, like a struck venomous snake; its function is to spread, like a dose of poison, or to burn up its own support, like a forest fire; it is manifested as corrupting, like an enemy who has found an opportunity; its proximate cause is a ground for resentment. The remaining factors are as previously described. Thus, it should be understood that these seventeen or eighteen factors become associated with the ninth citta. As with the ninth, so too with the tenth. Herein, its prompted nature and the occurrence of sloth and torpor are the distinctions.

Dvīsu pana mohamūlesu vicikicchāsampayuttena ekādasamena sampayuttā tāva phasso upekkhāvedanā saññā cetanā vitakko vicāro vīriyaṃ jīvitaṃ cittaṭṭhiti ahirikaṃ anottappaṃ moho vicikicchāti sarūpenāgatā terasa, uddhaccaṃ manasikāroti dve yevāpanakā niyatā. Tehi saddhiṃ pannarasa honti.

Now, in the two cittas rooted in delusion, associated with the eleventh citta, which is conjoined with doubt, thirteen factors arise as such: contact, equanimous feeling, perception, volition, initial application, sustained application, energy, life faculty, stability of mind, shamelessness, lack of moral dread, delusion, and doubt. Restlessness and attention are the two invariable particulars. Together with them, they become fifteen.

Tattha [M 0.0032] pavattaṭṭhitimattā ekaggatā. Vigatā cikicchāti vicikicchā. Sabhāvaṃ vicinanto [V 0.0028] etāya kicchati kilamatīti vicikicchā. Sā saṃsayalakkhaṇā, kampanarasā, anicchayapaccupaṭṭhānā, ayonisomanasikārapadaṭṭhānā. Sesā vuttanayā eva.

Herein, one-pointedness is the mere stability of occurrence. 'Devoid of remedy' is doubt. Or, investigating the intrinsic nature, one is troubled and wearied by it, thus it is doubt. It has the characteristic of perplexity, its function is wavering, it is manifested as indecisiveness, and its proximate cause is unwise attention. The remaining factors are just as stated.

Dvādasamena uddhaccasampayuttena sampayuttā sarūpenāgatā [P 0.0026] vicikicchāsahagate vuttesu vicikicchāhīnā uddhaccaṃ sarūpena āgataṃ, tasmā teraseva honti. Vicikicchāya abhāvena panettha adhimokkho uppajjati, tena saddhiṃ cuddasa honti. Adhimokkhasambhavato samādhi balavā hoti, adhimokkhamanasikārā dve yevāpanakā, tehi saha pannaraseva honti. Evaṃ tāva akusalacetasikā veditabbā.

With the twelfth citta, which is conjoined with restlessness, of the factors stated for the one accompanied by doubt, doubt is absent and restlessness arises as such; therefore, there are just thirteen factors that arise as such. Due to the absence of doubt, decision arises herein; with it, they become fourteen. Due to the arising of decision, concentration becomes strong. Decision and attention are the two particulars; with them, they become just fifteen. Thus far the unwholesome mental factors should be understood.

Idāni abyākatā vuccanti, abyākatā pana duvidhā vipākakiriyabhedato. Tattha vipākā kusalā viya bhūmivasena catubbidhā kāmāvacaraṃ rūpāvacaraṃ arūpāvacaraṃ lokuttarañceti. Tattha kāmāvacaravipākā sahetukāhetukavasena duvidhā. Tattha sahetukavipākasampayuttā sahetukā. Te sahetukakāmāvacarakusalasampayuttasadisā. Yā pana karuṇāmuditā aniyatā, tā sattārammaṇattā vipākesu nuppajjanti. Kāmāvacaravipākānaṃ ekantaparittārammaṇattā viratiyo panettha ekantakusalattā na labbhanti. Vibhaṅge “pañca sikkhāpadā kusalāyevā”ti hi vuttaṃ. Evaṃ kāmāvacarasahetukavipākacetasikā veditabbā.

Now, the indeterminate are spoken of. The indeterminate, however, are twofold, distinguished as resultant and functional. Therein, resultants, like wholesome states, are fourfold by way of plane: sense-sphere, fine-material sphere, immaterial sphere, and supramundane. Therein, sense-sphere resultants are twofold: with roots and without roots. Therein, those associated with resultants with roots are themselves with roots. They are similar to the mental factors associated with wholesome sense-sphere consciousness with roots. However, compassion and appreciative joy, being unfixed, do not arise in resultants because they have beings as their object. Because sense-sphere resultants have exclusively limited objects, the abstinences are not found here, as they are exclusively wholesome. For in the Vibhaṅga it is said: “The five precepts are exclusively wholesome.” Thus should the mental factors of rooted sense-sphere resultants be understood.

83.

83.

Tettiṃsādidvaye dhammā, dvattiṃseva tato pare;

Bāttiṃsa pañcame chaṭṭhe, ekatiṃsa tato pare.

In the first two there are thirty-three factors; in the next, thirty-two. In the fifth and sixth, thirty-two; and in those thereafter, thirty-one.

Ahetukacittasampayuttā [M 0.0033] pana ahetukā. Tesu cakkhuviññāṇasampayuttā tāva phasso upekkhāvedanā saññā cetanā jīvitaṃ cittaṭṭhitīti sarūpenāgatā cha, manasikārena ca satta honti. Sotaghānajivhākāyaviññāṇasampayuttāpi satta satteva cetasikā. Tattha kāyaviññāṇasampayuttesu pana upekkhāṭhāne sukhavedanā paviṭṭhā. Sā kāyikasātalakkhaṇā, pīṇanarasā, sesā vuttanayā eva.

Those associated with rootless consciousness are rootless. Among these, those associated with eye-consciousness are: contact, equanimous feeling, perception, volition, life faculty, and one-pointedness—these six are present in their own right; with attention, they become seven. Those associated with ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness also have seven mental factors each. Here, however, in the case of body-consciousness, pleasant feeling is included in place of equanimous feeling. It has the characteristic of bodily pleasure and the function of suffusing; the rest are as already stated.

84.

84.

Iṭṭhārammaṇayogasmiṃ, cakkhuviññāṇakādisu;

Sati kasmā upekkhāva, vuttā catūsu satthunā.

When there is connection with a desirable object in eye-consciousness and so on, why has only equanimity been stated by the Teacher in regard to the four?

85.

85.

Upādāya [V 0.0029] ca rūpena, upādārūpake pana;

Saṅghaṭṭanānighaṃsassa, dubbalattāti dīpaye.

It is explained that this is because of the weakness of the impact and friction on the derived matter on which it depends.

86.

86.

Pasādaṃ panatikkamma, kūṭaṃva picupiṇḍakaṃ;

Bhūtarūpena bhūtānaṃ, ghaṭṭanāya sukhādikaṃ.

But bypassing the sensitive matter, pleasure and so on arise from the impact of the primary elements with the primary elements, like a hammer striking through a ball of cotton.

Tasmā [P 0.0027] kāyaviññāṇaṃ sukhādisampayuttanti veditabbaṃ. Manodhātunā sampayuttā sarūpenāgatā cakkhuviññāṇena saddhiṃ vuttā cha, vitakkavicārehi saha aṭṭha, adhimokkhamanasikārehi dvīhi yevāpanakehi dasa dhammā honti. Tathā manoviññāṇadhātuupekkhāsahagatena. Somanassasahagatena pītiadhikā vedanāparivattanañca nānattaṃ. Tasmāvettha ekādasa dhammā honti. Evaṃ ahetukāpi kāmāvacaravipākacetasikā veditabbā.

Therefore, it should be understood that body-consciousness is associated with pleasure and so on. Associated with the mind-element are the six factors mentioned in connection with eye-consciousness that are present in their own right; with initial and sustained thought, they are eight; with the two occasional factors, decision and attention, they become ten factors. It is similar for the mind-consciousness-element accompanied by equanimity. For the one accompanied by joy, the difference is the addition of joy and the change of feeling. Therefore, here there are eleven factors. Thus should the rootless sense-sphere resultant mental factors also be understood.

Rūpāvacaravipākacittasampayuttā pana rūpāvacarā. Arūpāvacaravipākacittasampayuttā arūpāvacarā. Te sabbepi attano attano kusalacittasampayuttacetasikehi sadisāyevāti.

The mental factors associated with fine-material-sphere resultant consciousness are fine-material-sphere factors. The mental factors associated with immaterial-sphere resultant consciousness are immaterial-sphere factors. All of them are indeed similar to the mental factors associated with their respective wholesome consciousnesses.

Lokuttaravipākacittasampayuttā [M 0.0034] lokuttarā. Te sabbe tesaṃyeva lokuttaravipākacittānaṃ sadisā kusalacittasampayuttehi cetasikehi sadisā. Evaṃ rūpāvacarārūpāvacaralokuttaravipākacetasikā veditabbā.

The mental factors associated with supramundane resultant consciousness are supramundane factors. All of them are similar to the mental factors associated with the corresponding wholesome supramundane consciousnesses. Thus should the fine-material-sphere, immaterial-sphere, and supramundane resultant mental factors be understood.

Akusalavipākacittasampayuttā pana akusalavipākacetasikā nāma. Te pana kusalavipākāhetukacittesu cakkhuviññāṇādīsu vuttacetasikasadisā. Ettha pana kāyaviññāṇe dukkhavedanā paviṭṭhā. Sā kāyikābādhalakkhaṇā. Sesā vuttanayāyevāti. Evaṃ chattiṃsa vipākacittasampayuttacetasikā veditabbā.

The mental factors associated with unwholesome-resultant consciousness are called unwholesome-resultant mental factors. They are similar to the mental factors mentioned in connection with the rootless wholesome-resultant consciousnesses, such as eye-consciousness. Here, however, painful feeling is included in body-consciousness; it has the characteristic of bodily affliction. The rest are as already stated. Thus, the mental factors associated with the thirty-six resultant consciousnesses should be understood.

Kiriyābyākatā ca cetasikā bhūmito tividhā honti kāmāvacarā rūpāvacarā arūpāvacarāti. Tattha kāmāvacarā sahetukāhetukato duvidhā honti. Tesu sahetukakiriyacittasampayuttā sahetukā, te pana aṭṭhahi kāmāvacarakusalacittasampayuttehi samānā ṭhapetvā viratittayaṃ aniyatayevāpanakesu karuṇāmuditāyeva uppajjanti. Ahetukakiriyacittasampayuttā ahetukā, te kusalavipākāhetukamanodhātumanoviññāṇadhātucittasampayuttehi samānā. Manoviññāṇadhātudvaye [V 0.0030] pana vīriyindriyaṃ adhikaṃ. Vīriyindriyasambhavato panettha balappatto samādhi hoti. Hasituppādacittena sampayuttā dvādasa dhammā honti pītiyā saha. Ayamettha viseso.

Functional indeterminate mental factors are threefold by way of plane: sense-sphere, fine-material sphere, and immaterial sphere. Therein, the sense-sphere factors are twofold: with roots and without roots. Of these, those associated with rooted functional consciousness are rooted; they are the same as those associated with the eight sense-sphere wholesome consciousnesses, except for the three abstinences. Among the unfixed occasional factors, only compassion and appreciative joy arise. Those associated with rootless functional consciousness are rootless; they are the same as those associated with the rootless wholesome-resultant mind-element and mind-consciousness-element. However, in the two types of mind-consciousness-element, the faculty of energy is additional. Because of the presence of the faculty of energy, concentration here becomes strong. Associated with the smile-producing consciousness, there are twelve factors, including joy. This is the distinction here.

Rūpāvacarakiriyacittasampayuttā pana rūpāvacarā. Arūpāvacarakiriyacittasampayuttā arūpāvacarā. Te sabbepi sakasakabhūmikusalacittasampayuttehi samānāti. Evaṃ vīsati kiriyacittasampayuttā ca cetasikā veditabbā.

The mental factors associated with fine-material-sphere functional consciousness are fine-material-sphere factors. The mental factors associated with immaterial-sphere functional consciousness are immaterial-sphere factors. All of them are similar to those associated with the wholesome consciousness of their respective planes. Thus should the mental factors associated with the twenty functional consciousnesses be understood.

Ettāvatā [M 0.0035][P 0.0028] kusalākusalavipākakiriyabhedabhinnena ekūnanavutiyā cittena sampayuttā cetasikā niddiṭṭhā honti.

Thus far have been explained the mental factors associated with the eighty-nine consciousnesses as distinguished by the divisions of wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, and functional.

87.

87.

Kusalākusalehi vipākakriyā-

Hadayehi yutā pana cetasikā;

Sakalāpi ca sādhu mayā kathitā,

Sugatena mahāmuninā kathitā.

The mental factors associated with the wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, and functional consciousnesses—all these have been well explained by me as they were taught by the Sugata, the Great Sage.

88.

88.

Avagacchati yo imaṃ anunaṃ,

Paramaṃ tassa samantato mati;

Abhidhammanaye dūrāsade,

Atigambhīraṭhāne vijambhate.

Whoever understands this complete teaching, his wisdom becomes supreme in every way; he flourishes in the extremely profound domain of the Abhidhamma method, which is so difficult to approach.

Iti abhidhammāvatāre cetasikaniddeso nāma

Thus ends the chapter named 'The Exposition of Mental Factors' in The Introduction to the Abhidhamma.

Dutiyo paricchedo.

The Second Chapter.

3. Tatiyo paricchedo

3. The Third Chapter

Cetasikavibhāganiddeso

Exposition of the Classification of Mental Factors

89.

89.

Sabbe [P 0.0029][V 0.0031] cetasikā vuttā, buddhenādiccabandhunā;

Nāmasāmaññatoyeva, dvepaññāsa bhavanti te.

All mental factors were taught by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun. By name and in general, they are fifty-two.

Seyyathidaṃ – phasso vedanā saññā cetanā vitakko vicāro pīti cittekaggatā vīriyaṃ jīvitaṃ chando adhimokkho manasikāro tatramajjhattatā saddhā sati hirī ottappaṃ alobho adoso amoho kāyappassaddhiādīni cha yugāni, tisso viratiyo, karuṇā muditā lobho doso moho uddhaccaṃ māno diṭṭhi issā macchariyaṃ kukkuccaṃ thinaṃ middhaṃ vicikicchā ahirikaṃ anottappañcāti.

Namely: contact, feeling, perception, volition, initial thought, sustained thought, joy, one-pointedness of mind, energy, life faculty, desire, decision, attention, neutrality, faith, mindfulness, moral shame, moral dread, non-greed, non-hatred, non-delusion, the six pairs of factors beginning with tranquility, the three abstinences, compassion, sympathetic joy, greed, hatred, delusion, restlessness, conceit, wrong view, envy, stinginess, worry, sloth, torpor, doubt, shamelessness, and lack of moral dread.

90.

90.

Catupaññāsadhā [M 0.0036] kāme, rūpe pañcadaseritā;

Te honti dvādasārūpe, cattālīsamanāsavā.

Fifty-four are in the sense sphere, fifteen are stated for the fine-material sphere; they are twelve in the immaterial sphere, and forty in the supramundane.

91.

91.

Ekavīsasataṃ sabbe, cittuppādā samāsato;

Etesu tesamuppattiṃ, uddharitvā panekakaṃ.

In brief, all consciousnesses are one hundred and twenty-one. Having extracted from these the arising of those (mental factors) one by one,

92.

92.

Phassādīnaṃ tu dhammānaṃ, pavakkhāmi ito paraṃ;

Pāṭavatthāya bhikkhūnaṃ, cittacetasikesvahaṃ.

I shall now declare the distribution of the factors beginning with contact, for the proficiency of the bhikkhus in consciousness and mental factors.

93.

93.

Ekaggatā manakkāro, jīvitaṃ phassapañcakaṃ;

Aṭṭhete avinibbhogā, ekuppādā sahakkhayā.

One-pointedness, attention, life faculty, and the pentad beginning with contact; these eight are inseparable, arising and perishing together.

94.

94.

Phasso ca vedanā saññā, cetanā jīvitindriyaṃ;

Ekaggatā manakkāro, sabbasādhāraṇā ime.

Contact, feeling, perception, volition, life faculty, one-pointedness, and attention—these are common to all.

95.

95.

Vitakko pañcapaññāsa-cittesu samudīrito;

Cāro chasaṭṭhicittesu, jāyate natthi saṃsayo.

Initial thought is said to arise in fifty-five consciousnesses; sustained thought arises in sixty-six consciousnesses, there is no doubt.

96.

96.

Ekapaññāsacittesu[V 0.0032], pīti tesaṭṭhiyā sukhaṃ;

Upekkhā pañcapaññāsa-citte dukkhaṃ tu tīsu hi.

Joy arises in fifty-one consciousnesses, pleasure in sixty-three; equanimity in fifty-five consciousnesses, and pain indeed in three.

97.

97.

Hoti dvāsaṭṭhicittesu, somanassindriyaṃ pana;

Dukkhindriyaṃ panekasmiṃ, tathekamhi sukhindriyaṃ.

The faculty of joy is in sixty-two consciousnesses; the faculty of pain, however, is in one; and similarly, the faculty of pleasure is in one.

98.

98.

Pañcuttarasate [P 0.0030] citte, vīriyaṃ āha nāyako;

Catuttarasate citte, samādhindriyamabravi.

The Leader spoke of energy in one hundred and five consciousnesses; He declared the faculty of concentration in one hundred and four consciousnesses.

99.

99.

Sabbāhetukacittāni, ṭhapetvā cekahetuke;

Ekuttarasate citte, chandassuppattimuddise.

Excluding all rootless consciousnesses and the one-rooted consciousness, the arising of desire is declared in one hundred and one consciousnesses.

100.

100.

Ṭhapetvā dasa viññāṇe, vicikicchāyutampi ca;

Dasuttarasate citte, adhimokkho udīrito.

Excluding the ten sense-consciousnesses and that conjoined with doubt, decision is declared in one hundred and ten consciousnesses.

101.

101.

Saddhā [M 0.0037] sati hirottappaṃ, alobhādosamajjhatā;

Chaḷeva yugaḷā cāti, dhammā ekūnavīsati.

Faith, mindfulness, moral shame, moral dread, non-greed, non-hatred, neutrality, and the six pairs as well—these are the nineteen factors.

102.

102.

Ekanavutiyā citte, jāyanti niyatā ime;

Ahetukesu cittesu, apuññesu na jāyare.

These arise invariably in ninety-one consciousnesses; they do not arise in rootless and unwholesome consciousnesses.

103.

103.

Ekūnāsītiyā citte, paññā jāyati sabbadā;

Aṭṭhavīsatiyā citte, karuṇāmuditā siyuṃ.

Wisdom always arises in seventy-nine consciousnesses; compassion and sympathetic joy may arise in twenty-eight consciousnesses.

104.

104.

Kāmāvacarapuññesu, sabbalokuttaresu ca;

Cattālīsavidhe citte, sāṭṭhake viratittayaṃ.

The three abstinences arise in the eight sense-sphere meritorious consciousnesses and in all forty supramundane consciousnesses.

105.

105.

Saddhā sati hirottappaṃ, alobhādittayampi ca;

Yugaḷāni cha majjhattaṃ, karuṇāmuditāpi ca.

Faith, mindfulness, moral shame, and moral dread, the triad beginning with non-greed, the six pairs, neutrality, and also compassion and sympathetic joy.

106.

106.

Tathā viratiyo tisso, sabbe te pañcavīsati;

Kusalābyākatā cāpi, kusalena pakāsitā.

Likewise the three abstinences—all these are twenty-five. They are wholesome and also indeterminate, and are declared by the Wise One.

107.

107.

Ahirīkamanottappaṃ, moho uddhaccameva ca;

Dvādasāpuññacittesu, niyatāyeva jāyare.

Shamelessness, lack of moral dread, delusion, and restlessness—these invariably arise in the twelve unwholesome consciousnesses.

108.

108.

Lobho [V 0.0033] doso ca moho ca, māno diṭṭhi ca saṃsayo;

Middhamuddhaccakukkuccaṃ, thinaṃ macchariyampi ca.

Greed, hatred, and delusion; conceit, wrong view, and doubt; torpor, restlessness, and worry; sloth and stinginess as well.

109.

109.

Ahirīkamanottappaṃ, issā ca domanassakaṃ;

Ete akusalā vuttā, ekantena mahesinā.

Shamelessness and lack of moral dread, envy and displeasure—these are declared exclusively unwholesome by the Great Sage.

110.

110.

Lobho aṭṭhasu niddiṭṭho, vuttā catūsu diṭṭhitu;

Māno diṭṭhiviyuttesu, dosodvīsveva jāyate.

Greed is specified in eight, wrong view is stated in four; conceit in those dissociated from wrong view, hatred arises in two only.

111.

111.

Issāmaccherakukkuccā, dvīsu jāyanti no saha;

Vicikicchā panekasmiṃ, thinamiddhaṃ tu pañcasu.

Envy, stinginess, and worry arise in the two hatred-rooted consciousnesses, but not together; doubt, however, in one; sloth and torpor in five.

112.

112.

Phasso [M 0.0038] ca vedanā saññā, cetanā jīvitaṃ mano;

Vitakko ca vicāro ca, pīti vīriyasamādhi ca.

Contact, feeling, perception, volition, life faculty, mind, initial thought and sustained thought, joy, energy, and concentration.

113.

113.

Chando cevādhimokkho ca, manasikāro ca cuddasa;

Kusalākusalā ceva, honti abyākatāpi ca.

And desire, decision, and attention—these fourteen factors can be wholesome, unwholesome, and also indeterminate.

114.

114.

Ekūnatiṃsacittesu, jhānaṃ pañcaṅgikaṃ mataṃ;

Catujhānaṅgayuttāni, sattatiṃsāti niddise.

In twenty-nine consciousnesses, the five-factored jhāna is known; thirty-seven are specified as possessing four jhāna factors.

115.

115.

Ekādasavidhaṃ cittaṃ, tivaṅgikamudīritaṃ;

Catutiṃsavidhaṃ cittaṃ, duvaṅgikamudīritaṃ.

Eleven types of consciousness are said to have three factors; thirty-four types of consciousness are said to have two factors.

116.

116.

Sabhāvenāvitakkesu[P 0.0031], jhānaṅgāni na uddhare;

Sabbāhetukacittesu, maggaṅgāni na uddhare.

In consciousnesses naturally without initial thought, jhāna factors are not extracted; in all rootless consciousnesses, path factors are not extracted.

117.

117.

Tīṇi soḷasacittesu, indriyāni vade budho;

Ekasmiṃ pana cattāri, pañca terasasuddhare.

The wise one speaks of three faculties in sixteen consciousnesses; but four in one; and five are found in thirteen.

118.

118.

Satta dvādasacittesu, indriyāni jinobravi;

Ekenūnesu aṭṭheva, cattālīsamanesu ca.

The Conqueror declared seven faculties in twelve consciousnesses; and just eight faculties in thirty-nine.

119.

119.

Cattālīsāya [V 0.0034] cittesu, navakaṃ nāyakobravi;

Evaṃ indriyayogopi, veditabbo vibhāvinā.

In forty consciousnesses, the Leader declared nine; thus the combination of faculties should be understood by the discerning.

120.

120.

Amaggaṅgāni nāmettha, aṭṭhārasa ahetukā;

Jhānaṅgāni na vijjanti, viññāṇesu dvipañcasu.

Here, the eighteen rootless consciousnesses are without path factors; jhāna factors are not found in fifty-two consciousnesses.

121.

121.

Ekaṃ cittaṃ dumaggaṅgaṃ, timaggaṅgāni sattasu;

Cattālīsāya cittesu, maggo so caturaṅgiko.

One consciousness has two path factors, three path factors are in seven; in forty consciousnesses, the path is four-factored.

122.

122.

Pañcaddasasu cittesu, maggo pañcaṅgiko mato;

Vutto dvattiṃsacittesu, maggo sattaṅgikopi ca.

In fifteen consciousnesses, the path is known to be five-factored; and the path is said to be seven-factored in thirty-two consciousnesses.

123.

123.

Maggo [M 0.0039] aṭṭhasu cittesu, mato aṭṭhaṅgikoti hi;

Evaṃ tu sabbacittesu, maggaṅgāni samuddhare.

Indeed, the path in eight consciousnesses is known to be eight-factored; thus should one discern the path factors in all consciousnesses.

124.

124.

Balāni dve dvicittesu, ekasmiṃ tīṇi dīpaye;

Ekādasasu cattāri, cha dvādasasu niddise.

Two powers are in two consciousnesses, in one three are shown; in eleven four, and in twelve six are specified.

125.

125.

Ekūnāsītiyā satta, soḷasevābalāni tu;

Cittamevaṃ tu viññeyyaṃ, sabalaṃ abalampi ca.

Seven powers are in seventy-nine consciousnesses, but sixteen are without powers. Thus consciousness should be understood as being with powers and without powers.

126.

126.

Jhānaṅgamaggaṅgabalindriyāni,

Cittesu jāyanti hi yesu yāni;

Mayā samāsena samuddharitvā,

Vuttāni sabbānipi tāni tesu.

The jhāna factors, path factors, powers, and faculties, which arise in which consciousnesses—all of them, extracted by me in brief, have been explained in regard to those.

Iti abhidhammāvatāre cetasikavibhāganiddeso nāma

Thus in the Abhidhammāvatāra ends the exposition named the Division of Mental Factors.

Tatiyo paricchedo.

The Third Chapter.

4. Catuttho paricchedo

4. The Fourth Chapter.

Ekavidhādiniddeso

Exposition of the Singlefold and Other Methods.

127.

127.

Ito [P 0.0032][V 0.0035] paraṃ pavakkhāmi, nayamekavidhādikaṃ;

Ābhidhammikabhikkhūnaṃ, buddhiyā pana vuddhiyā.

Henceforth I shall explain the method of the singlefold and so on, for the growth of wisdom of bhikkhus skilled in the Abhidhamma.

128.

128.

Sabbamekavidhaṃ cittaṃ, vijānanasabhāvato;

Duvidhañca bhave cittaṃ, ahetukasahetuto.

All consciousness is singlefold by its nature of cognizing; and consciousness is twofold as rootless and with roots.

129.

129.

Puññāpuññavipākā hi, kāme dasa ca pañca ca;

Kriyā tissoti sabbepi, aṭṭhārasa ahetukā.

Indeed, the sense-sphere resultants of merit and demerit are ten and five, and the functional are three; thus all eighteen are rootless.

130.

130.

Ekasattati sesāni, cittuppādā mahesinā;

Sahetukāti niddiṭṭhā, tādinā hetuvādinā.

The remaining seventy-one arisings of consciousness were declared by the Great Sage, the Such-like One, the expounder of causes, as being with roots.

131.

131.

Savatthukāvatthukato[M 0.0040], tathobhayavasena ca;

Sabbaṃ vuttapakāraṃ tu, tividhaṃ hoti mānasaṃ.

All the aforementioned types of mind are threefold: as with a physical basis, without a physical basis, and as both.

132.

132.

Sabbo kāmavipāko ca, rūpe pañcadasāpi ca;

Ādimaggo situppādo, manodhātu kriyāpi ca.

All sense-sphere resultants, the fifteen of the form sphere, the consciousness-arising of the first path, and the functional mind-element...

133.

133.

Domanassadvayañcāpi, tecattālīsa mānasā;

Nuppajjanti vinā vatthuṃ, ekantena savatthukā.

...and the two consciousnesses accompanied by displeasure: these forty-three minds do not arise without a physical basis; they are exclusively with a physical basis.

134.

134.

Arūpāvacarapākā ca, ekantena avatthukā;

Dvācattālīsa sesāni, cittānubhayathā siyuṃ.

The formless-sphere resultants are exclusively without a physical basis; the remaining forty-two consciousnesses can be of both kinds.

135.

135.

Ekekārammaṇaṃ cittaṃ, pañcārammaṇameva ca;

Chaḷārammaṇakañceti, evampi tividhaṃ siyā.

Consciousness can also be threefold: as having a single object, as having five objects, and as having six objects.

136.

136.

Viññāṇāni ca dvepañca, aṭṭha lokuttarāni ca;

Sabbaṃ mahaggatañceva, ṭhapetvābhiññamānasaṃ.

The two sets of fivefold sense consciousnesses, the eight supramundane consciousnesses, and all the sublime consciousnesses—excluding the mind of supernormal knowledge...

137.

137.

Tecattālīsa [V 0.0036] viññeyyā, ekekārammaṇā pana;

Manodhātuttayaṃ tattha, pañcārammaṇamīritaṃ.

These forty-three should be known as having a single object. The three mind-elements are said to have five objects.

138.

138.

Tecattālīsa sesāni, chaḷārammaṇikā matā;

Tathā ca tividhaṃ cittaṃ, kusalākusalādito.

The remaining forty-three are considered to have six objects. And likewise, the mind is threefold: as wholesome, unwholesome, and so on.

139.

139.

Ahetuṃ ekahetuñca, dvihetuñca tihetukaṃ;

Evaṃ catubbidhaṃ cittaṃ, viññātabbaṃ vibhāvinā.

As rootless, with one root, with two roots, and with three roots—thus the mind is fourfold, to be understood by the discerning one.

140.

140.

Heṭṭhā mayāpi niddiṭṭhā, aṭṭhārasa ahetukā;

Vicikicchuddhaccasaṃyuttaṃ, ekahetumudīritaṃ.

The eighteen rootless were pointed out by me before. The consciousness associated with doubt and that with restlessness are declared to be single-rooted.

141.

141.

Kāme [P 0.0033] dvādasadhā puñña-vipākakriyato pana;

Dasadhākusalā cāti, bāvīsati duhetukā.

Now, in the sense sphere, there are twelve from the standpoint of wholesome, resultant, and functional, and ten unwholesome; thus there are twenty-two that are two-rooted.

142.

142.

Kāme [M 0.0041] dvādasadhā puñña-vipākakriyato pana;

Sabbaṃ mahaggatañceva, appamāṇaṃ tihetukaṃ.

Now, in the sense sphere, there are twelve from the standpoint of wholesome, resultant, and functional; also all the sublime and immeasurable consciousnesses are three-rooted.

143.

143.

Rūpīriyāpathaviññatti-janakājanakādito;

Evañcāpi hi taṃ cittaṃ, hoti sabbaṃ catubbidhaṃ.

From the standpoint of producing or not producing material form, deportment, and intimation, all consciousness is thus fourfold.

144.

144.

Dvādasākusalā tattha, kusalā kāmadhātuyā;

Tathā dasa kriyā kāme, abhiññāmānasaṃ dvayaṃ.

Therein, the twelve unwholesome, the wholesome of the sense sphere, likewise ten functional in the sense sphere, and the two minds of supernormal knowledge...

145.

145.

Samuṭṭhāpenti rūpāni, kappenti iriyāpathaṃ;

Janayanti ca viññattiṃ, ime dvattiṃsa mānasā.

...originate material forms, regulate deportment, and generate intimation—these are the thirty-two minds.

146.

146.

Kusalā ca kriyā ceva, te mahaggatamānasā;

Aṭṭhānāsavacittāni, chabbīsati ca mānasā.

The wholesome and functional sublime minds and the eight untainted consciousnesses—these are the twenty-six minds.

147.

147.

Samuṭṭhāpenti rūpāni, kappenti iriyāpathaṃ;

Copanaṃ na ca pāpenti, dvikiccā niyatā ime.

They originate material forms and regulate deportment, but they do not produce intimation. These are determined as having a dual function.

148.

148.

Ṭhapetvā dasa viññāṇe, vipākā dvīsu bhūmisu;

Kriyā ceva manodhātu, imānekūnavīsati.

The resultants in the two spheres, excluding the ten sense consciousnesses, and the functional mind-element—these are nineteen.

149.

149.

Samuṭṭhāpenti [V 0.0037] rūpāni, na karontitaradvayaṃ;

Puna dvepañcaviññāṇā, vipākā ca arūpisu.

They originate material forms, but do not perform the other two functions. Again, the two sets of fivefold sense consciousnesses and the resultants in the formless sphere...

150.

150.

Sabbesaṃ sandhicittañca, cuticittañcārahato;

Na karonti tikiccāni, ime soḷasa mānasā.

...and the rebirth-linking consciousness of all, and the death-consciousness of an Arahant—these sixteen minds do not perform any of the three functions.

151.

151.

Ekadviticatuṭṭhāna-pañcaṭṭhānapabhedato;

Pañcadhā cittamakkhāsi, pañcanimmalalocano.

By the division into having one, two, three, four, and five functions, the One with the Five Stainless Eyes taught that consciousness is fivefold.

152.

152.

Kusalākusalā sabbe, cittuppādā mahākriyā;

Mahaggatā kriyā ceva, cattāro phalamānasā.

All wholesome and unwholesome arisings of consciousness, the great functional, the sublime functional, and the four fruit-minds...

153.

153.

Sabbeva [M 0.0042] pañcapaññāsa, nippapañcena satthunā;

Javanaṭṭhānatoyeva, ekaṭṭhāne niyāmitā.

All these fifty-five are designated by the Teacher, who is free from proliferation, as having the single function of impulsion.

154.

154.

Puna dvepañcaviññāṇā, dassane savane tathā;

Ghāyane sāyane ṭhāne, phusane paṭipāṭiyā.

Again, the two sets of fivefold consciousnesses have the single functions of seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, and touching, respectively.

155.

155.

Manodhātuttikaṃ ṭhāne, āvajjane paṭicchane;

Aṭṭhasaṭṭhi bhavantete, ekaṭṭhānikataṃ gatā.

The threefold mind-element has the functions of adverting and receiving. Thus there are sixty-eight that have a single function.

156.

156.

Puna dviṭṭhānikaṃ nāma, cittadvayamudīritaṃ;

Somanassayutaṃ pañca-dvāre santīraṇaṃ siyā.

Again, two consciousnesses are declared, which are called 'two-functioned.' One is the investigating consciousness accompanied by joy, which occurs at the five doors.

157.

157.

Tadārammaṇaṃ chadvāre, balavārammaṇe sati;

Tathā voṭṭhabbanaṃ hoti, pañcadvāresu voṭṭhabo.

It becomes the registering consciousness at the six doors when there is a strong object. Likewise, there is determining; at the five doors, it is the determiner.

158.

158.

Manodvāresu sabbesaṃ, hoti āvajjanaṃ pana;

Idaṃ dviṭṭhānikaṃ nāma, hoti cittadvayaṃ pana.

But at all mind-doors, it becomes the adverting consciousness. This, then, is the pair of consciousnesses called 'two-functioned'.

159.

159.

Paṭisandhibhavaṅgassa, cutiyā ṭhānato pana;

Mahaggatavipākā te, nava tiṭṭhānikā matā.

Now, by way of the functions of rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and death, the nine sublime resultants are considered 'three-functioned'.

160.

160.

Aṭṭha [P 0.0034] kāmā mahāpākā, paṭisandhibhavaṅgato;

Tadārammaṇato ceva, cutiṭṭhānavasena ca.

The eight great sense-sphere resultants are four-functioned by way of rebirth-linking, life-continuum, registering, and the function of death.

161.

161.

Catuṭṭhānikacittāni[V 0.0038], aṭṭha hontīti niddise;

Kusalākusalapākaṃ tu-pekkhāsahagatadvayaṃ.

One should declare that the four-functioned consciousnesses are eight. But the two resultant consciousnesses accompanied by equanimity, which are the fruit of wholesome and unwholesome kamma...

162.

162.

Santīraṇaṃ bhave pañca-dvāre chadvārikesu ca;

Tadārammaṇataṃ yāti, balavārammaṇe sati.

They function as investigating at the five doors, and they become registering at the six doors when the object is strong.

163.

163.

Paṭisandhibhavaṅgānaṃ, cutiṭṭhānavasena ca;

Pañcaṭṭhānikacittanti, idaṃ dvayamudīritaṃ.

And by way of the functions of rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and death, this pair is declared to be the 'five-functioned consciousnesses'.

164.

164.

Pañcakiccaṃ [M 0.0043] dvayaṃ cittaṃ, catukiccaṃ panaṭṭhakaṃ;

Tikiccaṃ navakaṃ dve tu, dvikiccā sesamekakaṃ.

Two consciousnesses have five functions; eight have four functions; nine have three functions; two have two functions; and the rest have one function.

165.

165.

Bhavaṅgāvajjanañceva, dassanaṃ sampaṭicchanaṃ;

Santīraṇaṃ voṭṭhabbanaṃ, javanaṃ bhavati sattamaṃ.

Life-continuum, adverting, seeing, receiving, investigating, determining, and seventh is impulsion.

166.

166.

Chabbidhaṃ hoti taṃ channaṃ, viññāṇānaṃ pabhedato;

Sattadhā sattaviññāṇa-dhātūnaṃ tu pabhedato.

That is sixfold by the division of the six consciousnesses; but it is sevenfold by the division of the seven consciousness-elements.

167.

167.

Ekekārammaṇaṃ chakkaṃ, pañcārammaṇabhedato;

Chaḷārammaṇato ceva, hoti aṭṭhavidhaṃ mano.

By way of the six single-object types, the five-object type, and the six-object type, the mind becomes eightfold.

168.

168.

Tattha dvepañcaviññāṇā, honti ekekagocarā;

Rūpārammaṇikā dve tu, dve dve saddādigocarā.

Therein, the two sets of fivefold consciousnesses each have a single object: two have form as object, two have sound as object, and so on for the rest.

169.

169.

Sabbaṃ mahaggataṃ cittaṃ, pañcābhiññāvivajjitaṃ;

Sabbaṃ lokuttarañceti, ekekārammaṇaṃ bhave.

All sublime consciousness, with the exception of the five supernormal knowledges, and all supramundane consciousness, has a single object.

170.

170.

Ekekārammaṇaṃ chakka-midaṃ ñeyyaṃ vibhāvinā;

Pañcārammaṇikaṃ nāma, manodhātuttayaṃ bhave.

This sixfold single-object group should be known by the discerning one. The three mind-elements are what is called 'five-object consciousness'.

171.

171.

Kāmāvacaracittāni, cattālīsaṃ tathekakaṃ;

Abhiññāni ca sabbāni, chaḷārammaṇikāniti.

The forty-one sense-sphere consciousnesses and all the supernormal knowledges have six objects.

172.

172.

Cittaṃ navavidhaṃ hoti, sattaviññāṇadhātusu;

Pacchimañca tidhā katvā, kusalākusalādito.

The mind becomes ninefold by taking the seven consciousness-elements and dividing the last one, the mind-consciousness-element, threefold, as wholesome, unwholesome, and other.

173.

173.

Puññāpuññavaseneva[V 0.0039], vipākakriyabhedato;

Chasattatividho bhedo, manoviññāṇadhātuyā.

A seventy-six-fold division of the mind-consciousness-element is made solely by way of merit and demerit, and by the division into resultant and functional.

174.

174.

Manodhātuṃ dvidhā katvā, vipākakriyabhedato;

Navadhā pubbavuttehi, dasadhā hoti mānasaṃ.

By dividing the mind-element in two according to the distinction between resultant and functional, along with the nine previously mentioned types, the mind becomes tenfold.

175.

175.

Dhātudvayaṃ [M 0.0044] tidhā katvā, pacchimaṃ puna paṇḍito;

Ekādasavidhaṃ cittaṃ, hotīti paridīpaye.

The wise one further explains that the mind is elevenfold, by dividing each of the last two elements—mind-element and mind-consciousness-element—threefold.

176.

176.

Manoviññāṇadhātumpi, kusalākusalādito;

Catudhā vibhajitvāna, vade dvādasadhā ṭhitaṃ.

By dividing the mind-consciousness-element fourfold as wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, and functional, one should speak of consciousness as being established in twelve ways.

177.

177.

Bhave [P 0.0035] cuddasadhā cittaṃ, cuddasaṭṭhānabhedato;

Paṭisandhibhavaṅgassa, cutiyāvajjanassa ca.

Consciousness becomes fourteenfold through the division into fourteen functions: the functions of rebirth-linking, life-continuum, death, and adverting...

178.

178.

Pañcannaṃ dassanādīnaṃ, sampaṭicchanacetaso;

Santīraṇassa voṭṭhabba-javanānaṃ vasena ca.

...of the five functions beginning with seeing, of receiving, of investigating, of determining, and of impulsion...

179.

179.

Tadārammaṇacittassa, tatheva ṭhānabhedato;

Evaṃ cuddasadhā cittaṃ, hotīti paridīpaye.

...and the function of the registering consciousness. Thus it is explained that consciousness is fourteenfold.

180.

180.

Bhūmipuggalanānātta-vasena ca pavattito;

Bahudhā panidaṃ cittaṃ, hotīti ca vibhāvaye.

And since it proceeds according to the diversity of planes and persons, one should understand that this mind is in fact manifold.

181.

181.

Ekavidhādinaye panimasmiṃ,

Yo kusalo matimā idha bhikkhu;

Tassabhidhammagatā pana atthā,

Hatthagatāmalakā viya honti.

For whatever skilled and wise bhikkhu in this method of the singlefold and so on, the meanings contained in the Abhidhamma become like a myrobalan fruit in his own hand.

Iti abhidhammāvatāre ekavidhādiniddeso nāma

Here ends the Exposition of the Singlefold and Other Methods in the Abhidhammāvatāra.

Catuttho paricchedo.

The Fourth Chapter.

5. Pañcamo paricchedo

5. Chapter Five

Bhūmipuggalacittuppattiniddeso

Exposition on the Arising of Consciousness according to Planes and Individuals

182.

182.

Ito [P 0.0036][V 0.0040] paraṃ pavakkhāmi, buddhivuddhikaraṃ nayaṃ;

Cittānaṃ bhūmīsuppattiṃ, puggalānaṃ vasena ca.

Hereafter I shall explain the method that enhances wisdom: the arising of consciousness in the planes according to the different types of individuals.

183.

183.

Devāceva [M 0.0045] manussā ca, tisso vāpāyabhūmiyo;

Gatiyo pañca niddiṭṭhā, satthunā tu tayo bhavā.

Gods and human beings, and the three woeful planes: these five are pointed out as destinations. But the Teacher spoke of three planes of existence.

184.

184.

Bhūmiyo tattha tiṃseva, tāsu tiṃseva puggalā;

Bhūmīsvetāsu uppannā, sabbe ca pana puggalā.

Therein, the planes are thirty, and in them are thirty types of individuals. All these individuals, moreover, arise in these planes.

185.

185.

Paṭisandhikacittānaṃ, vasenekūnavīsati;

Paṭisandhi ca nāmesā, duvidhā samudīritā.

By way of rebirth-linking consciousnesses, there are nineteen. And this rebirth-linking is declared to be twofold.

186.

186.

Acittakā sacittā ca, asaññīnamacittakā;

Sesā sacittakā ñeyyā, sā panekūnavīsati.

Rebirth-linking is without consciousness and with consciousness. For non-percipient beings, it is without consciousness; the rest should be known as with consciousness. These latter are nineteen.

187.

187.

Paṭisandhivaseneva, honti vīsati puggalā;

Idha cittādhikārattā, acittā na ca uddhaṭā.

By way of rebirth-linking, there are twenty types of individuals. Since the topic here is consciousness, those without consciousness are not included.

188.

188.

Ahetudvitihetūti, puggalā tividhā siyuṃ;

Ariyā pana aṭṭhāti, sabbe ekādaseritā.

Individuals are of three kinds: rootless, two-rooted, and three-rooted. The noble ones are eight. In all, eleven are declared.

189.

189.

Etesaṃ pana sabbesaṃ, puggalānaṃ pabhedato;

Cittānaṃ bhūmīsuppattiṃ, bhaṇato me nibodhatha.

Now understand from me as I explain the arising of consciousness in the planes according to the distinctions of all these individuals.

190.

190.

Tiṃsabhūmīsu cittāni, kati jāyanti me vada;

Cuddaseva tu cittāni, honti sabbāsu bhūmisu.

Tell me, how many consciousnesses arise in the thirty planes? Fourteen consciousnesses, indeed, arise in all planes.

191.

191.

Sadā vīsati cittāni, kāmeyeva bhave siyuṃ;

Pañca rūpabhaveyeva, cattāreva arūpisu.

Twenty consciousnesses always occur only in the sense-sphere existence; five only in the fine-material existence, and four only in the immaterial planes.

192.

192.

Kāmarūpabhavesveva[V 0.0041], aṭṭhārasa bhavanti hi;

Dvecattālīsa cittāni, honti tīsu bhavesupi.

Eighteen consciousnesses arise only in the sense-sphere and fine-material existences; forty-two consciousnesses arise in the three existences.

193.

193.

Ṭhapetvā pana sabbāsaṃ, catassopāyabhūmiyo;

Teraseva ca cittāni, honti chabbīsabhūmisu.

Excluding the four woeful planes, thirteen consciousnesses arise in twenty-six planes.

194.

194.

Aparāni [M 0.0046] catassopi, ṭhapetvāruppabhūmiyo;

Cittāni pana jāyanti, cha ca chabbīsabhūmisu.

Excluding the four immaterial planes, another six consciousnesses arise in twenty-six planes.

195.

195.

Suddhāvāsikadevānaṃ[P 0.0037], ṭhapetvā pañca bhūmiyo;

Pañca cittāni jāyante, pañcavīsatibhūmisu.

Excluding the five planes of the Pure Abodes, five consciousnesses arise in twenty-five planes.

196.

196.

Aparāni duve honti, pañcavīsatibhūmisu;

Ṭhapetvā nevasaññañca, catassopāyabhūmiyo.

Another two consciousnesses arise in twenty-five planes, namely, all planes excluding the plane of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and the four woeful planes.

197.

197.

Dvepi cittāni jāyanti, catuvīsatibhūmisu;

Ākiñcaññaṃ nevasaññañca, ṭhapetvāpāyabhūmiyo.

Two consciousnesses also arise in twenty-four planes, namely, all planes excluding the plane of nothingness, the plane of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and the woeful planes.

198.

198.

Apāyabhūmiyo hitvā, tisso āruppabhūmiyo;

Dveyeva pana cittāni, honti tevīsabhūmisu.

Excluding the woeful planes and the three immaterial planes, only two consciousnesses arise in twenty-three planes.

199.

199.

Arūpe ca apāye ca, ṭhapetvā aṭṭha bhūmiyo;

Ekādasavidhaṃ cittaṃ, honti dvāvīsabhūmisu.

Excluding the eight planes of the immaterial sphere and the woeful states, eleven kinds of consciousness arise in twenty-two planes.

200.

200.

Suddhāvāse apāye ca, ṭhapetvā nava bhūmiyo;

Ekavīsāsu niccampi, cattārova bhavanti hi.

Excluding the nine planes of the Pure Abodes and the woeful states, four consciousnesses always arise in the remaining twenty-one planes.

201.

201.

Ekaṃ sattarasasveva, cittaṃ jāyati bhūmisu;

Suddhāvāse ṭhapetvā tu, apāyāruppabhūmiyo.

One consciousness arises in just seventeen planes, namely, all planes excluding the Pure Abodes, the woeful states, and the immaterial planes.

202.

202.

Dvādaseva tu jāyante, ekādasasu bhūmisu;

Ṭhapetvā pana sabbāpi, bhūmiyo hi mahaggatā.

Twelve consciousnesses arise in the eleven sense-sphere planes, that is, by excluding all the sublime planes.

203.

203.

Kāmāvacaradevānaṃ, manussānaṃ vasena tu;

Aṭṭha cittāni jāyante, sadā sattasu bhūmisu.

With respect to the sense-sphere gods and human beings, eight consciousnesses always arise in the seven planes of blissful sense-sphere existence.

204.

204.

Pañcamajjhānapākeko[V 0.0042], jāyate chasu bhūmisu;

Cattāri pana cittāni, tīsu tīsveva bhūmisu.

The one resultant consciousness of the fifth jhāna arises in six planes. Four other consciousnesses arise in three planes each.

205.

205.

Cattāri [M 0.0047] pana cittāni, honti ekekabhūmisu;

Arūpāvacarapākānaṃ, vasena paridīpaye.

Four consciousnesses arise in one plane each; this is explained by way of the immaterial-sphere resultants.

206.

206.

Kusalākusalā kāme,

Tesaṃ pākā ahetukā;

Āvajjanadvayañcāti,

Sattatiṃseva mānasā.

The wholesome and unwholesome consciousnesses in the sense-sphere, their rootless resultants, and the two advertings: these are the thirty-seven mental states.

207.

207.

Narakādīsvapāyesu, catūsupi ca jāyare;

Dvepaññāsāvasesāni, nuppajjanti kadācipi.

These arise in all four woeful states, such as the hells. The remaining fifty-two consciousnesses never arise there at any time.

208.

208.

Kāme devamanussānaṃ, nava pākā mahaggatā;

Neva jāyanti jāyanti, asīti hadayā sadā.

For gods and humans in the sense-sphere, the nine sublime resultants do not arise. Eighty consciousnesses always arise.

209.

209.

Kāme aṭṭha mahāpākā, domanassadvayampi ca;

Tathā ghānādiviññāṇa-ttayaṃ pākā apuññajā.

The eight great sense-sphere resultants, the two consciousnesses accompanied by displeasure, the triad of sense consciousnesses beginning with nose-consciousness, and the unwholesome resultants:

210.

210.

Natthi āruppapākā ca, rūpāvacarabhūmiyaṃ;

Imehi saha cittehi, tayo maggā phaladvayaṃ.

—these, and the immaterial resultants, are not found in the fine-material sphere. Along with these consciousnesses, the three lower paths and two lower fruits are also not found there.

211.

211.

Cattāro diṭṭhisaṃyuttā, vicikicchāyutampi ca;

Cattāro heṭṭhimā pākā, suddhāvāse na labbhare.

The four consciousnesses associated with wrong view, the one associated with doubt, and the four lower unwholesome resultants are not found in the Pure Abodes.

212.

212.

Sesāni ekapaññāsa, cittāni pana labbhare;

Rūpāvacarikā sabbe, vipākā kāmadhātuyā.

But the remaining fifty-one consciousnesses are found there. All fine-material resultants do not arise in the sense-sphere.

213.

213.

Domanassādimaggo ca, kriyā ca dve ahetukā;

Tecattālīsa cittāni, natthi āruppabhūmiyaṃ.

The consciousnesses accompanied by displeasure, the two rootless functional consciousnesses, and others; these forty-three consciousnesses are not found in the immaterial sphere.

214.

214.

Evaṃ [P 0.0038] bhūmivaseneva, cittuppattiṃ vibhāvaye;

Tathā ekādasannampi, puggalānaṃ vasena ca.

Thus one should understand the arising of consciousness by way of the planes, and likewise by way of the eleven types of individuals.

215.

215.

Kusalākusalā [M 0.0048][V 0.0043] kāme,

Tesaṃ pākā ahetukā;

Āvajjanadvayañcāti,

Sattatiṃseva mānasā.

The wholesome and unwholesome consciousnesses in the sense-sphere, their rootless resultants, and the two advertings: these are the thirty-seven mental states.

216.

216.

Ahetukassa sattassa, jāyante pañcabhūmisu;

Dvepaññāsāvasesāni, na jāyanti kadācipi.

For a rootless being, these thirty-seven consciousnesses arise in the five planes. The remaining fifty-two never arise at any time.

217.

217.

Ahetukassa vuttehi, kāmapākā duhetukā;

Duhetukassa jāyante, cattālīsaṃ tathekakaṃ.

For a two-rooted individual, forty-one consciousnesses arise: those mentioned for the rootless individual plus the two-rooted sense-sphere resultants.

218.

218.

Sabbe mahaggatā ceva, sabbepi ca anāsavā;

Tihetukā vipākā ca, kāme nava kriyāpi ca.

All sublime consciousnesses, all supramundane consciousnesses, the three-rooted resultants, and the nine sense-sphere functional consciousnesses:

219.

219.

Duhetuno na jāyanti, cattālīsaṃ tathāṭṭha ca;

Kāmāvacarasattassa, tihetupaṭisandhino.

—these forty-eight consciousnesses do not arise for a two-rooted individual. Now for a sense-sphere being with three-rooted rebirth-linking:

220.

220.

Puthujjanassa jāyante, catupaññāsa mānasā;

Dvihetukassa vuttāni, cattālīsaṃ tathekakaṃ.

For an ordinary person with three-rooted rebirth-linking, fifty-four mental states arise.

221.

221.

Cattāro ñāṇasaṃyuttā, vipākā kāmadhātuyā;

Rūpārūpesu puññāni, catupaññāsa mānasā.

For this person, the four sense-sphere resultants associated with knowledge and the wholesome consciousnesses of the fine-material and immaterial spheres may arise. In total, fifty-four mental states are possible.

222.

222.

Puthujjanassa jāyante, pañcatiṃsa na jāyare;

Chadevesu manussesu, sotāpannassa dehino.

Thirty-five consciousnesses do not arise for this ordinary person. For a stream-enterer embodied in the six heavens or among humans:

223.

223.

Paññāsevassa cittāni, jāyantīti viniddise;

Navatiṃseva cittāni, nuppajjantīti dīpaye.

It is specified that fifty consciousnesses arise for him, and it is shown that thirty-nine do not.

224.

224.

Sotāpannassa vuttāni, ṭhapetvā paṭhamaṃ phalaṃ;

Attanova phalenassa, sakadāgāmino siyuṃ.

For a once-returner, the consciousnesses are the same as those stated for the stream-enterer, but excluding the first fruit and including his own fruit.

225.

225.

Sotāpannassa [M 0.0049][V 0.0044] vuttāni, ṭhapetvā paṭighadvayaṃ;

Dutiyaṃ ca phalaṃ hitvā, yāni cittāni tāniti;

Anāgāmissa sattassa, jāyantīti viniddise.

The consciousnesses that arise for a non-returner are specified as those stated for a stream-enterer, but excluding the two consciousnesses rooted in aversion and replacing the second fruit with his own.

226.

226.

Kati cittāni jāyante, kāme arahato pana;

Cattārīsañca cattāri, kāme arahato siyuṃ.

But how many consciousnesses arise for an arahant in the sense-sphere? Forty-four consciousnesses arise for an arahant in the sense-sphere.

227.

227.

Maggaṭṭhānaṃ catunnampi, puggalānaṃ sakaṃ sakaṃ;

Maggacittaṃ siyā tesaṃ, ekacittakkhaṇā hi te.

For each of the four individuals standing on the path, their own respective path consciousness arises. For them, it lasts for only a single mind-moment.

228.

228.

Puthujjanassa tīsveva, paṭhamajjhānabhūmisu;

Pañcatiṃseva cittāni, jāyanteti viniddise.

For an ordinary person in the three first-jhāna planes, it is specified that thirty-five consciousnesses arise.

229.

229.

Ghānādīsu ca viññāṇa-ttayaṃ satta apuññajā;

Mahāpākā tathā pākā, uparijjhānabhūmikā.

The triad of consciousnesses beginning with nose-consciousness, the seven unwholesome resultants, the great resultants, and the resultants pertaining to the higher jhāna planes:

230.

230.

Vipākāpi ca āruppā, domanassadvayampi ca;

Aṭṭhārasa kriyā ceva, aṭṭha lokuttarāni ca.

—also the immaterial resultants, the two consciousnesses accompanied by displeasure, the eighteen functional consciousnesses, and the eight supramundane consciousnesses:

231.

231.

Paṭhamajjhānanibbatta-puthujjanasarīrino;

Etāni catupaññāsa, cittāni na ca labbhare.

—these fifty-four consciousnesses are not found in an ordinary person who has been reborn in a first-jhāna plane.

232.

232.

Sotāpannassa [P 0.0039] cittāni, tatthekatiṃsa jāyare;

Puthujjanassa vuttesu, hitvā cāpuññapañcakaṃ.

For a stream-enterer in those same planes, thirty-one consciousnesses arise; this is the set for the ordinary person, but excluding the five unwholesome consciousnesses connected with view and doubt.

233.

233.

Sakadāgāmino tattha, ṭhapetvā paṭhamaṃ phalaṃ;

Ekatiṃseva jāyante, pakkhipitvā sakaṃ phalaṃ.

For a once-returner there, thirty-one consciousnesses also arise: the set for the stream-enterer, but excluding the first fruit and including his own fruit.

234.

234.

Anāgāmissa tattheva, ṭhapetvā dutiyaṃ phalaṃ;

Ekatiṃseva jāyante, phalacittena attano.

For a non-returner in that same place, thirty-one consciousnesses also arise: the set for the once-returner, but excluding the second fruit and including his own fruit-consciousness.

235.

235.

Viññāṇaṃ cakkhusotānaṃ, puññajaṃ sampaṭicchanaṃ;

Santīraṇadvayañceva, kriyacittāni vīsati.

Eye-consciousness and ear-consciousness, wholesome-resultant receiving consciousness, the two investigating consciousnesses, and twenty functional consciousnesses,

236.

236.

Arahattaphalaṃ [M 0.0050][V 0.0045] pāko, paṭhamajjhānasambhavo;

Sattavīsati cittāni, arahantassa jāyare.

the fruit of Arahantship, and the resultant originating from the first jhāna: these twenty-seven consciousnesses arise for an Arahant.

237.

237.

Puthujjanassa tīsveva, dutiyajjhānabhūmisu;

Chattiṃsa dutiyajjhāna-tatiyajjhānapākato.

For an ordinary person in the three second-jhāna planes, thirty-six consciousnesses arise. This is also the case for one reborn from the third jhāna.

238.

238.

Puthujjanassa vuttesu, hitvā vāpuññapañcakaṃ;

Sotāpannassa bāttiṃsa, phalena saha attano.

For a stream-enterer, thirty-two consciousnesses arise: the set for the ordinary person, but excluding the five unwholesome ones, and including his own fruit.

239.

239.

Sotāpannassa vuttesu, ṭhapetvā paṭhamaṃ phalaṃ;

Bāttiṃsa phalacittena, sakadāgāmissa attano.

For a once-returner, thirty-two consciousnesses arise: the set for the stream-enterer, but excluding the first fruit and including his own fruit-consciousness.

240.

240.

Sakadāgāmīsu vuttesu, ṭhapetvā dutiyaṃ phalaṃ;

Anāgāmiphalenassa, bāttiṃseva bhavanti hi.

For a non-returner, thirty-two consciousnesses also arise: the set for the once-returner, but excluding the second fruit and including the fruit of non-returning.

241.

241.

Arahantassa tīsveva, aṭṭhavīsati attano;

Phalena dutiyajjhāna-tatiyajjhānapākato.

For an Arahant in the three planes of the second and third jhānas, twenty-eight consciousnesses arise, including his own fruit and the corresponding jhāna-resultant.

242.

242.

Parittakasubhādīnaṃ, devānaṃ tīsu bhūmisu;

Pañcatiṃseva jāyante, catutthajjhānapākato.

For the devas of the Parittasubha and other planes, in those three planes thirty-five consciousnesses arise, along with the resultant of the fourth jhāna.

243.

243.

Sotāpannassa tattheka-tiṃsa cittāni jāyare;

Sakadāgāmino evaṃ, tathānāgāminopi ca.

For a stream-enterer there, thirty-one consciousnesses arise. It is likewise for a once-returner and also for a non-returner.

244.

244.

Khīṇāsavassa tattheva, sattavīsati mānasā;

Tathā vehapphale cāpi, sabbesaṃ honti mānasā.
