For one whose taints are destroyed, twenty-seven minds arise there. Likewise, in the Vehapphala plane, the same sets of consciousnesses arise for all these respective individuals.

245.

245.

Ekatiṃseva cittāni, suddhāvāsikabhūmisu;

Anāgāmikasattassa, hontīti paridīpaye.

It is shown that thirty-one consciousnesses arise for a non-returner in the planes of the Pure Abodes.

246.

246.

Arahato pana tattheva, mānasā sattavīsati;

Evaṃ rūpīsu cittāni, viññeyyāni vibhāvinā.

But for an Arahant, twenty-seven minds arise there. Thus should the discerning person understand the consciousnesses that arise in the fine-material planes.

247.

247.

Catuvīsati [M 0.0051] cittāni, paṭhamāruppabhūmiyaṃ;

Puthujjanassa sattassa, jāyantīti viniddise.

It is specified that twenty-four consciousnesses arise for an ordinary being in the first formless plane.

248.

248.

Sotāpannassa [V 0.0046] tattheva, ṭhapetvāpuññapañcakaṃ;

Samavīsati cittāni, phalena saha attano.

For a stream-enterer there, excluding the five demeritorious consciousnesses, twenty consciousnesses arise, together with his own fruit.

249.

249.

Sakadāgāmino tattha, tathānāgāminopi ca;

Jāyanti vīsa cittāni, pubbapubbaphalaṃ vinā.

For a once-returner and also for a non-returner, twenty consciousnesses arise there, without the preceding fruit.

250.

250.

Khīṇāsavassa tattheva, dasapañca ca mānasā;

Puthujjanassa sattassa, dutiyāruppabhūmiyaṃ.

For one whose taints are destroyed, fifteen minds arise there. For an ordinary being in the second formless plane:

251.

251.

Honti [P 0.0040] tevīsa cittāni, iti vatvā vibhāvaye;

Tiṇṇannampettha sekhānaṃ, cittānekūnavīsati.

Twenty-three consciousnesses arise. Thus it should be analyzed. For the three trainees here, nineteen consciousnesses arise.

252.

252.

Cuddaseva tu cittāni, dutiyāruppabhūmiyaṃ;

Kriyādvādasa pākeko, phalaṃ khīṇāsavassa tu.

In the second formless plane, there are just fourteen consciousnesses: twelve are functional, and one is the resultant fruit for the one whose taints are destroyed.

253.

253.

Puthujjanassa sattassa, tatiyāruppabhūmiyaṃ;

Bāvīsati ca cittāni, bhavantīti pakāsaye.

It is declared that for an ordinary being in the third formless plane, twenty-two consciousnesses arise.

254.

254.

Aṭṭhāraseva cittāni, sotāpannassa jāyare;

Sakadāgāmino tāni, ṭhapetvā paṭhamaṃ phalaṃ.

Just eighteen consciousnesses arise for a stream-enterer. For a once-returner, the same arise, excluding the first fruition.

255.

255.

Sakadāgāmivuttesu, ṭhapetvā dutiyaṃ phalaṃ;

Aṭṭhāraseva cittāni, anāgāmissa jāyare.

For a non-returner, eighteen consciousnesses arise; these are the same as for a once-returner, but excluding the second fruition.

256.

256.

Teraseva ca cittāni, tatiyāruppabhūmiyaṃ;

Khīṇāsavassa sattassa, bhavantīti viniddise.

It should be declared that for a being whose taints are destroyed, just thirteen consciousnesses arise in the third formless plane.

257.

257.

Ekavīsati cittāni, catutthāruppabhūmiyaṃ;

Puthujjanassa sattassa, jāyantīti viniddise.

It should be declared that for an ordinary being, twenty-one consciousnesses arise in the fourth formless plane.

258.

258.

Sotāpannassa [M 0.0052] sattassa, sattarasa pakāsaye;

Sakadāgāmino tāni, ṭhapetvā paṭhamaṃ phalaṃ.

For a stream-entering being, seventeen consciousnesses should be declared. For a once-returner, the same arise, excluding the first fruition.

259.

259.

Sakadāgāmivuttesu, ṭhapetvā dutiyaṃ phalaṃ;

Honti sattarasevassa, anāgāmissa mānasā.

For a non-returner there are just seventeen minds; these are the same as for a once-returner, but excluding the second fruition.

260.

260.

Dvādaseva [V 0.0047] tu cittāni, catutthāruppabhūmiyaṃ;

Jāyanti arahantassa, iti vatvā vibhāvaye.

But in the fourth formless plane, just twelve consciousnesses arise for the Arahant; having stated this, one should understand.

261.

261.

Heṭṭhimānaṃ arūpīnaṃ, brahmānaṃ uparūpari;

Arūpakusalā ceva, uppajjanti kriyāpi ca.

For the formless brahmas of the lower planes, formless wholesome and functional consciousnesses arise in the planes successively higher up.

262.

262.

Uddhamuddhamarūpīnaṃ, heṭṭhimā heṭṭhimā pana;

Āruppāneva jāyante, diṭṭhādīnavato kira.

But for the formless beings of the higher and higher planes, the lower and lower formless consciousnesses do not arise, it is said, because they have seen the danger in them.

263.

263.

Ṭhapetvā paṭhamaṃ maggaṃ, kusalānuttarā tayo;

Kāmāvacarapuññāni, apuññāni tathā dasa.

The three wholesome supramundane consciousnesses, excluding the first path; the sense-sphere meritorious consciousnesses; and likewise the ten demeritorious consciousnesses.

264.

264.

Cattārāruppapuññāni, sabbe pākā anuttarā;

Paṭhamāruppapāko ca, nava kāmakriyāpi ca.

The four formless meritorious consciousnesses; all the supramundane resultants; the first formless resultant; and also the nine sense-sphere functional consciousnesses.

265.

265.

Āruppāpi kriyā sabbā, tecattālīsa mānasā;

Uppajjanti panetāni, paṭhamāruppabhūmiyaṃ.

And all the formless functional consciousnesses. These forty-three minds arise in the first formless plane.

266.

266.

Sabbo kāmavipāko ca, sabbo rūpomahaggato;

Cittuppādo manodhātu, domanassadvayampi ca.

All sense-sphere resultant consciousnesses; all fine-material sublime arisings of consciousness; the mind-element; and also the pair of consciousnesses accompanied by displeasure.

267.

267.

Ādimaggo tayo pākā, āruppā ca tathūpari;

Chacattālīsa natthettha, paṭhamāruppabhūmiyaṃ.

The first path, and likewise the three higher formless resultants. These forty-six are not found here in the first formless plane.

268.

268.

Vuttesu pana cittesu, paṭhamāruppabhūmiyaṃ;

Ṭhapetvā paṭhamāruppa-ttayaṃ pāko ca attano.

From the consciousnesses stated for the first formless plane, one excludes the triad of the first formless plane: the wholesome, its resultant, and the functional.

269.

269.

Tālīsetāni [M 0.0053] jāyante, dutiyāruppabhūmiyaṃ;

Evaṃ sesadvaye ñeyyā, hitvā heṭṭhimaheṭṭhimaṃ.

Forty such consciousnesses arise in the second formless plane. The same should be understood for the remaining two planes, having excluded the consciousnesses of the plane immediately below each time.

270.

270.

Attano [P 0.0041] attano pākā, cattāro ca anāsavā;

Vipākā honti sabbeva, catūsvāruppabhūmisu.

In the four formless planes, all the resultants that arise are their own respective resultants and the four taintless fruitions.

271.

271.

Voṭṭhabbanena cittena, kāme aṭṭha mahākriyā;

Catassopi ca āruppā, teraseva kriyā siyuṃ.

The determining consciousness, the eight great functional consciousnesses of the sense-sphere, and the four formless functional consciousnesses—these are the thirteen functional consciousnesses.

272.

272.

Khīṇāsavassa [V 0.0048] jāyante, paṭhamāruppabhūmiyaṃ;

Dvādaseva kriyā honti, dutiyāruppabhūmiyaṃ.

For one whose taints are destroyed, thirteen functional consciousnesses arise in the first formless plane; in the second formless plane, just twelve functional consciousnesses arise.

273.

273.

Ekādasa kriyā honti, tatiyāruppabhūmiyaṃ;

Daseva ca kriyā ñeyyā, catutthāruppabhūmiyaṃ.

In the third formless plane there are eleven functional cittas, and in the fourth formless plane just ten functional cittas should be known.

274.

274.

Arahato pana cittāni, honti ekūnavīsati;

Arahattaṃ kriyā sabbā, ṭhapetvāvajjanadvayaṃ.

But for the Arahant, there are nineteen cittas: the Arahantship fruition and all functional cittas, excluding the two adverting cittas.

275.

275.

Catunnañca phalaṭṭhānaṃ, tihetukaputhujjane;

Teraseva ca cittāni, bhavantīti pakāsaye.

It is declared that for the four established in the fruit and for the triple-rooted worldling, just thirteen resultant cittas arise.

276.

276.

Cattāro ñāṇasaṃyuttā, mahāpākā tathā nava;

Rūpārūpavipākā ca, teraseva bhavantime.

The four great resultants associated with knowledge, and likewise the nine fine-material and formless resultants—these become the thirteen.

277.

277.

Catunnañca phalaṭṭhānaṃ, duhetukaputhujjane;

Ñāṇahīnāni cattāri, vipākā eva jāyare.

For the four established in the fruit and for the double-rooted worldling, only the four resultants devoid of knowledge arise.

278.

278.

Puthujjanānaṃ tiṇṇampi, catunnaṃ ariyadehinaṃ;

Sattaraseva cittāni, sattannampi bhavanti hi.

For the three kinds of worldlings and for the four noble beings—for all seven kinds of persons, indeed—seventeen cittas exist.

279.

279.

Viññāṇāni duve pañca, manodhātuttayampi ca;

Santīraṇāni voṭṭhabbaṃ, honti sattarasevime.

The two sets of five sense-consciousnesses, the threefold mind-element, the three investigating cittas, and the determining citta—these are the seventeen.

280.

280.

Heṭṭhā tiṇṇaṃ phalaṭṭhānaṃ, tihetukaputhujjane;

Naveva kusalā honti, catunnampi mahaggatā.

For the lower three established in the fruit and for the triple-rooted worldling—for all four of these—the nine sublime wholesome cittas arise.

281.

281.

Tiṇṇaṃ [M 0.0054] puthujjanānañca, tiṇṇamariyānamādito;

Teraseva tu cittāni, uppajjantīti niddise.

It is pointed out that for the three kinds of worldlings and for the first three kinds of noble ones, just thirteen cittas arise.

282.

282.

Aṭṭheva kāmapuññāni, diṭṭhihīnā apuññato;

Cattāropi ca uddhacca-saṃyuttañcāti terasa.

The eight sense-sphere meritorious cittas; the four demeritorious cittas devoid of wrong view; and the one associated with restlessness—thus there are thirteen.

283.

283.

Heṭṭhā dvinnaṃ phalaṭṭhānaṃ, tathā sabbaputhujjane;

Domanassayuttaṃ cittaṃ, dvayameva tu jāyate.

For those established in the lower two fruits and likewise for all worldlings, only the pair of cittas associated with displeasure arises.

284.

284.

Tiṇṇaṃ [V 0.0049] puthujjanānaṃ tu, pañceva pana jāyare;

Cattāri diṭṭhiyuttāni, vicikicchāyutampi ca.

But for the three kinds of worldlings, just five cittas arise: the four associated with wrong view and the one associated with doubt.

285.

285.

Maggaṭṭhānaṃ catunnampi, maggacittaṃ sakaṃ sakaṃ;

Ekameva bhave tesaṃ, iti vatvā vibhāvaye.

For all four established in the path, their own respective path-consciousness—just one for each—arises. Having said this, one should understand.

286.

286.

Mayā bhavesu cittānaṃ, puggalānaṃ vasena ca;

Bhikkhūnaṃ pāṭavatthāya, cittuppatti pakāsitā.

By me, the arising of consciousness has been explained according to planes of existence and types of individuals, for the study of the monks.

287.

287.

Evaṃ sabbamidaṃ cittaṃ, bhūmipuggalabhedato;

Bahudhāpi ca hotīti, viññātabbaṃ vibhāvinā.

Thus, it should be understood by the discerning one that all this consciousness is indeed manifold through its divisions by plane and individual.

288.

288.

Sakkā [P 0.0042] vuttānusārena, bhedo ñātuṃ vibhāvinā;

Ganthavitthārabhītena, saṃkhittaṃ panidaṃ mayā.

A discerning one can know the divisions by following what has been said. Fearing an expansion of the text, this has been condensed by me.

289.

289.

Pubbāparaṃ viloketvā, cintetvā ca punappunaṃ;

Atthaṃ upaparikkhitvā, gahetabbaṃ vibhāvinā.

Having considered what comes before and after, having reflected again and again, and having investigated the meaning, it should be grasped by the discerning one.

290.

290.

Imañcābhidhammāvatāraṃ susāraṃ,

Varaṃ sattamohandhakārappadīpaṃ;

Sadā sādhu cinteti vāceti yo taṃ,

Naraṃ rāgadosā ciraṃ nopayanti.

This Abhidhammāvatāra, most essential, the excellent lamp for the darkness of beings' delusion—whoever constantly and well reflects upon or recites it, that person will not long be assailed by lust and hatred.

Iti abhidhammāvatāre bhūmipuggalavasena cittuppattiniddeso nāma

Thus ends the exposition on the arising of consciousness according to plane and individual in the Abhidhammāvatāra.

Pañcamo paricchedo.

The Fifth Chapter.

6. Chaṭṭho paricchedo

6. The Sixth Chapter

Ārammaṇavibhāganiddeso

Exposition of the Division of Objects

291.

291.

Etesaṃ [M 0.0055][P 0.0043][V 0.0050] pana cittānaṃ, ārammaṇamito paraṃ;

Dassayissāmahaṃ tena, vinā natthi hi sambhavo.

Hereafter I shall explain the objects of these consciousnesses, for without an object their arising is indeed impossible.

292.

292.

Rūpaṃ saddaṃ gandhaṃ rasaṃ, phoṭṭhabbaṃ dhammameva ca;

Chadhā ārammaṇaṃ āhu, chaḷārammaṇakovidā.

Visible form, sound, odor, taste, the tangible, and the mental object: those skilled in the six objects declare the object to be sixfold.

293.

293.

Tattha bhūte upādāya, vaṇṇo catusamuṭṭhito;

Sanidassanapaṭigho, rūpārammaṇasaññito.

Therein, color, which is dependent on the primary elements, has a fourfold origin. Being visible and impinging, it is designated as the visible-form object.

294.

294.

Duvidho hi samuddiṭṭho, saddo cittotusambhavo;

Saviññāṇakasaddova, hoti cittasamuṭṭhito.

Sound is declared to be twofold, arising from consciousness and from temperature. Sound accompanied by cognition arises from consciousness.

295.

295.

Aviññāṇakasaddo yo,

So hotūtusamuṭṭhito;

Duvidhopi ayaṃ saddo,

Saddārammaṇataṃ gato.

That sound which is without cognition arises from temperature. This sound, being of two kinds, is comprised under the sound object.

296.

296.

Dharīyatīti gacchanto, gandho sūcanatopi vā;

Ayaṃ catusamuṭṭhāno, gandhārammaṇasammato.

Odor has a fourfold origin and is regarded as the odor object.

297.

297.

Rasamānā rasantīti, rasoti parikittito;

Sova catusamuṭṭhāno, rasārammaṇanāmako.

It is called 'taste' because it is tasted. It has a fourfold origin and is named the taste object.

298.

298.

Phusīyatīti phoṭṭhabbaṃ, pathavītejavāyavo;

Phoṭṭhabbaṃ catusambhūtaṃ, phoṭṭhabbārammaṇaṃ mataṃ.

It is called 'the tangible' because it is touched; it consists of the earth, fire, and air elements. The tangible, which has a fourfold origin, is considered the tangible object.

299.

299.

Sabbaṃ nāmañca rūpañca, hitvā rūpādipañcakaṃ;

Lakkhaṇāni ca paññatti-dhammārammaṇasaññitaṃ.

All name-and-form—excluding the pentad beginning with form—as well as characteristics and concepts, are designated as the mind-object.

300.

300.

Chārammaṇāni [V 0.0051] labbhanti, kāmāvacarabhūmiyaṃ;

Tīṇi rūpe panārūpe, dhammārammaṇamekakaṃ.

In the sense-sphere plane, six objects are found. In the form sphere, three are found; but in the formless sphere, only the one mind-object.

301.

301.

Khaṇavatthuparittattā[M 0.0056], āpāthaṃ na vajanti ye;

Te dhammārammaṇā honti, yesaṃ rūpādayo kira.

It is said that for those consciousnesses whose objects are visible forms and so on, these forms become mind-objects because, being momentary and subtle, they do not enter the avenue of the senses.

302.

302.

Te paṭikkhipitabbāva, aññamaññassa gocaraṃ;

Neva paccanubhontānaṃ, mano tesaṃ tu gocaraṃ.

This view should be rejected, for they do not experience one another's object. For them, however, the mind is the object-field.

303.

303.

Tañca [P 0.0044] “paccanubhotī”ti, vuttattā pana satthunā;

Rūpādārammaṇāneva, honti rūpādayo pana.

And since it was said by the Teacher, 'He experiences,' visible forms and so on are indeed only objects consisting of visible form and the like.

304.

304.

Dibbacakkhādiñāṇānaṃ, rūpādīneva gocarā;

Anāpāthagatāneva, tānītipi na yujjati.

For knowledges such as the divine eye, visible forms and so on are indeed the objects. Therefore, the view that these are beyond the avenue of the senses is not tenable.

305.

305.

Yaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ hontaṃ, taṃ dhammārammaṇaṃ kathaṃ;

Evaṃ sati panetesaṃ, niyamoti kathaṃ bhave.

How can that which is a visible-form object be a mind-object? If this were so, how could there be a fixed rule for them?

306.

306.

Sabbaṃ ārammaṇaṃ etaṃ, chabbidhaṃ samudīritaṃ;

Taṃ parittattikādīnaṃ, vasena bahudhā mataṃ.

This entire object, declared as sixfold, is considered manifold by way of the triad of the limited, and so on.

307.

307.

Sabbo kāmavipāko ca, kriyāhetudvayampi ca;

Pañcavīsati ekantaṃ, parittārammaṇā siyuṃ.

All sense-sphere resultants and the two rootless functional consciousnesses—these twenty-five—invariably have limited objects.

308.

308.

Iṭṭhādibhedā pañceva, rūpasaddādayo pana;

Viññāṇānaṃ dvipañcannaṃ, gocarā paṭipāṭiyā.

The five sense objects beginning with visible form and sound, distinguished as desirable and so on, are respectively the objects of the two pentads of sense consciousnesses.

309.

309.

Rūpādipañcakaṃ sabbaṃ, manodhātuttayassa tu;

Terasannaṃ panetesaṃ, rūpakkhandhova gocaro.

The entire pentad beginning with form is the object for the mind-element-triad. For these thirteen in total, the object-field is only the aggregate of matter.

310.

310.

Nārūpaṃ na ca paññattiṃ, nātītaṃ na canāgataṃ;

Ārammaṇaṃ karonte ca, vattamāno hi gocaro.

They do not take as object the formless, concepts, the past, or the future; their object-field is only the present.

311.

311.

Terasetāni cittāni, jāyante kāmadhātuyaṃ;

Cattāri rūpāvacare, neva kiñci arūpisu.

These thirteen consciousnesses arise in the sense-sphere; four in the form-sphere; none at all in the formless planes.

312.

312.

Mahāpākānamaṭṭhannaṃ[M 0.0057][V 0.0052], santīraṇattayassapi;

Chasu dvāresu rūpādichaparittāni gocarā.

For the eight great resultants and the three investigating consciousnesses, the six limited objects beginning with visible form, arising at the six doors, are the object-field.

313.

313.

Rūpādayo parittā cha, hasituppādagocarā;

Pañcadvāre paṭuppannā, manodvāre tikālikā.

The six limited objects beginning with visible form are the object-field for the smile-producing consciousness. Occurring at the five doors, they are present; at the mind door, they can belong to the three times.

314.

314.

Dutiyāruppacittañca, catutthāruppamānasaṃ;

Chabbidhaṃ niyataṃ hoti, taṃ mahaggatagocaraṃ.

The six consciousnesses of the second and fourth formless attainments definitely have a sublime object.

315.

315.

Nibbānārammaṇattā hi, ekantena anaññato;

Aṭṭhānāsavacittānaṃ, appamāṇova gocaro.

Because they have Nibbāna as their object, exclusively and not otherwise, for the eight supramundane consciousnesses the object-field is the Immeasurable.

316.

316.

Cattāro ñāṇahīnā ca, kāmāvacarapuññato;

Kriyatopi ca cattāro, dvādasākusalāni ca.

The four sense-sphere wholesome consciousnesses dissociated from knowledge, the four functional consciousnesses dissociated from knowledge, and the twelve unwholesome consciousnesses:

317.

317.

Parittārammaṇā ceva, te mahaggatagocarā;

Paññattārammaṇattā hi, navattabbāva honti te.

These can have limited objects and sublime objects. Because they can also have a concept as object, they are said to be 'not-to-be-specified'.

318.

318.

Cattāro ñāṇasaṃyuttā, puññato kriyatopi ca;

Tathābhiññādvayañceva, kriyāvoṭṭhabbanampi ca.

The four wholesome and four functional consciousnesses associated with knowledge; likewise the two direct-knowledge consciousnesses; and the functional determining consciousness:

319.

319.

Ekādasannametesaṃ, tividho hoti gocaro;

Paññattārammaṇattā hi, navattabbāpi hontime.

For these eleven consciousnesses, the object-field is threefold. Because they can have a concept as object, they too are said to be 'not-to-be-specified'.

320.

320.

Yāni vuttāvasesāni, cittāni pana tāni hi;

Navattabbārammaṇānīti, viññeyyāni vibhāvinā.

The remaining consciousnesses that have been mentioned should be understood by the discerning one as having 'not-to-be-specified' objects.

Parittārammaṇattikaṃ samattaṃ.

The Triad on Limited Objects is completed.

321.

321.

Dutiyāruppacittañca[P 0.0045], catutthāruppamānasaṃ;

Chabbidhaṃ pana ekanta-atītārammaṇaṃ siyā.

The six consciousnesses of the second and fourth formless attainments may have an exclusively past object.

322.

322.

Viññāṇānaṃ dvipañcannaṃ, manodhātuttayassa ca;

Pañca rūpādayo dhammā, paccuppannāva gocarā.

For the two pentads of sense consciousnesses and the mind-element-triad, the five objects beginning with visible form are their object-field only in the present.

323.

323.

Aṭṭha [M 0.0058][V 0.0053] kāmamahāpākā, santīraṇattayampi ca;

Hasituppādacittanti, dvādasete tu mānasā.

The eight great sense-sphere resultants, the three investigating consciousnesses, and the smile-producing consciousness—these twelve minds:

324.

324.

Siyātītārammaṇā paccu-ppannānāgatagocarā;

Kusalākusalā kāme, kriyato nava mānasā.

The sense-sphere wholesome and unwholesome consciousnesses, and nine functional minds, may have past, present, or future objects.

325.

325.

Abhiññāmānasā dvepi, siyātītādigocarā;

Santapaññattikālepi, navattabbā bhavantime.

The two direct-knowledge minds may have past, etc., as their object. Since they can also take the Peaceful and concepts as object, they are 'not-to-be-specified'.

326.

326.

Sesāni pana sabbāni, rūpārūpabhavesupi;

Navattabbāni honteva, atītārammaṇādinā.

All the remaining consciousnesses in the form and formless spheres are indeed 'not-to-be-specified' on account of taking past objects and so on.

327.

327.

Kāmato ca kriyā pañca, rūpato pañcamī kriyā;

Cittānaṃ channametesaṃ, natthi kiñci agocaraṃ.

For the five functional consciousnesses from the sense-sphere and the fifth functional consciousness from the form-sphere—for these six consciousnesses—there is nothing that is not their object.

328.

328.

Nibbānañca phalaṃ maggaṃ, rūpañcārūpameva ca;

Sakkonti gocaraṃ kātuṃ, kati cittāni me vada.

Nibbāna, the fruit, the path, and form and the formless as well—tell me, how many consciousnesses are able to take these as their object?

329.

329.

Cattāro ñāṇasaṃyuttā,

Puññato kriyato tathā;

Abhiññāhadayā dvepi,

Kriyā voṭṭhabbanampi ca.

The four wholesome and four functional consciousnesses associated with knowledge; the two direct-knowledge consciousnesses; and the functional determining consciousness.

330.

330.

Sakkonti gocaraṃ kātuṃ, cittānekādasāpi ca;

Nibbānañca phalaṃ maggaṃ, rūpañcārūpameva ca.

These eleven consciousnesses are able to take as their object Nibbāna, the fruit, the path, and form and the formless as well.

331.

331.

Cittesu pana sabbesu, kati cittāni me vada;

Arahattaphalaṃ maggaṃ, kātuṃ sakkonti gocaraṃ.

But among all consciousnesses, tell me, how many are able to take as their object the path and fruit of Arahantship?

332.

332.

Sabbesu pana cittesu, cha ca cittāni me suṇa;

Arahattaphalaṃ maggaṃ, kātuṃ sakkonti gocaraṃ.

But among all consciousnesses, listen to me: six consciousnesses can make the path and fruit of Arahantship their object.

333.

333.

Cattāro ñāṇasaṃyuttā, kriyā voṭṭhabbanampi ca;

Kriyābhiññā manodhātu, cha ca sakkonti gocaraṃ.

The four functional consciousnesses associated with knowledge, the functional determining consciousness, and the functional direct-knowledge consciousness: these six are able to take it as their object.

334.

334.

Cattāro [M 0.0059][V 0.0054] ñāṇasaṃyuttā-bhiññācittañca puññato;

Nārahattaṃ phalaṃ maggaṃ, kātuṃ sakkonti gocaraṃ.

The four wholesome consciousnesses associated with knowledge and the wholesome direct-knowledge consciousness are not able to take the path and fruit of Arahantship as their object.

335.

335.

Kasmā arahato magga-cittaṃ vā phalamānasaṃ;

Puthujjanā vā sekkhā vā, na sakkonti hi jānituṃ.

Why is it that the path-consciousness or the fruit-consciousness of an Arahant cannot be known by ordinary people or trainees?

336.

336.

Puthujjano na jānāti,

Sotāpannassa mānasaṃ;

Sotāpanno na jānāti,

Sakadāgāmissa mānasaṃ.

A worldling does not know the mind of a stream-enterer; a stream-enterer does not know the mind of a once-returner.

337.

337.

Sakadāgāmī na jānāti, anāgāmissa mānasaṃ;

Anāgāmī na jānāti, arahantassa mānasaṃ.

A once-returner does not know the mind of a non-returner; a non-returner does not know the mind of an Arahant.

338.

338.

Heṭṭhimo [P 0.0046] heṭṭhimo neva, jānāti uparūpari;

Uparūpari jānāti, heṭṭhimassa ca mānasaṃ.

One on a lower stage never knows the mind of one on a higher stage, but one on a higher stage knows the mind of one on a lower stage.

339.

339.

Yo dhammo yassa dhammassa,

Hoti ārammaṇaṃ pana;

Tamuddharitvā ekekaṃ,

Pavakkhāmi ito paraṃ.

Hereafter I shall explain, taking them up one by one, which state becomes an object for which other state.

340.

340.

Kusalārammaṇaṃ kāme, kusalākusalassa ca;

Abhiññāmānasassāpi, kusalassa kriyassa ca.

Sense-sphere wholesome consciousness can be an object for wholesome and unwholesome consciousness, for the wholesome and functional direct-knowledge consciousness,

341.

341.

Kāmāvacarapākassa, tathā kāmakriyassa ca;

Etesaṃ pana rāsīnaṃ, channaṃ ārammaṇaṃ siyā.

and for sense-sphere resultant and functional consciousness. Thus it may be an object for these six classes of consciousness.

342.

342.

Rūpāvacarapuññāni, kāmapākaṃ tato vinā;

Pañcannaṃ pana rāsīnaṃ, honti ārammaṇāni hi.

Form-sphere wholesome consciousness can become an object for five classes of consciousness, that is, for the previous six excluding sense-sphere resultant consciousness.

343.

343.

Āruppakusalañcāpi, tebhūmakusalassa ca;

Tebhūmakakriyassāpi, tathevākusalassapi.

Formless-sphere wholesome consciousness can become an object for wholesome consciousness of the three planes, for functional consciousness of the three planes, for unwholesome consciousness,

344.

344.

Arūpāvacarapākānaṃ[M 0.0060][V 0.0055], dvinnaṃ pana catutthadu;

Imesaṃ aṭṭharāsīnaṃ, hotārammaṇapaccayo.

and for the second and fourth formless resultant consciousnesses. Thus it is an object-condition for these eight classes.

345.

345.

Apariyāpannapuññampi, kāmāvacaratopi ca;

Rūpato pañcamassāpi, kusalassa kriyassa ca.

Supramundane wholesome consciousness can be an object for sense-sphere wholesome and functional consciousness, and for the wholesome and functional consciousness of the fifth form-sphere jhāna.

346.

346.

Catunnaṃ pana rāsīnaṃ, hoti ārammaṇaṃ sadā;

Tathevākusalaṃ kāma-rūpāvacarato pana.

It is always an object for these four classes. Likewise, unwholesome consciousness can be an object for sense-sphere and form-sphere wholesome and functional consciousness,

347.

347.

Kusalassa kriyassāpi, tathevākusalassa ca;

Kāmāvacarapākānaṃ, channaṃ rāsīnamīritaṃ.

for unwholesome consciousness, and for sense-sphere resultant consciousness. It is said to be an object for these six classes.

348.

348.

Vipākārammaṇaṃ kāme, kāmāvacaratopi ca;

Rūpāvacarato ceva, kusalassa kriyassa ca.

Sense-sphere resultant consciousness can be an object for sense-sphere and form-sphere wholesome and functional consciousness,

349.

349.

Kāmāvacarapākānaṃ, tathevākusalassa ca;

Channañca pana rāsīnaṃ, hotārammaṇapaccayo.

for sense-sphere resultant consciousness, and for unwholesome consciousness. It is an object-condition for these six classes.

350.

350.

Vipākārammaṇaṃ rūpe, kāmāvacaratopi ca;

Rūpāvacarato ceva, kusalassa kriyassa ca.

Form-sphere resultant consciousness can be an object for sense-sphere and form-sphere wholesome and functional consciousness,

351.

351.

Apuññassāti pañcannaṃ, rāsīnaṃ hoti gocaro;

Arūpāvacarapākesu, ayameva nayo mato.

and for unwholesome consciousness. It is an object for these five classes. This same method is to be applied to the formless-sphere resultants.

352.

352.

Apariyāpannapākampi, kāmato rūpatopi ca;

Kusalassa kriyassāpi, hoti ārammaṇaṃ pana.

Supramundane resultant consciousness can be an object for sense-sphere and form-sphere wholesome and functional consciousness.

353.

353.

Kriyacittamidaṃ kāme, kāmāvacaratopi ca;

Rūpāvacarato ceva, kusalassa kriyassa ca.

Sense-sphere functional consciousness can be an object for sense-sphere and form-sphere wholesome and functional consciousness,

354.

354.

Kāmāvacarapākassa, tathevākusalassa ca;

Channaṃ rāsīnametesaṃ, hotārammaṇapaccayo.

for sense-sphere resultant consciousness, and for unwholesome consciousness. It is an object-condition for these six classes.

355.

355.

Yaṃ [M 0.0061] kriyāmānasaṃ rūpe, kāmapākaṃ tato vinā;

Pañcannaṃ pana rāsīnaṃ, hoti ārammaṇaṃ pana.

Form-sphere functional consciousness can be an object for five classes of consciousness, that is, for the previous six excluding sense-sphere resultant consciousness.

356.

356.

Kriyācittaṃ [P 0.0047][V 0.0056] panāruppe, tesaṃ pañcannameva ca;

Āruppassa kriyassāpi, channaṃ hoteva gocaro.

Formless-sphere functional consciousness can be an object for those same five classes and also for formless functional consciousness. Thus it is an object for six classes.

357.

357.

Rūpaṃ catusamuṭṭhānaṃ, rūpārammaṇasaññitaṃ;

Kāmāvacarapuññassa, tatheva kusalassa ca.

Material form of fourfold origin can be an object for sense-sphere wholesome and unwholesome consciousness,

358.

358.

Abhiññādvayacittassa, kāmapākakriyassa ca;

Channaṃ rāsīnametesaṃ, hotārammaṇapaccayo.

It is an object-condition for these six classes: for the two direct-knowledge consciousnesses, and for the sense-sphere resultant and functional consciousness.

359.

359.

Nibbānārammaṇaṃ kāma-rūpāvacarato pana;

Kusalassubhayassāpi, kāmarūpakriyassa ca.

Nibbāna can be an object for wholesome consciousness of both the sense-sphere and form-sphere, and for functional consciousness of the sense-sphere and form-sphere.

360.

360.

Apariyāpannato ceva, phalassa kusalassa ca;

Channaṃ rāsīnametesaṃ, hotārammaṇapaccayo.

And for the unincluded, and for the fruit and the wholesome, it is an object-condition for these six classes.

361.

361.

Nānappakārakaṃ sabbaṃ, paññattārammaṇaṃ pana;

Tebhūmakassa puññassa, tathevākusalassa ca.

The concept as object, being of all various kinds, is for the wholesome of the three planes, and likewise for the unwholesome.

362.

362.

Rūpārūpavipākassa, tebhūmakakriyassa ca;

Navannaṃ pana rāsīnaṃ, hotārammaṇapaccayo.

For the form-sphere and formless-sphere resultant, and for the three-plane functional; for these nine classes, it is an object-condition.

363.

363.

Rūpārammaṇikā dve tu, dve dve saddhādigocarā;

Pañcārammaṇikā nāma, cittuppādā tayo matā.

Two [consciousnesses] have form as their object, two each have sound and so forth as their domain; three arisings of consciousness are known as having the five sense-objects.

364.

364.

Idhekacattālīseva, chaḷārammaṇikā matā;

Kāmāvacaracittāna-mayamārammaṇakkamo.

Here indeed forty-one are understood as having six objects; this is the system of objects for sense-sphere consciousnesses.

365.

365.

Pañcābhiññā vivajjetvā, rūpārūpā anāsavā;

Cittuppādā ime sabbe, dhammārammaṇagocarā.

Excluding the five superknowledges, all these form-sphere, formless-sphere, and taintless arisings of consciousness have Dhamma as their object and domain.

366.

366.

Paṭhamāruppakusalaṃ, dutiyāruppacetaso;

Kusalassa vipākassa, kriyassārammaṇaṃ bhave.

The first formless wholesome consciousness can be the object for the second formless consciousness, whether wholesome, resultant, or functional.

367.

367.

Paṭhamāruppapākoyaṃ[M 0.0062], dutiyāruppacetaso;

Kusalassa vipākassa, kriyassārammaṇaṃ na hi.

This first formless resultant consciousness is indeed not the object for the second formless consciousness, be it wholesome, resultant, or functional.

368.

368.

Paṭhamaṃ [V 0.0057] tu kriyācittaṃ, dutiyāruppacetaso;

Na puññassa na pākassa, hoti ārammaṇaṃ pana.

The first functional consciousness, however, is not an object for a second formless consciousness that is wholesome or resultant.

369.

369.

Paṭhamaṃ tu kriyācittaṃ, dutiyāruppacetaso;

Kriyassārammaṇaṃ hoti, iti ñeyyaṃ vibhāvinā.

But the first functional consciousness is an object for a second formless consciousness that is functional; thus it should be understood by the discerning.

370.

370.

Puthujjanassa sekkhassa, arūpārammaṇaṃ dvidhā;

Kusalaṃ kusalassāpi, vipākassa ca taṃ siyā.

For the ordinary person and the learner, the formless object is twofold: a wholesome [consciousness] serves as an object for a wholesome and also for a resultant [consciousness].

371.

371.

Khīṇāsavassa bhikkhussa, paṭhamāruppamānasaṃ;

Ārammaṇaṃ tidhā hoti, iti vuttaṃ mahesinā.

For a monk whose taints are destroyed, the first formless consciousness is threefold as an object; so it was said by the great seer.

372.

372.

Kriyassāpi kriyā hoti, kusalampi kriyassa ca;

Kusalaṃ tu vipākassa, evaṃ hoti tidhā pana.

A functional [consciousness] is for a functional; a wholesome is also for a functional; and a wholesome is for a resultant. Thus, it is threefold.

373.

373.

Tatiyāruppacittampi, catutthāruppacetaso;

Evameva dvidhā ceva, tidhā cārammaṇaṃ siyā.

Likewise, the third formless consciousness, as an object for the fourth formless consciousness, may be twofold or threefold.

374.

374.

Yaṃ yaṃ pana idhārabbha,

Ye ye jāyanti gocaraṃ;

So so tesañca tesañca,

Hotārammaṇapaccayo.

Whatever object is taken up here, and whatever [consciousnesses] arise in relation to it, that very object is the object-condition for each and every one of them.

375.

375.

Yo [P 0.0048] panimassa naro kira pāraṃ,

Duttaramuttaramuttaratīdha;

So abhidhammamahaṇṇavapāraṃ,

Duttaramuttaramuttarateva.

Whatever man, it is said, crosses here to the further shore, difficult to cross and ever higher; he indeed crosses to the further shore of the great ocean of Abhidhamma, difficult to cross and ever higher.

Iti abhidhammāvatāre ārammaṇavibhāgo nāma

Thus in the Abhidhammāvatāra ends the chapter named the Analysis of Objects.

Chaṭṭho paricchedo.

The Sixth Chapter.

7. Sattamo paricchedo

7. The Seventh Chapter

Vipākacittappavattiniddeso

Exposition of the Occurrence of Resultant Consciousness

376.

376.

Anantañāṇena [M 0.0063][P 0.0049][V 0.0058] niraṅgaṇena,

Guṇesinā kāruṇikena tena;

Vutte vipāke matipāṭavatthaṃ,

Vipākacittappabhavaṃ suṇātha.

By him of infinite wisdom, unstained, compassionate, and seeking virtues; for the sake of mental dexterity regarding the resultants that have been spoken of, listen to the arising of resultant consciousness.

377.

377.

Ekūnatiṃsa kammāni, pākā dvattiṃsa dassitā;

Tīsu dvāresu kammāni, vipākā chasu dissare.

Twenty-nine kammas are shown, thirty-two resultants are indicated; kammas are performed through three doors, resultants appear in six.

378.

378.

Kusalaṃ kāmalokasmiṃ, pavatte paṭisandhiyaṃ;

Taṃ taṃ paccayamāgamma, dadāti vividhaṃ phalaṃ.

A wholesome kamma in the sense-sphere, in the course of existence and at rebirth-linking, depending on various conditions, yields diverse fruits.

379.

379.

Ekāya cetanāyekā, paṭisandhi pakāsitā;

Nānākammehi nānā ca, bhavanti paṭisandhiyo.

By a single volition, one rebirth-linking is declared; by various kammas, various rebirth-linkings come to be.

380.

380.

Tihetukaṃ tu yaṃ kammaṃ, kāmāvacarasaññitaṃ;

Tihetukaṃ duhetuñca, vipākaṃ detyahetukaṃ.

A three-rooted kamma, known as belonging to the sense-sphere, gives a three-rooted, a two-rooted, and a rootless resultant.

381.

381.

Duhetukaṃ tu yaṃ kammaṃ, taṃ na deti tihetukaṃ;

Duhetukamahetuñca, vipākaṃ deti attano.

A two-rooted kamma, however, does not yield a three-rooted resultant; it yields its own two-rooted and rootless resultant.

382.

382.

Tihetukena kammena,

Paṭisandhi tihetukā;

Duhetukāpi hoteva,

Na ca hoti ahetukā.

By a three-rooted kamma, rebirth-linking is three-rooted; it may also be two-rooted, but it is never rootless.

383.

383.

Duhetukena kammena,

Paṭisandhi duhetukā;

Ahetukāpi [V 0.0059] hoteva,

Na ca hoti tihetukā.

By a two-rooted kamma, rebirth-linking is two-rooted; it may also be rootless, but it is never three-rooted.

384.

384.

Asaṅkhāramasaṅkhāraṃ[M 0.0064], sasaṅkhārampi deti hi;

Sasaṅkhāramasaṅkhāraṃ, sasaṅkhāraṃ phalaṃ tathā.

Unprompted kamma indeed yields an unprompted and also a prompted result; prompted kamma yields an unprompted result, and likewise a prompted fruit.

385.

385.

Ekāya cetanāyettha, kusalassa ca soḷasa;

Vidhā vipākacittāni, bhavantīti pakāsaye.

Here, it is explained that from a single wholesome volition, sixteen types of resultant consciousnesses arise.

386.

386.

Ārammaṇena hoteva, vedanāparivattanaṃ;

Tadārammaṇacittampi, javanena niyāmitaṃ.

The change of feeling is indeed by the object; the tadārammaṇa-consciousness is also determined by the impulsion.

387.

387.

Kāmāvacaracittena, kusalenādinā pana;

Tulyena pākacittena, gahitā paṭisandhi ce.

If, however, rebirth-linking is taken up by a resultant consciousness of the same kind as a wholesome, or the like, sense-sphere consciousness...

388.

388.

Balavārammaṇe [P 0.0050] iṭṭhe, cakkhussāpāthamāgate;

Manodhātu bhavaṅgasmiṃ, tāya āvaṭṭite pana.

When a powerful, desirable object has come within range of the eye, and the mind-element has then adverted from the life-continuum on account of it...

389.

389.

Vīthicittesu jātesu, cakkhuviññāṇakādisu;

Jāyate javanaṃ hutvā, paṭhamaṃ kāmamānasaṃ.

When process-consciousnesses, such as eye-consciousness and so on, have arisen, the first sense-sphere consciousness arises as impulsion.

390.

390.

Sattakkhattuṃ javitvāna, paṭhame kusale gate;

Tadevārammaṇaṃ katvā, teneva sadisaṃ puna.

Having sped seven times, when the first wholesome impulsion has passed, making that same object its basis, again similar to it...

391.

391.

Vipākaṃ jāyate cittaṃ, tadārammaṇasaññitaṃ;

Sandhiyā tulyato mūla-bhavaṅganti pavuccate.

A resultant consciousness arises, known as 'tadārammaṇa'; because of its similarity to the rebirth-linking, it is called the root-life-continuum.

392.

392.

Tañca santīraṇaṃ ettha, dassanaṃ sampaṭicchanaṃ;

Gaṇanūpagacittāni, cattāreva bhavanti hi.

And here, the investigating, seeing, and receiving consciousnesses that enter into the calculation are indeed only four.

393.

393.

Yadā hi dutiyaṃ cittaṃ, kusalaṃ javanaṃ tadā;

Tena tulyavipākampi, tadārammaṇakaṃ siyā.

For when the second wholesome impulsion arises, then a resultant consciousness similar to it may become a tadārammaṇa.

394.

394.

Sandhiyā asamānattā, dve nāmānissa labbhare;

“Āgantukabhavaṅga”nti, “tadārammaṇaka”nti ca.

Due to its dissimilarity to the rebirth-linking, two names are obtained for it: 'adventitious life-continuum' and 'tadārammaṇa'.

395.

395.

Yadā [M 0.0065][V 0.0060] hi tatiyaṃ puññaṃ, javanaṃ hoti tena ca;

Sadisaṃ tatiyaṃ pākaṃ, tadārammaṇakaṃ siyā.

For when the third wholesome impulsion arises, then a similar third resultant consciousness may become a tadārammaṇa.

396.

396.

“Āgantukabhavaṅga”nti, idampi ca pavuccati;

Iminā pana saddhiṃ cha, purimāni ca pañcapi.

This too is called 'adventitious life-continuum'; with this one, there are now six, including the preceding five.

397.

397.

Yadā catutthaṃ kusalaṃ, javanaṃ hoti tena ca;

Tulyaṃ catutthaṃ pākaṃ tu, tadārammaṇataṃ vaje.

When the fourth wholesome impulsion arises, then a fourth resultant consciousness equal to it attains the state of tadārammaṇa.

398.

398.

Āgantukabhavaṅgaṃ tu, tadārammaṇanāmakaṃ;

Purimāni cha pākāni, iminā honti satta tu.

The adventitious life-continuum, named tadārammaṇa; with this one, the previous six resultant states become seven.

399.

399.

Tasmiṃ dvāre yadā iṭṭha-majjhattārammaṇaṃ pana;

Āgacchati tadāpāthaṃ, tadā vuttanayenidha.

When at that door a desirable-neutral object comes into range, then here the process proceeds by the method already explained.

400.

400.

Ārammaṇavaseneva, vedanā parivattati;

Upekkhāsahitaṃ tasmā, hoti santīraṇaṃ mano.

Feeling changes according to the object; therefore, the investigating mind is accompanied by equanimity.

401.

401.

Upekkhāsahitesveva, javanesu catūsupi;

Tehi tulyāni cattāri, pākacittāni jāyare.

From the four impulsions accompanied by equanimity, four resultant consciousnesses equal to them arise.

402.

402.

Vedanāyāsamānattā, accantaṃ purimehi tu;

Honti piṭṭhibhavaṅgāni, cattārīti ca nāmato.

Due to the complete dissimilarity of feeling from the preceding ones, there are, by name, four posterior life-continuum consciousnesses.

403.

403.

Pañcimāni vipākāni, purimehi ca sattahi;

Saddhiṃ dvādasa pākāni, bhavantīti viniddise.

It should be pointed out that these five resultant states, together with the previous seven, become twelve resultant states.

404.

404.

Cakkhudvāre tathā evaṃ, sotādīsvapi niddise;

Dvādasa dvādasa pākā, samasaṭṭhi bhavantime.

Likewise at the eye-door, so too should it be indicated for the ear-door and others; twelve resultant states for each, these become sixty in total.

405.

405.

Ekāya cetanāyeva, kamme āyūhite pana;

Samasaṭṭhi vipākāni, uppajjanti na saṃsayo.

When an action has been set in motion by a single volition, sixty resultant states arise without a doubt.

406.

406.

Gahitāgahaṇenettha[M 0.0066][P 0.0051], cakkhudvāresu dvādasa;

Sotaviññāṇakādīni, cattārīti ca soḷasa.

Here, by way of being grasped and not grasped, there are twelve at the eye-door; ear-consciousness and the like are four, thus making sixteen.

407.

407.

Evameva [V 0.0061] sasaṅkhāra-tihetukusalenapi;

Asaṅkhārasasaṅkhāru-pekkhāsahagatehipi.

Even so, by prompted three-rooted wholesome actions, and by unprompted and prompted actions accompanied by equanimity.

408.

408.

Kamme āyūhite tesaṃ, vipākehi ca tīhipi;

Eseva ca nayo tehi, dinnāya paṭisandhiyā.

When that action is set in motion, this same method applies to their three types of resultants and to the rebirth-linking given by them.

409.

409.

Paṭhamaṃ iṭṭhamajjhatta-gocarassa vasenidha;

Pavattiṃ pana dassetvā, upekkhāsahitadvaye.

First, having here shown the occurrence by way of the desirable-neutral object, then in the pair accompanied by equanimity...

410.

410.

Dassetabbā tappacchā tu, iṭṭhasmiṃ gocare idha;

Ekekasmiṃ pana dvāre, dvādasa dvādaseva tu.

Thereafter, they should be shown here in the case of a desirable object; indeed, twelve at each single door, twelve each.

411.

411.

Gahitāgahaṇenettha, pākacittāni soḷasa;

Pubbe vuttanayeneva, ñeyyaṃ sabbamasesato.

Here, the sixteen resultant consciousnesses, by way of being grasped and not grasped, should all be known completely by the method previously explained.

412.

412.

Tihetukena kammena, paṭisandhi tihetukā;

Bhavatīti ayaṃ vāro, vutto ettāvatā mayā.

That by a three-rooted action, rebirth-linking is three-rooted—this section has been spoken by me thus far.

413.

413.

Sandhimekaṃ tu kammekaṃ, janeti na tato paraṃ;

Anekāni vipākāni, sañjaneti pavattiyaṃ.

One action produces one rebirth-linking, no more than that; but in the course of existence, it generates many resultant states.

414.

414.

Ekasmā hi yathā bījā, jāyate ekamaṅkuraṃ;

Subahūni phalānissa, honti hetupavattito.

Just as from a single seed a single sprout is born, so from that many fruits arise due to the proceeding of causes.

415.

415.

Duhetukena kammena, paṭisandhi duhetukā;

Hotīti hi ayaṃ vāro, anupubbena āgato.

By a two-rooted kamma, rebirth-linking is two-rooted; thus this section has come in due sequence.

416.

416.

Duhetukena kammena, somanassayutenidha;

Asaṅkhārikacittena, kamme āyūhite pana.

Here, when kamma has been accumulated by a two-rooted, unprompted consciousness accompanied by joy.

417.

417.

Tena [M 0.0067] tulyena pākena, gahitā paṭisandhi ce;

Iṭṭhe ārammaṇe cakkhu-dvāre āpāthamāgate.

If rebirth-linking is taken by a resultant state similar to that, when a desirable object has come into range at the eye-door.

418.

418.

Somanassayute ñāṇa-hīne kusalamānase;

Sattakkhattuṃ javitvāna, gate tasmiṃ duhetuke.

When that two-rooted wholesome consciousness, accompanied by joy and devoid of knowledge, having sped seven times, has passed.

419.

419.

Tadevārammaṇaṃ [V 0.0062] katvā, jāyate tadanantaraṃ;

Taṃsarikkhakamekaṃ tu, asaṅkhārikamānasaṃ.

Taking that very same object, there arises immediately after, one unprompted consciousness similar to that.

420.

420.

Taṃ hi mūlabhavaṅganti, tadārammaṇamiccapi;

Ubhayampi ca tasseva, nāmanti paridīpitaṃ.

That, indeed, is called 'root bhavaṅga' and also 'tadārammaṇa'; it has been explained that both are names for that very same thing.

421.

421.

Duhetukasasaṅkhāre, javitepi ca taṃsamaṃ;

Hotāgantukasaṅkhātaṃ, tadārammaṇamānasaṃ.

And also when a two-rooted prompted javana has sped, a tadārammaṇa consciousness similar to it arises, which is designated 'adventitious'.

422.

422.

Tatheva ca duhetūnaṃ, iṭṭhamajjhattagocare;

Dvinnaṃ upekkhāyuttānaṃ, javanānamanantaraṃ.

And just so, immediately after the two two-rooted javanas accompanied by equanimity, which have a desirable-neutral object.

423.

423.

Dve tādisāni jāyante, tadārammaṇamānasā;

Tesaṃ “piṭṭhibhavaṅga”nti, nāmaṃ “āgantuka”nti ca.

Two such tadārammaṇa consciousnesses arise; their names are 'posterior bhavaṅga' and also 'adventitious'.

424.

424.

Santīraṇadvayañceva, dassanaṃ sampaṭicchanaṃ;

Imāni ca bhavaṅgāni, cakkhudvāre panaṭṭha hi.

The two investigating, seeing, and receiving consciousnesses, and these bhavaṅgas; indeed, there are eight such resultant states at the eye-door.

425.

425.

Evamaṭṭhaṭṭha [P 0.0052] katvāna, dvāresupi ca pañcasu;

Cattālīsa vipākāni, bhavantīti pavattiyaṃ.

Thus, taking eight for each of the five doors, it is said that forty resultant states arise in the course of existence.

426.

426.

Gahitāgahaṇenettha, cakkhudvāre panaṭṭha ca;

Sotaghānādinā saddhiṃ, dvādaseva bhavanti hi.

Here, by the method of inclusion and exclusion, the eight at the eye-door, together with those of the ear, nose, and so on, indeed become twelve.

427.

427.

Ekāya cetanāyevaṃ, kamme āyūhite pana;

Dvādaseva vipākāni, bhavantīti pakāsitaṃ.

Thus, when kamma is accumulated by a single volition, it is explained that twelve resultant states arise.

428.

428.

Duhetukattayenāpi[M 0.0068], sesena sadisena tu;

Pākenādinnasandhiyā, ayameva nayo mato.

This same method is to be understood also for the three two-rooted kammas and for the remainder in a similar way, in the case of a rebirth-linking given by a resultant state.

429.

429.

Duhetukena kammena, paṭisandhi duhetukā;

Hotītipi ayaṃ vāro, vutto ettāvatā mayā.

That 'by a two-rooted kamma, rebirth-linking is two-rooted'—this section has thus far been spoken by me.

430.

430.

Duhetukena kammena, paṭisandhi ahetukā;

Hotīti ca ayaṃ vāro, anupubbena āgato.

And that 'by a two-rooted kamma, rebirth-linking is rootless'—this section has now come in due sequence.

431.

431.

Duhetukesu [V 0.0063] cittesu, kusalesu catūsupi;

Tesu aññatareneva, kamme āyūhite pana.

When kamma has been accumulated by any one of those four two-rooted wholesome consciousnesses.

432.

432.

Tasseva pākabhūtāya, ādinnapaṭisandhino;

Upekkhāsahitāhetu, manoviññāṇadhātuyā.

For one who has taken rebirth-linking by means of the rootless mind-consciousness-element accompanied by equanimity, which is the result of that very kamma.

433.

433.

Paṭisandhi na vattabbā, sā kammasadisāti hi;

Kammaṃ duhetukaṃ hoti, paṭisandhi ahetukā.

The rebirth-linking should not be said to be similar to the kamma; for the kamma is two-rooted, while the rebirth-linking is rootless.

434.

434.

Tassa buddhimupetassa, iṭṭhamajjhattagocare;

Āpāthamāgate cakkhu-dvāre puna ca dehino.

And again, for that embodied being who has become conscious, when a desirable-neutral object has come into range at the eye-door.

435.

435.

Duhetūnaṃ catunnampi, puññānaṃ yassa kassaci;

Javanassāvasānasmiṃ, ahetukamidaṃ mano.

At the end of the impulsion of any one of the four two-rooted meritorious consciousnesses, this mind is rootless.

436.

436.

Tadārammaṇabhāvena, jāyate natthi saṃsayo;

Taṃ tu mūlabhavaṅgañca, tadārammaṇameva ca.

It arises as tadārammaṇa, there is no doubt; and that is both the root-bhavaṅga and the tadārammaṇa itself.

437.

437.

Vīthicittesu jātesu, cakkhuviññāṇakādisu;

Upekkhāsahitaṃyeva, hoti santīraṇampi ca.

When process-consciousnesses, such as eye-consciousness and so on, have arisen, the investigating consciousness is also only accompanied by equanimity.

438.

438.

Tesu ekaṃ ṭhapetvāna, gahitāgahaṇenidha;

Gaṇanūpagacittāni, tīṇiyeva bhavanti hi.

Here, having excluded one among them by the method of inclusion and exclusion, the consciousnesses that enter the calculation are indeed only three.

439.

439.

Iṭṭhe [M 0.0069] ārammaṇe cakkhu-dvāre āpāthamāgate;

Tadā santīraṇañceva, tadārammaṇamānasaṃ.

When a desirable object has come into range at the eye-door, then the investigating consciousness and the tadārammaṇa consciousness arise.

440.

440.

Somanassayutaṃyeva, gahetvā tesu ekakaṃ;

Purimāni ca tīṇīti, cattārova bhavanti hi.

Taking just one of them—the one accompanied by joy—along with the previous three, they indeed become four.

441.

441.

Evaṃ cattāri cittāni, dvāresupi ca pañcasu;

Honti vīsati cittāni, vipākāni pavattiyaṃ.

Thus, there being four consciousnesses in each of the five doors, there are twenty resultant consciousnesses in the course of existence.

442.

442.

Cakkhudvāre tu cattāri, gahitāgahaṇenidha;

Sotaghānādinā saddhiṃ, hotevāhetukaṭṭhakaṃ.

Here, by the method of inclusion and exclusion, the four in the eye-door, together with those of the ear, nose, and so on, indeed constitute the rootless octad.

443.

443.

Ahetupaṭisandhissa[V 0.0064], na tadārammaṇaṃ bhave;

Duhetukaṃ tihetuṃ vā, duhetupaṭisandhino.

For one with a rootless rebirth-linking, there would be no tadārammaṇa; for one with a two-rooted rebirth-linking, it may be two-rooted or three-rooted.

444.

444.

Jātā [P 0.0053] sugatiyaṃ yena, pākena paṭisandhi tu;

Tena tulyampi hīnaṃ vā, tadārammaṇakaṃ bhave.

For one whose rebirth-linking has arisen in a happy realm by whatever result, the tadārammaṇa may be equal to or inferior to that.

445.

445.

Manussalokaṃ sandhāya, vuttañcāhetukaṭṭhakaṃ;

Catūsupi apāyesu, pavatte pana labbhati.

The eight rootless consciousnesses are mentioned with reference to the human world, but they are found occurring in the cognitive process in all four woeful realms.

446.

446.

Thero nerayikānaṃ tu, dhammaṃ deseti vassati;

Gandhaṃ vāyuñca māpeti, yadā tesaṃ tadā pana.

The elder teaches the Dhamma to the hell-beings; and when it rains, he then creates fragrance and wind for them.

447.

447.

Theraṃ disvā ca sutvā ca, dhammaṃ gandhañca ghāyataṃ;

Pivatañca jalaṃ vāyuṃ, phusataṃ mudumeva ca.

Seeing the Elder, hearing the Dhamma, smelling the fragrance, drinking water, and feeling the soft wind.

448.

448.

Cakkhuviññāṇakādīni, puññajāneva pañcapi;

Santīraṇadvayaṃ ekā, manodhātūti aṭṭhakaṃ.

Eye-consciousness and the like, the five born of merit; the two investigating consciousnesses and one mind-element—thus the eight.

449.

449.

Ayaṃ tāva kathā iṭṭha-iṭṭhamajjhattagocare;

Kāmāvacarapuññānaṃ, javanānaṃ vasenidha.

This discussion so far concerns agreeable and agreeable-neutral objects; here, it is by way of the javanas of sense-sphere meritorious kamma.

450.

450.

Niyamatthaṃ [M 0.0070] tu yaṃ vuttaṃ, tadārammaṇacetaso;

Kusalaṃ pana sandhāya, taṃ vuttanti hi dīpitaṃ.

Whatever was stated for the sake of certainty concerning the tadārammaṇa consciousness, it is shown that this was stated with reference to the wholesome.

451.

451.

Idhākusalacittesu, somanassayutesupi;

Iṭṭhe ārammaṇe tesu, javitesu catūsupi.

Here, when the four unwholesome consciousnesses accompanied by joy have impelled regarding an agreeable object.

452.

452.

Somanassayutāhetu-manoviññāṇadhātu hi;

Tadārammaṇabhāvena, jāyate tadanantaraṃ.

The rootless mind-consciousness-element accompanied by joy indeed arises immediately thereafter as tadārammaṇa.

453.

453.

Chasvākusalacittesu, upekkhāya yutesu hi;

Gocare iṭṭhamajjhatte, javitesu anantaraṃ.

When the six unwholesome consciousnesses accompanied by equanimity have impelled regarding an agreeable-neutral object, immediately thereafter.

454.

454.

Upekkhāsahitāhetu-manoviññāṇadhātu hi;

Tadārammaṇabhāvena, jāyate pana puññajā.

Then the rootless mind-consciousness-element accompanied by equanimity, born of merit, arises as tadārammaṇa.

455.

455.

Iṭṭhārammaṇayogasmiṃ[V 0.0065], kaṅkhato uddhatassa vā;

Somanassayutaṃ hoti, tadārammaṇamānasaṃ.

When there is connection with a desirable object, for one who is doubting or restless, the tadārammaṇa consciousness is accompanied by joy.

456.

456.

Somanassayute citte, javane javite pana;

Gavesitabbā pañceva, tadārammaṇamānasā.

When the javana consciousness accompanied by joy has impelled, then five tadārammaṇa consciousnesses should be sought.

457.

457.

Upekkhāsahite citte, javane javite pana;

Chaḷeva gavesitabbā, tadārammaṇamānasā.

When the javana consciousness accompanied by equanimity has impelled, then six tadārammaṇa consciousnesses should be sought.

458.

458.

Tihetusomanassena, ādinnapaṭisandhino;

Jhānato parihīnassa, taṃ jhānaṃ paccavekkhato.

For one who has taken rebirth-linking with a three-rooted joyful consciousness, who has declined from jhāna, while reflecting upon that jhāna.

459.

459.

Domanassayutaṃ cittaṃ, hoti vippaṭisārino;

Tassa kiṃ jāyate brūhi, tadārammaṇamānasaṃ.

The mind of one with remorse is accompanied by displeasure. Tell me, what tadārammaṇa consciousness arises for him?

460.

460.

Paṭṭhāne paṭisiddhā hi, domanassaanantaraṃ;

Somanassassa uppatti, domanassassa cassa vā.

For in the Paṭṭhāna, the arising of joy or of displeasure immediately after displeasure is refuted.

461.

461.

Mahaggataṃ [M 0.0071] panārabbha, javane javitepi ca;

Tattheva paṭisiddhaṃ tu, tadārammaṇamānasaṃ.

But concerning an exalted object, even when the javana has impelled, the tadārammaṇa consciousness is indeed refuted there.

462.

462.

Tasmā [P 0.0054] bhavaṅgapātova, tadārammaṇameva vā;

Na hoti kiṃ nu kātabbaṃ, vada tvaṃ ābhidhammika.

Therefore, there is only a falling into bhavaṅga, and tadārammaṇa does not occur at all. What, then, is to be done? Tell me, O Abhidhammika.

463.

463.

Upekkhāsahitāhetu-manoviññāṇadhātu tu;

Puññāpuññavipākā hi, tadārammaṇikā siyā.

But the rootless mind-consciousness-element accompanied by equanimity, being the result of wholesome or unwholesome kamma, could indeed be the tadārammaṇa.

464.

464.

Āvajjanaṃ kimassāti, natthi taṃ jāyate kathaṃ;

Bhavaṅgāvajjanānaṃ kiṃ, maggassānantarassa ca.

What is its adverting? There is none. How then does it arise? What of bhavaṅga and adverting, and of the path and its immediate successor?

465.

465.

Phalassapi nirodhā ca, vuṭṭhahantassa bhikkhuno;

Phalacittassa vā evaṃ, natthi āvajjanaṃ kira.

For a bhikkhu emerging from the attainment of cessation or from the fruition consciousness, there is, it seems, no adverting.

466.

466.

Vinā āvajjanenāpi, hoti jāyatu mānasaṃ;

Kimassārammaṇaṃ brūhi, yadi jānāsi paṇḍita.

Let consciousness arise even without adverting. But tell me, what is its object, if you know, O wise one?

467.

467.

Vinā [V 0.0066] ārammaṇeneva, na hi jāyati mānasaṃ;

Rūpādīsu parittesu, yaṃ kiñcārabbha jāyate.

Indeed, consciousness does not arise without an object; it arises in dependence on some limited thing among forms and so on.

468.

468.

Utubījaniyāmo ca, kammadhammaniyāmatā;

Cittassa ca niyāmoti, ñeyyā pañca niyāmatā.

The fixed order of seasons, the fixed order of seeds, the fixed order of kamma, the fixed order of Dhamma, and the fixed order of consciousness—these five fixed orders should be known.

469.

469.

Tattha ekappahārena, phalapupphādidhāraṇaṃ;

Rukkhānaṃ pana sabbesaṃ, ayaṃ utuniyāmatā.

Therein, the bearing of fruits, flowers, and so on by all trees at once—this is the fixed order of seasons.

470.

470.

Tesaṃ tesaṃ tu bījānaṃ, taṃtaṃtulyaphalubbhavo;

Matthake nāḷikerassa, chiddattaṃ bījajo ayaṃ.

The arising of a fruit corresponding to each and every seed, and the hole at the top of a coconut—this is the fixed order of seeds.

471.

471.

Tihetukaṃ tihetuñca, duhetuñca ahetukaṃ;

Vipākaṃ tu yato deti, ayaṃ kammaniyāmatā.

That kamma gives a three-rooted, two-rooted, or rootless result—this is the fixed order of kamma.

472.

472.

Jātiyaṃ [M 0.0072] bodhisattassa, medanīkampanādikaṃ;

Visesattamanekampi, ayaṃ dhammaniyāmatā.

At the birth of the Bodhisatta, the trembling of the earth and so forth, and also numerous special states—this is the fixed order of Dhamma.

473.

473.

Gocarena pasādasmiṃ, ghaṭṭite pana tenidha;

Uppattāvajjanādīnaṃ, ayaṃ cittaniyāmatā.

When the sense-faculty is struck by an object here, then the arising of adverting and so forth—this is the fixed order of consciousness.

474.

474.

Andhajjanānaṃ hadayandhakāraṃ,

Viddhaṃsanaṃ dīpamimaṃ jalantaṃ;

Sikkhetha dhīro satataṃ payutto,

Mohandhakārāpagamaṃ yadiccheti.

This blazing lamp destroys the darkness in the hearts of the blind. Let the wise one, ever diligent, train, if one wishes for the removal of the darkness of delusion.

Iti abhidhammāvatāre vipākacittappavattiniddeso nāma

Thus ends the exposition on the process of resultant consciousness in the Abhidhammāvatāra.

Sattamo paricchedo.

The Seventh Chapter.

8. Aṭṭhamo paricchedo

8. The Eighth Chapter

Pakiṇṇakaniddeso

The Miscellaneous Exposition

475.

475.

Idāni [P 0.0055][V 0.0067] pana sabbesaṃ, etesaṃ mānasaṃ mayā;

Pāṭavatthāya bhikkhūnaṃ, kathīyati pakiṇṇakaṃ.

Now, however, for the monks, for the sake of their mastery of all these mental states, the miscellaneous section is explained by me.

476.

476.

Panthamakkaṭako nāma, disāsu pana pañcasu;

Tattha suttaṃ pasāretvā, jālamajjhe nipajjati.

A spider named Panthamakkaṭaka, having stretched out its thread in the five directions, lies down there in the middle of the web.

477.

477.

Paṭhamāya disāyettha, sutte pana pasārite;

Pāṇakena paṭaṅgena, ghaṭṭite makkhikāya vā.

When the thread stretched here in the first direction is touched by a small creature, a moth, or a fly,

478.

478.

Nipannaṭṭhānato kiñci, calitvā uṇṇanābhi tu;

Gantvā suttānusārena, yūsaṃ pivati tassa sā.

The spider, however, having moved a little from its lying place, goes along the thread and drinks the juice of that creature.

479.

479.

Punāgantvāna tattheva, nipajjati yathāsukhaṃ;

Evameva karoteva, disāsu dutiyādisu.

Having returned again to that very spot, it lies down at ease; it acts in just the same way in the second and other directions.

480.

480.

Pasādā [M 0.0073] pañca daṭṭhabbā, suttaṃ pañcadisāsviva;

Cittaṃ pana ca daṭṭhabbaṃ, majjhe makkaṭako viya.

The five sense-faculties should be seen like the thread in the five directions; and the mind, however, should be seen like the spider in the middle.

481.

481.

Pāṇakādīhi suttassa, tassa saṅghaṭṭanā viya;

Pasādānaṃ tu daṭṭhabbā, ghaṭṭanārammaṇena hi.

Just as there is the striking of that thread by creatures and so forth, so indeed should be seen the striking of the sense-faculties by the object.

482.

482.

Calanaṃ viya taṃmajjhe, nipannāyuṇṇanābhiyā;

Pasādaghaṭṭanaṃ tattha, gahetvārammaṇaṃ pana.

Like the stirring of the spider lying in the middle of that web, so too, upon grasping the object, is the impact on the sense-faculty.

483.

483.

Manodhātukriyācittaṃ, bhavaṅgāvaṭṭanaṃ mataṃ;

Tassā suttānusāraṃva, vīthicittapavattanaṃ.

The functional mind-element consciousness is considered the adverting of the life-continuum; the proceeding of the cognitive process is like its following of the thread.

484.

484.

Sīse panassa vijjhitvā, yūsapānaṃva cetaso;

Ārammaṇesu daṭṭhabbaṃ, javanassa pavattanaṃ.

And like the drinking of the juice after piercing the creature's head, so should the proceeding of impulsion be seen with respect to the objects of consciousness.

485.

485.

Punāgantvā [V 0.0068] yathā sutta-jālamajjhe nipajjanaṃ;

Vatthuṃyeva ca nissāya, cittassa parivattanaṃ.

And just as there is the returning again to lie down in the middle of the thread-web, so too, relying on the physical base itself, is the revolving of consciousness.

486.

486.

Idaṃ tu pana opammaṃ, atthaṃ dīpeti kiṃ tu hi;

Ārammaṇena paṭhamaṃ, pasāde ghaṭṭite pana.

This simile, however, what meaning does it indeed reveal? When the sense-faculty is first struck by the object,

487.

487.

Pasādavatthuto cittā, vatthusannissitaṃ mano;

Tato hi paṭhamaṃyeva, jāyatīti hi dīpitaṃ.

It is indeed revealed that from the sense-faculty base, the mind, which is dependent on a physical base, arises immediately after that consciousness.

488.

488.

Ekekārammaṇaṃ [P 0.0056] dvīsu, dvīsu dvāresu sabbaso;

Āgacchati tenāpāthaṃ, ayamatthopi dīpito.

This meaning is also revealed: that each single object comes completely into the cognitive range of two doors.

489.

489.

Rūpaṃ cakkhupasādamhi, ghaṭṭitvā taṅkhaṇe pana;

Manodvāre tathāpātha-māgacchati nisaṃsayo.

Form, having impacted the eye-sensitivity, in that very moment, however, without a doubt comes into range at the mind-door in the same way.

490.

490.

Khago yathā hi rukkhagge, nilīyantova sākhino;

Sākhaṃ ghaṭṭeti tassīdha, chāyā pharati bhūmiyaṃ.

For just as a bird, alighting on the top of a branching tree, shakes a branch, and its shadow here spreads upon the ground,

491.

491.

Sākhāya [M 0.0074] ghaṭṭanacchāyā, pharaṇāni ca sabbaso;

Apubbācarimaṃ eka-kkhaṇasmiṃyeva jāyare.

The shaking of the branch and the spreading of the shadow all arise in one single moment, without precedence or subsequence.

492.

492.

Evameva ca rūpassa, pasādassa ca ghaṭṭanaṃ;

Bhavaṅgacalanassāpi, paccayattena atthato.

In just the same way, the impact of the form on the sense-faculty is, in essence, the condition for the vibration of the life-continuum,

493.

493.

Tatheva ca manodvāre, āpāthagamanampi ca;

Apubbācarimaṃ eka-kkhaṇasmiṃyeva hotiti.

and similarly, the coming into range at the mind-door also occurs in one single moment, without precedence or subsequence.

494.

494.

Tato bhavaṅgaṃ chinditvā, cakkhudvāre yathākkamaṃ;

Āvajjane samuppanne, dassane sampaṭicchane.

Then, having cut off the life-continuum, when, in the eye-door in due order, adverting, seeing, and receiving have arisen,

495.

495.

Santīraṇe samuppanne, tato voṭṭhabbanepi ca;

Kusalaṃ javanaṃ cittaṃ, tathākusalameva vā.

and when investigating and then determining have also arisen, a wholesome or, likewise, an unwholesome impulsion consciousness occurs.

496.

496.

Eso eva nayo sota-dvārādīsupi viññunā;

Avisesena viññeyyo, saddādīnaṃ tu ghaṭṭane.

This very same method should be understood by the wise without distinction in the ear-door and other doors as well, in the case of the impact of sounds and so forth.

497.

497.

Dovārikopamādīni[V 0.0069], etassatthassa dīpane;

Uddharitvāna tānettha, dassetabbāni viññunā.

For the clarification of this meaning, the similes of the gatekeeper and others should be extracted and shown here by the wise.

498.

498.

Asambhedena cakkhussa, rūpāpāthagamena ca;

Ālokanissayenāpi, samanakkārahetunā.

Through the non-impairment of the eye, through a visible form coming into range, through the support of light, and through the condition of attention—

499.

499.

Paccayehi panetehi, sametehi catūhipi;

Jāyate cakkhuviññāṇaṃ, sampayuttehi taṃ saha.

through these four conditions being assembled, eye-consciousness arises together with its associated factors.

500.

500.

Asambhedena sotassa, saddāpāthagamena ca;

Ākāsanissayenāpi, samanakkārahetunā.

Due to the unobstructed ear, the coming into range of sound, dependence on space, and the condition of attention.

501.

501.

Paccayehi panetehi, sametehi catūhipi;

Jāyate sotaviññāṇaṃ, sampayuttehi taṃ saha.

When these four conditions are gathered together, ear-consciousness arises, together with its associated factors.

502.

502.

Asambhedena [M 0.0075] ghānassa, gandhāpāthagamena ca;

Vāyosannissayenāpi, samanakkārahetunā.

Due to the unobstructed nose, the coming into range of an odor, dependence on air, and the condition of attention.

503.

503.

Paccayehi panetehi, sametehi catūhipi;

Jāyate ghānaviññāṇaṃ, sampayuttehi taṃ saha.

When these four conditions are gathered together, nose-consciousness arises, together with its associated factors.

504.

504.

Asambhedena jivhāya, rasāpāthagamena ca;

Āposannissayenāpi, samanakkārahetunā.

Due to the unobstructed tongue, the coming into range of a taste, dependence on water, and the condition of attention.

505.

505.

Paccayehi panetehi, sametehi catūhipi;

Jāyate jivhāviññāṇaṃ, sampayuttehi taṃ saha.

When these four conditions are gathered together, tongue-consciousness arises, together with its associated factors.

506.

506.

Asambhedena [P 0.0057] kāyassa, phoṭṭhabbāpāthasaṅgamā;

Pathavīnissayenāpi, samanakkārahetunā.

Due to the unobstructed body, the coming into contact with a tangible object, dependence on earth, and the condition of attention.

507.

507.

Paccayehi panetehi, sametehi catūhipi;

Jāyate kāyaviññāṇaṃ, sampayuttehi taṃ saha.

When these four conditions are gathered together, body-consciousness arises, together with its associated factors.

508.

508.

Asambhedā manassāpi, dhammāpāthagamena ca;

Vatthusannissayenāpi, samanakkārahetunā.

Due to the unobstructed mind, the coming into range of mental objects, dependence on the physical base, and the condition of attention.

509.

509.

Paccayehi [V 0.0070] panetehi, sametehi catūhipi;

Manoviññāṇamevaṃ tu, sampayuttehi jāyate.

When these four conditions are gathered together, mind-consciousness thus arises, together with its associated factors.

510.

510.

Mano bhavaṅgacittanti, veditabbaṃ vibhāvinā;

Āvajjanakriyācittaṃ, samanakkāroti saññitaṃ.

The mind, by the discerning, is to be understood as the life-continuum consciousness. The functional adverting consciousness is known as attention.

511.

511.

Vatthusannissayenāti, nāyaṃ sabbattha gacchati;

Bhavaṃ tu pañcavokāraṃ, sandhāya kathito pana.

The phrase 'dependence on a base' does not apply in all cases; but it is spoken with reference to five-constituent existence.

512.

512.

Paṭisandhādicittāni, sabbānekūnavīsati;

Kāme dasa ca rūpesu, pañca cattārirūpisu.

The rebirth-linking and related consciousnesses, nineteen in all, are ten in the sensual realm, five in the fine-material realm, and four in the immaterial realm.

513.

513.

Kammaṃ [M 0.0076] kammanimittañca, tathā gatinimittakaṃ;

Idaṃ hi tividhaṃ tesaṃ, ārammaṇamudīritaṃ.

Kamma, the sign of kamma, and likewise the sign of destiny—these three are declared as their object.

514.

514.

Kāmāvacarasandhīnaṃ, parittārammaṇaṃ mataṃ;

Paccuppannamatītaṃ vā, hoti natthi anāgataṃ.

For rebirth-linking in the sensual sphere, the object is considered limited, being present or past; there is no future object.

515.

515.

Aṭṭheva ca mahāpākā, tīṇi santīraṇāni ca;

Ekādasavidhaṃ cittaṃ, tadārammaṇasaññitaṃ.

Eight great resultants and three investigating consciousnesses—these eleven types of consciousness are known as 'having that as object'.

516.

516.

Ekādasavidhe citte, tadārammaṇasaññite;

Dasa puññavipākāni, ekaṃ hoti apuññajaṃ.

Among these eleven types of consciousness known as 'having that as object', ten are results of merit, and one is a result of demerit.

517.

517.

Mahāpākā na jāyante, rūpārūpabhavadvaye;

Kāme rūpe bhave ceva, hoti santīraṇattayaṃ.

Great resultants do not arise in the two existences of form and formlessness; in the sensual and form realms, there are the three investigating consciousnesses.

518.

518.

Tadārammaṇacittāni, yāni vuttāni satthunā;

Tesu cittaṃ panekampi, rūpārūpabhavadvaye.

Those consciousnesses 'having that as object', which were spoken of by the Teacher; among them, not even a single consciousness arises in the two realms of form and formless existence.

519.

519.

Na tadārammaṇaṃ hutvā, pavattati kadācipi;

Kasmā na hoti ce tattha, bījassābhāvato pana.

It never occurs having that as an object. Why is it not there? Because, indeed, the seed is absent.

520.

520.

Paṭisandhibījaṃ natthettha, kāmāvacarasaññitaṃ;

Rūpādigocare tassa, bhaveyya janakaṃ tu yaṃ.

Here, there is no rebirth-linking seed designated as belonging to the sensual sphere; but whatever is its generator would have as its domain the sphere of form and so on.

521.

521.

Cakkhuviññāṇakādīnaṃ[V 0.0071], natthitāpajjatīti ce;

Nindriyānaṃ pavattānu-bhāvato cittasambhavo.

If it is said that eye-consciousness and the like would cease to exist, it is not so, for consciousness arises due to the operative influence of the faculties.

522.

522.

Ekantena yathā cetaṃ, tadārammaṇamānasaṃ;

Nappavattati sabbampi, rūpārūpabhavadvaye.

Just as this mind 'having that as object' absolutely does not occur at all in the two realms of form and formless existence.

523.

523.

Akāmāvacaradhammepi, tadetaṃ nānubandhati;

Kasmā ajanakattā hi, janakassāsamānato.

Even in non-sensual sphere phenomena, this does not follow. Why? Because it is not generative, being dissimilar to the generator.

524.

524.

Janakaṃ [M 0.0077] tena tulyaṃ vā, kāmāvacarasaññitaṃ;

Kusalākusalādiṃ tu, javanaṃ anubandhati.

However, impulsion follows that which is generative or similar to it, designated as belonging to the sensual sphere—namely, wholesome, unwholesome, and so forth.

525.

525.

Kāmāvacaradhammāpi[P 0.0058], ye mahaggatagocarā;

Hutvā vattanti te cāpi, idaṃ nevānubandhati.

Even those sensual sphere phenomena which have the sublime as their object, having occurred, do not follow this.

526.

526.

Parittārammaṇattā ca, ekantena panassa hi;

Tathāparicitattā ca, nānubandhati sabbadā.

Because its object is exclusively limited, and because it is unfamiliar in that way, it does not always follow.

527.

527.

Kiṃ tena yuttivādena, vuttaṃ aṭṭhakathāsu hi;

Tadārammaṇacittāni, ekādasapi sabbaso.

What use is that line of reasoning? For it is said in the commentaries: 'The eleven consciousnesses having that as object, altogether...'

528.

528.

Nāmagottaṃ panārabbha, javane javitepi ca;

Tadārammaṇaṃ na gaṇhanti, rūpārūpabhavesu vā.

...when impulsion has occurred concerning name and lineage, they do not take that as object, whether in the realms of form or formlessness.

529.

529.

Yadā paññattimārabbha, javane javitepi vā;

Tathā vipassanāyāpi, lakkhaṇārammaṇāya ca.

Or when impulsion has occurred concerning a concept; and similarly in the case of insight that has characteristics as its object.

530.

530.

Tadārammaṇā na labbhanti, micchattaniyatesupi;

Na lokuttaradhammepi, ārabbha javane gate.

Tadārammaṇas are not found, even in those fixed in wrongness; nor do they arise when impulsion has occurred with supramundane states as its object.

531.

531.

Tathā mahaggate dhamme, ārabbha javane pana;

Paṭisambhidāñāṇāni, ārabbha javitepi ca.

Similarly, when impulsion occurs with exalted states as its object, and also when impulsion has occurred with the analytical knowledges as its object.

532.

532.

Manodvārepi sabbesaṃ, javanānamanantaraṃ;

Tadārammaṇacittāni, bhavanti anupubbato.

Even at the mind-door, for all, immediately after the impulsions, tadārammaṇa-cittas arise in sequence.

533.

533.

Na [V 0.0072] vijjati manodvāre, ghaṭṭanārammaṇassa hi;

Kathaṃ bhavaṅgato hoti, vuṭṭhānaṃ pana cetaso.

At the mind-door, there is no impact of an object; how then does the arising of consciousness from the life-continuum occur?

534.

534.

Manodvārepi āpātha-māgacchanteva gocarā;

Ghaṭṭanāya vinā tasmā, cittānaṃ hoti sambhavo.

Even at the mind-door, objects come into range; therefore, the arising of consciousness occurs without impact.

535.

535.

Dvādasāpuññacittānaṃ[M 0.0078], vipākā sattasattati;

Bhavanti caturāsīti, pāpapākā pavattiyaṃ.

Of the twelve unwholesome consciousnesses, the results are seventy-seven; eighty-four unwholesome results arise in the course of existence.

536.

536.

Ekādasavidhānaṃ tu, hitvā uddhaccamānasaṃ;

Ekādasavidhā ceva, bhavanti paṭisandhiyo.

But, having excluded the consciousness accompanied by restlessness, there are indeed eleven kinds of rebirth-linking.

537.

537.

Kriyacittesu sabbesu, javanaṃ na ca hoti yaṃ;

Taṃ ve karaṇamattattā, vātapupphasamaṃ mataṃ.

Whatever among all functional consciousnesses is not an impulsion, that, being mere action, is considered to be like a flower in the wind.

538.

538.

Javanattaṃ tu sampattaṃ, kiccasādhanato pana;

Chinnamūlassa rukkhassa, pupphaṃva aphalaṃ siyā.

But that which has attained the state of impulsion, though it accomplishes its function, would be fruitless, like the flower of a tree with severed roots.

539.

539.

Paṭicca pana etasmā, phalametīti paccayo;

Yo dhammo yassa dhammassa, ṭhitiyuppattiyāpi vā.

However, because a fruit comes to be in dependence on it, it is a 'condition'. Whatever phenomenon aids another phenomenon in its stability or arising,

540.

540.

Upakāro hi so tassa, paccayoti pavuccati;

Sambhavopabhavo hetu, kāraṇaṃ paccayo mato.

that is indeed helpful to it and is called a 'condition'. Origin, source, reason, and cause are considered to be a condition.

541.

541.

Lobhādi pana yo dhammo, mūlaṭṭhenupakārako;

Hetūti pana so dhammo, viññātabbo vibhāvinā.

But whatever phenomenon, beginning with greed, is helpful in the sense of being a root, that phenomenon is to be known as a 'cause' by the discerning.

542.

542.

Lobho doso ca moho ca,

Tathālobhādayo tayo;

Chaḷeva hetuyo honti,

Jātito navadhā siyuṃ.

Greed, hatred, and delusion, and likewise the three beginning with non-greed; these six are causes. By classification, they may be ninefold.

543.

543.

Dhammānaṃ kusalādīnaṃ, kusalādittasādhako;

Mūlaṭṭhoti vadantevaṃ, eke ācariyā pana.

However, some teachers say thus: 'The meaning of

544.

544.

Evaṃ [P 0.0059][V 0.0073] sante tu hetūnaṃ, taṃsamuṭṭhānarūpisu;

Hetupaccayatā neva, sampajjati kadācipi.

But if this were so, the conditionality of a cause would never apply to the material forms arisen from those causes.

545.

545.

Na hi te pana rūpānaṃ, sādhenti kusalādikaṃ;

Na tesaṃ pana rūpānaṃ, paccayā na ca honti te.

For they [the causes] do not accomplish for the forms [any quality of] being wholesome, etc.; nor, then, would they be conditions for those forms.

546.

546.

Tasmā [M 0.0079] hi kusalādīnaṃ, kusalādittasādhako;

Mūlaṭṭhoti na gantabbo, viññunā samayaññunā.

Therefore, a wise person who knows the conventions should not understand the meaning of 'root' as that which accomplishes wholesomeness, etc.

547.

547.

Suppatiṭṭhitabhāvassa, sādhanenupakārako;

Mūlaṭṭhoti ca hetūnaṃ, viññātabbo vibhāvinā.

Rather, that which is helpful by accomplishing a well-established state is to be understood by the discerning as the meaning of 'root' for the causes.

548.

548.

Kusalākusalā hetū, kriyāhetū ca sabbaso;

Dhammānaṃ sampayuttānaṃ, taṃsamuṭṭhānarūpinaṃ.

Wholesome and unwholesome causes, and all functional causes, for their associated mental states and for the material form produced by them,

549.

549.

Hetupaccayataṃ yātā, pañcavokārabhūmiyaṃ;

Sampayuttānamevete, catuvokārabhūmiyaṃ.

attain the conditionality of a cause in the five-aggregate plane. In the four-aggregate plane, these are [causes] for their associated states only.

550.

550.

Kāme vipākahetūpi, kāmāvacarabhūmiyaṃ;

Attanā sampayuttānaṃ, paṭisandhikkhaṇe pana.

In the sense-sphere plane, resultant causes also, at the moment of rebirth-linking, for states associated with themselves,

551.

551.

Kaṭattārūpajātānaṃ, tatheva ca pavattiyaṃ;

Cittajānañca rūpānaṃ, hetupaccayataṃ gatā.

and for the kinds of material form produced by kamma, and likewise during the course of life for mind-produced material form, have attained the conditionality of a cause.

552.

552.

Rūpe vipākahetu ca, rūpāvacarabhūmiyaṃ;

Tathā vuttappakārānaṃ, honti te hetupaccayā.

In the fine-material sphere, resultant causes in the fine-material plane are also causal conditions for those of the types thus stated.

553.

553.

Hetuyo pañcavokāre, lokuttaravipākajā;

Cittajānañca rūpānaṃ, sampayuttānameva ca.

Causes in the five-aggregate plane that are born of supramundane results are [conditions] for mind-produced material form and for their associated states.

554.

554.

Te hetupaccayā honti, catuvokārabhūmiyaṃ;

Bhavanti sampayuttānaṃ, itare ca sabhūmiyaṃ.

They are causal conditions. In the four-aggregate plane, they are for their associated states; and the others are so in their respective planes.

555.

555.

Hetuttho hetuyo ceva, hetupaccayasambhavo;

Evameva ca viññeyyo, sañjātasukhahetunā.

The meaning of cause, the causes themselves, and the arising from the causal condition—thus should it be understood by one for whom the cause of happiness has arisen.

556.

556.

Chando [V 0.0074] cittañca vīriyaṃ, vīmaṃsā cāti satthunā;

Lokādhipatinā vuttā, catudhādhipatī siyuṃ.

Will, consciousness, energy, and investigation—these, declared by the Teacher, the Lord of the World, are the four dominants.

557.

557.

Chandaṃ [M 0.0080] tu jeṭṭhakaṃ katvā, chandaṃ katvā dhuraṃ pana;

Cittassuppattikālasmiṃ, chandādhipati nāmaso.

Having made will foremost, having made will the lead, at the time of the consciousness's arising, it is by name 'will-dominant'.

558.

558.

Eseva ca nayo ñeyyo, sesesupi ca tīsupi;

Adhippatīti niddiṭṭho, jeṭṭhaṭṭhenupakārako.

This same method should be understood for the remaining three as well. 'Dominant' is explained as that which is helpful in the sense of being chief.

559.

559.

Sumatimativibodhanaṃ vicittaṃ,

Kumatimatindhanapāvakaṃ padhānaṃ;

Imamatimadhuraṃ avedi yo yo,

Jinavacanaṃ sakalaṃ avedi so so.

This diverse awakening of good intelligence, this striving that is a fire for the fuel of wrong views; whoever has known this exceedingly sweet Word of the Conqueror, has known it in its entirety.

Iti abhidhammāvatāre pakiṇṇakaniddeso nāma

Thus ends the section called 'Miscellany' in the Abhidhammāvatāra.

Aṭṭhamo paricchedo.

The Eighth Chapter.

9. Navamo paricchedo

9. The Ninth Chapter.

Puññavipākapaccayaniddeso

Explanation of the Conditions for Meritorious Results.

560.

560.

Bāttiṃsa [P 0.0060] pākacittāni, lokikāneva yāni hi;

Etesaṃ pākacittānaṃ, paṭisandhipavattisu.

Thirty-two resultant consciousnesses, which are indeed only mundane; for these resultant consciousnesses, in rebirth-linking and in the course of life.

561.

561.

Puññāpuññādisaṅkhārā, yathā yesañca paccayā;

Bhavādīsu tathā tepi, viññātabbā vibhāvinā.

Meritorious, demeritorious, and other formations, and as they are conditions for them, so too in existences and the like should they be understood by the discerning.

562.

562.

Tayo bhavā catasso ca, yoniyo gatipañcakaṃ;

Viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo satta, sattāvāsā naveritā.

Three kinds of existence, four modes of generation, five destinations, seven stations of consciousness, and nine abodes of beings are taught.

563.

563.

Kāme [V 0.0075] puññābhisaṅkhāra-saññitā aṭṭha cetanā;

Navannaṃ pākacittānaṃ, kāme sugatiyaṃ pana.

In the sensual realm, eight volitions reckoned as meritorious formations are for the nine resultant consciousnesses in the happy destinations of the sensual realm.

564.

564.

Nānākkhaṇikakammūpa-nissayapaccayehi ca;

Dvedhā hi paccayā tesaṃ, bhavanti paṭisandhiyaṃ.

And by the different-moment kamma condition and the decisive support condition; for them, there are indeed two kinds of conditions at rebirth-linking.

565.

565.

Upekkhāsahitāhetu-manoviññāṇadhātuyā[M 0.0081];

Vinā parittapākānaṃ, honti dvedhā pavattiyaṃ.

They are conditions in two ways during the course of life for the minor resultants, with the exception of the rootless mind-consciousness element accompanied by equanimity.

566.

566.

Tāyeva cetanā rūpa-bhave dvedhāva paccayā;

Pañcannaṃ pākacittānaṃ, bhavanti hi pavattiyaṃ.

Those same volitions, in the form existence, are indeed conditions in two ways for the five resultant consciousnesses in the course of life.

567.

567.

Aṭṭhannaṃ tu parittānaṃ, kāme duggatiyaṃ tathā;

Pavatte paccayā honti, na honti paṭisandhiyaṃ.

But for the eight minor resultants, likewise in the unhappy destinations of the sensual realm, they are conditions in the course of life, but not at rebirth-linking.

568.

568.

Honti vuttappakārāva, kāme sugatiyaṃ tathā;

Soḷasannaṃ vipākānaṃ, pavatte paṭisandhiyaṃ.
