They are just of the kinds stated, likewise in the happy destinations of the sensual realm, for the sixteen results, in the course of life and at rebirth-linking.

569.

569.

Rūpe puññābhisaṅkhārā, rūpāvacarabhūmiyaṃ;

Pañcannaṃ pākacittānaṃ, paccayā paṭisandhiyaṃ.

Meritorious formations in the form realm are conditions for the five resultant consciousnesses at rebirth-linking in the form-sphere plane.

570.

570.

Hontimāpuññasaṅkhārā, kāme duggatiyaṃ dvidhā;

Viññāṇassa panekassa, paccayā paṭisandhiyaṃ.

These demeritorious formations, in the unhappy destinations of the sensual realm, are conditions in two ways for one consciousness at rebirth-linking.

571.

571.

Channaṃ pana pavatteva, honti no paṭisandhiyaṃ;

Sattannampi bhavanteva, pavatte paṭisandhiyaṃ.

But for the six, they are conditions only in the course of life, not at rebirth-linking; for the seven, they are conditions both in the course of life and at rebirth-linking.

572.

572.

Kāme sugatiyaṃ tesaṃ, sattannampi tatheva ca;

Pavatte paccayā honti, na honti paṭisandhiyaṃ.

In the happy destinations of the sensual realm, for those seven as well, they are likewise conditions in the course of life, but not at rebirth-linking.

573.

573.

Viññāṇānaṃ catunnampi, tesaṃ rūpabhave tathā;

Pavatte paccayā honti, na honti paṭisandhiyaṃ.

For those four consciousnesses, likewise in the form existence, they are conditions in the course of life, but not at rebirth-linking.

574.

574.

So [P 0.0061] ca kāmabhaveniṭṭha-rūpādiupaladdhiyaṃ;

Aniṭṭharūpādayo pana, brahmaloke na vijjare.

And that occurs in the sensual existence with the experience of disagreeable forms, etc.; but disagreeable forms and the like do not exist in the Brahma world.

575.

575.

Tathevāneñjasaṅkhāro[V 0.0076], arūpāvacarabhūmiyaṃ;

Catunnaṃ pākacittānaṃ, pavatte paṭisandhiyaṃ.

Likewise, the imperturbable formation, in the immaterial-sphere plane, is a condition for the four resultant consciousnesses in the course of life and at rebirth-linking.

576.

576.

Evaṃ [M 0.0082] tāva bhavesvete, paṭisandhipavattisu;

Yathā ca paccayā honti, tathā ñeyyā vibhāvinā.

Thus, in these existences, in rebirth-linking and in the course of life, as they are conditions, so should they be understood by the discerning.

577.

577.

Eseva ca nayo ñeyyo, yoniādīsu tatridaṃ;

Ādito pana paṭṭhāya, mukhamattanidassanaṃ.

And this same method should be understood for the modes of generation and so forth; what is given here from the beginning is merely an indication of the principal point.

578.

578.

Avisesena puññābhi-saṅkhāro dvibhavesupi;

Datvāna paṭisandhiṃ tu, sabbapākaṃ janeti so.

The meritorious formation, without distinction in the two existences, having given rebirth-linking, produces every result.

579.

579.

Tathā catūsu viññeyyo, aṇḍajādīsu yonisu;

Bahudevamanussānaṃ, gatīsu dvīsu eva ca.

Likewise, it should be understood in the four modes of generation, egg-born and the rest, and in the two destinations of many gods and humans.

580.

580.

Tathā nānattakāyādi-viññāṇānaṃ ṭhitīsupi;

Tathā vuttappakārasmiṃ, sattāvāse catubbidhe.

Similarly, in the stations of consciousness such as those with diverse bodies; and in the fourfold abodes of beings as described.

581.

581.

Evaṃ puññābhisaṅkhāro, bhavādīsu yathārahaṃ;

Ekavīsatipākānaṃ, paccayo hoti ca dvidhā.

Thus, the meritorious formation, as appropriate in existences and so forth, becomes the condition in two ways for twenty-one resultant states.

582.

582.

Kāme apuññasaṅkhāro, bhave catūsu yonisu;

Tīsu gatīsu ekissā, viññāṇaṭṭhitiyāpi ca.

The demeritorious formation in the sensual existence, in the four modes of generation, in the three destinations, and also in one station of consciousness.

583.

583.

Sattāvāse panekasmiṃ,

Uhoti so paccayo dvidhā;

Sattannaṃ pākacittānaṃ,

Pavatte paṭisandhiyaṃ.

And in one abode of beings, it is a condition in two ways for seven resultant consciousnesses, in the course of life and at rebirth-linking.

584.

584.

Tathevāneñjasaṅkhāro, ekārūpabhave puna;

Ekissā yoniyā ceva, ekissā gatiyāpi ca.

Similarly, the imperturbable formation, again in one formless existence, and in one mode of generation, and also in one destination.

585.

585.

Tīsu cittaṭṭhitīsveva, sattāvāse catubbidhe;

Catunnaṃ pākacittānaṃ, dvedhā so hoti paccayo.

In only three stations of consciousness and in the fourfold abodes of beings, it becomes the condition in two ways for four resultant consciousnesses.

586.

586.

Paṭisandhipavattīnaṃ[V 0.0077], vaseneva bhavādisu;

Vijānitabbā saṅkhārā, yathā yesañca paccayā.

Formations should be understood by way of rebirth-linking and the ongoing process in existences and so on, as well as their conditions.

587.

587.

Na [M 0.0083] rūpārūpadhammānaṃ, saṅkanti pana vijjati;

Saṅkantibhāve asati, paṭisandhi kathaṃ siyā.

There is no transmigration of material and immaterial phenomena; but when there is no transmigration, how can there be rebirth-linking?

588.

588.

Natthi cittassa saṅkanti, atītabhavato idha;

Tato hetuṃ vinā tassa, pātubhāvo na vijjati.

There is no transmigration of consciousness from a past existence to here; therefore, without a cause for it, its manifestation is not found.

589.

589.

Suladdhapaccayaṃ rūpā-rūpamattaṃ tu jāyati;

Uppajjamānamevaṃ tu, labhitvā paccayaṃ pana.

Indeed, only the material and immaterial, having well obtained conditions, arises; thus it arises, having obtained its conditions.

590.

590.

Bhavantaramupetīti, samaññāya pavuccati;

Na ca satto na ca jīvo, na attā vāpi vijjati.

It is said by designation that one takes on another existence; and no being, no life-principle, nor a self is found.

591.

591.

Tayidaṃ pākaṭaṃ katvā, paṭisandhikkamaṃ pana;

Dassayissāmahaṃ sādhu, nibodhatha sudubbudhaṃ.

Having made this evident, I will now clearly show the process of rebirth-linking; listen well to this, which is very difficult to understand.

592.

592.

Atītasmiṃ [P 0.0062] bhave tassa, āsannamaraṇassa hi;

Haritaṃ tālapaṇṇaṃva, pakkhittaṃ ātape pana.

Indeed, for one near death in a past existence, it is like a green palm leaf placed in the sun.

593.

593.

Sussamāne sarīrasmiṃ, naṭṭhe cakkhundriyādike;

Hadayavatthumattasmiṃ, ṭhite kāyappasādike.

When the body is withering, and the eye and other faculties have perished, when only the heart-basis and the body-sensitivity remain.

594.

594.

Vatthusannissitaṃ cittaṃ, hoti tasmiṃ khaṇepi ca;

Pubbānusevitaṃ kammaṃ, puññaṃ vāpuññameva vā.

Consciousness dependent on a basis exists even at that moment; and kamma previously practiced, whether meritorious or demeritorious,

595.

595.

Kammaṃ kammanimittaṃ vā, ālambitvā pavattati;

Evaṃ pavattamānaṃ taṃ, viññāṇaṃ laddhapaccayaṃ.

Taking kamma or a kamma-sign as its object, it proceeds; thus proceeding, that consciousness, having obtained conditions,

596.

596.

Avijjāya paṭicchannā-dīnave visaye pana;

Taṇhā nameti saṅkhārā, khipanti sahajā pana.

Towards the object, which is dangerous and obscured by ignorance, craving inclines it, and co-arisen formations impel it.

597.

597.

Na mīyamānaṃ taṇhāya, taṃ santativasā pana;

Orimā pana tīramhā, ālambitvāna rajjukaṃ.

That consciousness, not perishing through craving but by the power of continuity, is like one who, from this shore, clings to a rope

598.

598.

Mātikātikkamovetaṃ[M 0.0084][V 0.0078], purimaṃ jahati nissayaṃ;

Aparaṃ kammasambhūtaṃ, lambitvā vāpi nissayaṃ.

This is like crossing a canal: one abandons the former support, clinging to another support born of kamma.

599.

599.

Taṃ panārammaṇādīhi, paccayehi pavattati;

Purimaṃ cavanaṃ ettha, pacchimaṃ paṭisandhi tu.

That proceeds by conditions such as an object and so on; here, the former is passing away, and the latter is rebirth-linking.

600.

600.

Tadetaṃ nāpi purimā, bhavatopi idhāgataṃ;

Kammādiñca vinā hetuṃ, pātubhūtaṃ na ceva taṃ.

This has neither come here from a prior existence, nor has it manifested at all without a cause such as kamma.

601.

601.

Ettha cetassa cittassa, purimā bhavato pana;

Idhānāgamanetīta-bhavahetūhi sambhave.

Here, if this consciousness does not come here from a prior existence, it arises from causes in a past existence.

602.

602.

Paṭighosadīpamuddādī, bhavantettha nidassanā;

Yathā āgantvā aññatra, honti saddādihetukā.

Echoes, lamps, seals, and so on, are illustrations here; just as they arise elsewhere from causes such as sound, without having come from another place.

603.

603.

Evameva ca viññāṇaṃ, veditabbaṃ vibhāvinā;

Santānabandhato natthi, ekatā vāpi nānatā.

Just so should consciousness be understood by the discerning one; due to the linking of the continuity, there is neither identity nor difference.

604.

604.

Sati santānabandhe tu, ekantenekatā siyā;

Khīrato dadhisambhūtaṃ, na bhaveyya kadācipi.

However, if there were absolute identity in the linking of the continuity, curd arisen from milk would never come to be.

605.

605.

Athāpi pana ekanta-nānatā sā bhaveyya ce;

Khīrasāmī naro neva, dadhisāmī bhaveyya so.

And yet, if there were absolute difference, the man who owns the milk would not be the owner of the curd.

606.

606.

Tasmā ettha panekanta-ekatānānatāpi vā;

Na ceva upagantabbā, viññunā samayaññunā.

Therefore, here, neither absolute identity nor absolute difference should be accepted by the wise one who knows the doctrine.

607.

607.

Nanu evamasaṅkanti-pātubhāve tassa sati;

Ye imasmiṃ manussatta-bhāve khandhābhisambhavā.

Surely, when there is such a manifestation without transmigration, for those aggregates that have come into being in this human existence—

608.

608.

Tesaṃ idha niruddhattā, kammassa phalahetuno;

Paratthāgamato ceva, idha tassa katassa hi.

since they cease here, and since the cause of the fruit of kamma does not come from elsewhere—that kamma which was indeed done here—

609.

609.

Aññassa [M 0.0085] aññato ceva, kammato taṃ phalaṃ siyā;

Tasmā na sundaraṃ etaṃ, vidhānaṃ sabbameva ca.

the fruit would belong to another and arise from another's kamma. Therefore, this entire explanation is not sound.

Etthāha [V 0.0079] –

To this, it is said:

610.

610.

Santāne [P 0.0063] yaṃ phalaṃ etaṃ, nāññassa na ca aññato;

Bījānaṃ abhisaṅkhāro, etassatthassa sādhako.

This fruit which is in the continuity is neither of another, nor from another; the preparation of seeds is the proof of this meaning.

611.

611.

Ekasmiṃ pana santāne, vattamānaṃ phalaṃ pana;

Aññassātipi vā neva, aññato vā na hoti taṃ.

Indeed, the fruit occurring in a single continuity is neither of another, nor does it arise from another.

612.

612.

Bījānaṃ abhisaṅkhārā, etassatthassa sādhako;

Bījānaṃ abhisaṅkhāre, kate tu madhuādinā.

The preparation of seeds is the proof of this meaning. When the preparation of seeds is done with honey and so on,

613.

613.

Tassa bījassa santāne, paṭhamaṃ laddhapaccayo;

Madhuro phalaso tassa, hoti kālantare pana.

In the continuity of that seed, having received the initial condition, the taste of its fruit becomes sweet after some time.

614.

614.

Na hi tāni hi bījāni, abhisaṅkharaṇampi vā;

Pāpuṇanti phalaṭṭhānaṃ, evaṃ ñeyyamidampi ca.

For neither those seeds nor their preparation reach the state of fruit; thus, this too should be understood.

615.

615.

Bālakāle payuttena, vijjāsipposadhādinā;

Dīpetabbo ayaṃ vuddha-kālasmiṃ phaladāyinā.

That which is applied in youth, such as knowledge, crafts, and medicine, should be made manifest as fruit-bearing in old age.

616.

616.

Evaṃ santepi taṃ kammaṃ, vijjamānampi vā pana;

Phalassa paccayo hoti, atha vāvijjamānakaṃ.

Thus, that action, whether it be existing or non-existent, becomes a condition for the result.

617.

617.

Vijjamānaṃ sace hoti, tappavattikkhaṇe pana;

Bhavitabbaṃ vipākena, saddhimeva ca hetunā.

If it exists, then at the moment of its occurrence, the result must come to be, together with the cause.

618.

618.

Atha vāvijjamānaṃ taṃ, niruddhaṃ paccayo bhave;

Pavattikkhaṇato pubbe, pacchā niccaphalaṃ siyā.

Or, if that non-existent action, having ceased, were a condition, then both before and after the moment of its occurrence, there would be a constant result.

Vuccate [M 0.0086] –

It is said:

619.

619.

Kaṭattā paccayo kammaṃ, tasmā niccaphalaṃ na ca;

Pāṭibhogādikaṃ kammaṃ, veditabbaṃ nidassanaṃ.

Action is a condition due to its having been done; therefore its result is not constant. Action such as guaranteeing should be understood as an example.

620.

620.

Kaṭattāyeva [V 0.0080] taṃ kammaṃ, phalassa pana paccayo;

Na cassa vijjamānattaṃ, tassa vāvijjamānatā.

That action is a condition for the fruit precisely by reason of its having been done; not its existence, nor its non-existence.

621.

621.

Abhidhammāvatāroyaṃ, paramatthapakāsano;

Sotabbo pana sotūnaṃ, pītibuddhivivaḍḍhano.

This Abhidhammāvatāra, which illuminates the ultimate meaning, should be heard by listeners, for it increases joy and wisdom.

Iti abhidhammāvatāre puññavipākapaccayaniddeso nāma

Thus, in the Abhidhammāvatāra, the explanation of the condition for wholesome result.

Navamo paricchedo.

The Ninth Chapter.

10. Dasamo paricchedo

10. The Tenth Chapter

Rūpavibhāganiddeso

The Exposition of the Division of Material Form

622.

622.

Vuttamādimhi [P 0.0064] yaṃ rūpaṃ, cittajānamanantaraṃ;

Tassa dāni karissāmi, samāsena vibhāvanaṃ.

Now I shall briefly explain that material form which was mentioned at the beginning, immediately following the [section on] mind-born phenomena.

623.

623.

Yaṃ ruppatīti rūpanti, tathā rūpayatīti vā;

Rūpārūpabhavātīto, surūpo rūpamabravi.

It is called 'form' (rūpa) because it is afflicted (ruppati), or likewise because it manifests (rūpayati); the Beautiful One, who has transcended the realms of form and formless existence, spoke of form.

624.

624.

Taṃ rūpaṃ duvidhaṃ hoti, bhūtopādāyabhedato;

Catubbidhā mahābhūtā, upādā catuvīsati.

That material form is twofold, by division into primary elements and derived phenomena. The great primary elements are fourfold, and the derived are twenty-four.

625.

625.

Pathavīdhātu āpo ca,

Tejo vāyo tatheva ca;

Cattārome mahābhūtā,

Mahābhūtena desitā.

The earth element, water, fire, and also the wind element; these four are the great primary elements, taught by the Great Being.

626.

626.

Mahantā pātubhūtāti, mahābhūtasamāti vā;

Vañcakattā abhūtena, mahābhūtāti saññitā.

They are designated as 'great primary elements' because they have appeared as great, or because they are like great magicians, deceiving by means of the unreal.

627.

627.

Cakkhu [M 0.0087][V 0.0081] sotañca ghānañca, jivhā kāyo ca rūpatā;

Saddo gandho raso itthi-purisindriyajīvitaṃ.

The eye, the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, and visible form; sound, smell, taste, the faculties of femininity and masculinity, and life.

628.

628.

Vatthumāhāratā kāya-vacīviññattiyo duve;

Ākāso ceva rūpassa, lahutādittayampi ca.

The heart-base, nutriment, the two intimations of body and speech; space, and also the triad of lightness and so forth of material form.

629.

629.

Upacayo santatirūpaṃ, jaratāniccatāpi ca;

Upādāti pavuccanti, imāni catuvīsati.

Accumulation, continuity of form, decay, and also impermanence; these twenty-four are called derived phenomena.

630.

630.

Mahābhūtāni nissāya, amuñcitvā pavattito;

Upādārūpamiccāha, nirupādānamānaso.

The One whose mind is without clinging has said that because it proceeds depending on the great primary elements and without leaving them, it is called derived material form.

631.

631.

Pathavī patthaṭattā ca, vāyo vāyanato bhave;

Tejo tejeti rūpāni, āpo āpeti pālanā.

Earth is due to its being spread out, and air is due to its causing movement; fire heats material forms, water pervades by way of maintaining.

632.

632.

Tesaṃ dāni pavakkhāmi, rūpānaṃ lakkhaṇādikaṃ;

Lakkhaṇādīsu ñātesu, dhammā āvi bhavanti hi.

Now I shall explain the characteristics and so forth of these material forms; for when the characteristics and so on are known, the phenomena become manifest.

633.

633.

Sāmaññaṃ vā sabhāvo vā, dhammānaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ mataṃ;

Kiccaṃ vā tassa sampatti, rasoti paridīpito.

The general or intrinsic nature of phenomena is considered their characteristic; their function or accomplishment is explained as their function (rasa).

634.

634.

Phalaṃ vā paccupaṭṭhānaṃ, upaṭṭhānanayopi vā;

Āsannakāraṇaṃ yaṃ tu, taṃ padaṭṭhānasaññitaṃ.

Its manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna) is its result or its mode of appearance; and that which is its immediate cause is designated as its proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna).

Tattha [P 0.0065] kakkhaḷattalakkhaṇā pathavīdhātu, patiṭṭhānarasā, sampaṭicchanapaccupaṭṭhānā. Paggharaṇalakkhaṇā āpodhātu, upabrūhanarasā, saṅgahapaccupaṭṭhānā. Uṇhattalakkhaṇā tejodhātu, paripācanarasā, maddavānuppadānapaccupaṭṭhānā. Vitthambhanalakkhaṇā vāyodhātu, samudīraṇarasā, abhinīhārapaccupaṭṭhānā. Ekekāya cettha sesabhūtattayapadaṭṭhānāti veditabbā.

Therein, the earth element has the characteristic of hardness, its function is to provide a base, and its manifestation is receiving. The water element has the characteristic of flowing, its function is to cause cohesion, and its manifestation is binding. The fire element has the characteristic of heat, its function is to mature, and its manifestation is the provision of softness. The air element has the characteristic of distending, its function is to cause motion, and its manifestation is impelling. Here, it should be understood that each one has the remaining three primary elements as its proximate cause.

Cakkhatīti cakkhu, rūpaṃ vibhāvetīti attho.

It is called 'eye' (cakkhu) because it reveals (cakkhati), meaning it makes visible form manifest.

635.

635.

Tattha [M 0.0088][V 0.0082] cakkhu dvidhā vuttaṃ, paññāmaṃsappabhedato;

Tattha paññāmayaṃ cakkhu, hoti pañcavidhaṃ pana.

Therein, the eye is said to be twofold, by the distinction of the wisdom-eye and the flesh-eye; of these, the wisdom-eye is fivefold.

636.

636.

Buddhadhammasamantehi, ñāṇadibbehi nāmato;

Yathānukkamato tesaṃ, nānattaṃ me nibodhatha.

Understand from me the diversity of these, in their sequence, which are named: the Buddha-eye, the Dhamma-eye, the Universal-eye, the Knowledge-eye, and the Divine-eye.

637.

637.

Āsayānusaye ñāṇaṃ, indriyānaṃ paropare;

Buddhacakkhunti niddiṭṭhaṃ, muninā lokacakkhunā.

Knowledge of inclinations and underlying tendencies, and of the superiority and inferiority of faculties, is designated as the Buddha-eye by the Sage, the Eye of the World.

638.

638.

Heṭṭhāmaggattaye ñāṇaṃ, dhammacakkhunti saññitaṃ;

Ñeyyaṃ samantacakkhunti, ñāṇaṃ sabbaññutā pana.

The knowledge concerning the three lower paths is designated as the Dhamma-eye; the knowledge of omniscience, however, is to be known as the universal eye.

639.

639.

Yaṃ “cakkhuṃ udapādī”ti, āgataṃ ñāṇacakkhu taṃ;

Abhiññācittajā paññā, dibbacakkhunti vuccati.

That which is referred to by the phrase, 'the eye arose,' is the knowledge-eye; the wisdom born of the mind of direct knowledge is called the divine eye.

640.

640.

Maṃsacakkhupi duvidhaṃ, sasambhārapasādato;

Sasambhārañca nāmettha, akkhikūpe patiṭṭhitaṃ.

The flesh-eye is also twofold: that with its constituents and the sensitive element. And here, that which is established in the eye-socket is named 'the eye with its constituents'.

641.

641.

Akkhikūpaṭṭhinā heṭṭhā, uddhañca bhamukaṭṭhinā;

Ubhato akkhikūṭehi, matthaluṅgena antato.

Below, by the bone of the eye-socket, and above, by the bone of the brow; on both sides by the corners of the eye-sockets, and within by the brain.

642.

642.

Bahiddhā akkhilomehi, paricchinno ca yo pana;

Nhārusuttena ābandho, maṃsapiṇḍo pavuccati.

And that which is demarcated externally by the eyelashes and bound by sinew-threads, is called a lump of flesh.

643.

643.

Sakalopi ca lokoyaṃ, kamalassa dalaṃ viya;

Puthulaṃ vipulaṃ nīlaṃ, iti jānāti locanaṃ.

Like a lotus petal, the eye knows this entire world as broad, expansive, and blue.

644.

644.

Cakkhu nāma na taṃ hoti, vatthu tassāti vuccati;

Idaṃ pana sasambhāra-cakkhunti paridīpitaṃ.

That is not called the eye itself, but is said to be its physical basis; this, however, is explained as the eye with its constituents.

645.

645.

Vaṇṇo gandho raso ojā,

Catasso cāpi dhātuyo;

Bhāvasambhavasaṇṭhānaṃ,

Jīvitāni tatheva ca.

Color, odor, taste, nutritive essence, and also the four primary elements; gender, origination, configuration, and the life faculty as well.

646.

646.

Kāyacakkhupasādāti[M 0.0089][V 0.0083],

Sambhārā honti cuddasa;

Tathā vitthārato cetaṃ,

Catasso cāpi dhātuyo.

Including body-sensitivity and eye-sensitivity, the constituents are fourteen. Likewise, this is to be explained in detail, along with the four primary elements.

647.

647.

Vaṇṇo gandho raso ojā,

Saṇṭhānasambhavo tathā;

Dasete catusamuṭṭhānā,

Cattālīsa bhavanti te.

Color, odor, taste, nutritive essence, configuration, and origination, together with the four primary elements: these ten, arising from four causes, become forty.

648.

648.

Cakkhu [P 0.0066] kāyappasādo ca, bhāvo jīvitameva ca;

Cattālīsañca rūpāni, cattāri tu bhavanti hi.

Eye-sensitivity and body-sensitivity, gender, and the life faculty; along with the forty material forms, these four also indeed exist.

649.

649.

Imesaṃ pana rūpānaṃ, vasena paripiṇḍitaṃ;

Idaṃ sambhāracakkhunti, paṇḍitehi pakāsitaṃ.

Compounded by means of these material forms, this is declared by the wise as 'the eye with its constituents'.

650.

650.

Yo panettha sito atthi, paribandho parittako;

Catunnaṃ pana bhūtānaṃ, pasādo kammasambhavo.

Whatever slight, dependent bond exists herein is the sensitivity of the four primary elements, which is born of kamma.

651.

651.

Idaṃ pasādacakkhunti, akkhātaṃ pañcacakkhunā;

Tadetaṃ tassa majjhe tu, sasambhārassa cakkhuno.

This is declared as the 'sensitive eye' by the possessor of the five eyes; and it is in the middle of that eye with its constituents.

652.

652.

Setena maṇḍalenassa, parikkhittassa sabbaso;

Kaṇhamaṇḍalamajjhe vā, niviṭṭhe diṭṭhamaṇḍale.

Within that which is entirely surrounded by the white circle, it is settled in the sphere of vision in the middle of the black circle.

653.

653.

Sandhāraṇādikiccāhi, dhātūhi ca catūhipi;

Katūpakāraṃ hutvāna, utucittādinā pana.

Having been assisted by the four primary elements, with their functions beginning with sustaining, and further by season, mind, and so forth,

654.

654.

Upatthambhiyamānaṃ taṃ, āyunā katapālanaṃ;

Vaṇṇagandharasādīhi, rūpehi parivāritaṃ.

it is being sustained, protected by the life faculty, and surrounded by material forms such as color, odor, taste, and so forth.

655.

655.

Cakkhuviññāṇakādīnaṃ, vatthudvārañca sādhayaṃ;

Ūkāsirasamānena, pamāṇeneva tiṭṭhati.

Accomplishing its function as the physical basis and door for eye-consciousness and so forth, it exists, in measure, like the head of a louse.

Vuttaṃ [M 0.0090][V 0.0084] hetaṃ –

For this was said:

656.

656.

“Yena cakkhupasādena, rūpānimanupassati;

Parittaṃ sukhumaṃ etaṃ, ūkāsirasamūpama”nti.

‘By which sensitive eye one perceives visible forms—this is small, subtle, and comparable to the head of a louse.’

657.

657.

Sotādīsu ca eseva, nayo ñeyyo vibhāvinā;

Visesamattamevettha, pavakkhāmi ito paraṃ.

For the ear and so forth, this same method should be understood by the discerning one. Hereafter, I shall explain only the specific differences.

Suṇātīti sotaṃ, taṃ tanutambalomācite aṅgulivedhakasaṇṭhāne padese vuttappakārāhi dhātūhi katūpakāraṃ utucittāhārehi upatthambhiyamānaṃ āyunā paripāliyamānaṃ sotaviññāṇādīnaṃ vatthudvārabhāvaṃ sādhayamānaṃ tiṭṭhati.

It is called 'ear' (sota) because it hears (suṇāti). It exists in a place shaped like a finger-ring, covered with fine, copper-colored hairs; it is assisted by the elements of the aforementioned kind, sustained by season, mind, and nutriment, protected by the life faculty, and accomplishes its function as the physical basis and door for ear-consciousness and so forth.

Ghāyatīti ghānaṃ, taṃ sasambhāraghānabilassa anto ajapadasaṇṭhāne padese yathāvuttappakārā hutvā tiṭṭhati.

It is called 'nose' (ghāna) because it smells (ghāyati). It exists inside the nostril, in a place shaped like a goat's foot, being of the kind described above.

Sāyatīti jivhā, jīvitamavhāyatīti vā jivhā, sā sasambhārajivhāmajjhassa upari uppaladalaggasaṇṭhāne padese yathāvuttappakārā hutvā tiṭṭhati.

It is called 'tongue' (jivhā) because it tastes (sāyati), or because it calls forth life (jīvitamavhāyati). It exists on the surface of the middle of the tongue, in a place shaped like the tip of a lotus petal, being of the kind described above.

Kucchitānaṃ malānaṃ āyoti kāyo. Yāvatā pana imasmiṃ kāye upādinnakaṃ rūpaṃ atthi, sabbattha kāyapasādo kappāsapaṭale sneho viya yathāvuttappakāro hutvā tiṭṭhati.

It is called 'body' (kāya) because it is an abode (āya) of contemptible (kucchita) impurities (mala). However, wherever there is clung-to material form in this body, body-sensitivity exists throughout, like oil pervading a cotton cloth, being of the kind described above.

Ettha panetesaṃ lakkhaṇādīni pavakkhāmi – daṭṭhukāmatānidānakammasamuṭṭhānabhūtapasādalakkhaṇaṃ [P 0.0067] cakkhu, rūpesu āviñchanarasaṃ, cakkhuviññāṇassa ādhārabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, daṭṭhukāmatānidānakammajabhūtapadaṭṭhānaṃ.

Here I shall explain their characteristics and so forth. The eye has the characteristic of sensitivity of the primary elements, arisen from kamma rooted in the desire to see. Its function is to impinge upon visible forms. Its manifestation is the state of being a support for eye-consciousness. Its proximate cause is the primary elements born of kamma rooted in the desire to see.

Sotukāmatānidānakammasamuṭṭhānabhūtapasādalakkhaṇaṃ [M 0.0091] sotaṃ, saddesu āviñchanarasaṃ, sotaviññāṇassa ādhārabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, sotukāmatānidānakammajabhūtapadaṭṭhānaṃ.

The ear has the characteristic of sensitivity of the primary elements, arisen from kamma rooted in the desire to hear. Its function is to impinge upon sounds. Its manifestation is the state of being a support for ear-consciousness. Its proximate cause is the primary elements born of kamma rooted in the desire to hear.

Ghāyitukāmatānidānakammasamuṭṭhānabhūtapasādalakkhaṇaṃ ghānaṃ, gandhesu āviñchanarasaṃ, ghānaviññāṇassa ādhārabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, ghāyitukāmatānidānakammajabhūtapadaṭṭhānaṃ.

The nose has the characteristic of sensitivity of the primary elements, arisen from kamma rooted in the desire to smell. Its function is to impinge upon odors. Its manifestation is the state of being a support for nose-consciousness. Its proximate cause is the primary elements born of kamma rooted in the desire to smell.

Sāyitukāmatānidānakammasamuṭṭhānabhūtapasādalakkhaṇājivhā[V 0.0085], rasesu āviñchanarasā, jivhāviññāṇassa ādhārabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā, sāyitukāmatānidānakammajabhūtapadaṭṭhānā.

The tongue has the characteristic of sensitivity of the primary elements, arisen from kamma rooted in the desire to taste. Its function is to impinge upon flavors. Its manifestation is the state of being a support for tongue-consciousness. Its proximate cause is the primary elements born of kamma rooted in the desire to taste.

Phusitukāmatānidānakammasamuṭṭhānabhūtapasādalakkhaṇo kāyo, phoṭṭhabbesu āviñchanaraso, kāyaviññāṇassa ādhārabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāno, phusitukāmatānidānakammajabhūtapadaṭṭhāno.

The body has the characteristic of sensitivity of the primary elements, arisen from kamma rooted in the desire to touch. Its function is to impinge upon tangible objects. Its manifestation is the state of being a support for body-consciousness. Its proximate cause is the primary elements born of kamma rooted in the desire to touch.

Keci panāhu –

Some, however, say:

658.

658.

Tejādhikānaṃ bhūtānaṃ, pasādo pana cakkhuti;

Ākāsānilatoyubbiadhikānaṃ tu sesakā.

The sensitive element of the elements where fire predominates is the eye. But the remaining ones are of those where space, wind, water, and earth predominate.

659.

659.

Te panevaṃ tu vattabbā, “suttaṃ āharathā”ti hi;

Suttameva ca te addhā, na dakkhissanti kiñcipi.

They, however, should be told thus: ‘Bring a Sutta!’ But indeed, they will not see anything whatsoever in the Sutta itself.

660.

660.

Visese sati bhūtānaṃ, pasādo hi kathaṃ bhave;

Samānānaṃ hi bhūtānaṃ, pasādo paridīpito.

If there is a distinction among the elements, how can there be a sensitive element? For the sensitive element is explained as being among similar elements.

661.

661.

Tasmā nissayabhūtānaṃ, catunnaṃ sabbaso pana;

Pahāyeva panetesaṃ, visesaparikappanaṃ.

Therefore, this notion of distinctions concerning these four supporting elements should be completely abandoned.

662.

662.

Ñeyyā kammavisesena, pasādānaṃ visesatā;

Na hi bhūtavisesena, hoti tesaṃ visesatā.

The distinctions of the sensitive elements are to be known by distinctions in kamma, for their distinctions do not arise from distinctions in the elements.

663.

663.

Evametesu [M 0.0092] cakkhuñca, sotaṃ apattagāhakaṃ;

Sesaṃ tu pana ghānādittayaṃ sampattagāhakaṃ.

Thus, among these, the eye and ear are non-contact apprehenders, while the remaining three—nose, tongue, and body—are contact apprehenders.

Rūpanti rūpayatīti rūpaṃ, vaṇṇavikāramāpajjamānaṃ hadayaṅgatabhāvaṃ pakāsetīti attho. Taṃ pana cakkhupaṭihananalakkhaṇaṃ, cakkhuviññāṇassa visayabhāvarasaṃ, tasseva gocarabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, catumahābhūtapadaṭṭhānaṃ. Yathā cetaṃ, tathā sabbānipi upādārūpānīti[P 0.0068].

Form is called ‘form’ because it is afflicted; the meaning is that by undergoing a change of color, it reveals a state that is agreeable to the heart. It has the characteristic of impacting the eye; its function is to be the object of eye-consciousness; its manifestation is as the range of that same consciousness; and its proximate cause is the four great elements. Just as this is, so too are all derived forms.

Saddoti [V 0.0086] saddayatīti saddo, so pana sotapaṭihananalakkhaṇo, sotaviññāṇassa visayabhāvaraso, tasseva gocarabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāno.

Sound is called ‘sound’ because it sounds. It has the characteristic of striking the ear; its function is to be the object of ear-consciousness; and its manifestation is as the range of that very consciousness.

Rasoti rasanti tenāti raso, so jivhāpaṭihananalakkhaṇo, jivhāviññāṇassa visayabhāvaraso, tasseva gocarabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāno.

Taste is called ‘taste’ because one tastes by it. It has the characteristic of impacting the tongue; its function is to be the object of tongue-consciousness; and its manifestation is as the range of that same consciousness.

Gandhoti attānaṃ gandhayati sūcayatīti gandho, so ghānapaṭihananalakkhaṇo, ghānaviññāṇassa visayabhāvaraso, tasseva gocarabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāno.

Smell is called ‘smell’ because it scents itself, that is, makes itself known. It has the characteristic of impacting the nose; its function is to be the object of nose-consciousness; and its manifestation is as the range of that same consciousness.

Itthindriyanti –

The female faculty:

664.

664.

Kammajo itthibhāvoyaṃ, paṭisandhisamuṭṭhito;

Yañcetaṃ itthiliṅgādi, na tu taṃ indriyaṃ siyā.

This female state is produced by kamma, arisen at rebirth-linking. And those female characteristics and so forth are not the faculty itself.

665.

665.

Itthindriyaṃ paṭicceva, itthiliṅgādayo pana;

Pavatteyeva jāyante, na tāni paṭisandhiyaṃ.

Dependent on the female faculty, female characteristics and the like arise only during the course of life, not at rebirth-linking.

666.

666.

Na ca taṃ cakkhuviññeyyaṃ, manoviññeyyameva taṃ;

Itthiliṅgādayo cakkhuviññeyyā honti vā na vā.

That is not cognizable by eye-consciousness, but is cognizable only by mind-consciousness. Female characteristics and the like may or may not be cognizable by eye-consciousness.

667.

667.

Eseva ca nayo ñeyyo, sesepi purisindriye;

Idaṃ paṭhamakappānaṃ, ubhayaṃ tu pavattiyaṃ.

This same method should be understood for the remaining male faculty as well. For those of the first aeon, both of these arise in the course of existence.

668.

668.

Samuṭṭhātīti [M 0.0093] viññeyyaṃ, parato paṭisandhiyaṃ;

Pavattepi samuṭṭhāya, pavatte parivattati.

It should be understood that it originates from another at rebirth-linking. Even in the course of existence, having arisen, it changes in the course of existence.

669.

669.

Mahatā pāpakammena, purisattaṃ vinassati;

Mahatā kusaleneva, jāyate purisindriyaṃ.

Through great unwholesome kamma, manhood is destroyed. Through great wholesome kamma, the male faculty is produced.

670.

670.

Dubbalākusaleneva, itthiliṅgaṃ vinassati;

Dubbaleneva puññena, itthibhāvo hi jāyate.

Through weak unwholesome kamma, the female characteristic is destroyed. Through weak merit, the female state arises.

671.

671.

Ubhatobyañjanassāpi[V 0.0087], ekamevindriyaṃ siyā;

Evaṃ sante abhāvo ca, dutiyabyañjanassa tu.

Even for one with both sexual characteristics, there would be only one faculty. This being so, there would be an absence of the second characteristic.

672.

672.

Na cābhāvo siyā kasmā, na taṃ byañjanakāraṇaṃ;

Tassa kammasahāyaṃ hi, rāgacittaṃ tu kāraṇaṃ.

And why would there not be an absence? Because that is not the cause of the characteristic. Indeed, its companion is kamma, while the lustful mind is the cause.

Ubhayassa panetassa lakkhaṇādīni vuccati. Tattha itthibhāvalakkhaṇaṃ itthindriyaṃ, “itthī”ti pakāsanarasaṃ, itthiliṅganimittakuttākappānaṃ kāraṇabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ.

Now, the characteristics and so forth of both will be stated. Therein, the female faculty has the characteristic of the female state; its function is to indicate ‘woman’; and its manifestation is as the cause of female signs, features, deportment, and bearing.

Purisabhāvalakkhaṇaṃ purisindriyaṃ, “puriso”ti pakāsanarasaṃ, purisaliṅganimittakuttākappānaṃ kāraṇabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ.

The male faculty has the characteristic of the male state; its function is to indicate ‘man’; and its manifestation is as the cause of male signs, features, deportment, and bearing.

Jīvitanti –

The life faculty:

673.

673.

Jīvitindriyaniddese, vattabbaṃ yaṃ siyā idha;

Arūpajīvite vutta-nayeneva ca taṃ vade.

In the exposition of the life faculty, whatever should be said here, that should be said in the same way as was explained for immaterial life.

Lakkhaṇādīni [P 0.0069] panassa evaṃ veditabbāni. Sahajarūpaparipālanalakkhaṇaṃ jīvitindriyaṃ, tesaṃ pavattanarasaṃ, tesameva ṭhapanapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, yāpayitabbabhūtapadaṭṭhānanti.

Its characteristics and so forth should be understood thus: The life faculty has the characteristic of preserving co-nascent materiality; its function is to make them continue; its manifestation is the establishing of those same things; and its proximate cause is materiality that is to be maintained.

Vatthūti hadayavatthu.

The basis is the heart-basis.

674.

674.

Yaṃ nissāya manodhātu-manoviññāṇadhātuyo;

Vattanti pañcavokāre, taṃ “vatthū”ti pavuccati.

That depending on which the mind-element and mind-consciousness-element function in the five-aggregate existence, that is called ‘the basis’.

Manodhātumanoviññāṇadhātūnaṃ [M 0.0094] nissayalakkhaṇaṃ hadayavatthu, tāsañceva dhātūnaṃ ādhāraṇarasaṃ, ubbāhanapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ.

The heart-basis has the characteristic of being the support for the mind-element and mind-consciousness-element; its function is to sustain those very elements; and its manifestation is the upholding of them.

Āhāratāti kabaḷīkāro āhāro. Ojaṭṭhamakaṃ rūpaṃ āharatīti āhāro.

Nutriment is edible food. It is called ‘nutriment’ because it produces materiality that has nutritive essence as its eighth factor.

675.

675.

Yāya [V 0.0088] ojāya yāpenti, yattha yattha ca pāṇino;

Ayaṃ tu “kabaḷīkāro, āhāro”ti pavuccati.

By which nutritive essence beings sustain themselves, wherever they may be—this is called ‘edible food’.

676.

676.

Annapānādikaṃ vatthu, aggiṃ harati kammajaṃ;

Kevalaṃ na ca sakkoti, pāletuṃ jīvitaṃ pana.

Material food and drink can nourish the kamma-born fire, but cannot alone sustain life.

677.

677.

Ojā sakkoti pāletuṃ, harituṃ na ca pācakaṃ;

Haritumpi ca pāletuṃ, ubho sakkonti ekato.

Nutritive essence can sustain, but not nourish the digestive fire; both together are able to nourish and to sustain.

Lakkhaṇādito panassa ojālakkhaṇo kabaḷīkāro āhāro, rūpāharaṇaraso, upatthambhanapaccupaṭṭhāno, kabaḷaṃ katvā ajjhoharitabbavatthupadaṭṭhānoti veditabbo.

Its characteristic, etc., should be understood thus: Edible food has the characteristic of nutritive essence; its function is to produce material form; its manifestation is supporting; and its proximate cause is the object to be swallowed after making it into a mouthful.

Kāyaviññattiniddese kāyena attano bhāvaṃ viññāpentānaṃ kāyaggahaṇānusārena gahitāya etāya bhāvo viññāyatīti viññatti. Sayaṃ vā kāyaggahaṇānusārena viññāyatītipi viññatti. “Kāyena saṃvaro sādhu, sādhu vācāya saṃvaro”ti āgato copanasaṅkhāto kāyova viññatti kāyaviññatti. Kāyavipphandanena adhippāyaviññāpanahetuttā sayañca tathā viññeyyattā kāyena viññattītipi kāyaviññatti.

In the exposition of bodily intimation: ‘Intimation’ (viññatti) is so called because, for one who makes known one’s own state by means of the body, that state is known by this (intimation) in accordance with the apprehension of bodily action. Or, ‘intimation’ is so called because it is itself known according to the apprehension of bodily action. Moreover, the body itself, designated as conduct and mentioned in the saying ‘Restraint in body is good; restraint in speech is good,’ is ‘bodily intimation.’ Because it is the cause of making intention known through bodily movement, and because it is itself thus to be known, it is also called ‘bodily intimation.’

678.

678.

Tattha yā sahajātassa, cittajāniladhātuyā;

Rūpassa calane hetu, ekākāravikāratā.

Herein, that single mode of alteration which is the cause for the movement of co-nascent materiality of the mind-born wind element.

679.

679.

Kāyaviññatti nāmāyaṃ, kāyadvāranti sā matā;

Tattha yā cetanāsiddhā, puññāpuññavasā pana.

This is called bodily intimation; it is reckoned as the body-door. And that which is accomplished there by volition, according to what is wholesome and unwholesome—

680.

680.

Kāyakammanti [M 0.0095] niddiṭṭhā, satthunā sā hitesinā;

Sampavatti panetissā, vacīdvārepi jāyate.

that is called ‘bodily action,’ as taught by the Teacher, the Well-wisher. But its occurrence also arises at the speech door.

681.

681.

Labhitvā [P 0.0070] panupatthambhaṃ, ekāvajjanavīthiyaṃ;

Heṭṭhāhi chahi cittehi, vāyodhātusamuṭṭhitaṃ.

Having obtained support in a single adverting process by means of the six preceding consciousnesses, arisen from the wind element.

682.

682.

Sattamena tu cittena, vāyodhātusamuṭṭhitā;

Cāleti sahajaṃ rūpaṃ, viññattisahitāttanā.

But with the seventh consciousness, arisen from the wind element, it moves the co-nascent form, together with intimation itself.

Vacīviññattiniddese [V 0.0089] pana –

In the exposition of verbal intimation, however—

683.

683.

Paccayo cittajātāya, upādinnakaghaṭṭane;

Yo ākāravikāreko, ayaṃ pathavidhātuyā.

That single mode of alteration which is the condition for the mind-born (sound) through the impact on the appropriated (body), this is of the earth element.

684.

684.

Vacīviññatti viññeyyā, saha saddavasā pana;

Vacīdvāranti niddiṭṭhā, sāva sakyakulindunā.

Verbal intimation is to be understood as dependent on sound. It itself is declared as the verbal door by the Lord of the Sakyans.

685.

685.

Saddo na cittajo atthi, vinā viññattighaṭṭanaṃ;

Dhātusaṅghaṭṭaneneva, saha saddo hi jāyati.

There is no mind-born sound without the impact of intimation. Indeed, sound arises together with the collision of elements.

686.

686.

Sā viññāpanato ceva, ayaṃ viññeyyatopi ca;

Viññattīti siyā tassā, sambhavo kārakadvaye.

Because it makes known, and also because it is knowable, it is called ‘intimation’; its arising is in two factors.

687.

687.

Na viññattidvayaṃ aṭṭha, rūpāni viya cittajaṃ;

Cittajānaṃ vikārattā, cittajanti pavuccati.

The two intimations are not mind-born like the eight forms. Because they are modifications of mind-born (forms), they are called mind-born.

Tattha kāyaviññatti adhippāyapakāsanarasā, kāyavipphandanahetubhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā, cittasamuṭṭhānavāyodhātupadaṭṭhānā. Tathā vacīviññatti adhippāyapakāsanarasā, vacīghosassa hetubhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā, cittasamuṭṭhānapathavīdhātupadaṭṭhānā.

Here, bodily intimation has the function of revealing intention; its manifestation is as the cause of bodily movement; and its proximate cause is the mind-born wind element. Similarly, verbal intimation has the function of revealing intention; its manifestation is as the cause of speech sound; and its proximate cause is the mind-born earth element.

688.

688.

Na kassatīti ākāso, rūpānaṃ vivaro pana;

Yo rūpānaṃ paricchedo, svākāsoti pavuccati.

It is called ‘space’ (ākāsa) because it is not tilled. But it is an opening for forms. That which delimits forms is called ‘space’.

So [M 0.0096] rūpaparicchedalakkhaṇo, rūpapariyantapakāsanaraso, rūpamariyādapaccupaṭṭhāno, asamphuṭṭhabhāvachiddavivarabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāno vā, paricchinnarūpapadaṭṭhāno.

It has the characteristic of delimiting forms; its function is to reveal the extent of forms; its manifestation is as the limit of forms, or its manifestation is as un-impactedness, hollowness, and openness; and its proximate cause is delimited form.

Rūpassa lahutādittayaniddese –

In the exposition of the triad of lightness, etc., of form—

689.

689.

Heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva, rūpassa lahutādisu;

Tisso rūpavikārāti, viññātabbā vibhāvinā.

In the way explained below, the discerning should understand that lightness, etc., of form are three alterations of form.

690.

690.

Etāsaṃ [V 0.0090] pana tissannaṃ, kamato ca pavattiyaṃ;

Arogī madditaṃ cammaṃ, dhantahemaṃ nidassanaṃ.

For these three, in order of their occurrence, the examples are: a healthy person, softened leather, and refined gold.

691.

691.

Kammaṃ kātuṃ na sakkoti, lahutādittayaṃ pana;

Āhārādittayaṃyeva, taṃ karoti tato tijaṃ.

But the triad of lightness, etc., cannot perform action. Only the triad of nutriment, etc., makes it (the body) capable; therefore, it is threefold in origin.

Tattha [P 0.0071] adandhatālakkhaṇā rūpassa lahutā, rūpānaṃ garubhāvavinodanarasā, lahuparivattitāpaccupaṭṭhānā, lahurūpapadaṭṭhānā.

Here, the lightness of form has the characteristic of non-sluggishness; its function is removing the heaviness of forms; its manifestation is quick change; and its proximate cause is light form.

Athaddhatālakkhaṇā rūpassa mudutā, rūpānaṃ thaddhabhāvavinodanarasā, sabbakiriyāsu avirodhitāpaccupaṭṭhānā, mudurūpapadaṭṭhānā.

The softness of form has the characteristic of non-rigidity; its function is to eliminate the rigidity of forms; its manifestation is non-opposition to all activities; and its proximate cause is soft form.

Sarīrakiriyānukūlakammaññatālakkhaṇā rūpassa kammaññatā, akammaññatāvinodanarasā, adubbalabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā, kammaññatārūpapadaṭṭhānā. Etā pana tissopi na aññamaññaṃ vijahanti.

The wieldiness of form has the characteristic of suitability for bodily action; its function is removing unwieldiness; its manifestation is non-weakness; and its proximate cause is wieldy form. These three, however, do not abandon one another.

Upacayasantatiniddese –

In the exposition of accumulation and continuity—

692.

692.

Rūpānamācayo yo hi, vutto upacayoti so;

Anuppabandhatā tesaṃ, santatīti pavuccati.

That accumulation of forms, indeed, is called ‘growth’ (upacaya). Their unbroken sequence is called ‘continuity’ (santati).

693.

693.

Atthato [M 0.0097] ubhayampetaṃ, jātirūpanti dīpitaṃ;

Vuttamākāranānattā, veneyyānaṃ vasena vā.

In meaning, both of these are explained as 'birth-form'. They are spoken of separately owing to the diversity of their aspects, or according to the disposition of those to be trained.

Lakkhaṇādito pana ācayalakkhaṇo rūpassa upacayo, pubbantato rūpānaṃ ummujjāpanaraso, niyyātanapaccupaṭṭhāno, paripuṇṇabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāno vā, upacitarūpapadaṭṭhāno.

Furthermore, from the standpoint of its characteristic, etc., the accumulation of form has the characteristic of heaping up; its function is to cause forms to emerge from their initial point; its manifestation is as leading forth, or as completeness; and its proximate cause is accumulated form.

Pavattilakkhaṇā rūpassa santati, anuppabandhanarasā, anupacchedapaccupaṭṭhānā, anuppabandharūpapadaṭṭhānā.

The continuity of form has the characteristic of proceeding. Its function is unbroken succession. Its manifestation is non-severance. Its proximate cause is form that is an unbroken succession.

Jarāniddese [V 0.0091] jīraṇaṃ jarā.

In the explanation of aging, decay is aging.

694.

694.

Duvidhāyaṃ jarā nāma, pākaṭāpākaṭāti ca;

Pākaṭā rūpadhammesu, arūpesu apākaṭā.

Aging is twofold, namely, manifest and unmanifest. It is manifest in material phenomena, unmanifest in immaterial phenomena.

Rūpassa paripākatālakkhaṇā rūpassa jaratā, upanayanarasā, sabhāvānaṃ apagamepi nasabhāvāpagamapaccupaṭṭhānā vīhipurāṇabhāvo viya, paripaccamānarūpapadaṭṭhānā.

The characteristic of the aging of form is its ripening. Its function is drawing near. It is manifested as the non-disappearance of its intrinsic nature, even with the passing away of its former states, like the oldness of rice; its proximate cause is form that is in the process of ripening.

Paribhedalakkhaṇā rūpassa aniccatā, saṃsīdanarasā, khayavayapaccupaṭṭhānā, paribhijjamānarūpapadaṭṭhānāti veditabbāti.

The impermanence of form has the characteristic of disruption. Its function is to waste away. Its manifestation is decay and dissolution. Its proximate cause is form that is breaking apart—this should be understood.

Evaṃ catuvīsati upādārūpāni veditabbāni.

Thus, the twenty-four derived material phenomena should be understood.

695.

695.

Bhūtarūpāni cattāri, upādā catuvīsati;

Aṭṭhavīsati rūpāni, sabbāneva bhavanti hi.

Four are the primary elements, twenty-four are the derived forms; twenty-eight forms there are in total, all of them indeed.

696.

696.

Imesu pana rūpesu, asammohatthameva taṃ;

Samodhānaṃ samuṭṭhānaṃ, nipphannaṃ saṅkhatampi ca.

Now, concerning these forms, the following is solely for the purpose of non-delusion: combination, origination, the produced, and also the conditioned.

697.

697.

Codanaṃ [P 0.0072] parihārañca, nayamekavidhādikaṃ;

Saṅkhepena pavakkhāmi, pakiṇṇakamidaṃ suṇa.

Objection and rebuttal, and the method of one kind and so forth, I will explain briefly. Listen to this miscellaneous section.

Tattha [M 0.0098] samodhānanti sabbameva idaṃ rūpaṃ sabbasamodhānato pathavīdhātu āpodhātu tejodhātu vāyodhātu cakkhāyatanaṃ…pe… jaratā aniccatāti aṭṭhavīsatividhaṃ ca hoti, ito aññaṃ rūpaṃ nāma natthi. Keci pana middhavādino “middharūpaṃ nāma atthī”ti vadanti, te “addhā munīsi sambuddho, natthi nīvaraṇā tavā”ti ca “thinamiddhanīvaraṇaṃ avijjānīvaraṇañca nīvaraṇasampayutta”nti sampayuttavacanato ca mahāpakaraṇapaṭṭhāne “nīvaraṇaṃ dhammaṃ paṭicca nīvaraṇo dhammo uppajjati napurejātapaccayā”ti arūpepi “kāmacchandanīvaraṇaṃ paṭicca thinamiddhauddhaccakukkuccāvijjānīvaraṇa”nti evamādīhi pāḷīhi virujjhanato ca arūpameva middhanti paṭikkhipitabbā.

Herein, 'combination' means that all this form, by way of complete combination, is the earth element, water element, fire element, air element, the eye-base… up to aging and impermanence—thus it is of twenty-eight kinds. There is no other form besides this. However, some who are proponents of middha say, 'There is such a thing as middha-form.' They should be refuted because they contradict passages such as, 'Surely, you are a sage, enlightened; there are no hindrances for you,' and from the statement of association, 'The sloth-torpor hindrance and the ignorance hindrance are associated with hindrances.' Also, in the Great Treatise, the Paṭṭhāna, it is said, 'A hindrance-dhamma arises in dependence on a hindrance-dhamma, not by way of the pre-nascence condition,' and even in the immaterial realm, 'In dependence on the hindrance of sensual desire, [arise] the hindrances of sloth-torpor, restlessness-and-worry, and ignorance.' Thus, by contradicting such scriptural statements, it should be rejected that middha is form, for it is indeed immaterial.

698.

698.

Arūpepi [V 0.0092] panetassa, middhassuppatti pāṭhato;

Niṭṭhametthāvagantabbā, arūpanti ca viññunā.

Furthermore, since the arising of this middha even in the immaterial realm is known from the text, the wise should understand the conclusion here: that it is indeed immaterial.

Apare “balarūpena saddhiṃ ekūnatiṃsa, sambhavarūpena saddhiṃ tiṃsa, jātirūpena saddhiṃ ekatiṃsa, rogarūpena saddhiṃ dvattiṃsa rūpānī”ti vadanti. Tepi tesaṃ visuṃ visuṃ abhāvaṃ dassetvā paṭikkhipitabbā. Vāyodhātuyā gahitāya balarūpaṃ gahitameva, aññaṃ balarūpaṃ nāma natthi. Āpodhātuyā sambhavarūpaṃ, upacayasantatīti jātirūpaṃ, jaratāaniccatādīhi rogarūpaṃ gahitaṃ, aññaṃ rogarūpaṃ nāma natthīti, tasmā aṭṭhavīsatividhāneva rūpānīti.

Others say, 'There are twenty-nine forms when combined with strength-form, thirty with origination-form, thirty-one with birth-form, and thirty-two with disease-form.' These too should be refuted by showing their individual non-existence. When the air element is taken, strength-form is already taken; there is no other strength-form. With the water element, origination-form is taken; birth-form is accumulation and continuity; and with aging and impermanence, disease-form is taken—there is no other disease-form. Therefore, there are only twenty-eight kinds of forms.

Evaṃ samodhānato veditabbānīti.

Thus, it should be understood by way of combination.

Samuṭṭhānanti cattāri rūpasamuṭṭhānāni utucittāhārakammānīti.

Origination refers to the four originations of form: temperature, mind, nutriment, and kamma.

699.

699.

Kammaṃ [M 0.0099] utu ca cittañca, āhāro rūpahetuyo;

Eteheva ca rūpāni, jāyanti na panaññato.

Kamma, temperature, mind, and nutriment—these are the causes of form; by these alone do forms arise, and not from any other.

700.

700.

Tasmā ekasamuṭṭhānā, ekādasa bhavanti hi;

Aṭṭhindriyāni vatthuñca, viññattidvayameva ca.

Therefore, there are indeed eleven types of form that have a single origination: the eight faculties, the base, and the two intimations.

701.

701.

Aṭṭhindriyāni vatthuñca, ekanteneva kammajā;

Cittajaṃyeva viññatti-dvayaṃ vuttaṃ mahesinā.

The eight faculties and the base are solely born of kamma; the two intimations are said by the Great Sage to be born of mind.

702.

702.

Cittena utunā ceva, saddo dvīhi samuṭṭhito;

Utuāhāracittehi, lahutādittayaṃ kataṃ.

By mind and temperature, sound arises from two causes; by temperature, nutriment, and mind, the triad of lightness and so forth is produced.

703.

703.

Vaṇṇo [P 0.0073] gandho raso ojā,

Catasso cāpi dhātuyo;

Santatyupacayākāsā,

Ekādasa catubbhavā.

Color, odor, taste, and nutritive essence, and also the four elements; continuity, accumulation, and space—these eleven have a fourfold origin.

704.

704.

Ekādasekato [V 0.0093] jātā,

Dvijekova tijā tayo;

Catujekādasakkhātā,

Dve na kenaci jāyare.

Eleven are born from one cause; one is born from two causes; three are born from three causes; eleven are said to be from four causes; two are not born from any cause.

705.

705.

Kammena vīsati rūpā, sattarasa tu cetasā;

Utunā dasapañceva, cuddasāhārato pana.

From kamma, twenty forms; from mind, seventeen; from temperature, fifteen indeed; and from nutriment, fourteen.

706.

706.

Chasaṭṭhi sabbānetāni, samuṭṭhānavibhāgato;

Aṭṭhasaṭṭhi ca honteva, jaratāniccatāhi te.

All these are sixty-six, according to the division by origination; they become sixty-eight with aging and impermanence.

707.

707.

Jaratāniccatā ceva, na kenaci samuṭṭhitā;

Jātassa pākabhedattā, jāyeyyuṃ yadi tānipi.

Aging and impermanence are not originated by any cause, for they are the ripening and breaking up of what has been born. If they too were to arise...

708.

708.

Evaṃ sante tu tesampi, pākabhedā siyuṃ na hi;

Pāko paccati bhedo vā, na ca bhijjati natthi taṃ.

If that were so, then they too would have their own ripening and breaking up, which is not the case. Does ripening itself ripen, or does breaking up itself break up? That does not happen; there is no such thing.

709.

709.

Jātassa [M 0.0100] pākabhedattā, dvayametaṃ na jāyati;

Siyā katthaci buddhettha, “rūpassupacayo”ti hi.

Because they are the ripening and breaking up of what is born, this pair does not arise from a cause. But, it might be said, did not the Buddha state somewhere, 'the accumulation of form'?

710.

710.

Vacanena yathā “jāti, jāyatī”ti ca dīpitaṃ;

Pākopi paccatevaṃ tu, bhedopi paribhijjatu.

Just as it is explained by the expression 'birth is born,' so too let ripening ripen and let breaking up break up.

711.

711.

Na ceva jāyate jāti, iti ñeyyā vibhāvinā;

Jāyamānassa dhammassa, nibbattīti pakāsitā.

But birth itself is not born—thus it should be known by the discerning. It is proclaimed as the production of a phenomenon that is in the process of being born.

712.

712.

Tattha yathā siyā jāti, yesaṃ dhammānameva sā;

Tappaccayattavohāraṃ, abhinibbattisammutiṃ.

Therein, just as birth belongs to those very phenomena for which it occurs, it receives the designation of being dependent on them, the convention of arising.

713.

713.

Labhateva tathā tesaṃ, pākabhedā labbhanti te;

Tappaccayattavohāraṃ, abhinibbattisammutiṃ.

Just so, for those phenomena, their ripening and breaking up are obtained; they obtain the designation of being dependent on them, the convention of arising.

714.

714.

Evaṃ idaṃ dvayañcāpi, hoti kammādisambhavaṃ;

Na pākabhedā vohāraṃ, taṃ labhanti kadācipi.

Thus, while this pair pertains to what arises from kamma and so on, ripening and breaking up themselves never obtain that designation of arising.

715.

715.

Kasmā [V 0.0094] hi janakānaṃ tu, paccayānamabhāvato;

Ānubhāvakhaṇuppāde, jātiyā pana labbhati.

For what reason, indeed, is birth obtained at the moment of the arising of the effect, given the absence of the generative conditions?

716.

716.

Tappaccayattavohāraṃ, abhinibbattisammutiṃ;

Tasmā labhati jāti ca, labhatī netaradvayaṃ.

Therefore, birth obtains the designation of being dependent on those conditions and the convention of arising; it does not obtain the other two.

717.

717.

Jiyyatīti na vattabbaṃ, taṃ dvayaṃ bhijjatīti vā;

Ānubhāvakhaṇe tassa, paccayānamabhāvato.

It should not be said, 'It ages,' nor that 'This pair breaks up,' because at the moment of its effect, the conditions for that are absent.

718.

718.

“Aniccaṃ saṅkhatañcetaṃ, jarāmaraṇa”miccapi;

Vuttattā jāyaticcetaṃ, atha maññasi ce tuvaṃ.

If you think, 'This is impermanent and conditioned, and also aging and death,' because it is said, 'It is born,' then...

719.

719.

Evampi ca na vattabbaṃ, sā hi pariyāyadesanā;

Aniccānaṃ tu dhammānaṃ, jarāmaraṇato tathā.

Even so, it should not be said, for that is a teaching by way of an alternative expression; just as for impermanent phenomena, their impermanence is known from their aging and death.

720.

720.

Aniccaṃ [M 0.0101] saṅkhatañcāti, vuttaṃ viññattiyo viya;

Yadi evaṃ tayametaṃ, ajātattā ca sabbathā.

'Impermanent and conditioned' is said, like the intimations. If so, this triad would be altogether unoriginated.

721.

721.

Natthīti [P 0.0074] ce khaṃpupphaṃva, niccaṃ vāsaṅkhataṃ viya;

Nobhayaṃ panidaṃ kasmā, nissayāyattavuttito.

If it is argued that it 'does not exist,' like a sky-flower, or is 'permanent,' like the unconditioned—it is, however, neither of these. Why? Because its existence is dependent on a support.

722.

722.

Bhāve pathaviyādīnaṃ, nissayānaṃ tu bhāvato;

Tasmā hi ca khaṃpupphaṃva, na natthi pana taṃ tayaṃ.

Due to the existence of the supports, namely earth and the like, therefore that triad is not non-existent like a sky-flower.

723.

723.

Yasmā pathaviyādīnaṃ, abhāvena ca labbhati;

Tasmā na pana niccaṃ vā, nibbānaṃ viya taṃ tayaṃ.

Because it is subject to absence along with earth and the like, therefore that triad is not permanent like Nibbāna.

Nipphannanti ettha cattāro mahābhūtā cakkhusotaghānajivhākāyarūpasaddagandharasaitthipurisajīvitindriyakabaḷīkārāhārahadayavatthūti aṭṭhārasa rūpāni nipphannāni nāma. Sesāni dasa anipphannāni nāma.

Herein, 'produced': the four great elements; the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body faculties; visible form, sound, odor, taste; the femininity and masculinity faculties; the life faculty; edible food; and the heart-base—these eighteen forms are called 'produced'. The remaining ten are called 'unproduced'.

724.

724.

Aṭṭhārasa nipphannāni, anipphannāvasesakā;

Yadi honti anipphannā, bhaveyyuṃ te asaṅkhatā.

Eighteen are produced; the remaining are unproduced. If they were unproduced, they would be unconditioned.

725.

725.

Tesameva [V 0.0095] ca rūpānaṃ, vikārattā asaṅkhatā;

Kathaṃ nāma bhaveyyuṃ te, nipphannā ceva saṅkhatā.

Since they are but a modification of those very forms, how could they be unconditioned? They are indeed produced and conditioned.

Evaṃ nipphannasaṅkhato veditabbo.

Thus should the produced and conditioned be understood.

Codanāparihāranti ettha –

Herein, regarding 'Objection and Rebuttal'—

726.

726.

Itthibhāvo pumattañca, jīvitaṃ sambhavopi ca;

Tathā kāyappasādoti, sabbaṭṭhānāti vaṇṇitā.

Femininity, masculinity, life, and origination, as well as bodily sensitivity—these are described as pervading the entire body.

727.

727.

Evaṃ sante tu dhammānaṃ, hoti saṅkaradosatā;

Cakkhukāyapasādānaṃ, ekattaṃ upapajjati.

This being so, there would be the fault of the intermingling of phenomena; the oneness of the eye-sensitivity and the body-sensitivity would result.

728.

728.

Aññaṃ pana ca aññasmiṃ, na catthi paramatthato;

Tasmā kāyindriyaṃ cakkhu-pasādena na saṅkaraṃ.

But in an ultimate sense, one thing is not in another; therefore, the body faculty is not intermingled with the eye-sensitivity.

729.

729.

Aññamaññāvinibbhogavasena [M 0.0102] tu pavattito;

Tesaṃ ṭhānantaraṃ vattuṃ, na sakkā samayaññunā.

But due to their occurring in a state of mutual inseparability, it is not possible for one who knows the doctrine to state their separate locations.

730.

730.

Yāvatā anupādinnasantānaṃ atthi tattha so;

Atthi kāyapasādoti, tasmā evamudīritaṃ.

Insofar as the appropriated continuum exists, that bodily sensitivity is present there; therefore, it was stated thus.

731.

731.

Lakkhaṇādivasenāpi, nānattaṃ samupāgataṃ;

Dhajānaṃ pañcavaṇṇānaṃ, chāyā upamataṃ gatā.

Diversity is also established by way of characteristics and so on; this may be compared to the shadow of five-colored banners.

732.

732.

Tasmā [P 0.0075] hi pana dhammānaṃ, aññamaññaṃ vimissatā;

Na hotevāti viññeyyā, viññunā samayaññunā.

Therefore, it should be understood by the wise person who knows the doctrine that there is no intermingling of phenomena with one another.

Evaṃ nipphannānipphannabhāvo, codanāparihāro ca veditabbo.

Thus, the state of the produced and the unproduced, and the objection and rebuttal, should be understood.

Nayamekavidhādikanti –

Regarding 'The Method, of One Kind, etc.'—

733.

733.

Lokikattā [V 0.0096] nahetuttā, saṅkhatattā ca sāsavā;

Sabbamekavidhaṃ rūpaṃ, paccayāyattavuttito.

In that it is worldly, not a cause, conditioned, and with influxes, all form is of one kind, because its existence is dependent on conditions.

734.

734.

Ajjhattikabahiddhā ca, indriyānindriyāpi ca;

Sukhumoḷārikā ceva, upādinnādito dvidhā.

Internal and external; faculties and non-faculties; subtle and gross; and twofold as appropriated and unappropriated.

735.

735.

Cakkhuāyatanādīni, pañca ajjhattikāni tu;

Tevīsatividhaṃ sesaṃ, bāhiranti pavuccati.

The five beginning with the eye-base are internal; the remaining twenty-three kinds are said to be external.

736.

736.

Cakkhusotindriyādīni, indriyāni panaṭṭha tu;

Sesañca tu vīsaṃ rūpaṃ, anindriyamudīritaṃ.

The eight beginning with the eye faculty are faculties; the remaining twenty forms are declared as non-faculties.

737.

737.

Cakkhuāyatanādīni, nava phoṭṭhabbameva ca;

Taṃ bārasavidhaṃ rūpaṃ, oḷārikamudīritaṃ.

The nine forms beginning with the eye-base, and the tangible object as well; that twelvefold form is declared to be gross.

738.

738.

Sesāni pana rūpāni, sukhumāni tu soḷasa;

Kammajaṃ tu upādinnaṃ, anupādinnamaññathā.

But the remaining sixteen forms are subtle. Kamma-born form is appropriated; otherwise, it is unappropriated.

Evañca duvidhaṃ hoti.

And thus it is twofold.

Puna [M 0.0103] sanidassanasappaṭighaanidassanasappaṭigha- anidassanaappaṭighabhedato ca, kammajākammajanevakammajānākammajabhedato ca tividhaṃ. Tattha rūpāyatanaṃ sanidassanasappaṭighaṃ, ekādasavidhaṃ sesoḷārikarūpaṃ anidassanasappaṭighaṃ, sesaṃ soḷasavidhaṃ sukhumarūpaṃ anidassanaappaṭighaṃ. Kammato jātaṃ kammajaṃ, aṭṭhindriyāni, vatthu ca kammajaṃ, tadaññappaccayā jātaṃ akammajaṃ, nakutoci jātaṃ nevakammajānākammajaṃ jaratā aniccatā ca. Evaṃ tividhaṃ hoti.

Again, it is threefold by way of the distinction into visible and resistant, invisible and resistant, and invisible and non-resistant; and by way of the distinction into kamma-born, non-kamma-born, and neither kamma-born nor non-kamma-born. Herein, the form base is visible and resistant. The remaining eleven gross materialities are invisible and resistant. The remaining sixteen subtle materialities are invisible and non-resistant. Kamma-born are the eight faculties and the heart-basis. Non-kamma-born is that which is born from other conditions. Neither kamma-born nor non-kamma-born are decay and impermanence, which are born from no cause. Thus, it is threefold.

Puna diṭṭhasutamutaviññātavasena ca, dvārañceva vatthu ca, dvārameva hutvā na vatthu ca, vatthumeva hutvā na dvārañca, neva dvārañca na vatthu cāti evaṃ bhedato ca, dvārañcevindriyañca, dvāraṃyeva hutvā nevindriyañca, indriyameva hutvā na dvārañca, neva dvārañca nevindriyañcāti evaṃ [V 0.0097] bhedato ca, vatthu ceva indriyañca, indriyameva hutvā na vatthu ca, vatthumeva hutvā nevindriyañca, nevindriyaṃ na vatthu ceti evaṃ bhedato ca catubbidhaṃ.

Again, it is fourfold by way of the distinction into seen, heard, sensed, and cognized; and by way of the distinction into door and basis, only door and not basis, only basis and not door, and neither door nor basis; and by way of the distinction into door and faculty, only door and not faculty, only faculty and not door, and neither door nor faculty; and by way of the distinction into basis and faculty, only faculty and not basis, only basis and not faculty, and neither faculty nor basis.

Tattha [P 0.0076] diṭṭhaṃ nāma rūpāyatanaṃ, sutaṃ nāma saddāyatanaṃ, mutaṃ nāma gandharasaphoṭṭhabbāyatanattayaṃ, viññātaṃ nāma avasesacakkhāyatanādipañcakaṃ, soḷasavidhaṃ sukhumarūpañca. Cakkhāyatanādipañcakaṃ dvārañceva vatthu ca, viññattidvayaṃ dvārameva hoti, na vatthu, hadayavatthu vatthumeva hoti, na dvāraṃ, sesaṃ sabbaṃ rūpaṃ neva dvāraṃ na vatthu ca. Tatiyacatukke indriyameva hutvā na dvāranti itthindriyapurisindriyajīvitindriyāni. Imāni hi indriyāneva honti, na dvārāni, sesamanantaracatukke vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Catutthacatukke tatiyapadaṃ hadayavatthuṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, sesaṃ vuttanayameva. Evaṃ catubbidhaṃ hotīti veditabbaṃ.

Therein, the seen is the form base; the heard is the sound base; the sensed is the three bases of odor, taste, and the tangible; the cognized is the remaining five bases beginning with the eye base, and the sixteenfold subtle materiality. The five bases beginning with the eye base are both door and basis; the two kinds of intimation are only doors, not a basis; the heart-basis is only a basis, not a door; and all the remaining materiality is neither a door nor a basis. In the third tetrad, 'only faculty and not door' refers to the femininity faculty, masculinity faculty, and life faculty. These are indeed faculties, not doors. The rest should be understood in the way stated in the immediately preceding tetrad. In the fourth tetrad, the third term refers to the heart-basis; the rest is in the way stated. Thus, it should be understood as fourfold.

Puna ekajadvijatijacatujanakutocijātabhedato, dvārindriyaṃ vatthu ca, dvārameva hutvā nevindriyaṃ na vatthu ca, vatthumeva hutvā nevindriyaṃ na dvārañca, indriyameva hutvā na vatthu na dvārañca, nevindriyaṃ [M 0.0104] na vatthu na dvārañcāti evaṃ pabhedato pañcavidhaṃ.

Again, it is fivefold by way of the distinction into single-born, double-born, triple-born, four-born, and not-born-from-any-cause; and by way of the distinction into: door, faculty, and basis; only door, not faculty or basis; only basis, not faculty or door; only faculty, not basis or door; and neither faculty, nor basis, nor door.

Tattha –

Therein:

739.

739.

Aṭṭhindriyāni vatthuñca, viññattidvayameva ca;

Ekādasavidhaṃ rūpaṃ, ekajanti pavuccati.

The eight faculties, the basis, and the two kinds of intimation; this elevenfold materiality is said to be single-born.

740.

740.

Saddo eko dvijo nāma, lahutādittayaṃ tijaṃ;

Ekādasavidhaṃ sesaṃ, catujanti pakāsitaṃ.

Sound alone is called double-born; the triad beginning with lightness is triple-born; the remaining eleven kinds are proclaimed as four-born.

741.

741.

Jaratāniccatā ceva, nakutoci bhave pana;

Cakkhādipañcakaṃ dvāraṃ, indriyaṃ vatthumeva ca.

Decay and impermanence, moreover, are not born from any cause. The five beginning with the eye are door, faculty, and basis.

742.

742.

Viññattīnaṃ dvayaṃ dvāraṃ, nevindriyaṃ na vatthu ca;

Hadayavatthu vatthūva, na dvāraṃ nevindriyaṃ pana.

The two kinds of intimation are doors, neither faculty nor basis. The heart-basis is only a basis, neither a door nor a faculty.

Itthipurisajīvitindriyāni [V 0.0098] indriyameva na vatthu na dvārañca, sesaṃ pana rūpaṃ nevindriyaṃ na vatthu na dvāranti. Evaṃ pañcavidhanti veditabbaṃ.

The femininity, masculinity, and life faculties are only faculties, neither basis nor door. The remaining materiality is neither faculty, nor basis, nor door. Thus, it should be understood as fivefold.

Puna kammajacittajautucittajautucittāhārajacatujanakutocijātabhedato, cakkhuviññeyyasotaghānajivhākāyamanoviññeyyavasena chabbidhaṃ.

Again, it is sixfold by way of the distinction into kamma-born, mind-born, temperature-and-mind-born, temperature-mind-and-nutriment-born, four-born, and not-born-from-any-cause; and by way of the distinction into eye-cognizable, ear-cognizable, nose-cognizable, tongue-cognizable, body-cognizable, and mind-cognizable.

Tattha aṭṭhindriyāni vatthu ca kammajameva, viññattidvayaṃ cittajameva, saddo utucittajo, lahutādittayaṃ utucittāhārajameva, sesaṃ ekādasavidhaṃ catujaṃ nāma, jaratā aniccatā nakutocijātaṃ nāma. Dutiyachakke cakkhuviññeyyaṃ [P 0.0077] nāma cakkhuviññāṇena viññeyyaṃ rūpāyatanaṃ…pe… kāyaviññeyyaṃ nāma phoṭṭhabbāyatanaṃ, manoviññeyyaṃ nāma sesā pañca oḷārikā ca soḷasa sukhumarūpāni cāti ekavīsatividhaṃ hoti. Evaṃ chabbidhaṃ hoti.

Herein, the eight faculties and the basis are kamma-born alone; the two kinds of intimation are mind-born alone; sound is born of temperature and mind; the triad beginning with lightness is born of temperature, mind, and nutriment alone; the remaining eleven kinds are called four-born; decay and impermanence are called not-born-from-any-cause. In the second sixfold classification, the eye-cognizable is the form base, cognizable by eye-consciousness… and so on… the body-cognizable is the tangible base; the mind-cognizable is the remaining five gross and the sixteen subtle materialities, thus being twenty-one kinds. Thus, it is sixfold.

Puna chavatthuavatthubhedato ca, cakkhuviññeyyaṃ sotaghānajivhākāyaviññeyyaṃ manodhātuviññeyyaṃ manoviññāṇadhātuviññeyyanti sattavidhaṃ hoti.

Again, it is sevenfold by way of the distinction into six bases and non-bases; and by way of the distinction into eye-cognizable, ear-cognizable, nose-cognizable, tongue-cognizable, body-cognizable, mind-element-cognizable, and mind-consciousness-element-cognizable.

Tattha [M 0.0105] cakkhādipañcavatthūni hadayavatthunā saddhiṃ cha vatthūni, sesaṃ bāvīsatividhaṃ rūpaṃ avatthu nāma, dutiyasattakamuttānameva. Evaṃ sattavidhaṃ hoti.

Herein, the five bases beginning with the eye, together with the heart-basis, are the six bases. The remaining twenty-two types of materiality are called non-bases. The second sevenfold classification is just as stated. Thus, it is sevenfold.

Puna sattadvārādvārabhedato aṭṭhavidhaṃ. Tattha cakkhudvārādīni pañca kāyaviññattivacīviññattidvārehi saddhiṃ satta dvārāni, sesamadvāranti evaṃ aṭṭhavidhaṃ hoti.

Again, it is eightfold by way of the distinction into seven doors and non-door. Herein, the five doors beginning with the eye-door, together with the body-intimation and speech-intimation doors, are seven doors; the remainder is non-door. Thus, it is eightfold.

Puna aṭṭhindriyānindriyabhedato pana navavidhaṃ.

Again, it is ninefold by way of the distinction into the eight faculties and non-faculties.

Puna navakammajākammajabhedato dasavidhaṃ.

Again, it is tenfold by way of the distinction into the nine kamma-born and the non-kamma-born.

Puna āyatanabhedato ekādasavidhaṃ.

Again, it is elevenfold by way of the distinction of the bases.

Bhavesu rūpakalāpapavattibhedato bahuvidhanti veditabbaṃ.

In the realms of existence, it should be understood as manifold by way of the distinction in the occurrence of material groups.

743.

743.

Ito paraṃ pavakkhāmi, kāmarūpabhavadvaye;

Uppattiṃ pana rūpānaṃ, paṭisandhipavattisu.

From here onward, I shall explain the arising of materialities in the two realms of sense-desire and form, at rebirth-linking and during the course of life.

744.

744.

Bhummavajjesu [V 0.0099] devesu, niraye nijjhāmataṇhike;

Yoniyo purimā tisso, na santīti viniddise.

Among the deities, excluding the terrestrial ones, in hell, and among the 'parched with thirst' ghosts, the first three modes of generation do not exist—this should be declared.

745.

745.

Sese gatittaye bhumma-devesupi ca yoniyo;

Catasso ca bhavantīti, veditabbā vibhāvinā.

In the remaining three destinies and also among the terrestrial deities, all four modes of generation exist—this should be understood by the discerning.

746.

746.

Gabbhaseyyakasattassa, paṭisandhikkhaṇe pana;

Tiṃsa rūpāni jāyante, sabhāvasseva dehino.

For a womb-born being, at the moment of rebirth-linking, thirty materialities arise, as the inherent nature of the embodied one.

747.

747.

Abhāvagabbhaseyyānaṃ, aṇḍajānañca vīsati;

Bhavanti pana rūpāni, kāyavatthuvasena tu.

For those not womb-born and for the egg-born, twenty materialities arise, by way of the body and the basis.

748.

748.

Gahitāgahaṇenettha, ekādasa bhavanti te;

Eseva ca nayo ñeyyo, sabbesu dasakesupi.

Herein, by way of inclusion and non-inclusion, they are eleven. And this same method should be understood in all the decads.

749.

749.

Jīvitena yadā saddhiṃ, jāte suddhakamaṭṭhakaṃ;

Jīvitanavakaṃ nāma, hotīti samudīritaṃ.

When the pure octad arises together with the life-faculty, it is stated to be the 'life-ennead'.

750.

750.

Jīvitanavakaṃ [M 0.0106] kāyapasādenekato siyā;

Taṃ kāyadasakaṃ nāma, hotīti pariyāpuṭaṃ.

The life-ennead, when combined with body-sensitivity, becomes what is called the 'body-decad'—this is fully taught.

751.

751.

Eseva ca nayo ñeyyo, saddhiṃ bhāvena vatthunā;

Cakkhādīhi ca yojetvā, dasakā satta viññunā.

This same method should be understood by the wise, applying it together with the sex-faculty, the basis, and the eye and so forth, making seven decads.

752.

752.

Opapātikasattānaṃ, manussesūpapattiyaṃ;

Kāmāvacaradevānaṃ, niccaṃ rūpāni sattati.

For spontaneously arisen beings, for those arising among humans, and for sense-realm deities, there are always seventy materialities.

753.

753.

Cakkhu [P 0.0078] sotañca ghānañca, jivhā kāyo ca vatthu ca;

Bhāvo cāti hi sattannaṃ, dasakānaṃ vasā pana.

The eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, basis, and sex-faculty—this is by way of the seven decads.

754.

754.

Brahmānaṃ rūpinaṃ cakkhu-sotavatthuvasā pana;

Dasakāni ca tīṇeva, navakaṃ jīvitassa ca.

For form-realm Brahmās, by way of the eye-basis, ear-basis, and heart-basis, there are three decads and the life-ennead.

755.

755.

Catunnaṃ tu kalāpānaṃ, vasena pana rūpinaṃ;

Cattālīseva rūpāni, ekūnāni bhavanti hi.

For form-realm beings, by way of the four groups, there are indeed thirty-nine materialities.

756.

756.

Jīvitanavakeneva[V 0.0100], asaññuppatti dīpitā;

Jaccandhabadhirāghāna-rahite tu napuṃsake.

The arising of non-percipient beings is explained by the life-ennead alone. And in the case of a neuter who is born blind, deaf, and without the faculty of smell.

757.

757.

Vatthuno kāyajivhānaṃ, vasā tiṃsāvakaṃsato;

Ukkaṃsassāvakaṃsassa, antare anurūpato.

By way of the (heart-)basis, body, and tongue, there are thirty [materialities]. Between the maximum and the minimum, [the number is to be determined] accordingly.

758.

758.

Paripuṇṇānaṃ rūpānaṃ, vasena pana pāṇinaṃ;

Rūpānaṃ tu samuppatti, veditabbā vibhāvinā.

For beings who are complete in their materialities, the arising of those materialities should be understood by the discerning.

759.

759.

Sattavīsati rūpāni, kāmāvacaradehino;

Appavattanato honti, dvinnaṃ bhāvānamekato.

Twenty-seven materialities belong to a being of the sense-sphere, due to the non-occurrence of both sex-faculties together.

760.

760.

Ghānaṃ jivhā ca kāyo ca, tathā bhāvadvayampi ca;

Brahmānaṃ pana rūpīnaṃ, pañca rūpā na vijjare.

The nose, tongue, and body, and likewise the two sex-faculties; for form-realm Brahmās, these five materialities do not exist.

761.

761.

Catusantati kāmasmiṃ, rūpe honti tisantati;

Dvisantati asaññesu, bahiddhā ekasantati.

In the sense-sphere there are four continuities, in the form-sphere there are three continuities; in the non-percipient realm there are two continuities, and externally there is one continuity.

762.

762.

Rūpaṃ [M 0.0107] nibbattamānaṃ tu, sabbesaṃ pana pāṇinaṃ;

Paṭhamaṃ kammatoyeva, nibbattati na saṃsayo.

For all beings, when materiality is arising, it first arises from kamma alone; of this there is no doubt.

763.

763.

Gabbhaseyyakasattānaṃ, paṭisandhikkhaṇe pana;

Tañca kho sandhicittassa, uppādeyeva jāyare.

For womb-born beings, however, at the moment of rebirth-linking, that arises indeed at the very arising of the rebirth-linking consciousness.

764.

764.

Yatheva tassa uppāde, tiṃsa rūpāni jāyare;

Tatheva ṭhitibhaṅgesu, tiṃsa tiṃseva jāyare.

Just as at its arising thirty materialities come to be, so too at its static and dissolution moments, thirty materialities arise at each.

765.

765.

Sabbānetāni rūpāni, rūpakkhandhoti saññito;

Anicco addhuvonattā, dukkhakkhandhova kevalo.

All these materialities are designated as the materiality aggregate; impermanent, not lasting, not-self, merely an aggregate of suffering.

766.

766.

Rogato gaṇḍato rūpaṃ, parato ca palokato;

Disvāna dukkhato rūpaṃ, rūpe chandaṃ virājaye.

Seeing materiality as a disease, a boil, as alien, and as perishable; seeing materiality as suffering, one should dispel desire for materiality.

767.

767.

Gantuṃ panicche piṭakebhidhamme,

Yo dhammasenāpatinā samattaṃ;

Hitatthinā [V 0.0101] tena ca bhikkhunāyaṃ,

Sakkacca sammā pana sikkhitabbo.

Should a bhikkhu who is desirous of welfare wish to penetrate the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, which was completely mastered by the General of the Dhamma, this teaching should be properly and earnestly learned by him.

Iti abhidhammāvatāre rūpavibhāgo nāma

Thus in the Abhidhammāvatāra ends the chapter named the Division of Materiality.

Dasamo paricchedo.

The Tenth Chapter.

11. Ekādasamo paricchedo

11. The Eleventh Chapter

Nibbānaniddeso

The Exposition of Nibbāna

768.

768.

Rūpānantaramuddiṭṭhaṃ[P 0.0079], nibbānaṃ yaṃ panādito;

Tassidāni anuppatto, vibhāvananayakkamo.

Nibbāna, which was declared immediately after materiality and mentioned at the outset—now the methodical way of its exposition has been reached.

769.

769.

Tasmāhaṃ tassa dassetuṃ, dukkarassa yathābalaṃ;

Dubbodhassa pavakkhāmi, vibhāvanamito paraṃ.

Therefore, to explain that which is difficult to do and hard to comprehend, I shall hereafter speak, according to my ability, by way of an exposition.

Tattha [M 0.0108] nibbānanti bhavābhavaṃ vinanato vānaṃ vuccati taṇhā, vānato nikkhantattā nibbānanti ca pavuccati amataṃ asaṅkhataṃ paramaṃ sukhaṃ. Vuttaṃ hetaṃ “yo so sabbasaṅkhārasamatho sabbūpadhipaṭinissaggo taṇhākkhayo virāgo nirodho nibbāna”nti.

Therein, Nibbāna. Craving is called 'vāna' because it weaves together existence and non-existence. And because it is a departure from that 'vāna', it is called Nibbāna—the deathless, the unconditioned, the supreme bliss. For this has been said: 'That which is the stilling of all formations, the relinquishment of all substrata of existence, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation—that is Nibbāna.'

770.

770.

Yassa cādhigamā sabba-kilesānaṃ khayo bhave;

Nibbānamiti niddiṭṭhaṃ, nibbānakusalena taṃ.

And that by the attainment of which there is the destruction of all defilements—that is designated as Nibbāna by one skilled in Nibbāna.

Etaṃ ca nibbānaṃ nāma tayidaṃ santilakkhaṇaṃ, accutirasaṃ, assāsakaraṇarasaṃ vā, animittapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, nissaraṇapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ vāti veditabbaṃ.

And this Nibbāna is to be understood as having the characteristic of peace, the function of being deathless or the function of giving solace, and the manifestation of signlessness or the manifestation of deliverance.

Etthāha – na paramatthato nibbānaṃ nāma eko sabhāvo atthi, titthiyānaṃ attā viya, sasavisāṇaṃ [V 0.0102] viya ca anupalabbhanīyatoti? Na, paññācakkhunā upaparikkhiyamānānaṃ hitagavesīnaṃ yathānurūpāya paṭipattiyā upalabbhanīyato. Yaṃ hi puthujjanā nopalabbhanti, taṃ “natthī”ti na vattabbaṃ. Athāyasmatā sāriputtattherena dhammasenāpatinā “katamaṃ nu kho, āvuso, nibbāna”nti nibbānaṃ puṭṭhena “yo kho, āvuso, rāgakkhayo dosakkhayo mohakkhayo”ti rāgādīnaṃ khayova dassito, tasmā rāgādīnaṃ [P 0.0080] khayamattameva nibbānanti ce? Taṃ na. Kasmā? Arahattassāpi rāgādīnaṃ khayamattapasaṅgadosāpattito. Kathaṃ? Nibbānaṃ pucchānantarameva “katamaṃ nu kho, āvuso, arahatta”nti puṭṭhena “yo kho, āvuso, rāgakkhayo dosakkhayo mohakkhayo”ti rāgādīnaṃ khayova vutto, tasmā tava matena arahattaphalassāpi rāgādīnaṃ khayamattatā bhaveyya, na cetaṃ yuttaṃ anuttarassa lokuttaraphalacittassa rāgānaṃ khayamattatāpajjanaṃ, tasmā mā [M 0.0109] evaṃ byañjanacchāyāya vadesi, ubhinnaṃ pana suttānaṃ attho upaparikkhitabbo.

Here one might say: Is it not that in an ultimate sense there is no single nature called Nibbāna, being unattainable like the self of the sectarians or like a hare’s horn? No, for it is attainable through the appropriate practice by those who seek what is beneficial and who investigate with the eye of wisdom. For what ordinary people do not attain should not be declared as 'non-existent.' Furthermore, when the Venerable Sāriputta Thera, the General of the Dhamma, was asked, 'What, friend, is Nibbāna?' he replied, 'Friend, it is the destruction of greed, the destruction of hatred, the destruction of delusion.' Thus, only the destruction of greed and so forth was shown. If you say that Nibbāna is therefore merely the destruction of greed and so forth, that is not so. Why? Because of the fault that Arahantship too would consequently be merely the destruction of greed and so forth. How so? Immediately after the question about Nibbāna, when asked, 'What, friend, is Arahantship?' he answered, 'Friend, it is the destruction of greed, the destruction of hatred, the destruction of delusion,' again stating only the destruction of greed and so forth. Thus, according to your view, the fruit of Arahantship would also be merely the destruction of greed and so forth.
