But this is not fitting, for the unsurpassed, supramundane fruit-consciousness would be reduced to being merely the destruction of defilements. Therefore, do not speak thus, clinging to the shadow of the letter; rather, the meaning of both suttas should be examined.

Yassa pana dhammassādhigamena rāgādīnaṃ khayo hoti, so dhammo rāgādīnaṃ khayassa upanissayattā akkhayopi samāno “rāgādīnaṃ khayo nibbāna”nti khayopacārena vutto, “tipusaṃ jaro guḷo semho”tiādīsu viya phalūpacārena vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Arahattaṃ pana khayante uppannattā “khayo”ti vuttaṃ. Yadi rāgādīnaṃ khayamattaṃ nibbānaṃ bhaveyya, sabbe bālaputhujjanāpi samadhigatanibbānā sacchikatanirodhā bhaveyyuṃ. Kiñca bhiyyo – nibbānassa bahuttādidosāpattito ca. Evañhi sati rāgādikkhayānaṃ bahubhāvato nibbānassāpi bahubhāvo bhaveyya, saṅkhatalakkhaṇañca nibbānaṃ bhaveyya, saṅkhatalakkhaṇattā saṅkhatapariyāpannañca, saṅkhatapariyāpannattā aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ nibbānaṃ bhaveyyāti.

But the Dhamma, by the attainment of which the destruction of greed and so forth occurs—that Dhamma, being the supporting condition for the destruction of greed and so forth, though it is itself indestructible, is called 'the destruction of greed and so forth' by a figurative use of the word 'destruction'. This should be understood as being spoken of by a figurative use of the effect, just as in phrases like 'tin is rust' or 'molasses is phlegm'. Arahantship, however, is called 'destruction' because it arises at the end of the destruction. If Nibbāna were merely the destruction of greed and so forth, then all foolish ordinary people would have attained Nibbāna and realized cessation. What is more, there would also be the fault of Nibbāna being multiple. For if that were so, due to the multiplicity of the destructions of greed and so forth, there would also be a multiplicity of Nibbāna. And Nibbāna would have the characteristics of the conditioned; and because it has the characteristics of the conditioned, it would be included among conditioned things; and because it is included among conditioned things, Nibbāna would be impermanent and suffering.

Kiñca bhiyyo – yadi khayo nibbānaṃ bhaveyya, gotrabhuvodānamaggaphalacittānaṃ kiṃ nu ārammaṇaṃ vadesi, vada bhadramukhāti? Rāgādīnaṃ khayameva vadāmīti. Kiṃ pana rāgādayo gotrabhuādīnaṃ khaṇe khīyanti, udāhu khīyissanti, atha khīṇāti? Kiṃ panettha “khīṇesveva khayaṃ vadāmī”ti. Suṭṭhu upadhāretvā vada bhadramukhāti, yadi khīṇesveva khayaṃ vadesi, na gotrabhucittādīnaṃ nibbānārammaṇatā sijjhatīti. Kiṃ kāraṇaṃ? Gotrabhukkhaṇe rāgādayo khīyissanti, tathā vodānakkhaṇe, maggakkhaṇe pana khīyanti, na khīṇā, phalakkhaṇe khīṇā. Evaṃ sante bhavato matena phalameva khayārammaṇaṃ, na itare, itaresaṃ pana kimārammaṇaṃ vadesīti[V 0.0103]? Addhā so ārammaṇaṃ apassanto niruttaro [P 0.0081] bhavissati. Apica kilesakkhayo nāma sappurisehi karīyati, yathānurūpāya paṭipattiyā uppādīyatīti attho. Nibbānaṃ pana na kenaci karīyati na uppādīyati, tasmā nibbānamamatamasaṅkhataṃ. Tamakataṃ [M 0.0110] jānātīti ariyasāvako “akataññū”ti pavuccati. Vuttañcetaṃ –

What is more, if destruction were Nibbāna, what would you say is the object of the change-of-lineage, purification, path, and fruition consciousnesses? Speak, O fortunate one. 'I say it is the destruction of greed and so forth.' But do greed and so forth cease at the moment of change-of-lineage and so on, or will they cease, or have they ceased? 'Regarding this, I speak of destruction only when they have already ceased.' Consider carefully and speak, O fortunate one. If you speak of destruction only when they have already ceased, then the change-of-lineage consciousness and the others cannot have Nibbāna as their object. What is the reason? At the moment of change-of-lineage, greed and so forth will cease; similarly, at the moment of purification. At the moment of the path, however, they are ceasing, not yet ceased. At the moment of fruition, they have ceased. In that case, according to your view, only fruition has destruction as its object, not the others. Then what do you say is the object of the others? Surely, not seeing an object, you will be left without an answer. Moreover, the destruction of defilements is accomplished by noble persons; that is, it is produced through appropriate practice. But Nibbāna is not made by anyone, nor is it produced. Therefore, Nibbāna is deathless, unconditioned. The noble disciple who knows this unmade thing is called 'one who knows the unmade' (akataññū). And this has been said:

771.

771.

“Asaddho akataññū ca,

Sandhicchedo ca yo naro;

Hatāvakāso vantāso,

Sa ve uttamaporiso”ti.

'He who is beyond faith, who knows the Uncreated, who has severed the connection, destroyed the occasion, and abandoned all desire—he is indeed the supreme person.'

Apica “nissaraṇa”nti bhagavatā vuttattā ca. “Nissaraṇa”nti hi nibbānassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Yathāha “tayo khome, bhikkhave, dhammā duppaṭivijjhā. Katame tayo dhammā duppaṭivijjhā? Tisso nissaraṇadhātuyo. Kāmānametaṃ nissaraṇaṃ, yadidaṃ nekkhammaṃ. Rūpānametaṃ nissaraṇaṃ, yadidaṃ arūpaṃ. Yaṃ kho pana kiñci bhūtaṃ saṅkhataṃ paṭiccasamuppannaṃ, nirodho tassa nissaraṇa”nti hi vuttaṃ. Evaṃ vuttassa tassa nibbānassa abhāvapattidosato paṭhamajjhānākāsānañcāyatanānampi abhāvo bhaveyya, tasmā ayuttaṃ akkhayassa nibbānassa khayadosāpajjananti, na tu khayo nibbānaṃ.

Moreover, because it is called 'release' by the Blessed One. For 'release' is indeed a name for Nibbāna. As it is said: 'Monks, these three things are hard to penetrate. Which three things are hard to penetrate? The three elements of release. This is the release from sensual pleasures, namely, renunciation. This is the release from forms, namely, the formless. And whatever has come to be, is conditioned, and is dependently originated, cessation is its release.' Thus it has been said. If, due to the fault of arriving at the non-existence of that Nibbāna so described, then the first jhāna and the base of infinite space would also come to be non-existent. Therefore, it is inappropriate to impute the fault of destruction to the indestructible Nibbāna; for Nibbāna is not destruction.

“Atthi nissaraṇaṃ loke, paññāya me suphusita”nti ca “atthi, bhikkhave, ajātaṃ abhūtaṃ akataṃ asaṅkhata”nti ca dhammasāminā tathāgatena sammāsambuddhena anekesu suttantesu paramatthavasena vuttattā “atthi nibbānaṃ nāma eko dhammo”ti niṭṭhamettha gantabbaṃ. Apica parittattike “katame dhammā appamāṇā”ti padamuddharitvā – “cattāro maggā apariyāpannā cattāri ca sāmaññaphalāni nibbānañca, ime dhammā appamāṇā”ti vuttattā rāgādīnaṃ khayassa appamāṇattaṃ kathaṃ yujjati, tasmā paramatthato atthiyeva nibbānaṃ nāma eko sabhāvoti. Taṃ [M 0.0111] pana pakativādīnaṃ pakati viya, titthiyānaṃ attā viya ca sasavisāṇaṃ viya ca nāvijjamānaṃ.

'There is an escape in the world, well realized by my wisdom,' and also, 'There is, monks, the unborn, unbecome, unmade, unconditioned,' thus spoken by the Tathāgata, the Fully Enlightened One, the Lord of the Dhamma, in many discourses in terms of ultimate meaning; therefore it should be concluded that 'there is indeed a reality called Nibbāna.' Moreover, in the Parittattika, taking up the phrase 'Which things are immeasurable?' it is said: 'The four unincluded paths, the four fruits of recluseship, and Nibbāna—these things are immeasurable.' How then could the immeasurability of the destruction of greed, etc., be fitting? Therefore, ultimately, there indeed exists a reality with its own nature called Nibbāna. However, it is not non-existent like the 'nature' of the proponents of nature, the 'self' of the sectarians, or a hare's horn.

Atha paññattimattaṃ nibbānanti ce, tampi ayuttaṃ. Kasmā? Nibbānārammaṇānaṃ cittacetasikānaṃ navattabbārammaṇattā. Kathaṃ? Parittārammaṇattike ca pana “katame dhammā appamāṇārammaṇā”ti [V 0.0104] padamuddharitvā “cattāro maggā apariyāpannā cattāri ca sāmaññaphalāni[P 0.0082], ime dhammā appamāṇārammaṇā”ti hi vuttaṃ. Yadi panetesaṃ paññattiārammaṇaṃ siyā, appamāṇārammaṇatā na yujjeyya, navattabbārammaṇapakkhaṃ bhajeyyuṃ. “Navattabbārammaṇā pana rūpāvacarattikacatukkajjhānā kusalato ca vipākato ca kiriyato ca, catutthassa jhānassa vipāko, ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ kusalato ca vipākato ca kiriyato ca, ime dhammā navattabbārammaṇā”ti hi vuttaṃ, tasmā na paññattimattaṃ nibbānaṃ. Yasmā ca paṇṇattibhāvo nibbānassa na yujjati, tasmā maggaphalānaṃ ārammaṇapaccayabhūtaṃ uppādādīnamabhāvato niccaṃ, rūpasabhāvābhāvato arūpaṃ, papañcābhāvato nippapañcaṃ nibbānaṃ nāma atthīti upagantabbanti.

If it is said that Nibbāna is merely a concept, that too is inappropriate. Why? Because the minds and mental factors that take Nibbāna as their object do not have an object that is 'not to be spoken of'. How so? In the triad of limited objects, etc., the phrase 'Which states have immeasurable objects?' is raised, and it is said: 'The four unincluded paths and the four fruits of recluseship—these states have immeasurable objects.' But if these had a concept as their object, their nature of having an immeasurable object would not be fitting; they would fall into the category of having an object that is 'not to be spoken of'. For it is said: 'Now, these states have an object that is not to be spoken of: the four form-sphere jhānas—wholesome, resultant, and functional; the result of the fourth jhāna; the base of infinite space and the base of nothingness—wholesome, resultant, and functional. These states have an object that is not to be spoken of.' Therefore, Nibbāna is not merely a concept. And because the status of being a concept is not fitting for Nibbāna, it must be accepted that Nibbāna exists as the object-condition for the paths and fruits, being permanent due to the absence of arising, etc., formless due to the absence of a material nature, and free from proliferation due to the absence of proliferation.

772.

772.

Accantamanantaṃ santaṃ, amataṃ apalokitaṃ;

Paṇītaṃ saraṇaṃ khemaṃ, tāṇaṃ leṇaṃ parāyaṇaṃ.

The utterly boundless, the peaceful, the deathless, the undecaying; the sublime, the refuge, the secure, the protection, the shelter, the final goal.

773.

773.

Sivañca nipuṇaṃ saccaṃ, dukkhakkhayamanāsavaṃ;

Sududdasaṃ paraṃ pāraṃ, nibbānamanidassanaṃ.

The auspicious, the subtle, the true, the destruction of suffering, the taintless; the very hard to see, the further shore, Nibbāna, the unmanifest.

774.

774.

Taṇhākkhayaṃ dhuvaṃ dīpaṃ, abyāpajjhamanītikaṃ;

Anālayamarūpañca, padamaccutamakkharaṃ.

The destruction of craving, the stable, the island, the non-afflictive, the free from calamity; the unattached, the formless, the unfailing state, the imperishable.

775.

775.

Virāgañca nirodhañca, vimutti mokkhameva ca;

Imehi pana nāmehi, nibbānaṃ tu kathīyati.

And dispassion, and cessation, and liberation, and freedom itself; by these names, indeed, Nibbāna is spoken of.

776.

776.

Evañca [M 0.0112] pana viññāya, nibbānampi ca accutaṃ;

Tassa cādhigamūpāyo, kattabbo viññunā sadā.

And having thus understood Nibbāna, the unfailing state, the means to its attainment should always be undertaken by the wise.

777.

777.

Saddhābuddhikaraṃ tathāgatamate sammohaviddhaṃsanaṃ,

Paññāsambhavasampasādanakaraṃ jānāti yo ce imaṃ;

Atthabyañjanasālinaṃ sumadhuraṃ sāraññuvimhāpanaṃ,

Gambhīre nipuṇābhidhammapiṭake so yābhiniṭṭhaṃ padaṃ.

He who knows this teaching in the deep and subtle Abhidhamma Piṭaka—which generates faith and wisdom in the Tathāgata's doctrine, destroys delusion, produces clarity born of wisdom, is rich in meaning and expression, very sweet, and astonishing to those who know its essence—he attains the ultimate state.

Iti abhidhammāvatāre nibbānaniddeso nāma

Thus in the Abhidhammāvatāra ends the Exposition of Nibbāna.

Ekādasamo paricchedo.

The Eleventh Chapter.

12. Dvādasamo paricchedo

12. The Twelfth Chapter.

Paññattiniddeso

The Exposition of Concepts.

Etthāha [P 0.0083][V 0.0105] – “kiṃ ettakameva ñeyyaṃ, udāhu aññampi atthī”ti? Atthi paññatti nāmāti. Sā panesā paññapetabbato, paññāpanato ca “paññattī”ti vuccati. Tenevāha – “yā tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānaṃ saṅkhā samaññā paññatti vohāro nāmaṃ nāmakammaṃ nāmadheyyaṃ nirutti byañjanaṃ abhilāpo”ti. Tattha saṅkhāyatīti saṅkhā, kathīyatīti attho. Kinti kathīyati? “Aha”nti “mama”nti “paro”ti “parassā”ti “mañco”ti “pīṭha”nti anekehi ākārehi kathīyatīti saṅkhā. Samaññāyatīti samaññā. Paññāpīyatīti paññatti. Voharīyatīti vohāro. Kinti voharīyati? “Aha”nti “mama”nti “paro”ti “parassā”ti “mañco”ti “pīṭha”nti. Evaṃ tāva paññapetabbato paññattīti vuttā. “Aha”nti hi rūpādayo dhamme upādāya paṭicca kāraṇaṃ katvā yathā te rūpādayo dhammā uppādavayavanto, na evaṃvidhā, kevalaṃ lokasaṅketena [M 0.0113] siddhā yā ayaṃ “aha”nti kathīyati ceva paññāpīyati ca, esā paññattīti attho.

Here it is asked: "Is this all that is to be known, or is there something else?" There is indeed what is called a concept. This is called "paññatti" because it is to be made known and because of the making known. Therefore it is said: "Whatever is the reckoning, the convention, the concept, the expression, the name, the act of naming, the appellation, the term, the letter, the utterance concerning these various things." Here, "reckoning" (saṅkhā) is so called because one reckons, that is, one speaks of it. How does one speak of it? One speaks in many ways, such as "I," "mine," "another," "another's," "a bed," "a chair"—thus it is a reckoning. "Convention" (samaññā) is so called because one conventionally understands. "Concept" (paññatti) is so called because one makes it known. "Expression" (vohāro) is so called because one expresses. How does one express? As "I," "mine," "another," "another's," "a bed," "a chair." Thus far, it has been called a concept because it is to be made known. For, depending on and taking as a reason the phenomena of form, etc., this which is spoken of and made known as "I" is not of the same kind as those phenomena of form, etc., which are subject to arising and passing away, but is merely established by worldly convention. This is the meaning of concept.

Idāni paññāpanato paññattiṃ pakāsetuṃ “nāmaṃ nāmakamma”ntiādimāha. Tattha nāmanti taṃ taṃ dhammaṃ “esa itthannāmo nāmā”ti paññapeti, tasmā taṃ paññattīti pavuccati. Nāmakammantiādīni tassā eva vevacanāni. Ayaṃ paññāpanato paññatti nāma.

Now, to explain 'concept' from the side of making known, he says "name, act of naming," and so on. Therein, "name" makes known this or that thing, as in "this is named so-and-so"; therefore, it is called a concept. "Act of naming," and so on, are synonyms for that. This is what is called a concept from the side of making known.

Sā panesā tajjāpaññatti upādāpaññatti upanidhāpaññattīti tividhā hoti. Tattha tajjāpaññatti nāma cakkhusotarūpasaddapathavītejovāyotiādinayappavattā. Upādāpaññatti pana samūhāsamūhavasena duvidhā hoti. Tattha samūhapaññatti nāma rūpārūpadhammesu ekassa vā bahūnaṃ vā nāmaṃ gahetvā samūhamevopādāya vuccati. Kathaṃ? Acchataracchaghaṭapaṭādippabhedā. Ayaṃ samūhapaññatti [P 0.0084] nāma. Asamūhapaññatti pana disākāsakālanimittābhāvanirodhādibhedā.

This concept is threefold: concept corresponding to that, derivative concept, and concept by comparison. Herein, the concept corresponding to that proceeds by way of terms such as eye, ear, form, sound, earth, fire, wind, and so forth. The derivative concept, however, is twofold: collective and non-collective. Herein, the collective concept is spoken of based on a collection itself, having taken a name for one or many material or immaterial phenomena. How? For example, distinctions like a bear, a hyena, a pot, a cloth, and so on—this is called collective concept. The non-collective concept, on the other hand, includes distinctions like directions, space, time, signs, absence, cessation, and so forth.

Yadā pana sā vijjamānaṃ paramatthaṃ jotayati, tadā “vijjamānapaññattī”ti pavuccati. Yadā avijjamānaṃ samūhāsamūhabhedaṃ nāmamattaṃ jotayati, tadā “avijjamānapaññattī”ti pavuccati[V 0.0106]. Duvidhāpi panesā sotadvārajavanānantaraṃ gahitapubbasaṅketamanodvārajavanaviññāṇena viññāyati. Yāya gahitapubbasaṅketena manodvārajavanaviññāṇena paññāpīyati. Yaṃ sandhāya “vijjamānapaññatti, avijjamānapaññatti, vijjamānena avijjamānapaññatti, avijjamānena vijjamānapaññatti, vijjamānena vijjamānapaññatti, avijjamānena avijjamānapaññattī”ti chakkanayo vutto. Tattha paramatthato vijjamānānaṃ rūpādīnaṃ paññāpanā vijjamānapaññatti. Tathā avijjamānānamitthipurisādīnaṃ paññāpanā avijjamānapaññatti. Ṭhapetvā pana vacanatthaṃ kenaci ākārena anupalabbhamānānaṃ pañcamasaccādīnaṃ, titthiyaparikappitānaṃ vā pakatipurisādīnaṃ paññāpanāpi avijjamānapaññattiyeva[M 0.0114]. “Tevijjo, chaḷabhiñño”ti evamādinayappavattā vijjamānena avijjamānapaññatti. “Itthisaddo, purisasaddo”ti evamādikā avijjamānena vijjamānapaññatti. “Cakkhuviññāṇaṃ, sotaviññāṇa”nti evamādikā vijjamānena vijjamānapaññatti. “Khattiyakumāro, brāhmaṇakumāro, bhikkhukumāro”ti evamādikā avijjamānena avijjamānapaññattīti evaṃ vuttā cha paññattiyopi ettheva saṅgahaṃ gacchanti. Ayaṃ upādāpaññatti nāma.

When it illuminates an existing ultimate reality, it is called 'existent designation.' When it illuminates what does not exist—a mere name, a division into groups and non-groups—it is called 'non-existent designation.' Both of these are cognized by the mind-door impulsion consciousness which apprehends a previously grasped convention immediately after the ear-door impulsion. It is by means of that mind-door impulsion consciousness, which has apprehended a previously grasped convention, that one designates. In reference to this, the sixfold method is stated: 'existent designation, non-existent designation, designation of the non-existent by the existent, designation of the existent by the non-existent, designation of the existent by the existent, and designation of the non-existent by the non-existent.' Herein, the designation of things that exist in an ultimate sense, such as form, is existent designation. Likewise, the designation of things that do not exist, such as a woman or a man, is non-existent designation. Furthermore, the designation of things that cannot be apprehended in any way apart from the meaning of the words, such as a fifth truth, or of things imagined by sectarians, such as primordial nature and spirit, is also non-existent designation. Designations following the method of 'one with the threefold knowledge' or 'one with the sixfold higher knowledges' are designations of the non-existent by the existent. Designations such as 'the sound "woman"' or 'the sound "man"' are designations of the existent by the non-existent. Designations such as 'eye-consciousness' or 'ear-consciousness' are designations of the existent by the existent. Designations such as 'a kshatriya youth,' 'a brahmin youth,' or 'a bhikkhu youth' are designations of the non-existent by the non-existent. Thus, the six designations so stated are also included herein. This is called derivative designation.

Upanidhāpaññattipi etissā eva pabhedā, sā pana “dīghaṃ upanidhāya rasso, rassaṃ upanidhāya dīgho”tiādinayappavattā “kapaṇaṃ mānusakaṃ rajjaṃ dibbasukhaṃ upanidhāyā”ti evamādikā ca, tasmā paññapetabbato ca paññāpanato ca paññattīti veditabbā. Samaññā samattā.

The designation by comparison is also a subdivision of this. It proceeds by such methods as, 'in comparison to the long, there is the short; in comparison to the short, there is the long,' and so on, and also by such statements as, 'in comparison to wretched human kingship, there is divine bliss,' and the like. Therefore, it should be understood that it is a designation (paññatti) because it is what is to be designated and because of the act of designating. The exposition of designations is complete.

778.

778.

Paramatthato ca paññatti, tatiyā koṭi na vijjati;

Dvīsu ṭhānesu kusalo, paravādesu na kampati.

Ultimate reality and designation—a third category is not found; one who is skilled in these two standpoints is not shaken by the doctrines of others.

Iti abhidhammāvatāre paññattiniddeso nāma

Thus ends the Exposition of Designation in the Abhidhammāvatāra.

Dvādasamo paricchedo.

The Twelfth Chapter.

13. Terasamo paricchedo

13. The Thirteenth Chapter.

Kārakapaṭivedhaniddeso

The Exposition of the Analysis of the Agent.

Etthāha [P 0.0085][V 0.0107] – niddiṭṭhā kusalādayo nāma dhammā, na panetesaṃ kārako attā niddiṭṭho. Tassa hi kārakassa vedakassa attano abhāve kusalākusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ abhāvo siyā, tesamabhāve tadāyattavuttīnaṃ tesaṃ vipākānamabhāvo hoti, tasmā kusalādīnaṃ dhammānaṃ desanā niratthikāti? Atra vuccate – nāyaṃ [M 0.0115] niratthikā, sātthikāvāyaṃ desanā. Yadi kārakassābhāvā kusalādīnamabhāvo siyā, tassa parikappitassa attanopi abhāvo siyā. Kiṃ kāraṇanti ce? Tassa attano aññassa kārakassābhāvato. Kārakābhāvepi kattā attā atthīti ce? Tathā kusalādīnampi asatipi kattari atthitā upagantabbā, kutoyaṃ tava tatthānurodho, idha virodhoti. Athāpi yathā pana loke kārakābhāvepi pathavīāpatejautuādayo paṭicca aṅkurādīnaṃ abhinibbatti dissati, tathā etesampi kusalādīnaṃ dhammānaṃ hetupaccayasāmaggiyā abhinibbatti hotīti veditabbā.

Here one might say: "The wholesome and other states have been described, but their doer, the self, has not been described. For if there were no such doer and experiencer, the self, then wholesome and unwholesome states would not exist. If they did not exist, their results, which depend on them, would not exist. Therefore, is the teaching of wholesome and other states meaningless?" To this, it is replied: "This teaching is not meaningless; it is indeed meaningful. If, due to the absence of a doer, wholesome and other states were absent, then that imagined self would also be absent. And why? Because of the absence of another doer for that self. If you say that even in the absence of a doer, a self as agent exists, then likewise, the existence of wholesome and other states must be accepted even without an agent. Why this adherence of yours in that case, but opposition in this? Moreover, just as in the world, even without a doer, the arising of sprouts is seen to occur in dependence on earth, water, heat, and so on, so too should the arising of these wholesome and other states be understood as occurring from the assemblage of causes and conditions."

Athāpi cettha tassā paññāya parikappito nicco dhuvo kusalādīnaṃ kattā attā paramatthato atthīti ce? Tamupaparikkhissāma tāva, so pana tāva attā kārako vedako kiṃ sacetano vā, udāhu acetano vāti? Kiñcettha – yadi acetano siyā, pākāratarupāsāṇasadiso siyā. Tassa kārakavedakattābhāvo siyā. Yadi sacetano, so cetanāya añño vā siyā, anañño vā. Athānañño, cetanāya nāse attanopi nāso siyā. Kiṃ kāraṇanti ce? Cetanāya anaññattā.

And if it is held that here there exists in an ultimate sense a permanent, stable self, the doer of wholesome states and so forth, which is conceived by that understanding of yours, then we shall examine this. First, is that self, the agent and experiencer, conscious or unconscious? In this case, if it were unconscious, it would be like a wall, a tree, or a stone, and it would have no agency or experience. If it were conscious, would it be other than consciousness or not other? If it were not other, then with the cessation of consciousness, the self too would cease. And why? Because of its not being other than consciousness.

Athāpi bhavato adhippāyo evaṃ siyā, attano pana nāso [P 0.0086] na bhavati niccattā, cetanāyayeva nāso bhavatīti? Vuccate – attano anāse sati cetanāyapi nāso na bhavati. Kiṃ kāraṇanti ce? Cetanāya anaññattā. Cetanattānaṃ anaññatte sati cetanāyayeva nāso bhavati, na attanoti ayuttametaṃ. Atha cetanāyayeva vināse visesakāraṇaṃ natthi, attāva nassatu, tiṭṭhatu cetanā. Atha cetanāya nāse attano nāso [M 0.0116] na bhavatīti ce? Cetanāya attā añño siyā. Atha aññassa attassa nāse sati sayaṃ nāso na bhavati, evañca sati “cetanāya [V 0.0108] anañño attā”ti tava paṭiññā hīnā. Athāpi cetanattānaṃ anaññatte sati attano anāso cetanāyapi anāso bhavatu. Atha na bhavati, paṭiññā hīnā. Atha vuttappakārato viparītaṃ vā siyā, attā nassatu, cetanā tiṭṭhatu. Atha pana evaṃ na bhavatīti ce? Anaññattapakkhaṃ pariccaja. Atha pana na pariccajasi, paṭiññāhīno bhavasi.

Perhaps your opinion might be this: 'The destruction of the self does not occur, owing to its permanence; it is only the destruction of consciousness that occurs.' To this it is said: If there is no destruction of the self, there is no destruction of consciousness either. And why? Because it is not other than consciousness. If consciousness and the self are not other, this statement—'destruction occurs only of consciousness, not of the self'—is illogical. If there is no special reason for the destruction of consciousness alone, then let the self be destroyed and consciousness remain. If you say that with the destruction of consciousness the destruction of the self does not occur, then the self must be other than consciousness. And in that case, your thesis that 'the self is not other than consciousness' is defeated. Furthermore, if consciousness and the self are not other, then just as the self is not destroyed, so too consciousness should not be destroyed. But if it is destroyed, your thesis is defeated. Or, let the opposite of what was stated occur: let the self be destroyed and consciousness remain. If you say this does not happen, then you must abandon the position of non-otherness. If you do not abandon it, your thesis is defeated.

Athāyaṃ bhavato adhippāyo siyā “nāyaṃ mama attā cetanāya anañño, aññoyevā”ti? Tatra vuccate – idha pana aññattaṃ duvidhaṃ hoti lakkhaṇakatamaññattañca desantarakatamaññattañcāti. Tattha kiṃ tvaṃ cetanattānaṃ lakkhaṇakatamaññattaṃ vadesi, udāhu desantarakatamaññattanti? Ahaṃ lakkhaṇakatamaññattaṃ vadāmīti. Yathā hi rūparasagandhādīnamekadese vattamānānampi lakkhaṇato aññattaṃ hoti, evaṃ cetanattānamekadese vattamānānampi lakkhaṇato aññattaṃ hoti, tasmā lakkhaṇakatamaññattaṃ vadāmīti. Tatra vuccate – yathā hi jātavedassa ḍayhamāne āmakasaṅghaṭe āmakavaṇṇavināse rasādīnaṃ vināso bhavati, tatheva cetanāya vināse attanopi vināso siyā. Kiṃ kāraṇanti ce? Rūparasādīnaṃ viya ekadesattāti.

Now, could this be your opinion: 'This self of mine is not non-other than consciousness; it is indeed other'? To this it is said: Here, otherness is of two kinds—otherness due to characteristic and otherness due to different location. In this case, do you speak of otherness due to characteristic with regard to consciousness and the self, or otherness due to different location? 'I speak of otherness due to characteristic. For just as form, taste, smell, and so on, though existing in one place, are other by characteristic, so too consciousness and the self, though existing in one place, are other by characteristic. Therefore, I speak of otherness due to characteristic.' To this it is said: Just as when a fire is burning a raw lump of clay, with the destruction of its raw color, the destruction of its taste and so on occurs, so too, with the destruction of consciousness, the self also would be destroyed. And why? Because, like form, taste, and so on, they exist in one place.

Athevaṃ bhavato mati siyā “ekadesatte satipi attano pana nāso na bhavati, cetanāyayeva vināso bhavatī”ti? Atra vuccate – attano anāse cetanāyapi anāsova hoti. Kiṃ kāraṇanti ce? Rūparasādīnaṃ viya avinibbhogato. Atha samāne ekadesatte avinibbhogabhāvepi [M 0.0117] kena hetunā cetanāya eva nāso bhavati, na pana attano. Atha visesakāraṇaṃ natthi, tava laddhiyā attāva nassatu, tiṭṭhatu cetanā. Atha cetanāya nāse attano nāso [P 0.0087] na bhavati, ubhinnaṃ ekadesatā natthi. Evañca sati ko dosoti ce? Yaṃ pana tayā vuttaṃ, yathā rūparasagandhādīnaṃ ekadese vattamānānampi lakkhaṇato aññattaṃ, tathā cetanattānamekadese vattamānānampi lakkhaṇato aññattanti? Tamayuttanti tava paṭiññā hīnā. Atha rūparasādīnaṃ viya samānepi ekadesatte yadi attano anāse cetanāyapi anāso na bhavati, paṭiññāhīno asi. Atha vuttappakārato viparītaṃ vā siyā, tava attā nassatu, cetanā tiṭṭhatu. Athevaṃ na bhavatīti ce? Ekadesatāva natthīti.

Then, might your view be: 'Even though there is existence in one place, there is no destruction of the self; destruction occurs only for volition'? To this it is said: If there is no destruction of the self, there is also no destruction of volition. If you ask, 'What is the reason?' Because of their inseparability, like form, taste, and so on. Now, if, while there is the same existence in one place and inseparability, for what reason does destruction occur only for volition and not for the self? If there is no distinguishing reason, then according to your doctrine, let the self be destroyed and let volition remain. But if, with the destruction of volition, the self is not destroyed, then there is no existence in one place for the two. And if this is so, what is the fault? What you have said—'Just as form, taste, smell, and so on, though existing in one place, are distinct by their characteristics, so too volition and the self, though existing in one place, are distinct by their characteristics'—that is incorrect; your proposition is defeated. Furthermore, if, like form, taste, and so on, even with the same existence in one place, you maintain that when the self is not destroyed, volition is nevertheless destroyed, your proposition is defeated. Or let it be the opposite of what has been stated: let your self be destroyed, and let volition remain. And if you say, 'It is not so'? Then there is no existence in one place at all.

Atha desantarakatamaññattaṃ vadesi, cetanattānaṃ aññatte sati ghaṭapaṭasakaṭagehādīnaṃ viya aññattaṃ siyā. Cetanāya vinā anaññatā te attā na ghaṭena vinā paṭo viya añño siyā[V 0.0109]. Añño ca hi ghaṭo añño ca paṭoti? Na, evañca sati ko dosoti ce? “Acetano attā”ti pubbe vuttadosato na parimuccatīti. Tasmā paramatthato na koci kattā vā vedako vā attā atthīti daṭṭhabbanti.

If you speak of an otherness due to different locations, then if volition and self were other, their otherness would be like that of a pot, a cloth, a cart, a house, and so on. Your self, not being other than volition, would not be distinct in the way a cloth is distinct from a pot. For is a pot one thing and a cloth another? No. And if this is so, what is the fault? You do not escape the fault previously stated, that 'the self is non-sentient.' Therefore, it should be understood that in an ultimate sense, there is no self that is a doer or an experiencer.

Yadi evaṃ atha kasmā bhagavatā –

If that is so, then why did the Blessed One say:

779.

779.

“Asmā lokā paraṃ lokaṃ,

So ca sandhāvatī naro;

So ca karoti vedeti,

Sukhadukkhaṃ sayaṃkata”nti ca.

From this world to the next world, that person fares on; and he himself both does and experiences happiness and suffering of his own making.

780.

780.

“Satto [M 0.0118] saṃsāramāpanno,

Dukkhamassa mahabbhayaṃ;

Atthi mātā atthi pitā,

Atthi sattopapātiko”ti ca.

A being has fallen into saṃsāra; his suffering is a great fear. There is mother, there is father, there are beings who arise spontaneously.

781.

781.

“Bhārā have pañcakkhandhā,

Bhārahāro ca puggalo;

Bhārādānaṃ dukkhaṃ loke,

Bhāranikkhepanaṃ sukha”nti ca.

Indeed, the five aggregates are burdens, and the person is the burden-carrier. Taking up the burden is suffering in the world; laying down the burden is happiness.

782.

782.

“Yañhi karoti puriso,

Kāyena vācā uda cetasā;

Tañhi tassa sakaṃ hoti,

Tañca ādāya gacchatī”ti ca.

Whatever a person does, by body, speech, or mind, that is truly his own, and taking that he departs.

783.

783.

“Ekassekena kappena,

Puggalassaṭṭhisañcayo;

Siyā pabbatasamo rāsi,

Iti vuttaṃ mahesinā”ti ca.

In a single aeon, one person's accumulation of bones would be a heap equal to a mountain; so it was said by the Great Sage.

784.

784.

“Asaddho [V 0.0110] akataññū ca,

Sandhicchedo ca yo naro;

Hatāvakāso vantāso,

Sa ve uttamaporiso”ti ca. –

The one beyond faith, the knower of the Uncreated, who has severed the links, destroyed the opportunity, and renounced all desire—he is truly the supreme person.

Vuttanti. Saccaṃ evaṃ vuttaṃ bhagavatā, tañca kho sammutivasena, na paramatthato. Nanu bhagavatā idampi vuttaṃ –

It is said. It is true that the Blessed One spoke thus, but that was by way of convention, not in an ultimate sense. But has not the Blessed One also said this—

785.

785.

“Kiṃ [P 0.0088] nu sattoti paccesi, māra diṭṭhigataṃ nu te;

Suddhasaṅkhārapuñjoyaṃ, nayidha sattupalabbhatī”ti ca.

Why do you assume 'a being,' Māra? Is that a speculative view of yours? This is a heap of mere formations; no being is to be found here.

786.

786.

“Yathāpi [M 0.0119] aṅgasambhārā,

Hoti saddo ratho iti;

Evaṃ khandhesu santesu,

Hoti sattoti sammutī”ti ca.

Just as from an assemblage of parts the word 'chariot' arises, so when the aggregates are present, there is the convention 'a being.'

Tasmā na vacanamattamevāvalambitabbaṃ, na ca daḷhamūḷhagāhinā ca bhavitabbaṃ, garukulamupasevitvā suttapadānaṃ adhippāyo jānitabbo, suttapadesu abhiyogo kātabbo. Dve saccāni bhagavatā vuttāni – “sammutisaccaṃ, paramatthasaccañcā”ti. Tasmā dvepi sammutiparamatthasaccāni asaṅkarato ñātabbāni. Evaṃ asaṅkarato ñatvā koci kārako vā vedako vā nicco dhuvo attā paramatthato natthīti upaparikkhitvā paccayasāmaggiyā dhammānaṃ pavattiṃ sallakkhetvā paṇḍitena kulaputtena atthakāmena dukkhassantakiriyāya paṭipajjitabbanti.

Therefore, one should not rely on mere words, nor should one grasp stubbornly and foolishly. Having associated with a respected teacher, the meaning of the discourses should be understood, and effort should be applied to the scriptural passages. The Blessed One has spoken of two truths—'conventional truth' and 'ultimate truth.' Therefore, both conventional and ultimate truths should be known without confusing them. Having thus understood them without confusion, and having investigated that in an ultimate sense there is no agent or experiencer, no permanent, stable self, and having discerned the occurrence of phenomena through the combination of conditions, the wise son of good family, desiring his own welfare, should practice for the sake of making an end of suffering.

787.

787.

Yo imaṃ ganthaṃ accantaṃ, cinteti satatampi so;

Kamena paramā paññā, tassa gacchati vepulaṃ.

For one who constantly and thoroughly reflects on this text, supreme wisdom gradually grows vast.

788.

788.

Atimatikaramādhinīharaṃ,

Vimativināsakaraṃ piyakkaraṃ;

Paṭhati [V 0.0111] suṇati yo sadā imaṃ,

Vikasati tassa matīdha bhikkhuno.

For the monk who always recites and listens to this—which removes excessive conceit and delusion, destroys uncertainty, and is endearing—wisdom blossoms here.

Iti abhidhammāvatāre kārakapaṭivedhaniddeso nāma

Thus, in the Abhidhammāvatāra, the Exposition on the Penetration of the Agent.

Terasamo paricchedo.

The Thirteenth Chapter.

14. Cuddasamo paricchedo

14. The Fourteenth Chapter

Rūpāvacarasamādhibhāvanāniddeso

Exposition on the Development of Concentration in the Form Sphere

789.

789.

Bhāvanānayamahaṃ [M 0.0120][P 0.0089] hitānayaṃ,

Mānayañca sugataṃ sukhānayaṃ;

Byākaromi paramaṃ ito paraṃ,

Taṃ suṇātha madhuratthavaṇṇanaṃ.

Hereafter, I shall expound the supreme method of development, which leads to welfare, and the method of reverence for the Fortunate One, which leads to happiness. Listen to this sweet and meaningful exposition.

790.

790.

Uttaraṃ tu manussānaṃ, dhammato ñāṇadassanaṃ;

Pattukāmena kātabbaṃ, ādito sīlasodhanaṃ.

A person who desires to attain the higher knowledge and vision of the Dhamma must, from the outset, undertake the purification of virtue.

791.

791.

Saṅkassarasamācāre, dussīle sīlavajjite;

Natthi jhānaṃ kuto maggo, tasmā sīlaṃ visodhaye.

For one of discordant conduct, for the immoral, for one devoid of virtue, there is no jhāna; how then the path? Therefore, one should purify virtue.

792.

792.

Sīlaṃ cārittavārittavasena duvidhaṃ mataṃ;

Taṃ panācchiddamakkhaṇḍamakammāsamaninditaṃ.

Virtue is considered twofold: that of conduct and that of avoidance. It should be unbroken, unblemished, unspotted, and blameless.

793.

793.

Kattabbaṃ atthakāmena, vivekasukhamicchatā;

Sīlañca nāma bhikkhūnaṃ, alaṅkāro anuttaro.

It should be undertaken by one who desires his own welfare, who wishes for the happiness of seclusion. And virtue, indeed, is the unsurpassed ornament for monks.

794.

794.

Ratanaṃ saraṇaṃ khemaṃ, tāṇaṃ leṇaṃ parāyaṇaṃ;

Cintāmaṇi paṇīto ca, sīlaṃ yānamanuttaraṃ.

Virtue is a jewel, a refuge, security, protection, a shelter, a final resort; it is a precious wish-fulfilling gem, an unsurpassed vehicle.

795.

795.

Sītalaṃ [V 0.0112] salilaṃ sīlaṃ, kilesamaladhovanaṃ;

Guṇānaṃ mūlabhūtañca, dosānaṃ balaghāti ca.

Virtue is cool water, washing away the stain of defilements; it is the root of good qualities and the destroyer of the power of faults.

796.

796.

Tidivārohaṇañcetaṃ, sopānaṃ paramuttamaṃ;

Maggo khemo ca nibbānanagarassa pavesane.

This is the supreme stairway for ascending to heaven; it is a safe path for entering the city of Nibbāna.

797.

797.

Tasmā suparisuddhaṃ taṃ, sīlaṃ duvidhalakkhaṇaṃ;

Kattabbaṃ atthakāmena, piyasīlena bhikkhunā.

Therefore, that well-purified virtue, with its twofold characteristic, should be undertaken by a monk who desires his own welfare and who holds virtue dear.

798.

798.

Kātabbo pana sīlasmiṃ, parisuddhe ṭhitenidha;

Palibodhassupacchedo, palibodhā dasāhu ca.

Moreover, one established here in pure virtue should undertake the cutting off of obstacles; and the obstacles are said to be ten.

799.

799.

“Āvāso [M 0.0121] ca kulaṃ lābho,

Gaṇo kammañca pañcamaṃ;

Addhānaṃ ñāti ābādho,

Gantho iddhīti te dasā”ti.

Dwelling, family, gain, a group, and work as the fifth; a journey, relatives, sickness, study, and psychic power—these are the ten.

800.

800.

Palibodhassupacchedaṃ, katvā dasavidhassapi;

Upasaṅkamitabbo so, kammaṭṭhānassa dāyako.

Having cut off the ten kinds of obstacles, one should approach that giver of a meditation subject.

801.

801.

Piyo [P 0.0090] garu bhāvanīyo, vattā ca vacanakkhamo;

Gambhīrañca kathaṃ kattā, no caṭṭhāne niyojako.

He should be dear, respected, and worthy of esteem; a speaker who is patient when spoken to, a purveyor of profound discourse, and not one who engages another in what is unsuitable.

802.

802.

Evamādiguṇopetamupagantvā hitesinaṃ;

Kalyāṇamittaṃ kālena, kammaṭṭhānassa dāyakaṃ.

Having approached at the proper time such a spiritual friend, a giver of a meditation subject, who is endowed with these and other virtues and is a seeker of one's welfare.

803.

803.

Kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetabbaṃ, vattaṃ katvā panassa tu;

Tenāpi caritaṃ ñatvā, dātabbaṃ tassa bhikkhuno.

Having performed one's duties towards him, the meditation subject should be received. And he, having understood that monk's temperament, should give it to that monk.

804.

804.

Caritaṃ panidaṃ rāgadosamohavasena ca;

Saddhābuddhivitakkānaṃ, vasena chabbidhaṃ mataṃ.

Now, this temperament is considered to be sixfold: by way of lust, hatred, and delusion, and by way of faith, intelligence, and discursive thought.

805.

805.

Vomissakanayā tesaṃ, catusaṭṭhi bhavanti te;

Tehi attho na catthīti, na mayā idha dassitā.

By the method of their combination, they become sixty-four. As there is no purpose in them, they are not shown here by me.

806.

806.

Asubhā [V 0.0113] ca dasevettha, tathā kāyagatāsati;

Ekādasa ime rāga-caritassānukūlatā.

Herein, the ten meditations on foulness and likewise mindfulness directed to the body—these eleven are suitable for one of a lustful temperament.

807.

807.

Catasso appamaññāyo, savaṇṇakasiṇā ime;

Aṭṭheva ca sadā dosa-caritassānukūlatā.

The four immeasurables and the four color kasiṇas—these eight are always suitable for one of a hateful temperament.

808.

808.

Taṃ mohacaritassettha, vitakkacaritassa ca;

Anukūlanti niddiṭṭhaṃ, ānāpānaṃ panekakaṃ.

For one of a deluded temperament and for one of a discursive temperament, the single practice of mindfulness of breathing is declared herein to be suitable.

809.

809.

Purimānussatichakkaṃ, saddhācaritadehino;

Maraṇūpasamāyuttā, satimāhāranissitā.

The first six recollections are for a person of faithful temperament.

810.

810.

Saññā [M 0.0122] dhātuvavatthānaṃ, buddhippakatijantuno;

Ime pana ca cattāro, anukūlāti dīpitā.

Mindfulness of death, mindfulness of peace, the perception of loathsomeness in food, and the analysis of the four elements—these four are declared suitable for a person of intelligent nature.

811.

811.

Cattāropi ca āruppā, sesāni kasiṇāni ca;

Anukūlā ime sabba-caritānanti vaṇṇitā.

The four immaterial attainments and the remaining kasiṇas are described as suitable for all temperaments.

812.

812.

Idaṃ sabbaṃ panekanta-vipaccanīkabhāvato;

Atisappāyato vutta-miti ñeyyaṃ vibhāvinā.

This all should be understood by the discerning one as having been stated because it is entirely contrary to the defilements and exceedingly suitable.

813.

813.

Kammaṭṭhānāni sabbāni, cattālīsāti niddise;

Kasiṇāni dasa ceva, asubhānussatī dasa.

One should declare the meditation subjects to be forty in all: ten kasiṇas, ten foulnesses, and ten recollections.

814.

814.

Catasso appamaññāyo, cattāro ca arūpino;

Catudhātuvavatthānaṃ, saññā cāhāratā iti.

The four immeasurables, the four immaterial states, the analysis of the four elements, and the perception of loathsomeness in food.

815.

815.

Kammaṭṭhānesu etesu, upacāravahā kati;

Ānāpānasatiṃ kāya-gataṃ hitvā panaṭṭhapi.

Among these meditation subjects, how many lead only to access concentration? The eight recollections, excluding mindfulness of breathing and mindfulness directed to the body.

816.

816.

Sesānussatiyo saññā, vavatthānanti terasa;

Upacāravahā vuttā, sesā te appanāvahā.

The remaining recollections, the perception, and the analysis—these thirteen are said to lead to access concentration; the rest lead to absorption.

817.

817.

Appanāyāvahesvettha, kasiṇāni dasāpi ca;

Ānāpānasatī ceva, catukkajjhānikā ime.

Herein, among those that lead to absorption, the ten kasiṇas and mindfulness of breathing are subjects for the four jhānas.

818.

818.

Asubhāni [V 0.0114] dasa cettha, tathā kāyagatāsati;

Ekādasa ime dhammā, paṭhamajjhānikā siyuṃ.

Herein, the ten meditations on foulness and likewise mindfulness directed to the body; these eleven subjects are attainable only up to the first jhāna.

819.

819.

Ādibrahmavihārāti[P 0.0091], tikajjhānavahā tayo;

Catutthāpi ca āruppā, catutthajjhānikā matā.

The first three divine abodes lead to the first three jhānas; the fourth, along with the immaterial attainments, are considered to be subjects of the fourth jhāna.

820.

820.

Vasenārammaṇaṅgānaṃ, duvidho samatikkamo;

Gocarātikkamārūpe, rūpe jhānaṅgatikkamo.

By way of object and factors, the transcending is twofold: in the immaterial sphere, it is the transcending of the object-field; in the form sphere, it is the transcending of the jhāna factors.

821.

821.

Daseva kasiṇānettha, vaḍḍhetabbāni honti hi;

Na ca vaḍḍhaniyā sesā, bhavanti asubhādayo.

Herein, indeed, only the ten kasiṇas are to be enlarged; the rest, such as the meditations on foulness and so on, are not to be enlarged.

822.

822.

Daseva kasiṇānettha, asubhāni dasāpi ca;

Ānāpānasatī ceva, tathā kāyagatāsati.

Herein, the ten kasiṇas, and also the ten meditations on foulness, mindfulness of breathing, and likewise mindfulness directed to the body.

823.

823.

Paṭibhāganimittāni[M 0.0123], honti ārammaṇāni hi;

Sesāneva paṭibhāga-nimittārammaṇā siyuṃ.

Indeed, these have the counterpart sign as their object; the remaining subjects do not have the counterpart sign as their object.

824.

824.

Asubhāni dasāhāra-saññā kāyagatāsati;

Devesu nappavattanti, dvādasetāni sabbadā.

The ten meditations on foulness, the perception of loathsomeness in food, and mindfulness directed to the body—these twelve never occur among the devas.

825.

825.

Tāni dvādasa cetāni, ānāpānasatīpi ca;

Teraseva panetāni, brahmaloke na vijjare.

And these twelve, together with mindfulness of breathing—these thirteen are not found in the Brahmā world.

826.

826.

Ṭhapetvā caturārūpe, natthi kiñci arūpisu;

Manussaloke sabbāni, pavattanti na saṃsayo.

Except for the four immaterial meditations, there is nothing else in the immaterial realms; in the human world, all of them occur, without a doubt.

827.

827.

Catutthaṃ kasiṇaṃ hitvā, kasiṇā asubhāni ca;

Diṭṭheneva gahetabbā, ime ekūnavīsati.

The kasiṇas, excluding the fourth, and the meditations on foulness—these nineteen should be grasped by means of sight.

828.

828.

Satiyampi ca kāyamhi, diṭṭhena tacapañcakaṃ;

Sesamettha suteneva, gahetabbanti dīpitaṃ.

And in mindfulness directed to the body, the pentad ending with the skin should be grasped by sight; it is explained that the remainder herein should be grasped through hearing.

829.

829.

Ānāpānasatī ettha, phuṭṭhena paridīpitā;

Vāyokasiṇamevettha, diṭṭhaphuṭṭhena gayhati.

Herein, mindfulness of breathing is explained by way of touch; and the air kasiṇa is grasped by way of sight and touch.

830.

830.

Suteneva [V 0.0115] gahetabbā, sesā aṭṭhārasāpi ca;

Upekkhā appamaññā ca, arūpā ceva pañcime.

The remaining eighteen are also to be grasped through learning; equanimity, the immeasurable, and the four immaterial attainments—these five.

831.

831.

Āditova gahetabbā, na hontīti pakāsitā;

Pañcatiṃsāvasesāni, gahetabbāni ādito.

These are declared as not to be grasped from the very beginning; the remaining thirty-five should be grasped from the outset.

832.

832.

Kammaṭṭhānesu hetesu, ākāsakasiṇaṃ vinā;

Kasiṇā nava honte ca, arūpānaṃ tu paccayā.

Among these meditation subjects, except for the space kasiṇa, the nine kasiṇas are conditions for the immaterial attainments.

833.

833.

Dasāpi kasiṇā honti, abhiññānaṃ tu paccayā;

Tayo brahmavihārāpi, catukkassa bhavanti tu.

The ten kasiṇas are conditions for the higher knowledges; and the three divine abodes are conditions for the fourfold jhāna.

834.

834.

Heṭṭhimaṃ heṭṭhimāruppaṃ, uparūparimassa hi;

Tathā catutthamāruppaṃ, nirodhassāti dīpitaṃ.

Indeed, each lower immaterial attainment is a condition for the next higher one; likewise, the fourth immaterial attainment is said to be a condition for cessation.

835.

835.

Sabbāni ca panetāni, cattālīsavidhāni tu;

Vipassanābhavasampatti-sukhānaṃ paccayā siyuṃ.

And all these forty kinds of meditation subjects may be conditions for insight, higher becoming, attainment, and happiness.

836.

836.

Kammaṭṭhānaṃ [M 0.0124] gahetvāna, ācariyassa santike;

Vasantassa kathetabbaṃ, āgatassāgatakkhaṇe.

Having taken up a meditation subject in the teacher’s presence, one who is staying should report on it at the moment of arrival.

837.

837.

Uggahetvā [P 0.0092] panaññatra, gantukāmassa bhikkhuno;

Nātisaṅkhepavitthāraṃ, kathetabbaṃ tu tenapi.

But if a monk, having learned it, intends to go elsewhere, he too should speak of it, neither too concisely nor too elaborately.

838.

838.

Kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvāna, sammaṭṭhānaṃ manobhuno;

Aṭṭhārasahi dosehi, niccaṃ pana vivajjite.

Having taken up a meditation subject, the right foundation for the mind, one should always be free from the eighteen faults.

839.

839.

Anurūpe vihārasmiṃ, vihātabbaṃ tu gāmato;

Nātidūre naccāsanne, sive pañcaṅgasaṃyute.

One should reside in a suitable dwelling, not too far nor too near, auspicious and endowed with five qualities.

840.

840.

Khuddako palibodhopi, chinditabbo panatthi ce;

Dīghā kesā nakhā lomā, chinditabbā vibhāvinā.

Even a minor obstacle, if there is one, should be severed. Long hair, nails, and body hair should be cut by the discerning one.

841.

841.

Cīvaraṃ rajitabbaṃ taṃ, kiliṭṭhaṃ tu sace siyā;

Sace patte malaṃ hoti, pacitabbova suṭṭhu so.

The robe should be dyed if it is soiled; if the bowl is dirty, it should be thoroughly fired.

842.

842.

Acchinnapalibodhena[V 0.0116], pacchā tena ca bhikkhunā;

Pavivitte panokāse, vasantena yathāsukhaṃ.

Afterward, that monk, having severed the obstacles, should dwell at ease in a secluded place.

843.

843.

Vajjetvā mattikaṃ nīlaṃ, pītaṃ setañca lohitaṃ;

Saṇhāyāruṇavaṇṇāya, mattikāya manoramaṃ.

Having avoided blue, yellow, white, and red clay, a pleasing object should be made with smooth, reddish-brown clay.

844.

844.

Kattabbaṃ kasiṇajjhānaṃ, pattukāmena dhīmatā;

Senāsane vivittasmiṃ, bahiddhā vāpi tādise.

The kasiṇa meditation should be undertaken by the wise one desiring attainment, in a secluded dwelling, or in a similar place outside.

845.

845.

Paṭicchanne panaṭṭhāne, pabbhāre vā guhantare;

Saṃhārimaṃ vā kātabbaṃ, taṃ tatraṭṭhakameva vā.

In a hidden spot, on a mountain slope, or inside a cave, a portable one should be made, or one fixed right there.

846.

846.

Saṃhārimaṃ karontena, daṇḍakesu catūsvapi;

Cammaṃ vā kaṭasāraṃ vā, dussapattampi vā tathā.

When making a portable one, on four sticks, one may use hide, matting, or a piece of cloth.

847.

847.

Bandhitvā tathā kātabbaṃ, mattikāya pamāṇato;

Bhūmiyaṃ pattharitvā ca, oloketabbameva taṃ.

Having bound it thus, it should be made with clay according to the measure; and having spread it on the ground, it should be well examined.

848.

848.

Tatraṭṭhaṃ bhūmiyaṃ vaṭṭaṃ, ākoṭitvāna khāṇuke;

Vallīhi taṃ vinandhitvā, kātabbaṃ kaṇṇikaṃ samaṃ.

For a fixed one on the ground, having driven in a peg, a circle should be drawn; having bound it with creepers, a level rim should be made.

849.

849.

Vitthārato [M 0.0125] pamāṇena, vidatthicaturaṅgulaṃ;

Vaṭṭaṃ vattati taṃ kātuṃ, vivaṭṭaṃ pana micchatā.

The measure in width is a span and four fingerbreadths. It is proper to make it round; one should not wish it to be incomplete.

850.

850.

Bherītalasamaṃ sādhu, katvā kasiṇamaṇḍalaṃ;

Sammajjitvāna taṃ ṭhānaṃ, nhatvā āgamma paṇḍito.

Having made the kasiṇa-circle well, like the surface of a drum, the wise one, having swept that place, should bathe and then approach.

851.

851.

Hatthapāsapamāṇasmiṃ, tamhā kasiṇamaṇḍalā;

Padese tu supaññatte, āsanasmiṃ suatthate.

At a distance of two and a half cubits from that kasiṇa-circle, in a well-prepared spot, on a well-spread seat,

852.

852.

Ucce tattha nisīditvā, vidatthicaturaṅgule;

Ujukāyaṃ paṇidhāya, katvā parimukhaṃ satiṃ.

Sitting there on a high seat, a span and four fingerbreadths high, setting his body erect, establishing mindfulness before him,

853.

853.

Kāmesvādīnavaṃ disvā, nekkhammaṃ daṭṭhu khemato;

Paramaṃ pītipāmojjaṃ, janetvā ratanattaye.

Seeing the danger in sensual pleasures, seeing renunciation as security, generating supreme joy and gladness in the Triple Gem,

854.

854.

“Bhāgī [V 0.0117] assamahaṃ addhā, imāya paṭipattiyā;

Pavivekasukhassā”ti, katvā ussāhamuttamaṃ.

Having made the utmost effort, thinking, "Surely, through this practice, I will be a partaker in the bliss of seclusion,"

855.

855.

Ākārena [P 0.0093] sameneva, ummīlitvāna locanaṃ;

Nimittaṃ gaṇhatā sādhu, bhāvetabbaṃ punappunaṃ.

With a balanced posture, having opened the eyes, one grasping the sign should develop it well again and again.

856.

856.

Na vaṇṇo pekkhitabbo so, daṭṭhabbaṃ na ca lakkhaṇaṃ;

Vaṇṇaṃ pana amuñcitvā, ussadassa vasena hi.

The color should not be observed, nor should the characteristic be regarded; but without abandoning the color, one should attend by way of the concept.

857.

857.

Cittaṃ paṇṇattidhammasmiṃ, ṭhapetvekaggamānaso;

“Pathavī pathavi”ccevaṃ, vatvā bhāveyya paṇḍito.

The wise one, with a one-pointed mind, having placed it on the conceptual object, should develop it, saying, "Earth, earth."

858.

858.

Pathavī medanī bhūmi, vasudhā ca vasundharā;

Evaṃ pathavināmesu, ekaṃ vattumpi vaṭṭati.

Pathavī, medanī, bhūmi, vasudhā, and vasundharā—thus, among the names for earth, it is fitting to say any one.

859.

859.

Ummīlitvā nimīlitvā, āvajjeyya punappunaṃ;

Yāvuggahanimittaṃ tu, nuppajjati ca tāva so.

Opening and closing his eyes, he should attend again and again, for as long as the learning sign does not arise.

860.

860.

Evaṃ bhāvayato tassa, puna ekaggacetaso;

Yadā pana nimīletvā, āvajjantassa yogino.

Thus, for that yogi with a one-pointed mind who is developing it, when, having closed his eyes, he attends again,

861.

861.

Yathā ummīlitekāle, tathāpāthaṃ tu yāti ce;

Taduggahanimittaṃ ta-muppannanti pavuccati.

If it comes into range in the same way as when the eyes were open, then that learning sign is said to have arisen.

862.

862.

Nimitte [M 0.0126] pana sañjāte, tato pabhuti yoginā;

Nisīditabbaṃ no cevaṃ, tasmiṃ ṭhāne vijānatā.

When the sign has arisen, from then on, the yogi who knows should not sit in that place.

863.

863.

Attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ, pavisitvāna dhīmatā;

Tena tattha nisinnena, bhāvetabbaṃ yathāsukhaṃ.

Having entered his own dwelling place, the wise one, sitting there, should develop it as is comfortable.

864.

864.

Papañcaparihāratthaṃ, pādānaṃ pana dhovane;

Tassekatalikā dve ca, icchitabbā upāhanā.

For the purpose of avoiding proliferation and for washing the feet, single-soled or double-soled sandals are to be desired for him.

865.

865.

Samādhitaruṇo tassa, asappāyena kenaci;

Sace nassati taṃ ṭhānaṃ, gantvāvādāya taṃ pana.

His concentration is young; if it is destroyed by anything unsuitable, he should go to that place and take it up again.

866.

866.

Pīṭhe [V 0.0118] sukhanisinnena, bhāvetabbaṃ punappunaṃ;

Samannāharitabbañca, kare takkāhatampi ca.

Sitting comfortably on a seat, it should be developed again and again; and it should be brought to mind and struck with initial thought.

867.

867.

Nimittaṃ pana taṃ hitvā, cittaṃ dhāvati ce bahi;

Nivāretvā nimittasmiṃ, ṭhapetabbaṃ tu mānasaṃ.

But if the mind, having abandoned that sign, runs outside, one should restrain it and indeed fix the mind upon the sign.

868.

868.

Yattha yattha nisīditvā, tamicchati tapodhano;

Tattha tattha divārattiṃ, tassupaṭṭhāti cetaso.

Wherever the ascetic, having sat down, desires it, there, day and night, it appears to his mind.

869.

869.

Evaṃ tassa karontassa, anupubbena yogino;

Vikkhambhanti ca sabbāni, pañca nīvaraṇānipi.

Thus, for the yogi practicing in due order, all five hindrances are suppressed.

870.

870.

Samādhiyati cittampi, upacārasamādhinā;

Paṭibhāganimittampi, uppajjati ca yogino.

The mind also becomes concentrated with access concentration, and the counterpart sign arises for the yogi.

871.

871.

Ko panāyaṃ viseso hi, imassa purimassa vā;

Thavikā nīhatādāsa-maṇḍalaṃ viya majjitaṃ.

What, then, is the difference between this and the previous one? It is like a polished mirror-disc taken from its case.

872.

872.

Meghato viya nikkhantaṃ, sampuṇṇacandamaṇḍalaṃ;

Paṭibhāganimittaṃ taṃ, balākā viya toyade.

Like the full moon-disc emerged from a cloud, that counterpart sign is like a crane against a rain-cloud.

873.

873.

Taduggahanimittaṃ [P 0.0094] taṃ, padāletvāva niggataṃ;

Tatodhikataraṃ suddhaṃ, hutvāpaṭṭhāti tassa taṃ.

It emerges, having burst forth from that learning sign; having become exceedingly purer than that, it appears to him.

874.

874.

Tanusaṇṭhānavantañca, vaṇṇavantaṃ na ceva taṃ;

Upaṭṭhākāramattaṃ taṃ, paññajaṃ bhāvanāmayaṃ.

It is indeed without form, shape, or color; it is merely a mode of appearance, born of concept, a product of development.

875.

875.

Paṭibhāge [M 0.0127] samuppanne, nimitte bhāvanāmaye;

Honti vikkhambhitāneva, pañca nīvaraṇānipi.

When the counterpart sign, a product of development, has arisen, the five hindrances are indeed suppressed.

876.

876.

Kilesā sannisinnāva, yuttayogassa bhikkhuno;

Cittaṃ samāhitaṃyeva, upacārasamādhinā.

For the diligent monk, the defilements are indeed subsided, and his mind is indeed concentrated with access concentration.

877.

877.

Ākārehi pana dvīhi, samādhiyati mānasaṃ;

Upacārakkhaṇe tassa, paṭilābhe samādhino.

The mind becomes concentrated in two aspects: at the moment of access, and at the attainment of concentration.

878.

878.

Nīvāraṇappahānena[V 0.0119], upacārakkhaṇe tathā;

Aṅgānaṃ pātubhāvena, paṭilābhakkhaṇe pana.

At the moment of access, by the abandoning of the hindrances; and at the moment of attainment, by the manifestation of the factors.

879.

879.

Dvinnaṃ pana samādhīnaṃ, kiṃ nānākaraṇaṃ pana;

Aṅgāni thāmajātāni, upacārakkhaṇena ca.

What then is the distinction between the two concentrations? In access concentration, the factors are not yet strong.

880.

880.

Appanāya panaṅgāni, thāmajātāni jāyare;

Tasmā taṃ appanācittaṃ, divasampi pavattati.

But in absorption, the factors arise born of strength; therefore, that mind of absorption continues even for a whole day.

881.

881.

Pallaṅkena ca teneva, vaḍḍhetvā taṃ nimittakaṃ;

Appanaṃ adhigantuṃ so, sakkoti yadi sundaraṃ.

And with that very same cross-legged posture, having developed that sign, he is able to attain absorption, if it is well-established.

882.

882.

No ce sakkoti so tena,

Taṃ nimittaṃ tu yoginā;

Cakkavattiya gabbhova,

Ratanaṃ viya dullabhaṃ.

If he is not able to do so, that sign is as difficult for the yogi to obtain as a jewel from the womb of a universal monarch.

883.

883.

Satataṃ appamattena, rakkhitabbaṃ satīmatā;

Nimittaṃ rakkhato laddhaṃ, parihāni na vijjati.

It should be constantly guarded by one who is diligent and mindful; for one who guards the sign thus obtained, there is no decline.

884.

884.

Ārakkhaṇe asantamhi, laddhaṃ laddhaṃ vinassati;

Rakkhitabbaṃ hi tasmā taṃ, tatrāyaṃ rakkhaṇāvidhi.

When there is no guarding, whatever is gained is lost; therefore, it must indeed be guarded. Herein is the method of guarding.

885.

885.

Āvāso gocaro bhassaṃ, puggalo bhojanaṃ utu;

Iriyāpathoti sattete, asappāye vivajjaye.

Dwelling, alms-resort, speech, person, food, climate, and posture—these seven, if they are unsuitable, one should avoid.

886.

886.

Sappāye [M 0.0128] satta seveyya, evañhi paṭipajjato;

Na cireneva kālena, hoti bhikkhussa appanā.

One should cultivate the seven that are suitable; for a monk practicing thus, absorption arises before long.

887.

887.

Yassappanā na hoteva, evampi paṭipajjato;

Appanāya ca kosallaṃ, sammā sampādaye budho.

For one for whom absorption does not arise even when practicing thus, the wise one should properly accomplish skill in absorption.

888.

888.

Appanāya hi kosalla-midaṃ dasavidhaṃ idha;

Ganthavitthārabhītena, mayā vissajjitanti ca.

For this tenfold skill in absorption has been omitted here by me, fearing the expansion of the text.

889.

889.

Evañhi [V 0.0120] sampādayato, appanākosallaṃ pana;

Paṭiladdhe nimittasmiṃ, appanā sampavattati.

Thus indeed, for one accomplishing skill in absorption, when the sign has been obtained, absorption occurs.

890.

890.

Evampi paṭipannassa, sace sā nappavattati;

Tathāpi na jahe yogaṃ, vāyametheva paṇḍito.

Even for one thus practicing, if it does not arise, still, the wise one should not abandon the practice, but should indeed strive.

891.

891.

Cittappavattiākāraṃ[P 0.0095], tasmā sallakkhayaṃ budho;

Samataṃ vīriyasseva, yojayetha punappunaṃ.

Therefore, the wise one, discerning the manner of the mind's activity, should repeatedly apply evenness to his energy.

892.

892.

Īsakampi layaṃ yantaṃ, paggaṇhetheva mānasaṃ;

Accāraddhaṃ nisedhetvā, samameva pavattaye.

If the mind inclines even slightly to sluggishness, one should indeed uplift it. Having restrained the over-exerted mind, one should make it proceed evenly.

893.

893.

Līnatuddhatabhāvehi, mocayitvāna mānasaṃ;

Paṭibhāganimittābhi-mukhaṃ taṃ paṭipādaye.

Having freed the mind from states of sluggishness and restlessness, one should direct it toward the counterpart sign.

894.

894.

Evaṃ nimittābhimukhaṃ, paṭipādayato pana;

Idānevappanā tassa, sā samijjhissatīti ca.

For one who thus directs the mind toward the sign, that absorption will succeed for him right now.

895.

895.

Bhavaṅgaṃ pana pacchijja, pathavīkasiṇaṃ tathā;

Tadevārammaṇaṃ katvā, manodvāramhi yogino.

Then, for the yogi, having cut off the life-continuum, and having made that very earth-kasiṇa the object at the mind-door,

896.

896.

Jāyatevajjanaṃ cittaṃ, tatrevārammaṇe tato;

Javanāni ca jāyante, tassa cattāri pañca vā.

The adverting consciousness arises on that very object; then, four or five impulsion moments arise for him.

897.

897.

Avasāne panekaṃ tu, rūpāvacarikaṃ bhave;

Takkādayo panaññehi, bhavanti balavattarā.

At the end, however, one becomes a fine-material consciousness; and initial application and so forth become stronger than in the others.

898.

898.

Appanācetaso tāni, parikammopacārato;

Vuccanti parikammāni, upacārāni cātipi.

Those javanas preceding the absorption mind are called preliminary work and access, on account of being preliminary work and access.

899.

899.

Appanāyānulomattā[M 0.0129], anulomāni eva ca;

Yaṃ taṃ sabbantimaṃ ettha, gotrabhūti pavuccati.

Due to conformity with absorption, there are also the conformity-moments; that which is the very last here is called change-of-lineage.

900.

900.

Gahitāgahaṇenettha, parikammappanādikaṃ;

Dutiyaṃ upacāraṃ taṃ, tatiyaṃ anulomakaṃ.

Here, by the method of grasping and not grasping, in the process from preliminary work to absorption: the second is access, the third is adaptation.

901.

901.

Catutthaṃ [V 0.0121] gotrabhu diṭṭhaṃ, pañcamaṃ appanāmano;

Paṭhamaṃ upacāraṃ vā, dutiyaṃ anulomakaṃ.

The fourth is seen as change-of-lineage, the fifth is the absorption mind; or, the first is access, the second is adaptation.

902.

902.

Tatiyaṃ gotrabhu diṭṭhaṃ, catutthaṃ appanāmano;

Catutthaṃ pañcamaṃ vāti, appeti na tato paraṃ.

The third is seen as change-of-lineage, the fourth is the absorption mind; it absorbs at the fourth or fifth [impulsion], not beyond that.

903.

903.

Chaṭṭhe vā sattame vāpi, appanā neva jāyati;

Āsannattā bhavaṅgassa, javanaṃ pati tāvade.

In the sixth or seventh [impulsion], absorption does not arise; due to proximity to the life-continuum, the impulsion lasts only for that long.

904.

904.

Purimehāsevanaṃ laddhā, chaṭṭhaṃ vā sattamampi vā;

Appetīti panetthāha, godatto ābhidhammiko.

Having attained repetition from the preceding moments, the sixth or even the seventh 'it absorbs'—so declares the Abhidhammika Godatta here.

905.

905.

Dhāvanto hi yathā koci,

Naro chinnataṭāmukho;

Ṭhātukāmo pariyante,

Ṭhātuṃ sakkoti neva so.

Just as a man running, facing a collapsed bank, wishing to stop at the edge, is not able to do so.

906.

906.

Evameva panacchaṭṭhe, sattame vāpi mānaso;

Na sakkotīti appetuṃ, veditabbaṃ vibhāvinā.

In the same way, the mind in the sixth or seventh [impulsion] is not able to absorb; so it should be understood by the discerning one.

907.

907.

Ekacittakkhaṇāyeva, hotāyaṃ appanā pana;

Tato bhavaṅgapātova, hotīti paridīpitaṃ.

This absorption occurs for only a single mind-moment; then there is a falling into the life-continuum, so it has been explained.

908.

908.

Tato bhavaṅgaṃ chinditvā, paccavekkhaṇahetukaṃ;

Āvajjanaṃ tato jhāna-paccavekkhaṇamānasaṃ.

Then, having cut off the life-continuum, an adverting for the purpose of reviewing arises, followed by the mind that reviews the jhāna.

909.

909.

Kāmacchando [P 0.0096] ca byāpādo, thinamiddhañca uddhato;

Kukkuccaṃ vicikicchā ca, pahīnā pañcime pana.

Sensual desire and ill-will, sloth and torpor, and restlessness and remorse, and doubt—these five are abandoned.

910.

910.

Vitakkena vicārena, pītiyā ca sukhena ca;

Ekaggatāya saṃyuttaṃ, jhānaṃ pañcaṅgikaṃ idaṃ.

Endowed with initial application and sustained application, with joy, happiness, and one-pointedness, this jhāna has five factors.

911.

911.

Nānāvisayaluddhassa[M 0.0130], kāmacchandavasā pana;

Ito cito bhamantassa, vane makkaṭako viya.

For one greedy for various objects, under the power of sensual desire, wandering here and there like a monkey in a forest,

912.

912.

Ekasmiṃ [V 0.0122] visayeyeva, samādhāneva cetaso;

“Samādhi kāmacchandassa, paṭipakkho”ti vuccati.

When the mind is indeed concentrated on a single object, that concentration is called the antidote to sensual desire.

913.

913.

Pāmojjabhāvato ceva, sītalattā sabhāvato;

“Byāpādassa tato pīti, paṭipakkhā”ti bhāsitā.

From its nature of gladness and from its inherent coolness, joy is therefore spoken of as the antidote to ill-will.

914.

914.

Savipphārikabhāvena, nekkhammādipavattito;

“Vitakko thinamiddhassa, paṭipakkho”ti vaṇṇito.

By its expansive nature and its promotion of renunciation and so forth, initial application is described as the antidote to sloth and torpor.

915.

915.

Avūpasantabhāvassa, sayañcevātisantato;

“Sukhaṃ uddhaccakukkucca-dvayassa paṭipakkhakaṃ”.

Because it is itself exceedingly peaceful, happiness is the counteragent to the pair of restlessness and remorse, which is of an unpacified nature.

916.

916.

Matiyā anurūpattā, “anumajjanalakkhaṇo;

Vicāro vicikicchāya, paṭipakkho”ti dīpito.

Due to its conformity with wisdom and its characteristic of repeated pondering, sustained application is declared the antidote to doubt.

917.

917.

Pañcaṅgavippayuttaṃ taṃ, jhānaṃ pañcaṅgasaṃyutaṃ;

Sivaṃ tividhakalyāṇaṃ, dasalakkhaṇasaṃyutaṃ.

That jhāna, devoid of five factors and endowed with five factors, is auspicious, threefold beautiful, and endowed with ten characteristics.

918.

918.

Evañcādhigataṃ hoti, paṭhamaṃ tena yoginā;

Suciraṭṭhitikāmena, tassa jhānassa sabbaso.

Thus the first jhāna is attained by that yogi who desires the long-lasting stability of that jhāna in every way.

919.

919.

Taṃ samāpajjitabbaṃ tu, visodhetvāna pāpake;

Taṃ samāpajjato tassa, suciraṭṭhitikaṃ bhave.

Having purified away evil states, that jhāna should be attained; for one who attains it, it will be long-lasting.

920.

920.

Cittabhāvanavepullaṃ, patthayantena bhikkhunā;

Paṭibhāganimittaṃ taṃ, vaḍḍhetabbaṃ yathākkamaṃ.

A monk, aspiring to the full development of the mind, should develop that counterpart sign in due order.

921.

921.

Vaḍḍhanābhūmiyo dve ca, upacārañca appanā;

Upacārampi vā patvā, vaḍḍhetuṃ tañca vattati.

There are two grounds for growth: access and absorption. Or, having attained even access, it is fitting to develop that.

922.

922.

Appanaṃ pana patvā vā, tatrāyaṃ vaḍḍhanakkamo;

Kasitabbaṃ yathāṭhānaṃ, paricchindati kassako.

But having attained absorption, herein is the method of growth: just as a farmer defines the place to be cultivated.

923.

923.

Yoginā evamevampi, aṅguladvaṅgulādinā;

Paricchijja paricchijja, vaḍḍhetabbaṃ yathicchakaṃ.

So too the yogi, with measurements of one finger, two fingers, and so forth, having delimited again and again, should develop it as desired.

924.

924.

Pattepi [M 0.0131][V 0.0123] paṭhame jhāne, ākārehipi pañcahi;

Suciṇṇavasinā tena, bhavitabbaṃ tapassinā.

Even when the first jhāna has been attained, that ascetic should become well-practiced and masterful in the five modes.

925.

925.

Āvajjanaṃ samāpatti, adhiṭṭhānesu tīsu ca;

Vuṭṭhānapaccavekkhāsu, vasitā pañca bhāsitā.

Adverting, attainment, in the three resolutions, and in emergence and reviewing—the five masteries are declared.

926.

926.

Āvajjitvā adhiṭṭhitvā, samāpajja punappunaṃ;

Vuṭṭhitvā paccavekkhitvā, vasitā pañca sādhaye.

Having adverted, having resolved, having entered repeatedly, having emerged, and having reviewed—one should accomplish the five masteries.

927.

927.

Paṭhame [P 0.0097] avasipatte, dutiyaṃ yo panicchati;

Ubhato bhaṭṭhobhave yogī, paṭhamā dutiyāpi ca.

If one is unmastered in the first, and then desires the second, that yogi becomes fallen from both, the first and the second.

928.

928.

Kāmassahagatā saññā, manakkārā caranti ce;

Pamādayogino jhānaṃ, hoti taṃ hānabhāgiyaṃ.

If perceptions and applications of mind accompanied by sensual desire operate, for the negligent yogi that jhāna is conducive to decline.

929.

929.

Sati santiṭṭhate tasmiṃ, santā tadanudhammatā;

Mandassa yogino jhānaṃ, hoti taṃ ṭhitibhāgiyaṃ.

If mindfulness is firmly established in that, and its nature is peaceful, for the sluggish yogi that jhāna is conducive to stability.

930.

930.

Atakkasahitā saññā, manakkārā caranti ce;

Appamattassa taṃ jhānaṃ, visesabhāgiyaṃ siyā.

If perceptions and applications of mind without applied thought operate, for the heedful one that jhāna would be conducive to distinction.

931.

931.

Nibbidāsaṃyutā saññā, manakkārā caranti ce;

Nibbedhabhāgiyaṃ jhānaṃ, hotīti paridīpitaṃ.

If perceptions and applications of mind connected with disenchantment operate, it is declared to be the jhāna conducive to penetration.

932.

932.

Tasmā pañcasu etesu, suciṇṇavasinā pana;

Paṭhamā paguṇato jhānā, vuṭṭhāya vidhinā tato.

Therefore, having well-mastered these five, and having arisen methodically from the first jhāna that has been made familiar.

933.

933.

Yasmā ayaṃ samāpatti, āsannākusalārikā;

Thūlattā takkacārānaṃ, tatoyaṃ aṅgadubbalā.

Because this attainment is close to the unwholesome enemy, and due to the coarseness of applied and sustained thought, its factors are weak.

934.

934.

Iti ādīnavaṃ disvā, paṭhame pana yoginā;

Dutiyaṃ santato jhānaṃ, cintayitvāna dhīmatā.

Thus, having seen the danger in the first jhāna, the wise yogi should contemplate the second jhāna as peaceful.

935.

935.

Nikantiṃ pariyādāya, jhānasmiṃ paṭhame puna;

Dutiyādhigamatthāya, kātabbo bhāvanakkamo.

Having again abandoned delight in the first jhāna, the meditative process should be undertaken for the sake of attaining the second.

936.

936.

Athassa [V 0.0124] paṭhamajjhānā, vuṭṭhāya vidhinā yadā;

Satassa sampajānassa, jhānaṅgaṃ paccavekkhato.

Then, when he has arisen methodically from the first jhāna, mindful and clearly comprehending, he reviews the jhāna factors.

937.

937.

Thūlato [M 0.0132] takkacārā hi, upatiṭṭhanti yogino;

Sesamaṅgattayaṃ tassa, santamevopatiṭṭhati.

Indeed, applied and sustained thought appear to the yogi as coarse, while his remaining three factors appear as peaceful.

938.

938.

Thūlaṅgānaṃ pahānāya, tadā tassa ca yogino;

Santaṅgapaṭilābhāya, nimittaṃ tu tadeva ca.

Then, for that yogi, for the abandoning of the coarse factors and for the attainment of the peaceful factors, the sign is indeed the same.

939.

939.

“Pathavī pathavi”ccevaṃ, karoto manasā puna;

Idāni dutiyajjhāna-muppajjissati taṃ iti.

As he repeatedly makes the mind focus thus: 'earth, earth,' then the second jhāna will now arise.

940.

940.

Bhavaṅgaṃ pana pacchijja, pathavīkasiṇaṃ pana;

Tadevārammaṇaṃ katvā, manodvāramhi yogino.

Having cut off the life-continuum, and having made the earth-kasiṇa itself the object at the mind-door of the yogi.

941.

941.

Jāyatāvajjanaṃ cittaṃ, tasmiṃ ārammaṇe tato;

Javanāni hi jāyante, tassa cattāri pañca vā.

The adverting consciousness arises towards that object; then indeed four or five impulsions arise for him.

942.

942.

Avasāne panekampi, tesaṃ javanacetasaṃ;

Rūpāvacarikaṃ hoti, dutiyajjhānamānasaṃ.

At the end, however, one of those impulsion-consciousnesses becomes form-sphere, second jhāna consciousness.

943.

943.

Sampasādanamajjhattaṃ, pītiyā ca sukhena ca;

Ekaggatāya saṃyuttaṃ, jhānaṃ hoti tivaṅgikaṃ.

With internal serenity, united with joy, happiness, and one-pointedness, the jhāna is threefold in factors.

944.

944.

Heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva, sesaṃ samupalakkhaye;

Evaṃ duvaṅgahīnaṃ tu, tīhi aṅgehi saṃyutaṃ.

The rest should be understood in the same way as explained earlier. Thus, lacking two factors, it is combined with three factors.

945.

945.

Jhānaṃ [P 0.0098] tividhakalyāṇaṃ, dasalakkhaṇasaṃyutaṃ;

Dutiyādhigataṃ hoti, bhikkhunā bhāvanāmayaṃ.

The jhāna, excellent in three ways, endowed with ten characteristics, is attained by the monk through meditation as the second.

946.

946.

Dutiyādhigate jhāne, ākārehi ca pañcahi;

Suciṇṇavasinā hutvā, dutiyepi satīmatā.

The mindful one, having attained the second jhāna, should become well-practiced and masterful in the five modes.

947.

947.

Tasmā paguṇato jhānā, vuṭṭhāya dutiyā puna;

Āsannatakkacārāri, samāpatti ayaṃ iti.

Therefore, having arisen again from the second jhāna that has been made familiar, one reflects that this attainment is close to the enemy of applied and sustained thought.

948.

948.

Pītiyā [V 0.0125] piyato tassa, cetaso uppilāpanaṃ;

Pītiyā pana thūlattā, tatoyaṃ aṅgadubbalā.

Because of the mind's delight in joy, there is upliftment; but due to the coarseness of joy, this factor is weak.

949.

949.

Tattha [M 0.0133] ādīnavaṃ disvā, tatiye santato pana;

Nikantiṃ pariyādāya, jhānasmiṃ dutiye puna.

Having seen the danger in that, and the third jhāna as peaceful, having again abandoned delight in the second jhāna.

950.

950.

Tatiyādhigamatthāya, kātabbo bhāvanakkamo;

Athassa dutiyajjhānā, vuṭṭhāya ca yadā pana.

The meditative process should be undertaken for the sake of attaining the third [jhāna]. Then, when he has arisen from the second jhāna,

951.

951.

Satassa sampajānassa, jhānaṅgaṃ paccavekkhato;

Thūlato pītupaṭṭhāti, sukhādi santato pana.

For one who is mindful and clearly comprehending, as he reviews the jhāna factors, joy appears as coarse, while happiness and the rest appear as peaceful.

952.

952.

Thūlaṅgānaṃ pahānāya, tadā tassa ca yogino;

Santaṅgapaṭilābhāya, nimittaṃ tu tadeva ca.

Then, for that yogi, for the abandoning of the coarse factors and for the attainment of the peaceful factors, the sign is indeed the same.

953.

953.

“Pathavī pathavi”ccevaṃ, karoto manasā puna;

Idāni tatiyaṃ jhāna-muppajjissati taṃ iti.

As he repeatedly attends with the mind thus: 'earth, earth,' now that third jhāna will arise.

954.

954.

Bhavaṅgaṃ manupacchijja, pathavīkasiṇaṃ pana;

Tadevārammaṇaṃ katvā, manodvāramhi yogino.

Having cut off the life-continuum, and then having made that very earth-kasiṇa the object at the mind-door of the yogi,

955.

955.

Jāyatāvajjanaṃ cittaṃ, tasmiṃ ārammaṇe tato;

Javanāni ca jāyante, tassa cattāri pañca vā.

The adverting consciousness arises towards that object; then four or five impulsions arise for him.

956.

956.

Avasāne panekaṃ tu, tesaṃ javanacetasaṃ;

Rūpāvacarikaṃ hoti, tatiyajjhānamānasaṃ.

At the end, however, one of those impulsion-consciousnesses becomes the form-sphere, third jhāna consciousness.

957.

957.

Satiyā sampajaññena, sampannaṃ tu sukhena ca;

Ekaggatāya saṃyuttaṃ, duvaṅgaṃ tatiyaṃ mataṃ.

Endowed with mindfulness, clear comprehension, and happiness, and united with one-pointedness, the third [jhāna] is considered to have two factors.

958.

958.

Heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva, sesaṃ samupalakkhaye;

Evamekaṅgahīnaṃ tu, dvīhi aṅgehi saṃyutaṃ.

The rest should be understood in the same way as explained before. Thus, lacking one factor, it is combined with two factors.

959.

959.

Jhānaṃ tividhakalyāṇaṃ, dasalakkhaṇasaṃyutaṃ;

Tatiyādhigataṃ hoti, bhikkhunā bhāvanāmayaṃ.

The jhāna, excellent in three ways, endowed with ten characteristics, is attained as the third by the monk, being born of meditation.

960.

960.

Tatiyādhigate [V 0.0126] jhāne, ākārehi ca pañcahi;

Suciṇṇavasinā hutvā, tasmiṃ pana satīmatā.

When the third jhāna has been attained, and having become well-practiced and masterful in its five aspects, the mindful one continues in that.

961.

961.

Tasmā paguṇato jhānā, vuṭṭhāya tatiyā puna;

Āsannapītidosā hi, samāpatti ayanti ca.

Therefore, having arisen again from the third jhāna that has been made proficient, this attainment is indeed close to the fault of joy.

962.

962.

Yadevacettha [M 0.0134] ābhogo, sukhamicceva cetaso;

Evaṃ sukhassa thūlattā, hotāyaṃ aṅgadubbalā.

Whatever the advertence here, the mind intends only happiness; thus, due to the coarseness of happiness, this [attainment] is weak in its factor.

963.

963.

Iti [P 0.0099] ādīnavaṃ disvā, jhānasmiṃ tatiye puna;

Catutthaṃ santato disvā, cetasā pana yoginā.

Thus, having seen the danger in the third jhāna again, and having seen the fourth [jhāna] as peaceful, the yogi with his mind...

964.

964.

Nikantiṃ pariyādāya, jhānasmiṃ tatiye puna;

Catutthādhigamatthāya, kātabbo bhāvanakkamo.

Having again abandoned delight in the third jhāna, the meditative process should be undertaken for the sake of attaining the fourth.

965.

965.

Athassa tatiyajjhānā, vuṭṭhāya hi yadā pana;

Satassa sampajānassa, jhānaṅgaṃ paccavekkhato.

Then, when he has arisen from the third jhāna, for one who is mindful and clearly comprehending, as he reviews the jhāna factors,

966.

966.

Thūlato tassupaṭṭhāti, sukhaṃ taṃ mānasaṃ tato;

Upekkhā santato tassa, cittassekaggatāpi ca.

That mental happiness appears to him as coarse, while equanimity and one-pointedness of mind appear as peaceful.

967.

967.

Thūlaṅgassa pahānāya, santaṅgassūpaladdhiyā;

Tadeva ca nimittañhi, “pathavī pathavī”ti ca.

For the abandoning of the coarse factor and for the attainment of the peaceful factors, the sign is indeed the same, namely 'earth, earth.'

968.

968.

Karoto manasā eva, punappunañca yogino;

Catutthaṃ panidaṃ jhānaṃ, uppajjissati taṃ iti.

For the yogi who repeatedly attends with the mind thus, this fourth jhāna will then arise.

969.

969.

Bhavaṅgaṃ panupacchijja, pathavīkasiṇaṃ tathā;

Tadevārammaṇaṃ katvā, manodvāramhi yogino.

Then, having cut off the life-continuum, and in the same way having made that very earth-kasiṇa the object at the mind-door of the yogi,

970.

970.

Jāyatāvajjanaṃ cittaṃ, tasmiṃ ārammaṇe tato;

Javanāni ca jāyante, tassa cattāri pañca vā.

The adverting consciousness arises towards that object; then four or five impulsions arise for him.

971.

971.

Avasāne panekaṃ tu, tesaṃ javanacetasaṃ;

Rūpāvacarikaṃ hoti, catutthajjhānamānasaṃ.

At the end, however, one of those impulsion-consciousnesses becomes the form-sphere, fourth jhāna consciousness.

972.

972.

Ekaṅgavippahīnaṃ [V 0.0127] tu, dvīhi aṅgehi yogato;

Catutthaṃ panidaṃ jhānaṃ, duvaṅganti pavuccati.

Having abandoned one factor and being yoked with two factors, this fourth jhāna is thus said to have two factors.

973.

973.

Evaṃ tividhakalyāṇaṃ, dasalakkhaṇasaṃyutaṃ;

Catutthādhigataṃ hoti, bhikkhunā bhāvanāmayaṃ.

Thus, the jhāna, excellent in three ways, endowed with ten characteristics, is attained as the fourth by the monk, being born of meditation.

974.

974.

Yasmā sukhamupekkhāya, na hotāsevanaṃ pana;

Upekkhāsahagatāneva, javanāni javanti ca.

Because there is no cultivation of happiness with equanimity, the impulsions run accompanied only by equanimity.

975.

975.

Upekkhāsahagataṃ [M 0.0135] tasmā, catutthaṃ samudīritaṃ;

Ayamettha viseso hi, sesaṃ vuttanayaṃ pana.

Therefore, the fourth [jhāna] is declared to be accompanied by equanimity. This indeed is the distinction here, while the rest is according to the method stated.

976.

976.

Yaṃ catukkanaye jhānaṃ, dutiyaṃ taṃ dvidhā pana;

Katvāna pañcakanaye, dutiyaṃ tatiyaṃ kataṃ.

That which is the second jhāna in the fourfold system is twofold; in the fivefold system, it is made into the second and third.

977.

977.

Tatiyaṃ taṃ catutthañca, catutthaṃ pañcamaṃ idha;

Paṭhamaṃ paṭhamaṃyeva, ayamettha visesatā.

The third [of the fourfold system] becomes the fourth, and the fourth becomes the fifth here. The first is just the first. This is the distinction here.

978.

978.

Evamettāvatā vuttā, nātisaṅkhepato mayā;

Nātivitthārato cāyaṃ, rūpāvacarabhāvanā.

Thus far has this form-sphere meditation been stated by me, neither too briefly nor too extensively.

979.

979.

Sumadhuravarataravacano, kaṃ nu janaṃ neva rañjayati;

Atinisitavisadabuddhi-pasādajana vedanīyoyaṃ.

Whom indeed does this most sweet and excellent speech not delight? This is to be experienced by one who generates serene faith through exceedingly sharp and clear wisdom.

Iti abhidhammāvatāre rūpāvacarasamādhibhāvanāniddeso

Thus, in the Abhidhammāvatāra, the Exposition of the Cultivation of Form-Sphere Concentration.

Nāma cuddasamo paricchedo.

The Fourteenth Chapter.

15. Pannarasamo paricchedo

15. The Fifteenth Chapter

Arūpāvacarasamādhibhāvanāniddeso
