The Exposition of the Cultivation of Formless-Sphere Concentration

980.

980.

Rūpārūpamatītena[P 0.0100][V 0.0128], rūpārūpādivedinā;

Yāni cārūpapuññāni, sarūpenīritāni tu.

By one who has transcended form and the formless, by one who knows form, the formless, and so forth; and whatever formless merits have been set forth with their own characteristics.

981.

981.

Tesaṃ dāni pavakkhāmi, bhāvanānayamuttamaṃ;

Yogāvacarabhikkhūnaṃ, hitatthāya samāsato.

Now I shall briefly expound the supreme method of their cultivation, for the benefit of monks engaged in practice.

982.

982.

“Rūpe kho vijjamānasmiṃ, daṇḍādānādayo siyuṃ;

Anekāpi panābādhā, cakkhurogādayo”iti.

"Indeed, when form exists, there may be the taking up of weapons and so forth, and also many afflictions, such as eye-diseases and the like."

983.

983.

Rūpe ādīnavaṃ disvā, rūpe nibbindamānaso;

Tassātikkamanatthāya, arūpaṃ paṭipajjati.

Having seen the danger in form, with a mind disenchanted with form, one undertakes the practice of the formless in order to transcend it.

984.

984.

Tamhā [M 0.0136] kasiṇarūpāpi, so nibbijja visārado;

Apakkamitukāmo ca, sūkarābhihatova sā.

Therefore, that skilled one, having become disenchanted even with that kasiṇa-form, desires to depart from it, like one struck by a boar.

985.

985.

Catutthe pana jhānasmiṃ, hutvā ciṇṇavasī vasī;

Catutthajjhānato dhīmā, vuṭṭhāya vidhinā puna.

Having become a master with practiced mastery in the fourth jhāna, the wise one, emerging from that fourth jhāna, again proceeds according to the method.

986.

986.

Karoti panidaṃ cittaṃ, rūpamārammaṇaṃ yato;

Āsannasomanassañca, thūlasantavimokkhato.

One reflects thus: 'Because this jhāna has form as its object, is near to gladness, and is coarse compared to the peaceful liberation of the formless states.'

987.

987.

Iti ādīnavaṃ disvā, catutthe tattha sabbaso;

Nikantiṃ pariyādāya, paṭhamāruppañca santato.

Thus, seeing the danger in the fourth jhāna in every way, and having completely abandoned delight in it, one continuously applies oneself to the first formless attainment.

988.

988.

Cakkavāḷapariyantaṃ, yattakaṃ vā panicchati;

Tattakaṃ pattharitvāna, phuṭṭhokāsañca tena taṃ.

Having spread it out as far as the limit of the world-system, or as far as one wishes, one attends to that space pervaded by it.

989.

989.

Ākāso [V 0.0129] iti vānanto,

Ākāso iti vā puna;

Manasā hi karontova,

Ugghāṭeti pavuccati.

Mentally noting 'Space is infinite,' or again 'Space,' one is said to 'remove' it, as if doing so with the mind.

990.

990.

Ugghāṭento hi kasiṇaṃ, na saṃvelleti taṃ pana;

Na cuddharati so yogī, pūvaṃ viya kapālato.

Indeed, when removing the kasiṇa, one does not roll it up; nor does that yogi lift it up, like a cake from a pan.

991.

991.

Kevalaṃ pana taṃ neva, āvajjati na pekkhati;

Nāvajjanto napekkhanto, ugghāṭeti hi nāmaso.

But one simply neither attends to it nor looks at it; by not attending and not looking, one indeed removes it in name only.

992.

992.

Kasiṇugghāṭimākāsaṃ[P 0.0101], nimittaṃ pana taṃva so;

Ākāso iti cittena, āvajjati punappunaṃ.

He adverts again and again with the mind to that very sign, the space revealed by the removal of the kasiṇa, thinking, 'Space.'

993.

993.

Āvajjato hi tassevaṃ,

Karoto takkāhatampi ca;

Pañca nīvaraṇā tassa,

Vikkhambhanti hi sabbaso.

For one attending thus and also applying thought, the five hindrances are indeed entirely suppressed.

994.

994.

Āsevati [M 0.0137] ca bhāveti, taṃ nimittaṃ punappunaṃ;

Karoto pana tasseva, santacittassa yogino.

One frequents and cultivates that sign again and again; and for that yogi with a peaceful mind who is doing so,

995.

995.

Tatrākāse panāppeti, paṭhamāruppamānasaṃ;

Idhāpi purime bhāge, tīṇi cattāri vā pana.

in that space he attains absorption with the first formless consciousness. Here too, in the preliminary stage, there are three or four impulsions.

996.

996.

Javanāni upekkhāya, sampayuttāni honti hi;

Catutthaṃ pañcamaṃ vāpi, hoti āruppamānasaṃ.

Indeed, the impulsions are associated with equanimity; the fourth or the fifth is the formless consciousness.

997.

997.

Puna bhāvetukāmena, dutiyāruppamānasaṃ;

Suciṇṇavasinā hutvā, paṭhamāruppamānase.

By one desiring to cultivate the second formless consciousness further, having become one with well-practiced mastery in the first formless consciousness,

998.

998.

Āsannarūpāvacara-jjhānapaccatthikanti ca;

Dutiyāruppacittaṃva, na ca santamidanti ca.

one reflects that it has the form-sphere jhāna as a near obstacle, and that it is not as peaceful as the second formless consciousness.

999.

999.

Evamādīnavaṃ [V 0.0130] disvā, paṭhamāruppamānase;

Nikantiṃ pariyādāya, dutiyaṃ santato pana.

Thus, having seen the danger in the first formless consciousness and having completely abandoned craving for it, one then continuously applies oneself to the second.

1000.

1000.

Tamākāsaṃ pharitvāna, pavattamānasaṃ pana;

Tañca viññāṇamiccevaṃ, kattabbaṃ manasā bahuṃ.

That consciousness which arose pervading that space should be repeatedly made the object of mind, attending to it as 'consciousness.'

1001.

1001.

Āvajjanañca kattabbaṃ, tathā takkāhatampi ca;

“Ananta”nti “ananta”nti, kātabbaṃ manasā nidha.

Attention should be applied, and likewise the application of thought; here one should mentally repeat, 'Infinite, infinite.'

1002.

1002.

Tasmiṃ pana nimittasmiṃ, vicārentassa mānasaṃ;

Upacārena taṃ cittaṃ, samādhiyati yogino.

And as the yogi's mind investigates that sign, it becomes concentrated by way of access concentration.

1003.

1003.

Āsevati ca bhāveti, taṃ nimittaṃ punappunaṃ;

Tassa cevaṃ karontassa, satisampannacetaso.

One frequents and cultivates that sign again and again; and as one with a mindful mind continues to do so,

1004.

1004.

Ākāsaṃ phusaviññāṇe, dutiyāruppamānasaṃ;

Appeti appanā yasmiṃ, nayo vuttanayova so.

one attains absorption in the second formless consciousness, which has for its object the consciousness that pervaded space. The method for absorption is the same as that already described.

1005.

1005.

Ākāsoyamanantoti, evamākāsameva taṃ;

Pharitvā pavattaviññāṇaṃ, “viññāṇañca”nti vuccati.

The consciousness that arose having pervaded that very space with the thought, 'This space is infinite,' is called the 'Sphere of Infinite Consciousness.'

1006.

1006.

Manakkāravasenāpi, anantaṃ paridīpitaṃ;

“Viññāṇānanta”micceva, vattabbaṃ panidaṃ siyā.

By way of attention, the infinite is also illuminated; this, however, should be stated thus: 'Consciousness is infinite.'

1007.

1007.

Atha [M 0.0138] bhāvetukāmena, tatiyāruppamānasaṃ;

Suciṇṇavasinā hutvā, dutiyāruppamānase.

Then, by one who wishes to develop the third formless consciousness, having become well-practiced and mastered in the second formless consciousness,

1008.

1008.

Āsannapaṭhamāruppa-cittapaccatthikanti ca;

Tatiyāruppacittaṃva, na ca santamidanti ca.

The first formless consciousness, being near, is an obstacle; and this is not tranquil like the third formless consciousness.

1009.

1009.

Evamādīnavaṃ disvā, dutiyāruppamānase;

Nikantiṃ pariyādāya, tatiyaṃ santato pana.

Thus, having seen the danger in the second formless consciousness and having overcome craving for it, one then attends to the third as peaceful.

1010.

1010.

Evaṃ manasi katvāna, kātabbo manasā puna;

Paṭhamāruppaviññāṇā-bhāvo tasseva suññato.

Having thus attended in mind, it should be done again with the mind: the non-existence of that very first formless consciousness, as void.

1011.

1011.

Taṃ [P 0.0102][V 0.0131] panākāsaviññāṇaṃ, akatvā manasā puna;

“Natthi natthī”ti vātena, “suññaṃ suñña”nti vā tato.

But without again making that space-consciousness an object of mind, one should then attend, 'There is nothing, there is nothing,' or, 'It is void, it is void.'

1012.

1012.

Āvajjitabbamevañhi, kattabbaṃ manasāpi ca;

Takkāhatañca kātabbaṃ, punappunaṃva dhīmatā.

Indeed, one should advert thus, and it should also be done with the mind; and it should be struck with thought, again and again, by the wise one.

1013.

1013.

Tasmiṃ nimitte tassevaṃ, vicārentassa mānasaṃ;

Sati tiṭṭhati bhiyyopi, samādhiyati mānasaṃ.

As he thus investigates that sign, his mindfulness becomes further established, and his mind becomes concentrated.

1014.

1014.

Āsevati ca bhāveti, taṃ nimittaṃ punappunaṃ;

Tassa cevaṃ karontassa, satisampannacetaso.

He cultivates and develops that sign again and again; for him who does so with a mind endowed with mindfulness,

1015.

1015.

Kasiṇugghāṭimākāsaṃ, pharitvāna samantato;

Viññāṇassa pavattassa, natthibhāve abhāvake.

In the state of non-existence, the non-being, of the consciousness that arose pervading on all sides the space opened up from the kasiṇa,

1016.

1016.

Tatiyāruppaviññāṇaṃ,

Taṃ panāppeti yogino;

Appanāya nayopettha,

Hoti vuttanayova so.

Then, for the yogi, the third formless consciousness attains absorption. The method for absorption here is just that which has been described.

1017.

1017.

Ākāsagataviññāṇaṃ, dutiyāruppacakkhunā;

Passanto viharitvāna, “natthi natthī”tiādinā.

Having dwelt perceiving, with the eye of the second formless attainment, the consciousness that has gone to space, one reflects, 'There is nothing, there is nothing,' and so on.

1018.

1018.

Parikammamanakkāre[M 0.0139], tasmiṃ antarahite pana;

Tassāpagamamattaṃva, passanto vasatī ca so.

But when that preparatory mental advertence has disappeared, he dwells perceiving merely its passing away.

1019.

1019.

Sannipātaṃ yathā koci, disvā saṅghassa katthaci;

Gate saṅghe tu taṃ ṭhānaṃ, suññamevānupassati.

Just as someone, having seen an assembly of the Sangha somewhere, perceives that place as simply void when the Sangha has departed.

1020.

1020.

Puna bhāvetukāmena, catutthāruppamānasaṃ;

Suciṇṇavasinā hutvā, tatiyāruppamānase.

Again, by one who wishes to develop the fourth formless consciousness, having become well-practiced and mastered in the third formless consciousness,

1021.

1021.

Āsannadutiyāruppa-cittapaccatthikanti ca;

Catutthāruppacittaṃva, na ca santamidanti ca.

The second formless consciousness, being near, is an obstacle; and this is not tranquil like the fourth formless consciousness.

1022.

1022.

Evamādīnavaṃ [V 0.0132] disvā, tatiyāruppamānase;

Nikantiṃ pariyādāya, catutthaṃ santato pana.

Thus, having seen the danger in the third formless consciousness and having overcome craving for it, one then attends to the fourth as peaceful.

1023.

1023.

Evaṃ manasi katvāna, puna tattheva dhīmatā;

Abhāvārammaṇaṃ katvā, sampavattamidaṃ mano.

Having thus attended in mind, again right there by the wise one, having made the attainment of non-existence the object, this mind arises.

1024.

1024.

“Santaṃ santamidaṃ citta”-miccevaṃ taṃ punappunaṃ;

Hoti āvajjitabbañca, kātabbaṃ manasāpi ca.

Thus, 'Peaceful, peaceful is this mind'—that should be adverted to again and again, and should also be accomplished by the mind.

1025.

1025.

Tasmiṃ nimitte tassevaṃ, vicārentassa mānasaṃ;

Sati tiṭṭhati bhiyyopi, samādhiyati mānasaṃ.

As he thus investigates that sign, his mindfulness becomes further established, and his mind becomes concentrated.

1026.

1026.

Āsevati ca bhāveti, taṃ nimittaṃ punappunaṃ;

Tassa cevaṃ karontassa, satisampannacetaso.

He cultivates and develops that sign again and again; for him who does so with a mind endowed with mindfulness,

1027.

1027.

Tatiyāruppasaṅkhāta-khandhesu ca catūsupi;

Catutthāruppaviññāṇaṃ, taṃ panāppeti yogino.

And with respect to the four aggregates reckoned as the third formless attainment, the fourth formless consciousness then attains absorption for the yogi.

1028.

1028.

Appanāya [P 0.0103] nayopettha, heṭṭhā vuttanayūpamo;

Apicettha visesoyaṃ, veditabbo vibhāvinā.

The method of absorption here is similar to the method described before; moreover, this distinction should be understood by the discerning one.

1029.

1029.

“Aho santā vatāya”nti, samāpatti padissati;

Yā panābhāvamattampi, katvā ṭhassati gocaraṃ.

The attainment appears thus: 'Oh, how peaceful this is!' It is that which will remain, having made even mere non-existence its object.

1030.

1030.

Santārammaṇatāyeva, “santāya”nti vipassati;

Santato ce manakkāro, kathañca samatikkamo.

Precisely because its object is peaceful, one perceives it as 'peaceful.' If attention is on the peaceful, then how is there transcendence?

1031.

1031.

Anāpajjitukāmattā[M 0.0140], hoteva samatikkamo;

“Samāpajjāmahameta”-miccābhogo na vijjati.

Transcendence occurs precisely because of the desire not to enter into it; the advertence, 'I shall attain this,' is not found.

1032.

1032.

Santato taṃ karonto hi, manasā sukhumaṃ paraṃ;

Asaññaṃ pana dubbalyaṃ, pāpuṇāti mahaggataṃ.

Indeed, one who does that continuously with a supremely subtle mind attains the exalted state; however, it has the weakness of non-perception.

1033.

1033.

Nevasaññī ca nāsaññī,

Yāya saññāya hoti so;

He is one who is neither percipient nor non-percipient, by virtue of that perception which he has.

Na [V 0.0133] kevalaṃ tu saññāva,

Edisī atha kho pana.

And it is not only perception that is of such a kind; but rather...

1034.

1034.

Evameva bhavantettha, sukhumā vedanādayo;

Pattamakkhanatelena, maggasmiṃ udakena ca.

Just so, feeling and the other aggregates are subtle here, like oil with which a bowl is smeared, and like water on a path.

1035.

1035.

Sāvetabbo ayaṃ attho, catutthāruppabodhane;

Paṭusaññāya kiccassa, nevakkaraṇato ayaṃ.

This meaning should be understood concerning the awakening to the fourth formless attainment: it is so because of not performing the function of keen perception.

1036.

1036.

“Nevasaññā”ti niddiṭṭhā, catutthāruppasambhavā;

Paṭusaññāya kiccaṃ sā, kātuṃ sakkoti neva ca.

“Neither perception” is declared, arising from the fourth formless attainment; that perception is not able to perform the function of keen perception.

1037.

1037.

Yathā dahanakiccaṃ tu, tejodhātu sukhodake;

Sā saṅkhārāvasesattā, sukhumattena vijjati;

Tasmā pana ca sā saññā, “nāsaññā”ti pavuccati.

Just as the fire element has no burning function in pleasant water, that perception exists by its subtlety, because it is a residue of formations; therefore, that perception is indeed called 'not non-perception.'

1038.

1038.

Etā hi rūpamākāsaṃ,

Viññāṇaṃ tadabhāvakaṃ;

Atikkamitvā kamato,

Catasso honti āha ca.

Indeed, having sequentially transcended form, space, consciousness, and the non-existence of that, there come to be four attainments, so it was said.

1039.

1039.

“Ārammaṇātikkamato, catassopi bhavantimā;

Aṅgātikkamametāsaṃ, na icchanti vibhāvino.

“Through exceeding the object, these four states come to be; the discerning do not accept a transgression of their factors.”

1040.

1040.

Supaṇītatarā [M 0.0141] honti,

Pacchimā pacchimā idha;

Upamā tattha viññeyyā,

Pāsādatalasāṭikā”ti.

Here, each successive one is more exquisite; a simile should be understood in that regard: like a fine cloth on a palace terrace.

1041.

1041.

Saṅkhepena mayāruppa-samāpattinayo ayaṃ;

Dassito dassito suddha-dassinā piyadassinā.

Briefly, this method of the formless attainments has been well shown by me, the pure seer, the amiable seer.

1042.

1042.

Rūpārūpajjhānasamāpattividhānaṃ[V 0.0134],

Jānātimaṃ sārataraṃ yo pana bhikkhu;

Rūpārūpajjhānasamāpattīsu dakkho,

Rūpārūpaṃ yāti bhavaṃ so abhibhuyya.

Whatever monk, skilled in the attainments of form and formless jhānas, knows this more essential method for those attainments, he, having overcome existence, goes to the form and formless realms.

Iti abhidhammāvatāre arūpāvacarasamādhibhāvanāniddeso nāma

Thus in the Abhidhammāvatāra ends the section named the Exposition of the Development of Formless-Sphere Concentration.

Pannarasamo paricchedo.

The Fifteenth Chapter.

16. Soḷasamo paricchedo

16. The Sixteenth Chapter

Abhiññāniddeso

The Exposition of the Direct Knowledges

1043.

1043.

Ito [P 0.0104] paraṃ karissāmi, paññāsuddhikaraṃ paraṃ;

Pañcannampi abhiññānaṃ, mukhamattanidassanaṃ.

Hereafter, I shall compose a further treatise for the purification of wisdom: a brief exposition of the five direct knowledges.

1044.

1044.

Rūpārūpasamāpattī,

Nibbattetvā panaṭṭhapi;

Lokikāpi abhiññāyo,

Bhāvetabbā vibhāvinā.

And having produced the eight attainments of the form and formless spheres, the worldly direct knowledges should also be developed by the discerning one.

1045.

1045.

Catutthajjhānamattepi, suciṇṇavasinā satā;

Anuyogamabhiññāsu, kātuṃ vattati yogino.

Even with just the fourth jhāna, for a mindful one who has well-practiced mastery, it is fitting for the yogi to apply himself to the direct knowledges.

1046.

1046.

Abhiññā [M 0.0142] nāma bhikkhūnaṃ, sābhiññānaṃ anuttaro;

Alaṅkāro hi tāṇanti, satthanti ca pavuccati.

For monks with direct knowledge, this direct knowledge is indeed an unsurpassed ornament; it is called a refuge and a teacher.

1047.

1047.

Nibbattitāsvabhiññāsu, yogāvacarabhikkhunā;

Samādhibhāvanā hissa, tadā niṭṭhaṅgatā siyā.

When the direct knowledges have been produced by the meditating monk, his cultivation of concentration would then reach consummation.

1048.

1048.

Dibbāni [V 0.0135] cakkhusotāni, iddhicittavijānanaṃ;

Pubbenivāsañāṇanti, pañcābhiññā imā siyuṃ.

The divine eye and ear, psychic power, knowledge of others’ minds, and knowledge of previous abodes—these are the five direct knowledges.

1049.

1049.

Kasiṇānulomatādīhi, catuddasanayehi ca;

Dametabbamabhiññāyo, pattukāmena mānasaṃ.

The mind should be trained by means of the kasiṇas, conformity, and other such exercises, and through the fourteenfold method, by one who wishes to attain the direct knowledges.

1050.

1050.

Dante samāhite suddhe, pariyodāte anaṅgaṇe;

Nupaklese mudubhūte, kammanīye ṭhitācale.

Tamed, concentrated, purified, cleansed, stainless, free from defilements, pliant, workable, steady, and imperturbable.

1051.

1051.

Iti aṭṭhaṅgasampanne, citte iddhividhāya ca;

Abhinīharati ce cittaṃ, sijjhatiddhivikubbanaṃ.

Thus, with a mind possessed of these eight factors, if one directs the mind toward the kinds of psychic power, the manifestation of psychic power is accomplished.

1052.

1052.

Abhiññāpādakajjhānaṃ, samāpajja tato pana;

Vuṭṭhāya hi sataṃ vāpi, sahassaṃ vā yadicchati.

Having entered the jhāna that is the basis for direct knowledge, and then having emerged from it, if one wishes for a hundred or even a thousand…

1053.

1053.

“Sataṃ homi sataṃ homī”-ccevaṃ katvāna mānasaṃ;

Abhiññāpādakajjhānaṃ, samāpajja tato pana.

“May I be a hundred! May I be a hundred!”—having thus formed the mind, one enters the jhāna that is the basis for direct knowledge, and then…

1054.

1054.

Vuṭṭhāya punadhiṭṭhāti,

Sahādhiṭṭhānacetasā;

Sataṃ hoti hi so yogī,

Sahassādīsvayaṃ nayo.

Having emerged, one resolves again with a mind of resolution; indeed, that yogi becomes a hundred. This is the method for a thousand and so on.

1055.

1055.

Pādakajjhānacittaṃ tu, nimittārammaṇaṃ siyā;

Parikammamanānettha, satārammaṇikāni tu.

The mind of the base jhāna should have the sign as its object; but here, the preliminary minds have the hundred as their object.

1056.

1056.

Tadādhiṭṭhānacittampi[P 0.0105], satārammaṇameva taṃ;

Pubbe vuttappanācittaṃ, viya gotrabhunantaraṃ.

That mind of resolution also has the hundred as its object, just like the previously mentioned absorption mind that immediately follows the change-of-lineage mind.

1057.

1057.

Tamekaṃ [M 0.0143] jāyate tattha, catutthajjhānikaṃ mano;

Parikammavisesova, sesaṃ pubbasamaṃ idha.

There a single mind arises, a fourth-jhāna consciousness; only the preliminary work is special, the rest here is as before.

Iddhividhañāṇaṃ.

The Knowledge of the Kinds of Psychic Power.

1058.

1058.

Dibbasotamidaṃ [V 0.0136] tattha, bhāvetabbaṃ kathaṃ siyā;

Abhiññāpādakajjhānaṃ, samāpajja tato puna.

Here, this divine ear—how should it be developed? Having entered the jhāna that is the basis for direct knowledge, and then again…

1059.

1059.

Vuṭṭhāya parikammena, kāmāvacaracetasā;

Saddo āvajjitabbova, mahanto sukhumopi ca.

Having emerged, with a sense-sphere mind in the preliminary stage, sound should be attended to, whether it be loud or subtle.

1060.

1060.

Tassevaṃ pana saddassa, nimittaṃ manasi kubbato;

Dibbasotamidānissa, uppajjissati taṃ iti.

For one who thus gives attention to the sign of that sound in the mind, the divine ear will then arise for him.

1061.

1061.

Saddesvaññataraṃ saddaṃ, katvā ārammaṇaṃ tato;

Uppajjitvā niruddhe tu, manodvārāvajjane puna.

Having made a certain sound the object, then, when it has arisen and ceased, mind-door adverting occurs again.

1062.

1062.

Javanāni hi jāyante, tassa cattāri pañca vā;

Purimānettha cittesu, tīṇi cattāri vā pana.

For him, four or five javanas arise; of these, the first three or four.

1063.

1063.

Parikammopacārānu-lomagotrabhunāmakā;

Catutthaṃ pañcamaṃ vāpi, appanācittamīritaṃ.

They are named preparation, access, adaptation, and change-of-lineage; the fourth or fifth is called the absorption-mind.

1064.

1064.

Sahajātaṃ tu yaṃ ñāṇaṃ, appanāmānasena hi;

Taṃ ñāṇaṃ dibbasotanti, vadanti sutakovidā.

The knowledge that arises simultaneously with the mind of absorption—that knowledge is called the divine ear, declare those skilled in the scriptures.

1065.

1065.

Thāmajātaṃ karontena, taṃ ñāṇaṃ tena yoginā;

“Etthantaragataṃ saddaṃ, suṇāmī”ti ca cetasā.

That knowledge is to be made strong by that yogi with the thought: ‘I hear a sound that has entered this space.’

1066.

1066.

Aṅgulaṃ dvaṅgulaṃ bhiyyo,

Vidatthi ratanaṃ tathā;

Gāmo deso tato yāva,

Cakkavāḷā tato paraṃ.

A finger-breadth, two finger-breadths more, a span, a cubit likewise; a village, a region, then as far as the world-system, and beyond that.

1067.

1067.

Iccevaṃ tu paricchijja, vaḍḍhetabbaṃ yathākkamaṃ;

Eso adhigatābhiñño, pādakārammaṇena tu.

Thus, having delimited the range, it should be developed step by step. This one who has attained the higher knowledge does so by means of the basic object.

1068.

1068.

Phuṭṭhokāsagate [M 0.0144] sadde, sabbe pana suṇāti so;

Suṇanto pāṭiyekkampi, sallakkhetuṃ pahoti so.

He hears all sounds that have entered the pervaded space; and while hearing, he is able to discern each one individually.

Dibbasotañāṇaṃ.

The Knowledge of the Divine Ear.

1069.

1069.

Kathaṃ [V 0.0137] panuppādetabbaṃ, cetopariyamānasaṃ;

Dibbacakkhuvaseneva, idaṃ ñāṇaṃ panijjhati.

How then should the knowledge of others’ minds be developed? This knowledge is accomplished in the same way as the divine eye.

1070.

1070.

Ālokaṃ pana vaḍḍhetvā, tasmā dibbena cakkhunā;

Hadayaṃ pana nissāya, vattamānaṃ tu lohitaṃ.

Therefore, having expanded the light with the divine eye, and relying on the heart, one should see the blood present within it.

1071.

1071.

Disvā parassa viññeyyaṃ,

Hoti cittaṃ tu bhikkhunā;

Somanassayute citte,

Lohitaṃ lohitaṃ siyā.

Having seen another’s blood, the mind becomes discernible to the bhikkhu; when the mind is conjoined with joy, the blood is bright red.

1072.

1072.

Domanassayute citte, vattamāne tu kāḷakaṃ;

Upekkhāsahite citte, tilatelūpamaṃ siyā.

When a mind conjoined with displeasure is present, the blood is black; when the mind is accompanied by equanimity, it is like sesame oil.

1073.

1073.

Tasmā [P 0.0106] parassa sattassa, disvā hadayalohitaṃ;

Cetopariyañāṇaṃ taṃ, kātabbaṃ thāmataṃ gataṃ.

Therefore, having seen the heart-blood of another being, that knowledge of the minds of others should be made strong.

1074.

1074.

Evaṃ thāmagate tasmiṃ, yathānukkamato pana;

Cittameva vijānāti, vinā lohitadassanaṃ.

When that knowledge has thus become strong, then, in due course, one knows the mind itself, without the sight of blood.

1075.

1075.

Kāmāvacaracittañca, rūpārūpesu mānasaṃ;

Sabbameva vijānāti, sarāgādippabhedakaṃ.

He knows every mind of the sense-sphere, and mind in the form and formless realms, with its distinctions such as being with lust.

Cetopariyañāṇaṃ.

The Knowledge of the Minds of Others.

1076.

1076.

Pubbenivāsañāṇena, kattabbā tadanussati;

Taṃ sampādetukāmena, ādikammikabhikkhunā;

Jhānāni pana cattāri, samāpajjānupubbato.

A beginner bhikkhu who wishes to bring about the knowledge of past abodes should undertake that recollection by sequentially attaining the four jhānas.

1077.

1077.

Abhiññāpādakajjhānā, vuṭṭhāya hi tato puna;

Bhikkhunā vajjitabbāva, nisajjā sabbapacchimā.

Having arisen from the jhāna that is the basis for higher knowledge, the bhikkhu should then review the very last act of sitting.

1078.

1078.

Tato [M 0.0145][V 0.0138] pabhuti sabbampi, paṭilomakkamā pana;

Sabbamāvajjitabbaṃ taṃ, divase rattiyaṃ kataṃ.

From that point onwards, everything done during the day and at night should be reviewed in reverse order.

1079.

1079.

Paṭilomakkameneva, dutiye tatiyepi ca;

Divase pakkhamāsesu, tathā saṃvaccharesupi.

In reverse order, likewise on the second and third days, and also in fortnights, months, and years.

1080.

1080.

Yāva asmiṃ bhave sandhi, tāva tena ca bhikkhunā;

Katamāvajjitabbaṃ taṃ, purimasmiṃ bhavepi ca.

By that bhikkhu, everything done should be reviewed back to the rebirth-linking in this existence, and in the prior existence also.

1081.

1081.

Cutikkhaṇepi nibbattaṃ, nāmarūpañca sādhukaṃ;

Evamāvajjite tasmiṃ, nāmarūpe yadā pana.

And when the name-and-form that occurred at the moment of death has been thus well reviewed...

1082.

1082.

Tadevārammaṇaṃ katvā, nāmarūpaṃ cutikkhaṇe;

Manodvāre manakkāro, uppajjati tadā pana.

Then, having taken that very name-and-form at the death-moment as the object, attention arises at the mind-door.

1083.

1083.

Āvajjane niruddhasmiṃ, tadevārammaṇaṃ pana;

Katvā javanacittāni, honti cattāri pañca vā;

Pubbe vuttanayeneva, sesaṃ ñeyyaṃ vibhāvinā.

When the adverting has ceased, then, taking that same object, four or five javana-minds arise. The remainder should be understood by the discerning one in the manner previously stated.

1084.

1084.

Parikammādināmāni, purimāni bhavanti tu;

Pacchimaṃ appanācittaṃ, rūpāvacarikaṃ bhave.

The first minds are those named preparation, and so on; the last, the absorption-mind, belongs to the form-sphere.

1085.

1085.

Tena cittena yaṃ ñāṇaṃ, saṃyuttaṃ tena yā pana;

Saṃyuttā sati sā pubbe-nivāsānussatīritā.

The knowledge associated with that mind, and the mindfulness conjoined with it—that is called the recollection of past abodes.

Pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇaṃ.

The Knowledge of the Recollection of Past Abodes.

1086.

1086.

Rūpaṃ passitukāmena, bhikkhunā dibbacakkhunā;

Kasiṇārammaṇaṃ jhānaṃ, abhiññāpādakaṃ pana.

A bhikkhu desiring to see form with the divine eye should develop the jhāna that has a kasiṇa as its object and is the basis for higher knowledge.

1087.

1087.

Abhinīhārakkhamaṃ katvā, tejokasiṇameva vā;

Odātakasiṇaṃ vāpi, ālokakasiṇampi vā.

Having made [the mind] capable of resolve, [one develops] either the fire kasiṇa, or the white kasiṇa, or even the light kasiṇa.

1088.

1088.

Imesu [V 0.0139] katapuññehi, kasiṇesu ca tīsupi;

Ālokakasiṇaṃ ettha, seṭṭhanti paridīpitaṃ.

For those who have made merit with these, among the three kasiṇas, the light kasiṇa is here declared to be the best.

1089.

1089.

Tasmā [M 0.0146][P 0.0107] tamitaraṃ vāpi, uppādetvā yathākkamaṃ;

Upacārabhūmiyaṃyeva, ṭhatvā taṃ pana paṇḍito.

Therefore, a wise person, having generated that or another [kasiṇa] in due order, and having established himself only in the sphere of access concentration...

1090.

1090.

Vaḍḍhetvāna ṭhapetabbaṃ, na uppādeyya appanaṃ;

Uppādeti sace hoti, pādakajjhānanissitaṃ.

Having developed it, it should be maintained; one should not generate absorption. If one does generate it, it is based on the foundational jhāna.

1091.

1091.

Jhānassa vaḍḍhitassanto-gataṃ rūpaṃ tu yoginā;

Passitabbaṃ bhave rūpaṃ, passato pana tassa taṃ.

The form contained within the developed jhāna, however, should be seen by the yogi. But for one who is seeing it, it would be [merely] a visible object.

1092.

1092.

Parikammassa vāro hi, atikkamati tāvade;

Ālokopi tato tassa, khippamantaradhāyati.

For the period of preliminary work is indeed passed beyond at that very moment; then the light also quickly disappears for him.

1093.

1093.

Tasmiṃ antarahite rūpa-gatampi ca na dissati;

Tenātha pādakajjhānaṃ, pavisitvā tato puna.

When that has vanished, no object of form is seen; therefore, having entered the foundational jhāna, then again...

1094.

1094.

Vuṭṭhāya pana āloko, pharitabbova bhikkhunā;

Evaṃ anukkameneva, āloko thāmavā siyā.

But having emerged [from jhāna], the light should be made to pervade by the monk. In this way, by sequence, the light becomes strong.

1095.

1095.

“Āloko ettha hotū”ti,

Yattakaṃ ṭhānameva so;

Paricchindati tattheva,

Āloko pana tiṭṭhati.

“Let there be light here”—whatever space he determines, the light remains right there.

1096.

1096.

Divasampi nisīditvā, passato hoti dassanaṃ;

Tiṇukkāya gato maggaṃ, purisettha nidassanaṃ.

Even sitting for a day, for one who sees, there is vision. A person going along a path with a grass torch is the illustration here.

1097.

1097.

Uppādanakkamopissa, tatrāyaṃ dibbacakkhuno;

Vuttappakārarūpaṃ taṃ, katvā ārammaṇaṃ pana.

The process of arising for this divine eye is as follows: having made that form of the kind previously described an object,

1098.

1098.

Manodvāre manakkāre, jāte yāni tadeva ca;

Rūpaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā, jāyanti javanāni hi.

When attention arises at the mind-door, having taken that very form as the object, the javana moments indeed arise.

1099.

1099.

Kāmāvacaracittāni[V 0.0140], tāni cattāri pañca vā;

Heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva, sesaṃ ñeyyaṃ vibhāvinā.

Those are four or five sense-sphere consciousnesses. The remainder should be understood by the discerning one in the very manner stated before.

1100.

1100.

Atthasādhakacittaṃ taṃ, catutthajjhānikaṃ mataṃ;

Taṃcittasaṃyutaṃ ñāṇaṃ, dibbacakkhunti vuccati.

That mind which accomplishes the purpose is considered to be of the fourth jhāna. The knowledge associated with that mind is called the divine eye.

1101.

1101.

Anāgataṃsañāṇassa[M 0.0147], yathākammupagassa ca;

Parikammaṃ visuṃ natthi, ijjhanti dibbacakkhunā.

For the knowledge of the future and the knowledge of the faring of beings according to their kamma, there is no separate preliminary work; they are accomplished by means of the divine eye.

1102.

1102.

Cutūpapātañāṇampi, dibbacakkhunti vā pana;

Atthato ekamevedaṃ, byañjane pana nānatā.

The knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings is also called the divine eye. In meaning, this is one and the same, but in expression, there is diversity.

Dibbacakkhuñāṇaṃ.

The Knowledge of the Divine Eye.

1103.

1103.

Yodha suṇāti karoti ca citte,

Ganthamimaṃ paramaṃ pana bhikkhu;

So abhidhammamahaṇṇavapāraṃ,

Yāti anena tarena taritvā.

Whatever monk here hears and gives his mind to this supreme treatise, he crosses to the far shore of the great ocean of the Abhidhamma, having traversed it by means of this raft.

Iti abhidhammāvatāre abhiññāniddeso nāma

Thus, in the Abhidhammāvatāra, the exposition of the higher knowledges.

Soḷasamo paricchedo.

The Sixteenth Chapter.

17. Sattarasamo paricchedo

17. The Seventeenth Chapter.

Abhiññārammaṇaniddeso

Exposition of the Objects of the Higher Knowledges.

1104.

1104.

Anāgataṃsañāṇañca[P 0.0108], yathākammupagampi ca;

Pañca iddhividhādīni, sattābhiññā imā pana.

The knowledge of the future, and the knowledge of the faring of beings according to their kamma, and the five [knowledges] beginning with the kinds of psychic power—these, indeed, are the seven higher knowledges.

1105.

1105.

Etāsaṃ [V 0.0141] pana sattannaṃ, abhiññānamito paraṃ;

Pavakkhāmi samāsena, ārammaṇavinicchayaṃ.

Henceforth, I shall declare in brief the ascertainment of the objects of these seven higher knowledges.

1106.

1106.

Ārammaṇattikā vuttā, ye cattāro mahesinā;

Sattannamettha ñāṇānaṃ, sampavattiṃ suṇātha me.

The four triads of objects have been spoken of by the Great Seer; now listen to my [account of] the occurrence of these seven knowledges.

1107.

1107.

Tattha iddhividhañāṇaṃ, parittādīsu sattasu;

Ārammaṇavibhāgesu, pavattati kathaṃ pana.

Therein, how does the knowledge of the kinds of psychic power operate in the seven divisions of objects, beginning with the limited?

1108.

1108.

Kāyenādissamānena, gantukāmo yadābhave;

Cittasannissitaṃ katvā, kāyaṃ cittavasena taṃ.

When one wishes to go with an invisible body, having made the body dependent on the mind, [one directs] it according to the mind's power.

1109.

1109.

Mahaggate [M 0.0148] ca cittasmiṃ, samāropeti so tadā;

Kāyārammaṇato ñāṇaṃ, parittārammaṇaṃ siyā.

And when the mind is exalted, he then applies it; the knowledge, having the body as its object, would have a limited object.

1110.

1110.

Dissamānena kāyena, gantukāmo yadā bhave;

Kāyasannissitaṃ katvā, cittaṃ kāyavasena taṃ.

When one wishes to go with a visible body, having made the mind dependent on the body, [one directs] it according to the body's power.

1111.

1111.

Pādakajjhānacittaṃ taṃ, kāye ropeti so tadā;

Jhānārammaṇato ñāṇaṃ, taṃ mahaggatagocaraṃ.

He then implants that foundational jhāna-consciousness in the body; the knowledge, having the jhāna as its object, has the exalted sphere as its domain.

1112.

1112.

Anāgatamatītañca, karoti visayaṃ yadā;

Atītārammaṇaṃ hoti, tadānāgatagocaraṃ.

When it makes the future and the past its domain, it has the past as its object and the future as its range.

1113.

1113.

Kāyena dissamānena, gamane pana bhikkhuno;

Paccuppanno bhave tassa, gocaroti viniddise.

But for a monk moving with a visible body, the present should be defined as his sphere.

1114.

1114.

Kāyaṃ cittavasenāpi, cittaṃ kāyavasena vā;

Pariṇāmanakālasmiṃ, ajjhattārammaṇaṃ siyā.

The body by the influence of mind, or the mind by the influence of body; at the time of transformation, the object may be internal.

1115.

1115.

Bahiddhārammaṇaṃ hoti, bahiddhārūpadassane;

Evamiddhividhaṃ ñāṇaṃ, sampavattati sattasu.

The object is external when seeing external forms. Thus the knowledge of the kinds of psychic power operates in the seven.

1116.

1116.

Paccuppanne paritte ca, bahiddhajjhattikesupi;

Catūsvetesu dhammesu, dibbasotaṃ pavattati.

In the present and the limited, and in the external and internal; in these four phenomena, the divine ear operates.

1117.

1117.

Paccuppanno [P 0.0109][V 0.0142] paritto ca, saddo ārammaṇaṃ yato;

Parittārammaṇaṃ paccu-ppannārammaṇataṃ gataṃ.

Since the present and limited sound is the object, it becomes a limited object and a present object.

1118.

1118.

Attano kucchisaddassa, savanepi parassa ca;

Ajjhattārammaṇañceva, bahiddhārammaṇampi ca.

In hearing the sound of one's own stomach, and that of another, it is an internal object and also an external object.

1119.

1119.

Cetopariyañāṇampi, parittādīsu aṭṭhasu;

Ārammaṇavibhāgesu, pavattati kathaṃ pana.

How, then, does the knowledge of others' minds operate in the eight divisions of objects, beginning with the limited?

1120.

1120.

Parittārammaṇaṃ hoti, parittānaṃ pajānane;

Jānane majjhimānaṃ tu, taṃ mahaggatagocaraṃ.

It is a limited object in understanding the limited; but in understanding the middling, that has the exalted as its sphere.

1121.

1121.

Jānane pana maggassa, phalassāpi pajānane;

Tadā panassa ñāṇassa, appamāṇova gocaro.

But in knowing the path, and in understanding the fruit, then the range of this knowledge is indeed immeasurable.

1122.

1122.

Taṃ [M 0.0149] maggārammaṇaṃ hoti, maggacittassa jānane;

Pariyāyenevetassa, maggārammaṇatā matā.

That becomes a path-object in knowing the path-consciousness; by implication, its being a path-object is considered.

1123.

1123.

Atīte sattadivasa-bbhantare ca yadā pana;

Anāgate tathā satta-divasabbhantarepi ca.

And when within the past seven days, and likewise within the future seven days as well,

1124.

1124.

Paresaṃ pana cittassa, jānane samudīritaṃ;

Atītārammaṇañceva, tadānāgatagocaraṃ.

in knowing the minds of others, it is declared to be a past object, and then to have the future as its sphere.

1125.

1125.

Kathañca pana taṃ paccuppannagocarataṃ gataṃ;

Paccuppannaṃ tidhā vuttaṃ, khaṇasantatiaddhato.

And how, then, does it come to have the present as its sphere? The present is said to be threefold: by way of moment, continuity, and duration.

1126.

1126.

Tattha tikkhaṇasampattaṃ, paccuppannakhaṇādikaṃ;

Ekadvesantativārapariyāpannamidaṃ pana.

Therein, the momentary present and so on is that which is comprised of three moments; this, however, is included in a process of one or two continuities.

1127.

1127.

Santatipaccuppannanti, āhu santatikovidā;

Ekabbhavaparicchinnaṃ, paccuppannanti pacchimaṃ.

The continuity-present, say the experts in continuity; the last is called the duration-present, defined by a single existence.

1128.

1128.

Khaṇādikattayaṃ paccu-ppannaṃ tamāhu kecidha;

Cetopariyañāṇassa, hoti ārammaṇaṃ iti.

Some here say that this threefold present, beginning with the moment, becomes the object for the knowledge of others' minds.

1129.

1129.

Yathā [V 0.0143] ca pupphamuṭṭhimhi, ukkhitte gagane pana;

Avassaṃ ekamekassa, vaṇṭaṃ vaṇṭena vijjhati.

Just as when a handful of flowers is thrown into the sky, one stalk inevitably pierces another with its stalk.

1130.

1130.

Evaṃ mahājanassāpi, citte āvajjite pana;

Ekassa cittamekena, avassaṃ pana vijjhati.

So too, when adverting to the minds of a great multitude, one mind inevitably penetrates another.

1131.

1131.

Yenāvajjati cittena, yena jānāti cetasā;

Tesaṃ dvinnaṃ sahaṭṭhānā-bhāvato taṃ na yujjati.

By which mind one adverts, by which consciousness one knows; because these two do not coexist, that is not fitting.

1132.

1132.

Javanāvajjanānaṃ tu, nānārammaṇapattito;

Aniṭṭhe pana hi ṭhāne, ayuttanti pakāsitaṃ.

Because the impulsions and the adverting have different objects, it is declared to be inappropriate in an undesirable case.

1133.

1133.

Tasmā santatiaddhāna-paccuppannānameva tu;

Vasena paccuppannaṃ taṃ, hoti ārammaṇaṃ idaṃ.

Therefore, it is indeed by way of the continuity-present and the duration-present that this becomes the present object.

1134.

1134.

Paccuppannampi addhākhyaṃ, idaṃ javanavārato;

Dīpetabbanti niddiṭṭhaṃ, tatrāyaṃ dīpanānayo.

This present, also called duration, is indicated to be illuminated by the series of impulsions; therein is this method of illumination.

1135.

1135.

Yadā [M 0.0150][P 0.0110] parassa cittañhi, ñātumāvajjatiddhimā;

Āvajjanamano tassa, paccuppannakhaṇavhayaṃ.

When the one with psychic power adverts to know another's mind, his adverting mind is called the present moment.

1136.

1136.

Ārammaṇaṃ tadā katvā, tena saddhiṃ nirujjhati;

Javanāni hi jāyante, tassa cattāri pañca vā.

Having made that the object, it ceases together with it; for four or five impulsions arise for him.

1137.

1137.

Etesaṃ pacchimaṃ cittaṃ, iddhicittamudīritaṃ;

Kāmāvacaracittāni, sesānīti viniddise.

The last of these minds is called the psychic-power mind; the rest should be defined as sense-sphere minds.

1138.

1138.

Etesaṃ pana sabbesaṃ, niruddhaṃ tu tadeva ca;

Cittaṃ ārammaṇaṃ hoti, tasmā sabbāni tānipi.

But for all of these, that very mind which has ceased becomes the object; therefore, all those too...

1139.

1139.

Ekārammaṇataṃ yanti, na nānārammaṇāni hi;

Addhāvasā bhave paccu-ppannārammaṇato pana.

...attain a single object, for they do not have different objects; however, from the present object, it becomes the duration-present.

1140.

1140.

Ekārammaṇabhāvepi, iddhimānasameva ca;

Parassa cittaṃ jānāti, netarāni yathā pana.

Even in the state of having a single object, only the psychic mind knows another's mind, not the others, just as...

1141.

1141.

Cakkhudvāre [V 0.0144] tu viññāṇaṃ, rūpaṃ passati netaraṃ;

Evameva ca taṃ iddhi-cittameva ca jānāti.

...consciousness at the eye-door sees form and not another object; just so, that psychic mind alone knows.

1142.

1142.

Paracittārammaṇattā, bahiddhārammaṇaṃ siyā;

Cetopariyañāṇampi, aṭṭhasveva pavattati.

Because it has another's mind as its object, it would be an external object; the knowledge of penetration of mind also operates in these eight.

1143.

1143.

Pubbenivāsañāṇampi, parittādīsu aṭṭhasu;

Ārammaṇavibhāgesu, pavattati kathaṃ pana.

How, then, does the knowledge of past lives operate in the eight divisions of objects, beginning with the limited?

1144.

1144.

Kāmāvacarakhandhānaṃ, samanussaraṇe pana;

Parittārammaṇaṃyeva, hotīti paridīpaye.

When recollecting the aggregates pertaining to the sense-sphere, it is only a limited object—thus should it be explained.

1145.

1145.

Rūpāvacarikāruppakhandhānussaraṇe pana;

Bhavatīti hi ñātabbaṃ, taṃ mahaggatagocaraṃ.

But when recollecting the aggregates of the form-sphere and formless-sphere, it should be known that this has an exalted object.

1146.

1146.

Atīte attanā maggaṃ, bhāvitaṃ tu phalampi vā;

Samanussarato eva-ppamāṇārammaṇaṃ siyā.

When one recollects the path developed by oneself in the past, or the fruit attained, the object would be immeasurable.

1147.

1147.

Samanussarato maggaṃ, maggārammaṇameva taṃ;

Atītārammaṇaṃyeva, hoti ekantato idaṃ.

When recollecting the path, that has the path itself as its object; this is exclusively a past object.

1148.

1148.

Cetopariyañāṇampi[M 0.0151], yathākammupagampi ca;

Atītārammaṇā honti, kiñcāpi atha kho pana.

The knowledge of others’ minds and the knowledge of the passing on of beings according to their kamma have past objects, although, however...

1149.

1149.

Cetopariyañāṇassa, sattaddivasabbhantaraṃ;

Atītaṃ cittamevassa, ārammaṇamudīritaṃ.

For the knowledge of others' minds, the past mind within seven days is declared to be its only object.

1150.

1150.

Atīte cetanāmattaṃ, yathākammupagassapi;

Pubbenivāsañāṇassa, natthi kiñci agocaraṃ.

For the knowledge of past lives and the knowledge of the passing on of beings according to their kamma, there is nothing that is not their object, not even mere volition in the past.

1151.

1151.

Ajjhattārammaṇaṃ atta-khandhānussaraṇe siyā;

Bahiddhārammaṇaṃ añña-khandhānussaraṇe bhave.

It would be an internal object when recollecting one's own aggregates; it would be an external object when recollecting others' aggregates.

1152.

1152.

Saraṇe nāmagottassa, taṃ navattabbagocaraṃ;

Pubbenivāsañāṇampi, aṭṭhasveva pavattati.

When recollecting a name or clan, that is not an object to be spoken of; the knowledge of former abodes also operates only in these eight.

1153.

1153.

Paccuppanne [V 0.0145] paritte ca, bahiddhajjhattikesupi;

Catūsvetesu dhammesu, dibbacakkhu pavattati.

In the present and the limited, and also in the external and internal—in these four phenomena, the divine eye operates.

1154.

1154.

Dibbasotasamaṃ [P 0.0111] dibba-cakkhuārammaṇakkame;

Rūpaṃ saddoti dvinnaṃ tu, ayameva visesatā.

In the range of its objects, the divine eye is like the divine ear; the only distinction between the two is form and sound.

1155.

1155.

Anāgataṃsañāṇampi, parittādīsu aṭṭhasu;

Ārammaṇavibhāgesu, pavattati kathaṃ pana.

How, then, does the knowledge of the future operate in the eight divisions of objects, beginning with the limited?

1156.

1156.

Nibbattissati yaṃ kāmā-vacareti pajānato;

Parittārammaṇaṃ hoti, rūpārūpesvanāgate.

When one knows, 'What will arise is in the sense-sphere,' it is a limited object; in the future, in the form and formless realms...

1157.

1157.

Nibbattissati yañcāpi, siyā mahaggatagocaraṃ;

Bhāvessati ayaṃ maggaṃ, phalaṃ sacchikarissati.

...and what will arise there would be an exalted-sphere object. When knowing, 'This one will develop the path, will realize the fruit'...

1158.

1158.

Evaṃ pajānane appa-māṇārammaṇataṃ bhave;

Maggaṃ bhāvessaticceva, jānane maggagocaraṃ.

...in such understanding, it would be an immeasurable object. When knowing, 'One will develop the path,' it has the path as its object.

1159.

1159.

Ekantena idaṃ ñāṇaṃ, hotānāgatagocaraṃ;

Cetopariyaṃ tu kiñcāpi, hotānāgatagocaraṃ.

This knowledge is exclusively of the future sphere; although the knowledge of others' minds also has the future as its sphere.

1160.

1160.

Atha kho pana taṃ satta-divasabbhantaraṃ pana;

Cittameva ca jānāti, na hi taṃ aññagocaraṃ.

Yet that, within seven days, knows only the mind; for it does not have another object.

1161.

1161.

Anāgataṃsañāṇassa[M 0.0152], anāgataṃsagocaraṃ;

“Ahaṃ devo bhavissāmi”-ccevamajjhattagocaraṃ.

For the knowledge of the future, its sphere is the future. 'I will become a deva'—thus, it has an internal sphere.

1162.

1162.

“Tisso phusso amutrāyaṃ,

Nibbattissatināgate”;

Iccevaṃ jānane tassa,

Bahiddhārammaṇaṃ siyā.

'This Tissa or Phussa will arise there in the future'—in knowing thus, for that one it would be an external object.

1163.

1163.

Jānane nāmagottassa, yassa kassacināgate;

Pubbenivāsañāṇaṃva, taṃ navattabbagocaraṃ.

In knowing the name and clan of anyone in the future, like the knowledge of past lives, that is not an object to be spoken of.

1164.

1164.

Yathākammupagañāṇaṃ[V 0.0146], parittādīsu pañcasu;

Ārammaṇavibhāgesu, pavattati kathaṃ pana.

How, then, does the knowledge of the passing on of beings according to their kamma operate in the five divisions of objects, beginning with the limited?

1165.

1165.

Jānane kāmakammassa, parittārammaṇaṃ siyā;

Tathā mahaggatakammassa, taṃ mahaggatagocaraṃ.

In knowing sense-sphere kamma, it would be a limited object; likewise, for exalted kamma, that has an exalted object.

1166.

1166.

Atītameva jānāti, tasmā cātītagocaraṃ;

Ajjhattārammaṇaṃ hoti, attano kammajānane.

It knows only the past, and therefore has the past as its sphere; it becomes an internal object when knowing one's own kamma.

1167.

1167.

Bahiddhārammaṇaṃ hoti, parakammapajānane;

Evaṃ pavatti ñātabbā, yathākammupagassapi.

It becomes an external object when knowing the kamma of another; thus should the operation of the knowledge of the passing on of beings according to their kamma also be understood.

1168.

1168.

Sattannampi abhiññānaṃ, vutto ārammaṇakkamo;

Ettha vuttanayeneva, veditabbo vibhāvinā.

Of the seven higher knowledges, the range of objects has been stated; it should be understood by the discerning one according to the method explained herein.

1169.

1169.

Vividhatthavaṇṇapadehi sampannaṃ,

Madhuratthamatinīharaṃ ganthaṃ;

Sotujanassa hadayapītikaraṃ,

Suṇeyya koci manujo sacetano.

Endowed with words of varied meaning and description, a text that brings forth sweet meaning and profound thought, delighting the hearts of those who listen—may some wise person hear it.

Iti abhidhammāvatāre abhiññārammaṇaniddeso nāma

Thus, in the Abhidhammāvatāra, ends the chapter named 'The Exposition of the Objects of the Higher Knowledges'.

Sattarasamo paricchedo.

The Seventeenth Chapter.

18. Aṭṭhārasamo paricchedo

18. The Eighteenth Chapter

Diṭṭhivisuddhiniddeso

The Exposition of the Purification of View

1170.

1170.

Samādhiṃ [M 0.0153][P 0.0112] pana sābhiññaṃ, bhāvetvā tadanantaraṃ;

Bhāvetabbā yato paññā, bhikkhunā tena dhīmatā.

Since, having developed concentration together with the higher knowledges, wisdom should be developed immediately thereafter by that wise monk.

1171.

1171.

Tatohaṃ [V 0.0147] dāni vakkhāmi, paññābhāvanamuttamaṃ;

Samāseneva bhikkhūnaṃ, paraṃ pītisukhāvahaṃ.

Therefore, I shall now speak of the supreme development of wisdom, briefly for the monks, which brings supreme joy and happiness.

1172.

1172.

Kā paññā pana ko cattho,

Kimassā lakkhaṇādikaṃ;

Katidhā sā kathaṃ tena,

Bhāvetabbāti vuccate. –

What is wisdom? What is its meaning? What are its characteristics and so on? Of how many kinds is it? And how should it be developed? Thus it is asked.

1173.

1173.

Paññā vipassanāpaññā, puññacittasamāyutā;

Pajānātīti paññā sā, jānanā vā pakārato.

Wisdom is insight-wisdom, associated with meritorious consciousness. It is wisdom because it understands, or because it knows in a distinct way.

1174.

1174.

Saññāviññāṇapaññānaṃ, ko viseso kimantaraṃ;

Saññāviññāṇapaññānaṃ, jānanatte samepi ca.

What is the difference, what is the distinction, among perception, consciousness, and wisdom, even though they are the same in their act of knowing?

1175.

1175.

Yā sañjānanamattaṃva, saññā nīlādito pana;

Lakkhaṇappaṭivedhaṃ tu, kātuṃ sakkoti neva sā.

Perception is mere recognition of such things as blue; but it cannot accomplish the penetration of characteristics.

1176.

1176.

Viññāṇaṃ pana jānāti, nīlapītādigocaraṃ;

Sakkotipi aniccādilakkhaṇaṃ paṭivijjhituṃ.

Consciousness, however, knows objects such as blue and yellow; yet it is also unable to penetrate characteristics such as impermanence.

1177.

1177.

Ussakkitvā na sakkoti, maggaṃ pāpetumeva taṃ;

Paññā vuttanayaṃ kātuṃ, sakkoti tividhampi taṃ.

Though it strives, it cannot lead to the path; but wisdom can accomplish all three of these things in the way described.

1178.

1178.

Imesaṃ pana tiṇṇampi, viseso samudīrito;

Sabbesaṃ pana dhammānaṃ, sabhāvapaṭivedhanaṃ.

The distinction among these three has thus been declared. The meaning of wisdom, however, is the penetration of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.

1179.

1179.

Lakkhaṇaṃ pana paññāya, lakkhaṇaññūhi dīpitaṃ;

Sammohanandhakārassa, viddhaṃsanarasā matā.

The characteristic of wisdom has been illuminated by those who know characteristics; its function is considered to be the dispelling of the darkness of delusion.

1180.

1180.

Asammohapaccupaṭṭhānā[M 0.0154], samādhāsannakāraṇā;

Evamettha ca viññeyyā, paññāya lakkhaṇādikā.

Its manifestation is non-delusion; its proximate cause is concentration. Thus should the characteristics and so on of wisdom be understood here.

Katidhāti [V 0.0148] ettha –

Here, as to 'how many kinds':

1181.

1181.

Lakkhaṇenekadhā vuttā,

Lokikālokikā dvidhā;

Lokiyenettha maggena,

Yuttā sā lokikā siyā.

By its characteristic, it is spoken of as onefold; as worldly and supramundane, it is twofold. Here, that which is connected with the worldly path is worldly.

1182.

1182.

Lokuttarena [P 0.0113] maggena, yuttā lokuttarā matā;

Tividhāpi siyā paññā, cintāsutamayādito.

That which is connected with the supramundane path is considered supramundane. Wisdom may also be threefold: that born of reflection, of learning, and so on.

1183.

1183.

Tatthattanova cintāya, nipphannattāti tassa sā;

Hoti cintāmayā paññā, bhūripaññena desitā.

Therein, because it is produced by one's own reflection, it is wisdom born of reflection; so it was taught by the one of great wisdom.

1184.

1184.

Parato pana sutvāna, laddhā paññā ayaṃ idha;

Suteneva ca nipphannā, paññā sutamayā matā.

Furthermore, the wisdom gained here by hearing from another, and produced by that very hearing, is considered wisdom born of learning.

1185.

1185.

Yathā vāpi tathā cettha, bhāvanāya vasena tu;

Nipphannā appanāpattā, paññā sā bhāvanāmayā.

Similarly, wisdom produced here through the power of development and which has attained absorption is wisdom born of development.

1186.

1186.

Paṭisambhidācatukkassa, vasena catudhā siyā;

Atthadhammaniruttīsu, ñāṇaṃ ñāṇesu tīsupi.

By way of the fourfold discrimination, it may be fourfold: knowledge of meaning, of the Dhamma, of language, and knowledge concerning these three.

1187.

1187.

Yaṃ kiñci paccayuppannaṃ, vipākā ca kriyā tathā;

Nibbānaṃ bhāsitattho ca, pañcete atthasaññitā.

Whatever is conditionally arisen, results, functional consciousness, Nibbāna, and the meaning of what is spoken—these five are designated as 'meaning'.

1188.

1188.

Phalanibbattako hetu, ariyamaggo ca bhāsitaṃ;

Kusalākusalañceti, pañcete dhammasaññitā.

The cause that produces a fruit, the Noble Path, what is spoken, and the wholesome and unwholesome—these five are designated as 'Dhamma'.

1189.

1189.

Tasmiṃ atthe ca dhamme ca, yā sabhāvanirutti tu;

Niruttīti ca niddiṭṭhā, niruttikusalena sā.

The natural expression concerning that meaning and Dhamma is pointed out as 'language' by one skilled in language.

1190.

1190.

Ñāṇaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā, tividhaṃ paccavekkhato;

Tesu ñāṇesu yaṃ ñāṇaṃ, paṭibhānanti taṃ mataṃ.

The knowledge about those knowledges, for one who reflects upon that threefold knowledge as an object, is considered 'analytical knowledge of exposition' (paṭibhāna).

1191.

1191.

Pariyattiparipucchāhi[M 0.0155][V 0.0149], savanādhigamehi ca;

Pubbayogena gacchanti, pabhedaṃ paṭisambhidā.

Through study, inquiry, listening, attainment, and through prior practice, the discriminations attain their distinct kinds.

Kathaṃ bhāvetabbāti ettha –

Here, as to 'how it should be developed':

1192.

1192.

Khandhādīsu hi dhammesu, bhūmibhūtesu yoginā;

Uggahādivasenettha, katvā paricayaṃ pana.

A yogi should first establish familiarity with the phenomena such as the aggregates, which are the foundation, by means of comprehension and so on.

1193.

1193.

Sīlaṃ cittavisuddhiñca, sampādetvā tato paraṃ;

Diṭṭhisuddhādayo pañca, sampādentena suddhiyā.

Then, having perfected virtue and the purification of mind, he should accomplish the five purities beginning with the purity of view.

1194.

1194.

Tāya paññāya yuttena, bhītena jananādito;

Bhāvetabbā bhavābhāvaṃ, patthayantena bhikkhunā.

It should be developed by a monk who is endowed with that wisdom, fearful of birth and so on, and who aspires to the cessation of existence.

1195.

1195.

Rūpañca vedanā saññā, saṅkhārā ceva sabbaso;

Viññāṇañceti pañcete, khandhā sambuddhadesitā.

Form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness—these five aggregates are taught by the Perfectly Awakened One.

1196.

1196.

Tattha yaṃ kiñci rūpaṃ taṃ, atītānāgatādikaṃ;

Ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā, sukhumoḷārikampi vā.

Therein, whatever form there is, whether past, future, or otherwise; whether internal or external; whether subtle or gross;

1197.

1197.

Hīnaṃ vāpi paṇītaṃ vā, yaṃ dūre yañca santike;

Sabbaṃ tamekato katvā, rūpakkhandhoti vuccati.

Whether inferior or superior, whether far or near—having gathered all that together, it is called the aggregate of form.

1198.

1198.

Itaresupi yaṃ kiñci, taṃ vedayitalakkhaṇaṃ;

Sabbaṃ tamekato katvā, vedanākkhandhatā katā.

Among the others, too, whatever has the characteristic of being felt, having gathered all that together, is made the aggregate of feeling.

1199.

1199.

Cittajaṃ [P 0.0114] pana yaṃ kiñci, taṃ sañjānanalakkhaṇaṃ;

Sabbaṃ tamekato katvā, saññākkhandhoti vuccati.

Furthermore, whatever is mind-born has perceiving as its characteristic; gathering all of that together, it is called the aggregate of perception.

1200.

1200.

Yaṃ kiñci cittasambhūtaṃ, abhisaṅkhāralakkhaṇaṃ;

Sabbaṃ tamekato katvā, saṅkhārakkhandhatā katā.

Whatever is mind-produced has volitional formation as its characteristic; having gathered all of that together, it is made the aggregate of formations.

1201.

1201.

Tattha cittaṃ tu yaṃ kiñci, taṃ vijānanalakkhaṇaṃ;

Sabbaṃ tamekato katvā, viññāṇakkhandhatā katā.

Therein, whatever consciousness there is has the characteristic of cognizing; having gathered all of that together, it is made the aggregate of consciousness.

1202.

1202.

Cattāro [V 0.0150] ca mahābhūtā, upādā catuvīsati;

Aṭṭhavīsatidhā cetaṃ, rūpaṃ rūpanti gaṇhati.

The four great elements and the twenty-four derived forms; this form, being thus twenty-eightfold, is comprehended as form.

1203.

1203.

Ekāsītiyā [M 0.0156] cittena, saṃyuttā vedanādayo;

Vedanāsaññāsaṅkhāra-viññāṇakkhandhasaññitā.

Feeling and the rest, associated with the eighty-one types of consciousness, are designated as the aggregates of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness.

1204.

1204.

Cattārorūpino khandhe, nāmanti parigaṇhati;

Rūpakkhandho bhave rūpaṃ, nāmakkhandhā arūpino.

The four formless aggregates are comprehended as 'name'; the aggregate of form is form, the name-aggregates are formless.

1205.

1205.

Ruppanalakkhaṇaṃ rūpaṃ, nāmaṃ namanalakkhaṇaṃ;

Iti saṅkhepato nāma-rūpaṃ so parigaṇhati.

Form has the characteristic of being afflicted; name has the characteristic of inclining. Thus, in brief, he comprehends name-and-form.

1206.

1206.

Phālento viya tālassa, kandaṃ tu yamakaṃ dvidhā;

Vavatthapeti nāmañca, rūpañcāti dvidhā pana.

Like one splitting the paired trunk of a palm tree in two, he distinguishes name and form as twofold.

1207.

1207.

Nāmato rūpato añño,

Satto vā puggalopi vā;

Attā vā koci natthīti,

Niṭṭhaṃ gacchati sabbadā.

“Apart from name and form, no other being or person, nor any self exists”—thus he always reaches this conclusion.

1208.

1208.

Evaṃ vavatthapetvā so, nāmarūpaṃ sabhāvato;

Sattasammohaghātatthaṃ, bahusuttavasenidha.

Thus having determined name-and-form according to its intrinsic nature, here, by means of many suttas, for the purpose of striking down the delusion of beings.

1209.

1209.

Nāmarūpamattaññeva, natthi kocidha puggalo;

Evamettha paṇḍito poso, vavatthapeti taṃ pana.

There is only name-and-form; no person is found here. Thus the wise person here determines it.

Vuttaṃ hetaṃ –

For this has been said:

1210.

1210.

“Yathāpi aṅgasambhārā,

Hoti saddo ratho iti;

Evaṃ khandhesu santesu,

Hoti sattoti sammutī”ti.

“Just as from an assemblage of parts, the word ‘chariot’ arises, so, when the aggregates are present, the convention ‘a being’ arises.”

1211.

1211.

Yathāpi [V 0.0151] dāruyantampi, nijjīvañca nirīhakaṃ;

Dārurajjusamāyoge, taṃ gacchatipi tiṭṭhati.

Just as a wooden puppet, lifeless and without volition, moves and stands through the combination of wood and strings.

1212.

1212.

Tathedaṃ nāmarūpampi, nijjīvañca nirīhakaṃ;

Aññamaññasamāyoge, taṃ gacchatipi tiṭṭhati.

So too this name-and-form, lifeless and without volition, moves and stands through their mutual combination.

Tenāhu porāṇā –

Therefore the ancients have said:

1213.

1213.

“Nāmañca [M 0.0157] rūpañca idhatthi saccato,

Na hettha satto manujo ca vijjati;

Suññaṃ idaṃ yantamivābhisaṅkhataṃ,

Dukkhassa puñjo tiṇakaṭṭhasādiso”ti.

“Name and form truly exist here, but no being or person is found. This is empty, constructed like a machine, a heap of suffering, like grass and wood.”

1214.

1214.

Aññamaññūpanissāya[P 0.0115], daṇḍakesu ṭhitesu hi;

Ekasmiṃ patamāne tu, tatheva patatītaro.

Indeed, when sticks stand in mutual dependence, if one falls, the other falls in just the same way.

Tenāhu porāṇā –

Therefore the ancients have said:

1215.

1215.

“Yamakaṃ nāmarūpañca, ubho aññoññanissitā;

Ekasmiṃ bhijjamānasmiṃ, ubho bhijjanti paccayā”ti.

“Name and form are a pair, both mutually dependent; when one is broken, both, being conditioned, break.”

1216.

1216.

Utinnaṃ nāmarūpānaṃ, nāmaṃ nittejamettha taṃ;

Sakeneva hi tejena, na sakkoti pavattituṃ.

Of arisen name and form, that name here is without power; for by its own energy alone, it is not able to proceed.

1217.

1217.

Na byāharati no seti, na tiṭṭhati na gacchati;

Na bhedeti na coreti, na bhuñjati na khādati.

It does not speak, nor does it lie down, it does not stand, nor does it go; it does not break, nor does it steal, it does not eat, nor does it chew.

1218.

1218.

Tathā rūpampi nittejaṃ, vinā nāmañca sabbathā;

Sakeneva hi tejena, na sakkoti pavattituṃ.

So too, form is without power, entirely without name; by its own force alone, it is not able to proceed.

1219.

1219.

Bhuñjāmīti pivāmīti, khādāmīti tatheva ca;

Rodāmīti hasāmīti, rūpassetaṃ na vijjati.

“I eat,” “I drink,” and likewise “I chew”; “I weep,” “I laugh”—this is not found in form.

1220.

1220.

Nāmaṃ [V 0.0152] nissāya rūpaṃ tu, rūpaṃ nissāya nāmakaṃ;

Pavattati sadā sabbaṃ, pañcavokārabhūmiyaṃ.

Form proceeds in dependence on name, and name in dependence on form; thus does everything always proceed in the five-constituent realm.

1221.

1221.

Imassa pana atthassa, āvibhāvatthameva ca;

Jaccandhapīṭhasappīnaṃ, vattabbā upamā idha.

Furthermore, to make this meaning evident, the simile of the man blind from birth and the cripple should be stated here.

1222.

1222.

Yathā hi nāvaṃ nissāya, manussā yanti aṇṇave;

Evaṃ rūpampi nissāya, nāmakāyo pavattati.

Just as people, relying on a boat, travel on the ocean, so the name-body proceeds, relying on form.

1223.

1223.

Yathā [M 0.0158] manusse nissāya, nāvā gacchati aṇṇave;

Evaṃ nāmampi nissāya, rūpakāyo pavattati.

As a boat, relying on a man, goes on the ocean, so the material body continues, relying on name.

1224.

1224.

Sattasaññaṃ vinodetvā, nāmarūpassa sabbathā;

Yāthāvadassanaṃ etaṃ, “diṭṭhisuddhī”ti vuccati.

Having dispelled the perception of a being, this seeing of name-and-form completely as it truly is, is called 'purification of view'.

1225.

1225.

Parimuccitukāmo ca, dukkhato jātiādito;

Antadvayaṃ vivajjetvā, bhāvaye pana paṇḍito.

The wise one, desiring to be released from suffering, from birth and so on, should, avoiding both extremes, develop this.

1226.

1226.

Diṭṭhivisuddhimimaṃ parisuddhaṃ,

Suṭṭhutaraṃ tu karoti naro yo;

Diṭṭhigatāni malāni asesaṃ,

Nāsamupenti hi tassa narassa.

Whatever person cultivates this perfectly pure purification of view exceedingly well, for that person all stains of wrong views are destroyed without remainder.

Iti abhidhammāvatāre diṭṭhivisuddhiniddeso nāma

Thus, in the Abhidhammāvatāra, is the exposition called 'The Purification of View'.

Aṭṭhārasamo paricchedo.

The Eighteenth Chapter.

19. Ekūnavīsatimo paricchedo

19. The Nineteenth Chapter.

Kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhiniddeso

Exposition on the Purification by Overcoming Doubt.

1227.

1227.

Etassa [P 0.0116][V 0.0153] nāmarūpassa, jānitvā hetupaccaye;

Kaṅkhā tīsu panaddhāsu, vitaritvā ṭhitaṃ pana.

Having known the causes and conditions for this name-and-form, and having overcome doubt concerning the three periods of time, one is then established.

1228.

1228.

Kaṅkhāvitaraṇaṃ nāma, ñāṇaṃ taṃ samudīritaṃ;

Taṃ sampādetukāmena, atthakāmena bhikkhunā.

That knowledge called the Overcoming of Doubt has been declared; it is to be accomplished by the bhikkhu who desires his welfare.

1229.

1229.

Nāmarūpassa ko hetu, konu vā paccayo bhave;

Āvajjitvā tamiccevaṃ, rūpakāyassa tāvade.

What is the cause of name-and-form, and what is its condition? Having reflected thus, one should first consider the material body.

1230.

1230.

Kesā lomā nakhā dantā, taco maṃsaṃ nahāru ca;

Aṭṭhimiñjañca vakkañca, hadayaṃ yakanampi ca.

Head hairs, body hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, and sinews; bones, bone-marrow, and kidneys, heart, and liver.

1231.

1231.

Iccevamādibāttiṃsa-koṭṭhāsapaccayassa hi;

Pariggaṇhati kāyassa, manasā hetupaccaye.

Thus, with the mind, one comprehends the causes and conditions of this body, which is comprised of the thirty-two parts beginning in this way.

1232.

1232.

Avijjā [M 0.0159] taṇhupādānaṃ, kammaṃ hetu catubbidho;

Etassa rūpakāyassa, āhāro paccayo mato.

Ignorance, craving, clinging, and kamma are the fourfold cause. For this material body, nutriment is regarded as the condition.

1233.

1233.

Janako hetu akkhāto,

Paccayo anupālako;

Hetvaṅkurassa bījaṃ tu,

Paccayā pathavādayo.

The producer is said to be the cause; the condition is the sustainer. The cause of a sprout is the seed, but its conditions are the earth element and the others.

1234.

1234.

Itime pañca dhammā hi, hetupaccayataṃ gatā;

Avijjādayo tayo tattha, mātāva upanissayā.

Indeed, these five things have the nature of cause and condition. Among them, the three beginning with ignorance are a decisive support, like a mother.

1235.

1235.

Janakaṃ pana kammaṃ tu, puttassa hi pitā viya;

Dhātī viya kumārassa, āhāro dhārako bhave.

But generative kamma is like a father to a son; like a wet-nurse to a child, nutriment is the sustainer.

1236.

1236.

Iccevaṃ [V 0.0154] rūpakāyassa, so paccayapariggahaṃ;

Katvā punapi “cakkhuñca, rūpamālokameva ca.

Having thus comprehended the conditions for the material body, he again considers: 'The eye, form, and light...

1237.

1237.

Paṭicca cakkhuviññāṇaṃ, hoti”iccevamādinā;

Nayena nāmakāyassa, paccayaṃ parigaṇhati.

...dependent on which eye-consciousness arises.' By this method and others, he comprehends the conditions for the mental body.

1238.

1238.

So evaṃ nāmarūpassa, vuttiṃ disvāna paccayā;

Yathā etarahidaṃ tu, atītepi tathevidaṃ.

Having thus seen the occurrence of name-and-form from its conditions, he understands: 'Just as it is now, so too was it in the past.'

1239.

1239.

Paccayā ca pavattittha, tathevānāgatepi ca;

Pavattissati addhāsu, tīsvevaṃ anupassati.

From conditions it proceeded, and so too in the future it will proceed. Thus he contemplates it in the three periods of time.

1240.

1240.

Tassevaṃ [P 0.0117] passato yā sā, pubbante pañcadhā tathā;

Aparante siyā kaṅkhā, pañcadhā samudīritā.

For one who sees in this way, the fivefold doubt concerning the past and the fivefold doubt declared concerning the future...

1241.

1241.

Paccuppannepi addhāne, chabbidhā parikittitā;

Sabbā cānavasesāva, yogino sā pahiyyati.

...and the sixfold doubt described concerning the present time—all this is abandoned without remainder by the yogi.

1242.

1242.

Eko kammavipākānaṃ, vasenāpi ca paṇḍito;

Etassa nāmarūpassa, paccayaṃ parigaṇhati.

A wise person also comprehends the condition for this name-and-form by way of kamma and its result.

1243.

1243.

Kammaṃ catubbidhaṃ diṭṭha-dhammavedaniyaṃ tathā;

Upapajjāparāpariyā-hosikammavasā pana.

Kamma is fourfold: that which is experiencable in this very life, that experiencable in the next life, that experiencable in subsequent lives, and defunct kamma.

Tattha [M 0.0160] ekajavanavīthiyaṃ sattasu cittesu kusalā vā akusalā vā paṭhamajavanacetanā diṭṭhadhammavedanīyakammaṃ nāma. Taṃ imasmiṃyeva attabhāve vipākaṃ deti, tathā asakkontaṃ pana “ahosikammaṃ nāhosi kammavipāko, na bhavissati kammavipāko, natthi kammavipāko”ti imassa tikassa vasena ahosikammaṃ nāma hoti. Atthasādhikā pana sattamajavanacetanā upapajjavedanīyakammaṃ nāma. Tamanantare attabhāve vipākaṃ deti, tathā asakkontaṃ vuttanayena ahosikammaṃ nāma hoti. Ubhinnamantare pañcajavanacetanā aparāpariyavedanīyakammaṃ nāma. Tamanāgate yadā okāsaṃ labhati, tadā vipākaṃ deti, sati saṃsārappavattiyā ahosikammaṃ nāma na hoti.

Herein, in a single cognitive series with seven impulsions, the volition in the first impulsion, whether wholesome or unwholesome, is called kamma experiencable in this very life. It gives its result in this same existence. But if it is unable to do so, it becomes defunct kamma by way of the triad: 'There was kamma, but there was no kamma-result; there will be no kamma-result; and there is no kamma-result.' The volition in the seventh impulsion, which is effective in its purpose, is called kamma experiencable in the next life. It gives its result in the next existence. If it is unable to do so, it becomes defunct kamma in the way already stated. The five volitions in the impulsions between these two are called kamma experiencable in subsequent lives. This gives its result in the future whenever it finds an opportunity. As long as the round of existence continues, it does not become defunct kamma.

1244.

1244.

Aparaṃ [V 0.0155] catubbidhaṃ kammaṃ, garukaṃ bahulampi ca;

Āsannañca kaṭattā ca, kammanti samudīritaṃ.

Another fourfold classification of kamma has been declared: weighty kamma, habitual kamma, death-proximate kamma, and cumulative kamma.

1245.

1245.

Aññaṃ catubbidhaṃ kammaṃ, janakaṃ upathambhakaṃ;

Tathūpapīḷakaṃ kamma-mupaghātakameva ca.

Another fourfold kamma is: generative, supportive, obstructive, and destructive.

Tattha janakaṃ nāma kusalaṃ vā akusalaṃ vā kammaṃ paṭisandhiyampi pavattepi rūpārūpavipākakkhandhe janeti. Upatthambhakaṃ pana vipākaṃ janetuṃ na sakkoti, aññena kammena dinnāya paṭisandhiyā janite vipāke uppajjanakasukhadukkhaṃ upatthambheti, addhānaṃ pavatteti. Upapīḷakaṃ pana aññena kammena dinnāya paṭisandhiyā janite vipāke uppajjanakasukhadukkhaṃ pīḷeti bādhati, addhānaṃ pavattituṃ na deti. Upaghātakaṃ pana sayaṃ kusalampi akusalampi samānaṃ [P 0.0118] aññaṃ dubbalakammaṃ ghātetvā tassa vipākaṃ paṭibāhitvā attano vipākassa okāsaṃ karoti. Evaṃ pana kammena okāse kate taṃvipākamuppannaṃ nāma hoti. Iti imaṃ dvādasavidhaṃ kammaṃ kammavaṭṭe pakkhipitvā [M 0.0161] evameko kammavipākavasena nāmarūpassa paccayapariggahaṃ karoti.

Therein, generative kamma, whether wholesome or unwholesome, generates the material and immaterial resultant aggregates both at rebirth-linking and during the course of existence. Supportive kamma cannot generate a result itself; but when rebirth-linking has been given by another kamma and a result has been generated, it supports the pleasure and pain that arise and allows it to continue for its duration. Obstructive kamma, when rebirth-linking has been given by another kamma and a result has been generated, oppresses and afflicts the pleasure and pain that arise and does not allow it to continue for its duration. Destructive kamma, being itself wholesome or unwholesome, supplants another weaker kamma, obstructs its result, and creates an opportunity for its own result. Thus, when an opportunity has been created by a kamma, its result is said to have arisen. In this way, having included these twelve kinds of kamma in the round of kamma, one thus comprehends the conditions of name-and-form by way of kamma and its result.

Iti evaṃ kammavipākavaṭṭavasena nāmarūpassa pavattiṃ disvā “yathā idaṃ etarahi, evamatītepi addhāne kammavipākavasena paccayato pavattittha, anāgatepi pavattissatī”ti iti kammañceva vipāko cāti kammavipākavasena loko pavattatīti taṃ samanupassati. Tassevaṃ samanupassato sabbā soḷasavidhā kaṅkhā pahiyyati.

Thus, having seen the occurrence of name-and-form by way of the round of kamma and its result, one reflects: 'Just as it is now, so in the past it proceeded from conditions by way of kamma and its result, and so in the future it will proceed.' Thus one sees that the world proceeds by way of kamma and its result. For one who sees in this way, all sixteen kinds of doubt are abandoned.

1246.

1246.

Hetuphalassa sambandhavaseneva pavattati;

Kevalaṃ nāmarūpanti, sammā samanupassati.

It proceeds solely through the connection of cause and effect; one rightly sees that this is merely name-and-form.

1247.

1247.

Evaṃ kāraṇato uddhaṃ, kāraṇaṃ na ca passati;

Pākapavattito uddhaṃ, na pākapaṭivedakaṃ.

Beyond the cause, one sees no agent; beyond the occurrence of the result, one finds no experiencer.

Tenāhu porāṇā –

Therefore, the ancients have said:

1248.

1248.

“Kammassa kārako natthi, vipākassa ca vedako;

Suddhadhammā pavattanti, evetaṃ sammadassanaṃ.

“No doer of a deed is found, no one who experiences the result; bare phenomena roll on: this is the right view.

1249.

1249.

Evaṃ [V 0.0156] kamme vipāke ca, vattamāne sahetuke;

Bījarukkhādikānaṃva, pubbā koṭi na nāyati.

Thus, with kamma and its result revolving with their cause, like the sequence of seed and tree, a first beginning is not discerned.

1250.

1250.

Anāgatepi saṃsāre, appavatti na dissati;

Etamatthamanaññāya, titthiyā asayaṃvasī.

In the future of saṃsāra, too, its non-occurrence is not seen; not understanding this fact, the sectarians are not their own masters.

1251.

1251.

Sattasaññaṃ gahetvāna, sassatucchedadassino;

Dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhiṃ gaṇhanti, aññamaññavirodhino.

Having grasped the perception of a being, those who hold the views of eternalism and annihilationism adopt the sixty-two views, which are mutually contradictory.

1252.

1252.

Diṭṭhibandhanabaddhā te, taṇhāsotena vuyhare;

Taṇhāsotena vuyhantā, na te dukkhā pamuccare.

Bound by the fetters of views, they are carried off by the stream of craving. Being carried off by the stream of craving, they are not released from suffering.

1253.

1253.

Evametaṃ abhiññāya, bhikkhu buddhassa sāvako;

Gambhīraṃ nipuṇaṃ suññaṃ, paccayaṃ paṭivijjhati.

Having directly known this, the bhikkhu, a disciple of the Buddha, penetrates the conditionality that is profound, subtle, and empty.

1254.

1254.

Kammaṃ [M 0.0162] natthi vipākamhi, pāko kamme na vijjati;

Aññamaññaṃ ubho suññā, na ca kammaṃ vinā phalaṃ.

Kamma is not in the result, nor is the result found in the kamma; both are empty of each other, yet there is no result without kamma.

1255.

1255.

Yathā na sūriye aggi, na maṇimhi na gomaye;

Na tesaṃ bahi so atthi, sambhārehi ca jāyati.

Just as fire is not in the sun, nor in the gem, nor in cow-dung, nor does it exist outside of them; yet it is produced from their components.

1256.

1256.

Tathā na anto kammassa, vipāko upalabbhati;

Bahiddhāpi na kammassa, na kammaṃ tattha vijjati.

So too, the result is not found within the kamma, nor is it found outside the kamma; and the kamma is not found in the result.

1257.

1257.

Phalena [P 0.0119] suññaṃ taṃ kammaṃ, phalaṃ kamme na vijjati;

Kammañca kho upādāya, tato nibbattate phalaṃ.

That kamma is empty of its result; the result is not found in the kamma. But by depending on the kamma, the result is then produced.

1258.

1258.

Na hettha devo brahmā vā,

Saṃsārassatthi kārako;

Suddhadhammā pavattanti,

Hetusambhārapaccayā”ti.

Here there is no god or Brahmā who is the maker of saṃsāra. Bare phenomena proceed, conditioned by their constituent causes.”

1259.

1259.

Evaṃ nānappakārehi, nāmarūpassa paccayaṃ;

Pariggahetvā addhāsu, taritvā kaṅkhamuṭṭhitaṃ.

Thus, having in various ways comprehended the conditions for name-and-form, and having crossed over the doubt that had arisen about the periods of time,

1260.

1260.

Kaṅkhāvitaraṇaṃ [V 0.0157] nāma, ñāṇaṃ taṃ samudīritaṃ;

Dhammaṭṭhiti yathābhūtaṃ, taṃ sammādassanantipi.

That knowledge is called the Overcoming of Doubt; it is also right seeing, which is knowledge of the stability of phenomena as they really are.

1261.

1261.

Iminā pana ñāṇena,

Saṃyutto buddhasāsane;

Hoti laddhapatiṭṭhova,

Sotāpanno hi cūḷako.

One endowed with this knowledge becomes one who has gained a footing in the Buddha's Dispensation; he is indeed a 'lesser stream-enterer.'

1262.

1262.

Tasmā sapañño pana atthakāmo,

Yo nāmarūpassa hetupaccayāni;

Pariggahaṃ sādhu karoti dhīro,

Khippaṃ sa nibbānapuraṃ upeti.

Therefore, the wise and steadfast person who desires his welfare, who thoroughly comprehends the causes and conditions of name-and-form, quickly reaches the city of Nibbāna.

Iti abhidhammāvatāre kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhiniddeso nāma

Here ends the Exposition on the Purification by Overcoming Doubt in the Abhidhammāvatāra.

Ekūnavīsatimo paricchedo.

The Nineteenth Chapter.

20. Vīsatimo paricchedo

20. The Twentieth Chapter.

Maggāmaggañāṇadassanavisuddhiniddeso

The Exposition of the Purification by Knowledge and Vision of the Path and Not-Path.

1263.

1263.

Kalāpasammasaneneva[M 0.0163][P 0.0120],

Yogo karaṇiyo siyā;

Maggāmagge tu ñāṇaṃ ta-

Madhigantuṃ panicchatā.

The practice should be undertaken by the mere comprehension of groups, by one who wishes to attain that knowledge of the path and not-path.

1264.

1264.

Paccuppannassa dhammassa, nibbatti udayo mato;

Vayo vipariṇāmoti, tasseva samudīritā.

Of a present phenomenon, its production is considered its arising; its alteration is spoken of as its passing away.

1265.

1265.

Anupassanāpi [V 0.0158] ñāṇanti, varañāṇena desitaṃ;

So panevaṃ pajānāti, yogāvacaramāṇavo.

Contemplation, too, is knowledge, so it is taught by the one with supreme knowledge; but the meditating student understands it thus:

1266.

1266.

Imassa nāmarūpassa, pubbe uppattito pana;

Nicayo rāsi vā natthi, tathā uppajjatopi ca.

Of this name-and-form, before its arising there is no accumulation or mass, and neither is there as it arises.

1267.

1267.

Rāsito nicayā vāpi, natthi āgamananti ca;

Tathā nirujjhamānassa, na disāgamananti ca.

There is no coming from a mass or an accumulation; and likewise, for that which is ceasing, there is no departure to any direction.

1268.

1268.

Niruddhassāpi ekasmiṃ, ṭhāne natthi cayoti ca;

Ettha vīṇūpamā vuttā, etassatthassa dīpane.

And of that which has ceased, there is no accumulation in any single place; to illuminate this meaning, the simile of the lute is stated here.

1269.

1269.

Udabbayamanakkāramevaṃ saṅkhepato pana;

Katvā tasseva ñāṇassa, vibhaṅgassa vasena tu.

Having thus briefly treated the contemplation of arising and passing away, I will now proceed by way of the analysis of that very knowledge.

1270.

1270.

“Avijjāsamudayā rūpasamudayo”ti hi ādinā;

Nayenekekakhandhassa, udayabbayadassane.

By the method beginning with, 'With the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of form,' one is to see the arising and passing away of each single aggregate.

1271.

1271.

Dasa dasāti katvāna, vuttā paññāsalakkhaṇā;

Tesaṃ pana vasenāpi, dhamme samanupassati.

Taking them as ten each, fifty characteristics are mentioned; and by means of these, one contemplates the phenomena.

1272.

1272.

Evaṃ rūpudayo hoti, evamassa vayo iti;

Udeti evaṃ rūpampi, evaṃ rūpaṃ tu veti ca.

Thus is the arising of form, thus its passing away; thus form arises, and thus form passes away.

1273.

1273.

Evaṃ [M 0.0164] paccayatopettha, khaṇato udayabbayaṃ;

Passato sabbadhammā ca, pākaṭā honti tassa te.

To one who thus sees the arising and passing away by way of conditions and by way of moments, all those phenomena become manifest.

1274.

1274.

Udake daṇḍarājīva, āraggeriva sāsapo;

Vijjuppādāva dhammā te, parittaṭṭhāyino siyuṃ.

Like a line drawn on water, like a mustard seed on the point of an awl, like a flash of lightning are those phenomena; they are of brief duration.

1275.

1275.

Kadalīsupinālātacakkamāyupamā ime;

Asārā pana nissārā, hutvā khāyanti yogino.

Like a plantain tree, a dream, a firebrand-wheel, and a magical illusion, these appear to the yogi as being essenceless and pithless.

1276.

1276.

Evamettāvatā [P 0.0121] tena, udayabbayadassanaṃ;

Lakkhaṇāni ca paññāsa, paṭivijjha ṭhitaṃ pana.

Thus, by this much, the vision of arising and passing away and the fifty characteristics have been penetrated and established by him.

1277.

1277.

Ñāṇaṃ [V 0.0159] adhigataṃ hoti, taruṇaṃ paṭhamaṃ pana;

Yassa cādhigamā yogī, hotāraddhavipassako.

At first a tender knowledge is attained, and with its attainment the yogi becomes one who has commenced the practice of insight.

1278.

1278.

Vipassanāya hetāya,

Karuṇāyātha yogino;

Vipassakassa jāyante,

Upaklesā dasevime.

For the yogi, the insight meditator, because of this insight and then because of compassion, these ten imperfections arise.

1279.

1279.

Obhāso pīti passaddhi, ñāṇaṃ saddhā satī sukhaṃ;

Upekkhā vīriyaṃ nikantīti, upaklesā dasevime.

Illumination, rapture, tranquility, knowledge, faith, mindfulness, happiness, equanimity, energy, and delight—these are the ten imperfections.

1280.

1280.

Sampattapaṭivedhassa, sotāpannādinopi ca;

Tathā vippaṭipannassa, upaklesā na jāyare.

For one who has attained penetration, such as a stream-enterer and the others, and likewise for one who is practicing wrongly, these imperfections do not arise.

1281.

1281.

Sammāva paṭipannassa, yuttayogassa bhikkhuno;

Sadā vipassakasseva, uppajjanti kirassu te.

Indeed, they are said to arise only for a monk who is practicing rightly, who is devoted to the practice, and who is always developing insight.

1282.

1282.

Vipassanāya obhāso, obhāsoti pavuccati;

Tasmiṃ pana samuppanne, yogāvacarabhikkhu so.

The illumination that arises from insight is called 'illumination.' When that has arisen, that meditating monk...

1283.

1283.

Maggappatto phalappatto, ahamasmīti gaṇhati;

Amaggaṃyeva maggoti, tassevaṃ pana gaṇhato.

...grasps, 'I have attained the path, I have attained the fruit.' For one who grasps thus, he takes the not-path itself to be the path.

1284.

1284.

Evaṃ [M 0.0165] vipassanāvīthi,
