Okkantā nāma hoti sā;

Obhāsameva so bhikkhu,

Assādento nisīdati.

Thus that course of insight is embarked upon; that monk sits savoring only the illumination.

1285.

1285.

Pīti vippassanāpīti, tassa tasmiṃ khaṇe pana;

Tadā pañcavidhā pīti, jāyante khuddikādikā.

The rapture is insight-rapture. Then at that moment for him, the five kinds of rapture arise, beginning with the minor one.

1286.

1286.

Vipassanāya passaddhi, passaddhīti pavuccati;

Yogino kāyacittāni, passaddhāneva honti hi.

Tranquility from insight is called 'tranquility,' for the yogi's body and mind indeed become tranquil.

1287.

1287.

Lahūni [V 0.0160] ca mudūneva, kammaññāneva honti hi;

Passaddhādīhi so bhikkhu, anuggahitamānaso.

For they become light, pliant, and wieldy. That monk has his mind supported by tranquility and the other states.

1288.

1288.

Amānusiṃ ratiṃ nāma,

Anubhoti anuttaraṃ;

Yaṃ sandhāya ca gāthāyo,

Bhāsitā hi mahesinā.

He experiences an unsurpassed, non-human delight, concerning which verses were indeed spoken by the Great Seer.

1289.

1289.

“Suññāgāraṃ paviṭṭhassa, santacittassa bhikkhuno;

Amānusī rati hoti, sammā dhammaṃ vipassato.

For the monk who has entered an empty abode, whose mind is peaceful, there is a delight beyond the human as he rightly sees the Dhamma with insight.

1290.

1290.

“Yato yato sammasati, khandhānaṃ udayabbayaṃ;

Labhatī pītipāmojjaṃ, amataṃ taṃ vijānata”nti.

Whenever one comprehends the arising and passing away of the aggregates, one obtains rapture and joy. That is the deathless for those who understand.

1291.

1291.

Ñāṇādayo upaklesā, ñeyyā vuttanayenidha;

Ete dasa upaklesā, vajjanīyāva yoginā.

The imperfections beginning with knowledge are to be understood here in the manner described. These ten imperfections are certainly to be avoided by the yogi.

1292.

1292.

Etthobhāsādayo dhammā,

Upaklesassa vatthuto;

Upaklesāti niddiṭṭhā,

Upaklesanikanti tu.

Here, the states beginning with illumination are designated as 'imperfections' because they are the ground for them. The actual imperfection, however, is the delight in them.

1293.

1293.

Taṃ [M 0.0166] tamāvajjamānassa, bhāvanā parihāyati;

Asatte sattasaññī ca, hoti appassuto naro.

For one who adverts to these things, his meditation practice declines; and perceiving a self in what is not a self, the person becomes one of little learning.

1294.

1294.

Sabbobhāsādayo [P 0.0122] dhamme, na maggoti vicārayaṃ;

Maggo vipassanāñāṇaṃ, iccevaṃ pana paṇḍito.

The wise person, however, discriminates thus: 'All these states beginning with illumination are not the path. The path is the knowledge of insight itself.'

1295.

1295.

Vavatthapeti maggañca, amaggañceva cetasā;

Tassa cevaṃ ayaṃ maggo, nāyaṃ maggoti yogino.

With his mind he defines the path and the not-path. For that yogi, the thought arises: 'This is the path; this is not the path.'

1296.

1296.

Maggāmaggañca viññāya, ṭhitañāṇamidaṃ pana;

Maggāmaggesuñāṇanti, bhūriñāṇena desitaṃ.

Having known the path and the not-path, this established knowledge is taught by the one of vast wisdom as 'the knowledge of the path and not-path.'

1297.

1297.

Maggāmaggañāṇadassanesu [V 0.0161] kovidā,

Sārāsāravedino samāhitāhitā;

Maggāmaggañāṇadassananti taṃ idaṃ,

Buddhā buddhasāvakā vadanti vādino.

Skilled in the knowledge and vision of the path and not-path, knowing the essential from the unessential, composed and discerning of the beneficial and the harmful, the Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddhas, the great expounders, call this 'the knowledge and vision of the path and not-path'.

Iti abhidhammāvatāre maggāmaggañāṇadassanavisuddhiniddeso

Thus in the Abhidhammāvatāra ends the exposition of the purification by knowledge and vision of the path and not-path.

Nāma vīsatimo paricchedo.

The Twentieth Chapter.

21. Ekavīsatimo paricchedo

21. The Twenty-first Chapter.

Paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhiniddeso

Exposition of the Purification by Knowledge and Vision of the Way of Practice

1298.

1298.

Aṭṭhañāṇavaseneva[P 0.0123], sikhāpakkā vipassanā;

Navamaṃ paṭipadāñāṇa-dassananti pavuccati.

By the power of the eight knowledges, insight reaches its peak; the ninth is called the knowledge and vision of the way of practice.

1299.

1299.

Aṭṭha ñāṇāni nāmettha, veditabbāni viññunā;

Upaklesavinimuttaṃ, ñāṇaṃ suvisadaṃ pana.

Here, eight knowledges are to be understood by the wise; but the knowledge freed from the imperfections is exceedingly clear.

1300.

1300.

Udayabbaye ca bhaṅge ca, bhaye ādīnave tathā;

Nibbidāpassanāñāṇaṃ, ñāṇaṃ muccitukamyatā.

The knowledges of arising and passing away, of dissolution, of fearfulness, and of danger; the knowledge of disenchantment, and the knowledge of desire for deliverance.

1301.

1301.

Paṭisaṅkhā ca saṅkhāre, upekkhāñāṇamaṭṭhamaṃ;

Imāni aṭṭha ñāṇāni, navamaṃ saccānulomakaṃ.

Knowledge of reflection, and knowledge of equanimity towards formations as the eighth. These are the eight knowledges; the ninth is conformity with the truths.

1302.

1302.

Saccānulomañāṇanti[M 0.0167], anulomaṃ pavuccati;

Taṃ sampādetukāmena, yogāvacarabhikkhunā.

Knowledge conforming to the truths, which is called 'conformity', is to be accomplished by the bhikkhu, the practitioner of meditation, who wishes to attain it.

1303.

1303.

Udayabbayañāṇaṃ taṃ, ādiṃ katvā panaṭṭhasu;

Etesu pana ñāṇesu, yogo karaṇiyo pana.

Beginning with the knowledge of arising and passing away, practice should be undertaken in these eight knowledges.

1304.

1304.

Yathānukkamato [V 0.0162] tassa, tesu ñāṇesu aṭṭhasu;

Aniccādivaseneva, yogaṃ katvā ṭhitassa hi.

For one who abides having undertaken the practice in those eight knowledges in their proper sequence, by way of impermanence, etc.,

1305.

1305.

Aniccaṃ dukkhamanattāti, saṅkhāre anupassato;

Aṭṭhannaṃ pana ñāṇānaṃ, vasena pana yogino.

contemplating formations as impermanent, suffering, and non-self, for that yogi, by the power of the eight knowledges,

1306.

1306.

Vipassanā sikhāpattā, hoti vuṭṭhānagāminī;

Saccānulomañāṇanti, ayameva pavuccati.

insight reaches its peak and becomes conducive to emergence. This itself is called knowledge conforming to the truths.

1307.

1307.

Saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇaṃ taṃ, āsevantassa yogino;

Idāni tassa maggo ca, samuppajjissatīti hi.

For the yogi who cultivates that knowledge of equanimity towards formations, now indeed the path will arise for him.

1308.

1308.

Saṅkhārupekkhā saṅkhāre, aniccā dukkhāti vā tathā;

Sammasitvā bhavaṅgaṃ tu, puna votarateva sā.

Having comprehended formations as impermanent or suffering, the knowledge of equanimity towards formations then descends into the life-continuum.

1309.

1309.

Bhavaṅgānantaraṃ saṅkhāru-pekkhāgatanayena tu;

Aniccādivaseneva, saṅkhāre pana gocaraṃ.

Immediately after the life-continuum, in the same way as the knowledge of equanimity towards formations, taking formations as its object by way of impermanence, etc.,

1310.

1310.

Kurumānaṃ manodvāre, jāyatāvajjanaṃ tato;

Bhavaṅgāvaṭṭanaṃ katvā, jātassānantaraṃ pana.

then mind-door adverting arises, arresting the life-continuum. Immediately after that has arisen,

1311.

1311.

Saṅkhāre [P 0.0124] gocaraṃ katvā, paṭhamaṃ javanamānasaṃ;

Uppajjatīti taṃ cittaṃ, parikammanti vuccati.

taking formations as its object, the first impulsion-consciousness arises; that consciousness is called 'preparation'.

1312.

1312.

Tadanantaramevaññaṃ, saṅkhārārammaṇaṃ puna;

Dutiyaṃ javanaṃ hoti, upacāranti taṃ mataṃ.

Immediately after that, a second impulsion occurs, again with formations as its object; that is considered 'access'.

1313.

1313.

Tadanantaraṃ taṃ hoti, tathā saṅkhāragocaraṃ;

Tatiyaṃ javanacittaṃ, anulomanti saññitaṃ.

Immediately after that, the third impulsion-consciousness occurs, likewise with formations as its object; it is designated 'conformity'.

1314.

1314.

Purimānaṃ panaṭṭhannaṃ, ñāṇānaṃ anulomato;

Bodhipakkhiyadhammānaṃ, uddhañca anulomato.

Because it conforms to the preceding eight knowledges below and to the factors of enlightenment above,

1315.

1315.

Teneva [M 0.0168] taṃ hi saccānulomañāṇaṃ pavuccati;

Idaṃ hi pana saccānu-lomañāṇaṃ mahesinā.

for that very reason it is called knowledge conforming to the truths. This knowledge conforming to the truths has been spoken of by the Great Seer

1316.

1316.

“Vuṭṭhānagāminīyā [V 0.0163] hi, pariyosāna”nti bhāsitaṃ;

Ñeyyaṃ sabbapakārena, pariyosānanti gotrabhu.

as 'the culmination of insight conducive to emergence.' 'Culmination' should be understood in every way as change-of-lineage.

1317.

1317.

Itinekehi nāmehi, kittitāyā mahesinā;

Vuṭṭhānagāminī santā, parisuddhā vipassanā.

Thus praised by the Great Seer with these several names is the peaceful, purified insight conducive to emergence.

1318.

1318.

Vuṭṭhātukāmo saṃsāradukkhapaṅkā mahabbhayā;

Kareyya satataṃ tattha, yogaṃ paṇḍitajātiko.

One of wise birth, desiring to emerge from the great and fearful swamp of saṃsāric suffering, should constantly undertake the practice therein.

Iti abhidhammāvatāre paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhiniddeso nāma

Thus in the Abhidhammāvatāra ends the exposition named the Purification by Knowledge and Vision of the Way of Practice.

Ekavīsatimo paricchedo.

The Twenty-first Chapter.

22. Bāvīsatimo paricchedo

22. The Twenty-second Chapter.

Ñāṇadassanavisuddhiniddeso

Exposition of the Purification by Knowledge and Vision

1319.

1319.

Ito [P 0.0125] paraṃ tu bhikkhussa, hoti gotrabhumānasaṃ;

Āvajjaniyaṭhānattā, maggacittassa taṃ pana.

Hereafter, for the bhikkhu, the change-of-lineage consciousness occurs. It is the occasion for adverting to the path-consciousness.

1320.

1320.

Na cappaṭipadāñāṇa-dassanaṃ vā tatheva ca;

Ñāṇadassanasuddhiṃ vā, bhajate na kudācanaṃ.

It is neither the knowledge and vision of the way of practice, nor does it ever partake of the purification by knowledge and vision.

1321.

1321.

Ubhinnamantarā etaṃ, abbohārikameva taṃ;

Vipassanāya sotasmiṃ, patitattā vipassanā.

It stands between the two and is without designation. But because it has fallen into the stream of insight, it is called insight.

1322.

1322.

Pothujjanikagottaṃ vā, abhibhuyya pavattito;

Gottaṃ vuccati nibbānaṃ, tato bhavati gotrabhu.

Because it occurs having overcome the lineage of the worldling, and because Nibbāna is called the noble lineage, it is therefore 'change-of-lineage'.

1323.

1323.

Ñāṇaṃ catūsu maggesu, ñāṇadassanasuddhikaṃ;

Tattha taṃ paṭhamaṃ maggaṃ, sampādetuṃ panicchatā.

The knowledge in the four paths is the purification by knowledge and vision. For one desiring to accomplish the first path among them,

1324.

1324.

Aññaṃ [M 0.0169][V 0.0164] kiñcipi kātabbaṃ, bhikkhunā tena natthi taṃ;

Yañhi tena ca kātabbaṃ, siyā taṃ katameva tu.

there is nothing further to be done by that bhikkhu. For whatever should have been done by him has already been done.

1325.

1325.

Anulomāvasānañhi, sūraṃ tikkhaṃ vipassanaṃ;

Uppādentena taṃ sabbaṃ, katameva ca yoginā.

For by the yogi producing keen and sharp insight at the conclusion of conformity, all that has indeed been done.

1326.

1326.

Tassānulomañāṇassa, ante tu animittakaṃ;

Visaṅkhāraṃ nirodhañca, nibbānaṃ amataṃ padaṃ.

But at the end of that conformity knowledge, the signless, the unconditioned, cessation, Nibbāna, the deathless state,

1327.

1327.

Gocaraṃ kurumānaṃ taṃ, nibbānārammaṇe pana;

Paṭhamāvajjanañceva, paṭhamābhogatāpi ca.

is taken as its object. With Nibbāna as its object, it is the first adverting and the first turning towards it.

1328.

1328.

Maggassānantarādīhi, paccayehi panacchahi;

Tassa paccayabhāvañca, sādhayantaṃ tato pana.

And then, accomplishing its function as a condition for the path by the six conditions beginning with proximity,

1329.

1329.

Vipassanāya muddhañhi, sikhāpattāya tāya taṃ;

Uppajjati anāvattaṃ-rammaṇaṃ tassa gotrabhu.

for him that change-of-lineage consciousness arises as the crown of insight that has reached its peak, not reverting to its previous object.

1330.

1330.

Ekenāvajjaneneva, ekissāyeva vīthiyā;

Nānārammaṇatā cānu-lomagotrabhucetasaṃ.

Within a single cognitive process with a single adverting, there is a difference of object for the conformity and change-of-lineage consciousnesses.

1331.

1331.

Ṭhatvā [P 0.0126] āvajjanaṭṭhāne, tamanāvajjanampi ca;

Maggassa pana taṃ saññaṃ, datvā viya nirujjhati.

Standing in the place of adverting, though not adverting to it, it ceases as if giving a signal to the path.

1332.

1332.

Maggopi tena taṃ dinnaṃ, amuñcitvāva sañhitaṃ;

Taṃ ñāṇamanubandhanto, jāyate tadanantaraṃ.

The path, too, arises immediately after, following upon that knowledge and not abandoning the signal given by it.

1333.

1333.

Kadācipi anibbiddhapubbaṃ maggo panesa hi;

Lobhaṃ dosañca mohañca, viddhaṃsantova jāyati.

For this path, which has never before been penetrated, arises while destroying greed, hatred, and delusion.

1334.

1334.

Na kevalamayaṃ maggo, dosanāsanameva ca;

Karoti atha khopāyadvārānipi pidheti ca.

This path not only brings about the destruction of defilements, but it also closes the doors to the planes of misery.

1335.

1335.

Anāmataggasaṃsāravaṭṭadukkhamahodadhiṃ;

Apāramatighorañca, soseti ca asesato.

It dries up without remainder the boundless and most terrible great ocean of suffering in the round of saṃsāra, which is without discoverable beginning.

1336.

1336.

Micchāmaggaṃ [M 0.0170][V 0.0165] panaṭṭhaṅgaṃ, jāyamāno ca ujjhati;

Sabbaverabhayānettha, niccaṃ vūpasameti ca.

Arising, it abandons the wrong eightfold path, and it ever allays all enmity and fear.

1337.

1337.

Buddhassorasaputtattaṃ, upaneti nayaṃ pana;

Ānisaṃse anekepi, pavattayati yogino.

This guide leads one to the state of being a true-born son of the Buddha and produces numerous benefits for the yogi.

1338.

1338.

Dāyakenānisaṃsānaṃ, anekesamanena ca;

Ādimaggena saṃyuttaṃ, ñāṇanti ñāṇadassanaṃ.

The knowledge associated with the first path, this giver of numerous benefits, is the knowledge and vision.

Paṭhamamaggañāṇaṃ.

The Knowledge of the First Path.

1339.

1339.

Tassevānantaraṃ tassa, vipākā dvepi tīṇi vā;

Phalacittāni jāyante, na jāyante tato paraṃ.

Immediately after it, as its result, two or three fruition-consciousnesses arise; no more than that arise.

1340.

1340.

Keci ekañca dve tīṇi, cattārīti vadanti tu;

Na panetaṃ gahetabbaṃ, ajānitvā vadanti te.

Some say one, two, three, or four; but this should not be accepted, for they speak without knowing.

1341.

1341.

Ekassāsevanaṃ natthi, tasmā dve anulomakā;

Tehi āsevanaṃ laddhā, tatiyaṃ hoti gotrabhu.

There is no repetition of a single moment; therefore there are two conformity moments. Having gained repetition through them, the third is change-of-lineage.

1342.

1342.

Catutthaṃ maggacittaṃ tu,

Tasmā tīṇi phalāni hi;

Anulomā tayo honti,

Catutthaṃ hoti gotrabhu.

When the path-consciousness is the fourth, there are three fruitions. When there are three conformity moments, the fourth is change-of-lineage.

1343.

1343.

Pañcamaṃ maggacittañca, phalāni dve tato pana;

Sattacittaparamāva, ekāvajjanavīthi hi.

And when the path-consciousness is the fifth, there are two fruitions; for a cognitive process with a single adverting has a maximum of seven javana-consciousnesses.

1344.

1344.

Ettāvatā paneso hi, sotāpannoti vuccati;

Phalassa pariyosāne, bhavaṅgottaraṇaṃ siyā.

By this much, indeed, he is called a stream-enterer. At the end of the fruition, there is a descent into the life-continuum.

1345.

1345.

Tato bhavaṅgaṃ chinditvā, maggapekkhanahetukaṃ;

Uppajjati manodvāre, āvajjanamano pana.

Then, having arrested the life-continuum, the mind-door adverting consciousness arises for the purpose of reviewing the path.

1346.

1346.

Tasmiṃ [M 0.0171][V 0.0166] niruddhe maggassa, paccavekkhaṇasaññitā;

Javanāni hi jāyante, satteva paṭipāṭiyā.

When that has ceased, seven impulsions designated 'reviewing of the path' arise in sequence.

1347.

1347.

Eseva ca nayo ñeyyo, phalādīnampi pekkhane;

Paccavekkhaṇañāṇāni, bhavantekūnavīsati.

This same method should be understood also in reviewing the fruition and the others. The reviewing knowledges are nineteen in all.

1348.

1348.

Maggo [P 0.0127] phalaṃ pahīnā ca, kilesā avasiṭṭhakā;

Nibbānañceti pañcete, paccavekkhaṇabhūmiyo.

The path, the fruition, the abandoned defilements, the remaining defilements, and Nibbāna—these five are the grounds for reviewing.

1349.

1349.

Evaṃ so paccavekkhitvā, sotāpannopapattiyā;

Yogamārabhate dhīro, dutiyāya ca bhūmiyā.

The wise stream-enterer, having reviewed thus, undertakes the practice for the attainment of the second stage.

1350.

1350.

Khandhapañcakasaṅkhātaṃ, taṃ saṅkhāragataṃ puna;

Aniccaṃ dukkhamanattāti, ñāṇena parimajjati.

Again he comprehends with knowledge those formations comprised in the five aggregates as impermanent, suffering, and non-self.

1351.

1351.

Tato vipassanāvīthi-mogāhati ca tāvade;

Tassevaṃ paṭipannassa, heṭṭhā vuttanayena tu.

Then he enters upon the cognitive process of insight. For one who has thus entered the practice, the method is as stated above.

1352.

1352.

Tato saṅkhārupekkhāya, avasāne tatheva ca;

Ekāvajjanavārasmiṃ, gotrabhussa anantaraṃ.

Then, at the end of equanimity towards formations, just as before, in the single adverting turn, after the change-of-lineage consciousness,

1353.

1353.

Byāpādakāmarāgānaṃ, tanubhāvaṃ tu sādhayaṃ;

Sakadāgāmimaggoyaṃ, jāyate dutiyo pana.

this second path, the path of the once-returner, arises, accomplishing the attenuation of sensual lust and ill will.

Dutiyamaggañāṇaṃ.

The Knowledge of the Second Path.

1354.

1354.

Imassāpi ca ñāṇassa, heṭṭhā vuttanayenidha;

Phalacittāni ñeyyāni, viññunā dvepi tīṇi vā.

For this knowledge too, the wise should understand here, according to the method stated before, that there are two or three fruition-consciousnesses.

1355.

1355.

Ettāvatā paneso hi, sakadāgāmi nāmayaṃ;

Sakideva imaṃ lokaṃ, āgantvāntakaro bhave.

By this much, indeed, he is named a once-returner. Having come to this world only once more, he will make an end of suffering.

1356.

1356.

Heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva, pañcadhā paccavekkhaṇaṃ;

Evaṃ so paccavekkhitvā, sakadāgāmipattiyā.

The fivefold reviewing is just as stated before. Having reviewed thus, the once-returner...

1357.

1357.

Yogamārabhate [M 0.0172][V 0.0167] dhīro, tatiyāya ca bhūmiyā;

Byāpādakāmarāgānaṃ, pahānāya ca paṇḍito.

...the steadfast and wise one, undertakes the practice for the third stage and for the abandonment of sensual lust and ill will.

1358.

1358.

Khandhapañcakasaṅkhātaṃ, taṃ saṅkhāragataṃ pana;

Aniccaṃ dukkhamanattāti, ñāṇena parimajjati.

Again he comprehends with knowledge those formations comprised in the five aggregates as impermanent, suffering, and non-self.

1359.

1359.

Tato vipassanāvīthi-mogāhati ca tāvade;

Tassevaṃ paṭipannassa, heṭṭhā vuttanayena tu.

Then he enters upon the cognitive process of insight to that extent; and for one practicing thus, it is according to the method stated before.

1360.

1360.

Tato saṅkhārupekkhāya, avasāne tatheva ca;

Ekāvajjanavīthimhi, gotrabhussa anantaraṃ.

Then, at the end of equanimity towards formations, just as before, in the single adverting process, after the change-of-lineage consciousness,

1361.

1361.

Byāpādakāmarāgānaṃ, mūlaghātaṃ tu sādhayaṃ;

Tassānāgāmimaggoyaṃ, jāyate tatiyo pana.

this third path, the path of the non-returner, arises for him, accomplishing the eradication of the root of sensual lust and ill will.

Tatiyamaggañāṇaṃ.

The Knowledge of the Third Path.

1362.

1362.

Imassāpi ca ñāṇassa, heṭṭhā vuttanayenidha;

Pavatti phalacittānaṃ, veditabbā vibhāvinā.

For this knowledge too, the occurrence of the fruition-consciousnesses should be known here by the discerning one according to the method stated before.

1363.

1363.

Ettāvatā panesopi, hotināgāmi nāmayaṃ;

Tattheva parinibbāyī, anāvattisabhāvato.

By this much, he is named a non-returner. He attains final Nibbāna right there, because of his nature of non-returning.

1364.

1364.

Heṭṭhā [P 0.0128] vuttanayeneva, pañcadhā paccavekkhaṇaṃ;

Evaṃ so paccavekkhitvā, anāgāmiriyasāvako.

The fivefold reviewing is just as stated before. Having reviewed thus, the non-returner noble disciple...

1365.

1365.

Yogamārabhate dhīro, catutthāya ca bhūmiyā;

Pattiyārūparāgādi-pahānāya ca paṇḍito.

...the steadfast and wise one, undertakes the practice for the attainment of the fourth stage and for the abandoning of lust for form and so on.

1366.

1366.

Tatheva saṅkhāragataṃ, aniccādivasena so;

Parivattati ñāṇena, tatheva parimajjati.

In the same way, he reviews with wisdom conditioned phenomena by way of impermanence and so on; just so, he comprehends it.

1367.

1367.

Tato vipassanāvīthi-mogāhati ca tāvade;

Tassevaṃ paṭipannassa, heṭṭhā vuttanayena tu.

Then he enters upon the cognitive process of insight to that extent; and for one practicing thus, it is according to the method stated before.

1368.

1368.

Tato [M 0.0173][V 0.0168] saṅkhārupekkhāya, avasāne tatheva ca;

Ekāvajjanavārasmiṃ, gotrabhussa anantaraṃ.

Then, at the conclusion of equanimity towards formations, and likewise in the single adverting turn, immediately after the change-of-lineage consciousness,

1369.

1369.

Tassārahattamaggoyaṃ,

Jāyate tu tato paraṃ;

Rūparāgādidosānaṃ,

Viddhaṃsāya karo pana.

For him, this path to Arahantship arises immediately after that, and it brings about the destruction of the corruptions such as lust for form.

Catutthamaggañāṇaṃ.

The Knowledge of the Fourth Path.

1370.

1370.

Imassāpi ca ñāṇassa, heṭṭhā vuttanayenidha;

Pavatti phalacittānaṃ, veditabbā vibhāvinā.

For this knowledge too, the discerning one should understand the occurrence of the fruition-consciousnesses in accordance with the method stated here before.

1371.

1371.

Ettāvatā paneso hi,

Arahā nāma aṭṭhamo;

Ariyo puggalo hoti,

Mahākhīṇāsavo ayaṃ.

By this much, he is indeed the eighth noble person, called an Arahant; this one is the great one whose taints are destroyed.

1372.

1372.

Anuppattasadattho ca,

Khīṇasaṃyojano muni;

Sadevakassa lokassa,

Dakkhiṇeyyo anuttaro.

He has attained his own true benefit, the sage whose fetters are destroyed; in the world with its gods, he is the unsurpassed one worthy of offerings.

1373.

1373.

Ettāvatā catassopi, ñāṇadassanasuddhiyo;

Hitatthāya ca bhikkhūnaṃ, saṅkhepeneva dassitā.

Thus far, the four purifications of knowledge and vision have been shown in brief for the welfare of the bhikkhus.

1374.

1374.

Saddhena sammā pana bhāvanīyā,

Ariyāya paññāya ca bhāvanāya;

Visuddhikāmena tapodhanena,

Bhavakkhayaṃ patthayatā budhena.

With faith, indeed, they should be rightly cultivated, with noble wisdom and with development; by one who desires purity, rich in austerity, by the wise one who aspires to the destruction of becoming.

Iti abhidhammāvatāre ñāṇadassanavisuddhiniddeso nāma

Thus in the Abhidhammāvatāra ends the exposition on the Purification of Knowledge and Vision.

Bāvīsatimo paricchedo.

The Twenty-Second Chapter.

23. Tevīsatimo paricchedo

23. The Twenty-Third Chapter.

Kilesappahānakathā

The Treatise on the Abandonment of Defilements.

1375.

1375.

Etesu [M 0.0174][P 0.0129][V 0.0169] yena ye dhammā, pahātabbā bhavanti hi;

Tesaṃ dāni karissāmi, pakāsanamito paraṃ.

Hereafter I shall now set forth an explanation of which states are to be abandoned by which of these paths.

Imesu pana catūsu maggañāṇesu ye dhammā yena ñāṇena pahātabbā, tesaṃ pahānamevaṃ veditabbaṃ. Etāni hi yathāyogaṃ saṃyojanakilesamicchattalokadhammamacchariyavipallāsaganthāgatiāsava- oghayoganīvaraṇaparāmāsaupādānānusayamalaakusalakammapatha- akusalacittuppādasaṅkhātānaṃ pahānakarāni.

Now, among these four path-knowledges, the abandonment of those states that are to be abandoned by each knowledge should be understood thus. For these, as is appropriate, bring about the abandonment of what are designated as: fetters, defilements, wrongness, worldly conditions, stinginess, perversions, knots, wrong courses, taints, floods, yokes, hindrances, misapprehensions, clinging, underlying tendencies, stains, unwholesome courses of action, and the arising of unwholesome consciousness.

Tattha saṃyojanānīti dasa saṃyojanāni. Seyyathidaṃ – rūparāgārūparāgamānauddhaccāvijjāti ime pañca uddhaṃbhāgiyasaṃyojanāni nāma. Sakkāyadiṭṭhi vicikicchā sīlabbataparāmāso kāmarāgo paṭighoti ime pañca adhobhāgiyasaṃyojanāni nāma.

Therein, fetters are the ten fetters. That is: lust for form, lust for the formless, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance—these are called the five higher fetters. Identity view, doubt, clinging to precepts and vows, sensual lust, and ill will—these are called the five lower fetters.

Kilesāti dasa kilesā. Seyyathidaṃ – lobho doso moho māno diṭṭhi vicikicchā thinaṃ uddhaccaṃ ahirikaṃ anottappanti.

The defilements are ten. That is: greed, hatred, delusion, conceit, wrong view, doubt, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness, and lack of fear of wrongdoing.

Micchattāti dasa micchattā. Seyyathidaṃ – micchādiṭṭhi micchāsaṅkappo micchāvācā micchākammanto micchāājīvo micchāvāyāmo micchāsati micchāsamādhi micchāñāṇaṃ micchāvimuttīti.

Wrongness is the ten kinds of wrongness. That is: wrong view, wrong thought, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration, wrong knowledge, and wrong liberation.

Lokadhammāti aṭṭha lokadhammā lābho alābho yaso ayaso nindā pasaṃsā sukhaṃ dukkhanti. Idha pana kāraṇūpacārena [M 0.0175] lābhādivatthukassa anunayassa, alābhādivatthukassa paṭighassa cetaṃ lokadhammagahaṇena gahaṇaṃ katanti veditabbaṃ.

The worldly conditions are eight: gain and loss, fame and disgrace, blame and praise, pleasure and pain. Here, however, it should be understood that by a metaphorical usage, the term 'worldly conditions' is taken to refer to the attraction based on things like gain, and to the aversion based on things like loss.

Macchariyānīti pañca macchariyāni āvāsamacchariyaṃ kulamacchariyaṃ lābhamacchariyaṃ dhammamacchariyaṃ [V 0.0170] vaṇṇamacchariyanti. Imāni āvāsādīsu aññesaṃ sādhāraṇabhāvaṃ asahanākārena pavattāni macchariyāni.

Stinginess is of five kinds: stinginess regarding dwellings, stinginess regarding families, stinginess regarding gains, stinginess regarding the Dhamma, and stinginess regarding praise. These forms of stinginess arise from an inability to tolerate others sharing in one's dwellings and the like.

Vipallāsāti aniccadukkhaanattaasubhesuyeva [P 0.0130] vatthūsu “niccaṃ sukhaṃ attā subha”nti evaṃ pavattā saññāvipallāso cittavipallāso diṭṭhivipallāsoti ime tayo vipallāsā.

Perversions are the three perversions of perception, consciousness, and view that occur with respect to things that are impermanent, suffering, not-self, and foul, in that one perceives them as "permanent, pleasant, self, and beautiful."

Ganthāti cattāro ganthā abhijjhākāyagantho, byāpādo, sīlabbataparāmāso, idaṃsaccābhiniveso kāyaganthoti.

The knots are the four bodily knots: covetousness, ill will, clinging to precepts and vows, and adherence to the view 'this alone is the truth'.

Agatīti chandadosamohabhayāni. Āsavāti cattāro āsavā – kāmarāgabhavarāgamicchādiṭṭhiavijjāsavoti. Oghayogānītipi tesamevādhivacanaṃ. Nīvaraṇānīti kāmacchandādayo. Parāmāsoti micchādiṭṭhiyā adhivacanaṃ.

The wrong courses are desire, hatred, delusion, and fear. The taints are four: the taint of sensual pleasure, the taint of existence, the taint of views, and the taint of ignorance. 'Floods' and 'yokes' are also designations for these. The hindrances are sensual desire and so on. 'Misapprehension' is a designation for wrong view.

Upādānāti cattāri upādānāni kāmupādānādīnīti. Anusayāti satta anusayā kāmarāgānusayo paṭighamānadiṭṭhivicikicchābhavarāgāvijjānusayoti. Malāti tayo malā – lobho doso mohoti.

The clingings are the four kinds of clinging: clinging to sensual pleasures, clinging to views, clinging to precepts and vows, and clinging to a doctrine of self. The underlying tendencies are seven: the underlying tendency of sensual desire, aversion, conceit, views, doubt, craving for existence, and ignorance. The stains are three: greed, hatred, and delusion.

Akusalakammapathāti dasa akusalakammapathā. Seyyathidaṃ – pāṇātipāto adinnādānaṃ kāmesumicchācāro musāvādo pisuṇavācā pharusavācā samphappalāpo abhijjhā byāpādo micchādiṭṭhīti dasa.

The unwholesome courses of action are ten. Namely: destroying life, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, idle chatter, covetousness, ill will, and wrong view.

Akusalacittuppādāti [M 0.0176] lobhamūlāni aṭṭha, dosamūlāni dve, mohamūlāni dveti ime dvādasāti.

The arisings of unwholesome consciousness are these twelve: eight rooted in greed, two rooted in hatred, and two rooted in delusion.

Etesaṃ saṃyojanādīnaṃ etāni yathāsambhavaṃ pahānakarāni. Kathaṃ? Saṃyojanesu tāva sakkāyadiṭṭhivicikicchāsīlabbataparāmāsā apāyagamanīyā kāmarāgapaṭighāti ete paṭhamamaggañāṇavajjhā, sesā kāmarāgapaṭighā oḷārikā dutiyamaggañāṇavajjhā, sukhumā tatiyamaggañāṇavajjhā, rūparāgādayo pañcapi catutthamaggañāṇavajjhā eva.

These path-knowledges are the means of abandoning these things, the fetters and so on, as is appropriate. How? Regarding the fetters: identity view, doubt, clinging to precepts and vows, and those kinds of sensual desire and ill will that lead to the plane of misery are to be abandoned by the knowledge of the first path. The remaining gross sensual desire and ill will are to be abandoned by the knowledge of the second path. The subtle forms are to be abandoned by the knowledge of the third path. And the five beginning with lust for form are all to be abandoned by the knowledge of the fourth path.

Kilesesu [V 0.0171] diṭṭhivicikicchā paṭhamamaggañāṇavajjhā, doso tatiyamaggañāṇavajjho, lobhamohamānathinauddhaccaahirikānottappāni catutthamaggañāṇavajjhāni.

Regarding the defilements: wrong view and doubt are to be abandoned by the knowledge of the first path; hatred is to be abandoned by the knowledge of the third path; greed, delusion, conceit, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness, and lack of fear of wrongdoing are to be abandoned by the knowledge of the fourth path.

Micchattesu micchādiṭṭhi musāvādo micchākammanto micchāājīvoti ime paṭhamamaggañāṇavajjhā, micchāsaṅkappo pisuṇavācā pharusavācāti ime tatiyamaggañāṇavajjhā, cetanāyeva cettha micchāvācāti veditabbā, samphappalāpamicchāvāyāmasatisamādhivimuttiñāṇāni catutthamaggañāṇavajjhāni.

Regarding the wrongnesses: wrong view, false speech, wrong action, and wrong livelihood are to be abandoned by the knowledge of the first path. Wrong thought, divisive speech, and harsh speech are to be abandoned by the knowledge of the third path; here, wrong speech should be understood as the volition itself. Idle chatter, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration, wrong liberation, and wrong knowledge are to be abandoned by the knowledge of the fourth path.

Lokadhammesu paṭigho tatiyamaggañāṇavajjho, anunayo catutthamaggañāṇavajjho, yase pasaṃsāya ca anunayo catutthamaggañāṇavajjhoti eke.

Regarding the worldly conditions: aversion is to be abandoned by the knowledge of the third path, and attraction is to be abandoned by the knowledge of the fourth path. Some say that attraction to fame and praise is to be abandoned by the knowledge of the fourth path.

Macchariyāni paṭhamamaggañāṇavajjhāni eva.

The kinds of stinginess are to be abandoned by the knowledge of the first path alone.

Vipallāsesu pana anicce niccaṃ, anattani attāti ca saññācittadiṭṭhivipallāsā[P 0.0131], dukkhe sukhaṃ, asubhe subhanti diṭṭhivipallāso cāti ime paṭhamamaggañāṇavajjhā, asubhe subhanti saññācittavipallāsā tatiyamaggañāṇavajjhā, dukkhe sukhanti catutthamaggañāṇavajjhā.

Now, regarding the perversions: the perversions of perception, consciousness, and view that perceive the impermanent as permanent and the not-self as self, and the perversion of view that perceives the painful as pleasant and the foul as beautiful—these are to be abandoned by the knowledge of the first path. The perversions of perception and consciousness that perceive the foul as beautiful are to be abandoned by the knowledge of the third path. The perversions of perception and consciousness that perceive the painful as pleasant are to be abandoned by the knowledge of the fourth path.

Ganthesu sīlabbataparāmāsaidaṃsaccābhinivesakāyaganthā paṭhamamaggañāṇavajjhā, byāpādakāyagantho tatiyamaggañāṇavajjho, abhijjhākāyagantho catutthamaggañāṇavajjhova.

Regarding the knots: the bodily knots of clinging to precepts and vows and of adherence that 'this alone is the truth' are to be abandoned by the knowledge of the first path; the bodily knot of ill will is to be abandoned by the knowledge of the third path; and the bodily knot of covetousness is to be abandoned by the knowledge of the fourth path.

Agatiyo [M 0.0177] paṭhamamaggañāṇavajjhā.

The wrong courses are to be abandoned by the knowledge of the first path.

Āsavesu diṭṭhāsavo paṭhamañāṇavajjho, kāmāsavo tatiyañāṇavajjho, itare dve catutthañāṇavajjhā. Oghayogesupi eseva nayo.

Regarding the taints: the taint of views is to be abandoned by the knowledge of the first path; the taint of sensual pleasure is to be abandoned by the knowledge of the third path; the remaining two are to be abandoned by the knowledge of the fourth path. The same method applies to the floods and yokes.

Nīvaraṇesu vicikicchānīvaraṇaṃ paṭhamañāṇavajjhaṃ, kāmacchando byāpādo kukkuccanti tīṇi tatiyañāṇavajjhāni, thinamiddhauddhaccāni catutthañāṇavajjhāni.

Regarding the hindrances: the hindrance of doubt is to be abandoned by the knowledge of the first path. Sensual desire, ill will, and remorse are to be abandoned by the knowledge of the third path. Sloth and torpor, and restlessness are to be abandoned by the knowledge of the fourth path.

Parāmāso [V 0.0172] paṭhamañāṇavajjho.

Misapprehension is to be abandoned by the knowledge of the first path.

Upādānesu sabbesampi lokiyadhammānaṃ vatthukāmavasena “kāmā”ti āgatattā rūpārūpesu rāgopi kāmupādāne patati, tasmā tañca kāmupādānaṃ catutthañāṇavajjhaṃ, sesāni paṭhamañāṇavajjhāni.

Regarding the clingings: since all worldly things are called 'sensual pleasures' in the sense of being objects of desire, lust for the form and formless realms also falls under clinging to sensual pleasures. Therefore, that clinging to sensual pleasures is to be abandoned by the fourth knowledge, while the remaining kinds of clinging are to be abandoned by the first knowledge.

Anusayesu diṭṭhivicikicchānusayā paṭhamañāṇavajjhā, kāmarāgapaṭighānusayā tatiyañāṇavajjhā, mānabhavarāgāvijjānusayā catutthañāṇavajjhā.

Regarding the underlying tendencies: the underlying tendencies of views and doubt are to be abandoned by the knowledge of the first path. The underlying tendencies of sensual desire and aversion are to be abandoned by the knowledge of the third path. The underlying tendencies of conceit, craving for existence, and ignorance are to be abandoned by the knowledge of the fourth path.

Malesu dosamalaṃ tatiyañāṇavajjhaṃ, itarāni catutthañāṇavajjhāneva.

Regarding the stains: the stain of hatred is to be abandoned by the knowledge of the third path, while the others are to be abandoned only by the knowledge of the fourth path.

Akusalakammapathesu pāṇātipāto adinnādānaṃ micchācāro musāvādo micchādiṭṭhīti ime paṭhamañāṇavajjhā, pisuṇavācā pharusavācā byāpādoti tatiyañāṇavajjhā, samphappalāpo abhijjhā catutthañāṇavajjhāva.

Regarding the unwholesome courses of action: destroying life, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and wrong view are to be abandoned by the knowledge of the first path. Divisive speech, harsh speech, and ill will are to be abandoned by the knowledge of the third path. Idle chatter and covetousness are to be abandoned by the knowledge of the fourth path.

Akusalacittuppādesu cattāro diṭṭhigatacittuppādā, vicikicchāsampayutto cāti pañca paṭhamañāṇavajjhā, dve paṭighasampayuttā tatiyañāṇavajjhā, sesā catutthañāṇavajjhāti.

Regarding the arisings of unwholesome consciousness: the five consisting of the four arisings of consciousness accompanied by wrong view and the one associated with doubt are to be abandoned by the knowledge of the first path. The two associated with aversion are to be abandoned by the knowledge of the third path. The remaining ones are to be abandoned by the knowledge of the fourth path.

Yañca yena vajjhaṃ, taṃ tena pahātabbaṃ nāma. Tena vuttaṃ “etesaṃ saṃyojanādīnaṃ dhammānaṃ etāni yathāyogaṃ pahānakarānī”ti.

Whatever is to be abandoned by a certain means, that is what is meant by 'to be abandoned' by it. Therefore it was said: 'These are the means for abandoning these states, the fetters and so on, as is appropriate.'

1376.

1376.

Etesu [M 0.0178] ñāṇesu ca yena yena,

Yo yo hi dhammo samupeti ghātaṃ;

So so asesena ca tena tena,

Sandassito sādhu mayā panevaṃ.

Thus it has been well shown by me how, by each of these knowledges, each respective state is brought to complete destruction.

Kilesapahānakkamakathāyaṃ.

The Treatise on the Method of Abandoning Defilements.

1377.

1377.

Pariññādīni [P 0.0132][V 0.0173] kiccāni, yāni vuttāni satthunā;

Saccābhisamaye tāni, pavakkhāmi ito paraṃ.

The functions beginning with full understanding, which were taught by the Teacher—those functions at the time of the comprehension of the truths, I shall explain hereafter.

1378.

1378.

Ekekassa panetesu,

Ñāṇassekakkhaṇe siyā;

Pariññā ca pahānañca,

Sacchikiriyā ca bhāvanā.

Yet for each of these, in a single moment of knowledge, there can be: full understanding, abandoning, realization, and development.

1379.

1379.

Pariññādīni etāni, kiccānekakkhaṇe pana;

Yathāsabhāvato tāni, jānitabbāni viññunā.

These—full understanding and so on—are functions that occur over many moments; they should be known by the wise according to their intrinsic nature.

1380.

1380.

Padīpo hi yathā loke, apubbācarimaṃ idha;

Cattāri pana kiccāni, karotekakkhaṇe pana.

For just as a lamp in the world, simultaneously, performs four functions in a single moment.

1381.

1381.

Ālokañca vidaṃseti, nāseti timirampi ca;

Pariyādiyati telañca, vaṭṭiṃ jhāpeti ekato.

It reveals light and dispels darkness; it consumes the oil and burns up the wick all at once.

1382.

1382.

Evaṃ taṃ maggañāṇampi, apubbācarimaṃ pana;

Cattāripi ca kiccāni, karotekakkhaṇe pana.

So too that path-knowledge, simultaneously, performs all four functions in a single moment.

1383.

1383.

Pariññābhisamayeneva, dukkhaṃ abhisameti so;

Pahānābhisamayeneva, tathā samudayampi ca.

By the breakthrough of full understanding, one comprehends suffering; by the breakthrough of abandoning, so too the origin.

1384.

1384.

Bhāvanāvidhināyeva, maggaṃ abhisameti taṃ;

Ārammaṇakriyāyeva, nirodhaṃ sacchikaroti so.

By the method of development itself, one comprehends that path; by the act of taking it as object, one realizes cessation.

Vuttampi cetaṃ “maggasamaṅgissa ñāṇaṃ dukkhepetaṃ ñāṇaṃ, dukkhasamudayepetaṃ ñāṇaṃ, dukkhanirodhepetaṃ ñāṇaṃ, dukkhanirodhagāminiyā [M 0.0179] paṭipadāyapetaṃ ñāṇa”nti. Tattha yathā padīpo vaṭṭiṃ jhāpeti, evaṃ maggañāṇaṃ dukkhaṃ parijānāti. Yathā andhakāraṃ nāseti, evaṃ samudayaṃ pajahati. Yathā ālokaṃ vidaṃseti, evaṃ sahajātādipaccayatāya sammāsaṅkappādimaggaṃ bhāveti. Yathā telaṃ pariyādiyati, evaṃ kilesapariyādānena nirodhaṃ sacchikarotīti veditabbaṃ.

And this has been said: 'The knowledge of one endowed with the path is knowledge in regard to suffering, knowledge in regard to the origin of suffering, knowledge in regard to the cessation of suffering, and knowledge in regard to the path leading to the cessation of suffering.' Herein, just as a lamp burns up the wick, so path-knowledge fully understands suffering. Just as it dispels darkness, so it abandons the origin. Just as it reveals light, so by way of co-nascence condition and so on, it develops the path beginning with right intention. Just as it consumes the oil, so it realizes cessation through the consuming of the defilements. Thus it should be understood.

1385.

1385.

Uggacchanto yathādicco, apubbācarimaṃ pana;

Cattāri pana kiccāni, karotekakkhaṇe idha.

Just as the rising sun, simultaneously, performs four functions here in a single moment.

1386.

1386.

Obhāseti [V 0.0174] ca rūpāni, nāseti timirampi ca;

Ālokañca vidaṃseti, sītañca paṭihaññati.

It illuminates forms, dispels darkness, reveals light, and wards off cold.

1387.

1387.

Yathā ca mahatī nāvā, apubbācarimaṃ pana;

Cattāri pana kiccāni, karotekakkhaṇe pana.

And just as a great ship, simultaneously, performs four functions in a single moment.

1388.

1388.

Jahatī orimaṃ tīraṃ, sotaṃ chindati sā pana;

Tathā vahati bhaṇḍañca, tīramappeti pārimaṃ.

It leaves the near shore and cuts through the stream; it carries its cargo and reaches the far shore.

1389.

1389.

Nāvāyorimatīrassa, yathā pajahanaṃ pana;

Tatheva maggañāṇassa, dukkhassa parijānanaṃ.

Just as there is the leaving of the near shore by the ship, so there is the full understanding of suffering by the path-knowledge.

1390.

1390.

Yathā [P 0.0133] chindati taṃ sotaṃ, taṇhaṃ jahati taṃ tathā;

Yathā vahati taṃ bhaṇḍaṃ, sahajātādinā pana.

Just as it cuts through the stream, so it abandons craving; just as it carries the cargo, so by way of co-nascence and so on,

1391.

1391.

Tatheva paccayattena, maggaṃ bhāveti nāma so;

Yathā pāraṃ pana evaṃ, nirodhārammaṇaṃ bhave.

by its nature as a condition, it develops the path. And just as the far shore is reached, so cessation becomes its object.

1392.

1392.

Lokuttarena niddiṭṭhā, yā lokuttarabhāvanā;

Sā saṅkhepanayenevaṃ, mayā sādhu pakāsitā.

That supramundane development which was pointed out by the supramundane—that has thus been well explained by me in brief.

1393.

1393.

Ko [M 0.0180] hi nāma naro loke,

Lokuttarasukhāvahaṃ;

Bhāvanaṃ pana paññāya,

Na ca bhāveyya paṇḍito.

What wise person in the world, indeed, would not cultivate with wisdom the development that brings supramundane happiness?

1394.

1394.

Imaṃ viditvā hitabhāvanaṃ vanaṃ,

Upeti yo ve sukhasaṃhitaṃ hitaṃ;

Vidhūya cittassa anuttamaṃ tamaṃ,

Upeti cāviggahakampadaṃ padaṃ.

Having known this development for one's welfare, one who seeks happiness and benefit goes to the forest; having dispelled the mind's unsurpassed darkness, one reaches the state that is free from grasping and trembling.

Iti abhidhammāvatāre ñāṇadassanavisuddhiniddeso nāma

Thus in the Abhidhammāvatāra ends the chapter named 'The Exposition of the Purification of Knowledge and Vision'.

Tevīsatimo paricchedo.

The Twenty-Third Chapter.

24. Catuvīsatimo paricchedo

24. The Twenty-Fourth Chapter.

Paccayaniddeso

The Exposition of Conditions.

1395.

1395.

Yesaṃ [P 0.0134][V 0.0175] paccayadhammānaṃ, vasā sappaccayā ime;

Dhammā te paccaye cāhaṃ, dassayissāmito paraṃ.

Those conditioning phenomena by whose power these conditioned phenomena exist—those conditions I shall hereafter explain.

Katame paccayāti? Vuccate – hetārammaṇādhipatianantarasamanantarasahajāta- aññamaññanissayūpanissayapurejātapacchājātāsevanakammavipākāhārindriya- jhānamaggasampayuttavippayuttaatthinatthivigatāvigatavasena catuvīsatividhā honti.

What are the conditions? It is said: They are of twenty-four kinds, namely: root condition, object condition, predominance condition, contiguity condition, immediate contiguity condition, co-nascence condition, mutuality condition, support condition, decisive support condition, pre-nascence condition, post-nascence condition, repetition condition, kamma condition, result condition, nutriment condition, faculty condition, jhāna condition, path condition, association condition, dissociation condition, presence condition, absence condition, disappearance condition, and non-disappearance condition.

Tattha hetupaccayoti lobho doso moho alobho adoso amohoti ime cha dhammā hetupaccayā. Ārammaṇapaccayoti sabbalokiyalokuttaraṃ yaṃ yaṃ dhammaṃ ārabbha ye ye dhammā uppajjanti cittacetasikā dhammā, te te dhammā tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānaṃ ārammaṇapaccayena paccayo.

Herein, root condition: greed, hatred, delusion, non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion—these six states are root condition. Object condition: whatever worldly or supramundane phenomena are taken as object, in dependence on which mental and concomitant phenomena arise, those latter phenomena have the former as their condition by way of object condition.

Adhipatipaccayoti [M 0.0181] ettha sahajātādhipatiārammaṇādhipativasena duvidho. Tattha sahajātādhipati chandacittavīriyavīmaṃsāvasena catubbidho, ārammaṇādhipati pana domanassavicikicchuddhaccakiriyābyākatākusalavipāke ca aniṭṭhasammatañca rūpaṃ ṭhapetvā avasesaṃ. Anantarapaccayoti anantaraniruddhā cittacetasikā dhammā. Tathā samanantarapaccayopi.

Predominance condition: this is twofold, as co-nascent predominance and object predominance. Herein, co-nascent predominance is fourfold, by way of desire, consciousness, energy, and investigation. Object predominance, however, applies to the remainder after excluding displeasure, doubt, restlessness, functional-indeterminate states, unwholesome resultants, and material form considered undesirable. Contiguity condition: mind and mental factors that have ceased without an interval. So too is the immediate contiguity condition.

Sahajātapaccayoti cittacetasikā, mahābhūtā ceva hadayavatthu ca. Tathā aññamaññapaccayopi. Nissayapaccayoti vatthurūpāni ceva mahābhūtā, cittacetasikā ca. Upanissayapaccayoti ārammaṇānantarapakatūpanissayavasena tividho. Tattha ārammaṇūpanissayo ārammaṇādhipatiyeva, anantarūpanissayo pana anantarapaccayova, pakatūpanissayo pana kāyikasukhadukkhautubhojanasenāsanapuggalā saddhāsīlasutacāgapaññārāgadosamohādayo [P 0.0135] ca.

Co-nascence condition: mind and mental factors, the great elements, and the heart-base. So too is the mutuality condition. Support condition: base-materiality, the great elements, and mind and mental factors. Decisive support condition: this is threefold, as object decisive support, contiguity decisive support, and natural decisive support. Herein, object decisive support is just object predominance; contiguity decisive support is just contiguity condition; and natural decisive support includes bodily pleasure and pain, climate, food, lodging, persons, faith, morality, learning, generosity, wisdom, lust, hatred, delusion, and so on.

Purejātapaccayoti vatthārammaṇavasena duvidho. Tattha vatthupurejāto nāma vatthurūpāni, ārammaṇapurejāto nāma paccuppannarūpādīneva. Pacchājātapaccayoti cittacetasikā ca. Āsevanapaccayoti ṭhapetvā āvajjanadvayaṃ lokiyakusalākusalakiriyābyākatā dhammāva.

Pre-nascence condition: this is twofold, by way of base and object. Herein, base pre-nascence is base-materiality; object pre-nascence is only present material phenomena and so forth. Post-nascence condition: this is mind and mental factors. Repetition condition: only mundane wholesome, unwholesome, and functional-indeterminate phenomena, excluding the two advertings.

Kammapaccayoti [V 0.0176] sahajātanānakkhaṇikavasena duvidho. Tattha sahajātā lokiyalokuttarā eva, nānakkhaṇikā pana sāsavakusalākusalacetanā, anāsavakusalacetanā anantarameva attano vipākassa paccayo hoti. Vipākapaccayoti vipākacittacetasikā. Āhārapaccayoti kabaḷīkārāhāraphassacetanāviññāṇavasena catubbidho.

Kamma condition: this is twofold, by way of co-nascence and different-moment. Herein, co-nascent kamma is only mundane and supramundane volition. Different-moment kamma, however, is wholesome and unwholesome volition with taints; supramundane wholesome volition is a condition for its own result immediately after. Result condition: this is resultant mind and mental factors. Nutriment condition: this is fourfold, by way of physical food, contact, volition, and consciousness.

Indriyapaccayoti [M 0.0182] rūpasattakamanajīvitasukhadukkhasomanassadomanassaupekkhāsaddhāvīriya- satisamādhipaññāanaññātaññassāmītindriyaaññindriyaaññatāvindriyānīti vīsatindriyāni, tesu itthindriyapurisindriyāni vajjetvā vīsatindriyāni honti. Jhānapaccayoti vitakkavicārapītisukhacittekaggatāvasena pañcavidho. Maggapaccayoti diṭṭhisaṅkappavāyāmasatisamādhivācākammantājīvamicchādiṭṭhivasena navavidho.

Faculty condition: there are twenty-two faculties: the five physical sense faculties, mind faculty, life faculty, the five feeling faculties, the five spiritual faculties, and the three supramundane faculties—the faculty of 'I shall know the unknown,' the faculty of final knowledge, and the faculty of one who has final knowledge. Among these, excluding the femininity and masculinity faculties, there are twenty faculties that act as condition. Jhāna condition: this is fivefold, by way of initial application, sustained application, rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind. Path condition: this is ninefold, by way of the eight path factors beginning with right view, and wrong view.

Sampayuttapaccayoti cittacetasikāva. Vippayuttapaccayoti vatthupurejātāni ceva pacchājātā cittacetasikā ca. Atthipaccayoti jīvitindriyakabaḷīkāraāhāraārammaṇapurejātāni ceva nissayapaccaye vuttadhammāpi ca. Natthipaccayoti anantarapaccayova. Tathā vigatapaccayo ca. Avigatapaccayoti atthipaccayova. Evamime catuvīsati paccayā nāma.

Association condition: only mind and mental factors. Dissociation condition: pre-nascent bases and post-nascent mind and mental factors. Presence condition: the life faculty, physical food, pre-nascent objects, and also the phenomena stated under the support condition. Absence condition: this is just the contiguity condition. So too is the disappearance condition. Non-disappearance condition: this is just the presence condition. Thus, these are the twenty-four conditions by name.

Ettha pana katihākārehi rūpaṃ rūpassa paccayo hotīti? Yathārahaṃ sahajātaaññamaññanissayāhārindriyaatthiavigatavasena sattadhā paccayo hoti.

Herein, in how many ways is materiality a condition for materiality? As is appropriate, it is a condition in seven ways: by way of co-nascence, mutuality, support, nutriment, faculty, presence, and non-disappearance.

Rūpaṃ arūpassa yathārahaṃ ārammaṇādhipatisahajātaaññamaññanissayūpanissayapurejātindriyavippa- yuttaatthiavigatavasena ekādasahi ākārehi paccayo hoti.

Materiality is a condition for immateriality, as is appropriate, in eleven ways: by way of object, predominance, co-nascence, mutuality, support, decisive support, pre-nascence, faculty, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance.

Rūpaṃ rūpārūpassāti natthi.

There is no way for materiality to be a condition for materiality-and-immateriality.

1396.

1396.

Sattadhā rūpaṃ rūpassa, bhavatekādasehi taṃ;

Paccayo nāmadhammassa, missakassa na kiñci tu.

In seven ways materiality is a condition for materiality; in eleven ways it is a condition for mental phenomena; but for the mixed, it is not a condition at all.

Arūpaṃ arūpassa yathārahaṃ hetārammaṇādhipatianantarasamanantarasahajātaaññamaññanissayūpanissayā- sevanakammavipākāhārindriyajhānamaggasampayuttaatthinatthivigatāvigata- vasena [P 0.0136][V 0.0177] ekavīsatidhā paccayo hoti.

Immateriality is a condition for immateriality, as is appropriate, in twenty-one ways: by way of root, object, predominance, contiguity, immediate contiguity, co-nascence, mutuality, support, decisive support, repetition, kamma, result, nutriment, faculty, jhāna, path, association, presence, absence, disappearance, and non-disappearance.

Arūpaṃ [M 0.0183] rūpassa yathārahaṃ hetādhipatisahajātaaññamaññanissayapacchājātakammavipākāhārindriya- jhānamaggavippayuttaatthiavigatavasena pannarasadhā paccayo hoti.

Immateriality is a condition for materiality, as is appropriate, in fifteen ways: by way of root, predominance, co-nascence, mutuality, support, post-nascence, kamma, result, nutriment, faculty, jhāna, path, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance.

Arūpaṃ rūpārūpassa yathārahaṃ hetādhipatisahajātaaññamaññanissayakammavipākāhārindriyajhānamagga- atthiavigatavasena terasadhā paccayo hoti.

Immateriality is a condition for materiality-and-immateriality, as is appropriate, in thirteen ways: by way of root, predominance, co-nascence, mutuality, support, kamma, result, nutriment, faculty, jhāna, path, presence, and non-disappearance.

1397.

1397.

Ekavīsatidhā nāmaṃ, paccayo bhavatattano;

Tipañcahi taṃ rūpassa, ubhinnaṃ terasadhā pana.

In twenty-one ways name is a condition for itself; in fifteen ways for materiality; and in thirteen ways for both.

Rūpārūpaṃ rūpassa yathārahaṃ sahajātanissayaatthiavigatavasena catudhā paccayo hoti.

Materiality-and-immateriality are a condition for materiality, as is appropriate, in four ways: by way of co-nascence, support, presence, and non-disappearance.

Rūpārūpaṃ arūpassa yathārahaṃ sahajātaaññamaññanissayindriyaatthiavigatavasena chadhā paccayo hoti.

Materiality-and-immateriality are a condition for immateriality, as is appropriate, in six ways: by way of co-nascence, mutuality, support, faculty, presence, and non-disappearance.

Rūpārūpaṃ rūpassāti natthi.

There is no way for materiality-and-immateriality to be a condition for materiality-and-immateriality.

1398.

1398.

Ubhopi rūpadhammassa, catudhā honti paccayā;

Chabbidhā nāmadhammassa, missakassa na kiñci tu.

Both are conditions for material phenomena in four ways, and for mental phenomena in six ways; but for the mixed, not at all.

Etesu pana paccayesu kati rūpā, kati arūpā, katimissakāti? Purejātapaccayo eko rūpadhammova, hetuanantarasamanantarapacchājātāsevanakammavipākajhānamaggasampayuttanatthi- vigatānaṃ vasena dvādasa paccayā arūpadhammāva, sesā pana ekādasa paccayā rūpārūpamissakāti veditabbā.

Among these conditions, how many are material, how many are immaterial, and how many are mixed? The pre-nascence condition alone is a material phenomenon. Twelve conditions—root, contiguity, immediate contiguity, post-nascence, repetition, kamma, result, jhāna, path, association, absence, and disappearance—are exclusively immaterial phenomena. The remaining eleven conditions, however, are to be understood as mixed, being both material and immaterial.

Puna kālavasena hetusahajātaaññamaññanissayapurejātapacchājātavipākāhārindriyajhānamagga- sampayuttavippayuttaatthiavigatānaṃ [V 0.0178] vasena pannarasa paccayā paccuppannāva honti. Anantarasamanantarāsevananatthivigatapaccayā atītāva, kammapaccayo atīto vā hoti paccuppanno vā, ārammaṇādhipatiupanissayapaccayā [M 0.0184] pana tikālikā honti kālavinimuttā ca.

Again, with regard to time, fifteen conditions are present only: root, co-nascence, mutuality, support, pre-nascence, post-nascence, result, nutriment, faculty, jhāna, path, association, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance. Five conditions—contiguity, immediate contiguity, repetition, absence, and disappearance—are past only. The kamma condition is either past or present. The conditions of object, predominance, and decisive support, however, can pertain to the three times and can also be timeless.

1399.

1399.

Paccuppannāva hontettha,

Paccayā dasa pañca ca;

Atītā eva pañceko,

Dvekālikova dassito;

Tayo tikālikā ceva,

Vinimuttāpi kālato.

Herein, fifteen conditions

Are present only;

Five are past only, and one is shown

As pertaining to two times;

Three pertain to the three times

And are also free from time.

Sabbe [P 0.0137] panime catuvīsati paccayā yathārahaṃ ārammaṇūpanissayakammaatthipaccayānaṃ vasena catūsu paccayesu saṅgahaṃ gacchantīti veditabbā.

It should be understood that all these twenty-four conditions are included, according to their suitability, in four conditions: object, decisive support, kamma, and presence.

Iti abhidhammāvatāre paccayaniddeso nāma

Thus ends the Exposition of Conditions in the Abhidhammāvatāra.

Catuvīsatimo paricchedo.

The Twenty-Fourth Chapter.

Nigamanakathā

Concluding Verses

1400.

1400.

Abhidhammāvatāroyaṃ, varo paramagambhīro;

Icchatā nipuṇaṃ buddhiṃ, bhikkhunā pana sotabbo.

This Abhidhammāvatāra, excellent and supremely deep, should be studied by a monk who desires subtle wisdom.

1401.

1401.

Sumatimativicārabodhano,

Vimativimohavināsano ayaṃ;

Kumatimatimahātamonāso,

Paṭumatibhāsakaro mato mayā.

This work awakens good understanding and investigation,

It destroys doubt and delusion;

It dispels the great darkness of wrong views,

And is considered by me a light for the keen intellect.

1402.

1402.

Yato [V 0.0179] sumatinā mato nāmato,

Āyācitasammānato mānato;

Tato hi racito sadā tosadā,

Mayā hitavibhāvanā bhāvanā.

Since it was esteemed by the wise one, Sumati by name,

And requested with honor and respect;

Therefore it was composed by me, always giving delight,

A development that clarifies what is beneficial.

1403.

1403.

Atthato [M 0.0185] ganthato cāpi, yuttito cāpi ettha ca;

Ayuttaṃ vā viruddhaṃ vā, yadi dissati kiñcipi.

If anything whatsoever is seen here

That is improper or contradictory,

In meaning, text, or reasoning,

1404.

1404.

Pubbāparaṃ viloketvā, vicāretvā punappunaṃ;

Dhīmatā saṅgahetabbaṃ, gahetabbaṃ na dosato.

The wise should examine what comes before and after,

Investigate it repeatedly, and then accept its sense,

Not grasping at it with a fault-finding mind.

1405.

1405.

Tividhā byappathānañhi, gatiyo dubbidhāpi ce;

Tasmā upaparikkhitvā, veditabbaṃ vibhāvinā.

For the applications are threefold,

And the courses are twofold;

Therefore, the discerning one should investigate

And understand this thoroughly.

1406.

1406.

Nikāyantaraladdhīhi, asammisso anākulo;

Mahāvihāravāsīnaṃ, vācanāmagganissito.

Unmixed with the tenets of other schools and unconfused,

It is based on the textual tradition of the residents of the Mahāvihāra.

1407.

1407.

Madhurakkharasaṃyutto, attho yasmā pakāsito;

Tasmā hitatthakāmena, kātabbo ettha ādaro.

Because the meaning is made clear, joined with sweet-sounding syllables, therefore, one who desires what is beneficial should pay due respect to this work.

1408.

1408.

Saddhammaṭṭhitikāmena, karontena ca yaṃ mayā;

Puññamadhigataṃ tena, sukhaṃ pappontu pāṇino.

By the merit I have acquired in composing this work, desiring the stability of the true Dhamma, may all living beings attain happiness.

1409.

1409.

Antarāyaṃ vinā cāyaṃ, yathāsiddhimupāgato;

Tathā kalyāṇasaṅkappā, siddhiṃ gacchantu pāṇinaṃ.

Just as this work has reached completion without any hindrance, so too may the wholesome aspirations of all beings reach fulfillment.

1410.

1410.

Naranārigaṇākiṇṇe[P 0.0138], asaṃkiṇṇakulākule;

Phīte sabbaṅgasampanne, supasannasitodake.

Thronged with crowds of men and women, with well-ordered and numerous families, flourishing, complete in every aspect, with very clear and cool water—

1411.

1411.

Nānāratanasampuṇṇe, vividhāpaṇasaṅkaṭe;

Kāverapaṭṭane ramme, nānārāmopasobhite.

in the delightful port city of Kāvera, filled with various gems, crowded with diverse shops, and adorned with many parks;

1412.

1412.

Kelāsasikharākārapāsādapaṭimaṇḍite;

Kārite kaṇhadāsena, dassanīye manorame.

adorned with mansions like the peaks of Mount Kailāsa, built by Kaṇhadāsa, lovely and delightful to see;

1413.

1413.

Vihāre [V 0.0180] vividhākāracārupākāragopure;

Tattha pācīnapāsāde, mayā nivasatā sadā.

in a monastery with beautiful walls and gate-towers of various shapes—there, in the eastern mansion, I was always dwelling.

1414.

1414.

Asallekhamasākhalye, sīlādiguṇasobhinā;

Ayaṃ sumatinā sādhu, yācitena kato satā.

This work was composed by me, having been well requested by the good and wise Sumati, who is adorned with virtues such as morality and is not given to caustic or harsh speech.

1415.

1415.

Devā [M 0.0186] kālena vassantu, vassaṃ vassavalāhakā;

Pālayantu mahīpālā, dhammato sakalaṃ mahiṃ.

May the devas send rain in due season, may the rain clouds shower down; may the rulers of the earth protect the entire world in accordance with the Dhamma.

1416.

1416.

Yāva tiṭṭhati lokasmiṃ, himavā pabbatuttamo;

Tāva tiṭṭhatu saddhammo, dhammarājassa satthunoti.

As long as the Himālaya, the supreme mountain, stands in the world, so long may the true Dhamma of the Teacher, the King of Dhamma, endure.

Uragapuranivasanena ācariyena bhadantabuddhadattena sīlācārasampannena kato abhidhammāvatāro nāmāyaṃ.

This work named the Abhidhammāvatāra was composed by the teacher, the venerable Buddhadatta, a resident of Uragapura, who was endowed with virtue and good conduct.

Abhidhammāvatāro niṭṭhito.

The Abhidhammāvatāra is concluded.

Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Nāmarūpaparicchedo

The Demarcation of Name-and-Form

Ganthārambhakathā

Introduction to the Text

1.

1.

Sammā [M 0.0001][V 0.0001] sammābhisambuddhaṃ, dhammaṃ dhammappakāsanaṃ;

Saṃghaṃ saṃghuttamaṃ loke, vanditvā vandanārahaṃ.

Having paid homage to the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, to the Dhamma that makes the Teaching clear, and to the Sangha, supreme in the world, all of whom are worthy of veneration,

2.

2.

Nāmarūpaparicchedaṃ, pavakkhāmi samāsato;

Mahāvihāravāsīnaṃ, vaṇṇanānayanissitaṃ.

I shall explain in brief the Demarcation of Name-and-Form, relying on the method of exegesis of the residents of the Mahāvihāra.

1. Paṭhamo paricchedo

1. The First Chapter

Nāmattayavibhāgo

The Division of Name into Three

3.

3.

Tattha [V 0.0002] cittaṃ cetasikaṃ, nibbānanti mataṃ tidhā;

Nāmaṃ rūpaṃ tu duvidhaṃ, bhūtopādāyabhedato.

Therein, name is considered threefold: consciousness, mental factors, and Nibbāna. Form, however, is twofold, distinguished as primary matter and derived matter.

4.

4.

Kāmabhūmādibhedena, tattha cittaṃ catubbidhaṃ;

Cetoyuttā dvipaññāsa, dhammā cetasikā matā.

Therein, consciousness is fourfold, classified by way of the sense-sphere plane and so on. Fifty-two states associated with consciousness are considered mental factors.

5.

5.

Cakkhusotaghānajivhā-kāyaviññāṇadhātuyo;

Sampaṭicchanacittañca, tathā santīraṇadvayaṃ.

The consciousness-elements of eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body; the receiving consciousness, and likewise the two investigating consciousnesses.

6.

6.

Somanassasahagataṃ, upekkhāsahitanti ca;

Iccāhetukacittāni, puññapākāni aṭṭhadhā.

Accompanied by joy and accompanied by equanimity—thus the rootless consciousnesses that are wholesome-resultants are eightfold.

7.

7.

Somanassayutaṃ tattha, hitvā santīraṇaṃ tathā;

Sattākusalapākāni, tānevāti viniddise.

Omitting from these the investigating consciousness accompanied by joy, one should specify those very same seven as the unwholesome-resultant consciousnesses.

8.

8.

Pañcadvāramanodvārāvajjanaṃ [M 0.0002] hasananti ca;

Kriyacittamudīritaṃ, tividhampi ahetukaṃ.

The five-door adverting, the mind-door adverting, and the smile-producing consciousness—these three kinds of rootless consciousness are declared to be functional.

9.

9.

Evaṃ aṭṭhārasavidhaṃ, mānasaṃ hotihetukaṃ;

Mūlabhedenākusalaṃ, cittaṃ tu tividhaṃ mataṃ.

Thus, consciousness is of eighteen kinds that are rootless. Unwholesome consciousness, however, is considered threefold by distinction of its root.

10.

10.

Somanassasahagataṃ, upekkhāsahitaṃ tathā;

Diṭṭhigatasampayuttaṃ, vippayuttanti bheditaṃ.

Accompanied by joy or by equanimity; associated with wrong view or dissociated from it—thus it is divided.

11.

11.

Asaṅkhāraṃ sasaṅkhāramiti bhinnaṃ panaṭṭhadhā;

Lobhamūlaṃ pakāsenti, tatthākusalamānasaṃ.

Further divided as unprompted and prompted, the greed-rooted unwholesome consciousness is declared to be eightfold.

12.

12.

Domanassasahagataṃ, paṭighena samāyutaṃ;

Dosamūlamasaṅkhāraṃ, sasaṅkhārantipi dvidhā.

Accompanied by displeasure and associated with aversion, the hate-rooted consciousness is twofold: unprompted and prompted.

13.

13.

Vicikicchāsahagataṃ[V 0.0003], uddhaccasahitanti ca;

Mohamūlañca duvidhaṃ, upekkhāya samāyutaṃ.

Accompanied by doubt and accompanied by restlessness—the delusion-rooted consciousness is twofold, both associated with equanimity.

14.

14.

Dvādasākusalānevaṃ, cittānīti vibhāvaye;

Hitvāhetukapāpāni, sobhanāni tato paraṃ.

Thus one should understand the twelve unwholesome types of consciousness. After these come the beautiful types of consciousness, setting aside the rootless unwholesome-resultants.

15.

15.

Somanassasahagataṃ, upekkhāsahitaṃ tathā;

Dvidhā ñāṇena saṃyuttaṃ, vippayuttanti bheditaṃ.

Accompanied by joy, and likewise accompanied by equanimity; it is divided in two as associated with knowledge and dissociated from it.

16.

16.

Asaṅkhāraṃ sasaṅkhāramiti bhinnaṃ panaṭṭhadhā;

Sahetukāmāvacara-puññapākakriyā bhave.

Further divided as unprompted and prompted, they are eightfold. These are the rooted sense-sphere wholesome, resultant, and functional types of consciousness.

17.

17.

Kāme tevīsa pākāni, puññāpuññāni vīsati;

Ekādasa kriyā ceti, catupaññāsa sabbathā.

In the sense sphere there are twenty-three resultants, twenty wholesome and unwholesome types, and eleven functional types—thus fifty-four in all.

18.

18.

Takkacārapītisukhekaggatāsahitaṃ pana;

Paṭhamajjhānakusalaṃ, vipākañca kriyā tathā.

Accompanied by initial application, sustained application, rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness is the first jhāna wholesome consciousness; likewise its resultant and functional counterparts.

19.

19.

Dutiyaṃ takkato hīnaṃ, tatiyaṃ tu vicārato;

Catutthaṃ pītito hīnaṃ, upekkhekaggatāyutaṃ.

The second is without initial application; the third is without sustained application; the fourth is without rapture; the fifth is endowed with equanimity and one-pointedness.

20.

20.

Pañcamaṃ [M 0.0003] pañcadasadhā, rūpāvacaramīritaṃ;

Pañcamajjhānamevekamarūpāvacaraṃ pana.

The fine-material sphere consciousness is said to be fifteenfold, in five jhāna types. The immaterial sphere consciousness, however, is based only on the fifth jhāna.

21.

21.

Ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ, puññapākakriyā tathā;

Viññāṇañcāyatanañca, ākiñcaññāyatanakaṃ;

Nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ dvādasadhā bhave.

The base of infinite space, the base of infinite consciousness, the base of nothingness, and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—these, as wholesome, resultant, and functional, are twelvefold.

22.

22.

Sotāpattimaggacittaṃ, phalacittaṃ tathāparaṃ;

Sakadāgāmānāgāmi, arahattanti aṭṭhadhā.

The path consciousness of stream-entry and its fruit consciousness; likewise those of the once-returner, the non-returner, and the arahant—thus they are eightfold.

23.

23.

Jhānaṅgayogabhedena, katvekekaṃ tu pañcadhā;

Vitthārānuttaraṃ cittaṃ, cattālīsavidhaṃ bhave.

By making each one fivefold according to the distinction in jhāna factors, the expanded supramundane consciousness becomes fortyfold.

24.

24.

Rūpāvacaracittāni[V 0.0004], gayhantānuttarāni ca;

Paṭhamādijjhānabhede, āruppañcāpi pañcame.

The fine-material sphere consciousnesses and the supramundane consciousnesses are taken according to the divisions of the first jhāna and so on, and the immaterial consciousnesses are taken with the fifth jhāna.

25.

25.

Dvādasākusalānevaṃ, kusalānekavīsati;

Chattiṃseva vipākāni, kriyacittāni vīsati.

Thus, there are twelve unwholesome consciousnesses, twenty-one wholesome, thirty-six resultant, and twenty functional.

26.

26.

Ekavīsasataṃ vātha, ekūnanavutīvidhaṃ;

Cittaṃ taṃsampayogena, bhinnā cetasikā tathā.

Consciousness is thus of eighty-nine kinds, or one hundred twenty-one. The mental factors are similarly distinguished by their association with these.

27.

27.

Phasso ca vedanā saññā, cetanekaggatā tathā;

Jīvitaṃ manasīkāro, sabbasādhāraṇā matā.

Contact, feeling, perception, volition, one-pointedness, life faculty, and attention—these are considered universals.

28.

28.

Takkacārādhimokkhā ca, vīriyaṃ chandapītiyo;

Pakiṇṇakā cha akkhātā, terasaññasamānatā.

Initial application, sustained application, decision, energy, desire, and rapture—these six are called particulars. Thus there are thirteen common-to-others.

29.

29.

Pakiṇṇakā na viññāṇe, vitakko dutiyādisu;

Vicāro tatiyādimhi, adhimokkho tu kaṅkhite.

Among the particulars: initial application is absent in the second jhāna and higher; sustained application is absent in the third jhāna and higher; decision is absent in consciousness accompanied by doubt.

30.

30.

Santīraṇamanodhātuttikesu vīriyaṃ tathā;

Catutthasukhite pīti, chandohetumhi momuhe.

Energy is absent in the investigating consciousnesses and the three mind-element consciousnesses; rapture is absent in the fourth jhāna accompanied by happiness; desire is absent in rootless consciousness and in delusion-rooted consciousness.

31.

31.

Chasaṭṭhi pañcapaññāsa, ekādasa ca soḷasa;

Sattati vīsati ceva, tāni cittāni dīpaye.

One should point out those consciousnesses as sixty-six, fifty-five, eleven, sixteen, seventy, and twenty respectively.

32.

32.

Mohāhirikānottappa-muddhaccaṃ [M 0.0004] sabbapāpajaṃ;

Issāmaccherakukkuccadosā tu paṭighe tathā.

Delusion, shamelessness, fearlessness of wrongdoing, and restlessness arise in all unwholesome consciousness. Envy, avarice, worry, and hatred, however, arise likewise in consciousness accompanied by aversion.

33.

33.

Lobho lobhe tu diṭṭhi ca, diṭṭhiyutte viyuttake;

Māno ca thinamiddhaṃ tu, sasaṅkhāresu pañcasu.

Greed is in greed-rooted consciousness; wrong view is in that which is associated with wrong view, while conceit is in that which is dissociated from it. Sloth and torpor are in the five kinds of prompted consciousness.

34.

34.

Kaṅkhite vicikicchāti, cuddasākusalānime;

Dvādasākusalesveva, niyamena vavatthitā.

Doubt is in the consciousness accompanied by indecision. These are the fourteen unwholesome mental factors; they are established by rule in the twelve unwholesome consciousnesses.

35.

35.

Saddhā sati hirottappaṃ, alobhādosamajjhatā;

Kāyacittānaṃ passaddhi, lahutā mudutā tathā.

Faith, mindfulness, moral shame, moral dread, non-greed, non-hatred, neutrality, and the pairs: tranquility, lightness, and pliancy of body and mind.

36.

36.

Kammaññatā [V 0.0005] ca pāguññaujutāti yugā cha ca;

Ekūnavīsati dhammā, aññamaññāviyogino;

Ekūnasaṭṭhicittesu, sobhanesu pavattitā.

And the pairs: wieldiness, proficiency, and rectitude of body and mind—these nineteen states, inseparable from one another, arise in the fifty-nine beautiful types of consciousness.

37.

37.

Sammāvācā ca kammantājīvāti viratī imā;

Lokuttare sadā sabbā, saha kāmasubhe visuṃ.

The abstinences—right speech, right action, and right livelihood—are always all present in the supramundane, but arise separately in the wholesome sense-sphere consciousness.

38.

38.

Karuṇāmuditā nānā, rūpe pañcamavajjite;

Kadāci kāme kusale, kriyacitte sahetuke.

Compassion and appreciative joy arise variously in the fine-material sphere, except in the fifth jhāna; and sometimes in the wholesome and functional rooted consciousness of the sense sphere.

39.

39.

Tihetukesu cittesu, paññā sabbattha labbhati;

Ete saddhādayo dhammā, pañcavīsati sobhanā.

In consciousnesses with three roots, wisdom is found in all. These factors, faith and the others, are twenty-five beautiful ones.

40.

40.

Issāmaccherakukkuccaviratīkaruṇādayo;

Nānā kadāci māno ca, thinamiddhaṃ tathā saha.

Envy, avarice, worry, the abstinences, compassion and the others, and also conceit, and sloth and torpor, arise variously and sometimes together.

41.

41.

Satta sabbattha jāyanti, cha tu dhammā yathārahaṃ;

Cuddasākusalesveva, sobhanesveva sobhanā.

Seven arise in all, while six factors arise where appropriate; fourteen arise only in unwholesome states, the beautiful factors only in beautiful states.

42.

42.

Dvepaññāsa paniccevaṃ, dhamme saṅgayha mānase;

Labbhamāne vibhāveyya, paccekampi vicakkhaṇo.

Thus, having comprehended these fifty-two factors in the mind, a discerning person should analyze them individually as they are found.

43.

43.

Sobhanaññasamānā ca, paṭhame viratī vinā;

Dutiyādīsu takkañca, vicāraṃ tatiyādisu.

In the first [jhāna consciousness], the beautiful and common-to-others factors are present, without the abstinences; in the second and subsequent ones, also without initial application; in the third and subsequent ones, also without sustained application.

44.

44.

Catutthādīsu [M 0.0005] pītiñca, karuṇādiñca pañcame;

Hitvā neva viyojeyya, saṅkhipitvāna pañcadhā.

and also without rapture from the fourth [jhāna] onwards, and without compassion and the others in the fifth. Having thus summarized in five ways, one should disjoin them by abandoning them.

45.

45.

Pañcatiṃsa catuttiṃsa, tettiṃsa ca yathākkamaṃ;

Dvattiṃsa tiṃsa evātha, jāyantīti mahaggate.

Thirty-five, thirty-four, and thirty-three, in due order; then thirty-two and thirty: thus they arise in the sublime consciousness.

46.

46.

Gahetvā viratī sabbā, hitvāna karuṇādayo;

Paṭhame dutiyādimhi, vitakkādiṃ vinā tathā.

Taking all the abstinences, but excluding compassion and the others; so too in the first, second, and subsequent [supramundane jhānas], without initial thought and the other [factors that are progressively abandoned].

47.

47.

Pañcadhāva [V 0.0006] gaṇeyyevaṃ, chattiṃsā ca yathākkamaṃ;

Pañcatiṃsa catuttiṃsa, tettiṃsadvayamuttare.

Thus one should count in five ways: thirty-six, and in order, thirty-five, thirty-four, and a pair of thirty-threes in the supramundane states.

48.

48.

Sobhanaññasamānā ca, kāmesu kusale kriye;

Hitvā viratiyo pāke, viratīkaruṇādayo.

In sense-sphere wholesome and functional consciousness, the beautiful and ethically variable factors are present. In the resultants, one excludes the abstinences, and compassion and the others.

49.

49.

Ñāṇayutte somanasse, viyutte ñāṇavajjitā;

Upekkhake pītihīnā, vippayutte dvayaṃ vinā.

When associated with knowledge and accompanied by joy; when dissociated, it is without knowledge. When accompanied by equanimity, it is without joy; when dissociated from knowledge as well, it is without both.

50.

50.

Catudhā tividhesvevaṃ, vigaṇeyya dvayaṃ dvayaṃ;

Na santupekkhāsahite, karuṇādīti kecana.

Thus one should analyze the fourfold and threefold types, pair by pair. Some hold that compassion and the others are not present in consciousness accompanied by equanimity.

51.

51.

Aṭṭhatiṃsa sattatiṃsadvayaṃ chattiṃsakaṃ subhe;

Pañcatiṃsa catuttiṃsadvayaṃ tettiṃsakaṃ kriye.

In the wholesome: thirty-eight, a pair of thirty-sevens, and a thirty-six. In the functional: thirty-five, a pair of thirty-fours, and a thirty-three.

52.

52.

Tettiṃsa pāke dvattiṃsadvayekatiṃsakaṃ bhave;

Sahetukāmāvacarapuññapākakriyāmane.

In the resultants, there are thirty-three, a pair of thirty-twos, and a thirty-one. This concerns the rooted sense-sphere meritorious, resultant, and functional consciousness.

53.

53.

Mohādayo samānā ca, paṭhame lobhadiṭṭhiyā;

Tatiye lobhamānena, jāyantekūnavīsati.

With delusion and the other [universal unwholesome factors] and the ethically variable factors, nineteen arise: in the first [type of greed-rooted consciousness], with greed and wrong view; and in the third, with greed and conceit.

54.

54.

Aṭṭhārasa pītihīnā, pañcame sattame tathā;

Navame dosakukkuccamaccharissāhi vīsati.

In those devoid of joy—the fifth and seventh types—eighteen factors arise. In the ninth, with hatred, worry, avarice, and envy, twenty arise.

55.

55.

Paṭhamādīsu vuttāva, dutiyādīsu jāyare;

Thinamiddhenekavīsa, vīsa dvevīsatikkamā.

As stated for the first and following unprompted types, so they arise in the second and following prompted types. With the addition of sloth and torpor, there are twenty-one, twenty, and twenty-two respectively.

56.

56.

Chandapītiṃ [M 0.0006] vinuddhacce, kaṅkhite nicchayaṃ vinā;

Pañcadaseva kaṅkhāya, asubhesu vibhāvaye.

In the consciousness with restlessness, desire and joy are absent. In the one with doubt, decision is absent. In the consciousness with doubt, only fifteen factors arise. Thus one should analyze the unwholesome states.

57.

57.

Site samānā nicchandā, dvādasekādaseva tu;

Pītiṃ hitvāna voṭṭhabbe, vīriyaṃ sukhatīraṇe.

In smiling consciousness, the ethically variable factors, being without desire, are twelve. In determining consciousness, joy is excluded, and in pleasant investigating consciousness, energy is excluded, resulting in eleven factors.

58.

58.

Dvayaṃ hitvā manodhātu, upekkhātīraṇe dasa;

Satta sādhāraṇā eva, pañcaviññāṇasambhavā.

In the mind-element and in investigating consciousness with equanimity, having excluded two more factors, ten arise. In the five sense-consciousnesses, only the seven universal factors arise.

59.

59.

Iti [V 0.0007] cetasi sambhūtā,

Dvepaññāsa yathārahaṃ;

Ñeyyā cetasikā dhammā,

Cetobhedappabhedino.

Thus the fifty-two mental factors that arise in consciousness, each as is appropriate, are to be known as they are distinguished by the different types of consciousness.

60.

60.

Suññatañcānimittañca, tathāpaṇihitanti ca;

Tividhākāramīrenti, nibbānamamataṃ budhā.

The wise declare that deathless Nibbāna has a threefold aspect: namely, emptiness, the signless, and the undirected.

61.

61.

Yaṃ ārabbha pavattantaṃ, tatthānuttaramānasaṃ;

Suññatādivimokkhoti, nāmamālambato labhe.

That unsurpassed mind which proceeds having taken it as object obtains from its object the name 'liberation through emptiness,' and so forth.

62.

62.

Sopādisesanibbānadhātu ceva tathāparā;

Anupādisesā cāti, duvidhā pariyāyato.

The Nibbāna-element with residue remaining and, likewise, the other, the Nibbāna-element without residue remaining: thus it is twofold from a conventional point of view.

63.

63.

Tadetaṃ vānanikkhantamaccantaṃ santilakkhaṇaṃ;

Assāsakaraṇarasaṃ, khemabhāvena gayhati.

This Nibbāna, which has departed from craving, has ultimate peace as its characteristic. Its function is the causing of solace, and it is apprehended as a state of security.

64.

64.

Taṃ nāmetīti nibbānaṃ, namantīti tatopare;

Tepaññāsāti nāmāni, catupaññāsa sabbathā.

It is called Nibbāna because one names it so, or, according to others, because they bow to it. Its names are fifty-three, or fifty-four in all.

65.

65.

Cittacetasikayojanānayaṃ,

Cittamuttamamidaṃ pakāsitaṃ;

Sādhu cetasi nidhāya paṇḍitā,

Sādhu sāsanadharā bhavanti te.

This method of connecting mind and mental factors, this supreme mind, has been explained. The wise, having placed this well in their minds, truly become bearers of the Teaching.

66.

66.

Buddhappavattamavagāhitabodhiñāṇa-

Miccābhidhammamavagāhitasabbadhammaṃ[M 0.0007];

Ogayha nāmagatarāsimasesayitvā,

Saṅgayha sabbamidha yojitamādarena.

This Abhidhamma, which has come down from the Buddha, which fathoms the wisdom of enlightenment and fathoms all phenomena—having plunged into and completely mastered the collection of what is called 'name,' having comprehended it all, it is set forth here with reverence.

Iti nāmarūpaparicchede nāmattayavibhāgo nāma

Thus ends the section named 'The Division of the Threefold Name' in the 'Analysis of Name-and-Form'.

Paṭhamo paricchedo.

The First Chapter.

2. Dutiyo paricchedo

2. The Second Chapter.

Lakkhaṇarasupaṭṭhānavibhāgo

The Analysis of Characteristic, Function, Manifestation, and Proximate Cause

67.

67.

Sabhāvo [V 0.0008] lakkhaṇaṃ nāma, kiccasampajjanā raso;

Gayhākāro upaṭṭhānaṃ, padaṭṭhānaṃ tu paccayo.

Intrinsic nature is called the characteristic; the accomplishment of its task is the function; its mode of appearance is the manifestation; and the proximate cause is the immediate condition.

68.

68.

Attupaladdhisaṅkhātā, sampattā ca panatthato;

Lakkhaṇarasupaṭṭhānā, vohārābhogabheditā.

The characteristic, function, and manifestation are designated as the attainment of the essence, and are also arrived at by way of the meaning; they are distinguished by convention and by consideration.

69.

69.

Tepaññāsasabhāvesu, tasmā bhedaṃ yathārahaṃ;
