Lakkhaṇādippakārehi, pavakkhāmi ito paraṃ.

Therefore, from here on I shall explain the distinction, as is appropriate, among these fifty-three states, by way of their characteristics and other aspects.

70.

70.

Cintetīti bhave cittaṃ, cintanamattameva vā;

Sampayuttātha vā tena, cintentīti ca gocaraṃ.

It is 'citta' because it thinks, or because it is merely the act of thinking; or because the associated states think by means of it, or because it cognizes an object.

71.

71.

Phusatīti bhave phasso, phusanaṃ vātha kevalaṃ;

Sampayuttātha vā tena, phusantīti ca gocaraṃ.

It is contact (phassa) because it touches, or it is merely the act of touching; or because associated states touch the object by means of it.

72.

72.

Evaṃ kattari bhāve ca, karaṇe ca yathārahaṃ;

Tepaññāsasabhāvesu, saddanibbacanaṃ naye.

Thus, for the fifty-three states, one should understand the derivation of the words, as is appropriate, in the sense of agent, state, or instrument.

73.

73.

Ālambaṇamanaṃ cittaṃ, taṃvijānanalakkhaṇaṃ;

Sahajādhiṭṭhānarasaṃ, cintākappoti gayhati.

Citta is that which is aware of an object; it has knowing as its characteristic. Its function is to be the basis of co-arisen states. It is apprehended as a process of thought.

74.

74.

Ālambaṇasamodhāno[M 0.0008],

Phasso phusanalakkhaṇo;

Saṅghaṭṭanaraso tattha,

Sannipātoti gayhati.

Contact, the coming together with the object, has touching as its characteristic. Its function is impinging. It is apprehended as conjunction.

75.

75.

Vedanālambaṇarasā, sā vedayitalakkhaṇā;

Gocarānubhavarasā, anubhuttīti gayhati.

Feeling has the characteristic of being felt. Its function is to experience the object. It is apprehended as experience.

76.

76.

Ākāragahaṇaṃ [V 0.0009] saññā, sā sañjānanalakkhaṇā;

Nimittuppādanarasā, upalakkhāti gayhati.

Perception is the grasping of features; it has perceiving as its characteristic. Its function is to produce a sign. It is apprehended as marking.

77.

77.

Cetanā cittavipphārā, sāyaṃ byāpāralakkhaṇā;

Kammantāyūhanarasā, saṃvidhānanti gayhati.

Volition is the stirring of the mind; it has striving as its characteristic. Its function is the accumulation of kamma. It is apprehended as coordinating.

78.

78.

Ekaggatā avikkhepo, sāvisāhāralakkhaṇā;

Sampiṇḍanarasā cittaṃ, samodhānanti gayhati.

One-pointedness is non-distraction; it has non-wavering as its characteristic. Its function is to unify the mind. It is apprehended as composure.

79.

79.

Yāpanaṃ sahajātāna-manupālanalakkhaṇaṃ;

Jīvitaṃ jīvanarasaṃ, āyubandhoti gayhati.

The life faculty has the characteristic of maintaining co-arisen states. Its function is to make them live. It is apprehended as the continuation of their existence.

80.

80.

Sāraṇā manasīkāro, samannāhāralakkhaṇo;

Saṃyojanaraso citta-paṭipattīti gayhati.

Attention is the directing of the mind; it has the characteristic of directing towards an object. Its function is to yoke associated states to the object. It is apprehended as the mind's engagement.

81.

81.

Saṅkappanalakkhaṇo takko, sahajābhiniropano;

Ālambāhananaraso, sannirujjhoti gayhati.

Initial thought has applying the mind as its characteristic. Its function is to direct the co-arisen states onto the object. It is apprehended as the initial striking of the mind upon the object.

82.

82.

Vicāro anusandhāno, anumajjanalakkhaṇo;

Cittānuyojanaraso, anupekkhāti gayhati.

Sustained thought is continued connection; it has scrutinizing as its characteristic. Its function is to keep the mind yoked to the object. It is apprehended as continued examination.

83.

83.

Adhimokkho asaṃsappo, susanniṭṭhānalakkhaṇo;

Niccalāpādanaraso, daḷhavuttīti gayhati.

Decision is non-wavering; it has firm conviction as its characteristic. Its function is to produce steadfastness. It is apprehended as determination.

84.

84.

Vīriyaṃ pana vāyāmo, mahussāhanalakkhaṇo;

Kiccāsaṃsīdanaraso, upatthambhoti gayhati.

Energy is exertion; it has striving as its characteristic. Its function is to prevent co-arisen states from sinking. It is apprehended as support.

85.

85.

Ālambatthikatā [M 0.0009] chando, kattukāmatalakkhaṇo;

Ālambaṇesanaraso, hatthādānanti gayhati.

Desire is the need for an object; it has the wish-to-do as its characteristic. Its function is seeking an object. It is apprehended as the stretching forth of the hand.

86.

86.

Sahajātānupharaṇā, sampiyāyanalakkhaṇā;

Sampīnanarasā pīti, pāmojjamiti gayhati.

Joy, which suffuses the co-arisen states, has gladdening as its characteristic. Its function is to refresh. It is apprehended as elation.

87.

87.

Cetosaddahanaṃ saddhā, bhūtokappanalakkhaṇā;

Hitapakkhandanarasā, adhimuttīti gayhati.

Faith is the mind's trust; it has conviction in the true as its characteristic. Its function is to leap forward towards the beneficial. It is apprehended as resolution.

88.

88.

Asammosā [V 0.0010] sabhāvesu, sati dhāraṇalakkhaṇā;

Dhammāpilāpanarasā, appamādoti gayhati.

Mindfulness is non-confusion regarding states; it has bearing in mind as its characteristic. Its function is not to let phenomena float away. It is apprehended as heedfulness.

89.

89.

Hirī jegucchā pāpesu, sā harāyanalakkhaṇā;

Hīḷasaṃkocanarasā, pāpalajjāti gayhati.

Shame is disgust at evil; it has shrinking away as its characteristic. Its function is to recoil from blame. It is apprehended as shame at evil.

90.

90.

Pāpasārajjamottappaṃ, ubbeguttāsalakkhaṇaṃ;

Bhayasaṅkocanarasaṃ, avissāsoti gayhati.

Fear of wrongdoing is timidity regarding evil; it has agitation and dread as its characteristic. Its function is to shrink from fear. It is apprehended as unease.

91.

91.

Alobho anabhisaṅgo, apariggahalakkhaṇo;

Muttappavattanaraso, asaṃsaggoti gayhati.

Non-greed is non-attachment; it has non-grasping as its characteristic. Its function is to act with detachment. It is apprehended as non-adhesion.

92.

92.

Adoso cittasākhalyaṃ, abyāpajjanalakkhaṇo;

Saṇhappavattanaraso, sommabhāvoti gayhati.

Non-hatred is gentleness of mind; it has non-ill-will as its characteristic. Its function is to act gently. It is apprehended as a gentle state.

93.

93.

Amoho khalitābhāvo, paṭivijjhanalakkhaṇo;

Visayobhāsanaraso, paṭibodhoti gayhati.

Non-delusion is the absence of error; it has penetration as its characteristic. Its function is to illuminate the object. It is apprehended as understanding.

94.

94.

Tatramajjhattatopekkhā, samīkaraṇalakkhaṇā;

Apakkhapātanarasā, samavāhoti gayhati.

Equanimity is impartiality; it has balancing as its characteristic. Its function is not to take sides. It is apprehended as neutrality.

95.

95.

Passaddhi kāyacittānaṃ, darathābhāvalakkhaṇā;

Aparipphandanarasā, sītibhāvoti gayhati.

Tranquility of body and mind has the absence of distress as its characteristic. Its function is non-agitation. It is apprehended as a state of coolness.

96.

96.

Lahutā kāyacittānaṃ, adandhākāralakkhaṇā;

Avitthārarasā sallahukavuttīti gayhati.

Lightness of body and mind has the characteristic of non-sluggishness. Its function is to remove heaviness. It is apprehended as buoyancy.

97.

97.

Mudutā kāyacittānaṃ, kakkhaḷābhāvalakkhaṇā;

Kiccāvirodhanarasā, anukulyanti gayhati.

Pliancy of body and mind has the characteristic of absence of rigidity. Its function is non-opposition to the task. It is apprehended as compliance.

98.

98.

Kammaññatā [M 0.0010] ubhinnampi, alaṃkiccassa lakkhaṇā;

Pavattisampattirasā, yogabhāvoti gayhati.

Adaptability of both has the characteristic of fitness for the task. Its function is the successful carrying on of activity. It is apprehended as suitability.

99.

99.

Tathā pāguññatā dvinnaṃ, visadākāralakkhaṇā;

Sukhappavattanarasā, seribhāvoti gayhati.

Likewise, proficiency of the two has the characteristic of clarity. Its function is to proceed with ease. It is apprehended as mastery.

100.

100.

Ujutā [V 0.0011] kāyacittānaṃ, kuṭilābhāvalakkhaṇā;

Jimhanimmadanarasā, ujuvuttīti gayhati.

Straightness of body and mind has the absence of crookedness as its characteristic. Its function is to crush deceitfulness. It is apprehended as uprightness.

101.

101.

Sammāvācā vacīsuddhi, vācāsaṃyamalakkhaṇā;

Micchāvācoramarasā, vacīvelāti gayhati.

Right Speech has the characteristic of restraint in speech; its function is to abstain from wrong speech; it is apprehended as purity of speech.

102.

102.

Sammākammaṃ kriyāsuddhaṃ, sammākaraṇalakkhaṇaṃ;

Micchākammoramarasaṃ, kriyāvelāti gayhati.

Right Action has the characteristic of right doing; its function is to abstain from wrong action; it is apprehended as purity of action.

103.

103.

Sammājīvo visuddheṭṭhi, alliṭṭhājīvalakkhaṇo;

Micchājīvoramaraso, sammāvuttīti gayhati.

Right Livelihood has the characteristic of purity of livelihood; its function is to abstain from wrong livelihood; it is apprehended as right living.

104.

104.

Karuṇā dīnasattesu, dukkhāpanayalakkhaṇā;

Sotthitāpatthanarasā, anukampāti gayhati.

Compassion towards afflicted beings has the characteristic of removing suffering; its function is to wish for their well-being; it is apprehended as sympathy.

105.

105.

Sukhaṭṭhitesu muditā, anumodanalakkhaṇā;

Cetovikāsanarasā, avirodhoti gayhati.

Appreciative joy towards those established in happiness has the characteristic of rejoicing; its function is to gladden the mind; it is apprehended as non-opposition.

106.

106.

Cetosārajjanā lobho, apariccāgalakkhaṇo;

Ālambagijjhanaraso, abhilaggoti gayhati.

Greed has the characteristic of not letting go; its function is to covet an object; it is apprehended as clinging.

107.

107.

Cetobyāpajjanaṃ doso, sampadussanalakkhaṇo;

Ālambaṇaghātaraso, caṇḍikkamiti gayhati.

Hatred has the characteristic of corruption; its function is to destroy the object; it is apprehended as ferocity.

108.

108.

Cetosammuyhanaṃ moho,

So sammuyhanalakkhaṇo;

Sabhāvacchādanaraso,

Andhabhāvoti gayhati.

Delusion is the mind's confusion; its characteristic is bewilderment; its function is to conceal intrinsic nature; it is apprehended as blindness.

109.

109.

Pāpājigucchāhirikaṃ, nillajjākāralakkhaṇaṃ;

Pāpopalāpanarasaṃ, malaggāhoti gayhati.

Shamelessness is the absence of disgust for evil; it has the characteristic of impudence; its function is to conceal evil; it is apprehended as a stain.

110.

110.

Asārajjanamanottappamanuttāsanalakkhaṇaṃ[M 0.0011];

Pāpapakkhandanarasaṃ, pāgabbhamiti gayhati.

Recklessness is the absence of dread concerning evil; it has the characteristic of not being afraid of it; its function is to plunge into evil; it is apprehended as audacity.

111.

111.

Diṭṭhi [V 0.0012] daḷhavipallāso, sā parāmāsalakkhaṇā;

Tucchābhinivesanarasā, micchāgāhoti gayhati.

Wrong view is a firm perversion; its characteristic is misapprehension; its function is adherence to what is worthless; it is apprehended as wrong grasping.

112.

112.

“Ahasmī”ti maññamāno, so samunnatilakkhaṇo;

Ketusampaggaharaso, ahaṃkāroti gayhati.

Conceit is the conceiving 'I am'; its characteristic is haughtiness; its function is like raising a banner; it is apprehended as I-making.

113.

113.

Parasampattīsu issā, akkhamākāralakkhaṇā;

Cetovikucanarasā, vimukhattanti gayhati.

Envy regarding others' success has the characteristic of intolerance; its function is constriction of the mind; it is apprehended as turning away.

114.

114.

Pariggahesu maccheraṃ, sannigūhanalakkhaṇaṃ;

Sāmaññāsahanarasaṃ, vevicchamiti gayhati.

Stinginess is avarice regarding one's own possessions; it has the characteristic of their concealment; its function is intolerance of sharing them; it is apprehended as sordidness.

115.

115.

Cetopahananaṃ thīnaṃ, taṃ saṃsīdanalakkhaṇaṃ;

Ussāhabhañjanarasaṃ, saṃkhittattanti gayhati.

Sloth is the indisposition of the mind; it has the characteristic of sinking; its function is the destruction of effort; it is apprehended as contraction.

116.

116.

Vighāto sahajātānaṃ, middhaṃ mohanalakkhaṇaṃ;

Sattisaṃbhañjanarasaṃ, āturattanti gayhati.

Torpor is the affliction of the co-arisen factors; it has the characteristic of bewilderment; its function is the breaking of mindfulness; it is apprehended as sickness.

117.

117.

Uddhaccaṃ cittavikkhepo, avūpasamalakkhaṇaṃ;

Cetonavaṭṭhānarasaṃ, bhantattamiti gayhati.

Restlessness is agitation of mind; it has the characteristic of non-calm; its function is mental unsteadiness; it is apprehended as confusion.

118.

118.

Vippaṭisāro kukkuccamanusocanalakkhaṇaṃ;

Attānusocanarasaṃ, pacchātāpoti gayhati.

Worry is regret; it has the characteristic of lamenting; its function is self-reproach; it is apprehended as remorse.

119.

119.

Kaṅkhāyanā vicikicchā, asanniṭṭhānalakkhaṇā;

Anekagāhanarasā, appatiṭṭhāti gayhati.

Doubt is uncertainty; it has the characteristic of indecisiveness; its function is manifold grasping; it is apprehended as being unsettled.

120.

120.

Iccevaṃ lakkhaṇādīhi, vibhāveyya vicakkhaṇo;

Tepaññāsasabhāvesu, sabhāvākāralakkhaṇaṃ.

Thus, by way of their characteristics and so on, a discerning person should analyze the intrinsic nature, mode, and characteristic in these fifty-three states.

121.

121.

Lakkhaṇatthakusalā [M 0.0012] salakkhaṇe,

Lakkhaṇatthaparamepi kevalaṃ;

Lakkhaṇuggahasukhāya vaṇṇayuṃ,

Lakkhaṇādimukhato salakkhaṇaṃ.

Those skilled in the meaning of characteristics, and supreme in the meaning of characteristics alone, have described the specific characteristics by way of characteristic, function, and manifestation, for the sake of easily grasping them.

122.

122.

Atthaṃ [V 0.0013] tamevamanugamma mayettha vutta-

Matthānamatthanayanatthamanekadhāpi;

Pattheyya mettha vacanatthanayehi ñāṇa-

Matthesu buddhavacanatthanayatthikehi.

Following that very meaning, I have here explained in many ways the purpose of the method of meaning for the things to be understood. May those who seek the method of meaning in the Buddha's words attain knowledge of these things here through my methods of verbal explanation.

Iti nāmarūpaparicchede lakkhaṇarasupaṭṭhānavibhāgo nāma

Thus in the Determination of Mind-and-Matter ends the section named the Division of Characteristic, Function, and Manifestation.

Dutiyo paricchedo.

The Second Chapter.

3. Tatiyo paricchedo

3. The Third Chapter.

Bhedasaṅgahavibhāgo

The Division of Grouping by Classification

123.

123.

Evaṃ bhedasabhāvesu, tesveva puna saṅgahaṃ;

Sabhāvatthavisesehi, pavakkhāmi ito paraṃ.

From here on, I will again explain the grouping of these same states, classified by nature, with the special characteristics of their intrinsic reality.

124.

124.

Asādhāraṇañāṇehi, satthā vatthuvivecako;

Saṅgahetvā sabhāgehi, dhamme dassesi cakkhumā.

With his unique knowledges, the Teacher, the discerner of realities, having grouped the dhammas by similar categories, the Visionary One taught them.

125.

125.

Diṭṭhibhinivesaṭṭhena, yathābhūtasabhāvato;

Paramāmasaticcekā, parāmāsoti bhāsitā.

Because it wrongly apprehends, in the sense of adherence to views, from its actual intrinsic nature, it is called 'misapprehension' (parāmāsa).

126.

126.

Kilesāsucibhāvena, vaṇassāvaraso viya;

Ālimpantāva santānaṃ, savantīti pakāsitā.

Because of the impurity of the defilements, and because they stain the mental continuum like the discharge flowing from a wound, they are declared to 'flow out' (āsava).

127.

127.

Kāmataṇhā bhavataṇhā, diṭṭhāvijjāti āsavā;

Cattāro āsavaṭṭhena, tayo dhammā sabhāvato.

Craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, views, and ignorance are the taints. They are four in the sense of taints, but by intrinsic nature they are three phenomena: craving, views, and ignorance.

128.

128.

Etevo [M 0.0013] ghāti vuttāva, dvārālambābhivāhino;

Ottharitvā parābhūte, harantā pāṇino bhave.

These same are also called 'floods' (ogha), for they sweep beings away by way of the sense doors and objects; having overwhelmed them, they carry the conquered beings into the round of existence.

129.

129.

Yogāti [V 0.0014] cāhu te eva, pāṇino bhavayantake;

Dvārālambābhisambandhā, yantabandhāva yojitā.

These same are also called 'yokes' (yoga), for they yoke beings to the machine of existence through their connection with the sense doors and objects, as if bound to a machine.

130.

130.

Santānamadhigaṇhantā, māluvāva mahātaruṃ;

Gaṇhantā daḷhamālambaṃ, maṇḍūkamiva pannago.

They seize upon the mental continuum like a māluvā creeper on a great tree; they grasp a firm support like a snake grasping a frog.

131.

131.

Kāmataṇhā ca diṭṭhi ca, upādānā catubbidhā;

Diṭṭhi diṭṭhisīlabbata-mattavādoti bheditā.

There are four kinds of clinging, which are derived from sensual craving and from views. View is differentiated as clinging to views, clinging to rites and rituals, and clinging to a doctrine of self.

132.

132.

Kāyena kāyaṃ ganthentā, duppamuñcānuveṭhino;

Kathitā kāyaganthāti, taṇhābyāpādadiṭṭhiyo.

Because they bind the mental body to the physical body, entwining them in a way that is hard to release, they are called the 'bodily knots': covetousness, ill will, and views.

133.

133.

Sīlabbataparāmāso, iti diṭṭhi vibheditā;

Idaṃsaccābhiniveso, iti cevaṃ catubbidhā.

View is differentiated as the misapprehension of rites and rituals, and the dogmatic adherence that 'this alone is true'; thus the bodily knots are fourfold.

134.

134.

Nekkhammaṃ palibodhentā, bhāvanāparipanthakā;

Santānamaṇḍakosāva, pariyonandhakāti ca.

Because they obstruct renunciation and are obstacles to mental development, and because they envelop the mental continuum like a sheath on a bud, they are called 'envelopers' or hindrances.

135.

135.

Kāmacchando ca byāpādo, thinamiddhañca saṃsayo;

Avijjuddhaccakukkuccamiti nīvaraṇā matā.

Sensual desire, ill will, sloth-and-torpor, and doubt; ignorance, restlessness, and worry—these are considered the hindrances.

136.

136.

Āgāḷhaṃ pariyādāya, ogayhanuppavattino;

Yopparogāva santāna-manusentīti bhāsitā.

Because they arise repeatedly, having taken a firm hold, and because they lie latent in the mental continuum like chronic diseases, they are called 'latent tendencies' (anusaya).

137.

137.

Kāmarāgo bhavarāgo, paṭigho mānadiṭṭhiyo;

Kaṅkhāvijjāti satteva, cha dhammānusayā matā.

The seven latent tendencies are: sensual lust, lust for existence, aversion, conceit, views, doubt, and ignorance. By nature, they are considered to be six phenomena.

138.

138.

Dvārālambaṇabandhena, pāṇīnaṃ bhavamaṇḍale;

Saṃyojanāni vuttāni, pāsabandhāva pakkhinaṃ.

Because they bind beings in the circle of existence through the connection of sense doors and objects, they are called 'fetters' (saṃyojana), like snares that bind birds.

139.

139.

Kāmarūpārūparāgā, paṭigho mohasaṃsayo;

Diṭṭhi sīlabbataṃ māno, uddhaccena dasā bhave.

Lust for the sense-sphere, lust for the form realm, lust for the formless realm, aversion, delusion, doubt, views, clinging to rites and rituals, conceit, and restlessness—with these, there are ten fetters.

140.

140.

Rūpārūparāguddhaccaṃ, abhidhamme vinā puna;

Bhavarāgissa maccheraṃ, gahetvā dasadhā siyuṃ.

Again, in the Abhidhamma, without lust for the form realm, lust for the formless realm, and restlessness, but taking lust for existence, envy, and stinginess, they would be tenfold.

141.

141.

Saṃklepayanti [M 0.0014][V 0.0015] santānaṃ, upaghātenti pāṇino;

Sahajāteklesentīti, kilesāti pakāsitā.

Because they defile the mental continuum, harm living beings, and torment co-arisen states, they are declared to be 'defilements' (kilesa).

142.

142.

Lobho doso ca moho ca,

Diṭṭhi māno ca saṃsayo;

Thināhirikanottappa-

Muddhaccena siyuṃ dasa.

Greed, hatred, and delusion; view, conceit, and doubt; sloth, shamelessness, lack of moral dread, and restlessness—these are the ten defilements.

143.

143.

Navasaṅgahitā ettha, diṭṭhilobhā pakāsitā;

Sattasaṅgahitāvijjā, paṭigho pañcasaṅgaho.

Herein, view and greed are declared to be included in nine collections; ignorance is included in seven collections; and aversion is included in five collections.

144.

144.

Catusaṅgahitā kaṅkhā, mānuddhaccā tisaṅgahā;

Dukasaṅgahitaṃ thīnaṃ, kukkuccamekasaṅgahaṃ.

Doubt is included in four collections, conceit and restlessness in three; sloth is included in two collections, and remorse in one.

145.

145.

Dvidhāhirikanottappa-missāmacchariyaṃ tathā;

Iccevaṃ dasadhā vuttā, pāpakesveva saṅgahā.

Shamelessness and lack of moral dread, likewise envy and avarice; thus the ten defilements are declared, with these groupings occurring only in unwholesome states.

146.

146.

Parāmāsāsavoghā ca, yogupādānaganthato;

Nīvāraṇānusayato, saṃyojanakilesato.

Misapprehension, taints, and floods; yokes, clinging, and bodily knots; hindrances and latent tendencies; fetters and defilements.

147.

147.

Cuddaseva tu saṅkhepā, sattapaññāsa bhedato;

Yathādhammānusārena, cittuppādesu yojaye.

Fourteen in brief, fifty-seven by way of division; according to the nature of the phenomena, one should apply them to the arisings of consciousness.

148.

148.

Tatopare noparāmā-sādibheditasaṅgahā;

Cittaṃ cetasikaṃ rūpaṃ, nibbānamiti dīpaye.

Beyond this, the groupings are not differentiated by misapprehension and so forth. One should set forth: mind, mental factors, matter, and Nibbāna.

149.

149.

Iccākusaladhammānaṃ, ñatvā saṅgahamuttaraṃ;

Missakā nāma viññeyyā, yathāsambhavato kathaṃ;

Thus, having known the supreme grouping of unwholesome phenomena, the 'mixed' phenomena should be understood according to how they occur.

150.

150.

Lobho doso ca moho ca,

Ekantākusalā tayo;

Alobhādosāmoho ca,

Kusalābyākatā tathā.

Greed, hatred, and delusion—these three are exclusively unwholesome; likewise, non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion are wholesome or indeterminate.

151.

151.

Pādapasseva [V 0.0016] mūlāni, thirabhāvāya paccayā;

Mūlabhāvena dhammānaṃ, hetū dhammā cha dīpitā.

Just as the roots of a tree are the condition for its stability, so too, by being the roots of phenomena, six phenomena are explained as root-conditions.

152.

152.

Vitakko [M 0.0015] ca vicāro ca, pīti cekaggatā tathā;

Somanassaṃ domanassaṃ, upekkhāti ca vedanā.

Initial application, sustained application, joy, and likewise one-pointedness; and the feelings of mental pleasure, mental pain, and equanimity.

153.

153.

Āhaccupanijjhāyantā, nijjhānaṭṭhena paccayā;

Jhānadhammāti satthāha, pañca vatthusabhāvato.

Directing the mind and contemplating, they are conditions by way of contemplation; the Teacher declared them to be jhāna-factors, which by nature are five.

154.

154.

Sammādiṭṭhi ca saṅkappo, vāyāmo viratittayaṃ;

Sammāsati samādhī ca, micchādiṭṭhi ca sambhavā.

Right view, right intention, right effort, and the three abstinences; right mindfulness, right concentration, and also wrong view and its concomitants.

155.

155.

Sammāmicchā ca nīyantā, niyyānaṭṭhena paccayā;

Maggaṅgā dvādasakkhātā, nava dhammā sabhāvato.

The right and wrong paths lead out, being conditions by way of deliverance; twelve path factors are declared, which by intrinsic nature are nine phenomena.

156.

156.

Attabhāvaṃ pavattentā, ojaṭṭhamakavedanaṃ;

Paṭisandhināmarūpa-māharantā yathākkamaṃ.

Sustaining individual existence, feeling, and the nutritive octad; bringing about rebirth-linking name-and-form in due order.

157.

157.

Kabaḷīkāro āhāro,

Phasso sañcetanā tathā;

Viññāṇamiti cattāro,

Āhārāti pakāsitā.

Edible food, contact, volition, and consciousness: these four are declared as nutriments.

158.

158.

Dhammānaṃ sahajātānaṃ, indriyaṭṭhena paccayā;

Attānamissaraṭṭhena, anuvattāpakā tathā.

For co-arisen phenomena, faculties are a condition in the sense of mastery; and likewise, by way of their own lordship, they cause conformity.

159.

159.

Saddhā ca sati paññā ca, vīriyekaggatāpi ca;

Vedanā jīvitaṃ cittaṃ, aṭṭha rūpindriyāni ca.

Faith, mindfulness, and wisdom; energy and one-pointedness also; feeling, life, and mind; and the eight material faculties.

160.

160.

Kathaṃ jīvitamekaṃ tu, sukhaṃ dukkhanti vedanā;

Somanassaṃ domanassaṃ, upekkhāti ca bheditā.

How so? Life is indeed one; feeling is distinguished as pleasure, pain, mental pleasure, mental pain, and equanimity.

161.

161.

Paññādimaggenaññāta-ññassāmītindriyaṃ bhave;

Majjhe aññindriyamante, aññātāvindriyaṃ tathā.

The faculty of 'I shall know the unknown' arises by the path beginning with wisdom; in the middle is the faculty of knowing, and at the end, likewise, is the faculty of one who has known.

162.

162.

Soḷaseva [V 0.0017] sabhāvena, indriyaṭṭhavibhāgato;

Indriyānīti vuttāni, bāvīsati vibhāvaye.

By intrinsic nature, there are indeed sixteen; by the division of their function as faculties, they are called 'faculties', and one should understand them as twenty-two.

163.

163.

Daḷhādhiṭṭhitasantānā[M 0.0016], vipakkhehi akampiyā;

Balavantasabhāvena, baladhammā pakāsitā.

Firm in continuity of resolve, unshaken by opponents; by way of their powerful nature, the qualities of strength are proclaimed.

164.

164.

Saddhā sati hirottappaṃ, vīriyekaggatā tathā;

Paññāhirikānottappa-miccevaṃ navadhā matā.

Faith, mindfulness, moral shame, and moral dread; energy and one-pointedness likewise; wisdom, shamelessness, and lack of moral dread—thus they are considered ninefold.

165.

165.

Jeṭṭhā pubbaṅgamaṭṭhena, puññāpuññapavattiyaṃ;

Paccayādhippateyyena, sahajānaṃ yathārahaṃ.

Chief in the sense of being foremost in the occurrence of wholesome and unwholesome states; a condition by way of predominance for their co-arisen states, as is appropriate.

166.

166.

Cattārodhipatī vuttā, ādhippaccasabhāvato;

Chando cittañca vīriyaṃ, vīmaṃsāti ca tādinā.

Four predominances are declared by the Such-a-one, by way of their predominant nature: desire, mind, energy, and investigation.

167.

167.

Pañcasaṅgahitā paññā, vāyāmekaggatā pana;

Catusaṅgahitā cittaṃ, sati ceva tisaṅgahā.

Wisdom is included in five groups; energy and one-pointedness, however, are included in four; mind and mindfulness indeed are included in three.

168.

168.

Saṅkappo vedanā saddhā, dukasaṅgahitā matā;

Ekekasaṅgahā sesā, aṭṭhavīsati bhāsitā;

Iccevaṃ sattadhā bhedo, vutto missakasaṅgaho.

Intention, feeling, and faith are considered to be included in two groups; the remaining twenty-eight are said to be included in one group each. Thus the mixed grouping is declared, with its sevenfold division.

169.

169.

Hetujhānaṅgamaggaṅgā, āhārindriyato tathā;

Balādhippatito ceva, puññāpuññādimissatā;

Chattiṃseva sabhāvena, catusaṭṭhi pabhedato.

The roots, jhāna factors, path factors, nutriments, faculties, powers, and predominances, being mixed with wholesome, unwholesome, and other states, are thirty-six by intrinsic nature and sixty-four by way of division.

170.

170.

Iccevaṃ saṅgahetvāna, vibhāveyya tato paraṃ;

Cittuppādapabhedesu, yathāsambhavato kathaṃ.

Thus having grouped them, one should analyze them further in the divisions of mind-arisings, according to how they arise.

171.

171.

Sitāvajjanaviññāṇaṃ, sampaṭicchanatīraṇā;

Aṭṭhārasāhetukāva, momūhā ekahetukā.

The smiling, adverting, and sense consciousnesses, along with the receiving and investigating consciousnesses—these eighteen are indeed rootless; those rooted in delusion are single-rooted.

172.

172.

Sesā tu kusalā ñāṇaviyuttā ca dvihetukā;

Cittuppādāpare satta-cattālīsa tihetukā.

The remaining wholesome consciousnesses disjoined from knowledge are two-rooted; the other forty-seven mind-arisings are three-rooted.

173.

173.

Pañcaviññāṇamajjhānaṃ[V 0.0018], dvijhānaṅgikamīritaṃ;

Catutthapañcamajjhānaṃ, tijhānaṃ tatiyaṃ matā.

The five sense-consciousnesses are without jhāna factors; the fourth and fifth jhānas are said to have two jhāna factors; the third jhāna is considered to have three jhāna factors.

174.

174.

Catujhānaṃ tu dutiyaṃ, kāme ca sukhavajjitā;

Pañcajhānaṃ tu paṭhamaṃ, kāme ca sukhitā matā.

The second jhāna, however, has four factors, as do sense-sphere consciousnesses devoid of pleasure; the first jhāna has five factors, as are considered the sense-sphere consciousnesses accompanied by pleasure.

175.

175.

Paṭhamānuttaraṃ [M 0.0017] jhānaṃ, aṭṭhamaggaṅgikaṃ mataṃ;

Sattamaggaṅgikaṃ nāma, sesajhānamanuttaraṃ.

The first supreme jhāna is considered to have eight path factors; the remaining supreme jhānas indeed have seven path factors.

176.

176.

Lokiyaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ, tathā kāme tihetukā;

Pañcamaggaṅgikā nāma, cittuppādā pakāsitā.

The mundane first jhāna, and likewise the three-rooted mind-arisings in the sense sphere, are declared to have five path factors.

177.

177.

Sesaṃ mahaggataṃ jhānaṃ, sampayuttā ca diṭṭhiyā;

Ñāṇena vippayuttā ca, catumaggaṅgikā matā.

The remaining sublime jhānas, those associated with wrong view, and those disjoined from knowledge are considered to have four path factors.

178.

178.

Paṭighuddhaccayuttā ca, vippayuttā ca diṭṭhiyā;

Timaggaṅgaṃ dumaggaṅgaṃ, kaṅkhitaṃ samudīritaṃ.

Those associated with aversion or restlessness, and those disjoined from wrong view, have three or two path factors; the doubt-associated consciousness is declared to have two path factors.

179.

179.

Na hontāhetuke maggā, cittaṭṭhiti ca kaṅkhite;

Viditā niyatatā ca, lokiyesu na uddhaṭā.

There are no path factors in the rootless consciousnesses, and no mental stability in the doubt-associated; and known certainty is not found in these mundane states.

180.

180.

Kāmesu kabaḷīkāro, anāhāro asaññino;

Cittuppādesu sabbattha, āhārattayamīritaṃ.

Physical food exists in the sense sphere; for non-percipient beings, there are no mental nutriments; in all mind-arisings, the triad of mental nutriments is declared.

181.

181.

Indriyāni vibhāveyya, navadhānuttare budho;

Aṭṭhadhā samudīreyya, lokiyesu tihetuke.

The wise should analyze the faculties as ninefold in the supramundane; one should declare them as eightfold in the mundane, three-rooted consciousnesses.

182.

182.

Sattadhā pana ñāṇena, vippayutte pakāsaye;

Sitavoṭṭhabbanāpuññe, pañcadhā kaṅkhite pana.

However, one should declare them as sevenfold in those disjoined from knowledge; and as fivefold in the smiling, determining, and unwholesome consciousnesses, and in the doubt-associated consciousness.

183.

183.

Catudhā tividhā sese, cittuppāde samīraye;

Tihetukā sattabalā, chabalā tu duhetukā.

In the remaining mind-arisings, one should declare them as fourfold or threefold. Three-rooted consciousnesses have seven powers; two-rooted consciousnesses, however, have six powers.

184.

184.

Catubalā akusalā, kaṅkhitaṃ tibalaṃ mataṃ;

Dvibalaṃ sitavoṭṭhabba-mabalaṃ sesamīritaṃ.

The unwholesome consciousnesses have four powers, the doubt-associated is considered to have three powers; the smiling and determining consciousnesses have two powers, the remainder are said to be without power.

185.

185.

Javanedhipatīnaṃ [V 0.0019] tu, yo koceko tihetuke;

Dvihetuke vā kusale, vīmaṃsā nopalabbhati.

In a three-rooted or two-rooted wholesome javana, any one of the predominants may arise; however, investigation is not found as a predominant factor in the two-rooted.

186.

186.

Lokiyesu vipākesu,

Mohamūle ahetuke;

Yathāsambhavavuttittā,

Natthādhipati kocipi.

In mundane resultants, in those rooted in delusion, and in the rootless, no predominant factor whatsoever is found, due to their arising merely according to conditions.

187.

187.

Sambhoti [M 0.0018] kāyaviññāṇe, puññapāke sukhindriyaṃ;

Dukkhindriyampi tattheva, pāpapākamhi bhāsitaṃ.

In body-consciousness that is the result of merit, the pleasure faculty arises; the pain faculty, too, is said to arise therein when it is the result of demerit.

188.

188.

Santīraṇañca hasanaṃ, somanassāni soḷasa;

Paṭhamādicatujjhānaṃ, somanassayutaṃ bhave.

The investigating and smiling consciousnesses, sixteen joyful consciousnesses, and the first four jhānas are associated with joy.

189.

189.

Domanassayuttā dveva, cittuppādā pakāsitā;

Tadaññe pana sabbepi, pañcapaññāsupekkhakā.

Only two arisings of consciousness are declared to be associated with displeasure; all the others, however, are accompanied by equanimity in fifty-five cases.

190.

190.

Vedanāsampayogañca, vinibbhujjevamaṭṭhadhā;

Hetuyogādibhedehi, cittuppādā pakāsitā.

Thus have the arisings of consciousness been declared, analyzed in eight ways according to the distinctions of association with roots and so on, and association with feeling.

191.

191.

Taṃtaṃviyogabhedañca, paccekamatha missitaṃ;

Yathāvuttānusārena, yathāsambhavato naye.

One should infer the distinctions of dissociation from each factor, both singly and combined, in accordance with what has been said and as is appropriate.

192.

192.

Iccevaṃ pana yojetvā, cittuppādesu missakaṃ;

Tato ñeyyā visuddhā ca, bodhipakkhiyasaṅgahā.

Having thus applied the miscellaneous analysis to the arisings of consciousness, one should then understand the pure factors and the summary of the requisites of enlightenment.

193.

193.

Kāye ca vedanācitte, dhammesu ca yathārahaṃ;

Asubhaṃ dukkhamanicca-manattāti supaṭṭhitā.

In the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena, respectively, mindfulness is well established regarding foulness, suffering, impermanence, and non-self.

194.

194.

Sammāsati paniccekā, kiccagocarabhedato;

Satipaṭṭhānanāmena, cattāroti pakāsitā.

But right mindfulness is one; due to the distinction of function and object, it is declared as fourfold by the name 'Foundations of Mindfulness'.

195.

195.

Uppannānuppannapāpa-pahānānuppādanāya ca;

Anuppannuppannehi vā, nibbattiabhivuddhiyā.

For the abandoning of arisen evil and for the non-arising of the unarisen; and for the arising of unarisen good and for the increase of the arisen.

196.

196.

Padahantassa [V 0.0020] vāyāmo, kiccābhogavibhāgato;

Sammappadhānanāmena, cattāroti pakāsitā.

The effort of one who strives, by its division into task and purpose, is declared as fourfold by the name 'Right Exertions'.

197.

197.

Iddhiyā pādabhūtattā, iddhipādāti bhāsitā;

Chando cittañca vīriyaṃ, vīmaṃsāti catubbidhā.

Because they are the basis for spiritual power, they are called the bases of spiritual power. They are fourfold: zeal, consciousness, energy, and investigation.

198.

198.

Pañca saddhā sati paññā, vīriyekaggatā tathā;

Indriyānindriyaṭṭhena, balaṭṭhena balāni ca.

The five are faith, mindfulness, wisdom, energy, and concentration. They are faculties in the sense of exercising control, and powers in the sense of strength.

199.

199.

Sati dhammavicayo ca, tathā vīriyapītiyo;

Passaddhekaggatāpekkhā, bujjhantassaṅgabhāvato.

Mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, energy, rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity are factors for one who is awakening.

200.

200.

Bojjhaṅgāti [M 0.0019] visesena, satta dhammā pakāsitā;

Niyyānaṭṭhena maggaṅgā, sammādiṭṭhādiaṭṭhadhā.

These seven dhammas are specifically declared as the enlightenment factors. In the sense of leading out, they are the eight path factors, beginning with right view.

201.

201.

Chasaṅgahettha vāyāmo, satipaññā samīritā;

Pañcasaṅgahitā nāma, samādhi catusaṅgaho.

Herein, effort is comprised of six factors; mindfulness and wisdom are said to be comprised of five; concentration is comprised of four.

202.

202.

Saddhā dusaṅgahā vuttā, sesā ekekasaṅgahā;

Iccevaṃ sattadhā bhedo, bodhipakkhiyasaṅgaho.

Faith is said to be comprised of two factors; the remaining ones are comprised of one each. Thus is the sevenfold division, the summary of the requisites of enlightenment.

203.

203.

Satipaṭṭhānasammappadhānato iddhipādato;

Indriyabalabojjhaṅgā, maggabhedā ca bhāsitā.

The Foundations of Mindfulness, the Right Exertions, the Bases of Spiritual Power, the Faculties, the Powers, the Enlightenment Factors, and the divisions of the Path have been spoken of.

204.

204.

Chando cittamupekkhā ca, saddhāpassaddhipītiyo;

Sammādiṭṭhi ca saṅkappo, vāyāmo viratittayaṃ.

Zeal, consciousness, and equanimity; faith, tranquility, and rapture; right view and right intention; effort, and the three abstinences.

205.

205.

Sammāsati samādhīti, dīpitā bodhipakkhiyā;

Cuddasā dhammato honti, sattatiṃsa pabhedato.

Right mindfulness and right concentration—thus are the requisites of enlightenment illuminated. In terms of their nature, they are fourteen; by way of classification, they are thirty-seven.

206.

206.

Yehi dhammehi bujjhanto, saccāni paṭivijjhati;

Samattānuttare honti, na vā saṅkappapītiyo.

They are the dhammas by which one, in awakening, penetrates the truths. They are all present together in the supramundane, except for intention and rapture.

207.

207.

Pubbabhāgepi labbhanti, lokiyamhi yathārahaṃ;

Nibbedhabhāvanākāle, chabbisuddhipavattiyaṃ.

They are also found appropriately in the mundane sphere during the preliminary stage, at the time of developing penetration, during the process of the six purifications.

208.

208.

Iccevaṃ [V 0.0021] tividhā bhedaṃ, vibhāveyya yathārahaṃ;

Sabhāvabhedabhinnānaṃ, sabhāgatthehi saṅgahaṃ.

Thus one should appropriately discern the threefold division, and the grouping by common essence of those things that are distinct by their individual natures and divisions.

209.

209.

Bhedasaṅgahavidūhi vaṇṇitaṃ, bhedasaṅgahavimuttisāsane;

Bhedasaṅgahanayatthamuttamaṃ, bhedasaṅgahamukhaṃ pakāsitaṃ.

Praised by those skilled in analysis and synthesis in the Dispensation of liberation through analysis and synthesis; the supreme goal of this method, this introduction to analysis and synthesis, has been declared.

210.

210.

Dhammasabhāvavibhāgabudhevaṃ, dhammadisampatisāsanadhamme;

Dhammavibhūtivibhūsitacittā, dhammarasāmatabhāgi bhavanti.

Thus the wise who understand the analysis of the nature of phenomena in the Dhamma of the Dispensation, their minds adorned with the splendor of the Dhamma, become partakers of the deathless taste of the Dhamma.

Iti nāmarūpaparicchede bhedasaṅgahavibhāgo nāma

Thus ends the section named 'The Division of Analysis and Synthesis' in the 'Analysis of Name-and-Form'.

Tatiyo paricchedo.

The Third Chapter.

4. Catuttho paricchedo

4. The Fourth Chapter.

Pakiṇṇakavibhāgo

The Miscellaneous Division.

211.

211.

Ito [M 0.0020] paraṃ kiccato ca, dvārālambaṇavatthuto;

Bhūmipuggalato ṭhānā, janakā ca yathārahaṃ.

Hereafter, by function, door, object, and base; by plane, person, and occasion; and by generating causes, as is appropriate.

212.

212.

Saṅgaho ca pavatti ca, paṭisandhipavattisu;

Cittuppādavaseneva, saṃkhipitvāna niyyate.

The compendium and the process, in rebirth-linking and in the course of existence, are concisely set forth by way of the arising of consciousness.

213.

213.

Rūpārūpamahāpākā, mupekkhātīraṇadvayaṃ;

Cutisandhibhavaṅgāni, cittānekūnavīsati.

The form-sphere, formless-sphere, and great resultant consciousnesses, and the two investigating consciousnesses accompanied by equanimity; these nineteen consciousnesses perform the functions of death, rebirth-linking, and life-continuum.

214.

214.

Āvajjanaṃ tu yugaḷaṃ, dassanaṃ savanaṃ tathā;

Ghāyanaṃ sāyanañceva, phusanaṃ sampaṭicchanaṃ.

Adverting is twofold; then seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and receiving.

215.

215.

Tīṇi tīraṇacittāni, ekaṃ voṭṭhabbanaṃ mataṃ;

Pañcadvāre manodvāre, tadāvajjananāmakaṃ.

Three are the investigating consciousnesses, and one is reckoned as determining; that which is named adverting occurs in the five doors and the mind-door.

216.

216.

Pañcapaññāsa [V 0.0022] javanakiccānīti viniddise;

Kriyā cāvajjanaṃ hitvā, kusalākusalapphalaṃ.

Fifty-five are designated as having the function of impulsion: the functional consciousnesses (excluding adverting), and the wholesome, unwholesome, and [supramundane] resultant consciousnesses.

217.

217.

Tadālambaṇacittāni, bhavantekādaseva hi;

Mahāvipākacittāni, aṭṭha santīraṇattayaṃ.

Indeed, there are just eleven registration consciousnesses: the eight great resultants and the three investigating consciousnesses.

218.

218.

Pañcakiccanti bhāsanti, upekkhātīraṇadvayaṃ;

Catukiccā mahāpākā, tikakiccā mahaggatā.

They say the two investigating consciousnesses with equanimity have five functions; the great resultants have four functions, and the sublime resultants have three.

219.

219.

Dukiccamiti voṭṭhabbaṃ, sukhatīraṇamīritaṃ;

Pañcaviññāṇajavanamanodhātuttikaṃ pana.

The determining consciousness and the investigating consciousness with joy are said to have two functions. The five sense-consciousnesses, the impulsion consciousnesses, and the mind-element triad, however,

220.

220.

Ekakiccāti bhāsanti, aṭṭhasaṭṭhi vibhāvino;

Iccevaṃ kiccabhedena, cittuppādā vavatthitā.

the wise declare that sixty-eight have a single function. Thus, by the distinction of function, are the arisings of consciousness established.

221.

221.

Cakkhusotaghānajivhā-kāyadhātu yathākkamaṃ;

Pañcadvārā bhavaṅgaṃ tu, manodvāraṃ pavuccati.

The eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body sensitivities are, in order, the five doors. The life-continuum, however, is called the mind-door.

222.

222.

Ghānādayo [M 0.0021] tayo rūpe, pañca cakkhādayo tathā;

Arūpe natthubhayattha, tadālambaṇamānasaṃ.

The three [senses] beginning with smell, and likewise the five beginning with sight, are related to matter. In the formless sphere, neither exist; [there,] registration consciousness does not occur.

223.

223.

Cha dvārā vīthicittāni, satta kāmīsu rūpisu;

Dvārattayaṃ cha cittāni, manodvāramarūpisu.

In desire-sphere beings, seven kinds of process-consciousness arise through six doors. In form-sphere beings, six kinds arise through three doors. In formless-sphere beings, [processes arise] only at the mind-door.

224.

224.

Paṭisandhādibhūtā hi, avasāne cutiṭṭhitā;

Majjhe bhavaṅgaṃ chetvāna, paccekaṃ vīthi jāyati.

Beginning with rebirth-linking and ending with death, a process arises for each object by interrupting the intervening life-continuum.

225.

225.

Rūpādārammaṇe cakkhu-pasādādimhi ghaṭṭite;

Āvajjanādayo honti, bhavaṅgadvicalā paraṃ.

When a visible object and so on impinges on eye-sensitivity and so on, adverting and the rest arise, after the life-continuum has vibrated twice.

226.

226.

Pariṇāme bhavaṅgassa, ālambe gahaṇārahe;

Tathā vīthi manodvāre, yathāsambhavato bhave.

At the turning point of the life-continuum, when the object is ready to be cognized, a process likewise occurs at the mind-door, according to what is possible.

227.

227.

Āvajjā pañcaviññāṇaṃ, sampaṭicchanatīraṇaṃ;

Voṭṭhabbakāmajavanaṃ, tadālambaṇamānasaṃ.

Adverting, five-sense-consciousness, receiving, investigating; determining, sense-sphere impulsion, and registration consciousness.

228.

228.

Sattevaṃ [V 0.0023] vīthicittāni, cittuppādā catuddasa;

Catupaññāsa vitthārā, pañcadvāre yathārahaṃ.

Thus there are seven kinds of process-consciousness, fourteen arisings of consciousness in a process, and fifty-four consciousnesses in detail, as is appropriate to the five doors.

229.

229.

Uppādaṭṭhitibhaṅgānaṃ, vasā cittakkhaṇaṃ tayaṃ;

Rūpānaṃ ṭhiti ekūna-paññāsañca duke dukaṃ.

A consciousness-moment has three phases: arising, presence, and dissolution. The duration of a material phenomenon consists of forty-nine [sub-moments of] presence, plus a pair [for arising and dissolution].

230.

230.

Parittetiparitte ca, mahantetimahantake;

Voṭṭhabbamoghajavanaṃ, tadālambanti taṃ kamā.

For the very slight, slight, great, and very great processes, the corresponding outcomes are, in sequence, [ending at] determining, futile impulsion, and registration.

231.

231.

Āvajjanañca javanaṃ, manodvāre tu gocare;

Vibhūte tu tadālambaṃ, vitthārā sattasaṭṭhi te.

At the mind-door with a clear object, there is adverting and impulsion; registration also occurs. In detail, these consciousnesses are sixty-seven.

232.

232.

Kāme javanasattāla-mbaṇānaṃ niyame sati;

Vibhūtetimahante ca, tadālambaṇamīritaṃ.

In the sense-sphere, when the rule for seven impulsions and for registration is met, registration is said to occur with a clear and very great object.

233.

233.

Pañcadvāre manodhātu, paccekamhi yathākkamaṃ;

Pañcaviññāṇayugaḷaṃ, paccekaṃ tu pakāsitaṃ.

In the five doors, the mind-element functions for each separately in due order; the pairs of fivefold sense-consciousness are likewise revealed individually for each.

234.

234.

Manodvāre tu javanaṃ, mahaggatamanuttaraṃ;

Sukhatīraṇavoṭṭhabbaṃ, parittajavanaṃ chasu.

At the mind-door, impulsion can be sublime or supramundane. Investigating with joy, determining, and sense-sphere impulsion occur in the six doors.

235.

235.

Mahāvipākacittāni[M 0.0022], upekkhātīraṇadvayaṃ;

Chasu dvāresu jāyanti, vīthimuttāni cekadā.

The great resultant consciousnesses and the two investigating consciousnesses with equanimity arise in the six doors, and are sometimes process-free.

236.

236.

Sattati vīthicittāni, vipākā tu mahaggatā;

Nava vīthivimuttā ca, duvidhāpi dasīritā.

Seventy are process-consciousnesses. The nine sublime resultants are process-free. The [other] ten are said to be of two kinds.

237.

237.

Iccevaṃ dvārabhedena, vibhāvetvā tato paraṃ;

Ñeyyā gocarabhedena, cittuppādā yathārahaṃ.

Thus, having distinguished by the division of doors, thereafter the arisings of consciousness should be understood by the division of objects, as is appropriate.

238.

238.

Rūpasaddagandharasaphoṭṭhabbā pañca gocarā;

Sesañca rūpapaññattināmañca dhammagocaraṃ.

Visible form, sound, odor, taste, and tangible object are the five sense objects. The remainder—subtle matter, concepts, and mentality—is the mental object.

239.

239.

Pañcadvāre vattamānaṃ, pañcālambaṃ yathākkamaṃ;

Chālambaṇaṃ manodvāre, atītānāgatampi ca.

In the five doors, the five objects occur in due order and are exclusively present. At the mind-door, the six objects can be past, future, or present.

240.

240.

Paññattātītavattantaṃ[V 0.0024], chadvāraggahitaṃ pana;

Chaḷārammaṇasaṅkhātaṃ, yebhuyyena bhavantare.

That which was grasped by the six doors—be it a concept, past, or present object, known as the sixfold object—for the most part conditions a future existence.

241.

241.

Nimittagatikammānaṃ, kammamevātha gocaraṃ;

Paṭisandhibhavaṅgānaṃ, cutiyāva yathārahaṃ.

The object at the time of death—be it kamma, a kamma-sign, or a sign of destiny—becomes, as is appropriate, the object for rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and the final death-consciousness.

242.

242.

Pañcālambe manodhātu, paccekamhi yathākkamaṃ;

Pañcaviññāṇayugaḷaṃ, paccekaṃ tu pakāsitaṃ.

The mind-element arises in relation to each of the five sense-objects individually and in due order; the pairs of fivefold consciousness are likewise revealed individually for each.

243.

243.

Kāmapākāni sesāni, hasanañca parittake;

Ñāṇahīnānipuññāni, javanāni animmale.

The remaining sense-sphere resultants and laughter take a limited object; the impulsions devoid of knowledge and the unwholesome impulsions take an impure object.

244.

244.

Tihetukāmapuññāni, puññābhiññā ca lokiyā;

Sabbālambe pavattanti, aggamaggaphalaṃ vinā.

The three-rooted sense-sphere wholesome consciousnesses and the mundane wholesome supernormal knowledges arise with any kind of object, except for the highest path and fruit.

245.

245.

Kriyābhiññā ca voṭṭhabbaṃ, kriyā kāme tihetukā;

Sabbālambe pavattanti, nibbāne nimmalā siyuṃ.

The functional supernormal knowledges, determining, and the three-rooted functional consciousnesses of the sense-sphere arise with any kind of object. The pure supramundane consciousnesses have Nibbāna as their object.

246.

246.

Dutiyañca catutthañca, āruppesu mahaggate;

Mahaggataññe vohāre, ayamālambaṇe nayo.

The second and fourth formless consciousnesses, and the other sublime consciousnesses, take a concept as their object. This is the method regarding objects.

247.

247.

Cakkhusotaghānajivhā-kāyahadayavatthunā;

Kāmaloke chavatthūni, nissitā satta dhātuyo.

In the sense-sphere world, seven consciousness-elements arise dependent on the six bases: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and the heart-base.

248.

248.

Pañcaviññāṇadhātū [M 0.0023] ca, tāsaṃ pubbāparattayaṃ;

Manodhātu tato sesā, manoviññāṇadhātu ca.

There are the five sense-consciousness-elements. The triad that precedes and follows them is the mind-element; the rest are the mind-consciousness-element.

249.

249.

Catasso dhātuyo rūpe, tīṇi vatthūni nissitā;

Arūpe tu anissāya, dhātvekāva pavattati.

In the form realm, four consciousness-elements arise depending on three bases. In the formless realm, one element proceeds without dependence.

250.

250.

Pañcappasāde nissāya, paccekaṃ tu yathākkamaṃ;

Pañcaviññāṇayugaḷaṃ, bhavatīti pakāsitaṃ.

It is declared that the pairs of fivefold consciousness arise depending on the five sensitivities, each in its respective turn.

251.

251.

Kāmapākāni sesāni, maggāvajjanamādito;

Hasanaṃ paṭighārūpā-vacaraṃ vatthunissitaṃ.

The remaining sense-sphere resultants, mind-door adverting, laughter, consciousness rooted in aversion, and form-sphere consciousnesses are dependent on a physical base.

252.

252.

Dvecattālīsa [V 0.0025] nissāya, anissāya ca jāyare;

Anissāya vipākāni, āruppeti samīritaṃ.

Forty-two arise dependently and also without dependence. The resultants of the formless sphere are said to arise without dependence.

253.

253.

Iccevaṃ vatthubhedena, cittuppādā pakāsitā;

Tato paraṃ vibhāveyya, bhūmibhedena paṇḍito.

Thus the arisings of consciousness have been explained by way of the distinction of base. Hereafter, the wise one should discriminate by way of the distinction of planes.

254.

254.

Niraye petaloke ca, tiracchānāsure tathā;

Pāpakammopapajjanti, pāpapākāya sandhiyā.

In hell, the realm of ghosts, the animal realm, and the asura realm, beings are reborn through evil kamma, with a rebirth-linking of evil-resultant consciousness.

255.

255.

Bhūmissitesu devesu, manussesupi hīnakā;

Ahetukāya jāyanti, puññapākāya sandhiyā.

Among the earth-bound devas and among inferior human beings, they are born with a rootless, wholesome-resultant rebirth-linking.

256.

256.

Cātumahārājikā ca, tāvatiṃsā ca yāmakā;

Tusitā ceva nimmānaratino vasavattino.

The Four Great Kings, the Tāvatiṃsa, the Yāma, the Tusita, the Nimmānaratī, and the Vasavattī.

257.

257.

Iccevaṃ chasu devesu, manussesu ca jāyare;

Mahāvipākasandhīhi, kāmapuññakatā janā.

Thus in these six deva realms and among humans are people reborn who have done sense-sphere meritorious deeds, with a great-resultant rebirth-linking.

258.

258.

Brahmānaṃ pārisajjā ca, tathā brahmapurohitā;

Mahābrahmā ca jāyanti, paṭhamajjhānasandhiyā.

The Brahmā's Retinue, the Brahmā's Ministers, and the Great Brahmās are born through a rebirth-linking corresponding to the first jhāna.

259.

259.

Parittā appamāṇābhā, jāyantābhassarā tathā;

Dutiyajjhānapākāya, tatiyāya ca sandhiyā.

The devas of Limited Radiance, Immeasurable Radiance, and Streaming Radiance are born with a resultant of the second jhāna and the third jhāna as their rebirth-linking.

260.

260.

Parittasubhappamāṇasubhā ca subhakiṇhakā;

Catutthāya tu jāyanti, tatiyajjhānabhūmikā.

The devas of Limited Glory, Immeasurable Glory, and Refulgent Glory are born from the plane of the third jhāna; those of the fourth arise from the fourth jhāna plane.

261.

261.

Vehapphalā [M 0.0024] asaññī ca, suddhāvāsāti sattasu;

Pañcamāya ca jāyanti, asaññīcittavajjitā.

The Greatly Fruitful, the non-percipient beings, and the Pure Abodes—in these seven planes they are born through the fourth jhāna. The non-percipient beings are devoid of consciousness.

262.

262.

Avihā ca atappā ca, sudassā ca sudassino;

Akaniṭṭhāti pañcete, suddhāvāsā pakāsitā.

Avihā, Atappā, Sudassā, Sudassī, and Akaniṭṭhā—these five are declared as the Pure Abodes.

263.

263.

Ākāsānañcāyatanapākādīhi yathākkamaṃ;

Ākāsānañcāyatanabhūmikādīsu jāyare.

Through the resultants of the base of infinite space and so on, beings are born respectively in the planes of the base of infinite space and so on.

264.

264.

Cutisandhibhavaṅgānaṃ[V 0.0026], vasā pākā mahaggatā;

Kāme sahetukā pākā, tadālambaṇatopi ca.

The sublime resultants function as death, rebirth-linking, and life-continuum. In the sense-sphere, the rooted resultants also function as registration.

265.

265.

Yathāvuttaniyāmena, bhūmīsvekāva jāyare;

Cittuppādesu sabbattha, na tvevāsaññino matā.

According to the stated rule, they arise in one plane only. In all these arisings of consciousness, however, they are never considered to be non-percipient beings.

266.

266.

Ghānajivhākāyadhātu-nissitaṃ mānasaṃ tathā;

Paṭighadvayamiccevamaṭṭha honteva kāmisu.

Nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness, as well as the two types of aversion—these eight exist only in the sense-sphere.

267.

267.

Cakkhusotañca viññāṇaṃ, manodhātu ca tīraṇaṃ;

Kāmarūpesu jāyanti, yathāsambhavato dasa.

Eye- and ear-consciousness, the mind-element, and investigating consciousness—these ten arise in the sense-sphere and form realms, as is possible.

268.

268.

Voṭṭhabbakāmapuññāni, vippayuttāni diṭṭhiyā;

Uddhaccasahitañceti, sabbatthetāni cuddasa.

Determining, sense-sphere wholesome consciousnesses, those dissociated from wrong view, and consciousness accompanied by restlessness—these fourteen are found everywhere.

269.

269.

Kaṅkhitaṃ diṭṭhiyuttāni, suddhāvāsavivajjite;

Sitañca rūpajavana-māruppāpāyavajjite.

Consciousness accompanied by doubt and that associated with wrong view are absent in the Pure Abodes. Laughter and the form-sphere javanas are absent in the formless and woeful planes.

270.

270.

Kāmakriyā sahetū ca, uddhaṃ lokuttarattayaṃ;

Catutthāruppajavanaṃ, sabbatthāpāyavajjite.

The rooted functional consciousnesses of the sense-sphere, the three higher supramundane consciousnesses, and the fourth formless-sphere javana—all these occur everywhere except in the woeful planes.

271.

271.

Sesamāruppajavanaṃ, hitvāpāyaṃ yathākkamaṃ;

Uddhamāruppabhūmiñca, jāyatīti vibhāvaye.

One should discern that the remaining formless-sphere javanas arise in the higher formless planes, respectively, abandoning the woeful planes.

272.

272.

Sotāpattiphalādīni, cattārānuttarāni tu;

Suddhāvāsamapāyañca, hitvā sabbattha jāyare.

The four supramundane fruitions, from stream-entry onwards, arise everywhere except in the Pure Abodes and the woeful planes.

273.

273.

Suddhāvāsamapāyañca, hitvārūpañca sabbathā;

Paṭhamānuttaro maggo, sesaṭṭhānesu jāyati.

The first supramundane path arises in the remaining places, excluding the Pure Abodes, the woeful planes, and the formless realm entirely.

274.

274.

Sattatiṃsa [M 0.0025] apāyesu, kāmesīti pakāsitā;

Pañcapaññāsa suddhesu, rūpesvekūnasattati.

Thirty-seven types of consciousness are declared in the woeful planes, eighty in the sense-sphere planes, fifty-five in the Pure Abodes, and sixty-nine in the form planes.

275.

275.

Chacattālīsa āruppe, uppajjanti yathārahaṃ;

Iccevaṃ bhūmibhedena, cittuppādā pakāsitā.

Forty-six arise in the formless planes, as is appropriate. Thus the arisings of consciousness are explained by the distinction of planes.

276.

276.

Tihetusatte [V 0.0027] sabbāni, dvihetukāhetuke pana;

Parittāni vivajjetvā, ñāṇapākakriyājave.

For a three-rooted being, all consciousnesses arise. For two-rooted and rootless beings, however, the limited ones arise, excluding the resultant and functional javanas associated with knowledge.

277.

277.

Puthujjanānaṃ sambhonti, diṭṭhiyuttañca kaṅkhitaṃ;

Sotāpannāditiṇṇampi, phalaṃ hoti yathāsakaṃ.

For worldlings, consciousness associated with wrong view and doubt can arise. For the three noble ones from the stream-enterer onwards, their own respective fruition arises.

278.

278.

Vītarāgassa javanaṃ, kriyā cantimanuttaraṃ;

Puthujjanāditiṇṇampi, paṭighaṃ samudīritaṃ.

For one who is free from lust, the javana is functional, and the final supramundane consciousness arises. Aversion is said to arise in the three individuals beginning with the worldling.

279.

279.

Javā puthujjanādīnaṃ, catunnaṃ sesa sāsavā;

Sāsavāvajjapākāni, pañcannamapi dīpaye.

The remaining javanas with taints belong to the four types of individuals from the worldling onwards. The tainted adverting and resultant consciousnesses should be shown for all five.

280.

280.

Puthujjanesu tesaṭṭhi, sotāpannādikadvaye;

Ekūnasaṭṭhi cittāni, anāgāmikapuggale.

For worldlings, sixty-three consciousnesses can arise; for the stream-enterer and once-returner, fifty-nine; for the non-returner, fifty-seven.

281.

281.

Sattapaññāsa jāyanti, tepaññāsa anāsave;

Maggaṭṭhesu sako maggo, puggalesu ayaṃ nayo.

Fifty-seven arise; fifty-three for the taintless one. For those established in the path, their own path arises. This is the method concerning individuals.

282.

282.

Tihetukāmacutiyā, sabbāpi paṭisandhiyo;

Dvihetāhetucutiyā, kāmāvacarasandhiyo.

Following the death of a three-rooted sense-sphere being, all rebirth-linkings are possible; following the death of a two-rooted or rootless being, only sense-sphere rebirth-linkings.

283.

283.

Rūpāvacaracutiyā, sahetupaṭisandhiyo;

Āruppāruppacutiyā, heṭṭhimāruppavajjitā.

Following death in the fine-material sphere, rebirth-linking with roots occurs. Following death in a formless sphere, rebirth-linking occurs in a formless sphere, excluding the one below.

284.

284.

Paṭisandhi tathā kāme, tihetupaṭisandhiyo;

Bhavantīti ca medhāvī, cutisandhinayaṃ naye.

Similarly, in the sense-sphere, three-rooted rebirth-linkings occur. Thus the wise one should understand the method concerning death and rebirth-linking.

285.

285.

Cutiyānantaraṃ hoti, paṭisandhi tato paraṃ;

Bhavaṅgaṃ taṃ pana chetvā, hoti āvajjanaṃ tato.

Immediately after death comes rebirth-linking; after that, the life-continuum. Then, having interrupted that, adverting arises.

286.

286.

Aniṭṭhe pāpapākāva, cakkhuviññāṇakādayo;

Iṭṭhe tu puññapākāva, yathāsambhavato siyuṃ.

In the case of an undesirable object, eye-consciousness and so on are the results of unwholesome kamma. But in the case of a desirable object, they are the results of wholesome kamma, as may be possible.

287.

287.

Pubbe [M 0.0026] vuttanayeneva, vīthicittāni yojaye;

Pañcadvāre yathāyogaṃ, manodvāre ca paṇḍito.

The wise one should apply the cognitive process consciousnesses in the way previously explained: at the five doors as is appropriate, and also at the mind-door.

288.

288.

Santīraṇatadālamba-miṭṭhālambe [V 0.0028] pavattati;

Sukhitaṃ iṭṭhamajjhatte, aniṭṭhe ca upekkhitaṃ.

Investigating and registration occur with a desirable object. With a desirable or neutral object, they are accompanied by pleasure; with an undesirable object, by equanimity.

289.

289.

Sukhopetaṃ tadālambaṃ, upekkhākriyato paraṃ;

Na hoti domanassamhā, somanassaṃ tu sabbadā.

Registration accompanied by pleasure does not occur after a functional consciousness with equanimity, nor after impulsion with displeasure; but it always occurs after impulsion with joy.

290.

290.

Tathopekkhātadālambaṃ, sukhitakriyato paraṃ;

Aññattha niyamo natthi, tadālambapavattiyā.

Similarly, registration with equanimity does not occur after a functional consciousness with pleasure. In other cases, there is no fixed rule for the occurrence of registration.

291.

291.

Somanassabhavaṅgassa, javane domanassite;

Tadālambe asambhonte, upekkhātīraṇaṃ bhave.

For one whose life-continuum is accompanied by joy, when the impulsion is with displeasure and registration does not occur, investigating with equanimity may arise.

292.

292.

Parikammopacārānu-lomagotrabhuto paraṃ;

Pañcamaṃ vā catutthaṃ vā, javanaṃ hoti appanā.

After preparation, access, conformity, and change-of-lineage, the fourth or the fifth impulsion becomes absorption.

293.

293.

Catujhānaṃ sukhopetaṃ, ñāṇayuttānanantaraṃ;

Upekkhāñāṇayuttānaṃ, pañcamaṃ jāyate paraṃ.

The four jhānas accompanied by pleasure arise immediately after a consciousness associated with knowledge. The fifth jhāna arises after a consciousness associated with equanimity and knowledge.

294.

294.

Puthujjanāna sekkhānaṃ, kāmapuññatihetuto;

Tihetukāmakriyato, vītarāgānamappanā.

For worldlings and trainees, absorption arises from three-rooted wholesome sense-sphere consciousness. For those free from lust, it arises from three-rooted sense-sphere functional consciousness.

295.

295.

Āvajjapañcaviññāṇa-sampaṭicchanatīraṇaṃ;

Paṭisandhicuti sabbā, rūpārūpādikappanā.

Adverting, the five sense-consciousnesses, receiving, and investigating; all rebirth-linking and death; and the fine-material and immaterial absorptions.

296.

296.

Nirodhā vuṭṭhahantassa, upariṭṭhaphalaṃ dvayaṃ;

Pañcābhiññā tathā maggā, ekacittakkhaṇā matā.

For one emerging from the attainment of cessation, the two higher fruits, the five supernormal knowledges, and the paths are considered to last for a single mind-moment.

297.

297.

Dvikkhattuṃ hi nirodhassa, samāpattikkhaṇe pana;

Catutthāruppajavanaṃ, tadālambañca sabbathā.

At the moment of attaining cessation, the impulsion of the fourth immaterial jhāna arises twice; but registration is entirely absent.

298.

298.

Dvikkhattuṃ vātha tikkhattuṃ, maggassānantaraṃ phalaṃ;

Bhavaṅgādi ca voṭṭhabbaṃ, javanādi sakiṃ pana.

Immediately after the path, the fruit consciousness arises two or three times. But the preceding moments—life-continuum, determining, impulsion, etc.—arise only once.

299.

299.

Tihetukāmajavanaṃ, appanāghaṭitaṃ pana;

Tikkhattuṃ vā catukkhattuṃ, manodvāre pavattati.

However, a three-rooted sense-sphere impulsion that leads to absorption occurs three or four times at the mind-door.

300.

300.

Chadvāresu [M 0.0027][V 0.0029] panaññattha, javanaṃ kāmadhātujaṃ;

Pañca vāre cha vā satta, samuppajjati sambhavā.

But elsewhere, in a process at the six doors, a sense-sphere impulsion arises five, six, or seven times, as may be possible.

301.

301.

Samāpattibhavaṅgesu, niyamo na samīrito;

Vīthicittāvasāne tu, bhavaṅgaṃ cuti vā bhave.

Regarding the life-continuum during an attainment, no fixed number is stated. But at the end of a cognitive process, either life-continuum or death occurs.

302.

302.

Iccānantarabhedena, cittuppādaṭṭhitiṃ cutiṃ;

Thus, by way of the analysis of immediate succession, the arising, presence, and dissolution of consciousness...

Ñatvā gaṇeyya saṅgayha, labbhamānavasā kathaṃ?

Having known and comprehended this, how should one calculate according to what is obtainable?

303.

303.

Pañcadvārāvajjanato, dasa cittāni dīpaye;

Sesāvajjanato pañca-cattālīsanti bhāsitaṃ.

After five-door adverting, ten consciousnesses are shown to arise; after the remaining adverting, it is said that forty-five arise.

304.

304.

Pañcaviññāṇato pāpavipākā sampaṭicchanā;

Paramekaṃ duve puñña-vipākā sampaṭicchanā.

After the five sense-consciousnesses that are unwholesome-resultant, one receiving consciousness arises. After those that are wholesome-resultant, two receiving consciousnesses arise.

305.

305.

Santīraṇadvihetumhā, pākā dvādasa jāyare;

Tihetukāmapākamhā, ekavīsati bhāsitaṃ.

From a two-rooted investigating consciousness, twelve resultants arise. From a three-rooted sense-sphere resultant, it is said that twenty-one arise.

306.

306.

Rūpāvacarapākamhā, paramekūnavīsati;

Navaṭṭhāruppapākamhā, satta cha vā yathākkamaṃ.

From a fine-material sphere resultant, at most nineteen arise. From an immaterial resultant preceded by nine or eight impulsions, seven or six arise respectively.

307.

307.

Paṭighamhā tu satteva, sitamhā terasabravuṃ;

Dvihetupuññāpuññamhā, ekavīsati bhāvaye.

From a consciousness rooted in aversion, only seven arise; from one accompanied by joy, they say thirteen arise. From a two-rooted wholesome or unwholesome consciousness, one should understand that twenty-one arise.

308.

308.

Dvihetukāmakriyato, aṭṭhārasa upekkhakā;

Sukhitamhā sattarasa, vibhāventi vicakkhaṇā.

The discerning analyze thus: from a two-rooted sense-sphere functional consciousness with equanimity, eighteen arise; from one with pleasure, seventeen arise.

309.

309.

Kāmapuññā tihetumhā, tettiṃseva upekkhakā;

Sukhitamhā tipaññāsa, bhavantīti pakāsitaṃ.

It is declared that from a three-rooted wholesome sense-sphere consciousness with equanimity, thirty-three arise; from one with pleasure, fifty-three arise.

310.

310.

Tihetukāmakriyato, catuvīsatipekkhakā;

Sukhitamhā tu dīpeyya, pañcavīsati paṇḍito.

The wise one should show that from a three-rooted sense-sphere functional consciousness with equanimity, twenty-four arise; but from one with pleasure, twenty-five.

311.

311.

Dasa rūpajavamhekādasa dvādasa terasa;

Yathākkamaṃ pañcadasa, āruppā paridīpaye.

From the fine-material impulsions, ten, eleven, twelve, and thirteen arise respectively; from the immaterial, one should show fifteen.

312.

312.

Phalamhā [V 0.0030] cuddasevāhu, maggamhā tu sakaṃ phalaṃ;

Paraṃ saṅgahamiccevaṃ, vigaṇeyya visārado.

They say that from a fruition consciousness, fourteen arise; but from a path consciousness, its own fruit arises. Thus the expert should further analyze this compendium.

313.

313.

Pañcadasamhādyāvajja-mekavīsatitoparaṃ[M 0.0028];

Ekamhā pañcaviññāṇaṃ, pañcamhā sampaṭicchanaṃ.

Adverting arises from fifteen states; the next, from twenty-one. The five sense-consciousnesses arise from one; receiving consciousness arises from five.

314.

314.

Sukhasantīraṇaṃ hoti, pañcavīsatito paraṃ;

Sambhonti sattatiṃsamhā, upekkhātīraṇadvayaṃ.

Investigating with pleasure occurs after twenty-five states. The two investigating consciousnesses with equanimity arise from thirty-seven states.

315.

315.

Bhavanti cattālīsamhā, sukhapākā dvihetukā;

Tathekacattālīsamhā, sukhapākā dvihetukā;

Tathekacattālīsamhā, upekkhāya samāyutā.

Two-rooted resultants with pleasure arise from forty states; likewise, those associated with equanimity arise from forty-one.

316.

316.

Honti sattatito kāme,

Sukhapākā tihetukā;

Dvisattatimhā jāyanti,

Upekkhāsahitā puna.

From seventy sense-sphere states arise three-rooted resultants with pleasure. Again, from seventy-two arise those accompanied by equanimity.

317.

317.

Ekūnasaṭṭhito rūpā, pākā pākā arūpino;

Kamāṭṭhacattālīsamhā, tathekadvitihīnato.

The fine-material resultants arise from fifty-nine states. The immaterial resultants arise from forty-eight, and likewise from that number less one and less two, respectively.

318.

318.

Phaladvayaṃ catukkamhā, pañcamhāntaphaladvayaṃ;

Tikā mahaggatā javā, maggā kāmajavā dvayā.

The two lower fruits arise from four states; the final two fruits from five. The sublime impulsions arise from three; the paths and sense-sphere impulsions, from two.

319.

319.

Cittuppādānamiccevaṃ, gaṇito pubbasaṅgaho;

Ñeyyoyaṃ ṭhānabhedoti, pubbāparaniyāmito.

Thus is reckoned the preceding summary of the arisings of consciousness. This should be known as the analysis of conditions, which is determined by what precedes and what follows.

320.

320.

Rūpapākamahāpākā, manodhātu ca tīraṇaṃ;

Rūpameva janentīti, vuttā ekūnavīsati.

The fine-material resultants, the great resultants, the mind-element, and investigating consciousness: these nineteen are said to generate only matter.

321.

321.

Appanājavanaṃ sabbaṃ, mahaggatamanuttaraṃ;

Iriyāpatharūpāni, janetīti samīritaṃ.

All absorption impulsions—sublime and supramundane—are said to generate the material phenomena of posture.

322.

322.

Voṭṭhabbaṃ [V 0.0031] kāmajavanamabhiññā ca yathārahaṃ;

Iriyāpathaviññattirūpānaṃ janakā siyuṃ.

Determining, sense-sphere impulsions, and the supernormal knowledges, as appropriate, may be producers of the material phenomena of posture and intimation.

323.

323.

Pañcaviññāṇamāruppā, vipākā ca na kiñcipi;

Sabbesaṃ paṭisandhī ca, cuti cārahato tathā.

The five sense-consciousnesses and the immaterial resultants produce no matter whatsoever; likewise, all rebirth-linking consciousnesses and the death consciousness of an Arahant.

324.

324.

Rūpādittayamiccevaṃ[M 0.0029], samuṭṭhāpeti mānasaṃ;

Uppajjamānameveti, ñeyyo janakasaṅgaho.

Thus the mind, as it arises, generates the three kinds of matter. This should be known as the summary of generation.

325.

325.

Iti kiccādibhedesu, paccekasmiṃ pakāsitaṃ;

Nayaṃ vuttānusārena, samāsetvā viyojaye.

Thus, for each of the divisions by way of function and so on, it has been explained. Following the method that has been stated, one should summarize and analyze.

326.

326.

Panuṇṇasammohamalassa sāsane,

Vikiṇṇavatthūhi suganthitaṃ nayaṃ;

Pakiṇṇamogayha paratthaninnaye,

Vitiṇṇakaṅkhāva bhavanti paṇḍitā.

In the Dispensation which dispels the stain of delusion, this method is well-composed from scattered topics. By plunging into this miscellany to determine the meaning for the good of others, the wise overcome all doubt.

327.

327.

Bahunayavinibandhaṃ kullametaṃ gahetvā,

Jinavacanasamuddaṃ kāmamogayha dhīrā;

Hitasakalasamatthaṃ vatthusāraṃ haritvā,

Hadaya ratanagabbhaṃ sādhu sampūrayanti.

Taking this raft bound together by many methods, the wise plunge at will into the ocean of the Conqueror's word. Having extracted the essential substance, capable of benefiting all, they fill well the jewel-chamber of their hearts.

Iti nāmarūpaparicchede pakiṇṇakavibhāgo nāma

Thus ends the chapter named the Miscellaneous Section in the Delimitation of Mind and Matter.

Catuttho paricchedo.

The Fourth Chapter.

5. Pañcamo paricchedo

5. The Fifth Chapter.

Kammavibhāgo

The Analysis of Kamma.

328.

328.

Vibhāgaṃ [V 0.0032] pana kammānaṃ,

Pavakkhāmi ito paraṃ;

Kammapākakriyābhede,

Amohāya samāsato.

Now, from here on, I shall concisely explain the classification of kammas, regarding the distinctions of kamma, its result, and functional consciousness, for the dispelling of delusion.

329.

329.

Kammapaccayakammanti, cetanāva samīritā;

Tatthāpi nānakkhaṇikā, puññāpuññāva cetanā.

Kamma as a condition for kamma is said to be volition itself. Therein, those volitions, occurring at different moments, are wholesome and unwholesome.

330.

330.

Deti pākamadhiṭṭhāya, sampayutte yathārahaṃ;

Kammassāyūhanaṭṭhena, pavattattā hi cetanā.

For volition, since it occurs for the purpose of accumulating kamma, gives its result, having appropriately determined the associated states.

331.

331.

Klesānusayasantāne[M 0.0030], pākadhammā hi jāyare;

Pahīnānusayānaṃ tu, kriyāmattaṃ pavattati.

In the continuity of latent defilements, resultant states indeed arise; but for those who have abandoned the latent tendencies, only mere functional activity occurs.

332.

332.

Mūlabhāvā ca sabbesaṃ, tathevāvajjanadvayaṃ;

Janitāni ca kammehi, vipākāni pavattare.

And because of the root-nature of all, and likewise the two kinds of adverting, the results generated by kamma occur.

333.

333.

Cittuppādavaseneva, kammaṃ tettiṃsadhā ṭhitaṃ;

Kammacatukkabhedehi, vibhāveyya vicakkhaṇo.

By way of the arising of consciousness, kamma is established in thirty-three ways. The wise one should analyze it by the distinctions of the fourfold kamma.

334.

334.

Paccuppannādikaṇhādi-janakādigarādito;

Diṭṭhadhammādikāmādi-bhedā chadhā yathākkamaṃ.

The distinctions are sixfold in due order: (1) concerning the present, etc.; (2) dark, etc.; (3) generative, etc.; (4) weighty, etc.; (5) immediately effective, etc.; and (6) concerning the sensual sphere, etc.

335.

335.

Yaṃ pāpaṃ sukhavokiṇṇaṃ, akicchena karīyati;

Paccuppannasukhaṃ kammaṃ, āyatiṃ dukkhapākajaṃ.

Whatever evil deed mixed with pleasure is done without difficulty, that kamma brings pleasure in the present but has a painful result in the future.

336.

336.

Kicchena dukkhavokiṇṇaṃ, yadi pāpaṃ karīyati;

Paccuppanne ca taṃ dukkhaṃ, āyatiṃ dukkhapākajaṃ.

If an evil deed mixed with pain is done with difficulty, that kamma is painful in the present and has a painful result in the future.

337.

337.

Kicchena [V 0.0033] dukkhavokiṇṇaṃ, yadi puññaṃ karīyati;

Paccuppannamhi taṃ dukkhaṃ, āyatiṃ sukhapākajaṃ.

If a meritorious deed mixed with pain is done with difficulty, that kamma is painful in the present but has a pleasant result in the future.

338.

338.

Yaṃ puññaṃ sukhavokiṇṇaṃ, akicchena karīyati;

Paccuppannasukhañceva, āyatiṃ sukhapākajaṃ.

Whatever meritorious deed mixed with pleasure is done without difficulty, that kamma brings pleasure in the present and has a pleasant result in the future.

339.

339.

Visasaṃsaṭṭhamadhuraṃ, savisaṃ tittakaṃ tathā;

Gomuttamadhubhesajja-miccopammaṃ yathākkamaṃ.

The similes in due order are: sweetness mixed with poison; likewise, bitter poison; medicinal cow's urine; and honey.

340.

340.

Samādāne vipāke ca, sukhadukkhappabheditaṃ;

Kammamevaṃ catuddhāti, pakāsenti tathāgatā.

The Tathāgatas declare that kamma is thus fourfold, distinguished by pleasure and pain in its undertaking and in its result.

341.

341.

Ānantariyakammādi, ekantakaṭukāvahaṃ;

Kaṇhaṃ kaṇhavipākanti, kammaṃ duggatigāmikaṃ.

Kamma such as the heinous offenses, which brings exclusively bitter results, is called 'dark with a dark result'—kamma that leads to a woeful destination.

342.

342.

Paṭhamajjhānakammādi, ekantena sukhāvahaṃ;

Sukkaṃ sukkavipākanti, kammaṃ saggūpapattikaṃ.

Kamma such as that of the first jhāna, which brings exclusive happiness, is called 'bright with a bright result'—kamma that leads to rebirth in heaven.

343.

343.

Vokiṇṇakamma [M 0.0031] vokiṇṇa-sukhadukkhūpapattikaṃ;

Kaṇhasukkaṃ kaṇhasukka-vipākanti samīritaṃ.

Mixed kamma, which leads to the attainment of mixed pleasure and pain, is called 'dark-and-bright with a dark-and-bright result.'

344.

344.

Akaṇhasukkamīrenti, akaṇhasukkapākadaṃ;

Kammaṃ lokuttaraṃ loke, gatikammakkhayāvahaṃ.

The supramundane kamma, which brings about the destruction of kamma that leads to a destination, is called 'neither-dark-nor-bright' with a 'neither-dark-nor-bright' result.

345.

345.

Iti vaṭṭappavattamhi, klesavodānabheditaṃ;

Kammakkhayena saṅgayha, catudhā kammamīritaṃ.

Thus kamma is said to be fourfold: distinguished by defilement and purity within the course of the round of existence, and including that which leads to the exhaustion of kamma.

346.

346.

Janakañcevupatthambha-mupapīḷopaghātakaṃ;

Catudhā kiccabhedena, kammamevaṃ pavuccati.

Kamma is spoken of as fourfold by distinction of function: generative, supportive, obstructive, and destructive.

347.

347.

Janeti janakaṃ pākaṃ, taṃ chindatupapīḷakaṃ;

Taṃ pavattetupatthambhaṃ, taṃ ghātetopaghātakaṃ.

Generative kamma produces its result. Obstructive kamma obstructs it. Supportive kamma maintains it. Destructive kamma destroys it.

348.

348.

Karoti attano pāka-ssāvakāsanti bhāsitaṃ;

Pākadāyakakammaṃ tu, yaṃ kiñci janakaṃ bhave.

It is said that it creates an opportunity for its own result. Any kamma whatsoever that is generative may be a result-giving kamma.

349.

349.

Bādhamānakakammaṃ [V 0.0034] tu, taṃ pākamupapīḷakaṃ;

Upaghātakamīrenti, tadupacchedakaṃpare.

Obstructive kamma is that which obstructs the result. Destructive kamma is called that which cuts off the result of another kamma.

350.

350.

Garukāsannamāciṇṇaṃ, kaṭattākammunā saha;

Kammaṃ catubbidhaṃ pāka-pariyāyappabhedato.

Weighty, proximate, habitual, and residual kamma: thus kamma is fourfold, distinguished by the order of its ripening.

351.

351.

Mahaggatānantariyaṃ, garukammanti vuccati;

Kataṃ cintitamāsanna-māsannamaraṇena tu.

Sublime and heinous kamma are called weighty kamma. Proximate kamma is that which is done or remembered by one who is near death.

352.

352.

Bāhullena samāciṇṇamāciṇṇanti pavuccati;

Sesaṃ puññamapuññañca, kaṭattākammamīritaṃ.

What is frequently practiced is called habitual kamma. The remaining wholesome and unwholesome kamma is called residual kamma.

353.

353.

Diṭṭhadhamme vedanīyamupapajjāpare tathā;

Pariyāyavedanīyamiti cāhosikammunā.

Immediately effective, subsequently effective, indefinitely effective, and defunct kamma.

354.

354.

Pākakālavasenātha, kālātītavasena ca;

Catudhevampi akkhātaṃ, kammamādiccabandhunā.

Now, by way of the time of ripening and by way of having passed its time, kamma has been declared as fourfold by the Kinsman of the Sun.

355.

355.

Diṭṭhadhamme vedanīyaṃ, paṭhamaṃ javanaṃ bhave;

Aladdhāsevanattāva, asamatthaṃ bhavantare.

Immediately effective kamma is the first impulsion. Because it does not obtain repetition, it is incapable of giving a result in another existence.

356.

356.

Vedanīyaṃ [M 0.0032] tupapajjapariyosānamīritaṃ;

Pariniṭṭhitakammattā, vipaccati anantare.

Subsequently effective kamma is said to be the final impulsion. Because it is a completed kamma, it ripens in the immediately following life.

357.

357.

Sesāni vedanīyāni, pariyāyāpare pana;

Laddhāsevanato pākaṃ, janenti sati paccaye.

The remaining kamma to be experienced is indefinitely effective. Being the intermediate impulsions, they produce a result whenever the necessary conditions are obtained.

358.

358.

Vuccantāhosikammāni, kālātītāni sabbathā;

Ucchinnataṇhāmūlāni, paccayālābhato tathā.

Kamma is called defunct when it has completely passed its time for ripening, when its root of craving has been eradicated, or when it fails to obtain the necessary conditions.

359.

359.

Catudhā puna kāmādibhūmibhedena bhāsitaṃ;

Puññāpuññavasā dvedhā, kāmāvacarikaṃ bhave.

Again, kamma is spoken of as fourfold by the distinction of spheres, beginning with the sensual sphere. By way of the wholesome and unwholesome, sensual-sphere kamma is twofold.

360.

360.

Apuññaṃ tattha sāvajja-maniṭṭhaphaladāyakaṃ;

Therein, unwholesome kamma is blameworthy and gives an undesirable result.

Taṃ kammaphassadvārehi, duvidhaṃ sampavattati.+

It proceeds in two ways: by way of the kamma-doors and by way of the contact-doors.

361.

361.

Kāyadvāraṃ [V 0.0035] vacīdvāraṃ, manodvāranti tādinā;

Kammadvārattayaṃ vuttaṃ, phassadvārā cha dīpitā.

The body-door, the speech-door, and the mind-door: these are the three kamma-doors stated by the Such a One. The six contact-doors have also been explained.

362.

362.

Kammadvāre manodvāre, pañcadvārā samohitā;

Phassadvāramanodvāraṃ, kammadvārattayaṃ kataṃ.

The five doors are included in the mind-door, which is a kamma-door. The contact-doors and the mind-door are thus reckoned as the three kamma-doors.

363.

363.

Tathā hi kāyaviññattiṃ, janetvā jātacetanā;

Kāyakammaṃ vacīkammaṃ, vacībhedapavattikā.

For when a volition that has arisen generates bodily intimation, it is bodily kamma. Verbal kamma is that which occurs with the breaking forth of speech.

364.

364.

Viññattidvayasampattā, manokammanti vuccati;

Bhedoyaṃ pariyāyena, kammānamiti dīpito.

That which is accomplished without the two kinds of intimation is called mental kamma. This distinction of kammas is explained as being figurative.

365.

365.

Pāṇaghātādikaṃ kammaṃ, kāye bāhullavuttito;

Kāyakammaṃ vacīkammaṃ, musāvādādikaṃ tathā.

Kamma such as killing living beings is called bodily kamma because it occurs mostly through the body; likewise, kamma such as false speech is called verbal kamma.

366.

366.

Abhijjhādi manokammaṃ, tīsu dvāresu jāyati;

Dvīsu dvāresu sesāni, bhedoyaṃ paramatthato.

Mental kamma such as covetousness arises at the three doors; the other kinds of kamma arise at two doors. This is the distinction in the ultimate sense.

367.

367.

Phassadvāramanodvāre, viññattidvayamīritaṃ;

Pañcadvāre dvayaṃ natthi, ayamettha vinicchayo.

The two kinds of intimation are said to occur at the mind-door, which is a contact-door. At the five doors, the two do not occur. This is the ascertainment here.

368.

368.

Akkhantiñāṇa kosajjaṃ, dussilyaṃ muṭṭhasaccatā;

Iccāsaṃvarabhedena, aṭṭhadvāresu jāyati.

Lack of patience, ignorance, laziness, immorality, and forgetfulness: these arise at the eight doors by way of the breach of restraint.

369.

369.

Kammadvārattayañceva[M 0.0033], pañcadvārā tathāpare;

Asaṃvarānaṃ pañcannaṃ, aṭṭha dvārā pakāsitā.
