The three kamma-doors and the other five doors: for the five kinds of non-restraint, these eight doors are declared.

370.

370.

Tattha kammapathappattaṃ, paṭisandhiphalāvahaṃ;

Pāṇaghātādibhedena, dasadhā sampavattati.

Therein, that which constitutes a course of action and brings the result of rebirth-linking proceeds in ten ways, distinguished as killing living beings and so on.

371.

371.

Pāṇātipāto pharusaṃ, byāpādo ca tathāparo;

Iccevaṃ tividhaṃ kammaṃ, dosamūlehi jāyati.

Killing living beings, harsh speech, and ill will: these three kinds of kamma arise from the root of aversion.

372.

372.

Micchācāro abhijjhā ca, micchādiṭṭhi tathāparā;

Iccevaṃ tividhaṃ kammaṃ, lobhamūlehi jāyati.

Sexual misconduct, covetousness, and wrong view: these three kinds of kamma arise from the root of greed.

373.

373.

Theyyādānaṃ [V 0.0036] musāvādo, pisuṇaṃ samphalāpanaṃ;

Kammaṃ catubbidhammetaṃ, dvimūlehi pavattati.

Taking what is not given, false speech, slanderous speech, and frivolous chatter: these four kinds of kamma proceed from two roots.

374.

374.

Chandādosā bhayā mohā, pāpaṃ kubbanti pāṇino;

Tasmā chandādibhedena, cattālīsavidhaṃ bhave.

Beings commit evil through desire, aversion, fear, and delusion. Therefore, by the distinctions beginning with desire, it becomes fortyfold.

375.

375.

Iccāpuññaṃ pakāsenti, caturāpāyasādhakaṃ;

Aññatthāpi pavattamhi, vipattiphalasādhanaṃ.

Thus they explain unwholesome kamma, which leads to the four woeful states; and even when occurring elsewhere, it brings the result of misfortune.

376.

376.

Tividhaṃ pana puññaṃ tu, anavajjiṭṭhapākadaṃ;

Dānaṃ sīlaṃ bhāvanā ca, tīsu dvāresu jāyati.

But wholesome kamma is threefold, giving a blameless and desirable result: giving, virtue, and mental development. These arise at the three doors.

377.

377.

Mahattagāravā snehā, dayā saddhupakārato;

Bhogajīvābhayadhammaṃ, dadato dānamīritaṃ.

When one gives wealth, life, safety, and the Dhamma out of greatness, respect, affection, compassion, faith, or helpfulness, it is called giving.

378.

378.

Puññamācāravāritta-vattamārabbha kubbato;

Pāpā ca viramantassa, hoti sīlamayaṃ tadā.

For one who undertakes wholesome conduct, avoidance, and observances, and who refrains from evil, it then becomes kamma consisting in virtue.

379.

379.

Dānasīlavinimuttaṃ, bhāvanāti pavuccati;

Puññaṃ bhāventi santāne, yasmā tena hitāvahaṃ.

That which is distinct from giving and virtue is called mental development. Because one thereby develops wholesome states in one's mental continuity, it is beneficial.

380.

380.

Janetvā kāyaviññattiṃ, yadā puññaṃ karīyati;

Kāyakammaṃ tadā hoti, dānaṃ sīlañca bhāvanā.

When one does a meritorious deed—whether giving, virtue, or mental development—by generating bodily intimation, it is then bodily kamma.

381.

381.

Vacīviññattiyā [M 0.0034] saddhiṃ, yadā puññaṃ karīyati;

Vacīkammaṃ manokammaṃ, vinā viññattiyā kataṃ.

When a meritorious deed is done together with verbal intimation, it is verbal kamma. Mental kamma is that which is done without intimation.

382.

382.

Taṃtaṃdvārikamevāhu, taṃtaṃdvārikapāpato;

Viramantassa viññattiṃ, vinā vā saha vā puna.

For one who abstains from an evil deed pertaining to a particular door, that abstinence is called kamma of that same door, whether it occurs with or without intimation.

383.

383.

Dānaṃ sīlaṃ bhāvanā ca, veyyāvaccāpacāyanā;

Pattānumodanā patti-dānaṃ dhammassa desanā;

Savanaṃ diṭṭhijukamma-miccevaṃ dasadhā ṭhitaṃ.

Giving, virtue, mental development, service, reverence, rejoicing in merit, transference of merit, teaching the Dhamma, listening to the Dhamma, and straightening one's view: thus it is established in ten ways.

384.

384.

Kāmapuññaṃ [V 0.0037] pakāsenti, kāme sugatisādhakaṃ;

Aññatthāpi pavattamhi, sampattiphalasādhakaṃ.

They declare sensual-sphere merit to be that which leads to a happy destination in the sensual realm; and even when occurring elsewhere, it brings the result of good fortune.

385.

385.

Cittuppādappabhedena, kammaṃ vīsatidhā ṭhitaṃ;

Kāmāvacaramiccevaṃ, vibhāventi vibhāvino.

By the distinction in the arising of consciousness, kamma is established in twenty ways. Thus the wise explain sensual-sphere kamma.

386.

386.

Rūpāvacarikaṃ kamma-mappanābhāvanāmayaṃ;

Kasiṇādikamārabbha, manodvāre pavattati.

Form-sphere kamma consists in absorption-development. Taking a kasiṇa or other such object, it proceeds at the mind-door.

387.

387.

Pathavāpo ca tejo ca,

Vāyo nīlañca pītakaṃ;

Lohitodātamākāsaṃ,

Ālokoti visāradā.

Earth, water, fire, and air; blue, yellow, red, and white; space, and light: so say the experts.

388.

388.

Kasiṇāni dasīrenti, ādikammikayogino;

Uddhumātaṃ vinīlañca, vipubbakaṃ vikhāditaṃ.

The ten kasinas are spoken of for beginner yogis. The bloated, the livid, the festering, and the gnawed,

389.

389.

Vicchiddakañca vikkhittaṃ, hatavikkhittalohitaṃ;

Puḷavaṃ aṭṭhikañceti, asubhaṃ dasadhā ṭhitaṃ.

the dismembered, the scattered, the hacked and scattered, the bleeding, the worm-infested, and the skeleton: thus the foul meditations are established as tenfold.

390.

390.

Buddhe dhamme ca saṅghe ca, sīle cāge ca attano;

Devatopasamāyañca, vuttānussatibhāvanā.

The development of recollection is spoken of concerning: the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha; one's own virtue and generosity; and the deities and peace.

391.

391.

Maraṇe sati nāmekā, tathā kāyagatāsati;

Ānāpānasaticcevaṃ, dasadhānussatīritā.

Mindfulness of death, mindfulness directed to the body, and mindfulness of breathing: thus the ten recollections are declared.

392.

392.

Mettā [M 0.0035] karuṇā muditā, upekkhā bhāvanāti ca;

Catubrahmavihārā ca, appamaññāti bhāsitā.

The development of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity: these are the four divine abodes, and they are also called the boundless states.

393.

393.

Āhāre tu paṭikkūla-saññekāti pakāsitā;

Catudhātuvavatthānaṃ, catudhātupariggaho.

The perception of repulsiveness in food is declared as one. The analysis of the four elements is the defining of the four elements.

394.

394.

Cattāroruppakā ceti, cattālīsa samāsato;

Kammaṭṭhānāni vuttāni, samathe bhāvanānaye.

And the four formless states: thus, in brief, forty meditation subjects are spoken of in the method for developing serenity.

395.

395.

Ānāpānañca [V 0.0038] kasiṇaṃ, pañcakajjhānikaṃ tahiṃ;

Paṭhamajjhānikā vuttā, koṭṭhāsāsubhabhāvanā.

Therein, mindfulness of breathing and the kasinas are of the fivefold jhānas. The development of the foulness meditations and the parts of the body are said to be of the first jhāna.

396.

396.

Mettādayo catujjhānā, upekkhā pañcamī matā;

Āruppāruppakā sesā, upacārasamādhikā.

Loving-kindness and the others lead to the four jhānas; equanimity is considered to lead to the fifth. The formless meditations lead to the formless attainments; the remaining subjects lead only to access concentration.

397.

397.

Kasiṇāsubhakoṭṭhāse,

Ānāpāne ca jāyati;

Paṭibhāgo tamārabbha,

Tattha vattati appanā.

In the kasiṇas, the foulness meditations, the parts of the body, and in mindfulness of breathing, a counterpart sign arises. Taking that as its object, absorption proceeds there.

398.

398.

Kammaṭṭhānesu sesesu, paṭibhāgo na vijjati;

Tathā hi sattavohāre, appamaññā pavattare.

In the remaining meditation subjects, no counterpart sign is found; for the illimitables proceed in respect to the conventional designation of beings.

399.

399.

Kasiṇugghāṭimākāsaṃ, paṭhamāruppamānasaṃ;

Paṭhamāruppakābhāva-mākiñcaññañca gocaraṃ.

Space from the removal of the kasiṇa, the mind of the first formless attainment, the absence of the first formless attainment, and the base of nothingness serve as the respective objects.

400.

400.

Āruppā sampavattanti, ālambitvā yathākkamaṃ;

Aññattha pana sabbattha, nappavattati appanā.

The formless attainments proceed in sequence, taking the preceding one as their object; but in all other cases, absorption does not occur.

401.

401.

Parikammaṃ parikamma-samādhi ca tato paraṃ;

Upacārappanā ceti, bhāvanāyaṃ catubbidhaṃ.

Preliminary preparation, preparatory concentration, and after that access and absorption—thus development is fourfold.

402.

402.

Parikammanimittañca, uggaho ca tato paraṃ;

Paṭibhāgoti tīṇeva, nimittāni pakāsayuṃ.

The preparatory sign, the learning sign, and then the counterpart sign—thus they have declared three signs.

403.

403.

Nimittaṃ gaṇhato pubba-mādikammikayogino;

Parikammanimittanti, kasiṇādikamīritaṃ.

For a beginning yogi, the sign first grasped—such as a kasiṇa and so on—is called the preparatory sign.

404.

404.

Tasmiṃ [M 0.0036] pana nimittamhi, ārabhantassa bhāvanaṃ;

Paṭhamaṃ parikammanti, bhāvanāpi pavuccati.

When one undertakes development based on that sign, the initial development itself is called 'preliminary preparation'.

405.

405.

Cittenuggahite tasmiṃ, manodvāre vibhāvite;

Taduggahanimittaṃ tu, samuppannanti vuccati.

When that sign has been apprehended by the mind and has become clear at the mind-door, then the learning sign is said to have arisen.

406.

406.

Pañcadvāravinimuttā[V 0.0039], tamārabbha samāhitā;

Parikammasamādhīti, bhāvanā sā pakāsitā.

That development—freed from the five sense-doors and concentrated upon that sign—is declared to be 'preparatory concentration'.

407.

407.

Uggahākārasambhūtaṃ, vatthudhammavimuccitaṃ;

Paṭibhāganimittanti, bhāvanāmayamīritaṃ.

Arisen from the appearance of the learning sign and freed from the material basis, the counterpart sign is said to be born of mental development.

408.

408.

Rūpādivisayaṃ hitvā, tamārabbha tato paraṃ;

Bhavaṅgantaritaṃ hutvā, manodvāraṃ pavattati.

Having abandoned the object of form and so on, and then taking that sign as its object, the mind-door process occurs, after being interrupted by the life-continuum.

409.

409.

Sikhāpattasamādhāna-mupaklesavimuccitaṃ;

Upacārasamādhīti, kāmāvacaramīritaṃ.

The concentration that has reached its peak and is freed from the hindrances is called 'access concentration'; it is said to belong to the sense sphere.

410.

410.

Paṭibhāganimittamhi, upacārasamādhito;

Bhāvanābalanipphannā, samuppajjati appanā.

From access concentration on the counterpart sign, absorption arises, produced by the power of development.

411.

411.

Purimaṃ purimaṃ katvā, vasībhūtaṃ tato paraṃ;

Oḷārikaṅgamohāya, sukhumaṅgappavattiyā.

Having gained mastery over each preceding stage, one proceeds to the next for the sake of abandoning a grosser factor and for the arising of a subtler one.

412.

412.

Appanā padahantassa, pavattati yathākkamaṃ;

Vitakkādivinimuttā, vicārādisamāyutā.

For one who strives, absorption proceeds in due order, becoming free from initial application and so on, while accompanied by sustained application and so on.

413.

413.

Āvajjanā ca vasitā, taṃsamāpajjanā tathā;

Vuṭṭhānādhiṭṭhānā pacca-vekkhaṇāti ca pañcadhā.

Adverting, entering the attainment, resolving, emerging, and reviewing—mastery is thus fivefold.

414.

414.

Vitakkañca vicārañca, sahātikkamato pana;

Catukkajjhānamappeti, pañcakañca visuṃ visuṃ.

By overcoming initial and sustained application together, one attains the jhānas of the fourfold system; by overcoming them separately, one attains the jhānas of the fivefold system.

415.

415.

Appanāya ca paccekajhānassāpi visuṃ visuṃ;

Icchitabbā hi sabbattha, parikammādibhāvanā.

For absorption, and for each jhāna separately, the development of the preliminary stages and so on should be undertaken in every case.

416.

416.

Taṃ parittaṃ majjhimañca, paṇītanti vibhajjati;

Vimokkho ca vasībhūtamabhibhāyatananti ca.

That jhāna is divided as limited, middling, and excellent; and also as liberation, as the state of mastery, and as the bases of overcoming.

417.

417.

Parittādi [M 0.0037] parittādigocaranti catubbidhaṃ;

Dukkhāpaṭipadaṃ dandhābhiññamiccādito tathā.

It is fourfold as limited and so on, with a limited and so on object; and likewise fourfold as painful practice with slow direct knowledge, and so on.

418.

418.

Taṃ [V 0.0040] chandacittavīriyavīmaṃsādhippateyyato;

Visesaṭṭhitinibbedhahānabhāgiyatopi ca.

It is classified by the predominance of zeal, consciousness, energy, and investigation; and also as being conducive to distinction, to stability, to penetration, or to decline.

419.

419.

Pañcadhā jhānabhedena, catudhālambabhedato;

Samādhibhāvanāpuññamappanāpattamīritaṃ.

The meritorious kamma of concentration development that has reached absorption is said to be fivefold by the division of jhāna and fourfold by the division of its object.

420.

420.

Iti vikkhambhitaklesaṃ, rūpalokūpapattikaṃ;

Rūpāvacarakammanti, vibhāventi visāradā.

Thus the experts explain as fine-material-sphere kamma that which has suppressed the defilements and leads to rebirth in the fine-material world.

421.

421.

Arūpāvacarakammaṃ, catudhāruppasādhanaṃ;

Rūpadhammavibhāgena, bhāvitanti pavuccati.

The immaterial-sphere kamma, which accomplishes the four formless attainments, is said to be developed by turning away from material phenomena.

422.

422.

Catupārisuddhisīlaṃ, dhutaṅgaparivāritaṃ;

Sīlavisuddhisaṅkhātaṃ, pūrayitvā tato paraṃ.

Having first fulfilled the purification of virtue, which consists in the fourfold purification of morality and is accompanied by the ascetic practices,

423.

423.

Patvā cittavisuddhiñca, sopacārasamādhikaṃ;

Tathā diṭṭhivisuddhiñca, nāmarūpapariggahaṃ.

and having attained the purification of mind, which is concentration up to access, and likewise the purification of view, which is the discerning of mentality-materiality,

424.

424.

Kaṅkhāvitaraṇaṃ nāma, paccayaṭṭhitidassanaṃ;

Visodhetvā maggāmagga-ñāṇadassanameva ca.

and having accomplished the purification by overcoming doubt, which is the vision of established conditionality, and also the knowledge and vision of what is and is not the path,

425.

425.

Tato paraṃ vipassanto, visuddhīsu samāhito;

Sampādetvā paṭipadā-ñāṇadassanamuttamaṃ.

and thereafter, developing insight while concentrated in the purifications, having accomplished the supreme purification of knowledge and vision of the way,

426.

426.

Tato pappoti medhāvī, visuddhiṃ ñāṇadassanaṃ;

Catumaggasamaññātaṃ, sāmaññaphaladāyakaṃ.

the wise person then attains the purification of knowledge and vision, known as the four paths, which bestows the fruits of recluseship.

427.

427.

Chabbisuddhikamenevaṃ, bhāvetabbaṃ yathākkamaṃ;

Kammaṃ lokuttaraṃ nāma, sabbadukkhakkhayāvahaṃ.

Thus, by the method of the six purifications, supramundane kamma, which brings about the destruction of all suffering, should be developed in sequence.

428.

428.

Iti channaṃ catukkānaṃ, vasā kammaṃ vibhāvaye;

Yena kammavisesena, santānamabhisaṅkhataṃ.

Thus one should analyze kamma by way of the six tetrads, that specific kamma by which the mental continuum is conditioned.

429.

429.

Bhūmībhavayonigatiṭhitivāsesu sambhavā;

Paṭisandhādibhāvena, pākāya parivattati.

Arising in planes, existences, wombs, destinations, stations, and abodes, it proceeds to its ripening by way of rebirth-linking and so on.

430.

430.

Sāyaṃ [M 0.0038][V 0.0041] kammasamaññātā, kammajāni yathārahaṃ;

Janeti rūpārūpāni, manosañcetanā kathaṃ.

How does that mental volition, which is designated as kamma, generate, as is fitting, the material and immaterial phenomena born of kamma?

431.

431.

Bhūmi lokuttarā ceva, lokiyāti dvidhā ṭhitā;

Parittā ca mahaggatā, appamāṇāti bheditā.

The plane is twofold: mundane and supramundane. It is divided as limited, sublime, and immeasurable.

432.

432.

Ekādasa kāmabhavā, bhavā soḷasa rūpino;

Cattāroruppakā ceti, tividho bhava saṅgaho.

There are eleven sense-sphere existences, sixteen form-sphere existences, and four formless existences; thus the summary of existence is threefold.

433.

433.

Asaññeko bhavo neva-

Saññināsaññiko bhavo;

Sabbo saññibhavo seso,

Evampi tividho bhavo.

One existence is non-percipient; one is of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; all the rest are existences with perception. In this way, too, existence is threefold.

434.

434.

Āruppā catuvokārā, ekavokārasaññino;

Pañcavokārako nāma, bhavo seso pavuccati.

The formless existences are of four aggregates; the existence of non-percipient beings is of one aggregate; the remaining existence is said to be of five aggregates.

435.

435.

Niraye hoti deve ca, yonekā opapātikā;

Aṇḍajā jalābujā ca, saṃsedajopapātikā.

In hell and among the devas, birth is exclusively spontaneous. The four modes of birth are: egg-born, womb-born, moisture-born, and spontaneous.

436.

436.

Petaloke tiracchāne, bhummadeve ca mānuse;

Asure ca bhavantevaṃ, catudhā yoni saṅgahā.

In the realm of ghosts, the animal realm, among the earth-devas, humans, and asuras, all four modes of birth may be found.

437.

437.

Gatiyo nirayaṃ petā, tiracchānā ca mānavā;

Sabbe devāti pañcāha, pañcanimmalalocano.

The destinations are five, said the One with the Five Stainless Eyes: hell, the realm of ghosts, the animal realm, the human realm, and all the devas.

438.

438.

Tāvatiṃsesu devesu, vepacittāsurā gatā;

Kālakañcāsurā nāma, gatā petesu sabbathā.

The Vepacitti-asuras are included in the deva destination, among the Tāvatiṃsa devas; the asuras called Kālakañjas are included entirely within the ghost destination.

439.

439.

Sandhisaññāya nānattā, kāyassāpi ca nānato;

Nānattakāyasaññīti, kāmasuggatiyo matā.

Beings in the sense-sphere happy destinations are considered to have diverse bodies and diverse perceptions, owing to the diversity of their bodies and the diversity of their linking-perception.

440.

440.

Paṭhamajjhānabhūmī ca, caturāpāyabhūmiyo;

Nānattakāyaekatta-saññīti samudīritā.

The beings of the first-jhāna plane and the four woeful planes are said to have diverse bodies but uniform perception.

441.

441.

Ekattakāyanānatta-saññī [V 0.0042] dutiyabhūmikā;

Ekattakāyaekatta-saññī uparirūpino.

Those of the second-jhāna plane have uniform bodies but diverse perceptions; the higher fine-material beings have uniform bodies and uniform perceptions.

442.

442.

Viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo [M 0.0039] satta, tīhāruppehi heṭṭhato;

Asaññettha na gaṇhanti, viññāṇābhāvato sadā.

There are seven stations of consciousness, including the three lower formless realms. The non-percipient beings are not included among them, as they always lack consciousness.

443.

443.

Catutthāruppabhūmiñca, paṭuviññāṇahānito;

Taṃ dvayampi gahetvāna, sattāvāsā naveritā.

When the realm of non-percipient beings and the fourth formless realm are also included, the nine abodes of beings are enumerated.

444.

444.

Devā manussāpāyāti, tividhā kāmadhātuyo;

Paṭhamajjhānabhūmādi-bhedā bhūmi catubbidhā.

The sense-sphere planes are threefold: those of devas, humans, and the woeful states. The fine-material planes are fourfold, distinguished as the first-jhāna plane and so on.

445.

445.

Paṭhamāruppādibhedā, catudhāruppadhātuyo;

Sotāpannādibhedena, catudhānuttarā matā.

The immaterial-sphere planes are fourfold, distinguished as the first formless attainment and so on. The supramundane plane is considered fourfold, by the distinction of the stream-enterer and so on.

446.

446.

Nirayādippabhedena, bhinnā paccekato puna;

Ekatiṃsavidhā honti, sattānaṃ jātibhūmiyo.

When these are again divided individually, distinguished as the hells and so on, the birth-planes of beings become thirty-one-fold.

447.

447.

Evaṃ bhūmādibhedesu, sattā jāyanti sāsavā;

Kammāni ca vipaccanti, yathāsambhavato kathaṃ;

Thus, beings with taints are born in these various planes. But how do their kammas ripen according to the possibilities inherent in them?

448.

448.

Apāyamhā cutā sattā, kāmadhātumhi jāyare;

Sabbaṭṭhānesu jāyanti, sesakāmabhavā cutā.

Beings deceased from the woeful planes are reborn in the sense-sphere. Those deceased from the other sense-sphere existences can be reborn in any plane.

449.

449.

Suddhāvāsā cutā suddhā-vāsesupari jāyare;

Asaññimhā cutā kāma-sugatimhopapajjare.

Those deceased from the Pure Abodes are reborn in the Pure Abodes above them. Those deceased from the non-percipient realm are reborn in the sense-sphere happy destinations.

450.

450.

Sesarūpā cutā sattā, jāyantāpāyavajjite;

Āruppatopari kāma-sugatimhi tahimpi ca.

Beings deceased from the remaining form realms are reborn in planes apart from the woeful states: in the formless realms, in a higher form realm, or in the sense-sphere happy destinations.

451.

451.

Puthujjanāva jāyanti, asaññāpāyabhūmisu;

Suddhāvāsesu jāyanti, anāgāmikapuggalā.

Only worldlings are reborn in the non-percipient realm and the woeful planes. Non-returners are reborn in the Pure Abodes.

452.

452.

Vehapphale akaniṭṭhe, bhavagge ca patiṭṭhitā;

Na punaññattha jāyanti, sabbe ariyapuggalā.

All noble persons established in the Vehapphala, Akaniṭṭha, or the Peak of Existence realms are not reborn elsewhere.

453.

453.

Brahmalokagatā [V 0.0043] heṭṭhā, ariyā nopapajjare;

Dukkhamūlasamucchedā, parinibbantināsavā.

Noble ones who have gone to the Brahma worlds are not reborn in a lower plane; having eradicated the root of suffering, they attain final Nibbāna, free from taints.

454.

454.

Jāyantānañca jātāna-miti vuttaniyāmato;

Pavattātītakaṃ kammaṃ, paṭisandhipavattiyaṃ.

According to the principle thus stated for those being born and those already born, past kamma produces rebirth-linking and maintains the course of existence.

455.

455.

Arūpaṃ [M 0.0040] catuvokāre, rūpameva asaññisu;

Janeti rūpārūpāni, pañcavokārabhūmiyaṃ.

It generates only mentality in the four-aggregate existence, only materiality in the non-percipient existence, and both mentality and materiality in the five-aggregate existence.

456.

456.

Āruppānuttaraṃ kammaṃ, pākameva vipaccati;

Kaṭattārūpapākāni, kāmarūpaniyāmitaṃ.

Immaterial and supramundane kamma ripens only as result. The results of past kamma pertaining to the sense sphere and form sphere are confined to those spheres.

457.

457.

Kālopadhippayogānaṃ, gatiyā ca yathārahaṃ;

Sampattiñca vipattiñca, kammamāgamma paccati.

Depending on time, circumstance, effort, and destination, kamma ripens fittingly into fortune or misfortune.

458.

458.

Apāye sandhimuddhacca-hīnā datvā pavattiyaṃ;

Sabbāpi pañcavokāre, dvādasāpuññacetanā.

Of the twelve unwholesome volitions, the eleven apart from that associated with restlessness give rebirth-linking in the woeful planes; in the course of existence, all twelve yield their results in the five-aggregate existence.

459.

459.

Sattākusalapākāni, vipaccanti yathārahaṃ;

Kāmāvacarapuññāni, kāmesugatiyaṃ pana.

The seven unwholesome resultant consciousnesses ripen as is fitting. Wholesome kamma of the sense sphere, in turn, gives rebirth-linking in the happy destinations of the sense sphere.

460.

460.

Sahetukāni pākāni, paṭisandhipavattiyaṃ;

Janenti pañcavokāre, ahetupi yathārahaṃ.

In the five-aggregate existence, rooted wholesome kamma generates its results at rebirth-linking and in the course of existence; rootless kamma also generates its results as is fitting.

461.

461.

Tihetupuññamukkaṭṭhaṃ, paṭisandhiṃ tihetukaṃ;

Datvā soḷasa pākāni, pavatte tu vipaccati.

Superior wholesome kamma with three roots, having given a three-rooted rebirth-linking, ripens in the course of existence to yield sixteen kinds of results.

462.

462.

Tihetukomakukkaṭṭhaṃ, dvihetu ca dvihetukaṃ;

Sandhiṃ deti pavatte tu, tihetukavivajjitaṃ.

Inferior three-rooted kamma and superior two-rooted kamma give a two-rooted rebirth-linking, but in the course of existence they yield results apart from the three-rooted ones.

463.

463.

Dvihetukomakaṃ puññaṃ, paṭisandhimahetukaṃ;

Datvāhetukapākāni, pavatte tu vipaccati.

Inferior two-rooted wholesome kamma, having given a rootless rebirth-linking, ripens in the course of existence to yield rootless results.

464.

464.

Asaṅkhāraṃ sasaṅkhāra-vipākāni na paccati;

Sasaṅkhāramasaṅkhāra-vipākānīti kecana.

Unprompted kamma does not ripen as prompted results, nor prompted kamma as unprompted results—so some maintain.

465.

465.

Parittaṃ [V 0.0044] paṭhamajjhānaṃ, majjhimañca paṇītakaṃ;

Bhāvetvā jāyare brahma-pārisajjādi tīsupi.

Having developed the first jhāna as limited, middling, or superior, one is reborn in the three corresponding planes, beginning with the plane of Brahma's Retinue.

466.

466.

Tatheva dutiyajjhānaṃ, tatiyañca yathākkamaṃ;

Bhāvetvā jāyare jhānaṃ, parittābhādi tīsupi.

Similarly, having developed the second and third jhānas in due order, one is reborn in the three corresponding planes, beginning with the plane of Limited Radiance.

467.

467.

Tathā catutthaṃ tividhaṃ, bhāvetvāna samāhitā;

Parittasubhādikesu, tīsu jāyanti yogino.

Likewise, having developed the threefold fourth jhāna, a concentrated yogi is reborn in the three corresponding planes, beginning with the plane of Limited Glory.

468.

468.

Pañcamaṃ [M 0.0041] pana bhāvetvā, honti vehapphalūpagā;

Saññāvirāgaṃ bhāvetvā, asaññīsūpapajjare.

Having developed the fifth jhāna, they are reborn in the Vehapphala realm; having developed dispassion toward perception, they are reborn among the non-percipient beings.

469.

469.

Suddhāvāsesu jāyanti, anāgāmikapuggalā;

Āruppāni tu bhāvetvā, āruppesu yathākkamaṃ.

Non-returners are born in the Pure Abodes; but having developed the formless attainments, they are reborn in the corresponding formless realms in due order.

470.

470.

Evaṃ mahaggataṃ puññaṃ, yathābhūmivavatthitaṃ;

Janeti sadisaṃ pākaṃ, paṭisandhipavattiyaṃ.

Thus sublime merit, established according to its plane, produces a corresponding result at the time of rebirth-linking and in the course of existence.

471.

471.

Lokuttarāni puññāni, uppannānantaraṃ pana;

Samāpattikkhaṇe ceva, janenti sadisaṃ phalaṃ.

Supramundane merits, however, produce their corresponding fruit immediately after they have arisen and also at the moment of fruition attainment.

472.

472.

Mahaggatānantariyaṃ, paripakkasabhāvato;

Anantarabhavātītaṃ, kālātītaṃ na paccati.

Sublime kamma and immediately effective kamma, due to their mature nature, do not become defunct after the next life has passed or after a long time has passed.

473.

473.

Sukhumālasabhāvā ca, sukhumattā mahaggatā;

Santāne na vipaccanti, paṭipakkhehi dūsite.

Because of their subtle and tender nature, and on account of their sublimity, they do not ripen in a continuum corrupted by opposing factors.

474.

474.

Samānāsevane laddhe, vijjamāne mahabbale;

Aladdhā tādisaṃ hetuṃ, abhiññā na vipaccati.

Without obtaining such a cause—that is, the undertaking of suitable practice and the presence of great strength—the kamma for higher knowledge does not ripen.

475.

475.

Sakaṃ bhūmimatītānaṃ, na vipaccatānuttaraṃ;

Kammantarassadhiṭṭhānā, santānasseti dīpitaṃ.

For those who have passed beyond their own plane, the supreme kamma does not ripen; it is explained that this is due to the support of another kamma in the continuum.

476.

476.

Iti tettiṃsa kammāni, pākā chattiṃsa bhāsitā;

Cittuppādā kriyā sesā, kriyāmattappavattito.

Thus thirty-three types of consciousness are kamma, and thirty-six are spoken of as their results. The remaining consciousness-arisings are functional, since they proceed as mere activity.

477.

477.

Cittuppādavasenevamekūnanavutīvidhā[V 0.0045];

Tepaññāsa sabhāvena, cittacetasikā matā.

By way of the arisings of consciousness, they are of eighty-nine kinds; by their intrinsic nature, consciousness and mental factors are held to be fifty-three.

478.

478.

Iti cittaṃ cetasikaṃ, nibbānanti naruttaro;

Nāmaṃ tidhā pakāsesi, cakkhumā vadataṃ varo.

Thus the supreme man, the one with vision, the best of speakers, declared mentality to be threefold: consciousness, mental factors, and Nibbāna.

479.

479.

Iti kammavipākapaṇḍitā, mitakammavipākasāsane;

Hitakammavipākapāragū, catukammavipākamabravuṃ.

Thus, the wise in kamma and its result, who have gone to the far shore regarding beneficial kamma and its result, have spoken of the fourfold kamma and its result in this well-measured teaching.

480.

480.

Yatthāyaṃ [M 0.0042] paramatthavatthuniyame tulyena bāhulyato,

Atthānatthavicāraṇaṃ pati jano sammohamāpādito;

Buddho bodhitale yamāha sugato gantvāna devālayaṃ,

Svāyaṃ kammavipākanicchayanayo saṅkhepato dīpito.

Whereas people are often led to confusion when investigating what is beneficial and what is harmful in the domain of ultimate realities, this very method for the ascertainment of kamma and its result—which the Buddha, the Well-Gone One, taught after his enlightenment, having gone to the celestial abode—has here been explained in brief.

Iti nāmarūpaparicchede kammavibhāgo nāma

Thus ends the section named the Division of Kamma in the Analysis of Mind-and-Matter.

Pañcamo paricchedo.

The Fifth Chapter.

6. Chaṭṭho paricchedo

6. The Sixth Chapter.

Rūpavibhāgo

The Division of Matter.

481.

481.

Iti pañcapariccheda-paricchinnatthasaṅgahaṃ;

Nāmadhammamasesena, vibhāvetvā sabhāvato.

Thus having completely explained, according to their intrinsic nature, the mental phenomena comprising the subject matter defined in the preceding five chapters,

482.

482.

Sappabhedaṃ pavakkhāmi, rūpadhammamito paraṃ;

Bhūtopādāyabhedena, duvidhampi pakāsitaṃ.

Hereafter I shall explain the material phenomena with their divisions, which are revealed to be twofold, distinguished as primary elements and derived matter.

483.

483.

Uddesalakkhaṇādīhi, vibhāgajanakā tathā;

Kalāpuppattito cāpi, yathānukkamato kathaṃ?

How? In due order: by way of summary, characteristics, and so on; by way of division and genesis; and also by way of the arising of material groups.

484.

484.

Ruppatīti [V 0.0046] bhave rūpavikārappaccayesati;

Rūparūpaṃ tathā rūpapariyāpannatoparaṃ.

It is called 'matter' (rūpa) because it is afflicted (ruppati) when there are conditions for material transformation; and also because it is included in the category of matter.

485.

485.

Bhūtarūpaṃ tu pathavī, āpo tejo tathāparo;

Vāyo ca bhavatūpādārūpametthāti bhāsitaṃ.

The primary material elements are earth, water, fire, and air. What depends on these is said to be derived matter.

486.

486.

Bhūtarūpamupādāya[M 0.0043], pavattati na caññathā;

Iccupādāyarūpanti, rūpaṃ sesamudīritaṃ.

It exists in dependence on the primary elements and not otherwise; therefore the remaining matter is declared to be 'derived matter'.

487.

487.

Cakkhu sotañca ghānañca, jivhā kāyoti pañcadhā;

Pasādarūpamakkhātaṃ, nopasādaṃ panetaraṃ.

The eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body—these five are designated as sensitive matter; the other matter, however, is non-sensitive.

488.

488.

Rūpasaddagandharasā, phoṭṭhabbamiti pañcadhā;

Rūpaṃ pasādavisayaṃ, pasādo gocaraṃparaṃ.

Sights, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles are the fivefold material phenomena, the objects of the sensitivities; the sensitivity has the object for its domain.

489.

489.

Itthattaṃ purisattañca, bhāvarūpamudīritaṃ;

Jīvitindriyarūpanti, upādinnapavattikaṃ.

Femininity and masculinity are declared to be sexuality-matter. The life-faculty matter is that which maintains the continuity of what is produced by kamma.

490.

490.

Vatthurūpaṃ tu hadayaṃ, yaṃ dhātudvayanissayaṃ;

Kabaḷīkāramāhārarūpamiccāhu paṇḍitā.

The heart-base is the physical basis matter, which is the support for the two mental elements. The wise also declare edible food to be a material phenomenon.

491.

491.

Rūpadhammasabhāvattā, rūpanti paridīpitaṃ;

Iccevamaṭṭhārasadhā, rūparūpamudīritaṃ.

Because they have the nature of material phenomena, they are explained as 'matter.' Thus in eighteen ways concrete matter has been declared.

492.

492.

Anipphannasabhāvattā, rūpākāropalakkhitaṃ;

Anipphannaṃ nāma rūpaṃ, dasadhā paridīpitaṃ.

Because it has an unconcretized nature and is characterized by being a mode of matter, the so-called 'inconsubstantial matter' is explained as tenfold.

493.

493.

Rūpapparicchedaṃ rūpamiccākāso pakāsito;

Kāyabbacīviññattikaṃ, dvayaṃ viññattirūpakaṃ.

Space is revealed as the material phenomenon that is the delimitation of matter. Bodily intimation and verbal intimation are the two kinds of intimation-matter.

494.

494.

Lahutā mudutā kamma-ññatā viññattiyā saha;

Vikārarūpamiccāhu, pañcadhā ca vibhāvino.

Lightness, softness, and wieldiness, together with the two intimations, are said by the discerning to be the five kinds of alteration-matter.

495.

495.

Upacayo santati ca, jaratāniccatāti ca;

Catudhā lakkhaṇarūpaṃ, rūpakaṇḍe vibhāvitaṃ.

Production, continuity, decay, and impermanence: these four are distinguished in the section on matter as the matter of characteristics.

496.

496.

Iccevamaṭṭhavīsatividhānipi [V 0.0047] vicakkhaṇo;

Rūpāni lakkhaṇādīhi, vibhāveyya yathākkamaṃ.

Thus the discerning person should distinguish these twenty-eight kinds of matter in due order by their characteristics and so on.

497.

497.

Kharatā pathavīdhātu, sāyaṃ kakkhaḷalakkhaṇā;

Kalāpādhiṭṭhānarasā, paṭiggāhoti gayhati.

The earth element is hardness; its characteristic is roughness. Its function is to serve as a foundation for material groups; it is apprehended as that which supports.

498.

498.

Ābandhanamāpodhātu, sā paggharaṇalakkhaṇā;

Kalāpābandhanarasā, saṅgahattena gayhati.

The water element is cohesion; its characteristic is flowing. Its function is to bind material groups together; it is apprehended as that which holds them together.

499.

499.

Tejanattaṃ [M 0.0044] tejodhātu, sāyamuṇhattalakkhaṇā;

Pācanarasā maddavā-nuppādananti gayhati.

The fire element is heat; its characteristic is temperature. Its function is to mature things; it is apprehended as that which produces softness.

500.

500.

Vāyodhātu vāyanattaṃ, sā vitthambhanalakkhaṇā;

Samīraṇarasābhini-hārabhāvena gayhati.

The air element is distension; its characteristic is supporting. Its function is to cause motion; it is apprehended as that which conveys things from place to place.

501.

501.

Sabbatthāvinibhuttāpi, asammissitalakkhaṇā;

Taṃtaṃbhāvasamussannasambhāresupalakkhitā.

Although they are everywhere inseparable, their characteristic is that they do not mix; they are distinguished in those aggregates where their respective natures are predominant.

502.

502.

Aññamaññenupatthaddhā, sesarūpassa nissayā;

Catuddhevaṃ kalāpesu, mahābhūtā pavattare.

Mutually supported and serving as the basis for the other material phenomena, the great elements thus exist in groups of four.

503.

503.

Cakkhu sambhāracakkhumhi, sattakkhipaṭalocite;

Kaṇhamaṇḍalamajjhamhi, pasādoti pavuccati.

In the composite eye, which is covered by seven layers, in the middle of the black circle, is what is called the eye-sensitivity.

504.

504.

Yena cakkhupasādena, rūpāni anupassati;

Parittaṃ sukhumaṃ cetaṃ, ūkāsirasamūpamaṃ.

It is by means of this eye-sensitivity that one sees forms. It is tiny and subtle, comparable to the head of a louse.

505.

505.

Sotaṃ sotabilassanto,

Tambalomācite tathā;

Aṅgulivedhanākāre,

Pasādoti pavuccati.

The ear-sensitivity is located inside the ear canal, in a place fringed with fine, copper-colored hairs, and it has the shape of a small finger-ring.

506.

506.

Anto ajapadaṭṭhāne, ghānaṃ ghānabile ṭhitaṃ;

Jivhā jivhāya majjhamhi, uppalākārasannibhe.

The nose-sensitivity is situated inside the nostrils in a place shaped like a goat's hoof. The tongue-sensitivity is in the middle of the tongue in a place shaped like a blue lotus petal.

507.

507.

Iccevaṃ [V 0.0048] pana cattāro, taṃtaṃdesavavatthitā;

Kāyappasādo kāyamhi, upādinneti pañcadhā.

Thus these four sensitivities are established in their respective locations. The body-sensitivity is in the clung-to body; thus there are five kinds.

508.

508.

Kappāsapaṭalasneha-sannibhā bhūtanissitā;

Pasādā jīvitārakkhā, rūpādiparivāritā.

Resembling a film of cotton soaked in oil, these sensitivities are dependent on the primary elements, protected by the life-faculty, and surrounded by other material phenomena.

509.

509.

Dhītā rājakumārāva, kalāpantaravuttino;

Dvārabhūtāva paccekaṃ, pañcaviññāṇavīthiyā.

Like royal princesses, they dwell within material groups, each serving as a door for the cognitive processes of the five sense-consciousnesses.

510.

510.

Rūpādābhighātārahabhūtānaṃ vā yathākkamaṃ;

Daṭṭhukāmanidānādikammabhūtānameva vā.

Or, they are respectively those things capable of being impacted by sights and so on; or they are the kamma-born basis for the desire to see and so on.

511.

511.

Pasādalakkhaṇā [M 0.0045] rūpā-dāviñjanarasā tathā;

Pañcaviññāṇayugaḷaṃ, dvārabhāvena gayhare.

They have the characteristic of sensitivity and the function of receiving sights and so on; they are apprehended as being the door for the pair of fivefold consciousnesses.

512.

512.

Rūpaṃ nibhāso bhūtānaṃ, saddo nigghosanaṃ tathā;

Gandhova gandhanaṃ tattha, raso ca rasanīyatā.

Visible form is the radiance of the primary elements, sound their resonance, smell their scent, and taste their flavor.

513.

513.

Iccevaṃ pana cattāro, gocarā bhūtanissitā;

Bhūtattayañca phoṭṭhabbamāpodhātuvivajjitaṃ.

Thus these four sense objects are dependent on the primary elements. The tangible object consists of a triad of primary elements, excluding the water element.

514.

514.

Saddo aniyato tattha, tadañño sahavuttino;

Taṃtaṃsabhāvabhedena, taṃtaṃdvāropalakkhito.

Among these, sound is variable, while the others are co-existent. They are distinguished by their respective doors in accordance with the differences in their individual natures.

515.

515.

Pañceva pañcaviññāṇavīthiyā visayā matā;

Cakkhādipaṭihananalakkhaṇāva yathākkamaṃ.

These five are considered the objects for the cognitive processes of the five sense-consciousnesses; their characteristic is to impinge upon the eye and so on, respectively.

516.

516.

Pañcaviññāṇayugaḷālambabhāvarasā tathā;

Pañcaviññāṇayugaḷaṃ, gocarattena gayhare.

Their function is to serve as the object for the pair of fivefold consciousnesses; they are apprehended as the domain for that same pair of consciousnesses.

517.

517.

Itthindriyaṃ panitthattamitthibhāvoti bhāsito;

Purisattaṃ tathā bhāvo, purisindriyanāmako.

The female faculty is femininity, spoken of as the female state; likewise, masculinity, the male state, is what is named the male faculty.

518.

518.

Taṃ dvayaṃ panupādinnakāye sabbattha labbhati;

Kalāpantarabhinnañca, bhinnasantānavutti ca.

These two are found throughout the clung-to body; they are distinct within material groups and exist in separate individual continuums.

519.

519.

Vase [V 0.0049] vatteti liṅgāna-mitthipumbhāvalakkhaṇaṃ;

Itthīti ca purisoti, pakāsanarasaṃ tathā.

It has the characteristic of the female or male state, which controls the signs of gender. Its function is to manifest as 'woman' or 'man'.

520.

520.

Itthīnaṃ purisānañca, liṅgassa ca yathākkamaṃ;

Nimittakuttākappānaṃ, kāraṇattena gayhati.

It is apprehended as the cause of the respective signs, deportment, and appearance of women and of men.

521.

521.

Sattā maranti nāsena, yassa pāṇanti vuttiyā;

Sajīvamatakāyānaṃ, bhedo yenopalakkhito.

That by the destruction of which beings die, and by the presence of which they are said to live; that by which the distinction between a living and a dead body is recognized.

522.

522.

Tadetaṃ kammajātāna-manupālanalakkhaṇaṃ;

Jīvitaṃ jīvanarasaṃ, āyubaddhoti gayhati.

This life faculty has the characteristic of maintaining kamma-born material phenomena. Its function is to make them live. It is apprehended as that which is bound to the life-span.

523.

523.

Manodhātuyā ca tathā, manoviññāṇadhātuyā;

Nissayalakkhaṇaṃ vatthu-rūpaṃ hadayasammataṃ.

The heart-base is regarded as the material form that has the characteristic of being a support for the mind-element and for the mind-consciousness-element.

524.

524.

Samādhānarasaṃ [M 0.0046] tāsa-mubbāhattena gayhati;

Yasmiṃ kuppitakālamhi, vikkhittā honti pāṇino.

Its function is to stabilize them, and it is apprehended as that which bears them up. When it is agitated, beings become distracted.

525.

525.

Kāyo yassānusārena, cittakkhepena khijjati;

Yasmiṃ niruddhe viññāṇa-sotopi ca nirujjhati.

In dependence on it, the body is afflicted by mental agitation; when it ceases, the stream of consciousness also ceases.

526.

526.

Yaṃ nissāya patiṭṭhāti, paṭisandhi bhavantare;

Tadetaṃ kammasambhūtaṃ, pañcavokārabhūmiyaṃ.

Dependent on it, rebirth-linking is established in a future existence. This heart-base is produced by kamma in the five-aggregate planes.

527.

527.

Majjhe hadayakosamhi, aḍḍhapasatalohite;

Bhūtarūpamupādāya, cakkhādi viya vattati.

In the middle of the heart cavity, in about half a handful of blood, it exists in dependence on the primary elements, just like the eye-sensitivity and so on.

528.

528.

Kabaḷīkāro āhāro, rūpāharaṇalakkhaṇo;

Kāyānuyāpanaraso, upatthambhoti gayhati.

Edible food has the characteristic of conveying nutritive essence. Its function is to sustain the body. It is apprehended as that which provides support.

529.

529.

Ojāya yāya yāpenti, āhārasnehasattiyā;

Pāṇino kāmalokamhi, sāyamevaṃ pavuccati.

That nutritive essence by which beings in the sense-sphere sustain themselves, through the power of the succulence of food, is what is meant here.

530.

530.

Ākāsadhātu rūpānaṃ, pariyosānalakkhaṇā;

Paricchedarasā rūpamariyādoti gayhati.

The space element has the characteristic of terminating material phenomena. Its function is to delimit them. It is apprehended as the boundary of matter.

531.

531.

Salakkhaṇaparicchinnarūpadhammapariggahe[V 0.0050];

Yogīnamupakārāya, yaṃ desesi dayāparo.

That which the Compassionate One taught for the benefit of yogis, for the grasping of material phenomena as defined by their own characteristics.

532.

532.

Paricchinnasabhāvānaṃ, kalāpānaṃ yathārahaṃ;

Pariyantānamevesa, tadākāro pavuccati.

This is said to be the very boundary of material groups, whose nature is delimited as is appropriate.

533.

533.

Gamanādivacīghosapavattamhi yathākkamaṃ;

Vāyopathavidhātūnaṃ, yo vikāro samatthatā.

In the respective processes of movement and so forth, and of vocal sounds, there is an alteration and capacity of the air and earth elements.

534.

534.

Sahajopādinnakānaṃ, kriyāvācāpavattiyā;

Vipphandaghaṭṭanāhetu, cittānuparivattako.

It is the cause of vibration and impact for the process of bodily action and speech of co-nascent and clung-to phenomena, and it follows upon the mind.

535.

535.

Sa vikāravisesoyaṃ, viññattīti pakāsito;

Viññāpetīti kāyena, vācāya ca vicintitaṃ.

This specific alteration is declared as 'intimation' because it makes known, by means of the body and speech, what has been conceived.

536.

536.

Vāyopathavādhikānaṃ, bhūtānamiti kecana;

Pavuttā tādinā kāya-pariggahasukhāya yā.

Some say that this was taught by the Such-a-one for the sake of easily comprehending the body, which has a predominance of the air and earth elements.

537.

537.

Kāyo [M 0.0047] yassānubhāvena,

Sahābhogova khāyati;

Yaṃ nirodhā parābhūto,

Seti niccetano yathā.

The body, by whose power it appears as if with purpose; upon the cessation of which, it lies overcome, like a thing without consciousness.

538.

538.

Loke papañcā vattanti, bahudhā yāya nimmitā;

Kappenti kāyamattānaṃ, bālā yāya ca vañcitā.

Manifold conceptual proliferations, created by it, proceed in the world; and deceived by it, fools conceive of the body as a self.

539.

539.

Sāyaṃ kāyavacīkamma-dvārabhāvena lakkhitā;

Byāpāraghaṭṭanāhetu-vikārākāralakkhaṇā.

This intimation is characterized by being the door for bodily and verbal action, and by having the characteristic of an altered appearance caused by the impact of activity.

540.

540.

Kāyavācāadhippāya-pakāsanarasā tathā;

Kāyavipphandaghaṭṭana-hetubhāvena gayhati.

Its function is to reveal intention through body and speech; also, it is understood as being the cause of bodily movement and impact.

541.

541.

Lahutā pana rūpānaṃ, adandhākāralakkhaṇā;

Avitthānarasā salla-hukavuttīti gayhati.

Now, lightness of matter has the characteristic of non-sluggishness; its function is non-rigidity, and its manifestation is a light mode of occurrence.

542.

542.

Mudutāpi [V 0.0051] ca rūpānaṃ, kakkhaḷābhāvalakkhaṇā;

Kiccāvirujjhanarasā, anukulyanti gayhati.

And softness of matter has the characteristic of an absence of hardness; its function is non-opposition to actions, and its manifestation is pliancy.

543.

543.

Kammaññatā ca rūpānaṃ, alaṃkiccassa lakkhaṇā;

Pavattisampattirasā, yoggabhāvoti gayhati.

And workableness of matter has the characteristic of fitness for action; its function is the successful proceeding of actions, and its manifestation is a state of serviceability.

544.

544.

Sappāyamutumāhāraṃ, laddhā cittamanāmayaṃ;

Lahū mudu ca kammaññaṃ, yadā rūpaṃ pavattati.

When matter proceeds as light, soft, and workable, the mind, having obtained suitable climate and nutriment, is free from affliction.

545.

545.

Tathā pavattarūpassa, pavattākārabheditaṃ;

Lahutādittayampetaṃ, sahavutti tadā bhave.

For matter that has thus occurred, this triad beginning with lightness is its distinguished mode of occurrence; they then have a co-existent arising.

546.

546.

Sappāyapaṭivedhāya, paṭipattupakārikā;

Sākārā rūpasampatti, paññattevaṃ mahesinā.

Thus the perfection of matter with its characteristics, which is helpful for the practice and for the penetration of what is suitable, has been declared by the Great Sage.

547.

547.

Rūpassopacayo nāma, rūpassācayalakkhaṇo;

Rūpummujjāpanaraso, pāripūrīti gayhati.

The growth of matter has the characteristic of accumulation of matter; its function is to cause matter to emerge, and its manifestation is completion.

548.

548.

Pavattilakkhaṇā rūpa-santatīti pakāsitā;

Anuppabandhanarasā, avicchedoti gayhati.

Continuity of matter is declared to have the characteristic of proceeding; its function is unbroken succession, and it is understood as non-interruption.

549.

549.

Rūpamācayarūpena[M 0.0048], jāyaticcuparūpari;

Pekkhatopacāyākārā, jāti gayhati yoginā.

Matter arises in the mode of accumulation, again and again. For one who observes, birth is understood by the yogi as having the mode of increase.

550.

550.

Anuppabandhākārena, jāyatīti samekkhato;

Tadāyaṃ santatākārā, samupaṭṭhāsi cetasi.

For one who considers that it arises in a continuous manner, this mode of continuity then presents itself to the mind.

551.

551.

Evamābhogabhedena, jātirūpaṃ dvidhā kataṃ;

Atthūpaladdhibhāvena, jāyantaṃ vātha kevalaṃ.

Thus, by the distinction of application, the characteristic of birth is made twofold: either as being the obtaining of its nature, or merely as arising.

552.

552.

Rūpavivittamokāsaṃ, purakkhattena cīyati;

Abhāvā pana bhāvāya, pavattamiti santati.

Matter accumulates in a space devoid of matter, being set forth; continuity, for its part, is its proceeding from non-existence to existence.

553.

553.

Evamākārabhedāpi, sabbākāravarākaro;

Jātirūpaṃ dvidhākāsi, jātirūpavirocano.

Thus, even by the distinction of aspects, the Illuminator of the characteristic of birth, who is the source of the best of all aspects, made the characteristic of birth twofold.

554.

554.

Jaratā [V 0.0052] kālaharaṇaṃ, rūpānaṃ pākalakkhaṇā;

Navatāpāyanarasā, purāṇattanti gayhati.

Aging of matter has the characteristic of ripeness; its function is the disappearance of newness, and its manifestation is oldness.

555.

555.

Antimakkhaṇasampatti, paribhijjanalakkhaṇā;

Aniccatā haraṇarasā, khayabhāvena gayhati.

Impermanence, the attainment of the final moment, has the characteristic of breaking up; its function is carrying away, and its manifestation is the state of decay.

556.

556.

Iti lakkhaṇarūpaṃ tu, tividhaṃ bhinnakālikaṃ;

Sabhāvarūpadhammesu, taṃtaṃkālopalakkhitaṃ.

Thus, the characteristic-form is threefold, differentiated by time, and is observed in intrinsic material phenomena at their respective times.

557.

557.

Yena lakkhīyati rūpaṃ, bhinnākāraṃ khaṇe khaṇe;

Vipassanānayatthāya, tamiccāha tathāgato.

The Tathāgata has declared that by which matter is characterized as changing in aspect from moment to moment, for the sake of the method of insight.

558.

558.

Iccevaṃ saparicchedā, savikārā salakkhaṇā;

Akicchā paṭivedhāya, dayāpannena tādinā.

Thus, with limitations, variations, and characteristics, it has been taught by the compassionate Such-a-one so as to be easily penetrated.

559.

559.

Rūpadhammā sabhāvena, vijjamānāti bhāsitā;

Ajjhattikādibhedena, bahudhā bhijjare kathaṃ;

Material phenomena are said to exist by their intrinsic nature; how are they divided in many ways by distinctions such as internal and so forth?

560.

560.

Dvārabhūtā pavattenti, cittamattāti kappitaṃ;

Rūpamajjhattikaṃ tasmā, pasādā bāhiraṃparaṃ.

Functioning as doors, they proceed, being arranged as if from mind alone; therefore, the sensitive qualities are internal form, and the other is external.

561.

561.

Vaṇṇo [M 0.0049] gandho rasojā ca, bhūtarūpañca bhāsitaṃ;

Avinibbhogarūpaṃ tu, vinibbhogaṃ panetaraṃ.

Color, smell, taste, nutritive essence, and the primary elements are spoken of as inseparable matter; the rest, however, is separable.

562.

562.

Sattaviññāṇadhātūnaṃ, nissayattā yathārahaṃ;

Pasādā hadayañceva, vatthunā vatthu desitaṃ.

Because they are the appropriate basis for the seven consciousness-elements, the sensitive qualities and the heart-base are taught as the physical base.

563.

563.

Pañcaviññāṇupādinna-liṅgādi ca pavattito;

Pasādā jīvitaṃ bhāvā, cendriyaṃ nendriyaṃparaṃ.

The kamma-born [bases] for the five consciousnesses, sex, etc., are produced; the sensitive qualities, life, and the sexes are faculties, while the others are not faculties.

564.

564.

Pañcaviññāṇakammānaṃ, pavattimukhabhāvato;

Dvāraṃ pasādaviññatti-paramadvāramīritaṃ.

Because they are the portal for the occurrence of the five sense-consciousnesses and for actions, the sensitive qualities and the two intimations are a door; the other is said to be not a door.

565.

565.

Paṭihaññantaññamaññaṃ, pasādavisayā pana;

Tasmā sappaṭighaṃ nāma, rūpamappaṭighaṃparaṃ.

The sensitive material qualities and their objects impinge upon one another; therefore, such form is called resistant, and the other is non-resistant.

566.

566.

Dvārālambaṇabhāvena[V 0.0053], sabhāveneva pākaṭā;

Te evoḷārikaṃ tasmā, sesaṃ sukhumamīritaṃ.

By their nature of being doors and objects, they are clearly evident by their intrinsic nature; therefore, they are called coarse, and the rest are said to be subtle.

567.

567.

Oḷārikasabhāvena, pariggahasukhā tahiṃ;

Te eva santikerūpaṃ, dūrerūpaṃ panetaraṃ.

Because of their coarse nature, they are easy to apprehend; therefore, they are called near form, and the other is distant form.

568.

568.

Taṇhādiṭṭhīhupetena, kammunādinnabhāvato;

Kammajātamupādinnaṃ, anupādinnakaṃparaṃ.

Because they are produced by kamma associated with craving and views, kamma-born form is called 'grasped'; the other is 'ungrasped'.

569.

569.

Cakkhunā dissamānattā, sanidassananāmakaṃ;

Rūpameva tato sesa-manidassanamabravuṃ.

Because it is seen by the eye, visible form alone is called 'visible'; the rest after that, they called 'invisible'.

570.

570.

Sanidassanarūpañca, rūpaṃ sappaṭighaṃ tathā;

Anidassanamaññaṃ tu, thūlaṃ sappaṭighaṃ mataṃ.

Visible form is also resistant form; the other, invisible form, is considered coarse and resistant.

571.

571.

Anidassanarūpañca, sesaṃ appaṭighaṃ tathā;

Rūpaṃ tividhamiccevaṃ, vibhajanti vicakkhaṇā.

And the remaining invisible form is also non-resistant; thus, the wise discern form as threefold.

572.

572.

Appattagocaraggāhirūpaṃ cakkhādikaṃ dvayaṃ;

Sampattaggāhi ghānādi-ttayamaggāhikaṃ rūpaṃ.

The two, the eye and so forth, are forms that apprehend an object without contact; the three, the nose and so forth, apprehend by contact; other form is non-apprehending.

573.

573.

Diṭṭhaṃ rūpaṃ sutaṃ saddo, mutaṃ gandhādikattayaṃ;

Viññāṇeneva ñeyyattā, viññātamaparaṃ bhave.

Seen is visible form, heard is sound, sensed are the three beginning with smell; the other is to be known by consciousness alone.

574.

574.

Hadayaṃ [M 0.0050] vatthumevettha, dvāraṃ viññattikadvayaṃ;

Pasādā vatthu ca dvāraṃ, aññaṃ tubhayavajjitaṃ.

Here, the heart is a base indeed; the two intimations are a door; the sensitive qualities are both a base and a door; the other is devoid of both.

575.

575.

Bheditvā rūpamiccevaṃ, tasseva puna paṇḍito;

Samuṭṭhānajanakehi, vibhāveyya yathārahaṃ.

Having thus analyzed form, the wise person should again distinguish it appropriately by its originating causes.

576.

576.

Kusalākusalaṃ kamma-matītaṃ kāmikaṃ tathā;

Rūpāvacaramiccevaṃ, pañcavīsatidhā ṭhitaṃ.

Past wholesome and unwholesome kamma, belonging to the sense-sphere and also to the form-sphere—thus it is established in twenty-five ways.

577.

577.

Paṭisandhimupādāya, sañjaneti khaṇe khaṇe;

Kāmarūpesu rūpāni, kammajāni yathārahaṃ.

Beginning from rebirth-linking, it generates, moment by moment, appropriate kamma-produced forms in the sense and form realms.

578.

578.

Jāyantaṃ [V 0.0054] pañcaviññāṇa-pākāruppavivajjitaṃ;

Bhavaṅgādimupādāya, samuppādeti mānasaṃ.

Mind produces [form], beginning from the first life-continuum, but excluding the arising of the ten sense-consciousnesses, resultant consciousnesses, and formless-sphere consciousnesses.

579.

579.

Sītuṇhotusamaññātā,

Tejodhātu ṭhitikkhaṇe;

Tathevajjhohaṭāhāro,

Kāme kāyappatiṭṭhito.

The fire element, known as temperature (cold and heat), [produces form] at the moment of stability; likewise, ingested nutriment, when established in the body, [produces form] in the sense-sphere.

580.

580.

Ajjhattaṃ pana cattāro, bāhiro tupalabbhati;

Sabbe kāmabhave rūpe, āhāro na samīrito.

Internally, however, there are four [causes]; externally, only [temperature] is found. Nutriment is not said [to be a cause] for all forms in the sense-sphere existence.

581.

581.

Pavatte honti cattāro, kammamevopapattiyaṃ;

Jīvamānassa sabbepi, matassotu siyā na vā.

During the course of life, there are four [causes], but at rebirth, only kamma. For a living person, all are present; for one who is dead, [a cause] may or may not be present.

582.

582.

Kammaṃ cittotumāhāra-miccevaṃ pana paṇḍitā;

Rūpānaṃ janakattena, paccayāti pakāsayuṃ.

Kamma, mind, temperature, and nutriment—thus the wise declare them as causes, on account of their producing forms.

583.

583.

Hadayindriyarūpāni, kammajāneva cittajaṃ;

Viññattidvayamīrenti, saddo cittotujo mato.

The heart-base and faculty-forms are produced by kamma alone; they say the two intimations are produced by mind; sound is considered to be produced by mind and temperature.

584.

584.

Cittotukabaḷīkāra-sambhūtā lahutādayo;

Kammacittotukāhāra-jāni sesāni dīpaye.

Lightness, etc., arise from mind, temperature, and edible nutriment; the remaining forms should be explained as produced by kamma, mind, temperature, and nutriment.

585.

585.

Jāyamānādirūpānaṃ, sabhāvattā hi kevalaṃ;

Lakkhaṇāni na jāyanti, kehicīti pakāsitaṃ.

It is declared that the characteristic-forms, such as arising, are not produced by any cause, for they are merely the intrinsic nature of material phenomena.

586.

586.

Yadijātādayo [M 0.0051] tesa-mavassaṃ taṃsabhāvatā;

Tesañca lakkhaṇānanti, anavatthā bhavissati.

If birth and so forth were also to have their own characteristics, an infinite regress would occur.

587.

587.

Aṭṭhārasa pannarasa, terasa dvādasāti ca;

Kammacittotukāhāra-jāni honti yathākkamaṃ.

Eighteen, fifteen, thirteen, and twelve forms are produced respectively by kamma, mind, temperature, and nutriment.

588.

588.

Kalāpāni yathāyogaṃ, tāni saṅgayha paṇḍitā;

Nava cha caturo dveti, ekavīsati bhāvayuṃ.

The wise, having gathered those groups as appropriate, expound them as nine, six, four, and two—twenty-one in total.

589.

589.

Jīvitañcāvinibbhoga-rūpañca[V 0.0055], sahavuttito;

Saṅgayha cakkhudasakaṃ, cakkhumādāya bhāsitaṃ.

Taking the eye [sensitivity] as principal, the 'eye-decad' is spoken of, comprising it together with the inseparable qualities and life, due to their co-arising.

590.

590.

Tathā sotañca ghānañca, jivhaṃ kāyaṃ yathākkamaṃ;

Itthibhāvañca pumbhāvaṃ, vatthumādāya dīpaye.

Similarly, one should explain in due order the ear, nose, tongue, body, the female and male sexes, and the heart-base, taking each as the principal part of its respective decad.

591.

591.

Avinibbhogarūpena, jīvitanavakaṃ bhave;

Iccevaṃ kammajā nāma, kalāpā navadhā ṭhitā.

With the inseparable material qualities, the life-nonad arises; thus, the groups produced by kamma are established in nine ways.

592.

592.

Avinibbhogarūpañca, suddhaṭṭhakamudīritaṃ;

Kāyaviññattiyā saddhiṃ, navakanti pavuccati.

The inseparable material qualities are called the pure octad; this, together with body-intimation, is called a nonad.

593.

593.

Vacīviññattisaddehi, dasakaṃ bhāsitaṃ tathā;

Lahutādekādasakaṃ, lahutādīhi tīhipi.

With vocal intimation and sound, the decad is likewise spoken of; and the undecad, with the three qualities beginning with lightness.

594.

594.

Kāyaviññattilahutā-dīhi dvādasakaṃ mataṃ;

Vacīviññattilahutā-dīhi terasakaṃ tathā.

With bodily intimation and lightness, etc., a dodecad is understood; with vocal intimation and lightness, etc., a tredecad likewise.

595.

595.

Gahetvākārabhedañca, taṃtaṃkālopalakkhitaṃ;

Iti cittasamuṭṭhānā, cha kalāpāti bhāsitā.

Having taken up the various modes distinguished by their respective times, thus the groups originating from mind are spoken of as six.

596.

596.

Suddhaṭṭhakaṃ tu paṭhamaṃ, saddena navakaṃ mataṃ;

Lahutādekādasakaṃ, lahutādisamāyutaṃ.

First is the pure octad; with sound, it is regarded as a nonad. The undecad is that which is combined with lightness and so forth.

597.

597.

Saddena lahutādīhi, tathā dvādasakaṃ bhave;

Kalāpā utusambhūtā, catuddhevaṃ pakāsitā.

With sound, lightness, and so forth, a dodecad likewise arises; thus, the groups born of temperature are declared to be four.

598.

598.

Suddhaṭṭhakañca lahutā-dekādasakamiccapi;

Kalāpāhārasambhūtā, duvidhāva vibhāvitā.

The groups born of nutriment are distinguished as twofold: namely, the pure octad and the undecad beginning with lightness.

599.

599.

Kalāpānaṃ [M 0.0052] pariccheda-lakkhaṇattā vicakkhaṇā;

Na kalāpaṅgamiccāhu, ākāsaṃ lakkhaṇāni ca.

Because they have the characteristic of delimiting the groups, the wise say that space and the characteristics are not components of a group.

600.

600.

Iccevaṃ catusambhūtā, kalāpā ekavīsati;

Sabbe labbhanti ajjhattaṃ, bāhirotusamuṭṭhitā.

Thus, the twenty-one groups arisen from four causes are all found internally; those arisen from temperature are also found externally.

601.

601.

Aṭṭhakaṃ [V 0.0056] saddanavaka-miti dvedhāva bhāsitā;

Matakāyepi te eva, siyumiccāhu paṇḍitā.

The octad and the sound-nonad are thus spoken of as twofold; the wise say that these same two may be present even in a dead body.

602.

602.

Kāme sabbepi labbhanti, sabhāvānaṃ yathārahaṃ;

Sampuṇṇāyatanānaṃ tu, pavatte catusambhavā.

In the sensuous realm, all are obtained according to the respective nature of beings. But for those with complete sense-bases, the four modes of generation occur in the course of existence.

603.

603.

Dasakāneva sabbāni, kammajāneva jātiyaṃ;

Cakkhusotaghānabhāva-dasakāni na vā siyuṃ.

All decads are indeed kamma-born at birth; but the eye, ear, nose, and sex decads may or may not be present.

604.

604.

Vatthukāyadasakāni, sabhāvadasakāni vā;

Gabbhaseyyakasattānaṃ, tato sesāni sambhavā.

The base, body, and sex decads arise for beings in the womb; thereafter, the remaining groups come into being.

605.

605.

Kammaṃ rūpaṃ janetevaṃ,

Mānasaṃ sandhito paraṃ;

Tejodhātu ṭhitippattā,

Āhārajjhohaṭo tathā.

Thus kamma generates materiality. Mind does so after the rebirth-linking. The fire element does so upon reaching the static phase, and likewise nutriment, when it has been consumed.

606.

606.

Iccevaṃ catusambhūtā, rūpasantati kāminaṃ;

Dīpajālāva sambandhā, yāvajīvaṃ pavattati.

Thus, for beings in the sensuous realm, the material continuity arisen from four causes continues as long as life lasts, connected like the flame of a lamp.

607.

607.

Āyuno vātha kammassa, khayenobhinnameva vā;

Aññena vā marantāna-mupacchedakakammunā.

By the exhaustion of life-span or of kamma, or by the exhaustion of both; or by the destructive kamma of those dying from another cause.

608.

608.

Sattarasacittakkhaṇamāyu rūpānamīritaṃ;

Sattarasamacittassa, cuticittoparī tato.

Seventeen mind-moments is declared as the lifespan of materiality; its production ceases from the seventeenth mind-moment prior to the death-consciousness.

609.

609.

Ṭhitikālamupādāya, kammajaṃ na paraṃ bhave;

Tato bhijjatupādinnaṃ, cittajāhārajaṃ tato.

From the static phase of the death-consciousness onwards, kamma-born materiality no longer arises. Then the appropriated matter breaks up, followed by that born of mind and nutriment.

610.

610.

Iccevaṃ matasattānaṃ, punadeva bhavantare;

Paṭisandhimupādāya, tathā rūpaṃ pavattati.

Thus, for deceased beings, again in another existence, from rebirth onwards, materiality continues in that way.

611.

611.

Ghānajivhākāyabhāvadasakāhārajaṃ [M 0.0053] pana;

Rūpaṃ rūpabhave natthi, paṭisandhipavattiyaṃ.

However, the decads of nose, tongue, body, and sex, and nutriment-originated materiality, do not exist in the form realm, either at rebirth or during the course of existence.

612.

612.

Tattha [V 0.0057] gandharasojā ca, na labbhantīti kecana;

Kalāpā ca gaṇetabbā, tatthetaṃ rūpavajjitā.

Some say that there, smell, taste, and nutritive essence are not found; and the groups should be reckoned there as being devoid of these material qualities.

613.

613.

Ṭhitikkhaṇañca cittassa, te eva paṭisedhayuṃ;

Cittabhaṅgakkhaṇe rūpa-samuppattiñca vārayuṃ.

They also deny the static moment of consciousness, and they reject the arising of materiality at the moment of the mind's dissolution.

614.

614.

Cakkhusotavatthusaddacittajampi asaññisu;

Arūpe pana rūpāni, sabbathāpi na labbhare.

In the realm of non-percipient beings, there is no eye, ear, heart-base, sound, or mind-born materiality; and in the immaterial realm, material phenomena are not found in any way at all.

615.

615.

Itthaṃ panettha vimalena vibhāvanatthaṃ,

Dhammaṃ sudhammamupagamma surādhivāsaṃ;

Rūpaṃ arūpasavibhāgasalakkhaṇaṃ taṃ,

Vuttaṃ pavuttamabhidhammanaye mayāpi.

Thus here, for the sake of stainless clarification, having relied upon the good Dhamma, the abode of the devas, that doctrine of materiality and the immaterial, with its divisions and characteristics, has been spoken and proclaimed by me also, according to the Abhidhamma method.

616.

616.

Rūpavibhāgamimaṃ suvibhattaṃ, rūpayato pana cetasi niccaṃ;

Rūpasamiddhajineritadhamme, rūpavatī abhivaḍḍhati paññā.

This classification of materiality is well-divided. For one who constantly contemplates form in the mind, in accordance with the Dhamma proclaimed by the Conqueror, which is rich in form, a beautiful wisdom grows abundantly.

Iti nāmarūpaparicchede rūpavibhāgo nāma

Thus, in the Chapter on Name-and-Materiality, this is the Section on the Analysis of Materiality.

Chaṭṭho paricchedo.

The Sixth Chapter.

7. Sattamo paricchedo

7. The Seventh Chapter

Sabbasaṅgahavibhāgo

The Analysis of the Compendium of All

617.

617.

Catupaññāsa dhammā hi, nāmanāmena bhāsitā;

Aṭṭhārasavidhā vuttā, rūpadhammāti sabbathā.

Indeed, fifty-four phenomena are spoken of under the designation 'mind'; and eighteen kinds are declared, in all, as 'material phenomena'.

618.

618.

Abhiññeyyā sabhāvena, dvāsattati samīritā;

Saccikaṭṭhaparamatthā, vatthudhammā salakkhaṇā.

Seventy-two things are said to be directly knowable by their intrinsic nature; they are ultimate realities in the true sense, real phenomena with their own characteristics.

619.

619.

Tesaṃ [M 0.0054][V 0.0058] dāni pavakkhāmi, sabbasaṅgāhikaṃ nayaṃ;

Ābhidhammikabhikkhūnaṃ, hatthasāramanuttaraṃ.

Now I shall explain to them the method that encompasses everything, the supreme manual for monks versed in Abhidhamma.

620.

620.

Dukā tikā ca khandhāyatanato dhātusaccato;

Paṭiccasamuppādā ca, paccayā ca samaññato.

The dyads and triads; and in terms of the aggregates, sense bases, elements, and truths; and dependent origination and conditions, in summary.

621.

621.

Paccayo eva nibbānamapaccayamasaṅkhataṃ;

Asaṅkhāramanuppādaṃ, sassataṃ niccalakkhaṇaṃ.

Nibbāna, which is unconditioned and uncompounded, is indeed a condition; the uncompounded is non-arising, eternal, with the characteristic of immovability.

622.

622.

Paccayā ceva saṅkhārā, saṅkhatā ca tatopare;

Uppādavayadhammā ca, paccayaṭṭhitikā tathā.

Formations are indeed conditioned, and other things are also compounded; they have the nature of arising and passing away, and likewise persist due to conditions.

623.

623.

Nibbānaṃ rūpadhammā ca, vippayuttāva kevalaṃ;

Ārammaṇā eva nāma, nālambanti hi kiñcipi.

Nibbāna and material phenomena are indeed entirely dissociated; they are only objects for the mind, for they do not take any object at all.

624.

624.

Ekuppādanirodhā ca, ekālambaṇavatthukā;

Saṃsaṭṭhā sampayuttā ca, sahajātā yathārahaṃ.

With single arising and cessation, with a single object and base; intermingled, associated, and conascent, each as is fitting.

625.

625.

Aññamaññenupatthaddhā, sabbattha sahavuttino;

Sārammaṇārammaṇā ca, cittacetasikā matā.

Mutually supported, they occur together everywhere; having an object and being objects, mind and mental factors are known.

626.

626.

Vipassanāya bhūmīti, tattha tebhūmakā matā;

Lokiyā pariyāpannā, vaṭṭadhammā sauttarā.

As the ground for insight, they are known as pertaining to the three planes; they are mundane, included, states of the round of existence, with a superior.

627.

627.

Sakkāyadhammā sabhayā, tīramorimanāmakaṃ;

Saṃyojaniyā samalā, tathā nīvaraṇīyakā.

States pertaining to personality are fearful, called 'this shore'; they are subject to fetters and defilement, and likewise subject to hindrances.

628.

628.

Saṃklesikā parāmaṭṭhā, upādānīyasāsavā;

Oghanīyā yoganīyā, ganthanīyāti bhāsitā.

Defiling, clung to, subject to clinging and with taints; subject to floods, subject to yokes, subject to ties, so it is said.

629.

629.

Aññe apariyāpannā, vivaṭṭā cāvipassiyā;

Lokuttarānuttarā ca, nosaṃyojaniyādayo.

Others are unincluded, devoid of the round, and not subject to perversion; supramundane and unsurpassed, they are not subject to fetters and so on.

630.

630.

Kammajātā [V 0.0059] upādinnā, nāma vuccanti sāsavā;

Anupādinnakā nāma, tato sesā pavuccare.

Those born of kamma are called 'acquired' and are with taints; the rest are called 'unacquired'.

631.

631.

Dhammā sappaṭibhāgāti, kusalākusalā matā;

Appaṭibhāgadhammāti, tadaññe paridīpaye.

Wholesome and unwholesome states are known as states with a counterpart; the others are declared to be states without a counterpart.

632.

632.

Saraṇā [M 0.0055] ca pahātabbā, dvādasākusalā pana;

Tadaññe araṇā nāma, pahātabbā na kehici.

The twelve unwholesome states are with defilement and should be abandoned; the others are called 'without defilement' and are not to be abandoned by anyone.

633.

633.

Rūpino rūpadhammā ca, nāmadhammā arūpino;

Evamādippabhedena, dvidhā bhedaṃ vibhāvaye.

States with form are material phenomena, and mental phenomena are formless; thus, by such initial distinctions, one should discern the twofold division.

634.

634.

Bālā dhammā tapanīyā, kaṇhā ca kaṭukapphalā;

Asevitabbā sāvajjā, dvādasākusalā matā.

Foolish states are tormenting, dark and bitter in their result; they should not be cultivated, are blameworthy, and are known as the twelve unwholesome states.

635.

635.

Paṇḍitā cātapanīyā, sukkā ca sukhadāyakā;

Sevitabbānavajjā ca, kusalā ekavīsati.

States of the wise are untormenting, bright and happiness-yielding; they should be cultivated, are blameless, and are the twenty-one wholesome states.

636.

636.

Kriyā vipākā rūpañca, nibbānanti catubbidhā;

Vuttā abyākatā nāma, dhammā tabbiparītato.

Functional consciousness, resultants, form, and Nibbāna—these four kinds are declared to be indeterminate states, being contrary to the others.

637.

637.

Hīnā dhammā parittā ca, kāmāvacarabhūmikā;

Rūpārūpā pavuccanti, majjhimā ca mahaggatā.

Inferior and limited states are those of the sense-sphere plane; form and formless states are called intermediate and sublime.

638.

638.

Appamāṇā paṇītā ca, dhammā lokuttarā matā;

Saṃkiliṭṭhasaṃklesikā, dvādasākusalā tathā.

Immeasurable and sublime are the supramundane states known to be; likewise, defiled and defiling are the twelve unwholesome states.

639.

639.

Asaṃkiliṭṭhasaṃklesikā, dhammā tebhūmakāpare;

Asaṃkliṭṭhāsaṃklesikā, nava lokuttarā siyuṃ.

Undefiled and defiling are the other states pertaining to the three planes; undefiled and undefiling are the nine supramundane states.

640.

640.

Vipākā te pavuccanti, vipākā catubhūmakā;

Vipākadhammā nāmāti, kusalākusalā matā.

Resultants are said to be those pertaining to the four planes; wholesome and unwholesome states are known as 'states that yield results'.

641.

641.

Kriyā rūpañca nibbānaṃ, na pākaṃ na tu paccati;

Ācayagāmino dhammā, puññāpuññāva sāsavā.

Functional consciousness, form, and Nibbāna are neither a result nor do they ripen; states leading to accumulation are merit and demerit with taints.

642.

642.

Vuttāpacayagāmino[V 0.0060], kusalānuttarā pana;

Kriyā rūpañca nibbānaṃ, pākā cobhayavajjitā.

Declared as leading to non-accumulation are the unsurpassed wholesome states; but functional consciousness, form, Nibbāna, and resultants are devoid of both accumulation and non-accumulation.

643.

643.

Paṭhamānuttaro maggo, dassanaṃ bhāvanāpare;

Tadaññe dvayanimmuttā, sabbepi paramatthato.

The first supramundane path is abandoned by vision, the others by development; all other states, in the ultimate sense, are free from this pair.

644.

644.

Satta lokuttarā heṭṭhā, vuttā sekkhāti tādinā;

Arahattaphalameva, asekkhanti pakāsitaṃ.

The seven lower supramundane states are said by the Such One to be those of trainees; the fruit of arahantship alone is declared to be that of one beyond training.

645.

645.

Lokiyāpi [M 0.0056] ca nibbānaṃ, bhāsitobhayavajjitā;

Evamādippakārehi, tividhāti vibhāvaye.

Mundane states and Nibbāna are spoken of as devoid of both; thus, in these and similar ways, one should discern the threefold division.

646.

646.

Atītānāgataṃ rūpaṃ, paccuppannamathāparaṃ;

Ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā, sukhumoḷārikaṃ tathā.

Form that is past, future, or present; internal or external; likewise, subtle or gross.

647.

647.

Hīnaṃ paṇītaṃ yaṃ dūre, santike vā tadekato;

Sabbaṃ rūpaṃ samodhāya, rūpakkhandhoti vuccati.

Inferior or superior, that which is far or near—all form, taken together and gathered, is called the form aggregate.

648.

648.

Tatheva vedanākkhandho, nāma yā kāci vedanā;

Saññākkhandhoti saññā ca, rāsibhāvena bhāsitā.

Likewise, the aggregate of feeling is whatever feeling there is; and the aggregate of perception is perception, spoken of in the sense of a mass.

649.

649.

Vaṭṭadhammesu assādaṃ, tadassādopasevanaṃ;

Vinibhujja nidassetuṃ, khandhadvayamudāhaṭaṃ.

To discern and demonstrate the allure in the states of the round of existence, and the cultivation of that allure, two aggregates are declared.

650.

650.

Vivādamūlasaṃsāra-kamahetunidassanaṃ;

Sandhāya vedanā saññā, katā nānāti kecana.

With reference to demonstrating the root of contention and the cause of the course of saṃsāra, some say that feeling and perception are made diverse.

651.

651.

Cittasaṃsaṭṭhadhammānaṃ, cetanāmukhato pana;

Saṅkhārakkhandhanāmena, dhammā cetasikā matā.

Of states associated with mind, with volition as their chief, the mental factors are known by the name 'aggregate of formations'.

652.

652.

Sabbabhedaṃ tathā cittaṃ, viññāṇakkhandha sammataṃ;

Bhedābhāvena nibbānaṃ, khandhasaṅgahanissaṭaṃ.

Likewise, mind in all its diversity is considered the aggregate of consciousness; Nibbāna, by reason of its non-division, is excluded from the aggregation of the aggregates.

653.

653.

Ālambanīyabhāvena, upādānopakārato;

Pañcupādānakkhandhāti, lokuttaravivajjitā.

By way of being an object and by aiding clinging, the five aggregates subject to clinging are so called, excluding the supramundane.

654.

654.

Yathā [V 0.0061] thūlaṃ hitatthāya, pariggāhakayoginaṃ;

Dhammā tebhūmakā eka-bhūmibhāvāya desitā.

For the benefit of yogis who grasp the coarse, the states pertaining to the three planes are taught for the purpose of attaining the state of one plane.

655.

655.

Bhājanaṃ bhojanaṃ tassa, byañjanaṃ bhojako tathā;

Bhuñjitā cāti pañcete, upamenti yathākkamaṃ.

The vessel, the food, its condiment, the eater, and likewise the act of eating—these five are compared in due order.

656.

656.

Gilānasālā gelaññaṃ, asappāyopasevanā;

Samuṭṭhānaṃ gilānoti, upamenti ca paṇḍitā.

The sickroom, sickness, indulgence in the unsuitable, the arising of sickness, and the sick person—thus do the wise make comparison.

657.

657.

Cārako kāraṇaṃ tattha, aparādho ca kārako;

Aparādhakato coro, iti copamitā puna.

The prison, the cause thereof, the offense, the perpetrator, and the thief who has committed an offense—thus again are they compared.

658.

658.

Niccādhipīḷanaṭṭhena[M 0.0057], bhārāti paridīpitā;

Klesadukkhamukhenete, khādakā ca nirantaraṃ.

By the meaning of constant oppression, they are declared as burdens; through defilements and suffering, they are also ceaseless devourers.

659.

659.

Anatthāvahitā niccamukkhittāsikaverino;

Maccumārābhidheyyattā, vadhakāti ca bhāsitā.

Constantly bringing harm, they are enemies with drawn swords; by reason of being called Death-Māra, they are also spoken of as killers.

660.

660.

Vimaddāsahanaṃ rūpaṃ, pheṇapiṇḍaṃva dubbalaṃ;

Muhuttaramaṇīyattā, vedanā bubbuḷūpamā.

Form is unable to endure crushing, weak like a lump of foam; feeling is like a water bubble, by reason of being delightful for a moment.

661.

661.

Marīcikūpamā saññā, vipallāsakabhāvato;

Saṅkhārāpi ca nissārā, kadalikkhandhasādisā.

Perception is like a mirage, by reason of its delusive nature; and formations are also without substance, like a plantain trunk.

662.

662.

Nānappakāraṃ cintentaṃ, nānāklesavimohitaṃ;

Palambhatīti viññāṇaṃ, māyāsamamudīritaṃ.

Consciousness deceives one who ponders in various ways, bewildered by diverse defilements; thus, it is declared to be like an illusion.

663.

663.

Iccevaṃ pañcupādānakkhandhā khandhā ca kevalaṃ;

Pañcakkhandhāti nāmena, desitāti vibhāvaye.

Thus, one should discern that the five aggregates subject to clinging and the mere aggregates are taught by the name 'the five aggregates'.

664.

664.

Ajjhattañca bahiddhā ca, viññāṇuppattikāraṇaṃ;

Dvārālambaṇabhedena, dvedhāyatanamīritaṃ.

The cause for the arising of consciousness, both internal and external, is declared as the twofold base, distinguished by way of door and object.

665.

665.

Cakkhādajjhattikaṃ tattha, chadvārāyatanaṃ bhave;

Bāhirāyatanaṃ nāma, tathā rūpādigocaraṃ.

Therein, the eye and so forth are the six internal door-bases; likewise, the external base is that which has forms and so forth as its range.

666.

666.

Iti [V 0.0062] vīthippavattānaṃ, dvārālambaṇasaṅgaho;

Āgame abhidhamme tu, sabbathāpi yathārahaṃ.

Thus is the summary of doors and objects for the cognitive process, explained in the Suttas and the Abhidhamma in every way as is appropriate.

667.

667.

Tathāhanantarātīto, jāyamānassa pacchato;

Mano sabbopi sabbassa, manassāyatanaṃ bhave.

Likewise, all mind that has immediately ceased becomes the mind-base for all that is arising afterwards.

668.

668.

Tathā pubbaṅgamaṭṭhena, sahajānamarūpinaṃ;

Dvārabhāvena viññāṇaṃ, sabbamāyatanaṃ mataṃ.

Likewise, by being a forerunner for the co-arisen immaterial states and by way of being a door, all consciousness is regarded as a base.

669.

669.

Manāyatanamiccevaṃ, pasādāyatanaṃ tathā;

Pañcaviññāṇadhammānaṃ, iti chaddhā vibhāvaye.

The mind-base, and likewise the sensitive bases for the phenomena of the five consciousnesses—thus one should discern in six ways.

670.

670.

Pañcappasādavisayā, pañcāyatanasammatā;

Sesaṃ rūpañca nibbānaṃ, sabbe cetasikāti ca.

The five objects of the sensitive faculties are considered the five bases; the remaining form, Nibbāna, and all mental factors.

671.

671.

Ekūnasaṭṭhidhammānaṃ[M 0.0058], dhammāyatanasaṅgaho;

Iti chaddhā pakāsenti, bāhirāyatanaṃ budhā.

The summary of fifty-nine phenomena is the mind-object base; thus the wise declare the external bases in six ways.

672.

672.

Suññagāmova daṭṭhabba-majjhattikamasārato;

Gāmaghātakacorāva, taṃ hanantaṃva bāhiraṃ.

The internal should be seen as an empty village, being essenceless; the external, like village-plundering robbers, striking it down.

673.

673.

Nāmappavattimuḷhānaṃ, taduppattikakāraṇaṃ;

Dvādasāyatanānīti, vuttamitthaṃ mahesinā.

For those bewildered by the process of mentality, the twelve bases were taught as the cause of its arising—thus it was spoken here by the Great Sage.

674.

674.

Samattā bhāvamattena, dhārentīti salakkhaṇaṃ;

Dvārālambataduppanna-pariyāyena bheditā.

Because, by their very nature, they bear their own characteristics, they are called elements; they are divided by way of door, object, and what has arisen from them.

675.

675.

Manāyatanametthāha, satta viññāṇadhātuyo;

Ekādasa yathāvuttā, iccaṭṭhārasa dhātuyo.

Here, the mind-base is said to be the seven consciousness-elements; the other eleven are as stated—thus there are eighteen elements.

676.

676.

Antādikā manodhātu, manoviññāṇadhātuyā;

Pavesāpagame dvāra-pariyāyena tiṭṭhati.

The mind-element, functioning at the beginning and the end, stands as a door for the mind-consciousness-element at its entrance and departure.

677.

677.

Bherītaladaṇḍaghosa-samaṃ chakkaṃ yathākkamaṃ;

Kaṭṭhāraṇipāvakādi-samañca tividhaṃ bhave.

The sixfold group, respectively, is like the drum, the stick, and the sound; and the threefold group is like the fire-sticks and the fire.

678.

678.

Dukkhaṃ [V 0.0063] samudayo ceva, nirodho ca tathāparo;

Maggo cāti catuddhāha, saccaṃ saccaparakkamo.

Suffering, its origin, and likewise its cessation, and the path—thus the truth is declared in four ways by the one whose striving is for truth.

679.

679.

Bhāro ca bhāradānañca, bhāranikkhepanaṃ tathā;

Bhāranikkhepanūpāyo, iccopammaṃ yathākkamaṃ.

The burden, the taking up of the burden, and likewise the laying down of the burden; the means of laying down the burden—this is the simile in due order.

680.

680.

Rogo roganidānañca, rogavūpasamo tathā;

Rogabhesajjamicceva-mupamāhi ca dīpitaṃ.

Disease, the cause of disease, and likewise the allaying of disease; and the medicine for disease—thus it is illuminated by similes.

681.

681.

Visarukkho rukkhamūlaṃ, rukkhacchedo tathāparo;

Rukkhacchedakasatthanti, catudhopamitaṃ tathā.

The poisonous tree, the root of the tree, and likewise the cutting of the tree; and the axe for cutting the tree—thus it is compared in four ways.

682.

682.

Tīramorimasaṅkhātaṃ, mahogho pārimaṃ tathā;

Tadatikkamupāyoti, upamenti ca taṃ budhā.

The near shore, the great flood, and likewise the far shore; and the means to cross beyond—thus the wise compare it.

683.

683.

Sacchikatvāna paccakkha-miccopammaṃ yathākkamaṃ;

Samācikkhi vimokkhāya, saccaṃ tacchaniyāmato.

Having realized it directly, he explained the similes in due order; for the sake of liberation, he taught the truth according to its unfailing nature.

684.

684.
