Tathā [M 0.0059] hi dukkhaṃ nābādhaṃ, nāññaṃ dukkhā ca bādhakaṃ;

Bādhakattaniyāmena, dukkhasaccamitīritaṃ.

For suffering is indeed affliction, and nothing other than suffering is an afflicter; by the principle of being an afflicter, it is declared the truth of suffering.

685.

685.

Taṃ vinā nāññato dukkhaṃ, na hoti na ca taṃ tato;

Dukkhahetuniyāmena, saccamāha visattikaṃ.

Without it, suffering does not arise from any other source, nor does it come from anywhere else; by the fixed law of the cause of suffering, he declared the truth to be craving.

686.

686.

Nāññā nibbānato santi, na ca santaṃ na taṃ yato;

Santabhāvaniyāmena, nibbānaṃ saccamuttamaṃ.

There is no peace other than Nibbāna, nor is there peace from what is other than that; by the fixed nature of peace, Nibbāna is the supreme truth.

687.

687.

Nāññaṃ maggāca niyyānaṃ, aniyyāno na cāpi so;

Tasmā niyyānabhāvena, maggo saccanti sammato.

There is no deliverance apart from the path, nor is it not a means of deliverance; therefore, by its nature as deliverance, the path is regarded as truth.

688.

688.

Iti tacchāvipallāsa-bhūtabhāvo catūsupi;

Saccaṭṭhoti viniddiṭṭho, dukkhādīsvavisesato.

Thus, the meaning of truth is indicated as the true, unperverted, and real nature in all four—suffering and the rest—without distinction.

689.

689.

Pīḷanaṭṭho saṅkhataṭṭho, santāpaṭṭho ca bhāsito;

Viparīṇāmaṭṭho cāti, dukkhassevaṃ catubbidhā.

The meaning of oppression, the meaning of being conditioned, and the meaning of burning are declared; and the meaning of change—thus the meanings of suffering are fourfold.

690.

690.

Āyūhanā [V 0.0064] nidānā ca, saṃyogā palibodhato;

Dukkhassamudayassāpi, catudhatthā pakāsitā.

Accumulation, origin, connection, and obstruction; thus the meanings of the origin of suffering are also declared in four ways.

691.

691.

Nissāraṇā vivekā cā-saṅkhatāmatato tathā;

Atthā dukkhanirodhassa, catudhāva samīritā.

Escape, seclusion, and likewise the unconditioned and the deathless; the meanings of the cessation of suffering are thus stated in four ways.

692.

692.

Niyyānato hetuto ca,

Dassanādhipateyyato;

Maggassāpi catuddheva-

Miti soḷasadhā ṭhitā.

Leading out, cause, seeing, and supremacy; the meanings of the path are also fourfold—thus they stand as sixteen aspects.

693.

693.

Saccikaṭṭhaparamatthaṃ, tacchābhisamayaṭṭhato;

Tathatthamapi saccaṭṭhaṃ, paṭṭhapentettha paṇḍitā.

Because its meaning is the direct realization of the real, the wise here establish the meaning of truth as the ultimate meaning of reality and the meaning of 'thusness'.

694.

694.

Tadetaṃ paṭivijjhanti, ariyāva catubbidhaṃ;

Vuttamariyasaccanti, tasmā nāthena taṃ kathaṃ;

The noble ones alone penetrate this fourfold truth; therefore it was spoken of by the Protector as the Noble Truth.

695.

695.

Jāti [M 0.0060] jarā ca maraṇaṃ, soko ca paridevanā;

Dukkhañca domanassañca, upāyāso tathāparo.

Birth, aging, and death, sorrow and lamentation, pain, grief, and also despair.

696.

696.

Appiyehi ca saṃyogo, vippayogo piyehi ca;

Yampi na labhaticchanto, tampi dukkhamidaṃ mataṃ.

Association with the disliked, and separation from the liked; not getting what one desires—this too is considered suffering.

697.

697.

Apāyesupapajjantā, cavantā devalokato;

Manussesu ca jīrantā, nānābyasanapīḷitā.

Being reborn in the lower realms, passing away from the deva world, and aging among humans, afflicted by various calamities.

698.

698.

Socantā paridevantā, vedentā dukkhavedanaṃ;

Domanassehi santattā, upāyāsavighātino.

Grieving, lamenting, experiencing painful feelings, tormented by grief, overcome by despair.

699.

699.

Aniṭṭhehi akantehi, appiyehi samāyutā;

Saṅkhārehi ca sattehi, nānānatthavidhāyibhi.

Associated with the undesired, the unlovely, the disagreeable—with conditioned things and beings that bring about diverse harms;

700.

700.

Iṭṭhehi piyakantehi, manāpehi viyojitā;

Saṅkhārehi ca sattehi, nānāsampattidāyibhi.

Separated from the desired, the dear and lovely, the delightful—from conditioned things and beings that bestow various blessings;

701.

701.

Dukkhāpagamamicchantā[V 0.0065], patthayantā sukhāgamaṃ;

Alabbhaneyyadhammesu, pipāsāturamānasā.

Desiring the cessation of suffering, longing for the arrival of happiness, with minds tormented by thirst for things unattainable.

702.

702.

Kicchādhipannā kapaṇā, vipphandantā rudammukhā;

Taṇhādāsā parābhūtā, bhavasaṃsārasaṃkaṭe.

Overcome by hardship, miserable, struggling, with tearful faces, enslaved by craving, defeated in the perilous round of existence.

703.

703.

Yaṃ tebhūmakanissandaṃ, kaṭukaṃ gāḷhavedanaṃ;

Vedenti saṃsāraphalaṃ, taṃjātādiṃ vinā kuto.

That bitter, intense pain, the outcome of the three realms, which they experience as the fruit of saṃsāra—how could that be without birth and so forth?

704.

704.

Tasmā jātādibhedehi, bādhamānā bhayāvahā;

Dukkhā ca dukkhavatthu ca, bahudhāpi papañcitā.

Therefore, suffering, which is oppressive and fear-bringing, and the basis of suffering, are expounded in manifold ways through the divisions of birth and so forth.

705.

705.

Te sabbe pañcupādāna-kkhandhā eva samāsato;

Dukkhādhiṭṭhānabhāvena, dukkhatāya niyāmitā.

All these, in brief, are simply the five aggregates subject to clinging; by their nature as a basis for suffering, they are determined to be suffering.

706.

706.

Tasmā tebhūmakā dhammā, sabbe taṇhāvivajjitā;

Dukkhasaccanti desesi, desanākusalo muni.

Therefore, the Sage skilled in teaching declared all phenomena of the three realms, excluding craving, to be the truth of suffering.

707.

707.

Virāgatejālābhena[M 0.0061], taṇhāsnehasinehitaṃ;

Visarukkhova jātādinānānatthaphalodayaṃ.

Through the power of the fire of dispassion, the arising of the fruit of various harms such as birth—which, like a poison tree, is moistened by the oil of craving—is ended.

708.

708.

Nandirāgānubandhena, santānamavakaḍḍhitaṃ;

Punabbhavābhinibbattibhāvena parivattati.

Bound by attachment to delight and lust, the stream of being is drawn along; it revolves through the process of rebirth into new existence.

709.

709.

Patiṭṭhitañca tatthetamattasnehānusevanaṃ;

Gocarānunayābaddhaṃ, rāgamucchāsamohitaṃ.

Established there, pursuing affection for self, bound by longing for its pastures, deluded by the intoxication of passion.

710.

710.

Klesarāsiparikliṭṭhaṃ, byasanopaddavāhataṃ;

Dukkhasallasamāviddhaṃ, vihaññati nirantaraṃ.

Defiled by a mass of defilements, struck by calamity and disaster, pierced by the dart of suffering, it is constantly afflicted.

711.

711.

Have virāgatejena, vicchinne sati sabbathā;

Kena bandhena santāna-mānessati bhavantaraṃ.

When craving is completely severed by the power of dispassion, by what bond will the continuity be led to another existence?

712.

712.

Bhavantaramasampatte, santānamhi vivaṭṭite;

Kimadhiṭṭhāya jātādidukkhadhammā pavattare.

When another existence is not attained and the continuum has ceased to revolve, upon what foundation will the suffering of birth and so on come to pass?

713.

713.

Tasmā [V 0.0066] mokkhavipakkhena, taṇhādukkhavidhāyinī;

Dukkhasamudayo nāma, saccamiccāha nāyako.

Therefore, the Leader declared that craving, which produces suffering and is the antithesis of liberation, is the truth of the origin of suffering.

714.

714.

Sabbadukkhavinimuttaṃ, sabbaklesavinissaṭaṃ;

Dukkhanirodhanāmena, saccaṃ vuccati accutaṃ.

Freed from all suffering, released from all defilements, the unchanging truth is called by the name 'cessation of suffering'.

715.

715.

Dukkhañca parijānanto, pajahaṃ dukkhasambhavaṃ;

Nibbānaṃ padamārabbha, bhāvanāvīthimosaṭo.

Fully understanding suffering, abandoning the origin of suffering, making the state of Nibbāna one's aim, one enters upon the path of development.

716.

716.

Niyyānaṭṭhaṅgiko maggo, sabbadukkhavimuttiyā;

Dukkhanirodhagāmīti, saccaṃ tasmā tamīritaṃ.

The eightfold path is the way of release for liberation from all suffering; leading to the cessation of suffering, it was therefore proclaimed as that truth.

717.

717.

Catusaccavinimuttā, sesā lokuttarā matā;

Maggaṅgasampayuttā ca, phaladhammā ca sabbathā.

Separate from the Four Truths, the remaining supramundane states and the fruition states, which are in every way associated with the path factors, are so considered.

718.

718.

Itthaṃ sahetukaṃ dukkhaṃ, sopāyāmatanibbutiṃ;

Paṭipattihitatthāya, vibhāveti vināyako.

Thus, suffering with its cause, and the deathless quenching with its path, the Guide elucidates for the benefit of the practice.

719.

719.

Sappāṭihāriyaṃ dhammaṃ, desetvāna anuttaro;

Catudhāriyasaccāni, vibhajīti vibhāvaye.

Having taught the Dhamma with its wonders, the Incomparable One distinguishes and makes clear the four noble truths.

720.

720.

Tabbhāvabhāvibhāvena[M 0.0062], paccayākāralakkhitaṃ;

Tiyaddhaṃ dvādasaṅgañca, vīsatākārasaṅgahaṃ.

Marked by the mode of conditions through the nature of arising when that exists, it has three periods, twelve factors, and is gathered in twenty aspects.

721.

721.

Tisandhi catusaṅkhepaṃ, tivaṭṭañca tilakkhaṇaṃ;

Tebhūmakaṃ dvimūlañca, catukkanayamaṇḍitaṃ.

Three junctions, four summaries, three rounds, and three characteristics; three planes, two roots, and adorned with four methods.

722.

722.

Paccekaṃ catugambhīra-manupubbavavatthitaṃ;

Avijjākūṭasaṅkhātaṃ, bandhāvicchedamaṇḍalaṃ.

Individual, fourfold profound, gradually established; known as the peak of ignorance, the circle of uninterrupted bondage.

723.

723.

Sokādīnatthanissandaṃ, kevalaṃ dukkhapiṇḍitaṃ;

Paṭiccasamuppādoti, bhavacakkaṃ pavuccati.

The source of sorrow and the like, entirely a mass of suffering, Dependent Origination is thus called the wheel of existence.

724.

724.

Paṭividdhāya vijjāya, bhaṅgāvijjāya sabbathā;

Vivaṭṭatānupubbena, hetubhaṅgā yathākathaṃ.

When ignorance has been pierced through by knowledge and is completely destroyed, by a gradual turning back, the breaking of the causes occurs accordingly.

725.

725.

Asmiṃ [V 0.0067] sati idaṃ hoti, assuppādā idaṃ bhave;

Asatāsmiṃ na taṃ hoti, tassa bhaṅgāva bhijjati.

When this exists, this comes to be; with the arising of this, this arises. When this does not exist, this does not come to be; with the cessation of this, this ceases.

726.

726.

Etamatthaṃ purakkhatvā, paccayaṭṭhiti dassitā;

Paṭiccasamuppādassa, idappaccayatā naye.

Having taken this meaning as foremost, the stability of conditions is shown in the method of Dependent Origination, that is, the principle of specific conditionality.

727.

727.

Tathā hi jātiyāpāha, paccayattaṃ mahāmuni;

Jarāmaraṇadhammānaṃ, mattābhedepi vatthuto.

For the Great Sage declared birth as a condition for the phenomena of aging and death, even when there is only a slight distinction in substance.

728.

728.

Āhaccapaccayaṭṭhamhi, nedisī paccayaṭṭhiti;

Tattha dhammantarasseva, paccayaṭṭho vibhāvito.

In the state of being an adventitious condition, such stability of a condition is not found; there, the state of the condition is clarified only through a different phenomenon.

729.

729.

Vuttamācariyenetaṃ, paṭṭhānanayasaṅgahe;

Labbhamānanayaṃ tāva, dassanatthaṃ papañcito.

This was stated by the Teacher in the compilation on the method of relations; the obtainable method, however, is elaborated for the purpose of demonstration.

730.

730.

Ettha tasmānupekkhitvā, āhacca niyamaṃ budho;

Tabbhāvabhāvimattena, paccayatthaṃ vibhāvaye.

Therefore, the wise one, having paid attention here and having applied the principle, should discern the meaning of conditionality by the mere fact of arising when that exists.

731.

731.

Tatthāvijjā ca saṅkhārā, addhātītoti bhāsitā;

Viññāṇaṃ nāmarūpañca, saḷāyatanasaññitaṃ.

Therein, ignorance and formations are said to be the past; consciousness, name-and-form, that designated as the six sense spheres,

732.

732.

Phasso ca vedanā taṇhā, upādānaṃ bhavoti ca;

Paccuppanno bhave addhā, bhave addhā anāgato.

contact, feeling, craving, clinging, and existence—these are certainly the present period; existence is also certainly the future period.

733.

733.

Jāti [M 0.0063] jarā maraṇanti, dvedhā hoti ca sabbathā;

Kālattayavavatthānaṃ, tiyaddhamiti dīpaye.

Birth, aging, and death—these are invariably twofold; the establishment of the three times thus reveals the three periods.

734.

734.

Tatthāvijjāti aññāṇaṃ, catusaccesu bhāsitaṃ;

Pubbante cāparante ca, paccayaṭṭhitiyaṃ tathā.

Therein, ignorance is the unknowing spoken of in regard to the Four Noble Truths, to the past and the future, and likewise to the stability of conditions.

735.

735.

Apuññātisaṅkhāroti, vuttā dvādasa cetanā;

Tathā puññābhisaṅkhāro, kāmarūpesu bhāsito.

The demeritorious formation is said to be the twelve volitions; likewise, the meritorious formation is spoken of in the desire and form realms.

736.

736.

Āneñjātisaṅkhāroti, vuttāruppā catubbidhā;

Kāyabbacīmanodvāraṃ, patvā tāyeva cetanā.

The imperturbable formation is said to be the fourfold immaterial volitions; those same volitions, having arisen through the doors of body, speech, and mind,

737.

737.

Vuttā [V 0.0068] kāyavacīcittasaṅkhārāti mahesinā;

Saṅkhārāti vibhattevamekūnatiṃsa cetanā.

are called the bodily, verbal, and mental formations by the Great Seer. Thus are the formations analyzed as twenty-nine volitions.

738.

738.

Ekūnavīsatividhaṃ, paṭisandhikkhaṇe tathā;

Pavatte dvattiṃsavidhaṃ, viññāṇaṃ pākamānasaṃ.

Nineteen-fold at the moment of rebirth-linking and likewise thirty-two-fold in the course of existence is consciousness, the resultant mind.

739.

739.

Tividhaṃ vedanā saññā, saṅkhārāti vibheditaṃ;

Nāmarūpaṃ tu duvidhaṃ, bhūtopādāyabhedato.

Feeling, perception, and formations are distinguished as threefold; name-and-form, however, is twofold, by the distinction between primary and derived matter.

740.

740.

Saḷāyatanasaṅkhātaṃ, cakkhādajjhattikaṃ mataṃ;

Cakkhusamphassādibhedā, phasso chadhā pakāsito.

The sixfold sense base, known as the internal, is considered to be the eye and so forth. Contact, distinguished as eye-contact and so on, is declared to be sixfold.

741.

741.

Sukhā dukkhā upekkhāti, vedanā tividhā bhave;

Kāme bhave ca vibhave, taṇhāti tividhā matā.

Pleasant, painful, and neutral—thus feeling is threefold; for sensual pleasure, for existence, and for non-existence—thus craving is considered threefold.

742.

742.

Kāmupādānādibhedā, upādānā catubbidhā;

Kammopapattibhedena, bhavo nāma dvidhā mato.

By the distinction of clinging to sensual pleasures and so on, grasping is fourfold; by the distinction of kamma and rebirth, becoming is considered twofold.

743.

743.

Attabhāvābhinibbatti, jāti nāma jarā pana;

Purāṇabhāvo maraṇaṃ, pariyosānamīritaṃ.

The production of a personal existence is called birth; aging, then, is the state of decay; death is said to be the final end.

744.

744.

Dvādasaṅgappabhedena, vibhattevaṃ mahesinā;

Paṭiccasamuppādoti, paccayā eva kevalā.

Thus, with its division into twelve factors, was it distinguished by the Great Sage; this Dependent Origination is merely and solely conditions.

745.

745.

Paṭicca phalabhāvena, sāpekkhaṃ ṭhitamattani;

Apaccakkhāya saṅgantvā, uppādentīti paccayā.

They exist in mutual reliance for the arising of a fruit; not rejecting one another, they come together and produce it. Thus they are called 'conditions'.

746.

746.

Avijjāsaṅkhārānaṃ [M 0.0064] tu, gahaṇe gahitāva te;

Taṇhupādānabhavāpi, iti pañcettha hetuyo.

With the taking of ignorance and formations, craving, clinging, and becoming are also included; thus, these five here are the causes.

747.

747.

Taṇhupādānabhavānaṃ, gahaṇe gahitā puna;

Avijjā saṅkhārā cāti, pañcevetthāpi hetuyo.

When craving, clinging, and becoming are taken, ignorance and formations are also taken again; thus, these five here are also the causes.

748.

748.

Viññāṇādisarūpena, dassitaṃ phalapañcakaṃ;

Jātijjarāmaraṇena, tadeva gahitaṃ puna.

The fivefold fruit is shown in the form of consciousness and so on; by birth, aging, and death, that same fruit is taken up again.

749.

749.

Atīte [V 0.0069] hetavo pañca, idāni phalapañcakaṃ;

Idāni hetavo pañca, āyatiṃ phalapañcakaṃ.

In the past, five causes; in the present, the fivefold fruit. In the present, five causes; in the future, the fivefold fruit.

750.

750.

Itthaṃ bhedena saṅgayha, dvādasaṅgaṃ vicakkhaṇā;

Atthāpattivisesena, vīsatākāramīrayuṃ.

Thus, comprehending the twelve factors by way of division, the discerning ones, through specific inferences of meaning, declared twenty aspects.

751.

751.

Hetuphalaṃ phalahetu, puna hetuphalanti ca;

Tisandhi catusaṅkhepaṃ, tamevāhu vibhāvino.

Cause-and-fruit, fruit-and-cause, and again cause-and-fruit; three connections, four summaries—the discerning ones declare it thus.

752.

752.

Avijjātaṇhupādānā, klesavaṭṭanti bhāsitā;

Bhavekadeso saṅkhārā, kammavaṭṭaṃ tatoparaṃ.

Ignorance, craving, and clinging are declared to be the round of defilements; formations and a part of becoming are the round of kamma.

753.

753.

Vipākavaṭṭamiccevaṃ, vivaṭṭenāvivaṭṭitaṃ;

Tivaṭṭavaṭṭitaṃ hutvā, vaṭṭametaṃ pavattati.

And so the round of result. Not being made to cease by the path to cessation, having become turned by the three rounds, this cycle proceeds.

754.

754.

Aniccañca khayaṭṭhena, dukkhametaṃ bhayaṭṭhato;

Anattāsārakaṭṭhena, vaṭṭamevaṃ tilakkhaṇaṃ.

Impermanent in the sense of decay, suffering in the sense of fear, non-self in the sense of being without substance—thus the round has three characteristics.

755.

755.

Saṃsārasseva vuttāyaṃ, paccayānaṃ paramparā;

Paṭiccasamuppādoti, tato tebhūmako mato.

This succession of conditions is said to be the very round of existence; it is Dependent Origination, and is therefore considered to pertain to the three planes.

756.

756.

Bandhāvijjāṇḍakosena, vijjādibhedavajjitā;

Vimuttirasamappattā, bhavataṇhāpipāsitā.

Bound by the eggshell of ignorance, devoid of the distinctions of knowledge, not having attained the taste of liberation, they are thirsty with the craving for becoming.

757.

757.

Abhisaṅkhārabhāvena, paṭibandhati santati;

Tathābhisaṅkhatā pāka-bhāvāya parivattati.

By its nature as a volitional formation, the continuity is bound; thus volitionally formed, it proceeds toward a state of ripening.

758.

758.

Vipākā [M 0.0065] puna kammāni, pākāni puna kammato;

Iccevaṃ pariyāyena, saṃsāroyaṃ pavattati.

From results, actions arise again; and from kamma, results arise again. Thus in this cycle does this round of existence proceed.

759.

759.

Iccāvijjābhavataṇhā, vaṭṭopatthambhakā matā;

Sampayuttānusayitā, tasmā vaṭṭaṃ dvimūlakaṃ.

Thus ignorance and craving for becoming are considered the supports of the round. Because they are associated with and latent, the round is therefore said to have two roots.

760.

760.

Paccayapaccayuppanna-santānabhedato pana;

Nānābhūtānamekantaṃ, bījarukkhādayo viya.

However, due to the continuity between condition and conditioned phenomenon, they are not absolutely separate, just like a seed and a tree.

761.

761.

Tathāpi [V 0.0070] tesaṃ dhammānaṃ, vatthulakkhaṇabhedato;

Dīpavaṭṭisikhānaṃva, natthi ekantamekatā.

Yet for these phenomena, due to the difference in their basis and characteristic, there is no absolute identity, just as for a lamp's wick and its flame.

762.

762.

Hetuhetusamuppannā, īhābhogavivajjitā;

Paccayāya ca paccetu-mabyāpārā tato matā.

Causes and things arisen from causes are devoid of striving and deliberation; therefore they are considered to be without agency in conditioning or in being conditioned.

763.

763.

Avijjādīnamevātha, sambhave sambhavanti ca;

Saṅkhārādisabhāvāti, ṭhitevaṃdhammatāya te.

When ignorance and so on exist, formations and so on also come to be; they stand thus by this specific conditionality of phenomena.

764.

764.

Itthamekattanānattā, abyāpāro tathāparo;

Etthevaṃdhammatā ceti, nayā vuttā catubbidhā.

Thus, neither-oneness-nor-otherness, non-agency, and likewise this specific conditionality—these four principles have been stated.

765.

765.

Phalānaṃ paccayuppatti, paccayattho ca hetusu;

Sabhāvapaṭivedho ca, desanā cittatāti ca.

The conditional arising of fruits, the meaning of condition in the causes, the penetration of their own-nature, and the diversity of the teaching.

766.

766.

Atthadhammapaṭivedha-desanānaṃ yathākkamaṃ;

Atigambhīrabhāvena, catugambhīramīritaṃ.

Because of the exceeding profundity, respectively, of the meaning, the phenomena, the teaching, and the penetration, it is called the four profundities.

767.

767.

Padhānakāraṇattā hi, avijjādiparamparā;

Kamena saṅkhārādīnaṃ, paccayāti vavatthitā.

Indeed, because of being the principal cause, the succession beginning with ignorance is established, in due order, as the condition for formations and the rest.

768.

768.

Tathā hi jātiyā eva, jarāmaraṇasambhavo;

Ajātānaṃ jarā vātha, maraṇaṃ vā kuto bhave.

For thus, from birth itself, aging and death arise; for those who are not born, how could there be aging or death?

769.

769.

Sāvopapattisaṅkhātā, jāti kammabhavoditā;

Aṅkuro viya bījamhā, tattha tatthopalabbhati.

That birth, known as re-arising, originates from kamma-becoming; like a sprout from a seed, it is found in this or that existence.

770.

770.

Sampayogānusayato, upādānappatiṭṭhitā;

Āyūhanti ca kammāni, ākaḍḍhantopapattikaṃ.

Through association and latent tendency, established in clinging, kammas are accumulated, drawing one toward a new birth.

771.

771.

Upādāniyadhammesu[M 0.0066], taṇhāsnehapipāsitā;

Daḷhī kubbantupādānaṃ, piyarūpābhinandino.

Thirsty with craving and affection for things that are a basis for clinging, those who delight in pleasing forms make their clinging strong.

772.

772.

Vedanīyesu dhammesu, assādamanupassato;

Vedanāpaccayā taṇhā, samuṭṭhāya pavaḍḍhati.

For one who sees gratification in things that are to be felt, craving arises from feeling as its condition and grows.

773.

773.

Iṭṭhāniṭṭhañca [V 0.0071] majjhattaṃ, phusantā pana gocaraṃ;

Vedenti vedanaṃ nāma, nāphusantā kudācanaṃ.

When one contacts a desirable, undesirable, or neutral object, one experiences what is called feeling; but without contacting an object, one never does.

774.

774.

Phusatālambaṇañceso, saḷāyatanasambhave;

Dvārābhāve kuto tassa, samuppatti bhavissati.

This contact, which has an object, arises when the six sense bases are present; without the sense doors, how could its arising possibly occur?

775.

775.

Saḷāyatanametañca, nāmarūpūpanissitaṃ;

Chaphassadvārabhāvena, pavattati yathārahaṃ.

And this sixfold sense base, dependently supported by name-and-form, proceeds as is fitting by way of being the six doors for contact.

776.

776.

Pubbaṅgamādhiṭṭhānena, viññāṇena patiṭṭhahe;

Nāmarūpaṃ upatthaddhaṃ, paṭisandhipavattiyaṃ.

With consciousness as its forerunner and foundation, name-and-form is established and sustained, both at rebirth-linking and in the course of existence.

777.

777.

Saṅkhārajanitaṃ hutvā, patiṭṭhāti bhavantare;

Viññāṇaṃ janakābhāve, tassuppatti kathaṃ bhave.

Having been generated by volitional formations, consciousness becomes established in another existence; in the absence of a generator, how could its arising occur?

778.

778.

Avijjāyānusayite, paṭivedhavirodhite;

Vaṭṭānugatasantāne, paṭisandhiphalāvahe.

In a continuum that follows the round, in which ignorance lies latent, which is opposed to penetration, and which brings the fruit of rebirth-linking,

779.

779.

Pākadhammā sabhāvena, pavattanti hi cetanā;

Avijjāpaccayā honti, saṅkhārāti tato matā.

volitions, which by nature are ripening phenomena, indeed proceed. Since they are conditioned by ignorance, they are therefore known as 'volitional formations'.

780.

780.

Paṭividdhesu saccesu, paccayānaṃ paramparā;

Vighātīyati sabbāpi, tato vaṭṭaṃ vivaṭṭati.

When the truths have been penetrated, the entire succession of conditions is terminated; thereby the round ceases to revolve.

781.

781.

Iccāvijjāvirodhena, tassā vaṭṭappavattiyā;

Saṅghātanikabhāvena, avijjā kūṭasammatā.

Thus, because of its opposition to knowledge, its making the round proceed, and its nature of consolidating, ignorance is considered the ridge-pole.

782.

782.

Jarāmaraṇasaṅghāṭa-paṭipīḷitacetasaṃ;

Klesamucchāparetānaṃ, sā cāvijjā pavaḍḍhati.

For those whose minds are oppressed by the mass of aging and death, for those overcome by the swoon of the defilements, that very ignorance grows.

783.

783.

Iccābaddhamavicchedaṃ, idappaccayamaṇḍalaṃ;

Cakkanemisamāvaṭṭaṃ, kamena parivattati.

Thus this circle of specific conditionality, bound and unbroken, revolves in sequence, like the rim of a wheel.

784.

784.

Vaṭṭassa [M 0.0067] dvādasaṅgassa, tassa tebhūmakassa tu;

Dukkhakkhandhassa dassesi, nissandena nidassanaṃ.

The Great Seer showed the demonstration of the mass of suffering as the outflow of this twelve-linked round pertaining to the three planes.

785.

785.

Sokañca [V 0.0072] paridevañca, tathā dukkhañca kāyikaṃ;

Domanassamupāyāsaṃ, nānābyasanasambhavaṃ.

Sorrow and lamentation, and also bodily pain, mental displeasure and despair, arise from various misfortunes.

786.

786.

Iccāturamaniccantaṃ, mahopaddavasaṅkulaṃ;

Bahupaklesupassaṭṭhaṃ, dukkhametanti piṇḍitaṃ.

Thus, it is afflicted and impermanent, crowded with great calamities, assailed by many corruptions—this, in brief, is suffering.

787.

787.

Iccevaṃ pañcupādāna-kkhandhabheditasaṅgaho;

Attabhāvabhavaratho, hatthamuttaṃva yantakaṃ.

Thus this collection, distinguished as the five aggregates subject to clinging, is the chariot of individual existence, like a puppet released from the hand.

788.

788.

Gatiṭṭhitinivāsesu, saṃsaranto nirantaraṃ;

Cakkenetena yātīti, bhavacakkamidaṃ mataṃ.

Wandering unceasingly through destinies, stations, and abodes, one travels by this wheel—thus this is known as the wheel of becoming.

789.

789.

Avijjāṇḍaṃ padāletvā, paṭivedhappavattiyā;

Paccayappaccayuppannā, supaṭṭhanti sabhāvato.

Having split open the egg of ignorance through the arising of penetration, conditions and conditioned phenomena are well established by their own nature.

790.

790.

Aniccā dukkhanattā ca, bhaṅgavanto bhayāvahā;

Sādīnavāti saṅkhāya, vivaṭṭamabhitiṭṭhati.

Having comprehended them as impermanent, suffering, and not-self, as perishable and bringing fear, as disadvantageous, one stands firm in the unrolling of the round.

791.

791.

Tato sānusayā taṇhā, nirujjhati punabbhave;

Santānaratiyābhāvā, na pakkhandati sandhiyaṃ.

Then craving with its latent tendencies ceases in regard to future existence; due to the absence of delight in the continuum, it does not leap forward to relinking.

792.

792.

Aviruḷhikabhāvena, tattha vaṭṭavirodhite;

Abhisaṅkhārabhāvena, na pavattanti cetanā.

Therein, through the state of non-sprouting and opposition to the round, volitions no longer proceed by way of karmic formation.

793.

793.

Paṭisandhipavattīpi, na janenti bhavantare;

Iccāvijjānirodhena, niruddhā kammacetanā.

They no longer generate rebirth-linking and the ongoing process in another existence. Thus, with the cessation of ignorance, kammic volitions cease.

794.

794.

Paccayatthanirodhena, saṅkhārānaṃ nirodhato;

Viññāṇaṃ janakābhāvā, niruddhamiti vuccati.

With the cessation of their condition, and from the cessation of the formations, consciousness, lacking a generator, is said to have ceased.

795.

795.

Viññāṇādinirodhā ca, nāmarūpādikaṃ tathā;

Dukkhakkhandhassimassevaṃ, nirodhoti pavuccati.

And from the cessation of consciousness and so on, likewise name-and-form and so on cease. Thus is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering declared.

796.

796.

Iti [M 0.0068] vaṭṭavivaṭṭānaṃ, vasā dvedhā vibhāvito;

Paṭiccasamuppādoti, desitoyaṃ mahesinā.

Thus, this Dependent Origination, explained in a twofold way by means of the round and its unrolling, was taught by the Great Seer.

797.

797.

Sabbasaṅkhatadhammānaṃ[V 0.0073], sabbe dhammāpi paccayā;

Janakā cevupatthambhā, saṃvibhattā yathārahaṃ.

For all conditioned phenomena, all phenomena are conditions, both generative and supportive, distinguished appropriately.

798.

798.

Āhacca paccayaṭṭhena, catuvīsatidhā ṭhitā;

Hetālambaṇādhipatānantarasamanantarā.

By way of specific conditionality, they are established in twenty-four ways: root condition, object condition, dominance condition, contiguity condition, immediate contiguity condition,

799.

799.

Sahajātaaññamañña-nissayā copanissayo;

Purejātā pacchājātā-sevanā kammameva ca.

Conascence condition, mutuality condition, dependence condition, decisive support condition, prenascence condition, postnascence condition, repetition condition, and kamma condition,

800.

800.

Pākāhārindriyajjhāna-maggaṅgasampayuttakā;

Vippayuttatthi natthi ca, vigatāvigatanti ca.

Result condition, nutriment condition, faculty condition, jhāna condition, path condition, association condition, dissociation condition, presence condition, absence condition, disappearance condition, and non-disappearance condition.

801.

801.

Pañcātītāva kammaṃ tu, vattamānañca īritaṃ;

Sabbathāpi tayo vuttā, vattamānā tatopare.

Five are past, while kamma is said to be present. Three are said to be of all times; the others are present.

802.

802.

Chadhā nāmaṃ tu nāmassa, pañcadhā nāmarūpinaṃ;

Ekadhā puna rūpassa, rūpaṃ nāmassa cekadhā.

Name is a condition for name in six ways; for name-and-form in five ways. Again, form is a condition for form in one way, and form is a condition for name in one way.

803.

803.

Paññattināmarūpāni, nāmassa duvidhā dvayaṃ;

Dvayassa navadhā ceti, chabbidhā paccayā kathaṃ.

Concept, name, and form are conditions for name in two ways; for the pair (name-and-form) in nine ways. How are there six kinds of conditions?

804.

804.

Niruddhānantarā eva, jāyantānamanantaraṃ;

Nāmadhammāva nāmānaṃ, janakattopakārakā.

Mental phenomena, immediately upon ceasing, are generative and supportive conditions for other mental phenomena that arise without interval.

805.

805.

Nirantarappavattiyā, anurūpamanantarā;

Anantarapaccayena, paccayoti pakāsitā.

Because of their continuous and suitable procession, they are revealed to be a condition by way of contiguity condition.

806.

806.

Samanantarabhāvena, tesaṃ te eva paccayā;

Samanantaranāmena, paccayoti pakāsitā.

Through their nature of immediate contiguity, those very same phenomena are conditions; they are revealed to be a condition by the name 'immediate contiguity condition'.

807.

807.

Atthibhāvāya dhammānaṃ, natthitāyopakārakā;

Natthipaccayanāmena, vuttā te eva tādinā.

Those very same phenomena, being helpful to the existence of other phenomena by their non-existence, are spoken of by the Tathāgata by the name 'absence condition'.

808.

808.

Okāsadānabhāvena, vigatāvopakārakā;

Dhammā te eva vuccanti, vigatappaccayoti ca.

Those very same phenomena, being helpful by giving an opportunity through their disappearance, are also called 'disappearance condition'.

809.

809.

Javā [M 0.0069][V 0.0074] paguṇabhāvāya, javānamupakārakā;

Āsevanapaccayoti, niruddhānantarā matā.

Those that have ceased immediately before are helpful for the proficiency of subsequent javanas; they are known as the repetition condition.

810.

810.

Saṃsaṭṭhasahajātānaṃ, sampayogena paccayā;

Sampayuttapaccayoti, nāmā nāmānamīritā.

For conjoined and co-arisen phenomena, mental phenomena are a condition by way of association; thus they are called the 'association condition' for other mental phenomena.

811.

811.

Icceko vattamāno ca, pañcātītā yathārahaṃ;

Arūpānamarūpā ca, paccayā chabbidhā matā.

Thus, one present and five past conditions, as appropriate, are the six kinds of conditions that are immaterial for the immaterial.

812.

812.

Pavatte cittajātānaṃ, kammajānañca sandhiyaṃ;

Rūpānaṃ sahajātāna-marūpānañca tādinā.

In the course of existence, for mind-born and kamma-born phenomena; at relinking, for co-arisen material and immaterial phenomena, the Tathāgata taught:

813.

813.

Hetubhūtā cha dhammāpi, mūlaṭṭhenopakārakā;

Hetupaccayabhāvena, paccayoti pakāsitā.

The six phenomena that are roots are helpful by way of being a foundation; they are revealed as a condition by way of root condition.

814.

814.

Tathā nijjhāyanaṭṭhena, tesamevopakārakā;

Jhānapaccayanāmena, jhānadhammā vibhāvitā.

Likewise, the jhāna-factors are helpful to those same phenomena by way of close meditation; they are explained by the name 'jhāna condition'.

815.

815.

Tatheva niyyānaṭṭhena, paccayāti pakāsitā;

Maggapaccayanāmena, maggaṅgā ca mahesinā.

Similarly, the path-factors are revealed by the Great Seer as a condition by the name 'path condition' because they have the characteristic of leading out.

816.

816.

Tesameva ca dhammānaṃ, sahajātāti cetanā;

Kammabyāpārābhāvena, vattamānā ca paccayā.

For those same phenomena, the co-arisen volition, being present, is a condition by way of its kamma-function.

817.

817.

Kaṭattārūpapākānaṃ, nānakkhaṇikacetanā;

Abhisaṅkhārabhāvena, janakappaccayā matā.

For the resultant immaterial phenomena produced by it, the volition of a different moment is known as a generative condition by way of being a volitional formation.

818.

818.

Iccevaṃ duvidhā bhedā, vipphāraṭṭhena cetanā;

Kammapaccayanāmena, paccayoti pakāsitā.

Thus volition, of two kinds by way of its pervasive influence, is revealed as a condition by the name 'kamma condition'.

819.

819.

Rūpānaṃ sahajātānaṃ, aññamaññamarūpinaṃ;

Paccayā santabhāvena, vipākā samudīritā.

Resultant phenomena are declared to be conditions by their peaceful presence for co-arisen material phenomena and for immaterial phenomena mutually.

820.

820.

Ekotītopi cattāro, vattamānāti pañcadhā;

Paccayā nāmadhammāva, nāmarūpānamīritā.

One past and four present, thus in five ways, mental phenomena alone are said to be conditions for name-and-form.

821.

821.

Imassa [V 0.0075] rūpakāyassa, pacchājātopakārako;

Pacchājātapaccayoti, nāmaṃ rūpānamekadhā.

Name is helpful to this material body by arising after it; thus name is a condition for form in one way, as postnascence condition.

822.

822.

Sattaviññāṇadhātūnaṃ[M 0.0070], cha vatthūni pavattiyaṃ;

Pañcaviññāṇavīthiyā, pañcālambā yathākkamaṃ.

In the course of existence, the six bases are conditions for the seven consciousness-elements; in the five-door cognitive process, the five objects are conditions respectively.

823.

823.

Purejātavisesena, nāmānamupakārakā;

Purejātapaccayoti, rūpaṃ nāmassa cekadhā.

By the specific mode of prenascence, they are helpful to mental phenomena; thus form is a condition for name in one way, as prenascence condition.

824.

824.

Cittacetasikā dhammā, yaṃ yamārabbha jāyare;

Ālambaṇapaccayoti, sabbametaṃ pavuccati.

Whatever object mind and mental factors arise depending on—all that is called the object condition.

825.

825.

Yamālambaṃ garuṃ katvā, nāmadhammā pavattare;

Svāyamevālambaṇūpa-nissayoti pakāsito.

When mental phenomena proceed by taking a certain object as weighty, this very same is explained as the object-decisive-support condition.

826.

826.

Anantarapaccayena, ye dhammā paccayā matā;

Te eva vānantarūpa-nissayoti pakāsito.

Those states that are regarded as conditions by way of contiguity—these are explained as the contiguity-decisive-support condition.

827.

827.

Rāgasaddhādayo dhammā, ajjhattamanuvāsitā;

Sattasaṅkhāradhammā ca, bahiddhopanisevitā.

States such as lust and faith, internally pervading, and the seven supportive conditions, externally cultivated—

828.

828.

Rāgasaddhādidhammānaṃ, kammaṃ pākānamiccayaṃ;

Pakatūpanissayoti, paṭṭhapesi tathāgato.

For states such as lust and faith, and for kamma in relation to its results, the Tathāgata established the natural decisive-support condition.

829.

829.

Iccevaṃ balavaṭṭhena, nissayenopakārakā;

Upanissayanāmena, paccayoyaṃ tidhā mato.

Thus, by way of being a strong factor, helpful by way of support, this condition is considered threefold under the name of decisive support.

830.

830.

Rūpārūpaṃ paniccevaṃ, tekālikamakālikā;

Paññatti ceva nāmānaṃ, paccayo duvidho mato.

For mental states, the condition is considered twofold: temporal form and non-form, and timeless concepts.

831.

831.

Ālambādhippatibhūtaṃ, nāmānaṃ garugocaraṃ;

Sahajādhippatīdhammā, sahajānaṃ yathārahaṃ.

The object as predominant condition, the sphere of weighty objects for mental states; co-nascent predominant states, for co-nascent states, as appropriate.

832.

832.

Nāmarūpānamicceva-mādhippaccena paccayo;

Adhippatipaccayoti, duvidhā paridīpito.

Thus, by way of predominance, it is a condition for mind and matter; the predominance condition is explained as twofold.

833.

833.

Sahajā [V 0.0076] nāmarūpānaṃ, mahābhūtā ca rūpinaṃ;

Paṭisandhikkhaṇe vatthu, nāmānamiti sabbathā.

Co-nascent phenomena for mind and matter; the great elements for material form; and at the moment of rebirth-linking, the base for mental states—thus in every way.

834.

834.

Sahajātavisesena, dhammānamupakārakā;

Sahajātapaccayoti, tividhevaṃ vibhāvitā.

By the distinction of co-nascence, they are helpful to phenomena; the co-nascence condition is thus explained as threefold.

835.

835.

Arūpino [M 0.0071] catukkhandhā, mahābhūtā catubbidhā;

Sandhiyaṃ vatthunāmāni, sahajānīti sabbathā.

The four immaterial aggregates, the fourfold great elements; at the moment of linking, the base and mental states are co-nascent, in every way.

836.

836.

Upakārapavattā ca, aññamaññassa tādinā;

Aññamaññapaccayoti, vibhattā tividhā matā.

Being helpful in their occurrence to one another, and being of such a nature to each other, the condition of mutuality is considered to be divided threefold.

837.

837.

Sattaviññāṇadhātūnaṃ, bhūtopādāyarūpinaṃ;

Sahajātanāmarūpa-dhammānañca yathākkamaṃ.

For the seven consciousness-elements, for material form derived from the great elements, and for co-nascent mind-and-matter phenomena, each in due order.

838.

838.

Vatthu bhūtā catukkhandhā, nissayenopakārakā;

Nissayappaccayo nāma, paccayoti mato tidhā.

The base, the great elements, and the four aggregates, being helpful by way of support—the condition called 'support condition' is considered threefold.

839.

839.

Kabaḷīkāro āhāro, rūpakāyassa paccayo;

Arūpino panāhārā, sahajānaṃ yathārahaṃ.

Edible food is a condition for the material body; immaterial nutriments, however, are for co-nascent phenomena, as appropriate.

840.

840.

Nāmarūpānamiccevaṃ, yāpanaṭṭhena paccayā;

Āhārapaccayoteva, duvidhevaṃ pakāsito.

Thus, being a condition for mind and matter by way of sustaining, the nutriment condition is explained as twofold.

841.

841.

Pasādajīvitārūpi-ndriyadhammā yathākkamaṃ;

Pañcaviññāṇupādinna-rūpānaṃ nāmarūpinaṃ.

The faculties of sensitivity, life, and immaterial states, in due order, are conditions for the five consciousnesses, for kamma-born matter, and for mind and matter.

842.

842.

Sahajātānamicceva-missaraṭṭhena paccayā;

Indriyappaccayoteva, tividhā samudāhaṭo.

Thus, for co-nascent states, being conditions by way of sovereignty, the faculty condition is declared as threefold.

843.

843.

Sattaviññāṇadhātūnaṃ, cha vatthūni yathārahaṃ;

Pacchājātā ca kāyassa, cittacetasikā tathā.

For the seven consciousness-elements, the six bases as appropriate; and likewise, post-nascent mind and mental factors for the body.

844.

844.

Arūpā sahajātānaṃ, rūpānanti matā tidhā;

Vippayuttapaccayoti, vippayogopakārakā.

Immaterial states for co-nascent material forms are regarded as threefold; the dissociation condition is thus helpful by way of dissociation.

845.

845.

Sahajātaṃ [V 0.0077] purejātaṃ, pacchājātañca sabbathā;

Kabaḷīkāro āhāro, rūpajīvitamiccayaṃ.

Co-nascent, pre-nascent, and post-nascent in every way; edible food, and the life faculty of form—such are these.

846.

846.

Atthipaccayasaṅkhāto, paccayo pañcadhā mato;

Vijjamānasabhāvena, paccayaṭṭhā yathārahaṃ.

The condition termed 'presence' is regarded as fivefold; by way of their existing nature, they stand as conditions, as appropriate.

847.

847.

Te evāvigatā hutvā, vattamānopakārakā;

Avigatapaccayoti, sugatena vavatthitā.

These very same conditions, being non-disappeared, are helpful while present; thus was the 'non-disappearance condition' determined by the Well-Gone One.

848.

848.

Aṭṭhevaṃ [M 0.0072] vattamānāni, nāmarūpāni paccayā;

Sabbatthādhippatī cāti, navadhā nāmarūpinaṃ.

Thus, eight present mind-and-matter phenomena act as conditions; and with the all-pervading predominance, there are thus nine conditions for mind and matter.

849.

849.

Itthamuddiṭṭhaniddiṭṭhā, paṭṭhānanayasaṅgahā;

Kusalākusalādīhi, suvibhattā mahesinā.

Thus, the collected methods of the Paṭṭhāna, both outlined and detailed, have been well-divided by the Great Sage by way of the skillful, unskillful, and so on.

850.

850.

Paññattināmarūpānaṃ, vasena tividhā ṭhitā;

Paccayāti pakāsenti, catuvīsati paṇḍitā.

Distinguished threefold by way of concept, mind, and matter, the wise declare that there are twenty-four conditions.

851.

851.

Paññatti paññapīyattā, paññāpetīti ca dvidhā;

Nāmarūpavinimuttā, paññattā tādinā kathaṃ.

A concept is twofold: because it is made known and because it makes known. How is that which is free from mind and matter designated by the Such a One?

852.

852.

Bhūtapariṇāmākāramupādāya tathā tathā;

Bhūmipabbatapāsāṇatiṇarukkhalatādayo.

Depending on the various forms of the transformation of the great elements, there are concepts such as earth, mountains, rocks, grass, trees, and creepers.

853.

853.

Sambhārākāramārabbha, sannivesavisesitā;

Yānagāmavanuyyānakaṭasārapaṭādayo.

Based on the form of their components, distinguished by their particular arrangement, are concepts such as vehicles, villages, forests, parks, mats, ponds, and cloths.

854.

854.

Kārakavedakākāraṃ, viññattindriyalakkhitaṃ;

Khandhapañcakamāhacca, maccāsurasurādayo.

Based on the five aggregates, the appearance of a doer and an experiencer, characterized by intimation and faculties, gives rise to concepts such as mortals, asuras, and devas.

855.

855.

Candādāvaṭṭanādīhi, disākālādisammuti;

Pārampariyakādīhi, jātigottakulādayo.

By the revolution of the moon and sun and so forth, conventions of direction, time, and so on are established; by tradition and the like, birth, clan, family, and so on.

856.

856.

Taṃtaṃkriyādibhedehi, paññattā kathinādayo;

Taṃtaṃkalāpāsamphuṭṭhā, kūpākāsaguhādayo.

By distinctions of various actions and so forth, concepts such as the kathina ceremony are designated; and based on the non-contact with various material groups, concepts such as a well, space, and a cave are designated.

857.

857.

Taṃ [V 0.0078] taṃ nimittamārabbha, cintayantassupaṭṭhitā;

Kasiṇādikavohārā, bhāvanāmayagocarā.

Based on a particular sign, present for one who contemplates, are the designations of kasiṇa and so forth, which are the sphere of meditative development.

858.

858.

Pubbopalabbhābhāvena, kasiṇugghāṭimādayo;

Nirodhā ca samāpatti, visesābhāvalakkhitā.

By the non-existence of a previously apprehended object, concepts such as the removal of the kasiṇa are designated; and the attainment of cessation is characterized by the absence of particulars.

859.

859.

Iti taṃ tamupādāya, samaññātā tathā tathā;

Saṅkhā samaññā paññatti, vohāroti pakāsitā.

Thus, dependent on this and that, they are designated in such and such a way. They are declared as convention, designation, concept, and expression.

860.

860.

Ālambaṇaṭṭhākārena, santābhāvepi vatthuto;

Cintāvohāranipphannā, atthacchāyāva bhāsinī.

By way of object and mode, though in reality non-existent, produced by thought and expression, it shines like a shadow of meaning.

861.

861.

Paññāpīyattā [M 0.0073] paññatti, nāmāyamiti bhāsitā;

Upādāya ca paññatti, sā evopanidhāya ca.

It is called 'designation' because it is made known; it is spoken of as 'name'. And that designation is by way of grasping, and also by way of placing near.

862.

862.

Paññatti paññāpanato, paṇḍitehi pakāsitā;

Avijjamānā paññatti, vijjamānātipi dvidhā.

Designation, because it makes known, is declared by the wise as twofold: non-existent designation and existent designation.

863.

863.

Lokavohārikaṭṭhena, paññattaṃ paramatthato;

Avijjamānametāya, paññāpenti yadā tadā.

When, by way of worldly usage, they designate with this that which is non-existent in ultimate reality, then...

864.

864.

Avijjamānapaññatti, vijjamānaṃ yadā puna;

Paññāpenti tadā esā, vijjamānanti vuccati.

That is non-existent designation. When, however, they designate that which exists, then this is called 'existent designation'.

865.

865.

Itthaṃ paññattidhammañca, sammatatthavisesato;

Bhāvadhammañca rūpādi-salakkhaṇavisesato.

Thus, there is the phenomenon of designation, by way of the particular meaning of convention; and the phenomenon of existence, such as form and so forth, by way of its own specific characteristics.

866.

866.

Paññāpetīti paññatti, nāmāyamiti bhāsitā;

Yā nāmaṃ nāmakammādināmena samudīritā.

'It makes known,' thus it is a 'designation'; 'this is a name,' thus it is spoken of. It is that which is proclaimed as 'name' by terms such as 'the act of naming'.

867.

867.

Sā evāvijjamānena-vijjamānādibheditā;

Itthisaddo chaḷābhiñño, rājaputto tu bhāsitā.

That very designation is divided into non-existent, existent, and so forth. The word 'woman' can refer to one with the six super-knowledges, while 'prince' is also spoken of.

868.

868.

Kriyānimittatthayoga-ruḷhijātopacārikā;

Sambandhopacayāvatthā, saṇṭhānāpekkhitā tathā.

Designations are based on action, sign, meaning, connection, conventional usage, origin, and figurative usage; and likewise on relation, accumulation, state, and dependence on shape.

869.

869.

Devadattotha [V 0.0079] medhāvī, vedanā candimā tathā;

Khattiyo narasīho ca, bhātā lohitakaṃ yuvā.

Devadatta, and the wise one; feeling, and likewise the moon; the warrior, and the lion among men; brother, the red one, and the youth.

870.

870.

Kuṇḍalaṃ dussamiccevamādibheditasaṅgahā;

Sammatatthasabhāvesu, vohārākāralakkhitā.

The collection is distinguished by such things as 'earring' and 'cloth'; they are characterized by modes of expression concerning conventional meanings and inherent natures.

871.

871.

Sāyaṃ yādicchakānvatthasaṅketakkhaṇasambhavā;

Vohāratthavisesena, ñeyyākārānusārinī.

This designation, arising from arbitrary usage, underlying meaning, convention, and moment, follows the mode of what is to be known by way of the particular meaning of expression.

872.

872.

Vacīghosānusārena, sotaviññāṇavīthiyā;

Pavattānantaruppanna-manodvārassa gocarā.

Following the sound of speech, by way of the ear-consciousness process, it is the object of the mind-door arising immediately after.

873.

873.

Atthā [M 0.0074] yassānusārena, viññāyanti tato paraṃ;

Sammatā ca sabhāvā ca, pubbasaṅketabhāgino.

Meanings, following which, are understood thereafter. Both conventions and inherent natures partake in prior convention.

874.

874.

Yāyaṃ vālambaṇākāravisese paṭidissati;

Vedanādivacīghosaṃ, sabhāvānugacetaso.

That which appears as a specific mode of object—the sound of speech such as 'feeling'—is of the mind that follows its own nature.

875.

875.

Sāyaṃ paññatti viññeyyā, lokasaṅketanimmitā;

Vacīviññattisahito, saddo evāti kecana.

This designation should be understood as fashioned by worldly convention. Some say it is just sound accompanied by verbal intimation.

876.

876.

Itthaṃ paññattidhammāti, vuttaṃ paññattikadvayaṃ;

Tathādhivacanā dhammā, niruttīti ca tādinā.

Thus has the twofold designation been stated as 'the phenomena of designation,' and likewise by such terms as 'the phenomena of appellation' and 'linguistic analysis'.

877.

877.

Avisaṃvādakaṭṭhena, lokavohārasādhakaṃ;

Samaññāsaccamiccevaṃ, ācikkhanti vicakkhaṇā.

By way of being non-deceptive and accomplishing worldly usage, the wise thus declare this to be conventional truth.

878.

878.

Satthā yaṃ paramatthamuttamaguṇo nāmañca rūpanti ca,

Dvedhākāsi sabhāvadhammakusalo nibbijjha dhammantaraṃ;

Vohāratthavisesañeyyamaparaṃ byākāsi paññattito,

Āraddhaṃ kamato mayevamakhilaṃ taṃ suṭṭhu niṭṭhāpitaṃ.

The Teacher, of supreme virtue in the ultimate truth, skilled in the nature of things, having penetrated other phenomena, divided that which is name and form into two. He explained another thing to be known as the particular meaning of expression, by way of designation. Thus, all that was begun by me in due order has been thoroughly completed.

879.

879.

Yaṃ dhammaṃ dhammarājā niratikamabhisambodhi maggena buddhā,

Katvā kaṇḍambamūle paramamanupamaṃ pāṭihīraṃ khaṇena;

Pātvākā [V 0.0080] tattha patvā puravaragaṇamullāpalāvaṇṇaraṃsi,

Tatthādāyatthasāraṃ kathitamaticiraṃ ṭhātu pāṭhānukūlaṃ.

The Dhamma to which the King of Dhamma, the Buddha, fully awakened by the unsurpassed path; having performed in an instant the supreme, incomparable miracle at the foot of the mango tree; having arrived there and made it manifest, gladdening the host of the excellent city with waves of loveliness—may that essence of meaning spoken there, conforming to the text, endure for a very long time.

Iti nāmarūpaparicchede sabbasaṅgahavibhāgo nāma

Thus, in the Analysis of Name and Form, this is the chapter named the 'Division Comprising Everything'.

Sattamo paricchedo.

The Seventh Chapter.

Niṭṭhito ca nāmarūpaparicchede sabbathāpi

And thus the Analysis of Name and Form is in every way completed.

Abhidhammaparamatthavibhāgo.

The Division of the Ultimate Realities of the Abhidhamma.

8. Aṭṭhamo paricchedo

8. The Eighth Chapter

Kasiṇāsubhavibhāgo

The Division of the Kasiṇas and the Foul

880.

880.

Ito [M 0.0075] paraṃ pavakkhāmi, bhāvanānayamuttamaṃ;

Nāmarūpaṃ pariggayha, paṭipajjitumīhato.

Hereafter I shall explain the supreme method of development for one who, having comprehended name and form, wishes to practice.

881.

881.

Bhāvanā duvidhā tattha, samatho ca vipassanā;

Samatho duvidho tattha, paritto ca mahaggato.

Therein, development is twofold: tranquility and insight. Therein, tranquility is twofold: limited and exalted.

882.

882.

Upacāramanuppatto, parittoti pavuccati;

Mahaggatappanāpatto, samatho lokiyo mato.

That which has attained access is called limited. The tranquility that has attained absorption in the exalted state is considered mundane.

883.

883.

Kasiṇāni dasāsubhā, dasadhānussatī tathā;

Appamaññā ca saññā ca, vavatthāruppakāni ca.

The ten kasiṇas, the ten impurities, likewise the ten recollections; the immeasurables, the one perception, the defining of the elements, and the immaterial states.

884.

884.

Kammaṭṭhānāni tatthāhu, cattālīsa vicakkhaṇā;

Yatthānuyogaṃ kubbantā, bhāventi samathadvayaṃ.

Therein, the wise have declared forty meditation subjects; by applying themselves to which, they develop the twofold tranquility.

885.

885.

Taṃ [V 0.0081] payogavisuddhena, patvānopāyasampadaṃ;

Ajjhāsayaṃ visodhetvā, bhāvetabbanti bhāsitaṃ.

It is said that this should be developed through purified effort, having attained the accomplishment of means and having purified one's disposition.

886.

886.

Kathaṃ karonto cārittaṃ, vārittañca vivajjiya;

Pātimokkhaṃ samādāya, saddhāya paripūraye.

How should one, practicing proper conduct and avoiding what is prohibited, having undertaken the Pātimokkha, fulfill it with faith?

887.

887.

Paṭisaṅkhāya sodhetvā, chadvāresu malāsavaṃ;

Chaḷindriyāni medhāvī, satārakkhena gopaye.

Having reflected and purified the defilements and taints at the six doors, the wise one should guard the six faculties with mindfulness as protector.

888.

888.

Pāpakājīvanissaṅgo, kuhakācāranissaṭo;

Ājīvaṃ parisodheyya, pahitatteṭṭhisuddhiyā.

Free from evil livelihood, freed from deceitful conduct, one should purify one's livelihood by the purity of resolute striving.

889.

889.

Idamatthitamārabbha, paṭisaṅkhāya yoniso;

Paññavā sampajaññena, paribhuñjeyya paccaye.

Having reflected wisely on this purpose, the wise one, with clear comprehension, should make use of the requisites.

890.

890.

Saṃvaraṃ pātimokkhe ca, sīlamindriyasaṃvaraṃ;

Ājīvapārisuddhiñca, tathā paccayanissitaṃ.

Restraint in the Pātimokkha, restraint of the sense faculties, purity of livelihood, and likewise the virtue dependent on the requisites.

891.

891.

Samādāya [M 0.0076] catuddheva-madhiṭṭheyya tato paraṃ;

Tasseva parivārāya, dhutaṅgāni yathārahaṃ.

Having undertaken these four, one should then be resolute; and for their support, one should undertake the ascetic practices as is appropriate.

892.

892.

Paṃsukūlikamaṅgaṃ ti-cīvaraṃ cīvarāyugaṃ;

Piṇḍapātikamaṅgañca, sapadānikamuttamaṃ.

The practice of wearing rag-robes, the practice of wearing the triple robe—the pair concerning robes; the practice of eating almsfood, and the excellent practice of eating in succession.

893.

893.

Khalupacchābhattikaṅgaṃ, dhutaṅgaṃ pattapiṇḍikaṃ;

Ekāsanikamiccevaṃ, pañcadhā bhojane ṭhitaṃ.

The practice of refusing food after the proper time, the ascetic practice of eating only from the bowl, and the practice of eating in one session; thus are the five established with regard to food.

894.

894.

Āraññikaṃ yathāsantha-

Tikaṅgaṃ rukkhamūlikaṃ;

Abbhokāsikasosāni-

Kaṅgā nesajjikaṃ tathā.

The practice of the forest-dweller, the practice of dwelling in any assigned lodging, the practice of dwelling at the root of a tree, the practice of dwelling in the open air, the practice of dwelling in a charnel ground, and likewise the practice of the sitter.

895.

895.

Cha senāsanamārabbha, dhutaṅgānīti terasa;

Kappiyepi ca loluppa-samācāravimuttiyā.

Thus there are thirteen ascetic practices, six concerning the dwelling place, for the purpose of freedom from greedy behavior even regarding what is allowable.

896.

896.

Sāmīcipaṭipattīti[V 0.0082], katvā sallekhavuttiyā;

Paccayattayamāhacca, paññattāni mahesinā.

As the proper course of conduct for a life of effacement, and based on the three requisites, they were prescribed by the Great Sage.

897.

897.

Catupārisuddhisīlaṃ, dhutaṅgaparivāritaṃ;

Pūretvāna visuddhevaṃ, payogaparisuddhiyā.

Having thus fulfilled the fourfold purity of virtue, supported by the ascetic practices, through purity of effort.

898.

898.

Tato paṇidhisampanno, bhāvanāya visārado;

Upāyaṃ paṭipādeyya, pavivekarato kathaṃ?

Then, endowed with resolution and skilled in development, how might one who delights in seclusion put the means into practice?

899.

899.

Āvāso ca kulaṃ lābho,

Gaṇo kammañca pañcamaṃ;

Addhānaṃ ñāti ābādho,

Gantho iddhīti te dasa.

Dwelling, supporters, gain, a group, and work as the fifth; a journey, relatives, sickness, study, and psychic power—these are the ten.

900.

900.

Chetvāna nipako yogī,

Palibodhe yathārahaṃ;

Nirālayo nirārambho,

Papañcopasame rato.

The wise yogi, having cut off obstacles as is fitting, without attachment, without new undertakings, delights in the stilling of proliferation.

901.

901.

Piyaṃ [M 0.0077] garuṃ bhāvaniyaṃ, vattāraṃ vacanakkhamaṃ;

Kattāramatigambhīrakathaṃ ṭhānaniyojakaṃ.

One who is dear, respected, and venerable; an admonisher who is patient with words; a speaker of profound discourse, who urges one on to a higher state.

902.

902.

Bahussutaṃ guṇavanta-māgammācariyaṃ budho;

Khamo padakkhiṇaggāhī, niyyātattuju bhadrako.

The wise one, having approached a learned and virtuous teacher, is patient, receptive to instruction, self-surrendered, upright, and good.

903.

903.

Ārādhetvāna gaṇheyya, taṃ kammaṭṭhānadāyakaṃ;

Kammaṭṭhānaṃ parikkhitvā, cariyārahamattano.

Having pleased that giver of a meditation subject, and having examined a meditation subject suitable for one's own temperament, one should receive it.

904.

904.

Rāgo doso ca moho ca,

Cariyā tīhi paṇḍitā;

Saddhābuddhivitakkehi,

Chabbidhā ca vibhāvayuṃ.

Greed, hatred, and delusion are the three temperaments. With faith, intelligence, and discursive thought, they are understood as sixfold.

905.

905.

Rāgussannassa [V 0.0083] sappāyā, koṭṭhāsāsubhabhāvanā;

Dosussannassappamaññā, nīlādi ca catubbidhā.

For one abounding in lust, the development of the body's parts and of impurity is suitable; for one abounding in hatred, the immeasurables and the four kinds of kasiṇas, beginning with blue.

906.

906.

Vitakkaṃ mohussannānaṃ, ānāpānaṃ pakāsitaṃ;

Cha saddhācaritassāhu, buddhānussatiādayo.

For those of a discursive and deluded temperament, mindfulness of breathing is declared; for one of faithful temperament, they say the six recollections beginning with the Buddha are suitable.

907.

907.

Maraṇopasamāsaññāvavatthānāni buddhino;

Sesāni pana sabbesaṃ, tatthāpi kasiṇaṃ budhā.

Recollection of death, recollection of peace, the one perception, and the defining of the elements are for the intelligent one. The remaining, however, are for all; and among those, the wise recommend the kasiṇas.

908.

908.

Vitakkapakatikassa, parittaṃ mohacārino;

Mahantamiti sappāyaṃ, gahetvāna tato paraṃ.

For one of a discursive nature, a limited object is suitable; for one of a deluded temperament, a vast one is suitable. Having grasped this, one should proceed further.

909.

909.

Mahāvāsaṃ navaṃ jiṇṇaṃ, panthasoṇḍikasantikaṃ;

Paṇṇapupphaphalākiṇṇaṃ, bahusammānapatthitaṃ.

A great dwelling, a new or dilapidated one, one near a road or a tavern, one abounding in leaves, flowers, and fruits, or one that is famous and sought after.

910.

910.

Sīmantadārunagara-kkhettapaccantanissitaṃ;

Visabhāgamasappāyaṃ, paṭṭanaṃ mittadullabhaṃ.

A place situated on a state border, near timber, a city, or a field; a place in a border region; a place with disagreeable people or otherwise unsuitable; a port town where a good friend is difficult to find.

911.

911.

Ṭhānāniṭṭhārasetāni, parivajjeyya paṇḍito;

Seveyya bhāvanāyoggaṃ, senāsanamatandito.

The wise one should avoid these eighteen places. Unweariedly, one should resort to a dwelling fit for development.

912.

912.

Nātidūraṃ nāccāsannaṃ, appasaddamanākulaṃ;

Gamanāgamanasampannaṃ, appaḍaṃsānupaddavaṃ.

Not too far, not too near, with little noise and not crowded, convenient for coming and going, with few biting insects and free from dangers.

913.

913.

Akicchapaccayuppādaṃ[M 0.0078], lajjībhikkhugaṇocitaṃ;

Vivekaṭṭhānabahulaṃ, bahussutanisevitaṃ.

Where requisites are easily obtained, frequented by conscientious monks, abounding in solitary places, resorted to by the well-learned—

914.

914.

Appabhayaṃ nirāsaṅkaṃ, appadosaṃ mahāguṇaṃ;

Vihāramanusevanto, tattha nissaṅgacetasā.

Free from fear, without anxiety, with few faults and great qualities—dwelling there with a detached mind.

915.

915.

Tato kesanakhaccheda-rajanādimasesato;

Khuddakaṃ palibodhañca, chinditvāna yathārahaṃ.

Then, having rightly cut off all minor obstacles, such as cutting hair and nails, and dyeing.

916.

916.

Āvāsaṃ gocaraṃ bhassaṃ, puggalaṃ bhojanaṃ tathā;

Vajjentotumasappāyaṃ, iriyāpathamattano.

Avoiding unsuitable lodgings, alms-round resorts, speech, persons, and food, as well as one's own deportment—

917.

917.

Sevanto [V 0.0084] satta sappāye, te evāti padhānavā;

Bhāvanūpāyasampanno, vūpakaṭṭho rahogato.

Cultivating the seven suitable things, truly they are energetic, endowed with the means for development, secluded, and gone into solitude.

918.

918.

Kāmesvādīnavaṃ disvā, nekkhammaṃ daṭṭhu khemato;

Pariyuṭṭhānanibbindo, sodheyyajjhāsayaṃ kathaṃ.

Seeing the danger in sensual pleasures, perceiving renunciation as safety, weary of the mental obsessions—how should one purify one's disposition?

919.

919.

Appassādā mahādukkhā, kāmā hi kaṭukapphalā;

Dussaṃhārā durārakkhā, bahvādīnavasaṇṭhitā.

Sensual pleasures give little enjoyment and great suffering, for they are bitter in result; hard to restrain, hard to guard, established in many drawbacks.

920.

920.

Aṭṭhikā khajjamānāva, vighātāya pabhijjitā;

Gayhantattavadhāyete, maṃsapesīva pakkhibhi.

Like bones being gnawed, broken for one's torment; like a piece of flesh seized by birds, they are grasped for one's own destruction.

921.

921.

Paṭivāte tiṇukkāva, pariggāhakadāhino;

Aṅgārakāsusaṅkāsā, sabbaṅgaparitāsakā.

Like a grass torch carried against the wind, burning the one who holds it; like a pit of coals, scorching every limb.

922.

922.

Supine paribhuttāva, nālaṃ kassaci tittiyā;

Na tu kassaci accantā, alaṅkārāva yācitā.

Like things enjoyed in a dream, they are not enough for anyone's satisfaction; like borrowed ornaments, they are not anyone's permanently.

923.

923.

Chajjantā phalarukkhāva, paṭipannapabhañjino;

Asisūnūpamā nicca-madhikoṭṭenti pāṇino.

Like fruit trees that are stripped bare, they destroy those who approach them; like a sword and a butcher's block, they constantly cut down living beings.

924.

924.

Sattisūlūpamā daḷhaṃ, taṇhāsallānuvedhino;

Ghorānatthavisākiṇṇā, kaṇhasappasirūpamā.

Like a spear or a stake, they pierce firmly with the dart of craving; full of terrible harm and poison, they are like the head of a black snake.

925.

925.

Sabbāsavaparikliṭṭhā[M 0.0079], sabbāsaṃklesavatthukā;

Gammā ca capalā nīcā, puthujjanamamāyitā.

Defiled by all taints, the basis of all defilements; they are vulgar, fickle, and low, clung to as 'mine' by ordinary people.

926.

926.

Bahusādhāraṇā cete, sapattajanapatthitā;

Mahopaddavupayaṭṭhā, bahvāyāsā bhayāvahā.

These are common to many, desired by rival people; beset by great dangers, bringing much trouble and fear.

927.

927.

Mahārambhasamāraddhā, khippākāravidhaṃsino;

Sokasallaṃ pavesentā, vigacchanti suve suve.

Begun with great undertakings, they are swiftly destructive; implanting the dart of sorrow, they disappear day by day.

928.

928.

Nālaṃ kassaci tāṇāya, nālamassāsanāya ca;

Avisāsaniyāvassaṃ, kitavā mārakiṃkarā.

They are no refuge for anyone, nor are they fit for consolation; they are certainly untrustworthy, like gamblers, the minions of Māra.

929.

929.

Sattānamupaghātāya[V 0.0085], madhurākāranimmitā;

Rakkhasī viya santāna-māvisanti manoharā.

Fashioned in a sweet guise for the injury of beings, like a charming demoness, they possess one's being.

930.

930.

Āviṭṭhā yehi dummedhā, byasanāhitasambhavā;

Vipallāsaparābhūtā, byāpajjantā vihaññare.

The foolish who are possessed by them, whose arising is from misfortune and harm, overcome by perversions, come to ruin and are destroyed.

931.

931.

Cetosaṅkapparacitā, nandirāgopasevanā;

Madhulittāsidhārāva, byāpārenopasevitā.

Fashioned by the mind's intentions, frequented with delight and lust; like a honey-smeared razor's edge, they are attended with harm.

932.

932.

Manoramasubhākārā, piyarūpopalambhino;

Mittamukhaṃ sapattāva, vañcayanti mahājanaṃ.

With charming and beautiful appearances, providing the perception of lovely forms, like enemies with the face of a friend, they deceive the multitude.

933.

933.

Vañcitā yehi dummedhā, sabbasampattidhaṃsitā;

Khemamaggā paribbhaṭṭhā, dhārenti vadhamattano.

The foolish who are deceived by them, their every attainment destroyed, having strayed from the path of safety, incur their own destruction.

934.

934.

Virūparūpākārena, nimmathentā palobhino;

Abhāvitānaṃ bālānaṃ, mānasaṃ nihanantime.

With their manifold forms and appearances, crushing and enticing, they destroy the minds of undeveloped fools.

935.

935.

Yattha rāgasallaviddhā, salleneva vane migā;

Tattha tatthānudhāvantā, vipphandanti nirantaraṃ.

Wherein those pierced by the dart of lust, like deer in the forest pierced by a dart, run about here and there, thrashing about incessantly.

936.

936.

Mamaṃkārena vuḍḍhantā, ghoramāsīvisaṃ yathā;

Vissaṭṭhā bhogadhammesu, assādenti aviddasu.

Growing with possessiveness, like a deadly viper, the unwise, given over to things of enjoyment, relish them.

937.

937.

Anayabyasanāyete[M 0.0080], vasī kubbanti pāṇino;

Vicittākārasaṇṭhānā, pisācanagaraṃ yathā.

These subdue beings for their ruin and calamity; with their diverse forms and appearances, they are like a city of demons.

938.

938.

Anatthāvahitā bālā, vāguraṃ nāvabujjhare;

Tattheva paṭivamanti, yathā haññanti mucchitā.

Fools, intent on what is harmful, do not understand the snare; right there they fall into it, so that they are struck down, senseless.

939.

939.

Sīghavāhī mahoghoyaṃ, klesavaṭṭaṃ mahabbhayo;

Sakaṇṭakañca gahanaṃ, paṅkova duratikkamo.

This mighty flood is swiftly flowing, the round of defilements is a great danger; it is a thorny thicket, and like a bog, hard to cross.

940.

940.

Cetosaṃmohanaṭṭhānaṃ, pamādapaṭisandhitaṃ;

Ohāri sithilaṃ cetaṃ, duppamuñcañca bandhanaṃ.

A ground for the mind's bewilderment, rooted in negligence; it is a dragging, lax, and hard-to-release bond.

941.

941.

Jālaṃva [V 0.0086] vitthataṃ loke,

Mārapāso samoḍḍito;

Pañjaraṃ cārako ceso,

Sattānamanayāvaho.

Like a net spread wide in the world, Māra's snare is set; this is a cage and a prison, bringing ruin to beings.

942.

942.

Yatthānurāgasambaddhā, paliguṇṭhitasāyino;

Makkaṭālepabaddhāva, nitthunanti vighātino.

Wherein those bound by attachment, clinging while entangled, like monkeys stuck with birdlime, lament, being afflicted.

943.

943.

Baḷisaṃvāmisacchannaṃ, savisaṃ viya bhojanaṃ;

Migaluddanivāpova, vināsāya samoḍḍitā.

Like a hook concealed by bait, or food laced with poison; like a hunter's decoy, it is set for destruction.

944.

944.

Mīnakā vaṅkagiddhāva, ye gilitvā puthujjanā;

Ghoraṃ maccumukhaṃ patvā, socantāpāyabhāgino.

Like fish greedy for the hook, ordinary people, having swallowed it, fall into Death’s grim jaws, lamenting, destined for the woeful states.

945.

945.

Pāpakkhettamidaṃ ṭhānaṃ, micchālobhanisevanaṃ;

Duccarītaṅkurārohaṃ, apāyaphalapūraṇaṃ.

This place is a field of evil, cultivated with wrong greed, where sprouts of misconduct grow, fulfilling the fruit of the lower realms.

946.

946.

Ajjhositā panettha ca, lobhamucchāvidāhino;

Kodhūpanāhajalitā, issāmaccheradhūpitā.

And here they are engrossed, burning with the fever of greed and delusion, blazing with anger and resentment, smoldering with envy and stinginess.

947.

947.

Sārambhāyudhasannaddhā, vipphurantā manorathā;

Ābandhicchā mahākacchā, ṭhanti lokavipattiyā.

Armed with the weapon of rivalry, their desires quivering, bound by craving like a great marsh, they stand for the world's ruin.

948.

948.

Avajjaṃ [M 0.0081] natthi etesa-makattabbaṃ na vijjati;

Sammuṭṭhasaccatā tesu, na patiṭṭhāti sādhutā.

There is nothing blameless about them, nothing they will not do; truthfulness is forgotten in them, goodness is not established.

949.

949.

Paropaghātābhiratā, dayādhammaparammukhā;

Sabbasattesvavissāsī, sabbattha parisaṅkitā.

Delighting in harming others, averse to the principle of compassion; distrustful of all beings, apprehensive everywhere.

950.

950.

Bhayasantāsabahulā, sabbānatthānusārino;

Sādhentā caturāpāyaṃ, pāpakammapurakkhakā.

Full of fear and dread, pursuing all that is unbeneficial; they bring about the four woeful states, with evil actions as their vanguard.

951.

951.

Mahāsaṅkaṭupabyuḷhā, palibodhaparipphuṭā;

Haññanti dukkhadhammehi, kāme bālā bhavepare.

Overwhelmed by great peril, pervaded by hindrances, fools are afflicted by states of suffering in sensual pleasures and future existences.

952.

952.

Tato [V 0.0087] maccunirāsaṅkā, khiḍḍārativimohitā;

Kimpakkamiva bhakkhantā, rammakāravirodhino.

Then, fearless of death, deluded by play and pleasure, like those eating the kimpakka fruit, they are hostile to those who bring about well-being.

953.

953.

Gāmasūkarapotāva, kāmāsucipariplutā;

Camarīkatakammantā, asmiṃ loke palobhitā.

Like village piglets, wallowing in the impurity of desires; like yaks attached to their tails, they are enticed in this world.

954.

954.

Khajjamānā kilesehi, kimīhiva nirantaraṃ;

Parihāniṃ panaññāya, parivārenti mucchitā.

Gnawed by defilements as if by worms, incessantly; unaware of their decline, deluded, they persist.

955.

955.

Tato jarāhi santattaṃ, yobbanañcopamuyhati;

Kāmā ca parihāyanti, jīvitañcoparujjhati.

Then, scorched by aging, youth is bewildered; sensual pleasures wane, and life is brought to an end.

956.

956.

Paraṃ pamādābhivaṭṭhā, pāpaklesamahodakā;

Tato taṇhānadī pūrā, pāpetāpāyasāgaraṃ.

Furthermore, from heedlessness grows a great flood of evil defilements; then the river of craving, full, leads them to the ocean of misery.

957.

957.

Idhalokapariccattā, paralokatthadhaṃsitā;

Gaṅgākuṇapakākāva, senti sokaparāyaṇā.

Abandoned by this world, having destroyed their welfare in the next, like crows on a corpse in the Ganges, they lie down, given over to sorrow.

958.

958.

Iccattatthaṃ paratthañca, sattā kāmanibandhanā;

Viddhaṃsetvā vinassanti, idha ceva parattha ca.

Thus, beings bound by desire, having destroyed their own good and that of others, perish both here and hereafter.

959.

959.

Iti sādīnavā kāmā, ghorā sālasilūpamā;

Yattha bālā visīdanti, natthi saṅgo vijānataṃ.

Such are the dangers of sensual pleasures—terrible, like a great rock; where fools sink down, for the discerning there is no attachment.

960.

960.

Itthaṃ [M 0.0082] kāmabhayaṭṭānaṃ, sikkhattayamanuttaraṃ;

Samācikkhi vimokkhāya, nekkhammamiti cakkhumā.

Thus the One with Vision expounded the state of fear in sensual pleasures and, for the sake of liberation, the supreme threefold training, which is renunciation.

961.

961.

Sabbāsavavighātāya, paṭipatti anuttarā;

Antadvayamanāgamma, majjhimāyaṃ pakāsitā.

For the destruction of all taints, the unsurpassed practice, not approaching the two extremes, is revealed as the middle way.

962.

962.

Sabbadukkhasamugghātī, visuddhi paramuttamā;

Vijjācaraṇasampatti, sabbasampattisādhikā.

It is the uprooter of all suffering, the supreme, ultimate purity; the accomplishment in knowledge and conduct, the fulfiller of all attainments.

963.

963.

Puññakkhettamidaṃ ṭhānaṃ, tapokammanisevanaṃ;

Saddhāsīlaṅkurārohaṃ, sampattiphalapūraṇaṃ.

This place is a field of merit, cultivated with ascetic practice, where sprouts of faith and virtue grow, fulfilling the fruit of attainment.

964.

964.

Klesacārakamokkhāya[V 0.0088], dvārametamanuttaraṃ;

Mahoghuttaraṇaṃ kullaṃ, sotthi pārimapāpakaṃ.

This is the unsurpassed door to release from the prison of defilements, a raft for crossing the great flood, bringing safety to the further shore.

965.

965.

Pāpacoravighātāya, khemamaggo anuttaro;

Akaṇṭako agahano, uju sabbhi pavedito.

For the destruction of the thieves of evil, it is the unsurpassed path of security; thornless, unobstructed, and straight, it is proclaimed by the good.

966.

966.

Mahābandhanamokkhāya,

Abbhuto jinaghosito;

Palibodhapariccāgo,

Abbhokāso alepano.

For release from the great bondage, wondrous is the proclamation of the Conqueror; it is the abandonment of hindrances, an open space, unstained.

967.

967.

Saṅgapaṅkasamuttāro, ganthānaṃ viniveṭhanaṃ;

Taṇhādāsabyanitthāro, seribhāvo sukhāvaho.

It is the escape from the mud of attachment, the disentangling of fetters; the release from the slavery of craving, a state of freedom that brings happiness.

968.

968.

Sabbayogavisaṃyogo, sabbasokanirundhano;

Sabbālayavisaṅkhāro, sabbadukkhaviniggamo.

It is the release from all yokes, the cessation of all sorrow; the dismantling of all attachments, the escape from all suffering.

969.

969.

Mārapāsasamucchedī, pattametamanuttaraṃ;

Mohandhakāraviddhaṃsī, vijjālokavirocano.

It is the cutter of Māra's snare, this unsurpassed attainment; the destroyer of the darkness of delusion, radiating the light of knowledge.

970.

970.

Abyāpajjamidaṃ ṭhāna-mabhayaṃ nirupaddavaṃ;

Tapokammānamokāso, māracakkhuvimohano.

This state is free from ill will, fearless, and without affliction; an opportunity for ascetic practice, bewildering to Māra’s eye.

971.

971.

Sabbasantāpaharaṇamidaṃ sītaṃva candanaṃ;

Nimmalaṃ dhammasalilaṃ, saṃklesamalasodhanaṃ.

This is the remover of all torment, cool like sandalwood; the stainless water of the Dhamma, the cleanser of the stain of defilements.

972.

972.

Saṃsārasetu [M 0.0083] suhatā, bodhipakkhiyapatthatā;

Sokasallasamuddhārī, yantaṃ sukatayojitaṃ.

The bridge over saṃsāra is well-constructed, the factors of enlightenment are laid out; it is the extractor of the dart of sorrow, an instrument well-applied.

973.

973.

Cittātaṅkasamuddhaṃsī, paribhogasukhosadhaṃ;

Lokāmisānaṃ vamanaṃ, cetodosavirecanaṃ.

The destroyer of mental anguish, the medicine that is the bliss of its partaking; the emetic for worldly allurements, the purgative for mental defilements.

974.

974.

Accantatittikāraṇamīrenti dhammabhojanaṃ;

Pipāsaharaṇaṃ pānaṃ, vimuttirasapesalaṃ.

They partake of the Dhamma-food, the cause of utmost satisfaction; the drink that quenches thirst, delightful with the taste of liberation.

975.

975.

Vaṇṇakittisugandhāya[V 0.0089], guṇamālā suganthitā;

Pāpakopīnavasanaṃ, hirottappavicittitaṃ.

Fragrant with praise and renown, a garland of qualities well-strung; a garment against evil, adorned with shame and moral dread.

976.

976.

Accantaparisuddho ca, saddhammaratanāvali;

Ariyānamalaṅkāro, anupāyi siriṅkaro.

Utterly pure, a garland of the true Dhamma’s jewels; an ornament of the Noble Ones, a constant bringer of glory.

977.

977.

Cintānaṃ dunnimittānamidaṃ santikaraṃ paraṃ;

Vipattipaṭighātāya, parittamidamuttamaṃ.

The supreme pacifier of thoughts and ill omens; the supreme protection for warding off misfortune.

978.

978.

Antarāyavināsāya, maṅgalaṃ jinadesitaṃ;

Micchāgāhavimokkhāya, sotthi sambuddhabhāsitā.

For the destruction of obstacles, the auspiciousness taught by the Conqueror; for liberation from wrong grasping, the well-being spoken by the Perfectly Enlightened One.

979.

979.

Anivatti ca paccakkhamāvenikamabhāriyaṃ;

Amatosadhamaccantamajarāmarasādhanaṃ.

Irreversible, direct, unique, and unburdensome; the deathless medicine, the ultimate means for attaining the ageless and immortal.

980.

980.

Yametaṃ samadhiṭṭhāya, sambodhittayamuttamaṃ;

Papponti sabbasampattiguṇapāramipūritaṃ.

Having firmly resolved upon this, they attain the supreme threefold enlightenment, which is filled with all accomplishments, qualities, and perfections.

981.

981.

Sabbākāravaropeta-metaṃ nekkhammasammataṃ;

Sīlagambhīraparikkhaṃ, dhutaṅgoditatoraṇaṃ.

Endowed with all excellent aspects, esteemed as renunciation; surrounded by a moat of profound virtue, its arched gateways proclaimed by the ascetic practices.

982.

982.

Samādhivīthivitthinnaṃ, satipākāragopuraṃ;

Saddhāsamiddhisamphullaṃ, paññāpāsādasobhitaṃ.

With broad avenues of concentration, its ramparts and gate-towers of mindfulness; flourishing with the prosperity of faith, adorned with a palace of wisdom.

983.

983.

Sammājīvadhajaṃ rammaṃ, hirottappapaṭicchadaṃ;

Vimuttāmatasambhogaṃ, veneyyajanasevitaṃ.

Its lovely banner is Right Livelihood, its covering is shame and moral dread; partaking of the deathless bliss of liberation, frequented by those fit to be guided.

984.

984.

Abhejjaṃ pāpaverīhi, puraṃ sugatamāpitaṃ;

Anītimanupasaggaṃ, paṭipannā mahesayo.

Impregnable to evil foes, the city built by the Sugata; free from calamity and affliction, the great sages have entered upon it.

985.

985.

Paramassāsasampattā[M 0.0084], paripuṇṇamanorathā;

Sabbasaṅgamatikkamma, nikkhantā akuto bhayā.

Having attained the highest solace, their heart's desires fulfilled; having overcome all attachments, they have gone forth, fearless from any quarter.

986.

986.

Sammadatthamabhiññāya, maccudheyyapahāyino;

Sabbadukkhoghanittiṇṇā, pāraṃ gacchanti paṇḍitā.

Having fully understood the true meaning, abandoning the realm of death; having crossed the flood of all suffering, the wise go to the far shore.

987.

987.

Iti [V 0.0090] sabbaṅgasampannaṃ, mahesigaṇasevitaṃ;

Nekkhammaṃ kāmanikkhantaṃ, saddhammapathamuttamaṃ.

Thus complete in every aspect, frequented by hosts of great sages, is renunciation, the departure from sensual pleasures, the unsurpassed path of the true Dhamma.

988.

988.

Virādhenti parābhūtā, mucchitā yena dujjanā;

Taṃ pāpasamudācāraṃ, pariyuṭṭhānamabravuṃ.

That by which the wicked—defeated and infatuated—are ruined, that evil course of conduct, they have called an obsession.

989.

989.

Cetonīvaraṇaṃ cetaṃ, paññācakkhunirodhanaṃ;

Sīlopaghātakaraṇaṃ, cittavikkhepasaṅgamo.

This is a hindrance to the mind, an obstruction of the eye of wisdom; a cause of damage to virtue, an association with mental distraction.

990.

990.

Ayasānaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ, guṇatejavināsanaṃ;

Sabbasampattidahanaṃ, caturāpāyasādhakaṃ.

A basis for dishonor, a destroyer of virtue and glory; the burning of all success, that which leads to the four states of woe.

991.

991.

Sabbāsavamalopeto, sabbopaklesasañcayo;

Pāpayakkhasamo ceso, dosāsīvisasaṅgamo.

Endowed with the stain of all taints, an accumulation of all corruptions; this is like an evil demon, an encounter with the venomous snake of hatred.

992.

992.

Pamādapathamakkantaṃ, amittagaṇasaṅgamaṃ;

Mahabbhayasamuṭṭhānaṃ, mahābyasanasaṅkaraṃ.

The treading of the path of heedlessness, an association with a host of enemies; the origin of great fear, a mixture of great misfortune.

993.

993.

Apāyadukkhamāruḷhaṃ, ahitāvahitaṃ padaṃ;

Sabbānatthakaraṃ ghoraṃ, sabbadukkhavidhāyakaṃ.

The ascent to the suffering of the lower realms, a state bringing what is unbeneficial; causing all harm, dreadful, and bringing about all suffering.

994.

994.

Dhiratthu pāpadhammānaṃ, sabbakalyāṇahāyinaṃ;

Laddhāpi khaṇasampatti, dullabhā yehi nāsitā.

Shame on those with evil qualities, who destroy all that is good; by whom the attainment of the opportune moment, though difficult to obtain, is destroyed.

995.

995.

Tesaṃ hi samudācāro, dullabhaṃ buddhasāsanaṃ;

Samuddhaṃseti asani, yathā ratanapabbataṃ.

For their conduct destroys the Buddha’s teaching, which is difficult to obtain, just as a thunderbolt destroys a jeweled mountain.

996.

996.

Saddhammadhanacorā te, nekkhammapatibandhakā;

Paṭipattiṃ vilumpantā, palibundhanti pāṇino.

They are thieves of the true Dhamma's wealth, hinderers of renunciation; plundering the practice, they obstruct living beings.

997.

997.

Vissāsivadhakāpete, vissaṭṭhāvassaghātino;

Yehi bālāhatā senti, nissayejinasāsane.

Killers of the trusting, destroyers of reliance; by whom fools lie struck down within the refuge of the Victor’s teaching.

998.

998.

Tepi [M 0.0085] vāsenti dummedhā, nissaṅkā mohapārutā;

Antomanasi ucchaṅke, ghoramāsīvisaṃ yathā.

Unhesitating and veiled by delusion, even those dull-witted ones harbor it within their minds, just as one would a dreadful viper in one's lap.

999.

999.

Attano [V 0.0091] ca vināsāya, nissaṭaṃ klesapañjare;

Cinantā nāvabujjhanti, vipattipathayāyino.

For their own ruin, they accumulate what has emerged from the cage of defilements; traveling the path of downfall, they do not understand.

1000.

1000.

Halāhalaṃva khādantā, āliṅgantāva pāpakaṃ;

Avassamupahaññanti, pāpadhammopalāḷino.

Like eating deadly poison, like embracing evil; they are inevitably destroyed, those who indulge in evil qualities.

1001.

1001.

Pāpacintā paribyuḷhā, vitakkamathitā janā;

Lokadvayāpi dhaṃsenti, atthadvayavināsino.

People overwhelmed by evil thoughts, agitated by thinking, fall away from both worlds, being destroyers of both benefits.

1002.

1002.

Kodhūpanāhi vigacchā, issāmaccheradūsitā;

Makkhī palāsī sārambhī, appatissā agāravā.

Full of anger and enmity, defiled by envy and stinginess; disparaging, spiteful, contentious, without deference, and disrespectful.

1003.

1003.

Mānātimānabahulā, mudhāmukharacaṇḍikā;

Uddhatā ca pamattā ca, dabbitā ketugāhino.

Abounding in pride and conceit, vainly talkative and fierce; arrogant and heedless, haughty, grasping at false views.

1004.

1004.

Cetokhilakhilabhūtā, vinibandhānuveṭhitā;
