1328.

1328.

Vihiṃsāratisārambha-paṭirodhavimocanaṃ;

Verikibbisaviddhaṃsī, lokānuggahakāraṇaṃ.

The prevention of harming, discontent, and contention; the release from enmity and evil deeds, the cause of benefiting the world.

1329.

1329.

Dhammapajjotakaraṇaṃ[V 0.0121], saṃyogamalasodhanaṃ;

Sammohatimiruddhāri, sampattipaṭipādanaṃ.

The illumination of the Dhamma, the cleansing of the stain of fetters; the remover of the darkness of delusion, the attainment of accomplishment.

1330.

1330.

Iccattatthaṃ paratthañca, sampādetvā khamāparo;

Sādheti sabbasampatti-midha ceva parattha ca.

Thus, having accomplished one's own welfare and that of others, one devoted to patience achieves all accomplishments, both here and in the hereafter.

1331.

1331.

Titikkhāguṇasampanno[M 0.0114], pāṇabhūtānukampako;

Anākulitakammanto, sorato sakhilo suci.

Endowed with the quality of patience, compassionate towards living beings; of untroubled actions, gentle, friendly, and pure.

1332.

1332.

Nivāto samitācāro, subhago piyadassano;

Paṭisaṅkhābalappatto, dhitimā matipāṭavo.

Humble, of restrained conduct, charming, pleasant to behold; having attained the power of reflection, resolute, and mentally astute.

1333.

1333.

Akkhobho adhivāsento,

Sabbānatthe parissaye;

Bhīmasaṅgāmāvacaro,

Hatthināgova sobhati.

Unshaken, enduring all misfortunes and dangers, he shines like a noble elephant moving through a terrible battle.

1334.

1334.

Itthaṃ samantato bhaddaṃ, titikkhaṃ paccavekkhato;

Passambheti samuṭṭhāya, khamā byāpādasambhamaṃ.

Thus, for one contemplating patience, which is auspicious in every way, patience calms the agitation of ill-will that has arisen.

1335.

1335.

Dibbosadhamivātaṅkaṃ, meghajjavaṃ hutāsanaṃ;

Khippamantaradhāpeti, titikkhā kodhamattano.

Like a divine medicine for sickness, or a torrent of rain for a fire, patience quickly makes one's own anger disappear.

1336.

1336.

Tatonekaguṇopetaṃ, nekadosappabhañjanaṃ;

Khantidhammamadhiṭṭhāya, pasannadhīramānaso.

Therefore, having established oneself in the virtue of patience—which is endowed with many qualities and destroys numerous faults—with a serene and steadfast mind,

1337.

1337.

Bhāveyya paṭhamaṃ tāva, mettābhāvanamuttamaṃ;

Attānamupamaṃ katvā, sattesu hitavuḍḍhiyā.

First of all, one should cultivate the supreme meditation of loving-kindness, taking oneself as the example, for the increase of welfare among beings.

1338.

1338.

Sabbe sattā ca pāṇā ca, bhūtā jīvā ca puggalā;

Abyāpajjā tathāverā, anīghā ca sukhedhino.

May all beings, all creatures, all that have come to be, all that have life, and all individuals be free from affliction, likewise free from enmity, untroubled, and may they flourish in happiness.

1339.

1339.

Vijjāsampattibhogehi, pavaḍḍhantu yasassino;

Parivārabalappattā, bhayopaddavavajjitā.

May those of good repute prosper with knowledge, accomplishments, and wealth; may they attain the strength of a retinue, and be free from fear and calamity.

1340.

1340.

Sakhilā [V 0.0122] sukhasambhāsā, aññamaññāvirodhino;

Modantu suhitā sabbe, mā kiñci pāpamāgamā.

Friendly, pleasant in speech, not in conflict with one another; may all rejoice, content and well-disposed, and may they meet with no evil.

1341.

1341.

Saddhāpāmojjabahulā, dānasīlamahussavā;

Guṇabhūsitasantānā, āyuṃ pālentanāmayaṃ.

Abounding in faith and joy, celebrating great festivals of giving and virtue; with characters adorned by good qualities, may they maintain a long life free from illness.

1342.

1342.

Sammādiṭṭhiṃ [M 0.0115] purodhāya, saddhammapaṭipattiyā;

Ārādhentu hitopāya-maccantaṃ sukhasādhanaṃ.

Having established right view as foremost, through the practice of the true Dhamma, may they attain the beneficial path, the ultimate means to happiness.

1343.

1343.

Iti nānappakārena, sattesu hitamānasaṃ;

Mātāva piyaputtamhi, pavatteyya nirantaraṃ.

Thus, in various ways, one should continuously maintain a mind set on the welfare of beings, just as a mother does for her own dear son.

1344.

1344.

Sinehaṃ parivajjento, byāpādañca vināsayaṃ;

Parisuddhena cittena, hitakāmova kevalaṃ.

Avoiding fondness and destroying ill-will, with a completely pure mind, wishing only for their welfare.

1345.

1345.

Mettāya mitte majjhatte, verike ca yathākkamaṃ;

Karonto sīmasambhedaṃ, attani ca samaṃ phare.

Breaking the boundaries between friend, neutral, and foe, one should pervade them respectively with loving-kindness, and equally so oneself.

1346.

1346.

Āsevantassa tassevaṃ, hitābhogasamāhitaṃ;

Sattapaññattimārabbha, samādhiyati mānasaṃ.

For one thus practicing, whose mind is composed with an inclination towards their welfare, the mind becomes concentrated with regard to the concept of 'a being'.

1347.

1347.

Tato anīgho ekaggo, upasantamanoratho;

Jhānattikaṃ catukkaṃ vā, mettācetovimuttiyā.

Then, free from distress, one-pointed, with mental aspirations calmed, he attains the triad or tetrad of jhānas through the liberation of mind by loving-kindness.

1348.

1348.

Bhūmidesadisāsatta-bhedabhinnesu odhiso;

Yathāsambhavamappeti, sabbasattesvanodhiso.

He applies it with specified limits among the divisions of beings by realm, region, and direction; and he applies it without specified limits to all beings.

1349.

1349.

Tadevamekasattamhi, paricchedaniyāmato;

Bahukesu ca sattesu, sabbesu ca pavattati.

Thus it operates towards a single being by way of a specified limit, and towards many beings, and towards all.

1350.

1350.

Tathāsevitasantāno,

Mettācetovimuttiyā;

Karuṇābhāvanāyoga-

Mārabheyya tato paraṃ.

His mental continuity thus cultivated by the liberation of mind through loving-kindness, he should next undertake the practice of cultivating compassion.

1351.

1351.

Sattānaṃ [V 0.0123] dukkhitākāra-māvajjitvāna yoniso;

“Aho dukkhā vimuccantu, sabbe sattā”ti cintayaṃ.

Having wisely adverted to the state of suffering in beings, one should think: 'Oh, may all beings be released from suffering!'

1352.

1352.

Kathaṃ māṇavakoyañca, bhayabheravakampito;

Byasanopaddavāviddho, vipphandati vighātavā.

And how this young man, trembling with fear and terror, afflicted by calamity and disaster, struggles in his distress!

1353.

1353.

Tathā hete vimosāya, paṭipannā virodhino;

Sabyāpajjā vihaññanti, cetodukkhasamappitā.

Thus indeed, these who are in conflict with one another, striving for release, are afflicted with ill-will and are overcome by mental suffering.

1354.

1354.

Athaññe [M 0.0116] paridevanti, vipattivinipātikā;

Padhupāyikasaṅkappā, sokopāyāsabhāgino.

Then others lament, having fallen into misfortune and ruin; with smouldering intentions, they are partakers in sorrow and despair.

1355.

1355.

Athāpare parābhūtā, kāmaklesavasīkatā;

Mohandhakārapakkhantā, sattā gacchanti duggatiṃ.

Then others are defeated, brought under the power of sensual defilements; fallen into the darkness of delusion, beings go to a state of woe.

1356.

1356.

Te tattha kaṭukaṃ ghoramanubhontā sakaṃ phalaṃ;

Dukkhasūlasamāviddhā, bāhā paggayha kandare.

There, experiencing their own bitter, dreadful fruit, pierced by the stakes of suffering, raising their arms, they wail.

1357.

1357.

Dīgharattādhimuttāya, devalokasamiddhiyā;

Devakāyā vihāyanti, akāmā parivattino.

For a long time devoted to the prosperity of the divine world, divine hosts abandon it, unwillingly revolving.

1358.

1358.

Cirakālaṃ jalitvāna, sūriyova nabhantare;

Brahmānopi patanteva, brahmalokāparāyaṇā.

Having blazed for a long time like the sun in the sky, even Brahmās fall, whose ultimate resort is the Brahma-world.

1359.

1359.

Khandhapañcakamiccevaṃ, dukkhāgāraṃ samubbahaṃ;

Nānāgatīsu vikkhittaṃ, pāṇajātaṃ vihaññati.

Thus, bearing the house of suffering that is the five aggregates, the mass of living beings, scattered in various destinations, is afflicted.

1360.

1360.

Anāthamanayāpannaṃ, parihānibhayākulaṃ;

Vātamaṇḍalikakkhittapakkhīva parivattati.

Helpless, fallen into misfortune, agitated by the fear of decline, one revolves like a bird thrown by a whirlwind.

1361.

1361.

Iti disvāna sutvā vā, sambhāvetvāna vā puna;

Dukkhāpagamamicchanto, dukkhāpagama patthayaṃ.

Thus, having seen or heard this, or having reflected upon it again, desiring and aspiring for the removal of suffering.

1362.

1362.

Sukhitesu ca medhāvī, dukkhākāramanussaraṃ;

Pavatteyya dayāpanno, karuṇābhāvanappanaṃ.

And the wise one, recalling the aspect of suffering even among the happy, should, filled with pity, engage in the development of compassion.

1363.

1363.

“Aho [V 0.0124] sattā vimuccantu, dukkhadhammehi sabbathā;

Sādhu samentupāyāsā, sokā ca paridevanā.

“Oh, may beings be freed from all things of a suffering nature! May vexations, sorrows, and lamentations utterly cease.

1364.

1364.

“Khīyantu pāpadhammā ca, passambhentāmayā tathā;

Saṃklesā palibodhā ca, samucchijjantu pāṇinaṃ.

“May evil qualities be destroyed, and may afflictions likewise be calmed; and may the defilements and hindrances of beings be utterly cut off.

1365.

1365.

“Byāpādā ca vihāyantu, vinivattantupaddavā;

Byasanāni vinassantu, vigacchantu vipattiyo.

“May ill will be abandoned, and may calamities be averted; may misfortunes perish, and may adversities vanish.

1366.

1366.

“Vihesā [M 0.0117] ca vighātā ca, khīyantu bhayabheravā;

Paṭikkamantu vissaṭṭhā, sotthiṃ passantu pāṇino”.

“May harassment and harm cease, and may fears and terrors be destroyed; may they retreat, dispersed, and may beings see well-being.”

1367.

1367.

Iccevamanukampanto, sabbasattepi sabbathā;

Sabbadukkhasamugghātaṃ, patthento karuṇāyati.

Thus, feeling compassion for all beings in every way, aspiring for the uprooting of all suffering, one is compassionate.

1368.

1368.

Sokuppattaṃ nivārento, vihiṃsaṃ dūrato haraṃ;

Mettāyamiva pāpeti, karuṇājhānamappanaṃ.

Dispelling the arising of sorrow, keeping harm far away, it leads to the absorption of compassion-jhāna, just like loving-kindness.

1369.

1369.

Karuṇānantaraṃ yogī, bhāveyya muditaṃ tato;

Sattānaṃ sukhitākāramāvajjetvāna yoniso.

After compassion, the yogi should then cultivate appreciative joy, wisely bringing to mind the happy state of beings.

1370.

1370.

Kathaṃ cirāya brahmāno, mahātejā mahiddhikā;

Pītibhakkhā subhaṭṭhāyī, pamodanti nirāmayā.

How the Brahmās, of great splendor and great power, feeding on joy, abiding in excellent states, and free from affliction, delight for a long time.

1371.

1371.

Devakāyā mahābhogā,

Mahesakkhā yasassino;

Accharāparivārehi,

Paricārenti nandane.

The divine hosts, of great possessions, great authority, and glorious, attended by throngs of celestial nymphs, enjoy themselves in the Nandana grove.

1372.

1372.

Rājābhisekasampattā, chattacāmarabhūsitā;

Ādhippaccamadhiṭṭhāya, sukhitā rājabhogino.

Having attained the prosperity of royal consecration, adorned with parasols and yak-tail whisks, having established supreme authority, the enjoyers of royal pleasures are happy.

1373.

1373.

Yathopaṭṭhitabhogehi, tadaññepi ca pāṇino;

Yathākāmitanipphannā, modanti sukhapītikā.

With the enjoyments that have come to hand, other beings too, having fulfilled their desires, rejoice with happiness and joy.

1374.

1374.

Caturāpāyikā [V 0.0125] sattā, pāpakammaparikkhayā;

Tato cutābhinandanti, sukhaṭṭhāne patiṭṭhitā.

Beings in the four woeful states, through the exhaustion of evil kamma, having passed away from there, rejoice, established in a happy state.

1375.

1375.

Sabbālayasamugghātaṃ, patvā lokuttaraṃ padaṃ;

Paṭipassaddhadarathā, sukhaṃ modantanappakaṃ.

Having attained the transcendent state, the complete uprooting of all attachments, with their vexations subsided, they rejoice in no small happiness.

1376.

1376.

Iti disvāna sutvā vā, sambhāvetvā punappunaṃ;

Sattānamadhivāsento, sukhākāraṃ pamodati.

Thus, having seen or heard this, or having repeatedly considered it, dwelling upon the happy state of beings, one rejoices.

1377.

1377.

“Aho [M 0.0118] sādhu aho suṭṭhu,

Modanti vata pāṇino;

Aho suladdhaṃ sattānaṃ,

Samiddhimabhipatthitaṃ.

“Oh, how good! Oh, how excellent! Indeed, beings rejoice! Oh, how well gained by beings is the prosperity they aspire to.

1378.

1378.

“Pasannamukhavaṇṇā ca, paripuṇṇamanorathā;

Pītipāmojjabahulā, ciraṃ jīvantunāmayā.

“With radiant faces, with fulfilled wishes, abounding in joy and gladness, may they live long, free from affliction.

1379.

1379.

“Bhayamaggamatikkantā, dukkhasaṅghāṭanissaṭā;

Khemamaggamanuppattā, pītisampattiphullitā.

“Having crossed the path of fear, escaped from the mass of suffering, attained the path of safety, blossoming with the wealth of joy.

1380.

1380.

“Samaggā suhitā cete, paṭisandhānapesalā;

Sampattimabhivedenti, kalyāṇaguṇabhūsitā”.

“And these, united and well-disposed, skilled in reconciliation, adorned with virtuous qualities, proclaim their attainment.”

1381.

1381.

Iti sammā pihāyanto, sukhādhigamasampadaṃ;

Sattānamabhirocento, muditāya samaṃ pharaṃ.

Thus, rightly yearning for the wealth of attaining happiness, gladdening beings, one pervades equally with appreciative joy.

1382.

1382.

Hitvā palāsābhisaṅgaṃ, issāratiniraṅkato;

Mettāyamiva pāpeti, muditājhānamappanaṃ.

Having abandoned the entanglement of rivalry, having dispelled envy and discontent, it leads to the absorption of appreciative joy-jhāna, just like loving-kindness.

1383.

1383.

Muditaṃ pana bhāvetvā, bhāveyyupekkhamuttamaṃ;

Virodhānunayaṃ hitvā, hutvā majjhattamānaso.

But having cultivated appreciative joy, one should cultivate supreme equanimity, having abandoned opposition and compliance, having become of neutral mind.

1384.

1384.

Sabhāvabhūta lokassa,

Lābhālābhaṃ yasāyasaṃ;

Nindāpasaṃsaṃ [V 0.0126] passanto,

Sukhaṃ dukkhañca kevalaṃ.

Seeing the natural state of the world: gain and loss, fame and disrepute, censure and praise, and purely happiness and suffering.

1385.

1385.

Kathaṃ kammassakatattāyaṃ lokānuparivattati;

Lokadhamme parābhūto, attādheyyavivajjito.

How does this world revolve according to the principle of kamma-ownership? Overcome by worldly conditions, devoid of self-mastery.

1386.

1386.

Kiṃ nāmatthi samatthettha, pavattetuṃ yathāruci;

Kassa vā ruciyā honti, sukhitā vātha dukkhitā.

What is there here that is able to act according to its own liking? Or by whose liking do beings become either happy or suffering?

1387.

1387.

Yathāpaccayasambhūtā, sukhadukkhā hi pāṇino;

Na sakkā parivattetuṃ, aññena puna kenaci.

Indeed, the happiness and suffering of beings arise according to conditions; they cannot be altered by anyone else whatsoever.

1388.

1388.

Micchāmaggamadhiṭṭhāya[M 0.0119], vipajjanti ca mānavā;

Sammāmaggaṃ purodhāya, sampajjanti punattanā.

Having undertaken the wrong path, people come to ruin; having placed the right path foremost, they prosper once more.

1389.

1389.

Tattha kāyavasenete, parivattanti aññathā;

Yathārucitakammantā, paccekavasavattino.

There, by means of the body, they change in various ways, their actions according to their liking, each subject to their own power.

1390.

1390.

Niratthakavihesāyaṃ, maññe lokavicāraṇā;

Santametaṃ paṇītañca, yadidaṃ tatrupekkhanaṃ.

This pondering of the world I deem a useless vexation; peaceful and sublime is this, namely, equanimity in that regard.

1391.

1391.

Ahaṃ ko nāma ke cete, kimaṭṭhānabudhantaro;

Paresupari pekkhanto, vihaññāmīti attano.

‘Who am I? And who are these? What is the basis of understanding between us?’ Thus looking excessively at others, I vex myself.

1392.

1392.

Sukhitā hontu vā mā vā, dukkhā muccantu vā na vā;

Samiddhā vā daliddā vā, kā mamettha vicāraṇā.

Whether they be happy or not, whether they be freed from suffering or not, whether prosperous or poor—what concern is that of mine here?

1393.

1393.

Attānaṃ parihārantu, yathākāmaṃ tu pāṇino;

Palibodho papañco vā, byāpādo vā na me tahiṃ.

Let beings conduct themselves as they wish; for me there is no hindrance, proliferation, or ill will in that.

1394.

1394.

Iti saṅkhāyupekkhanto, hitakāmopi pāṇinaṃ;

Apakkhapātupekkhāya, samaṃ pharati yoniso.

Thus, reflecting with equanimity, though wishing for the welfare of beings, one pervades evenly and wisely with impartial equanimity.

1395.

1395.

Aññāṇupekkhā nikkhanto, anurodhaṃ virājiya;

Mettāyamiva pāpeti, pañcamajjhānamappanaṃ.

Having emerged from ignorance-based equanimity, having become dispassionate towards favor, it leads to the absorption of the fifth jhāna, just like loving-kindness.

1396.

1396.

Appamaññā [V 0.0127] catasseva-mācikkhi vadataṃ varo;

Mahāpurisadhorayho, hitakāmo mahāmuni.

Thus the four immeasurables were declared by the best of speakers, the great leader of men, the great sage who desired what is beneficial.

1397.

1397.

Na liṅgavisabhāgamhi, ādikammikayoginā;

Bhāvetabbā matasatte, mettameva na sabbathā.

By a beginner meditator, loving-kindness should not be developed towards a person of a dissimilar gender, nor towards a dead being at all.

1398.

1398.

Pattabbasampadākāraṃ, dukkhākārañca pāṇisu;

Āvajjaṃ muditākāramanattādhīnataṃ tathā.

Reflecting on the aspect of prosperity to be attained and the aspect of suffering in beings, and likewise on the aspect of appreciative joy and their being subject to what is not-self.

1399.

1399.

Attani duggate mitte, majjhatteti yathākkamaṃ;

Paṭhamaṃ bhāvanāyogamārabhitvā tato paraṃ.

First, having undertaken the practice of development in due order towards oneself, an unfortunate person, a friend, and a neutral person; then afterwards...

1400.

1400.

Attani mitte majjhatte, veriketi catūsupi;

Karonto sīmasambhedaṃ, sabbattha samamānaso.

Towards oneself, a friend, a neutral person, and an enemy—in these four also—one breaks the boundaries, with an even mind towards all.

1401.

1401.

Bhūmikādippabhedehi[M 0.0120], paricchijjodhiso tathā;

Aparicchijja vā cetā, bhāvetabbāti bhāsitā.

Thus, by limiting them specifically through distinctions such as realms, or by not limiting them, these are to be cultivated, so it is said.

1402.

1402.

Asaṅkhotitasantānā, tāhi bhūtānukampakā;

Viharantuttamā brahmavihārāti tato matā.

Because they are supreme abidings for those compassionate to beings, whose mental continuity is unbroken, they are therefore known as the divine abodes.

1403.

1403.

Appamāṇālambaṇattā, tathā suppaṭipattiyā;

Sattesu appamāṇattā, appamaññāti sammatā.

Because their object is boundless, likewise because of the excellence of the practice, and because of their boundlessness towards beings, they are known as the 'immeasurables'.

1404.

1404.

Asampattahitā sattā, dukkhitā laddhasampadā;

Kammassakāti cintetvā, tato tesu yathākkamaṃ.

Beings who have not attained welfare, those who are suffering, and those who have gained prosperity—reflecting, 'They are owners of their kamma,' one then directs the mind towards them accordingly:

1405.

1405.

“Sampattīhi samijjhantu,

Dukkhā muccantu pāṇino;

Aho sattā sukhappattā,

Hontu sattā yathā tathā”.

‘May they be successful in their attainments! May beings be freed from suffering! Wonderful, that beings have attained happiness! Let beings be as they are.’

1406.

1406.

Iccābhivuddhimicchanto, dukkhāpagamanaṃ tathā;

Samiddhe anumodanto, upekkhanto ca pīṇite.

Thus, desiring their growth, and likewise the removal of their suffering, rejoicing with the prosperous, and being equanimous towards the gratified.

1407.

1407.

Mātāva [V 0.0128] dahare putte, gilāne yobbane ṭhite;

Sakiccapasute ceva, catudhā sampavattati.

Just as a mother towards her child—when it is young, when it is sick, when it is in the prime of youth, and when it is engaged in its own affairs—so does this practice unfold in four ways.

1408.

1408.

Itthaṃ catudhā sattesu, sammā cittapavattanā;

Sabbathāpi catuddhāva, tato vuttā mahesinā.

Thus, the right directing of the mind towards beings is fourfold; therefore it was declared fourfold in every way by the great seer.

1409.

1409.

Iccetā pana bhāvento, pasannamukhamānaso;

Sukhaṃ supati suttopi, pāpaṃ kiñci na passati.

Indeed, one who cultivates these, with a serene face and mind, sleeps in comfort; even while asleep, one sees nothing evil.

1410.

1410.

Paṭibujjhatanutrāso, jāgarova pamodati;

Cetaso ca samādhānaṃ, khippamevādhigacchati.

One awakens without terror and rejoices while awake; and one quickly attains concentration of mind.

1411.

1411.

Parissayā pahīyanti, vigacchanti cupaddavā;

Devatāpi ca rakkhanti, amuyhantaṃ anākulaṃ.

Dangers are overcome, calamities disappear, and deities also protect the one who is unbewildered and untroubled.

1412.

1412.

Phullaṃva [M 0.0121] kamalaṃ kāle, candaṃva vimalaṃ jano;

Sommakomaladhammehi, piyacakkhūhi passati.

People look upon him with pleasing eyes, as upon a lotus blooming in season or the spotless moon, for he is endowed with gentle and tender qualities.

1413.

1413.

Asaṃhīro asaṃkuppo, sabbāvatthāsu paṇḍito;

Samaṃ pavattitārambho, lokamesonugaṇhati.

Unshaken, imperturbable, wise in all circumstances, with effort evenly directed, such a one treats this world with kindness.

1414.

1414.

Khaṇamattopacārekā, pavattekamhi puggale;

Appamāṇā phalitveva, vaṇṇayanti mahesino.

Even a moment's service to a single person engaged in the practice, the great seers declare, indeed bears immeasurable fruit.

1415.

1415.

Pageva sabbasattesu, appanāpattabhāvanā;

Catassopi samībhūtā, vasībhūtā nirantaraṃ.

How much more so with regard to all beings, with the cultivation of the attainment of absorption—the four are balanced and mastered without interruption.

1416.

1416.

Puññadhārābhisandantā, paripūrenti paṇḍitaṃ;

Appameyyamahoghova, sāgaraṃ vīcimālinaṃ.

Streams of merit flow forth, filling the wise person, like an immeasurable great flood fills the wave-crested ocean.

1417.

1417.

Appamaññāmayānaṃ hi, puññānaṃ soḷasiṃ kalaṃ;

Sabbopadhikapuññāni, nāgghantīti pakāsitaṃ.

Indeed, a sixteenth part of the merits born of the immeasurables does not equal all merits connected to the aggregates; thus it is proclaimed.

1418.

1418.

Avañjhā tassa pabbajjā, yassa hetāsu gāravo;

Sukhumodagyabahulo, tisso sikkhā susikkhati.

His going forth is not in vain whose reverence is for these qualities; abounding in subtlety and loftiness, he trains well in the three trainings.

1419.

1419.

Amoghaṃ [V 0.0129] raṭṭhapiṇḍañca, bhuñjateso visesato;

Tampi mahapphalaṃ hoti, saddhādeyyaṃ patiṭṭhitaṃ.

Not in vain does he eat the country's almsfood, in a special way; and that gift of faith, being well-established, is also of great fruit.

1420.

1420.

Saddhādikusalā dhammā, pavaḍḍhanti akhaṇḍitā;

Sambuddhicariyānañca, mahattaṃ tassa pākaṭaṃ.

Wholesome states beginning with faith grow uninterrupted; and his greatness in conduct for perfect enlightenment becomes evident.

1421.

1421.

Akicchapaṭivedhāya, pādakajjhānamuttamaṃ;

Uju cekāyano maggo, brahmalokūpapattiyā.

For swift penetration, it is the supreme foundation jhāna; and it is the straight, one-way path for rebirth in the Brahma-world.

1422.

1422.

Vāsanābhāgiyā cetā, bodhisambhārakūlikā;

Sovaggikā sukhāhārā, lokārakkhā niruttarā.

These are states conducive to wholesome dispositions, contributing to the accumulation of requisites for enlightenment; leading to heaven, bringing happiness, protecting the world, unsurpassed.

1423.

1423.

Appameyyānisaṃsevaṃ, appameyyaguṇodayā;

Appamaññā tato tāsu, na pamajjeyya paṇḍito.

Thus, the immeasurables have immeasurable benefits and give rise to immeasurable virtues; therefore, a wise person should not be negligent towards them.

1424.

1424.

Paṭikkūlaṃ [M 0.0122] panāhāre, bhāvento saññamuttamaṃ;

Kabaḷīkāramāhāra-mannapānādisaṅgahaṃ.

Now, cultivating the supreme perception of repulsiveness in food, that is, in physical food which is a collection of meals, drinks, and so on.

1425.

1425.

Asitaṃ khāyitaṃ pītaṃ, sāyitañca rahogato;

Paṭikkūlanti cinteyya, gamanādivasā kathaṃ.

What has been eaten, chewed, drunk, and tasted, one should, in solitude, reflect upon as repulsive, considering how it passes through the body and so on.

1426.

1426.

Tapovanamidaṃ hitvā, ramaṇīyamanākulaṃ;

Āhārahetu gantabbo, gāmo gāmajanākulo.

Having left this delightful, undisturbed hermitage, one must go to the village, crowded with villagers, for the sake of food.

1427.

1427.

Tatthāsuciparikliṭṭhe, dujjanāvārasaṅkare;

Dīnamesayatuttiṭṭhaṃ, gehe gehe tu bhojanaṃ.

There, in an unclean and defiled place, a heap of wicked people and refuse, one stands miserably, seeking food from house to house.

1428.

1428.

Taṃ kheḷamalasaṃkliṭṭhaṃ, jivhaggaparivattitaṃ;

Dantacuṇṇitasambhinnaṃ, vaṇṇagandhaṃ vilissati.

That food, stained with saliva and impurities, turned about by the tip of the tongue, crushed and broken by the teeth, loses its color and smell.

1429.

1429.

Pittasemhaparibyuḷhaṃ, pubbalohitamissitaṃ;

Pavisantaṃ paṭikkūlaṃ, jegucchaṃ dhikkatāsivaṃ.

Overwhelmed by bile and phlegm, mixed with pus and blood, it is, upon entering, repulsive, disgusting, contemptible, and dreadful.

1430.

1430.

Kucchiyaṃ kuṇapākiṇṇe, duggandhaparibhāvite;

Suvānavamathākāraṃ, vantaṃva svānadoṇiyaṃ.

In the belly, filled with carrion, pervaded by foul odors; it is like a dog's vomit, like vomit in a dog's trough.

1431.

1431.

Tattacandanikāyaṃva[V 0.0130], nānākimisamākule;

Tattha bubbuḷakacchannaṃ, kuthitaṃ paripaccati.

Like a heated cauldron, teeming with various worms; there, covered with bubbles, it putrefies and is digested.

1432.

1432.

Saṃpaccantaṃ panetañca, sabhāvañca visevitaṃ;

Vaḍḍheti kesalomādiṃ, nānākuṇapasañcayaṃ.

And as this is being digested, and its nature thoroughly partaken of, it increases the hair of the head, body hair, and so on—a collection of various putrid things.

1433.

1433.

Vipaccantamathopetamanekopaddavāvahaṃ;

Kuṭṭhagaṇḍakilāsādimahābyādhisatodayaṃ.

Then, as it is being digested, it brings many troubles; it is the origin of hundreds of great diseases such as leprosy, boils, skin eruptions, and so on.

1434.

1434.

Pūtibhūtañca taṃ pakka-manekadvārasañcitaṃ;

Medapiṇḍaṃva kuthitaṃ, parissavati santataṃ.

And that putrid, digested food, gathered at many openings, like a putrefied lump of fat, constantly oozes forth.

1435.

1435.

Yena pūtigato kāyo, niccaṃ duggandhavāyiko;

Dhoviyantopi satataṃ, sucibhāvaṃ na gacchati.

By which the body becomes putrid, constantly emitting a foul odor; even when constantly washed, it does not attain purity.

1436.

1436.

Kucchito [M 0.0123] soyamāhāro,

Kāyāsucinisevano;

Nissandamalaniṭṭhāno,

Upaklesaphalāvaho.

This food is contemptible, serving the body's impurity; its outcome is filth, bringing forth the fruit of defilements.

1437.

1437.

Kāmarāgasamuṭṭhānaṃ, rogajātinibandhanaṃ;

Madappamādādhiṭṭhānaṃ, pāpakammamahāpatho.

It is the origin of sensual desire, the cause of disease and birth, the basis of intoxication and negligence, the great path of evil deeds.

1438.

1438.

Ahitodayamaggoyaṃ, bhayabheravasambhavo;

Byasanāgamanadvāraṃ, apāyāvahitaṃ mukhaṃ.

This is a path to the arising of what is unbeneficial, a source of fear and terror, a doorway to misfortune, a mouth leading to the lower realms.

1439.

1439.

Carantattasamattāva, yatthodariyamucchitā;

Kliṭṭhakammāni dummedhā, karontā dukkhabhāgino.

Those who wander, entirely self-absorbed, infatuated with their bellies—the foolish, performing defiled actions, become partakers of suffering.

1440.

1440.

Tattha cittavirāgāya, kiṃ pakkaphalasannibhe;

Rasassādapiyākāre, ghorādīnavasañcite.

How necessary is dispassion of mind towards that which is like a ripe fruit, pleasant in taste, and beloved in appearance, yet is fraught with dreadful disadvantages.

1441.

1441.

Bhāventassa paṭikkūla-saññamevaṃ vibhāvino;

Upacārapathaṃ patvā, cittaṃ hoti samāhitaṃ.

For one thus cultivating and discerning the perception of repulsiveness, upon reaching the path of access, the mind becomes concentrated.

1442.

1442.

Soyaṃ [V 0.0131] passambhitāhāra-

Visado so vicakkhaṇo;

Madappamādanikkhanto,

Rasassādanirālayo.

That discerning one, tranquil and pure regarding food, is free from intoxication and heedlessness, without attachment to savoring tastes.

1443.

1443.

Limpento viya bhesajja-makkharabbhañjako yathā;

Puttamaṃsaṃva khādanto, āhāraṃ paribhuñjati.

Like one smearing medicine on a wound, like one anointing an axle, like one eating the flesh of one's own child, so he consumes food.

1444.

1444.

Ariyavaṃsānupajāto,

Appicchādiguṇodito;

Kāmajālaṃ padāletvā,

Sotthiṃ pappoti paṇḍito.

Born into the lineage of the noble ones, endowed with virtues such as having few desires, having burst through the net of sensual pleasures, the wise one attains well-being.

1445.

1445.

Catudhātuvavatthānaṃ, bhāvento pana pañcadhā;

Dhātuyo parigaṇheyya, catassopi sabhāvato.

One developing the analysis of the four elements should comprehend the four elements in a fivefold way, according to their intrinsic nature.

1446.

1446.

Saṅkhepena [M 0.0124] ca vitthārā, sambhārā ca salakkhaṇā;

Ajjhattañca bahiddhā ca, catudhā vibhaje kathaṃ.

Briefly and in detail, with their constituent parts and characteristics, internally and externally, how should one divide them fourfold?

1447.

1447.

Yaṃ kiñci kesalomādi, kakkhaḷattaṃ pavuccati;

Ajjhattaṃ pathavīdhātu, bahiddhā tu tatoparā.

Whatever has the characteristic of hardness, such as head-hair and body-hair, is called the internal earth element; the external, however, is other than that.

1448.

1448.

Yūsabhūtanti yaṃ kiñci,

Āpova paripācakaṃ;

Tejo vāyoti gaṇheyya,

Vitthambhakamasesato.

Whatever is of a fluid nature is water; that which digests is fire; that which supports is wind—thus should one understand them completely.

1449.

1449.

Vitthāratopi sambhārā, kesalomādi vīsati;

Pathavīdhātu pittādi, dvādasāpoti bhāvaye.

In detail, as to the constituents: the twenty parts beginning with head-hair are the earth element; the twelve parts beginning with bile are the water element—thus should one develop it.

1450.

1450.

Tejena yena kāyoyaṃ, santappati jirīyati;

Paridayhati sammā ca, paccanti asitādayo.

By that fire with which this body is heated, ages, and is consumed with fever, and by which what is eaten and so forth is properly digested.

1451.

1451.

Tadetaṃ [V 0.0132] catukoṭṭhāsaṃ, kāyasambhavamattano;

Tejodhātūti gaṇheyya, vāyodhātūticāparaṃ.

This fourfold portion, originating in one's own body, one should understand as the fire element, and the next as the wind element.

1452.

1452.

Uddhañcādhogamāvātā, kucchikoṭṭhāsayā tathā;

Aṅgamaṅgānusārī ca, chadhānāpānamiccapi.

The winds that go upwards and downwards, those in the belly and in the bowels, those that pervade the limbs, and also the in-breath and out-breath—thus are the six kinds.

1453.

1453.

Taṃ taṃ lakkhaṇamārabbha, niddhāretvā salakkhaṇaṃ;

Parigaṇheyya sabbattha, catudhā dhātusaṅgahaṃ.

Having taken up each respective characteristic, and having determined its own characteristic, one should comprehend everywhere the fourfold collection of elements.

1454.

1454.

Iccevaṃ catukoṭṭhāso,

Dhātumatto kaḷevaro;

Niccetano ca nissatto,

Nissāro parabhojano.

Thus this body, with its four parts, is merely a collection of elements; mindless and without a being, essenceless, and food for others.

1455.

1455.

Ritto tuccho ca suñño ca,

Vivitto ca pavajjito;

Attā vā attanīyaṃ vā,

Natthevettha kathañcipi.

Empty, hollow, and void, secluded and forsaken; no self or anything belonging to a self exists here in any way whatsoever.

1456.

1456.

Kevalaṃ [M 0.0125] cetanāviddho, kāyoyaṃ parivattati;

Kampito yāya yantaṃva, sādhippāyova khāyati.

Merely impelled by volition, this body moves about; moved by that volition, like a machine, it appears as if with purpose.

1457.

1457.

Āyu usmā ca viññāṇaṃ, yadā kāyaṃ jahantimaṃ;

Apaviddho tadā seti, niratthaṃva kaliṅgaraṃ.

When life, heat, and consciousness abandon this body, then it lies cast aside, useless as a log of wood.

1458.

1458.

Viparītaṃ papañcentā, bahudhā mohapārutā;

Yattha micchāvipallāsaparābhūtā puthujjanā.

Proliferating in a distorted way, shrouded in delusion in many ways, are the ordinary people who are overcome by wrong perception and distortion.

1459.

1459.

Saṃsāraddhānakantāraṃ, caturāpāyasaṅkaraṃ;

Byasanekāyanopāyaṃ, nātivattanti dujjanā.

Such wicked people do not transcend the wilderness of the long journey of saṃsāra, which is a mixture of the four woeful states and the sole resort for many calamities.

1460.

1460.

Soyamevaṃ catuddhāti,

Dhātubhedena passato;

Tassopacāriko [V 0.0133] nāma,

Samatho hoti cetasi.

For one who thus sees the fourfold division of the elements, there arises in the mind the calm that is called access.

1461.

1461.

Itthaṃ dhātuvavatthānaṃ, katvā tadanusārato;

Upādārūpadhamme ca, nāmadhamme ca sabbathā.

Having thus made the analysis of the elements, and in accordance with that, also the derived material phenomena and the mental phenomena in every way,

1462.

1462.

Bhūmibhūte pariggayha, passanto paccayaṭṭhitiṃ;

Ajjhattañca bahiddhā ca, vipassantodayabbayaṃ.

Having grasped them as the ground, seeing the conditioned nature of things, contemplating arising and passing away both internally and externally,

1463.

1463.

Yathābhūtamabhiññāya, nibbindanto virajjati;

Virāgā ca vimuccitvā, pāragūti pavuccati.

Having directly known things as they really are, becoming disenchanted, one becomes dispassionate; and being liberated through dispassion, one is called 'one who has gone beyond'.

1464.

1464.

Āruppaṃ pana bhāvento, kammaṭṭhānamanāvilaṃ;

Catukkapañcakajjhānaṃ, patvā kasiṇamaṇḍale.

But one developing the formless, an unclouded meditation subject, having attained the fourfold and fivefold jhānas in the kasiṇa-sphere,

1465.

1465.

Pariciṇṇavasībhūtā, jhānā vuṭṭhāya pañcamā;

Cinteti daṇḍādānādirūpadosamabhiṇhaso.

Having become a master of the jhānas through practice, emerging from the fifth jhāna, one reflects repeatedly on the faults of form, such as being liable to be struck with sticks.

1466.

1466.

Nibbindanto tato rūpe, tadākāre ca gocare;

Tadālambaṇadhamme ca, patthento samatikkamaṃ.

Becoming disenchanted with form, with its appearance and its domain, and with the phenomena that have it as their object, one aspires for its transcendence.

1467.

1467.

Pattharitvāna yaṃ kiñci, ākāsakasiṇaṃ vinā;

Ugghāṭeti tamevātha, kasiṇaṃ dhitimā sato.

Having spread out any kasiṇa whatsoever, except for the space kasiṇa, the resolute and mindful one then removes that very kasiṇa.

1468.

1468.

Na [M 0.0126] taṃ manasi karoti, nāvajjati na pekkhati;

Cintābhogavinimutto, kasiṇaṃ pati sabbathā.

One does not pay attention to it, does not advert to it, does not look at it; one is completely freed from thought and reflection with regard to the kasiṇa.

1469.

1469.

Tadappāyasamaññātamākāsaṃ pati mānasaṃ;

Sādhukaṃ paṭipādeti, yoniso paṭicintayaṃ.

Reflecting wisely, one skillfully directs the mind toward the space designated as the basis for that attainment.

1470.

1470.

Tassāvajjanasampannaṃ, upāyapaṭipāditaṃ;

Kasiṇāpagamākāsaṃ, cintanārabbha vattati.

Endowed with attention to that and established by skillful means, the contemplation proceeds, taking as its object the space that is the departure of the kasiṇa.

1471.

1471.

Itthamantaradhāpetvā, kasiṇaṃ tu tato paraṃ;

Sabbāvantamanantaraṃ, pharatākāsagocaraṃ.

Having thus made the kasiṇa disappear, then immediately thereafter, one pervades the entire sphere of space.

1472.

1472.

Tattha [V 0.0134] vuttanayeneva, bhāventassopacārato;

Paṭhamāruppamappeti, ākāsānantagocare.

For one developing it by way of access, in accordance with the method described therein, one attains the first formless attainment in the sphere of infinite space.

1473.

1473.

Tato tamhā vasībhūtā, vuṭṭhahitvā vicintayaṃ;

“Āsannarūpāvacarajjhānapaccatthika”nti taṃ.

Then, having become a master of that, emerging from it, one reflects thus: 'That attainment is an adversary, being close to the form-realm jhānas.'

1474.

1474.

Nikantiṃ pariyādāya, tamhā ākāsagocarā;

Appetuṃ dutiyāruppa-matisantanti gacchati.

Having overcome delight in that sphere of space, one proceeds to attain the second formless attainment, thinking, 'It is exceedingly peaceful.'

1475.

1475.

Paṭhamāruppaviññāṇa-manantaṃ pharato tato;

Dutiyāruppamappeti, viññāṇānantagocare.

Then, by pervading the infinite consciousness of the first formless attainment, one attains the second formless attainment, which has the sphere of infinite consciousness.

1476.

1476.

Paṭhamāruppaviññāṇa-mabhāvento tato paraṃ;

Appeti tatiyāruppa-mākiñcaññamhi gocare.

Then, by no longer developing the consciousness of the first formless attainment, one attains the third formless attainment in the sphere of nothingness.

1477.

1477.

Tato ca tatiyāruppaṃ, “santameta”nti passato;

Catutthāruppamappeti, tatiyāruppagocare.

Then, perceiving the third formless attainment as 'this is peaceful,' one attains the fourth formless attainment, which has the third formless attainment as its sphere.

1478.

1478.

Gūthamhi maṇḍape laggo, eko tannissitoparo;

Eko bahi anissāya, taṃ taṃ nissāya cāparo.

One is attached in a pavilion of dung, another is dependent on it; one is outside, independent, and yet another is dependent on that one.

1479.

1479.

Ṭhito catūhi etehi, purisehi yathākkamaṃ;

Samānatāya ñātabbā, catassopi vibhāvinā.

These four persons, standing thus in order, should be understood by the discerning one through their similarity.

1480.

1480.

Iccālambaṇabhedehi[M 0.0127], catudhāruppabhāvanā;

Aṅgabhedaṃ panetāsaṃ, na kathenti tathāpi ca.

Thus, the development of the formless attainments is fourfold, distinguished by their objects. Yet, even so, they do not speak of the distinction of their factors.

1481.

1481.

Suppaṇītatarā honti, uddhamuddhaṃ yathākkamaṃ;

Cātumahārājikādidibbasampattiyo yathā.

They become increasingly sublime, higher and higher in due order, just like the divine attainments beginning with those of the Cātumahārājika realm.

1482.

1482.

Āneñjamiti bhāvetvā, samāpattiṃ catubbidhaṃ;

Susamāhitasaṅkappo, sampannācalamānaso.

Having developed the fourfold attainment called 'imperturbable,' with well-composed intention and a mind perfected in steadfastness,

1483.

1483.

Vipassanto yathābhūtaṃ, sacchikatvā phaluttamaṃ;

Ubhatobhāgavimutto, arahāti pavuccati.

Seeing with insight things as they truly are, having realized the supreme fruit, freed in both ways, he is called an Arahant.

1484.

1484.

Kammaṭṭhānavidhiṃ [V 0.0135] ñatvā, cattālīsavidhaṃ tato;

Abhiññāyopi viññeyyā, samathe bhāvanānaye.

Having known the method of the forty kinds of meditation subjects, the higher knowledges should then also be understood in the practice of serenity.

1485.

1485.

Iddhividhā dibbasotā, cetopariyajānanā;

Pubbenivāsānussati, dibbacakkhu tathāparā.

The kinds of psychic power, the divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, recollection of past lives, and likewise the other, the divine eye.

1486.

1486.

Cetosamādhinissaṭṭhā, pañcābhiññā pakāsitā;

Rūpāvacaradhammāva, pañcamajjhānabhūmikā.

The five higher knowledges, arisen from concentration of mind, are declared; they are indeed phenomena of the form realm, on the plane of the fifth jhāna.

1487.

1487.

Bahubhāvādidhiṭṭhānaṃ, komārādivikubbanā;

Manomayābhinimmānamiccevaṃ tividhiddhiyo.

The determination of being manifold and so on, transformation into a youth and so on, and the creation of a mind-made body—thus are the three kinds of psychic power.

1488.

1488.

Dibbe ca mānuse sadde,

Tathā dūre ca santike;

Suṇanti yāya sā dibbā,

Sotadhātūti bhāsitā.

That by which they hear sounds both divine and human, likewise those far and near, is called the divine ear-element.

1489.

1489.

Cetopariyañāṇanti, parapuggalacetaso;

Sarāgavītarāgādiparicchedakamīritaṃ.

Knowledge of encompassing the mind is said to be the discernment of the minds of other individuals, as to whether they are with lust, without lust, and so on.

1490.

1490.

Pubbenivutthakhandhānussaraṇe ñāṇamīritaṃ;

Pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa nāmena tādinā.

The knowledge in recollecting the aggregates previously dwelt in is spoken of; by such a one, it is called by the name 'knowledge of the recollection of past lives'.

1491.

1491.

Cavamāne ca jāyante, satte rūpamarūpakaṃ;

Tathā mānusakaṃ rūpaṃ, thūlaṃ sukhuma santikaṃ.

Beings passing away and being reborn, with form and without form, likewise human form, gross, subtle, and near,

1492.

1492.

Dūre [M 0.0128] pakāsaṃ channañca, yena passanti yogino;

Cutūpapātañāṇaṃ taṃ, dibbacakkhūti vuccati.

And the distant, the manifest, and the hidden—that by which yogis see, that knowledge of passing away and reappearance, is called the divine eye.

1493.

1493.

Anāgataṃsañāṇañca, yathākammupagaṃ tathā;

Tannissitattā gacchanti, dibbacakkhumhi saṅgahaṃ.

Knowledge of the future and likewise how beings fare according to their deeds; because they are dependent on it, they are included in the divine eye.

1494.

1494.

Iti pañcavidhaṃ pattumabhiññaṃ pana paṇḍito;

Katvāna pañcamajjhāne, pañcadhā vasitaṃ cidaṃ.

Thus, the wise one, in order to attain the fivefold higher knowledge, having achieved the fivefold mastery in the fifth jhāna,

1495.

1495.

Tathā [V 0.0136] samāhite citte, parisuddhe niraṅgaṇe;

Mudubhūte kammaniye, āneñjamhi patiṭṭhite.

When the mind is thus concentrated, purified, stainless, become soft, workable, and established in imperturbability,

1496.

1496.

Abhiññāpādakajjhānā, tato vuṭṭhāya pañcamā;

Abhiññāparikammāya, ninnāmeyyātha mānasaṃ.

Having emerged from the fifth jhāna, which is the basis for higher knowledge, one should then direct the mind towards the preliminary work for higher knowledge.

1497.

1497.

Adhiṭṭheyyādikaṃ taṃ tamāvajjitvā yathārahaṃ;

Parikammaṃ karitvāna, samāpajjeyya pādakaṃ.

Having adverted to each particular thing to be determined as is appropriate, and having performed the preliminary work, one should attain the foundational jhāna.

1498.

1498.

Punadeva ca vuṭṭhāya, parikammaṃ yathā pure;

Karontassa panappeti, abhiññāṇena pañcamaṃ.

And emerging once again, for one performing the preparatory work as before, the fifth jhāna which is the higher knowledge is attained.

1499.

1499.

Adhiṭṭhantaṃ vikubbantaṃ, nimminantaṃ yathārahaṃ;

Sadde suṇantaṃ sattānaṃ, parijānañca mānasaṃ.

Determining, transforming, creating as is fitting; hearing the sounds of beings, and fully knowing their minds;

1500.

1500.

Saraṃ pubbenivāsañca, passaṃ sugatiduggatiṃ;

Yathākammaṃ vipākañca, pajānantamanāgataṃ.

Recalling past lives, seeing happy and unhappy destinies, and knowing the future result according to kamma—

1501.

1501.

Yathāsambhavamiccevamupāyakusalo muni;

Upanissayasampanno, abhiññamadhigacchati.

Thus, as is possible, the sage skilled in means, endowed with supporting conditions, attains higher knowledge.

1502.

1502.

Pattābhiñño mahāyogī, pariyodātamānaso;

Paripakkena ñāṇena, vipassitvā tilakkhaṇaṃ.

The great yogi who has attained the higher knowledges, with a perfectly pure mind, having seen with insight the three characteristics with ripened wisdom,

1503.

1503.

Laddhāsavakkhayaṃ ñāṇaṃ, chadhābhiññamanuttaraṃ;

Mahākhīṇāsavo nāma, chaḷabhiñño pavuccati.

Having obtained the knowledge of the destruction of taints, the unsurpassed sixth higher knowledge, he is called the Great One with Taints Destroyed, the possessor of the six higher knowledges.

1504.

1504.

Cattālīsavidhaṃ [M 0.0129] panitthamamalocetomalakkhālanaṃ,

Kammaṭṭhānanayaṃ yamāha sugato sammā samādhānakaṃ;

Saṃkhittaṃ kathitaṃ tamettha sakalaṃ sābhiññamettāvatā,

Kattabbā muninettha sādhumatinā sambhāvanā sabbathā.

Thus this fortyfold method of meditation, a stainless cleansing of the mind's defilements, which the Well-Gone-One rightly called the means of concentration—all that, along with the higher knowledges, has been briefly explained here to this extent. Herein, reverence should be shown in every way by the wise sage.

1505.

1505.

Varaguṇagaṇabhūsitānusiṭṭhaṃ,

Iti samathamimaṃ tu bhāvayitvā;

Paramamanupamaṃ [V 0.0137] bhajanti dhīrā,

Hitasukhamukhamuttamānubuddhaṃ.

Having thus cultivated this serenity, instructed and adorned with a multitude of excellent qualities, the wise resort to the supreme, incomparable, perfectly enlightened one, the highest source of benefit and happiness.

Iti nāmarūpaparicchede sesakammaṭṭhānavibhāgo nāma

Thus ends the section named 'The Division of the Remaining Meditation Subjects' in the Discernment of Name-and-Form.

Dasamo paricchedo.

The Tenth Chapter.

Niṭṭhito ca nāmarūpaparicchede sabbathāpi

And thus is completed in every way, within the Discernment of Name-and-Form,

Samathabhāvanāvibhāgo.

The Division of the Development of Serenity.

11. Ekādasamo paricchedo

11. The Eleventh Chapter.

Vipassanāvibhāgo

The Division of Insight.

1506.

1506.

Dvidhā samuṭṭhānadhurā, tividhā bhūmiyo matā;

Tividhābhinivesā ca, sarīraṃ tu catubbidhaṃ.

The primary undertakings are twofold, the grounds are considered threefold; the applications are threefold, and the substance is fourfold.

1507.

1507.

Tividhā bhāvanā tattha, saṅkhāresu yathārahaṃ;

Duvidhākāramārabbha, nijjhāyati tilakkhaṇaṃ.

Therein, the development is threefold, as is appropriate regarding formations; having undertaken the twofold mode, one contemplates the three characteristics.

1508.

1508.

Aṭṭhārasākārabhinnā, dasāvatthā vibhāvitā;

Tidhā vibhāgā sādheti, vimokkhattayamuttamaṃ.

Distinguished by eighteen aspects, made clear in ten stages, and divided in three ways, it accomplishes the supreme triad of liberations.

1509.

1509.

Catusaccapaṭivedhā, sattaṭṭhāriyapuggalā;

Klesahānī yathāyogaṃ, catasso paṭisambhidā.

The penetration of the four truths, the seven noble individuals, the abandonment of defilements as is appropriate, and the four analytical knowledges.

1510.

1510.

Tividhā [M 0.0130] ca samāpatti, nirodhā ca tathāparā;

Nissandaphalamiccāhu, tassā sāsanakovidā.

And threefold are the attainments, and likewise the other, cessation; the experts in the teaching declare this to be its resultant fruit.

1511.

1511.

Vipassanābhāvanāya-miti bhāsanti paṇḍitā;

Tamidāni pavakkhāmi, yathānukkamato kathaṃ.

Thus do the wise speak of the development of insight; that I shall now explain in due order, how it is.

1512.

1512.

Bhūmidhamme [V 0.0138] pariggayha, vicinantassa yogino;

Satiyā samathā vātha, samuṭṭhāti vipassanā.

For the yogi who comprehends and investigates the phenomena of the grounds, insight arises from mindfulness or from serenity.

1513.

1513.

Sabhāvapaṭivedhe ca, saddhammapaṭipattiyaṃ;

Paññāsaddhādvayaṃ tassā, dhuramāhu dhurandharā.

Concerning the penetration of inherent nature and the practice of the true Dhamma, the burden-bearers declare the pair of wisdom and faith to be its yoke.

1514.

1514.

Tebhūmakasabhāvānaṃ, sappaccayapariggaho;

Ñātapariññā nāmāyaṃ, bhūmīti paṭhamā matā.

The comprehension of the inherent natures of the three realms, together with their conditions—this, named 'full understanding through knowing,' is considered the first ground.

1515.

1515.

Kalāpato sammasanaṃ, udayabbayadassanaṃ;

Pariññātīraṇā nāma, dutiyā bhūmi bhāsitā.

Comprehension by way of groups and the vision of arising and passing away—this, named 'full understanding through investigation,' is spoken of as the second ground.

1516.

1516.

Pahānapariññā bhūmi, tatiyāhu tatoparaṃ;

Bhaṅgādiñāṇamiccevaṃ, tividhā bhūmiyo matā.

Beyond that, they say, is the third ground, that of 'full understanding through abandoning,' which consists of the knowledge of dissolution and so forth; thus the grounds are considered threefold.

1517.

1517.

Khaṇasantatiaddhāna-vasenettha samīritā;

Aniccā dukkhānattāti, tividhābhinivesanā.

Here, by way of moment, continuity, and time-period, the threefold application—as impermanent, suffering, and not-self—is declared.

1518.

1518.

Diṭṭhikaṅkhāvitaraṇā, maggāmaggapaṭippadā;

Visuddhiyo catassopi, sarīranti nidassitā.

Purification of View, the Overcoming of Doubt, the Knowledge and Vision of the Path and Not-Path, and of the Way—these four purifications are shown to be the substance.

1519.

1519.

Salakkhaṇavavatthānaṃ, paccayākāranicchayo;

Kummaggaparihāro ca, tilakkhaṇavipassanā.

The determination of individual characteristics, the ascertainment of conditions and causes, the avoidance of the wrong path, and insight into the three characteristics.

1520.

1520.

Iti lakkhaṇabhinnattā, labbhantekakkhaṇepi ca;

Desitā hetubhūtena, kamenevaṃ visuddhiyo.

Thus, due to the distinctness of their characteristics, and although they are obtainable even in a single moment, the purifications were taught in this sequence, which is based on causality.

1521.

1521.

Sīlabbisuddhiādīnaṃ, tathā sāva paramparā;

Cittabbisuddhiādīnamatthāyāti pakāsitā.

Thus, that very succession of the purification of virtue and so forth is declared to be for the sake of the purification of mind and so forth.

1522.

1522.

Dissamānasabhāvānaṃ, passanto paccayaṭṭhiti;

Paripanthavimutto hi, paṭipādeti bhāvanaṃ.

Seeing the conditioned nature of phenomena as they are manifest, one, being indeed free from obstacles, undertakes the development.

1523.

1523.

Tathāpi [M 0.0131] ca visesena, paṭipannassa yogino;

Tattha tattha vibhūtattā, ṭhānato bheditā kathaṃ.

Nevertheless, for the yogi who is especially practicing the way, since clarity becomes manifest in various places, how is this teaching divided according to stages?

1524.

1524.

Rūpapubbaṅgamaṃ [V 0.0139] vātha, nāmapubbaṅgamaṃ tathā;

Ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā, yathāpākaṭadhammato.

Either with form as the forerunner, or similarly with name as the forerunner; either internally or externally, according to whichever phenomenon is manifest.

1525.

1525.

Nāmarūpādibhedena, bhūmidhammapariggaho;

Vuttā diṭṭhivisuddhīti, attadiṭṭhippahānato.

The comprehension of the phenomena of the grounds, by way of the analysis of name-and-form and so forth, is called the Purification of View, because it is the abandoning of the view of a self.

1526.

1526.

Āhacca paccayuppannā, tathā tabbhāvabhāvino;

Pavattantīti saṅkhāre, passato pana yoniso.

For one who wisely sees that formations proceed thus: arisen from their respective conditions and existing only while those conditions obtain,

1527.

1527.

Paccayaggāhinī paññā, nāmarūpappavattiyā;

Kaṅkhā taranti tāyāti, kaṅkhāvitaraṇā matā.

there arises the wisdom that grasps the conditions for the occurrence of name-and-form. Because one crosses over doubt by means of it, this is considered the 'Overcoming of Doubt'.

1528.

1528.

Aniccā dukkhānattāti, paccayāyattavuttito;

Saṅkhipitvā kalāpena, sammasīyanti saṅkhatā.

Because their occurrence is dependent on conditions, conditioned things are comprehended as impermanent, suffering, and not-self, after having been summarized by way of groups.

1529.

1529.

Uppādavayabhāvopi, lakkhaṇattayasādhako;

Paccayākāramārabbha, lakkhīyati visesato.

The nature of arising and passing away also establishes the three characteristics; it is especially discerned based on the mode of conditions.

1530.

1530.

Tasmā sammasanañāṇaṃ, udayabbayadassanaṃ;

Kaṅkhāvitaraṇāyaṃ tu, saṅgayhati visuddhiyaṃ.

Therefore, the knowledge of comprehension and the vision of arising and passing away are included in the Purification of Overcoming Doubt.

1531.

1531.

Tattha saṃklesavikkhepaṃ, kummaggaṃ parivajjato;

Maggāmaggavisuddhīti, ñāṇadassanamīritaṃ.

Therein, for one who avoids defilement, distraction, and the wrong path, the Purification by Knowledge and Vision of What Is Path and Not-Path is declared.

1532.

1532.

Tato kathenti akliṭṭhamudayabbayadassanaṃ;

Ādiṃ katvā paṭipadāñāṇadassanasuddhiyaṃ.

Then they speak of the unafflicted vision of arising and passing away, beginning with the Purification of Knowledge and Vision of the Course of Practice.

1533.

1533.

Paccayapaccayuppanne, yathāvatthuvavatthite;

Pahātumīhamānānaṃ, niyyānapaṭipattito.

For those striving to abandon, by means of the practice leading to liberation, conditions and conditionally arisen phenomena, established according to their true nature.

1534.

1534.

Upaklesavisuddho hi, punadevodayabbayaṃ;

Adhiṭṭhahitvā bhaṅgādi-ñāṇehi paṭipajjati.

Indeed, one purified of corruptions, having again determined upon arising and passing away, proceeds by means of the knowledges of dissolution and so forth.

1535.

1535.

Tathā [M 0.0132] cābhinavuppanne, bhijjamāne vipassato;

Saṃvegakaḍḍhitaṃ ñāṇaṃ, bhaṅgādimanutiṭṭhati.

And similarly, for one who sees with insight the newly arisen as breaking up, knowledge, drawn along by spiritual urgency, persists in dissolution and so forth.

1536.

1536.

Tato [V 0.0140] pubbe pavattā hi, saṃklesāpāyasambhavā;

Paṭipattivisuddhīti, na saṅgayhati bhāvanā.

Indeed, the development that occurred previously, arising from defilements and states of loss, is not included as the Purification of Practice.

1537.

1537.

Sampādento paniccetā, catassopi visuddhiyo;

Aniccā dukkhānattāti, bhāveyya tividhā kathaṃ.

But while accomplishing these four purifications, how should one develop in three ways the contemplation of impermanence, suffering, and not-self?

1538.

1538.

Paccayapaccayuppannā, jātānantarabhedino;

Aniccā ca pabhaṅgū ca, palujjanti cavanti ca.

Conditionally and dependently arisen, breaking up immediately after arising, they are impermanent and fragile; they dissolve and pass away.

1539.

1539.

Addhuvā ca asārā ca, vibhavā ca vināsino;

Saṅkhatā vipariṇāma-dhammā ittarakālikā.

They are unstable and without essence, subject to dissolution and destruction; conditioned, subject to change, and temporary.

1540.

1540.

Khayadhammā vayadhammā, lahukālappavattino;

Tāvakālikadhammā ca, parittaṭṭhitikā tathā.

They are subject to decay and subject to vanishing, occurring for a brief time; and they are temporary phenomena, and similarly of short duration.

1541.

1541.

Khaṇattayaparicchinnā, pubbāparavicittakā;

Purakkhatā nirodhassa, sassatā na kudācanaṃ.

Bounded by the three moments, diverse in their before and after, with cessation as their forerunner, they are never eternal.

1542.

1542.

Jāyanti parihānāya, na tu jāyanti vuddhiyā;

Jiyyamānāva tiṭṭhanti, jiṇṇā bhaṅgaparāyaṇā.

They are born for decline, not for growth; they remain only while decaying; having aged, they are headed for dissolution.

1543.

1543.

Ahutvāyevuppajjanti, na kutocipi āgatā;

Hutvā antaradhāyanti, na tu katthaci sañcitā.

They arise without having been, not having come from anywhere; having been, they vanish, not stored anywhere.

1544.

1544.

Taṃ taṃ paccayasāmaggi-mattalābhāya nissitā;

Nirodhadhammā jāyanti, jātā byanti bhavanti te.

Dependent on this and that combination of conditions for their mere attainment, they arise as subject to cessation; having arisen, they vanish.

1545.

1545.

Yathā nadī pabbateyyā, yathā dīpasikhā tathā;

Sīghasīghaṃ pavattantā, uppajjanti vayanti ca.

Like a mountain river, and like a lamp's flame, occurring very swiftly, they arise and cease.

1546.

1546.

Jātā jātā nirujjhanti, aññe aññe tu jāyare;

Avīci anusambandhā, na jānanti visesato.

As soon as they arise, they cease, while others and others are born; connected without interruption, one does not know this specifically.

1547.

1547.

Iti [M 0.0133] nānappakārena, vipassanto vicakkhaṇo;

Aniccabhāvanaṃ dhīro, paripāceti sādhukaṃ.

Thus, in various ways, the discerning one, practicing insight, the wise one, brings the development of impermanence to maturity.

1548.

1548.

Dukkhā [V 0.0141] ca dukkhavatthū ca, abhiṇhaparipīḷitā;

Rogā gaṇḍā ca sallā ca, aghato ca upaddavā.

They are suffering and the basis of suffering, constantly oppressed; they are diseases, tumors, and darts, misfortune and calamities.

1549.

1549.

Bhayopasaggāghamūlā,

Sāsavādīnavītitā;

Aleṇāsaraṇātāṇā,

Vadhakā mārakāmisā.

They are rooted in fear, danger, and misfortune, afflicted by taints and drawbacks; without shelter, without refuge, without protection, they are killers, the bait of Māra.

1550.

1550.

Jātidhammā jarābyādhi-

Sokopāyāsabhāgino;

Paridevasabhāvā ca,

Saṃklesā dukkhabhāgino.

Subject to birth, they share in aging, sickness, sorrow, and despair; they have the nature of lamentation, are defilements, and share in suffering.

1551.

1551.

Jegucchā paṭikūlā ca, bībhacchā ca virūpino;

Ajaññā capalā hīnā, duggandhā bālasevitā.

They are repulsive and loathsome, disgusting and misshapen; ignoble, fickle, and base, foul-smelling, frequented by fools.

1552.

1552.

Sokantarikatāniccaṃ, taṇhāya kaḍḍhitā bhusaṃ;

Kapaṇā duggatā dīnā, vipannā ca vighātino.

Always interspersed with sorrow, they are strongly drawn by craving; they are wretched, miserable, and distressed, ruined and destructive.

1553.

1553.

Attalābhaṃ gavesanti, taṃtaṃpaccayanissitā;

Dukkhādhiṭṭhānamaccantaṃ, jātā puna vihaññare.

Seeking their own existence, dependent on this and that condition, they are utterly a basis for suffering; having been born, they are again afflicted.

1554.

1554.

Aggikūpe nimuggāva, klesasantāpabhāgino;

Oviddhā viya sattīhi, saṅkhārā niccadukkhitā.

Like those sunk in a pit of fire, sharing in the torment of defilements, pierced as if by spears, formations are constantly afflicted.

1555.

1555.

Jāyamānā ca jiyyantā, miyyantā ca khaṇe khaṇe;

Pasukā viya niccammā, haññanti serikāturā.

Being born, decaying, and dying moment by moment, like flayed cattle, they are slain, afflicted by sensuality.

1556.

1556.

Tilāni tilayanteva, ucchuyanteva ucchuyo;

Udayabbayāvassaṃ te, pīḷayanti abhiṇhaso.

Just as sesame seeds in a press and sugarcane in a mill, they are constantly oppressed by the power of arising and passing away.

1557.

1557.

Manoramanavākārā[M 0.0134], vipallāsaparikkhatā;

Iriyāpathasañchannā, nopatiṭṭhanti dukkhato.

Pleasing in speech and manner, adorned with distortions, and concealed by their deportment, suffering is not apparent.

1558.

1558.

Saṅkhāresu [V 0.0142] panetesu, vedanāssādarodhino;

Sāva sandulasambaddhā, sammohaparivāritā.

But in these formations, which obstruct the enjoyment of feeling, craving is bound by defilement and surrounded by delusion.

1559.

1559.

“Aduṃ dukkhamidaṃ dukkha”-miti saṃsāracārino;

Dukkhahetumajānantā, sambhamanti aviddasu.

“This is suffering, this is suffering”—thus do those who wander in saṃsāra, not knowing the cause of suffering, stumble on, unwise.

1560.

1560.

Sukhākāramapassantā, dukkhabhāranipīḷitā;

Patthenti dukkhamevaññaṃ, bālā byasanabhāgino.

Not seeing the aspect of happiness, crushed by the burden of suffering, fools long for still other suffering, partakers of misfortune.

1561.

1561.

Cavantā upapajjantā, rukkhasākhaṃva makkaṭo;

Dukkhamekaṃ vimuccanti, tato gaṇhanti cāparaṃ.

Falling away and reappearing, like a monkey releasing one branch only to seize another, they relinquish one suffering only to grasp another.

1562.

1562.

Te dīgharattaṃ socanti, taṇhāsallasamappitā;

Diṭṭhipāsasamupetā, mānatthambhānusāyino.

They grieve for a long time, afflicted by the dart of craving, bound by the noose of views, and with the underlying tendency of the pillar of conceit.

1563.

1563.

Tamākāraṃ paniccevaṃ, vipassanto visārado;

Dukkhānupassanaṃ nāma, paripāceti bhāvanaṃ.

And thus, observing in that manner, the skilled one perfects the development called 'contemplation of suffering'.

1564.

1564.

Dhammaṭṭhitiniyāmā hi, khandhāyatanadhātuyo;

Anattāsassatantā ca, īhābhogavivajjitā.

For the aggregates, sense bases, and elements are fixed by the law of the Dhamma's stability; they are not-self, not eternal, and devoid of striving and purpose.

1565.

1565.

Payojanamadhiṭṭhāya, na tu byāpārayanti ca;

Paccayapaccayuppannā, janetuṃ vātha jāyituṃ.

They do not exert themselves with a set purpose, either to generate or to be generated; they are arisen dependent on conditions.

1566.

1566.

Tathāpi hetusāmaggi-sambhave sambhavanti te;

Tabbhāvabhāvibhāvena, aññamaññapavattitā.

Nevertheless, when there is a concurrence of causes, they arise; by the nature of one's existence causing the other's existence, they proceed in mutual dependence.

1567.

1567.

Ajāyituṃ na sakkonti, sati paccayasambhave;

Paccayānamalābhe tu, na jāyanti kudācanaṃ.

They are unable not to arise when there is the arising of conditions; but when conditions are not obtained, they never arise at all.

1568.

1568.

Na kiñcettha apekkhitvā, samaggā honti paccayā;

Na janetuṃ na sakkonti, samaggā ca kudācanaṃ.

Not depending on anything here, conditions come together; and when united, they are never unable to generate.

1569.

1569.

Yathāpaccayalābhena[M 0.0135], pavattanti yathā tathā;

Rakkhitā vā vidhātā vā, natthi assāmikā tathā.

According to the obtaining of conditions, they proceed just so; there is no guard or director, thus they are ownerless.

1570.

1570.

“Ahaṃ [V 0.0143] mama”nti gaṇhantā, pariṇāmenti aññathā;

Vissasantā harantete, parābhūtā palambhino.

Grasping 'I' and 'mine,' they transform things otherwise. Trusting, they are carried away, defeated, and self-deceived.

1571.

1571.

Rittā tucchā ca suññā ca, vivittā sāravajjitā;

Salakkhaṇaparicchinnā, dhammā natthettha puggalo.

Empty, hollow, and void, isolated, devoid of essence, phenomena are defined by their own characteristics; there is no person here.

1572.

1572.

Jāyamānā ca jiyyantā, miyyamānā ca saṅkhatā;

Vivasā parivattanti, vaso tesaṃ na katthaci.

Being born, decaying, and dying, conditioned things revolve, powerless; there is no control over them anywhere.

1573.

1573.

Na tesu kassacisseraṃ, na tesañcatthi katthaci;

Na cattanīti saṅkhārā, ādhipaccavivajjitā.

No one has mastery over them, nor do they have mastery over anything anywhere. And thus, these formations are not self, devoid of sovereignty.

1574.

1574.

Kadalīpattavaṭṭīva, aññamaññapatiṭṭhitā;

Sahajātagghanībhūtā, nopaṭṭhanti anattato.

Like the layers of a banana stalk, resting on one another, born together and densely packed, they do not appear as a self.

1575.

1575.

Arūpanissitaṃ rūpaṃ, arūpaṃ rūpanissitaṃ;

Jaccandhapīṭhasappīva, aññamaññavavatthitaṃ.

Form is dependent on the formless, the formless is dependent on form; like a man born blind and a cripple, they are mutually established.

1576.

1576.

Yantasuttena yantaṃva, kāyayantaṃ pavattati;

Nāmāvakaḍḍhitaṃ tattha, natthi attā sayaṃvasī.

Like a machine driven by a string, the body-machine proceeds. Dragged by name, there is no self there, no self-controller.

1577.

1577.

Cetovipphāranipphannā, vāyodhātusamuṭṭhitā;

Iriyāpathaviññattivikārā pālakā matā.

Produced by the mind's expansion, arisen from the wind element, the changes in deportment and expressions of communication are regarded as governors.

1578.

1578.

Oviddhavedanāsallavikārapariṇāmato;

Bālānaṃ cittanipphannā, attāti parikappanā.

From the alteration and transformation caused by the piercing dart of feeling, the fools' mind-produced conception 'self' arises.

1579.

1579.

Suddhasaṅkhārapuñjoyaṃ, nettha sattopalabbhati;

Taṃ taṃ paccayamāgamma, dukkhakkhandhova jāyati.

This is a heap of mere formations; no being is found here. Depending on this or that condition, just a mass of suffering arises.

1580.

1580.

Evamādippakārehi, vipassanto anattato;

Anattabhāvanaṃ nāma, bhāvetīti pavuccati.

Thus, observing in this and similar ways as not-self, it is said that one develops the meditation called 'development of not-self'.

1581.

1581.

Bhāvento tividhampetaṃ, nijjhāyati tilakkhaṇaṃ;

Nimittañca pavattañca, samārabbha yathākkamaṃ.

Developing this threefold meditation, one contemplates the three characteristics, taking up the sign and the occurrence in due order.

1582.

1582.

Attalābhanimittañca[M 0.0136][V 0.0144], taṃtaṃpaccayanissitā;

Tabbhāvabhāvibhāvena, lakkhīyanti nimittato.

Dependent on this or that condition, they are marked by the sign of the acquisition of existence, which proceeds by the nature of one thing causing another to be.

1583.

1583.

Jāyamānā ca jiyyantā, miyyamānā ca saṅkhatā;

Taṃ taṃ bhāvamatikkamma, pavattanti khaṇe khaṇe.

Being born, decaying, and dying, conditioned, having passed beyond each state, they proceed moment by moment.

1584.

1584.

Hetunissayanākāro, nimittanti tato mato;

Pavattaṃ vattanākāro, khaṇasantatiaddhato.

The aspect of dependence on causes is thus considered the sign; the occurrence is the aspect of proceeding, through the duration of the continuity of moments.

1585.

1585.

Apubbābhinavuppatti, uppādoti pakāsito;

Pubbāpariyasandhānaṃ, paṭisandhīti bhāsitā.

The arising, unprecedented and new, is declared as 'uppāda'; the connection of prior and subsequent states is spoken of as 'paṭisandhi'.

1586.

1586.

Āyūhantīti vuccanti, tadatthaṃ pana vāvaṭā;

Iccādipariyāyehi, bahvākārāpi saṅkhatā.

They are called 'striving' and are 'engaged' for that purpose; by these and other modes, the conditioned is of manifold aspects.

1587.

1587.

Nimitte ca pavatte ca, vatthuto yanti saṅgahaṃ;

Taṃ dvayākāramārabbha, patiṭṭhāti tilakkhaṇaṃ.

In the sign and in the occurrence, they are comprised in substance; based on this twofold aspect, the three characteristics are established.

1588.

1588.

Paccayādhīnadhammānaṃ, uppādavayalakkhitā;

Aniccatānimittaṭṭhā, pavattesu na pākaṭā.

Of phenomena dependent on conditions, impermanence—marked by arising and passing away and standing as the sign—is not evident in their occurrences.

1589.

1589.

Pubbāparavicittānamasamatthānamattani;

Sannissayena nipphanno, bhāvadubbalyasādhako.

Of those diverse before and after, incapable in themselves, it is produced by dependence, establishing the weakness of existence.

1590.

1590.

Hetusaṅkhātabhāvo hi, saṅkhārānamaniccatā;

Pavattamānā dasseti, taṃ sabhāvaṃ panattano.

For the impermanence of formations is the state of being reckoned as caused; as it proceeds, it reveals that intrinsic nature of its own.

1591.

1591.

Niccā dhuvā ce saṅkhārā, kasmā pekkhanti paccaye;

Ahutvā yadi nissāya, jātā kā tattha niccatā;

If formations were permanent and stable, why would they depend on conditions? If, not having been, they arise through dependence, what permanence is there in that?

1592.

1592.

Attalābhaṃ labhitvāna, hetusāmaggilābhato;

Yāpessanti tamaññatra, kathaṃ nāmattadubbalā.

Having attained their own being from the gain of a causal combination, how indeed, being weak in themselves, could they sustain it elsewhere?

1593.

1593.

Paccaye anapekkhitvā, yadi natthi samatthatā;

Attalābhūpalābhāya, kiṃ samatthānupālane;

If, without depending on conditions, there is no capacity to attain one's own being, what is the point of maintaining that capacity?

1594.

1594.

Janakā [M 0.0137][V 0.0145] paccayānañhi, tadāyūhanato paraṃ;

Parihāritumāraddhā, jiyā khittasaro yathā.

For the causes are the producers; beyond their initial striving, the effects have begun to diminish, like an arrow shot from a bowstring.

1595.

1595.

Accīva vaṭṭinikkhantā, meghamuttāva vijjutā;

Paccayuddhaṭavissaṭṭhā, dhammā bhaṅgaparāyaṇā.

Like a flame that has left the wick, like lightning freed from a cloud, phenomena, sent forth and raised up by conditions, are destined for dissolution.

1596.

1596.

Tasmā nimittamākāraṃ, passanto sa vipassako;

“Vinassanti avassa”nti, saddahanto vimuccati.

Therefore, that insight meditator, seeing the sign and its mode, and having faith that 'They will surely perish,' is liberated.

1597.

1597.

Aniccato tathā hevaṃ, vipassantassa yogino;

Saddhāvimokkha bāhulyaṃ, bhavatīti pakāsitaṃ.

Thus, for the yogi who sees with insight in this very way that it is impermanent, an abundance of faith-deliverance occurs—this is declared.

1598.

1598.

Iti saṅkhāradhammesu, nimittākāranicchitaṃ;

Aniccalakkhaṇaṃ dhīro, nijjhāyati niyāmato.

Thus, the wise one unfailingly contemplates the characteristic of impermanence in conditioned phenomena, having ascertained it by its sign and mode.

1599.

1599.

Bādhakattabhayākārā, pavatte dukkhitā viya;

Pavattamānā pīḷenti, saṅkhārā ca bhayāvahā.

Being oppressive and having the aspect of fear, like those who suffer in the round of existence, formations oppress as they occur, and they are fear-producing.

1600.

1600.

Uppādābhinavākāraṃ, atikkamma tato paraṃ;

Jarājaccaritā hutvā, bhañjamānā kathaṃ sukhā.

Having passed beyond the fresh aspect of arising, thereafter, having become subject to aging and decay, how can they be happy when breaking apart?

1601.

1601.

Tasmā pavattamākāraṃ, nijjhāyanto nirantaraṃ;

Saṅkhāre dukkhato disvā, hitvāna paṇidhiṃ tahiṃ.

Therefore, constantly contemplating the mode of occurrence, seeing formations as suffering, and having abandoned aspiration for them,

1602.

1602.

Tadāyūhananissaṅgo, passaddhadaratho sukhī;

Samādhibahulo yogī, vūpasantoti vuccati.

detached from that striving, with tranquilized distress, at ease, the yogi, abounding in concentration, is called 'calmed.'

1603.

1603.

Byāpāravasitākāraṃ, saṅkhārānaṃ vipassato;

Nimitte ca pavatte ca, upaṭṭhāti anattato.

For one who sees with insight the aspect of formations as being under the sway of activity, the characteristic of not-self appears in the sign and in the occurrence.

1604.

1604.

Anattādhīnanipphannā, vasātītappavattino;

Bhāvadubbalyanissārā, kathamattā bhavissare.

Produced not under the control of a self, occurring beyond one's sway, essenceless due to the weakness of their nature, how could they be a self?

1605.

1605.

Tamevaṃ paṭivijjhanto, maññatānattalakkhaṇaṃ;

Vipassanārasassādī, saṃvegabahulo bhave.

Thus penetrating the characteristic of not-self in what is conceived, savoring the taste of insight, one should abound in spiritual urgency.

1606.

1606.

Iccāhacca [V 0.0146] pavattānaṃ, lakkhaṇānaṃ sabhāvato;

Vavatthito tattha tattha, taṃtaṃlakkhaṇanicchayo.

Thus, for the characteristics that occur repeatedly, the determination of each respective characteristic is established in each case according to its own nature.

1607.

1607.

Tathāpipākaṭaṭṭhāne[M 0.0138], hetubhūte ca yoniso;

Vavatthapeti saṅkhāya, lakkhaṇāni vicakkhaṇo.

Likewise, the discerning one, having reflected wisely, determines the characteristics both in the manifest instance and in that which has become the cause.

1608.

1608.

Uppādavayabhāvena, dissamānā hi saṅkhatā;

Pubbāparavivekena, dassenti tadaniccataṃ.

Indeed, conditioned things, being seen by way of their arising and passing away, show their impermanence through the discernment of before and after.

1609.

1609.

Tathā ca vipariṇāmaṃ, vipassanto visārado;

Nimittaphalanipphannaṃ, tamatthamadhimuccati.

And similarly, the expert one, seeing change with insight, resolves upon that meaning produced from signs and results.

1610.

1610.

Dukkhappavattihetuttā, nimittamapi paṇḍito;

Bhayāvahaniyāmena, bādhakanteva passati.

Because it is the cause of the occurrence of suffering, the wise one sees even the sign as merely oppressive, by its fearful inevitability.

1611.

1611.

Tathā hi paccayārabbha, saṅkhārā nissayanti ce;

Tatovassaṃ bhavissanti, mahabbhayasamohitā.

Thus indeed, if formations are dependent, arising from conditions, they will surely be accompanied by great fear.

1612.

1612.

Nirodhadhammā jāyanti, sallaviddhāva dukkhitā;

Jarāturā vipajjantā, bhijjantāva vighātino.

Phenomena whose nature is cessation are born, suffering as if pierced by a dart; afflicted by aging, they perish, breaking up like destructive forces.

1613.

1613.

Tenevāniccato diṭṭhā, dukkhabhāvena khāyare;

Saṅkhatattā sabhāvo hi, dukkhāya parivattati.

Therefore, seen as impermanent, they appear as a state of suffering; for their own nature, being conditioned, turns to suffering.

1614.

1614.

Aniccā puna saṅkhārā, dukkhāti ca vavatthitā;

Anattattaniyāmena, nidassenti salakkhaṇaṃ.

Moreover, formations are impermanent and are established as suffering; by the principle of not-self, they reveal their own characteristic.

1615.

1615.

Kathaṃ attaparādhīnā, paccayuppannabhaṅgurā;

Vipattiniyatā vātha, bādhamānā bhayāvahā.

How can they be a self, being dependent on others, arisen from conditions and fragile, or destined for ruin, oppressing and fear-producing?

1616.

1616.

Āhaccākārabhedena, tividhā hi vipassanā;

Aniccā dukkhānattāti, ayamettha vinicchayo.

By the difference in the mode of approach, insight is indeed threefold: impermanence, suffering, and not-self—this is the determination here.

1617.

1617.

Tidhābhūtā paniccetā, pahānākārabheditā;

Mahāvipassanā nāma, aṭṭhārasavidhā kathaṃ.

But these, being threefold and distinguished by the mode of abandoning, how do they become the eighteenfold Great Insight, so-called?

1618.

1618.

Hetusāmagginipphannamaniccanti [V 0.0147] tilakkhaṇaṃ;

Aniccataṃ vipassanto, niccasaññaṃ vimuñcati.

The characteristic of impermanence is to be produced by an aggregation of causes. By seeing impermanence with insight, one abandons the perception of permanence.

1619.

1619.

Aniccatāyādhiṭṭhānanimittaṃ [M 0.0139] pana passato;

Animitte vimuccantī, animittānupassanā.

But for one who sees the sign of the basis of impermanence, the contemplation of the signless liberates in the signless.

1620.

1620.

Nirujjhamānadhammānaṃ, byantibhāvaṃ vipassato;

Samudayaṃ pajahantī, nirodhāanupassanā.

For one who sees with insight the vanishing of phenomena as they cease, the contemplation of cessation abandons arising.

1621.

1621.

Sithilā jātu nissārā, dubbalā lahughātino;

Khayadhammāti saṅkhāya, ghanasaññaṃ vimuñcati.

They are loose, indeed without essence, weak, easily destroyed; having understood that they are subject to decay, one abandons the perception of solidity.

1622.

1622.

Attalābhamatikkamma, vayantīti vicintayaṃ;

Jahatāyūhanaṃ tattha, putte sūtipajā viya.

Having surpassed the acquisition of self, reflecting, 'They pass away,' one there abandons accumulation, like a mother who has given birth her offspring.

1623.

1623.

Anavattitabhāvānaṃ, aññathattaṃ vipassato;

Vikārapariṇāmesu, dhuvasaññā virajjati.

For one who sees the otherness of things that do not recur, in their alterations and transformations, the perception of permanence fades away.

1624.

1624.

Ālambañca tadālamba-ñāṇabhaṅgañca bhāvayaṃ;

Sārādānābhinivesaṃ, adhipaññāya muccati.

Developing both the object and the dissolution of the knowledge concerning that object, one is liberated by higher wisdom from the adherence to grasping at an essence.

1625.

1625.

Iccāniccānimittā ca, nirodhā ca khayā vayā;

Viparīṇāmādhisaññā, dhammānupassanāti ca.

Thus: impermanence, the signless, and cessation, and decay, passing away, the perception of change, and the contemplation of phenomena.

1626.

1626.

Sattānupassanābhedamaniccākāradassanaṃ;

Niccasaññādibhaṅgāya, paridīpenti paṇḍitā.

The wise explain the sevenfold distinction of contemplation, which is the seeing of the aspect of impermanence, for the breaking of the perception of permanence and so on.

1627.

1627.

Taṃ tamākāramārabbha, tathā bāhulyavuttito;

Taṃlakkhaṇānugatā ca, bhedā tasseva sattadhā.

With reference to that very aspect, and likewise due to its frequent mention, its divisions, following that characteristic, are indeed sevenfold.

1628.

1628.

Sukhasaññaṃ nissajjantī, vuttā dukkhānupassanā;

Nibbinnā nibbidāñāṇaṃ, virāgā rāgavajjitā.

Abandoning the perception of happiness, the contemplation of suffering is so called; it is disenchanted, the knowledge of disenchantment, dispassionate, devoid of lust.

1629.

1629.

Jātāppaṇihitā nāma, muñcantī paṇidhiṃ tathā;

Nirālayābhinivesā, ādīnavānupassanā.

By name, it is born as the undirected, thus releasing aspiration; the contemplation of drawbacks is adherence to non-clinging.

1630.

1630.

Pañcānupassanābhedaṃ[V 0.0148], tadidaṃ dukkhadassanaṃ;

Sukhasaññādibhaṅgāya, pavattanti pakāsitaṃ.

This vision of suffering is declared to be the fivefold division of contemplation; they proceed for the breaking of the perception of happiness and so on.

1631.

1631.

Anattato [M 0.0140] vipassanto, attasaññā vimuccati;

Jahatattābhinivesaṃ, jhāyanto puna suññato.

Seeing with insight things as not-self, one is freed from the perception of self; abandoning adherence to self, one meditates moreover on emptiness.

1632.

1632.

Dvayānupassanābhedamanattākāradassanaṃ;

Attasaññābhinivesaṃ, vimokkhāya vibhāvituṃ.

The twofold distinction of contemplation, which is the seeing of the aspect of not-self, is to be cultivated for liberation from the adherence to the perception of self.

1633.

1633.

Paṭinissaggato disvā, saṅkhāresu tilakkhaṇaṃ;

Jahanto saṅkhatādānaṃ, pakkhandati asaṅkhate.

Having seen the three characteristics in formations from the aspect of relinquishment, and abandoning the grasping of the conditioned, one plunges into the unconditioned.

1634.

1634.

Yathābhūtena ñāṇena, vipassanto vimuccati;

Sammohābhinivesamhā, avipallatthadassano.

Seeing with insight by means of knowledge of things as they really are, one is liberated from adherence to delusion, being one who sees without distortion.

1635.

1635.

Mohatābhogavimuttā, paṭisaṅkhānupassanā;

Jahantappaṭisaṅkhaṃ tu, paṭisaṅkhāya lakkhaṇaṃ.

The contemplation by reflection is freed from the expanse of delusion; but abandoning non-reflection, having reflected upon the characteristic, one is liberated.

1636.

1636.

Diṭṭhisaṅkhātadosattā, vibhāvento vivaṭṭato;

Saṃyogābhinivesamhā, paṭilīno vimuccati.

Because of the fault designated as 'views', distinguishing things from the aspect of turning away, being withdrawn, one is freed from adherence to the fetters.

1637.

1637.

Muccītukamyatāñāṇaṃ, paṭinissaggasammataṃ;

Yathā bhūtaṃ tathā ñāṇaṃ, paccayākāranissitaṃ.

The knowledge of the desire for deliverance is regarded as relinquishment; the knowledge of things as they are is based on the mode of conditionality.

1638.

1638.

Saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇaṃ tu, paṭisaṅkhānupassanā;

Vuṭṭhānagāminī nāma, vivaṭṭanti pavuccati.

The knowledge of equanimity towards formations, however, is the contemplation by reflection; by name 'leading to emergence', it is called 'turning away'.

1639.

1639.

Catassopi paniccetā, ādānādippabhañjitā;

Lakkhaṇattayamāhacca, pavattanti yathā tathā.

And indeed these four also, which shatter grasping and so on, having struck upon the three characteristics, proceed accordingly.

1640.

1640.

Nimittamārabbha tathā pavattaṃ,

Tilakkhaṇaṃ jhāyati yāya yogī;

Tamitthamaṭṭhārasabhedabhinnaṃ,

Vipassanābhāvanamāhu dhīrā.

That development of insight, by which the yogi, taking a sign as object, contemplates the three characteristics thus arisen—that which is divided into eighteen kinds—the wise declare it to be so.

1641.

1641.

Vipassanānayamimamuttamaṃ [M 0.0141][V 0.0149] subhaṃ,

Nidassitaṃ jinavacanānusārato;

Vibhāvayaṃ manasi hitāvahaṃ paraṃ,

Nirāmayaṃ padamanupāpuṇissati.

By developing in mind this supreme and auspicious method of insight, which was shown in accordance with the Victor's word and brings supreme benefit, one will attain the unafflicted state.

Iti nāmarūpaparicchede vipassanāvibhāgo nāma

Thus ends the section named 'The Analysis of Insight' in the 'Delineation of Name and Form'.

Ekādasamo paricchedo.

The Eleventh Chapter.

12. Dvādasamo paricchedo

12. The Twelfth Chapter.

Dasāvatthāvibhāgo

The Analysis of the Ten States.

1642.

1642.

Iccaṭṭhārasadhā bhinnā, paṭipakkhappahānato;

Lakkhaṇākārabhedena, tividhāpi ca bhāvanā.

Thus, it is divided in eighteen ways by the abandoning of opposing factors; and by the distinction of characteristic and mode, the development is also threefold.

1643.

1643.

Kalāpato sammasanaṃ, udayabbayadassanaṃ;

Bhaṅge ñāṇaṃ bhaye ñāṇaṃ, ñāṇamādīnavepi ca.

Comprehension by groups, the seeing of arising and passing away, knowledge of dissolution, knowledge of fear, and also knowledge of drawback.

1644.

1644.
