Tatheva nibbidāñāṇaṃ, ñāṇaṃ muccitukamyatā;

Paṭisaṅkhā ca saṅkhāru-pekkhāñāṇānulomakaṃ.

Likewise, knowledge of disenchantment, knowledge of the desire for deliverance, reflection, knowledge of equanimity towards formations, and conformity knowledge.

1645.

1645.

Iccāvatthāpabhedena, dasadhāpi vibhāvitā;

Sabhāgatthavisesena, tidhā saṅgahitā puna.

Thus, they are explained in ten ways according to the division of stages, and again, grouped into three based on the distinction of their common meaning.

1646.

1646.

Yathābhūtaṃ nāma ñāṇattayaṃ sammasanādikaṃ;

Bhayādiñāṇaṃ tividhaṃ, nibbidāti pavuccati.

The threefold knowledge beginning with comprehension is knowledge of things as they are; the threefold knowledge of fear and so on is called disenchantment.

1647.

1647.

Tathā muccitukāmādi, virāgova catubbidhaṃ;

Lakkhaṇattayanijjhānavasena puna vuṭṭhitā.

Likewise, the fourfold knowledge beginning with the desire for deliverance, and dispassion itself, arise again by means of contemplation on the three characteristics.

1648.

1648.

Suññatañcānimittañca[V 0.0150], tathāppaṇihitanti ca;

Sādheti maggasaṅkhātaṃ, vimokkhattayamuttamaṃ.

That which is called the path, through emptiness, signlessness, and likewise desirelessness, accomplishes the supreme triad of liberations.

1649.

1649.

Iti bhāvetukāmassa, vibhāveti yathākkamaṃ;

Dasāvatthāvibhāgena, samādāya yathā kathaṃ.

Thus, for one who wishes to develop this, it is explained in sequence, by means of a division into ten stages, how to undertake it appropriately.

1650.

1650.

Visuddho [M 0.0142] paṭhamaṃ tāva, sādhu sīlavisuddhiyā;

Upacārappanāyañca, ṭhatvā cittavisuddhiyaṃ.

First, one is properly purified by the purification of morality; and having been established in the purification of mind through access and absorption,

1651.

1651.

Sappaccayaṃ pariggayha, nāmarūpaṃ sabhāvato;

Diṭṭhikaṅkhāvitaraṇaṃ, patvā suddhiṃ tato paraṃ.

Having comprehended name-and-form with its conditions according to its intrinsic nature, and having attained the purity that is the overcoming of wrong view and doubt, one then attains further purity.

1652.

1652.

Atītānāgate khandhe, paccuppanne ca sāsave;

Kalāpato sammasitvā, sammaseyya tilakkhaṇaṃ.

Having comprehended by way of groups the past, future, and present aggregates with their taints, one should then contemplate the three characteristics.

1653.

1653.

Ādānanikkhepanato,

Vayovuddhatthagāmito;

Āhāratopi ututo,

Kammato cāpi cittato.

From taking up and putting down, from the process of decay and growth, from nutriment and from climate, from kamma and also from mind.

1654.

1654.

Dhammatārūpato cāpi, rūpasattakato naye;

Kalāpato yamakato, khaṇikā paṭipāṭito.

And also from the natural state of things, from the sevenfold method regarding form, from groups, from pairs, and from the sequence of moments.

1655.

1655.

Diṭṭhimugghāṭayanto ca, mānamugghāṭayaṃ tathā;

Nikantipariyādāno, nāmasattakato naye.

Uprooting view, and likewise uprooting conceit, thoroughly consuming craving, one should be skilled in the sevenfold method regarding name.

1656.

1656.

Niccā ce na nirujjheyyuṃ, na bādheyyuṃ sukhā yadi;

Vase vatteyyumattā ce, tadabhāvā na tādisā.

If they were permanent, they would not cease; if pleasant, they would not be painful; if self, they would be under one's control. Due to the absence of these, they are not so.

1657.

1657.

Sambhavanti hi saṅkhārā, sati paccayasambhave;

Tato paccayanipphannā, avassaṃ bhedagāmino.

For formations arise when there is an arising of conditions; therefore, being produced by conditions, they inevitably proceed to dissolution.

1658.

1658.

Tadaniccā khayaṭṭhena, dukkhā nāma bhayaṭṭhato;

Anattāsārakaṭṭhena, saṅkhārāti vibhāvayaṃ.

Thus one should discern formations: as impermanent in the sense of destruction, as suffering in the sense of being fearful, and as not-self in the sense of being without essence.

1659.

1659.

Kālena [V 0.0151] sammase rūpaṃ, nāmaṃ kālena sammase;

Ajjhattañca bahiddhā ca, samāsabyāsato tato.

At times one should comprehend form, at times one should comprehend name; then, both internally and externally, by way of summary and detail.

1660.

1660.

Yathopaṭṭhitabhedena, sammasanto samūhato;

Kalāpato sammasanamiti bhāveti paṇḍito.

Contemplating according to the distinctions as they appear, and as a whole—thus the wise one develops comprehension by way of groups.

1661.

1661.

Tassevaṃ sammasantassa, kammaññaṃ hoti mānasaṃ;

Sūpaṭṭhanti ca saṅkhārā, vodāyati ca bhāvanā.

For one contemplating thus, the mind becomes pliable, formations appear clearly, and the development becomes bright.

1662.

1662.

Tato [M 0.0143] paraṃ vipassanto, pariggaṇhāti paṇḍito;

Paccuppannasabhāvānaṃ, khandhānamudayabbayaṃ.

Then, the wise one, observing further, comprehends the arising and passing away of the presently existing aggregates.

1663.

1663.

Taṇhāsammohakammehi,

Khandhapañcakasabhāvo;

Rūpamāhārato hoti,

Phassato vedanādayo.

From craving, delusion, and kamma is the nature of the five aggregates; form is from nutriment, and feeling and so on are from contact.

1664.

1664.

Viññāṇaṃ nāmarūpamhā, sambhotīti ca passato;

Tassa paccayato hoti, khandhesudayadassanaṃ.

For one who sees that consciousness arises from name-and-form, the vision of the arising of the aggregates occurs through seeing their conditionality.

1665.

1665.

Taṇhādīnaṃ nirodhā ca,

Nirodho hoti passato;

Tathā vīsatidhā hoti,

Tattheva vayadassanaṃ.

And for one who sees that from the cessation of craving and so on, cessation occurs, likewise the vision of dissolution occurs right there in twenty ways.

1666.

1666.

Nibbattivipariṇāmalakkhaṇaṃ pana passato;

Khaṇato dasadhā nesamudayabbayadassanaṃ.

Now, for one who sees the characteristic of production and change, the vision of their arising and passing away occurs tenfold, moment by moment.

1667.

1667.

Itthaṃ paññāsadhā bhedo,

Khandhānamudayabbayo;

Āyatanādibhedopi,

Yojetabbo yathārahaṃ.

Thus, the arising and passing away of the aggregates is divided in fifty ways; the division of the sense bases and so on should also be applied appropriately.

1668.

1668.

Tadevamanupassanto[V 0.0152], khandhāyatanadhātuyo;

Aniccā dukkhānattāti, bhāveti bahudhā budho.

Thus contemplating the aggregates, sense-bases, and elements, the wise one develops them in many ways as impermanent, suffering, and not-self.

1669.

1669.

Bhāvanāpasutassevaṃ, passato bodhipakkhiyā;

Pātubhūtā pavattanti, visesena visāradā.

For one devoted to development, seeing thus, the factors of enlightenment, having become manifest, proceed with distinction and clarity.

1670.

1670.

Salakkhaṇaparicchinne, tilakkhaṇavavatthite;

Chando sāsavasaṅkhāre, sāradaṃ pariyesati.

When their own characteristics are defined and the three characteristics are determined, desire seeks for an essence in formations connected with taints.

1671.

1671.

Tattha [M 0.0144] pubbaṅgamaṃ hutvā, saṃpakkhandati mānasaṃ;

Saṅkappobhiniropeti, āharanto punappunaṃ.

There, the mind, acting as the forerunner, plunges in; intention, bringing it forth again and again, implants it.

1672.

1672.

Yathāvatthusabhāvena, tato saddhādhimuccati;

Sati sūpaṭṭhitā hoti, pariggayha sabhāvato.

Then, in accordance with the intrinsic nature of the object, faith becomes resolute; mindfulness becomes well-established, having comprehended that intrinsic nature.

1673.

1673.

Paññā sampaṭivijjhantī, samāhacca vipassati;

Paggahetvāna vāyāmo, paṭipādeti bhāvanaṃ.

Wisdom, penetrating and focusing, sees with insight; energy, having been exerted, accomplishes the development.

1674.

1674.

Tato pītimano hoti, nipphāditamanoratho;

Pāmojjabahulo hutvā, passaddhadaratho pana.

Then one becomes joyful in mind, with one's wish fulfilled; having become abundant in delight, one's anxiety is then calmed.

1675.

1675.

Vikkhepuddhaccanittiṇṇo, samādhiyati niccalo;

Upekkhā bhāvanāvīthiṃ, adhiṭṭhāti tato paraṃ.

Having crossed beyond distraction and restlessness, one becomes concentrated and unmoving; thereafter, one establishes equanimity upon the path of development.

1676.

1676.

Āruḷhayoggācariyo, ājānīyaratho viya;

Vātābhāve padīpova, pasannekamukhaṭṭhitā.

Like a practitioner mounted upon the vehicle of his practice, like a chariot of thoroughbreds, like a lamp in a windless place, it stands serene and one-pointed.

1677.

1677.

Sukhumā nipuṇākārā, khuradhārāgatā viya;

Gaṇhantī bhāvanāgabbhaṃ, pavaḍḍhati vipassanā.

Subtle and skillful in nature, like treading on a razor's edge, insight takes hold of the womb of development and grows.

1678.

1678.

Sampattapaṭivedhassa,

Tassevaṃ taṃ vipassato;

Jāyateko upakleso,

Dasopaklesavatthukā.

For one who has attained penetration, while thus contemplating it, a corruption arises, founded on the ten bases of corruption.

1679.

1679.

Obhāso [V 0.0153] pīti passaddhi, adhimokkho ca paggaho;

Sukhaṃ ñāṇamupaṭṭhānamupekkhā ca nikanti ca.

Illumination, rapture, tranquility, resolution, and exertion; happiness, knowledge, mindfulness, equanimity, and craving.

1680.

1680.

Jātesvetesu yaṃ kiñci, uḷāraṃ jātavimhayo;

Disvā vipassanāmaggā, vokkamitvā tato paraṃ.

When any of these lofty things arise, one becomes astonished; having seen them, one thereafter deviates from the path of insight.

1681.

1681.

Tamahaṃkāravikkhitto, assādento mamāyati;

Hotādhimāniko vātha, maññanto tamanuttaraṃ.

Distracted by that I-making, savoring it, one regards it as 'mine'; or one becomes conceited, considering it to be supreme.

1682.

1682.

Siyā [M 0.0145] cevamupakliṭṭhā, patitā vātha bhāvanā;

Tatthevaṃ paṭisaṅkhāya, paṭivijjhati paṇḍito.

If the development is thus corrupted, or has fallen away, the wise person, reflecting upon it thus, penetrates it.

1683.

1683.

Na taṇhādiṭṭhimānehi, pariyogāhahetuto;

Lakkhaṇālambaṇattā ca, lokiyāyaṃ vipassanā.

Because it is overwhelmed by craving, views, and conceit, and because it has characteristics as its object, this insight is mundane.

1684.

1684.

Diṭṭhimānanikantī ca, kummaggā paripanthakā;

Maggo visuddhiyā nāma, visuddhā ca vipassanā.

Views, conceit, and craving are wrong paths and obstacles; the path is for the sake of purity, and insight is to be purified.

1685.

1685.

Sārathīva rathaṃ bhantamiti saṅkhāya sādhukaṃ;

Paviṭṭhamaggaṃ vikkhittaṃ, sampādeti yathā pure.

Just as a charioteer restores a straying chariot, so too, discerning this well, one restores the distracted mind that has entered a wrong path to the course as before.

1686.

1686.

Itthaṃ magge amagge ca, yāthāvapaṭivedhakaṃ;

Maggāmaggavisuddhīti, ñāṇadassanamīritaṃ.

Thus, the knowledge and vision that penetrates the path and the not-path as they really are is called the Purity of Knowledge and Vision of Path and Not-Path.

1687.

1687.

Cetopavattanākāramiti sallakkhayaṃ budho;

Sādhukaṃ paṭivijjhanto, sukhumaṃ nipuṇaṃ tato.

The wise one, thus discerning well the mode of the mind's occurrence, then thoroughly penetrates its subtle and skillful nature.

1688.

1688.

Paripanthe vimocetvā, bodhetvā bodhipakkhiye;

Bhāvanaṃ paṭipādento, punadevodayabbayaṃ.

Having freed oneself from the obstacles and having awakened the factors of enlightenment, one undertakes the development, contemplating rise and fall once again.

1689.

1689.

Samadhiṭṭhāya medhāvī, vipassati tilakkhaṇaṃ;

Udayabbayañāṇanti, tamīrenti tato paraṃ.

The wise one, established in concentration, sees with insight the three characteristics; thereafter, this is called the knowledge of rise and fall.

1690.

1690.

Saṅkhārānaṃ vibhūtattā, sākārānaṃ visesato;

Tilakkhaṇānaṃ diṭṭhattā, saṅkhāresu sabhāvato.

Because the formations, especially those with specific characteristics, are clearly manifest, and because the three characteristics are seen in the formations according to their intrinsic nature.

1691.

1691.

Paripanthā [V 0.0154] vimuttassa, maggāmaggavisuddhiyā;

Yathāvīthippavattassa, paṭipattivisuddhiyā.

For one who is freed from obstacles through the purity of knowledge and vision of path and not-path, and who proceeds along the proper course through the purity of the way of practice:

1692.

1692.

Indriyānaṃ sutikkhattā, paripakkā vipassanā;

Udayamhā vimuccitvā, bhaṅge ṭhāti yathā kathaṃ.

With faculties very sharp and insight mature, having been freed from arising, one stands, as it were, in dissolution.

1693.

1693.

Uppādo paccayāyatto, dhammānamiti nicchite;

Nirodhānugatā jāti, siddhāvassaṃ niyāmato.

When it is determined that the arising of phenomena is dependent on conditions, it is established as an invariable rule that birth is followed by cessation.

1694.

1694.

Tatodayāva paṭṭhāya, atthāya sūriyo viya;

Vināsāya pavattantā, vayantevāti pekkhati.

Beginning from their very arising, one sees that they proceed toward destruction and vanish, just as the sun rises only to set.

1695.

1695.

Udayābhogamohāya[M 0.0146], vayanticceva sabbathā;

Bhedassabhāvamārabbha, dhammesu sati tiṭṭhati.

Leaving behind the delusion of attending to arising, one sees that they vanish in every way; taking the intrinsic nature of dissolution as the object, mindfulness is established in phenomena.

1696.

1696.

Atītā ca niruddhāva, nirujjhissantināgatā;

Nirujjhanteva vattantā, iccevamanupassato.

Past phenomena have ceased, future phenomena will cease, and present phenomena are ceasing—thus one contemplates.

1697.

1697.

Nijjharova giraggamhi, vārivoṇatapokkhare;

Padīpo viya jhāyanto, āraggeriva sāsapo.

Like a waterfall from a mountain peak, like water from a tilted lotus leaf, like a lamp being consumed, like a mustard seed on the point of an awl,

1698.

1698.

Ātape viya ussāvo, parissāve jalaṃ viya;

Madditaṃ pheṇapiṇḍaṃva, loṇapiṇḍamivodake.

like dew in the sunshine, like water through a strainer, like a crushed ball of foam, like a lump of salt in water,

1699.

1699.

Udake daṇḍarājīva, vijjutāva valāhake;

Jalaṃ tattakapāleva, salile viya bubbuḷaṃ.

like a line drawn with a stick on water, like lightning in a cloud, like water on a hot pan, like a bubble in water,

1700.

1700.

Vātabbhāhatatūlaṃva, tīraṃ pattāva vīciyo;

Phalaṃ bandhanamuttaṃva, tiṇānīva hutāvahe.

like cotton struck by the wind, like waves that have reached the shore, like fruit freed from its stalk, like grass in a fire.

1701.

1701.

Jāyantāpi ca jiyyantā, miyyantā ca nirantaraṃ;

Nirodhāyābhidhāvantā, bhaṅgābhimukhapātino.

Being born, aging, and dying without interruption, they rush toward cessation, falling headlong toward dissolution.

1702.

1702.

Vigacchantāva dissanti, khīyantantaradhāyino;

Viddhaṃsayantā saṅkhārā, patantā ca vināsino.

The formations are seen as departing, wasting away, and disappearing; they are shattering, falling, and perishing.

1703.

1703.

Bhaṅgañāṇaṃ [V 0.0155] tamakkhātaṃ, yena ñāṇena passato;

Aniccantānudhāvanti, tividhāpi vipassanā.

That is called the knowledge of dissolution. For one who sees with this knowledge, the threefold insight pursues impermanence.

1704.

1704.

Udayabbayabhaṅgesu, pākaṭā hi aniccatā;

Bhayādīnavanibbede, dukkhatānattatā tato.

In arising, passing away, and dissolution, impermanence is manifest; from that, in fear, danger, and disenchantment, suffering and not-self become manifest.

1705.

1705.

Itthaṃ bhaṅgamadhiṭṭhāya, passantassa tilakkhaṇaṃ;

Saṅkhārā sabhayā hutvā, samupaṭṭhanti yogino.

Thus, for the yogi who is established in dissolution and sees the three characteristics, the formations appear as fearful.

1706.

1706.

Vāḷamigānubaddhāva, nimmujjantā viyaṇṇave;

Amanussagahitāva, parikkhittāva verihi.

Like one pursued by beasts of prey, like one sinking in the ocean, like one seized by non-human beings, like one surrounded by enemies,

1707.

1707.

Kaṇhasappasamālīḷhā[M 0.0147], caṇḍahatthisamuṭṭhitā;

Papātāvāṭapakkhantā, patantāva hutāvahe.

like one embraced by a black serpent, like one confronted by a fierce elephant, like one who has fallen into a pit at a precipice, like one falling into a fire,

1708.

1708.

Vajjhappattā mahācorā, chijjantā viya sīsato;

Sūlamāropiyantāva, pabbatenotthaṭā viya.

like great thieves condemned to death, like one whose head is being cut off, like one being impaled on a stake, like one being crushed by a mountain,

1709.

1709.

Jātisaṅkaṭapakkhantā, jarābyādhinipīḷitā;

Maraṇāsanisammaddā, mahābyasanabhāgino.

Having entered the peril of birth, oppressed by aging and sickness, crushed by the thunderbolt of death, they are partakers in great disaster.

1710.

1710.

Maccunabbhāhatā niccaṃ, dukkhabhārasamotthaṭā;

Sokopāyāsanissandā, paridevaparāyaṇā.

Always struck by death, overwhelmed by the burden of suffering, they are an outflow of sorrow and despair, given over to lamentation.

1711.

1711.

Taṇhādiṭṭhimamattena, sattā etthādhimucchitā;

Baddhā bhayena baddhāva, muttāva bhayamuttakā.

Deluded by craving, views, and the sense of 'mine', beings here are deeply infatuated; bound by fear like captives, while those freed are freed from fear.

1712.

1712.

Iti saṅkhāradhammesu, bhayuppattimudikkhato;

Bhayañāṇanti bhāsanti, bhayamuttā mahesayo.

Thus, contemplating the arising of fear in conditioned phenomena, the great sages, freed from fear, declare it to be the knowledge of fear.

1713.

1713.

Sabhayā puna saṅkhārā, sandissanti samantato;

Ahitāvahitāniccamādīnavaṃ nirantaraṃ.

Moreover, formations are fearful, appearing all around as a perpetual and constant harm, disadvantage, and danger.

1714.

1714.

Gūthakūpaṃva kuthitaṃ, bhasmacchannova pāvako;

Sarakkhasaṃva salilaṃ, savisaṃ viya bhojanaṃ.

Like a festering cesspool, like fire covered with ashes; like water haunted by ogres, like food mixed with poison.

1715.

1715.

Vanaṃ [V 0.0156] vāḷamigākiṇṇaṃ, maggo coramahabbhayo;

Bhijjamānā mahānāvā, phalantā asanī yathā.

Like a forest teeming with wild beasts, a path beset by great danger from thieves; like a great ship breaking apart, like lightning striking.

1716.

1716.

Āvudhākulasannaddhā, yuddhabhūmipatiṭṭhitā;

Saṅgatāva mahāsenā, ghorānatthaniyāmitā.

Armed and fully equipped, stationed on the battlefield; like a vast army assembled, destined for terrible ruin.

1717.

1717.

Rathaṃ cakkasamāruḷhaṃ, vuyhantaṃ vaḷavāmukhaṃ;

Kappuṭṭhānamahārambhaṃ, kappo pattantaro yathā.

Like a chariot, mounted on wheels, being swept away by the mare's mouth; like the great upheaval at the beginning of an eon, like an eon fallen into ruin.

1718.

1718.

Tathā [M 0.0148] lokā tayopete,

Mahopaddavasaṅkulā;

Ḍayhantekādasaggīhi,

Paripphandaparāyaṇā.

So too are these three worlds, beset by great calamities; they are burning with the eleven fires, intent on convulsive writhing.

1719.

1719.

Mahāraññamivādittaṃ, bhavayonigatiṭṭhiti-

Sattāvāsā samībhūtā, jalitaṅgārakāsukā.

Like a great forest ablaze, the wombs of becoming, destinations, and states of existence—the dwellings of beings—are reduced to ashes, like a pit of burning coals.

1720.

1720.

Āsīvisā mahābhūtā, vadhakā khandhapañcakā;

Cakkhādayo suññā gāmā, gocarā gāmaghātakā.

Like venomous snakes are the great elements, and killers are the five aggregates; the sense bases are empty villages, their domains village-destroyers.

1721.

1721.

Iccānayasamākiṇṇaṃ, bhavasāgaramaṇḍalaṃ;

Leṇaṃ tāṇaṃ patiṭṭhā vā, saraṇaṃ vā na vijjati.

Thus, this sphere of the ocean of becoming is crowded with dangers; no shelter, protection, foundation, or refuge is found.

1722.

1722.

Etthābhirodhino bālā, vaṅkaghastāva mīnakā;

Mahāsakaṭupabbuḷhā, mahabbhayapatiṭṭhitā.

Fools delight here, like fish caught in a weir; oppressed by great burdens, they are established in great fear.

1723.

1723.

Jāyamānāva jiyyantā, nānābyasanapīḷitā;

Vipattāvaṭṭapatitā, maraṇābaddhanicchayā.

Born only to decay, afflicted by various troubles; fallen into misfortune's whirlpool, destined for certain death.

1724.

1724.

Mohandhakārapihitā, caturoghasamotthaṭā;

Vitunnā dukkhasallena, vihaññanti vighātino.

Shrouded in the darkness of delusion, swept away by the four floods; pierced by the dart of suffering, the destructive ones are afflicted.

1725.

1725.

Itthañca visapupphaṃva, nānānatthaphalāvahaṃ;

Dukkhānubandhasambādhaṃ, ābādhaṃva samuṭṭhitaṃ.

Thus, like a poisonous flower, bearing fruits of diverse harm; oppressed by suffering's consequence, like a disease arisen.

1726.

1726.

Āsīvisaṃva [V 0.0157] kupitaṃ, ghoraṃ bhayanibandhanaṃ;

Asisūnaṃva sārambhaṃ, dukkhāyūhanakaṃ padaṃ.

Like an angry viper, fearsome, the source of danger; like the violence of a sword-blade, a state that heaps up suffering.

1727.

1727.

Savidāhaparipphandapakkabandhamivodakaṃ;

Uppādañca pavattañca, nimittāyūhanaṃ tathā.

Like water boiling, churning, and bound in a bubble; so too are arising, continuation, signs, and accumulation.

1728.

1728.

Paṭisandhiñca passantaṃ, ñāṇamādīnavaṃ mataṃ;

Tebhūmakesu tenāyamavuddhiṃ paṭivijjhati.

For one who sees rebirth, that knowledge is considered the knowledge of danger; by this, one penetrates non-growth in the three realms.

1729.

1729.

Bhayabheravapakkhante, bahvādīnavapaccaye;

Saṅkhāre samavekkhanto, nibbindati nirālayo.

In the face of fear and dread, amidst conditions for many dangers, observing formations, one becomes disenchanted, without longing.

1730.

1730.

Visaṃ [M 0.0149] jīvitukāmova, verike viya bhīruko;

Supaṇṇaṃ nāgarājāva, coraṃ viya mahaddhano.

Like one desiring to live avoids poison, like a timid man avoids an enemy, like a serpent king avoids a garuḍa, like a wealthy man avoids a thief.

1731.

1731.

Dukkhānusayasambādhe, bādhamāne vibhāvayaṃ;

Saṃvejeti nirānande, paripanthabhayākule.

Discerning the oppressive affliction from the latent tendencies of suffering, one feels spiritual urgency towards that which is joyless, perilous, and filled with fear.

1732.

1732.

Suddho muttakarīsaṃva, suhito vamitaṃ viya;

Suvilittova duggandhaṃ, sunhāto aṅgaṇaṃ viya.

Like a clean person (is disgusted by) urine and feces, like a well-fed person (is disgusted by) vomit, like one well-anointed (is disgusted by) a foul smell, like one well-bathed (is disgusted by) dirt.

1733.

1733.

Rāgadosaparikliṭṭhe, caturāsavapūtike;

Hīnalokāmisāsāre, saṃklesavisadūsite.

Stained by lust and hatred, foul with the four taints, low, essenceless, worldly gain, polluted by the poison of defilements.

1734.

1734.

Saṅkhārepi jigucchanto, nābhinandati paṇḍito;

Tassetaṃ nandinissaṭṭhaṃ, nibbidāñāṇamabravuṃ.

Disgusted even by formations, the wise one does not delight. This abandoning of delight, they call the knowledge of disenchantment.

1735.

1735.

Sabhayādīnave disvā, saṅkhāre puna paṇḍito;

Nibbindanto tato tehi, parimuccitumicchati.

Having seen fear and danger in formations, the wise person, moreover, growing disenchanted with them, wishes to be completely released.

1736.

1736.

Mīnāva kumīne baddhā, pañjare viya pakkhino;

Coro cārakabaddhova, peḷāyantova pannago.

Like fish bound in a fish-trap, like birds in a cage, like a thief bound in prison, like a snake inside a basket.

1737.

1737.

Paṅke sanno mahānāgo, cando rāhumukhaṃ gato;

Migo yathā pāsagato, tathā saṃsāracārake.

Like a great elephant sunk in the mud, like the moon gone into Rāhu's mouth, like a deer caught in a snare—so it is in the prison of saṃsāra.

1738.

1738.

Avijjāpariyonaddhe[V 0.0158], khandhapañcakasanthare;

Diṭṭhijālapaṭicchanne, vipallāsaparikkhite.

Enveloped by ignorance, on the bed of the five aggregates, concealed by the net of views, confined by distortions.

1739.

1739.

Pañcanīvaraṇābaddhe, mānatthambhasamussaye;

Icchāpapātagambhīre, vipattivinipātane.

Bound by the five hindrances, raised on the pillar of conceit, in the deep chasm of craving, in the downfall of misfortune and ruin.

1740.

1740.

Jarābyādhisamuppāde, dhūmaketupapattike;

Kodhūpanāhadahane, sokopāyāsadhūpite.

In the arising of aging and sickness, in the appearance of a comet, in the burning of anger and resentment, fumigated by sorrow and despair.

1741.

1741.

Madappamādāvarodhe, bhavataṇhāvakaḍḍhane;

Vippayogasamuttāse, niccāpāyabhayākule.

Obstructed by intoxication and heedlessness, dragged down by craving for becoming, terrified by separation, agitated by constant fear of the lower realms.

1742.

1742.

Chālambābhihate [M 0.0150] niccaṃ, phassadvārādhikuṭṭane;

Sañcetanākāraṇike, vedanākammakāraṇe.

Constantly struck by the six sense-objects, battered at the door of contact, caused by volition, with feeling as a cause for kamma.

1743.

1743.

Anatthālāpanigghose, klesarakkhasalālite;

Maraṇārambhaniṭṭhāne, baddho muttiṃ gavesati.

In the clamor of useless talk, indulged by the ogres of defilement, culminating in the onset of death, one who is bound seeks liberation.

1744.

1744.

Aggiṃ viya ca samphuṭṭha-masuciṃ gahitaṃ viya;

Petaṃ khāditukāmaṃva, vikkantentamivāvudhaṃ.

Like one who has touched fire, like one who has grasped filth, like a hungry ghost wanting to devour, like one advancing with a weapon.

1745.

1745.

Mahābyasanupassaṭṭhe, saṅkhāre mottumicchato;

Muccitukamyatāñāṇamuppannanti pavuccati.

When afflicted by great disaster, for one wishing to be freed from formations, the knowledge of the desire for release is said to arise.

1746.

1746.

Dujjahe palibajjhante, ganthānusayasaṅgame;

Taṇhupādānagahaṇe, nandirāgānubandhane.

Hard to abandon, tenaciously clinging, in the confluence of bonds and latent tendencies, in the grip of craving and clinging, bound by delight and passion.

1747.

1747.

Diṭṭhimānamadatthaddhe, lobhapāsanirantare;

Saṃyojanamahādugge, cirakālappapañcite.

Stiff with views, conceit, and intoxication, constantly in the snare of greed, in the great fortress of the fetters, long proliferated.

1748.

1748.

Saṅkhāre muñcataccantaṃ, āvijjhitvāva pannagaṃ;

Lakkhaṇānupanijjhāya, sukhumaṃ pana yoniso.

One completely releases formations—like having pierced a snake—by contemplating their characteristics subtly and with wise attention.

1749.

1749.

Majjhattagahaṇo tasmā, nirapekkhavimuttiyā;

Vaggulīvāphalaṃ rukkhaṃ, vīmaṃsati visesato.

Therefore, for the sake of liberation without attachment, one grasps equanimity and examines it thoroughly, like a bat examining the fruit on a tree.

1750.

1750.

Vihataṃ [V 0.0159] viya kappāsaṃ, vihananto punappunaṃ;

Gandhaṃ viya ca pisento, pisitaṃyeva sādhukaṃ.

Beating them again and again, like beating cotton; and grinding them well, like grinding perfume.

1751.

1751.

Aniccā dukkhānattāti, satimā susamāhito;

Āhacca paṭivijjhanto, lakkhaṇāni vipassati.

Mindful and well-concentrated, penetrating them directly, one sees with insight the characteristics as impermanent, suffering, and non-self.

1752.

1752.

Vipassantassa tassevaṃ, paṭisaṅkhānupassanā-

Ñāṇamiccāhu nipuṇaṃ, vicinantaṃ visāradā.

For one who thus sees with insight, the experts declare that the discerning knowledge of reflective contemplation is subtle.

1753.

1753.

Iti sammā vipassanto, sacchikatvā tilakkhaṇaṃ;

Yathābhūtasabhāvena, tatthevamanupassati.

Thus, seeing with insight rightly and having realized the three characteristics, one contemplates them right there in accordance with their real nature.

1754.

1754.

Aniccā [M 0.0151] vata saṅkhārā, niccāti gahitā pure;

Dukkhāva sukhato diṭṭhā, anattāva panattato.

Alas, formations are impermanent, though formerly they were grasped as permanent; they are indeed suffering, though seen as happiness; and they are indeed non-self, though seen as self.

1755.

1755.

Aniccā dukkhānattā ca, saṅkhatā puna sabbathā;

Alabbhaneyyadhammā ca, tathevākāmakāriyā.

Moreover, in every way, conditioned things are impermanent, suffering, and non-self; they have a nature that cannot be obtained, and likewise they act against one's will.

1756.

1756.

Dhātumattā parādhīnā, attādheyyavivajjitā;

Maccudheyyavasānītā, upadhihatagocarā.

They are mere elements, dependent on others, devoid of self-governance; they are brought under the sway of death's domain, their resort afflicted by the substrates of existence.

1757.

1757.

Ahaṃ mamanti vohāro, paro vātha parassa vā;

Attā vā attanīyaṃ vā, vatthuto natthi katthaci.

The designations “I” and “mine,” or “another” and “another's,” or “a self” and “what belongs to a self”—in reality, these exist nowhere.

1758.

1758.

Yathāpi aṅgasambhārā, hoti saddo ratho iti;

Evaṃ khandhesu santesu, hoti sattoti sammuti.

Just as from a collection of parts the term “chariot” comes to be, so too, when the aggregates are present, there is the convention “a being.”

1759.

1759.

Tattha kappenti attānaṃ, bālā dummedhino janā;

Ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā, passato natthi kiñcanaṃ.

Therein foolish, witless people fashion a self, either internally or externally. But for one who sees, there is no impediment whatsoever.

1760.

1760.

Sukhito dukkhito vātha, puggalo nāma katthaci;

Vatthuto natthi sabbattha, saṅkhārā taṃsabhāvino.

In reality, a person by name, whether happy or suffering, exists nowhere at all; there are only formations, which have that nature.

1761.

1761.

Jāyamānā ca jiyyantā, miyyamānā ca saṅkhatā;

Attāva dukkhitā hete, na tu dukkhāya kassaci.

Being born, decaying, and dying—such are conditioned things. Indeed, these are themselves afflicted with suffering, but the suffering belongs to no one.

1762.

1762.

Dukkhameva [V 0.0160] hi sambhoti, dukkhaṃ tiṭṭhati veti ca;

Nāññatra dukkhā sambhoti, nāññaṃ dukkhā nirujjhati.

Suffering alone arises, suffering persists and passes away. Nothing other than suffering arises, nothing other than suffering ceases.

1763.

1763.

Ettha gayhūpagaṃ natthi, palāsetaṃ papañcitaṃ;

Niruddhassa samāyūhā, niratthakasamubbhavā.

Here there is nothing to be grasped; this is malice and mental proliferation. The accumulations of what has ceased arise without purpose.

1764.

1764.

Aniccā hontu saṅkhārā, dukkhitā vā mamettha kiṃ;

Anattā vāti? Saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇaṃ pavattati.

‘Let formations be impermanent, or afflicted with suffering, or non-self—what is that to me?’ Thus proceeds the knowledge of equanimity towards formations.

1765.

1765.

Iti disvā yathābhūtaṃ, yāva bhaṅgā tato paraṃ;

Gaṇhantī bhāvanāgabbhaṃ, paripakkā vipassanā.

Thus having seen as it really is, up to their dissolution and beyond, fully ripened insight conceives the embryo of development.

1766.

1766.

Avassaṃ bhaṅganiṭṭhāne, bhayādīnavanicchite;

Nibbinditvā virajjanto, paṭisaṅkhāyupekkhati.

Since their final state is inevitably dissolution, and having ascertained the danger and peril, one becomes disenchanted, grows dispassionate, and reflects with equanimity.

1767.

1767.

Tattha [M 0.0152] muttakarīsaṃva, kheḷapiṇḍaṃva ujjhitaṃ;

Vissaṭṭhaparaputtaṃva, vissaṭṭhabhariyaṃ viya.

Like discharged excrement, like a thrown-away lump of phlegm, like another’s abandoned son, like a repudiated wife.

1768.

1768.

Pavattañca nimittañca, paṭisaṅkhāyupekkhato;

Sabbasaṅkhāradhammesu, gatiyonibhavesu vā.

Thus one reflects with equanimity on the process and its sign in all formations, or in destinies, origins, and states of existence.

1769.

1769.

Vāri pokkharapatteva, sūcikaggeva sāsapo;

Khittaṃ kukkuṭapattaṃva, daddulaṃva hutāvahe.

Like water on a lotus leaf, like a mustard seed on a needle's point, like a thrown chicken feather, like tinder in a fire.

1770.

1770.

Na pasārīyatī cittaṃ, na tu sajjati bajjhati;

Ālayā patilīyanti, parivattati vaṭṭato.

The mind does not spread outwards, nor does it cling or become bound; attachments recede, and one turns away from the round of existence.

1771.

1771.

Sītaṃ ghammābhitattova,

Chātajjhattova bhojanaṃ;

Pipāsitova pānīyaṃ,

Byādhitova mahosadhaṃ.

As one scorched by heat longs for coolness, as one afflicted by hunger for food, as one who is thirsty for water, and as one who is sick for a great medicine.

1772.

1772.

Bhīto khemantabhūmiṃva, duggatova mahānidhiṃ;

Añjasaṃ maggamuḷhova, dīpaṃ viya ca aṇṇave.

As a frightened person seeks a land of safety, as a destitute person a great treasure, as one who has lost the way the straight path, and as one at sea an island in the ocean.

1773.

1773.

Ajarāmaramaccantaṃ[V 0.0161], asaṅkhāramanāsavaṃ;

Sabbadukkhakkhayaṃ ṭhānaṃ, nibbānamabhikaṅkhati.

He longs for Nibbāna—the ageless, deathless, and ultimate state, the unconditioned and taintless, the destruction of all suffering.

1774.

1774.

Vuṭṭhānagāminī cāyaṃ, sikhappattā vipassanā;

Sakuṇī tīradassīva, sānulomā pavattati.

This insight, which leads to emergence and has reached its peak, proceeds in conformity, like a shore-seeing bird.

1775.

1775.

Appavattamanimittaṃ, passanto pana santato;

Pakkhīva nipphalaṃ rukkhaṃ, hitvā vuṭṭhāti saṅkhatā.

Continuously seeing the signless, the state of non-occurrence, he emerges from the conditioned, like a bird abandoning a fruitless tree.

1776.

1776.

Upacārasamādhīti, kāmāvacarabhāvanā;

Muttoyaṃ lokiyo maggo, pubbabhāgavipassanā.

Development in the sense sphere is access concentration; this mundane path is preliminary insight.

1777.

1777.

Paripakkā kamenevaṃ, paribhāvitabhāvanā;

Pariccajantī saṅkhāre, pakkhandantī asaṅkhate.

Thus gradually ripened by well-developed cultivation, she abandons formations, leaping into the unconditioned.

1778.

1778.

Janetānuttaraṃ [M 0.0153] magga-māsevanavisesato;

Kaṭṭhasaṅghaṭṭanā jātā, accidhūmāva bhāsuraṃ.

Through excellence in cultivation, it generates the unsurpassed path, like a bright flame and smoke are generated from the rubbing of sticks.

1779.

1779.

Uggacchati yathādicco, purakkhatvāruṇaṃ tathā;

Vipassanaṃ purakkhatvā, maggadhammo pavattati.

Just as the sun rises, preceded by the dawn, so the Dhamma of the path proceeds, preceded by insight.

1780.

1780.

Tathā pavattamāno ca, nibbānapadagocaro;

Vimokkhattayanāmena, yathārahamasesato.

Thus it proceeds, with the state of Nibbāna as its resort, suitably and completely, by the name of the three liberations.

1781.

1781.

Klesadūsitasantāne, abhihantvā vigacchati;

Ekacittakkhaṇuppādo, asanī viya pabbataṃ.

The path, arising for a single mind-moment, departs, having destroyed the mental continuity defiled by the defilements, like a thunderbolt striking a mountain.

1782.

1782.

Pubbe vuttanayeneva, appanānayamīraye;

Pādakajjhānabhedena, jhānaṅganiyamo bhave.

One should apply the method of absorption in the way previously stated. According to the different basic jhānas, there is a determination of the jhāna factors.

1783.

1783.

Parikammopacārānu-lomasaṅkhātagocarā;

Yaṃ kiñci lakkhaṇākāraṃ, vipassantā pavattare.

They proceed in insight, contemplating whatever signs and characteristics fall within the domain of what is known as preparation, access, and conformity.

1784.

1784.

Tato gotrabhu nibbāna-mālambitvāna jāyati;

Bahiddhā khandhato tasmā, vuṭṭhānanti pavuccati.

Then change-of-lineage consciousness arises, taking Nibbāna as its object. Therefore, because it is external to the aggregates, it is called 'emergence'.

1785.

1785.

Tato [V 0.0162] maggo kilesamhā, vimuccanto pavattati;

Vuṭṭhānaṃ ubhato tasmā, khandhato ca kilesato.

Then the path proceeds, liberating one from the defilements. Therefore it is an emergence from both: from the aggregates and from the defilements.

1786.

1786.

Dve tathā tīṇi vā honti, phalāni ca tato paraṃ;

Bhavaṅgapāto taṃ chetvā, jāyate paccavekkhaṇā.

Then two or three fruition moments occur. A lapse into the life-continuum cuts this off, and then reviewing consciousness arises.

1787.

1787.

Maggaṃ phalañca nibbānaṃ, paccavekkhati paṇḍito;

Hīne kilese sese ca, paccavekkhati vā na vā.

The wise one reviews the path, the fruit, and Nibbāna. He may or may not review the defilements that have been abandoned and those that still remain.

1788.

1788.

Bhāvetvā paṭhamaṃ magga-mitthamādiphale ṭhito;

Tato paraṃ pariggayha, nāmarūpaṃ yathā pure.

Thus, having developed the first path and being established in the first fruit, he thereafter comprehends name-and-form as before.

1789.

1789.

Kamena ca vipassanto, punadeva yathārahaṃ;

Yathānukkamamappeti, sakadāgāmiādayo.

And gradually practicing insight again, according to suitability, he attains in due order the stages beginning with the once-returner.

1790.

1790.

Itthaṃ [M 0.0154] vibhattaparipākavibhāvanāyaṃ,

Buddhānubuddhaparibhāvitabhāvanāyaṃ;

Paccuddhareti bhavasāgarapāragāmī,

Maggo mahesi guṇasāgarapāragāmī.

Thus, in this unfolding of distinct maturation, this development cultivated by the Buddhas and their disciples, the path lifts one up—the path that goes to the far shore of the ocean of existence, the path of the great sage that goes to the far shore of the ocean of virtues.

1791.

1791.

Iccetaṃ dasavidha bhāvanāvibhāgaṃ,

Bhāvetvā paramahitāvahaṃ kamena;

Papponti padamajarāmaraṃ cirāya,

Saṃklesaṃ sakalamavassajanti dhīrā.

Thus, having gradually developed this tenfold classification of meditation, which brings the highest benefit, the wise attain the ageless, deathless state and abandon all defilements.

Iti nāmarūpaparicchede dasāvatthāvibhāgo nāma

Thus ends the division into ten stages in the analysis of name and form.

Dvādasamo paricchedo.

The Twelfth Chapter.

13. Terasamo paricchedo

13. The Thirteenth Chapter.

Nissandaphalavibhāgo

The Division of Consequential Fruit

1792.

1792.

Vipassanāya [V 0.0163] nissandamiti vuttamito paraṃ;

Saccānaṃ paṭivedhādiṃ, pavakkhāmi yathākkamaṃ.

The consequence of insight has thus been stated. Hereafter, I shall explain, in due order, the penetration of the Truths and so forth.

1793.

1793.

Pariññā ca pahānañca, sacchikiriyā ca bhāvanā;

Iti dukkhādisaccesu, kiccamāhu catubbidhaṃ.

Full understanding, abandoning, realization, and development: thus, concerning the Truths of Suffering and so forth, the task is said to be fourfold.

1794.

1794.

Taṃ sabbaṃ maggakālamhi, karissati tato paraṃ;

Paṭipassaddhakiccattā, kataṃ hoti phale kathaṃ.

All that is to be accomplished is done at the time of the path; thereafter, since the task is pacified, how can it be said to be accomplished in the fruition?

1795.

1795.

Chinnatālo phalasseva, chinnānusayamūlakā;

Khandhā nālamadhiṭṭhānaṃ, vipallāsapavattiyā.

Like a palm tree with its crown cut off, with the roots of the underlying tendencies severed, the aggregates are no longer a basis for the arising of perversions.

1796.

1796.

Accantapaṭipakkhattā, catumaggapavattiyā;

Paraṃ klesā na jāyanti, daḍḍhabījaṅkuraṃ yathā.

Due to complete opposition, through the arising of the four paths, no further defilements arise, just as a sprout from a burnt seed does not.

1797.

1797.

Niyyānaṭṭhavisesena, aññamaññassa paccayo;

Maggova maggaṃ bhāveti, jāyamānotha vā puna.

By the special characteristic of leading out, each is a condition for the other. The path itself develops the path, or when it arises again.

1798.

1798.

Maggappavattisantāne[M 0.0155], bhāvanāti pavuccati;

Vattamānena taṃ kiccaṃ, nipphāditamasesato.

In the continuum of the path's arising, it is called development. By the present moment, that task is accomplished in its entirety.

1799.

1799.

Iti tīṇipi saccāni, kiccato paṭivijjhati;

Nibbānaṃ sacchikubbanto, maggo ekakkhaṇe saha.

Thus, the path, while realizing Nibbāna, penetrates the three Truths in terms of their functions, together in a single moment.

1800.

1800.

Kiccappavattito cettha, paṭivedhoti vuccati;

Tañca sādheti maggoyaṃ, niyyanto santigocaro.

Here, from its engagement in the task, it is called penetration. And this path, leading out to the sphere of peace, accomplishes that.

1801.

1801.

Pariccajitvā saṅkhāre, maggassārabbha nibbutiṃ,

Niyyānameva saccesu, kiccasādhanamīritaṃ.

Having abandoned formations and taken Nibbāna as the object for the path, the leading out itself concerning the Truths is declared to be the accomplishment of the task.

1802.

1802.

Maggo [V 0.0164] eva hi niyyāti, sesā tassopakārakā;

Appentā jhānadhammā ca, bujjhantā bodhipakkhiyā.

For the path alone leads out; the rest are its helpers: the jhana factors applying it, and the factors of enlightenment awakening.

1803.

1803.

Tasmā tasseva vuṭṭhānaṃ, pakāsenti visesato;

Khandhehi ca kilesehi, vimokkhattayato kathaṃ.

Therefore, they explain in particular the emergence from that, and how liberation from the aggregates and defilements is threefold.

1804.

1804.

Katvānābhinivesaṃ tu, yattha tattha yathā tathā;

Bhūmidhammaṃ pariggayha, vipassitvā tato paraṃ.

Having made a resolve, in whatever way, having grasped the phenomena of the plane and practiced insight upon them, thereafter...

1805.

1805.

Yato kutoci vuṭṭhānaṃ, yadi hoti aniccato;

Hutvādhimokkhabahulo, saddhindriyavisesato.

If the emergence from any of these is through impermanence, it occurs, being abundant in resolute conviction, specifically through the faculty of faith.

1806.

1806.

Animittavimokkhena, niyyanto sattapuggalo;

Saddhānusārī paṭhame, majjhe saddhāvimuttako.

Leading out by way of the signless liberation, such a person is one of seven types: the faith-follower at the first stage, the faith-liberated one in the middle stages,

1807.

1807.

Ante paññāvimuttoti, tamīrenti tathāgatā;

Saṅkhāre dukkhato disvā, vuṭṭhahanto sa puggalo.

and at the end, the one liberated by wisdom—thus the Tathāgatas declare. That person, having seen formations as suffering, emerges.

1808.

1808.

Passaddhibahulo hutvā, samādhindriyalābhato;

Tathevāppaṇihitena, niyyanto tividho bhave.

Having become one abounding in tranquility, through the acquisition of the faculty of concentration, just so, leading out by way of the desireless, one becomes threefold.

1809.

1809.

Anattato vuṭṭhahitvā, vedabāhulyayogato;

Suññatenātha niyyanto, paññindriyavisesato.

Having emerged through non-self, due to the application of abundant insight, then leading out through emptiness, specifically by the faculty of wisdom.

1810.

1810.

Dhammānusārī paṭhame, diṭṭhippatto tato paraṃ;

Ante paññāvimuttoti, tampi dīpenti paṇḍitā.

The Dhamma-follower is at the first stage, the view-attainer after that; and at the end, the one liberated by wisdom—this too the wise illuminate.

1811.

1811.

Āneñjapādakajjhāna-nāmakāyavisesato[M 0.0156];

Sacchikatvāna nibbānaṃ, majjhe cha kāyasakkhino.

Having realized Nibbāna specifically through the mental body that has the imperturbable jhānas as its basis, six types of persons in the middle stages are body-witnesses.

1812.

1812.

Arūpato ca maggena, āneñjena ca rūpato;

Vimutto ubhatobhāga-vimutto arahā bhave.

Liberated from the formless by the path, and from form by the imperturbable, one liberated in both ways becomes an Arahant.

1813.

1813.

Tivimokkhamukhībhūtā, iti vuṭṭhānasādhikā;

Sattapuggalabhedañca, sampādeti vipassanā.

Thus, having become the gateway to the three liberations and accomplishing emergence, insight also brings about the distinction of the seven kinds of persons.

1814.

1814.

Adhimuccati [V 0.0165] saddhā ca, yathāvatthusabhāvato;

Ñeyyadhammesu sabbattha, paññā ca paṭivijjhati.

Faith is resolved according to the true nature of the object; and wisdom penetrates everywhere among all knowable phenomena.

1815.

1815.

Tasmā saddhā ca paññā ca, vatthunicchayalakkhaṇā;

Vatthuppatiṭṭhitā cāyaṃ, tilakkhaṇavipassanā.

Therefore, faith and wisdom are characterized by the determination of the object. And this insight into the three characteristics is established upon that object.

1816.

1816.

Tasmā saddhādhuro yogī, disvoḷārikalakkhaṇaṃ;

Tato paramanattāti, sukhume adhimuccati.

Therefore, the yogi led by faith, having seen the gross characteristic, is then resolved upon the subtle, that is, non-self.

1817.

1817.

Tassevamadhimuttassa, saddhā vā pana kevalā;

Samādhindriyādhikā ca, vuṭṭhānaghaṭikā bhave.

For one who is thus resolved, faith, or even faith alone, along with the predominant faculty of concentration, becomes the condition for emergence.

1818.

1818.

Thūlalakkhaṇamohāya, paññādhure vipassato;

Dhammasabhāvamāhacca, sukhumaṃ paṭivijjhati.

For one led by wisdom who practices insight to dispel delusion regarding gross characteristics, having penetrated the true nature of phenomena, one penetrates the subtle.

1819.

1819.

Tasmā saddhādhurasseva, vuṭṭhānadvayamādito;

Ante saddhānugatassa, paññā suparipūrati.

Therefore, for one led by faith, the two kinds of emergence are from the beginning; at the end, for one who follows faith, wisdom becomes fully perfected.

1820.

1820.

Paññādhurassa sesanti, keci ācariyā pana;

Dhurasaṃsandanaṃ nāma, vuṭṭhānesu vibhāvayuṃ.

Some teachers, however, say the rest pertains to the one led by wisdom; they explained the 'confluence of faculties' in the emergences.

1821.

1821.

Sattakkhattuparamo ca,

Kolaṃkolo tathāparo;

Ekabījīti tividho,

Sotāpanno pavuccati.

The stream-enterer is said to be of three kinds: the one with at most seven more lives, the one who goes from family to family, and the one-seeder.

1822.

1822.

Sakiṃdeva imaṃ lokaṃ, āgantvā puna puggalo;

Sakadāgāmināmena, dutiyopi pakāsito.

The person who comes to this world only once more is also declared as the second, by the name of once-returner.

1823.

1823.

Antarāparinibbāyī[M 0.0157], upahaccāparo tathā;

Asaṅkhāraṃ sasaṅkhāraṃ, uddhaṃsototi pañcadhā.

The one who attains Nibbāna in the interim, and likewise the one who attains Nibbāna upon landing; the one who attains it without exertion, with exertion, and the one who goes upstream—thus they are fivefold.

1824.

1824.

Anāgāmī ca tatiyo, catuttho arahāti ca;

Itthaṃ phalaṭṭhā cattāro, maggaṭṭhā ca tatopare.

The non-returner is the third, and the Arahant the fourth. Thus, there are four established in the fruits, and the others are those established in the paths.

1825.

1825.

Bhāvanāpariyāyena[V 0.0166], paṭivedhānurūpato;

Cattāro ca yugā honti, aṭṭha cāriyapuggalā.

According to the method of development, corresponding to penetration, there are four pairs and eight noble individuals.

1826.

1826.

Diṭṭhikaṅkhā pahīyanti, ādimaggena sabbathā;

Apāyagamanīyampi, pāpamaññaṃ pahīyati.

Wrong view and doubt are entirely abandoned by the first path; and other evil leading to states of woe is also abandoned.

1827.

1827.

Sakadāgāmimaggena, khīyantoḷārikā tathā;

Anāgāmikamaggena, kāmadosāva sabbathā.

By the path of the once-returner, the grosser defilements are thus diminished; by the path of the non-returner, sensual lust and ill will are entirely abandoned.

1828.

1828.

Arahattena sabbepi, klesā khīyanti sabbathā;

Klesahāni yathāyoga-miti ñeyyā vibhāvinā.

By Arahantship, all defilements are entirely destroyed. The destruction of defilements should be understood by the discerning one as is appropriate.

1829.

1829.

Paṭisambhidā catasso, atthe dhamme niruttiyaṃ;

Paṭibhāne ca bhāsanti, ñāṇaṃ bhedagataṃ budhā.

The wise declare the four analytical knowledges—in meaning, Dhamma, language, and eloquence—to be knowledge that has reached distinction.

1830.

1830.

Hetupphalañca nibbānaṃ, bhāsitattho tathāparo;

Pākākriyāti pañcete, atthanāmena bhāsitā.

Cause, fruit, Nibbāna, the meaning of what is spoken, and resultant and functional consciousness—these five are spoken of by the name of 'meaning'.

1831.

1831.

Hetu cāriyamaggo ca, bhāsitañca tathāparaṃ;

Kusalākusalañceti, pañca dhammo pakāsito.

The cause, the noble path, and likewise what was spoken, the wholesome, and the unwholesome—these five are declared as 'Dhamma'.

1832.

1832.

Tatthevaṃ dasadhā bhede, atthadhamme yathārahaṃ;

Yo vohāro sabhāvena, sā niruttīti sammatā.

Therein, regarding the tenfold division of meaning and Dhamma, the appropriate conventional expression in its own nature is considered 'nirutti'.

1833.

1833.

Taṃtaṃgocarakiccādi-bhedabhinnaṃ tahiṃ tahiṃ;

Pavattamānaṃ yaṃ ñāṇaṃ, paṭibhānaṃ tamīritaṃ.

That knowledge which proceeds in various contexts, differentiated by the distinctions of its respective objects, functions, and so on, is called 'eloquence'.

1834.

1834.

Pubbayogo bāhussaccaṃ,

Desabhāsā tathāgamo;

Paripucchā cādhigamo,

Nissayo mittasampadā.

Previous effort, extensive learning, knowledge of local languages, knowledge of the scriptures, questioning, attainment, support, and good friendship.

1835.

1835.

Iccūpanissayaṃ [M 0.0158] laddhā, bhijjati paṭisambhidā;

Asekkhabhūmiyaṃ vātha, sekkhabhūmiyameva vā.

Having obtained these supporting conditions, analytical knowledge breaks forth, whether in the stage of a non-learner or, indeed, in the stage of a learner.

1836.

1836.

Sarassato [V 0.0167] āgamato, tathālambaṇatopi ca;

Nāmuppattiṃ pakāsenti, phalassa tividhaṃ budhā.

The wise declare the threefold origination of the fruit by name: from sound, from scripture, and likewise from its object.

1837.

1837.

Tidhā tato samāpatti, sotāpattiphalādikā;

Suññatā cānimittā ca, tathāppaṇihitāti ca.

From that, the attainments, beginning with the fruit of stream-entry, are threefold: emptiness, the signless, and likewise the desireless.

1838.

1838.

Tañca vuttanayeneva, samāpajjitumicchato;

Vipassantassa saṅkhāre, phalamappeti attano.

And for one desiring to attain it in the manner just described, while contemplating formations, the fruit accrues to oneself.

1839.

1839.

Nirodhaṃ tu samāpattiṃ, rūpārūpassa lābhako;

Samāpajjatānāgāmī, arahā ca yathā tathā.

As for the attainment of cessation, one who has obtained the form and formless attainments—a non-returner or an Arahant, as the case may be—enters it.

1840.

1840.

Rūpārūpasamāpattiṃ, samāpajja yathākkamaṃ;

Vuṭṭhahitvā vipassanto, tattha tattheva saṅkhate.

Having attained the form and formless attainments in sequence, and upon emerging, one contemplates the conditioned states right then and there.

1841.

1841.

Yuganandhaṃ pavattetvā, samathañca vipassanaṃ;

Yāvākiñcaññāyatana-mitthaṃ patvā tato paraṃ.

Having made serenity and insight proceed in harmony, and having thus reached as far as the sphere of nothingness, thereafter...

1842.

1842.

Adhiṭṭheyyamadhiṭṭhāya, katvābhogaṃ yathārahaṃ;

Maggārūpasamāpattiṃ, samāpajjati paṇḍito.

Having determined what should be determined and having made the appropriate inclination, the wise one enters the formless attainment of the path.

1843.

1843.

Tato nirodhaṃ phusati, cittuppādadvayā paraṃ;

Tassevaṃ manasābhāvo, nirodhoti pavuccati.

Then he touches cessation, after a pair of mind-arisings. The non-existence of mind in this way is called cessation.

1844.

1844.

Phalacittasamuppādā, vuṭṭhānaṃ tassa dīpitaṃ;

Tato bhavaṅgaṃ chetvāna, paccavekkhati buddhimā.

From the arising of the fruit-consciousness, his emergence is indicated. Then, having cut off the life-continuum, the wise one reviews.

1845.

1845.

Iccānekaguṇādhāraṃ, paññābhāvanamuttamaṃ;

Bhāveyya matimā yogī, patthento hitamattano.

Thus, the wise yogi, desiring his own welfare, should cultivate the supreme development of wisdom, the support of many virtues.

1846.

1846.

Itthaṃ susampāditasīlacitta-

Paññāvisuddhī paṭipādayantā;

Patvāna sambodhimapetasokā,

Pālenti sotthiṃ paramaṃ cirāya.

Thus, undertaking the well-accomplished purity of virtue, mind, and wisdom, having attained enlightenment and become sorrowless, they maintain the supreme welfare for a long time.

1847.

1847.

Te [M 0.0159][V 0.0168] pattipattā paramappatītā,

Pakkhālitaklesamalā mahesī;

Those great sages have reached the attainment, are supremely delighted, and have washed away the stain of the defilements;

Accantavodātaguṇoditattā,

Lokassa hontuttamadakkhiṇeyyā.

Because their virtues are utterly pure and manifest, they become the supreme recipients of offerings in the world.

Iti nāmarūpaparicchede nissandaphalavibhāgo nāma

Thus, in The Delimitation of Name and Form, ends the section named The Division of the Resultant Fruit.

Terasamo paricchedo.

The Thirteenth Chapter.

Niṭṭhito ca sabbathāpi vipassanāvibhāgo.

Thus, the exposition of insight is completely finished.

Nigamanakathā

Concluding Remarks

1848.

1848.

Ettāvatā paṭiññāto, pavakkhāmīti ādito;

Nāmarūpaparicchedo, pariniṭṭhāpito mayā.

Thus far, the promise declared from the beginning, 'I will explain,' has been fulfilled; the analysis of name and form has been completed by me.

1849.

1849.

Teraseva paricchedā, vibhattā satta sādhikā;

Nāmarūpaparicchede, bhāṇavārā pakāsitā.

In the Analysis of Name and Form, thirteen chapters, divided into seven and a half recitation portions, have been declared.

1850.

1850.

Abhidhammaparamatthā, samatho ca vipassanā;

Visuṃ visuṃ vibhattāti, vibhāgettha tidhā matā.

The ultimate realities of the Abhidhamma, serenity, and insight are each separately distinguished; thus, the division here is considered threefold.

1851.

1851.

Soyaṃ vijjāvimokkhā ca, hadayesu vibhāvinaṃ;

Vallabhattamadhiṭṭhāya, sāsanettha gavesinaṃ.

This knowledge and liberation shine in the hearts of the discerning who, holding it dear, seek the Teaching here.

1852.

1852.

Manogatatamuddhaṃsī, raviraṃsīva paṇḍito;

Dassetu ciramālokaṃ, saddhammaratanālaye.

May the wise one, like the sun's rays dispelling the darkness of a bewildered mind, long reveal the light in the abode of the jewel of the true Dhamma.

1853.

1853.

Paṇḍiccaṃ [V 0.0169] paramatthesu, pāṭavaṃ paṭipattiyaṃ;

Patthayantena bhikkhūna-mitthaṃ sugatasāsane.

For monks in the Sugata's Dispensation aspiring to wisdom in the ultimate realities and skill in the practice, thus it is.

1854.

1854.

Nāmarūpapariccheda-masaṃkiṇṇamanākulaṃ;

Kubbatā hitakāmena, sukatena katena me.

This unmixed and unconfused Analysis of Name and Form was composed by me as a well-done deed, out of a desire for the welfare of others.

1855.

1855.

Mahāmerunibhaṃ [M 0.0160] gehaṃ, mahācetiyabhūsitaṃ;

Mahāvihāramāruḷha-mahābodhimahussavaṃ.

The Mahāvihāra, a dwelling like Mount Meru, adorned with great cetiyas, celebrating the great festival of the lofty Great Bodhi tree.

1856.

1856.

Alaṅkātuṃ pahontālaṃ, cirakālaṃ tapodhanā;

Laṅkādīpassalaṅkāraṃ, kalaṅkāpagatālayaṃ.

For a long time, the ascetics, whose wealth is austerity, have been fully capable of adorning this ornament of the isle of Laṅkā, a dwelling free from stain.

1857.

1857.

Nāmarūpaparicchedo,

Antarāyaṃ vinā yathā;

Niṭṭhitoyaṃ tathā loke,

Niṭṭhantajjhāsayā subhā.

Just as this Analysis of Name and Form has been completed without hindrance, so may the noble intentions of beings in the world be fulfilled.

Iti anuruddhācariyena viracitaṃ

Thus was this composed by the teacher Anuruddha.

Nāmarūpaparicchedapakaraṇaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Treatise on the Analysis of Name and Form is completed.

Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Paramatthavinicchayo

The Determination of the Ultimate Realities

Ganthārambhakathā

Introduction to the Text

1.

1.

Vanditvā [M 0.0001][V 0.0001] vandaneyyānaṃ, uttamaṃ ratanattayaṃ;

Pavakkhāmi samāsena, paramatthavinicchayaṃ.

Having paid homage to the supreme Triple Gem, which is worthy of homage, I shall explain in brief the determination of the ultimate realities.

Paṭhamo paricchedo

First Chapter

1. Cittavibhāgo

1. The Analysis of Consciousness

1. Sarūpasaṅgahakathā

1. Exposition of the Summary of Essences

2.

2.

Cittaṃ [V 0.0002] cetasikaṃ rūpaṃ, nibbānanti niruttaro;

Catudhā desayī dhamme, catusaccappakāsano.

The Unsurpassed One, the Illuminator of the Four Noble Truths, taught the phenomena as fourfold: consciousness, mental factors, material form, and Nibbāna.

3.

3.

Cittamekūnanavutividhaṃ tattha vibhāvaye;

Ekanavutividhaṃ vā, ekavīsasatampi vā.

Therein, one should understand consciousness to be of eighty-nine kinds, or of ninety-one kinds, or of one hundred and twenty-one kinds.

4.

4.

Dvepaññāsa sarūpena, dhammā cetasikā matā;

Cittuppādavasā bhinnā, sampayogānusārato.

The mental factors are held to be fifty-two in essence; they are distinguished according to their association with the consciousness with which they arise.

5.

5.

Aṭṭhavīsavidhaṃ rūpaṃ, bhūtopādāyabhedato;

Duvidhaṃ rūparūpaṃ tu, aṭṭhārasavidhaṃ bhave.

Material form is twenty-eightfold, distinguished as primary elements and derived matter. Concrete matter, in turn, is of eighteen kinds.

6.

6.

Nibbānaṃ pana dīpenti, asaṅkhatamanuttaraṃ;

Atthanāmavasā dvedhā, paññattīti pavuccati.

They explain Nibbāna as the unconditioned and unsurpassed. Concept, it is said, is twofold by way of meaning and name.

7.

7.

Tesaṃ dāni pavakkhāmi, vibhāgaṃ tu yathākkamaṃ;

Catudhā paramatthānaṃ, dvidhā paññattiyā kathaṃ.

Now I shall explain their classification in due order: how the ultimate realities are fourfold and concept is twofold.

8.

8.

Kusalādivibhāgena[M 0.0002], tattha cittaṃ catubbidhaṃ;

Tathā bhūmivibhāgena, kāmabhūmādito kathaṃ.

Therein, consciousness is fourfold by classification as wholesome, etc. Likewise, by classification according to plane, it is explained as beginning with the sense-sphere plane.

9.

9.

Somanassasahagataṃ, upekkhāsahitaṃ tathā;

Ñāṇena sampayuttañca, vippayuttanti bheditaṃ.

It is distinguished as accompanied by joy or accompanied by equanimity, and as associated with knowledge or dissociated from it.

10.

10.

Asaṅkhāraṃ sasaṅkhāramiti bhinnaṃ punaṭṭhadhā;

Kāmāvacarakusalaṃ, kāme sugatisādhakaṃ.

Distinguished again as unprompted and prompted, it becomes eightfold. This is the sense-sphere wholesome consciousness, which is conducive to a good destination in the sense sphere.

11.

11.

Takkacārapītisukha-cittassekaggatāyutaṃ[V 0.0003];

Paṭhamajjhānakusalaṃ, pañcaṅgikamudāhaṭaṃ.

Accompanied by initial application, sustained application, rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind, the wholesome first jhāna is declared to have five factors.

12.

12.

Vitakkahīnaṃ dutiyaṃ, jhānaṃ tu caturaṅgikaṃ;

Vicārahīnaṃ tatiyaṃ, jhānaṃ pana tivaṅgikaṃ.

The second jhāna, lacking initial application, has four factors; the third jhāna, lacking sustained application, has three factors.

13.

13.

Pītihīnaṃ catutthañca, upekkhekaggatāyutaṃ;

Pañcamañca pakāsenti, ubhayampi duvaṅgikaṃ.

The fourth jhāna is without rapture and endowed with equanimity and one-pointedness. And they declare a fifth; both of these have two factors.

14.

14.

Evaṃ jhānaṅgabhedena, cittaṃ pañcavidhaṃ bhave;

Rūpāvacarakusalaṃ, rūpabhūmipavattakaṃ.

Thus, by the distinction of the jhāna factors, this consciousness becomes fivefold. This is the fine-material sphere wholesome consciousness, which occurs on the fine-material plane.

15.

15.

Ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ, kusalaṃ paṭhamaṃ bhave;

Viññāṇañcāyatananti, dutiyaṃ tatiyaṃ tathā.

The wholesome consciousness of the base of infinite space is the first; the consciousness of the base of infinite consciousness is the second, and the third is likewise.

16.

16.

Ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ tu, catutthaṃ pana mānasaṃ;

Nevasaññānāsaññāya-tanañceti catubbidhaṃ.

The consciousness of the base of nothingness is the third, while the fourth is that of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Thus this immaterial wholesome consciousness is fourfold.

17.

17.

Āruppakusalaṃ nāma, upekkhekaggatāyutaṃ;

Duvaṅgikamidaṃ sabbaṃ, āruppabhavasādhakaṃ.

This is called the immaterial wholesome consciousness, accompanied by equanimity and one-pointedness. All of this is two-factored and brings about existence in the immaterial realm.

18.

18.

Sotāpattimaggacittaṃ, paṭhamānuttaraṃ tathā;

Sakadāgāmi anāgāmi, arahattanti sabbathā.

The path consciousness of stream-entry is the first supramundane consciousness. Likewise there are the paths of the once-returner, the non-returner, and arahantship.

19.

19.

Catudhā maggabhedena, jhānabhedena pañcadhā;

Vīsatāpariyāpannakusalaṃ dvayamissitaṃ.

By division of path it is fourfold, and by division of jhāna, fivefold. Thus the supramundane wholesome consciousness is of twenty kinds.

20.

20.

Itthaṃ bhūmivibhāgena, kusalaṃ tu catubbidhaṃ;

Ekavīsāpi bāvīsaṃ, sattatiṃsavidhampi vā.

Thus, by classification according to plane, wholesome consciousness is fourfold. In total, it is of twenty-one kinds, or twenty-two, or even thirty-seven kinds.

21.

21.

Somanassasahagataṃ[M 0.0003], upekkhāsahitaṃ tathā;

Diṭṭhigatasampayuttaṃ, vippayuttanti bheditaṃ.

It is distinguished as: accompanied by joy or accompanied by equanimity; and as associated with wrong view or dissociated from it.

22.

22.

Asaṅkhāraṃ sasaṅkhāramiti bhinnaṃ punaṭṭhadhā;

Lobhamūlaṃ pakāsenti, lobhamohadvihetukaṃ.

Distinguished again as unprompted and prompted, they become eightfold. They declare these to be rooted in greed, having two causes: greed and delusion.

23.

23.

Domanassasahagataṃ[V 0.0004], paṭighena samāyutaṃ;

Asaṅkhāraṃ sasaṅkhāramiti bhinnaṃ dvidhā pana.

Accompanied by displeasure and associated with aversion, and distinguished as unprompted and prompted, these are again twofold.

24.

24.

Dosamūlaṃ pakāsenti, dosamohadvihetukaṃ;

Vicikicchāsahagataṃ, uddhaccasahitanti ca.

They declare these to be rooted in aversion, having two causes: aversion and delusion. And there are those accompanied by doubt and accompanied by restlessness.

25.

25.

Upekkhāvedanāyuttaṃ, momūhaṃ duvidhaṃ pana;

Mohamūlaṃ pakāsenti, mohenevekahetukaṃ.

These two types of consciousness rooted in sheer delusion are accompanied by equanimous feeling. They are declared to be rooted in delusion, having only one cause, which is delusion itself.

26.

26.

Dvādasākusalā nāma, caturāpāyasādhakā;

Ete sugatiyañcāpi, vipattiphaladāyakā.

These are called the twelve unwholesome types of consciousness, which lead to the four woeful planes. Even in a good destination, they yield adverse fruit.

27.

27.

Cakkhusotaghānajivhā-kāyaviññāṇanāmakā;

Pañcaviññāṇayugaḷā, yugaḷaṃ sampaṭicchanaṃ.

There are the pairs of eye-, ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness; and the pair of receiving consciousness.

28.

28.

Santīraṇadvayañceva, upekkhāsahitaṃ tathā;

Puññāpuññavaseneva, vipākā duvidhā ṭhitā.

And there are the two investigating consciousnesses, which are also accompanied by equanimity. Depending on whether the kamma was meritorious or demeritorious, these resultants are of two kinds.

29.

29.

Upekkhāsahitā tattha, mānasā dvādaseritā;

Kāyaviññāṇayugaḷaṃ, sukhadukkhayutaṃ kamā.

The pair of body-consciousness is accompanied by pleasure and pain respectively. Among these, twelve consciousnesses are said to be accompanied by equanimity.

30.

30.

Somanassasahagataṃ, yaṃ santīraṇamānasaṃ;

Taṃ puññapākamevāhu, pāpapākaṃ na vijjati.

That investigating consciousness which is accompanied by joy, they say, is a resultant of merit only; it is not found as a resultant of demerit.

31.

31.

Pañcadvāramanodvāra-vasena duvidhaṃ pana;

Upekkhāvedanāyuttaṃ, kriyāvajjananāmakaṃ.

The functional adverting consciousness, accompanied by equanimous feeling, is twofold: five-door-adverting and mind-door-adverting.

32.

32.

Somanassasahagataṃ, hasituppādamānasaṃ;

Kriyājavanamiccevaṃ, tividhāhetukakriyā.

The smile-producing consciousness is accompanied by joy. Thus the rootless functional consciousnesses are threefold.

33.

33.

Aṭṭheva puññapākāni, pāpapākāni sattadhā;

Kriyacittāni tīṇīti, aṭṭhārasa ahetukā.

There are eight wholesome-resultants, seven unwholesome-resultants, and three functional types of consciousness. Thus there are eighteen rootless types in all.

34.

34.

Sapuññehi [M 0.0004] samānā ca, mahāpākamahākriyā;

Mahaggatakriyā pākā, phalacittāni ca kamā.

Similarly, there are the great resultants and great functional types of consciousness; the sublime resultants and functional types; and the fruition consciousnesses, in order.

35.

35.

Itthamekūnanavuti-vidhaṃ [V 0.0005] cittaṃ bhave tathā;

Ekanavutividhaṃ vā, ekavīsasatampi vā.

Thus consciousness may be of eighty-nine kinds; or of ninety-one kinds; or of one hundred and twenty-one kinds.

36.

36.

Takkacārapītisukhacittassekaggatāyutaṃ;

Sotāpattimaggacittaṃ, paṭhamajjhānikaṃ mataṃ.

The path consciousness of stream-entry, when accompanied by initial application, sustained application, rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness, is considered to be of the first jhāna level.

37.

37.

Dutiyaṃ takkato hīnaṃ, tatiyaṃ tu vicārato;

Catutthaṃ pītito hīnaṃ, upekkhekaggatāyutaṃ.

The second is without initial application; the third is without sustained application; the fourth is without rapture; and the fifth is endowed with equanimity and one-pointedness.

38.

38.

Pañcamanti ca pañcete, paṭhamānuttarā matā;

Diṭṭhikaṅkhāsīlabbataparāmāsappahāyino.

The fifth, and thus these five, are considered the first unsurpassed paths, those who have abandoned wrong view, doubt, and clinging to rites and rituals.

39.

39.

Tatheva sakadāgāmimaggacittañca pañcadhā;

Rāgadosamohattayatanuttakaramīritaṃ.

Similarly, the path-consciousness of a once-returner is fivefold; it is said to weaken lust, hatred, and delusion.

40.

40.

Kāmadosasamugghātakaraṃ niravasesato;

Tatiyānuttarañcāpi, kusalaṃ pañcadhā tathā.

Completely eradicating sensual lust and ill-will, the third unsurpassed path, likewise, is fivefold wholesome.

41.

41.

Rūparāgārūparāgamānuddhaccāpi cāparā;

Avijjā ceti pañcuddhaṃbhāgiyānamasesato.

Lust for form, lust for the formless, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance—these five are the upper fetters, abandoned entirely.

42.

42.

Saṃyojanānaṃ sesānaṃ, samugghātakaraṃ paraṃ;

Catutthānuttaraṃ maggacittaṃ pañcavidhanti ca.

The fourth unsurpassed path-consciousness, which completely uproots the remaining fetters, is also fivefold.

43.

43.

Cattāri pañcakāneva, maggesu ca phalesu ca;

Sesāni cekāsītīti, ekavīsasataṃ bhave.

Four sets of five for the paths and for the fruits; the remaining eighty-one thus become one hundred and twenty-one.

44.

44.

Lokuttarānaṃ aṭṭhannaṃ, iccevaṃ pañcadhā puna;

Jhānaṅgamaggabojjhaṅga-vibhāgāya yathārahaṃ.

Thus again, the eight supramundane consciousnesses are divided fivefold, according to their suitability, by way of the divisions of jhāna factors, path factors, and enlightenment factors.

45.

45.

Pādakajjhānamāmaṭṭhajhānaṃ ajjhāsayo tathā;

Vuṭṭhānagāminī ceva, niyāmeti vipassanāti.

The foundational jhāna, the contemplated jhāna, and also the disposition, and insight leading to emergence—this is the fixed course of insight.

Iti cittavibhāge sarūpasaṅgahakathā niṭṭhitā.

Thus concludes the exposition summarizing the nature of consciousness in the Analysis of Consciousness.

Paṭhamo paricchedo.

The First Chapter.

Dutiyo paricchedo

The Second Chapter.

2. Pakiṇṇakakathā

2. Miscellaneous Discourse.

46.

46.

Kusalānekavīseva[M 0.0005][V 0.0006], dvādasākusalāni ca;

Chattiṃsati vipākāni, kriyācittāni vīsati.

Twenty-one are wholesome, and twelve unwholesome; thirty-six are resultant, and twenty are functional consciousnesses.

47.

47.

Kāmesu catupaññāsa, rūpesu dasa pañca ca;

Dvādasāruppacittāni, aṭṭhānuttaramānasā.

Fifty-four in the sense-sphere, fifteen in the form-sphere; twelve formless-sphere consciousnesses, eight supramundane minds.

48.

48.

Kāme tevīsa pākāni, puññāpuññāni vīsati;

Ekādasa kriyā ceti, catupaññāsa sabbathā.

In the sense-sphere, there are twenty-three resultants, twenty wholesome and unwholesome, and eleven functional—thus, fifty-four in all.

49.

49.

Puññapākakriyābhedā, tayo rūpesu pañcakā;

Āruppeti catukkāni, sattavīsa mahaggatā.

By the division of wholesome, resultant, and functional, there are three sets of five in the form-sphere and three sets of four in the formless—thus, twenty-seven are the sublime consciousnesses.

50.

50.

Catumaggaphalānaṃ tu, vasenaṭṭhapi jhānato;

Dasobhayampi missetvā, tālīsānuttarā siyuṃ.

The eight consciousnesses of the four paths and fruits, by way of the jhānas, become forty supramundane consciousnesses.

51.

51.

Puññapākakriyāpāpā, santi kāme mahaggate;

Pāpaṃ natthi kriyāpāpā, na vijjanti anuttare.

Wholesome, resultant, functional, and unwholesome exist in the sense-sphere. In the sublime sphere, the unwholesome does not exist. In the supramundane, the functional and the unwholesome are not found.

52.

52.

Pāpāhetukamuttāni, anavajjāni sabbathā;

Ekūnasaṭṭhi cittāni, puññapākakriyāvasā.

Fifty-nine consciousnesses—comprising wholesome, resultant, and functional types—are entirely blameless, being distinct from the unwholesome and the rootless.

53.

53.

Kammacittāni tettiṃsa, puññāpuññāni sabbathā;

Chattiṃsa tesaṃ pākāni, kriyā vīsa na cobhayaṃ.

Thirty-three are kamma-producing consciousnesses, comprising all wholesome and unwholesome types. Thirty-six are their resultants, and twenty are functional, being neither kamma-producing nor resultant.

54.

54.

Cakkhuviññāṇadhātādi, pañcaviññāṇanāmakā;

Pañcadvārāvajjanañca, duvidhaṃ sampaṭicchanaṃ.

The eye-consciousness element and so forth, which are named the five sense-consciousnesses; the five-door adverting consciousness, and the two kinds of receiving consciousness.

55.

55.

Manodhātuttayaṃ nāma, chasattati tato pare;

Manoviññāṇadhātūti, sattadhā dhātubhedato.

The mind-element is threefold, and the seventy-six that remain are the mind-consciousness element; thus, by division into elements, they are of seven kinds.

56.

56.

Manoviññāṇadhātuñca[V 0.0007], manodhātuttayaṃ tathā;

Katvā manoviññāṇanti, cha viññāṇā pakittitā.

By grouping the mind-consciousness element and likewise the threefold mind-element together as mind-consciousness, the six consciousnesses are declared.

57.

57.

Āvajjanaṃ dassanañca, savanaṃ ghāyanaṃ tathā;

Sāyanaṃ phusanañceva, sampaṭicchanatīraṇaṃ.

Adverting, seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, receiving, and investigating.

58.

58.

Voṭṭhabbanañca [M 0.0006] javanaṃ, tadārammaṇanāmakaṃ;

Bhavaṅgaṃ cuti sandhīti, cittaṃ cuddasadhā ṭhitaṃ.

Determining, impulsion, and registration; life-continuum, decease, and rebirth-linking—thus consciousness is established with fourteen functions.

59.

59.

Āvajjanādayo dve dve, yugā satta yathākkamaṃ;

Tīṇi tīraṇacittāni, ekaṃ voṭṭhabbanaṃ mataṃ.

The seven functions beginning with adverting are performed by pairs of consciousnesses in due order; three are the investigating consciousnesses, and one is reckoned as the determining consciousness.

60.

60.

Kusalākusalā sabbe, phalā cāvajjanaṃ vinā;

Kriyā ca pañcapaññāsa, javananti pavuccare.

All wholesome and unwholesome consciousnesses, the fruit consciousnesses, and the functional consciousnesses apart from adverting—these fifty-five are called impulsion.

61.

61.

Santīraṇamahāpākā, tadārammaṇanāmakā;

Ekādasa pavattanti, javanārammaṇe yato.

The eleven consciousnesses—the investigating and the great-resultant—perform the function of registration, as they arise with the object of the impulsion.

62.

62.

Mahaggatamahāpākā, upekkhātīraṇadvayaṃ;

Cutisandhibhavaṅgāni, cittānekūnavīsati.

The sublime-resultant, the great-resultant, and the two investigating consciousnesses with equanimity—these nineteen consciousnesses perform the functions of decease, rebirth-linking, and life-continuum.

63.

63.

Javanāvajjanādīni, voṭṭhabbasukhatīraṇā;

Mahaggatamahāpākā, upekkhātīraṇāti ca.

Impulsion, adverting, and the others; determining, investigating with pleasure; sublime-resultant and great-resultant; and investigating with equanimity.

64.

64.

Aṭṭhasaṭṭhi tathā dve ca, navaṭṭha dve yathākkamaṃ;

Ekadviticatuppañcakiccaṭṭhānāni niddise.

Sixty-eight, and also two, nine, eight, and two, in due order, are specified for the states having one, two, three, four, and five functions respectively.

65.

65.

Rūpapākā mahāpākā, manodhātu ca tīraṇaṃ;

Rūpaṃ janenti ekūnavīsati netaradvayaṃ.

The form-sphere resultants, the great-resultants, the mind-element, and the investigating consciousnesses—these nineteen generate material form; the other two do not.

66.

66.

Abhiññāvajjitā sabbe, appanājavanā pana;

Rūpaṃ janenti chabbīsa, paṇāmentiriyāpathaṃ.

All absorption javanas except for the higher knowledges—twenty-six in number—generate material form and regulate the bodily postures.

67.

67.

Abhiññādvayavoṭṭhabbaparittajavanā pana;

Dvattiṃsa rūpaviññattiiriyāpathasādhakā.

The two higher knowledges, the determining consciousness, and the sense-sphere javanas—these thirty-two accomplish material form, bodily intimation, and bodily postures.

68.

68.

Pañcaviññāṇamāruppa-vipākā [V 0.0008] sabbasandhiyo;

Cuti khīṇāsavasseti, soḷasete na kiñcipi.

The ten sense-consciousnesses, the immaterial resultants, all rebirth-linking consciousnesses, and the death-consciousness of the Arahant—these sixteen produce nothing whatsoever.

69.

69.

Rūpaṃ janenti cittāni, sattasattati sabbathā;

Aṭṭhapaññāsa cittāni, paṇāmentiriyāpathaṃ.

Seventy-seven consciousnesses in total produce form; fifty-eight consciousnesses produce bodily movement.

70.

70.

Dvattiṃsa [M 0.0007] catuviññattiṃ, samuṭṭhāpenti mānasā;

Na janenti tassampekaṃ, yathāvuttāni soḷasa.

Thirty-two consciousnesses produce the four intimations; the sixteen previously mentioned do not produce even one of them.

71.

71.

Somanassasahagatā, parittajavanā pana;

Hasanampi janentīti, catukiccāni terasa.

Accompanied by joy, the sense-sphere javanas also produce laughter; thus, thirteen perform four functions.

72.

72.

Sabbampi pañcavokāre, kiccametaṃ pakāsitaṃ;

Āruppe pana sabbampi, rūpāyattaṃ na vijjati.

All this function is explained regarding the five-aggregate realm; but in the formless realm, nothing dependent on form is found.

73.

73.

Asaññīnaṃ tu sabbāni, cittāneva na labbhare;

Rūpakkhandhova tesaṃ tu, attabhāvoti vuccati.

For the non-percipient beings, no consciousnesses are obtainable; only the aggregate of form is said to be their existence.

74.

74.

Pāṇātipātatheyyādivasenopacitaṃ pana;

Uddhaccarahitāpuññaṃ, caturāpāyabhūmiyaṃ.

The unwholesome kamma accumulated through killing, stealing, and so on, devoid of restlessness, leads to the four realms of misery.

75.

75.

Datvā sandhiṃ pavatte tu, pañcavokārabhūmiyaṃ;

Uddhaccasahitañcāpi, satta pākāni paccati.

Having given rebirth-linking in the five-aggregate realm, seven results ripen in the course of existence; and likewise for the kamma accompanied by restlessness.

76.

76.

Dānasīlādibhedena, pavattaṃ kusalaṃ pana;

Kāme mānasamukkaṭṭhaṃ, catukkaṃ tu tihetukaṃ.

However, wholesome kamma arisen through giving, virtue, and so forth, in the sensual realm, is fourfold and triple-rooted, excelling in mental states.

77.

77.

Datvā tihetukaṃ sandhiṃ, kāme sugatiyaṃ pana;

Soḷasa puññapākāni, pavatte tu vipaccati.

When it gives a triple-rooted rebirth-linking in the happy sensual realm, sixteen meritorious results ripen in the course of existence.

78.

78.

Tihetukomakaṃ puññaṃ, ukkaṭṭhañca dvihetukaṃ;

Datvā dvihetukaṃ sandhiṃ, kāme sugatiyaṃ tathā.

Triple-rooted inferior wholesome kamma and superior double-rooted wholesome kamma, having given a double-rooted rebirth-linking, likewise lead to the happy sensual realm.

79.

79.

Pavatte pana ñāṇena, sampayuttaṃ vivajjiya;

Dvādasa puññapākāni, vipaccati yathārahaṃ.

But in the course of existence, excluding those associated with knowledge, twelve meritorious results ripen as is fitting.

80.

80.

Dvihetukomakaṃ [V 0.0009] puññaṃ, paṭisandhimahetukaṃ;

Deti mānusake ceva, vinipātāsure tathā.

Double-rooted inferior wholesome kamma, giving a rootless rebirth-linking, yields results in the human realm and likewise among the fallen asuras.

81.

81.

Aṭṭhāhetukapākāni, pavatte tu vipaccare;

Cattāripi catukkāni, pañcavokārabhūmiyaṃ.

Eight rootless results ripen in the course of existence; and also four tetrads in the five-aggregate realm.

82.

82.

Bhāvanāmayapuññaṃ [M 0.0008] tu, mahaggatamanuttaraṃ;

Yathābhūminiyāmena, deti pākaṃ yathāsakaṃ.

But the wholesome kamma born of development, sublime and unsurpassed, yields results according to the rule of the plane, each in its own way.

83.

83.

Kaṭattārūpapākāni, pañcavokārabhūmiyaṃ;

Āruppānuttare pākaṃ, tathā rūpamasaññisu.

The results of kamma-born materiality ripen in the five-aggregate realm; resultants ripen in the formless and supramundane states, and likewise form in the realm of non-percipient beings.

84.

84.

Puññāpuññāni kammāni, tettiṃsāpi ca yabbathā;

Sañjanenti yathāyogaṃ, paṭisandhipavattiyaṃ.

The thirty-three wholesome and unwholesome kammas, in their respective ways, generate rebirth-linking and continuity as is fitting.

Iti cittavibhāge pakiṇṇakakathā niṭṭhitā.

Thus concludes the miscellaneous discussion in the analysis of consciousness.

Dutiyo paricchedo.

The Second Chapter.

Tatiyo paricchedo

The Third Chapter.

3. Vīthisaṅgahakathā

3. Discussion on the Compendium of Cognitive Processes.

85.

85.

Cakkhusotaghānajivhā-kāyāyatana pañcadhā;

Pasādā hadayañceti, cha vatthūni viniddise.

The five sense-sensitivities—eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body—and the heart-base: these six bases are declared.

86.

86.

Cakkhusotaghānajivhā-kāyadvārā ca pañcadhā;

Manodvāraṃ bhavaṅganti, cha dvārā cittavīthiyā.

The five sense-doors—eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body—and the mind-door, that is, the life-continuum: these are the six doors of a cognitive process.

87.

87.

Rūpasaddagandharasa-phoṭṭhabbā pañca gocarā;

Dhammārammaṇapaññatti, cha dvārārammaṇakkamā.

Visible forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tactile objects are the five sense objects; the dhamma-object is designated as the sixth. These are, in sequence, the objects of the six doors.

88.

88.

Nimittagatikammāni[V 0.0010], kammamevātha gocarā;

Paṭisandhibhavaṅgānaṃ, cutiyā ca yathārahaṃ.

Kamma, the kamma-sign, and the destination-sign are the objects, as is fitting, for rebirth-linking, the life-continuum, and death.

89.

89.

Maraṇāsannasattassa, yathopaṭṭhitagocaraṃ;

Chadvāresu tamārabbha, paṭisandhi bhavantare.

For a being nearing death, according to the object that has appeared, having taken that as object at any of the six doors, rebirth-linking occurs in a future existence.

90.

90.

Ekacittakkhaṇā hoti, yāvajīvaṃ tato paraṃ;

Bhavaṅgaṃ pariyosāne, cuti cekakkhaṇā bhave.

Rebirth-linking is a single thought-moment; thereafter, the life-continuum lasts for a lifetime; at the end, the death-consciousness is also a single moment.

91.

91.

Duhetāhetucutiyā, kāmāvacarasandhiyo;

Tihetukāmacutiyā, sabbāpi paṭisandhiyo.

From double-rooted or rootless death-consciousness, sensual-sphere rebirth-linkings arise; from triple-rooted sensual death-consciousness, all rebirth-linkings arise.

92.

92.

Rūpāvacaracutiyā[M 0.0009], sahetupaṭisandhiyo;

Āruppatopari kāme, tattha vāpi tihetukā.

From a form-sphere death, rooted rebirth-linkings arise; from a formless-sphere death, rebirth in a higher realm, in the sensual realm, or in that same realm, is triple-rooted.

93.

93.

Paṭisandhi bhavaṅgañca, ekamevekajātiyaṃ;

Cuti cārammaṇañcassa, evameva yathārahaṃ.

In a single existence, the rebirth-linking and life-continuum are of one and the same type; its death-consciousness and its object are likewise the same, as is fitting.

94.

94.

Rūpādārammaṇe cakkhu-ppasādādimhi ghaṭṭite;

Majjhe bhavaṅgaṃ chinditvā, vīthi nāma pavattati.

When a visible object strikes the eye-sensitivity, and so forth, a process, so-called, proceeds, having cut off the life-continuum in its midst.

95.

95.

Āvajjapañcaviññāṇasampaṭicchanatīraṇā;

Voṭṭhabbakāmajavanatadārammaṇanāmakā.

Adverting, fivefold sense-consciousness, receiving, investigating, determining, sensual-sphere impulsion, and registration—so are they named.

96.

96.

Satteva ṭhānasaṅkhepā, pañcadvārikamānasā;

Catupaññāsa sabbepi, vitthārena sarūpato.

In brief, there are just seven stages of the five-door mental process; in detail, all fifty-four are of their own nature.

97.

97.

Āvajjasabbajavanatadārammaṇanāmakā;

Sattasaṭṭhi sarūpena, manodvārikamānasā.

Adverting, all impulsions, and registration—so are named the mind-door mental states, sixty-seven in their own nature.

98.

98.

Iṭṭhe ārammaṇe honti, puññapākāni sabbathā;

Aniṭṭhe pāpapākāni, niyamoyaṃ pakāsito.
