Six causes are in the group of causes: the triads beginning with greed and non-greed. With doubt and restlessness included with delusion, they are there spoken of as eightfold.

401.

401.

Micchādiṭṭhi abhijjhā ca, byāpādo viratittayaṃ;

Sammādiṭṭhinabhijjhā ca, abyāpādo ca cetanā.

Wrong view, covetousness, and ill will, the three abstinences; right view, non-covetousness, and non-ill will, and volition.

402.

402.

Dasa kammapathānettha, vuttā viraticetanā;

Lokapālavināsāti, vuttā lokadukā dvidhā.

Herein, the ten courses of action are spoken of as abstinences and volitions; the two pairs concerning the world are spoken of as twofold: the guardians and the destroyers.

403.

403.

Passaddhiādiyugaḷā, niravajjā cha rāsayo;

Sati ca sampajaññañca, upakāradukaṃ bhave.

The pairs beginning with tranquility are six blameless groups; mindfulness and clear comprehension are the helpful pair.

404.

404.

Yuganandhadukaṃ nāma, samatho ca vipassanā;

Paggaho ca avikkhepo, samathaddukamīritaṃ.

The pair called 'yoked together' consists of serenity and insight; exertion and non-distraction are said to be the pair of serenity.

405.

405.

Ye sarūpena niddiṭṭhā, cittuppādesu tādinā;

Te ṭhapetvāvasesā tu, yevāpanakanāmakā.

Those that have been pointed out by their own nature in the arisings of consciousness by the Tathāgata—setting those aside, the remainder are named adventitious.

406.

406.

Chando ca adhimokkho ca, tatramajjhattatā tathā;

Uddhaccaṃ manasikāro, pañcāpaṇṇakanāmakā.

Intention and decision, and likewise neutrality of mind; restlessness and attention—these five are named the 'āpaṇṇaka'.

407.

407.

Māno ca thinamiddhañca, issā macchariyaṃ tathā;

Kukkuccamappamaññā ca, tisso viratiyopi ca.

Conceit, sloth and torpor, envy, and avarice; worry, the illimitables, and the three abstinences as well.

408.

408.

Ete [M 0.0036] aniyatā nāma, ekādasa yathārahaṃ;

Tato ca sesā sabbepi, niyatāti pakittitā.

These eleven, as appropriate, are named 'indeterminate'; all the rest are then declared to be 'determinate'.

409.

409.

Keci [V 0.0040] rāsiṃ na bhajanti, keci cāniyatā yato;

Tasmā yevāpanāteva, dhammā soḷasa desitā.

Since some do not belong to a fixed group, and some are indeterminate, therefore sixteen such factors are taught as 'adventitious' (yevāpanaka).

410.

410.

Sattatiṃsāvasesā tu, tattha tattha yathārahaṃ;

Sarūpeneva niddiṭṭhā, cittuppādesu sabbathā.

The remaining thirty-seven, however, are pointed out by their own nature, as is appropriate here and there in all arisings of consciousness.

411.

411.

Desitānuttaruddhacce, nāmato viratuddhavā;

Tathānuttaracittesu, niyataṃ viratittayaṃ.

Abstinence and restlessness are taught by name in the supramundane and restlessness contexts; likewise, in supramundane consciousnesses, the three abstinences are fixed.

412.

412.

Cittaṃ vitakko saddhā ca,

Hirottappabaladvayaṃ;

Alobho ca adoso ca,

Lobho doso ca diṭṭhi ca.

Consciousness, applied thought, and faith; the pair of powers, conscience and moral dread; non-greed and non-hatred; greed, hatred, and wrong view.

413.

413.

Ahirīkamanottappaṃ,

Uddhaccaṃ viratittayaṃ;

Soḷasete yathāyogaṃ,

Dvīsu ṭhānesu desitā.

Shamelessness and lack of moral dread, restlessness, and the three abstinences; these sixteen, as appropriate, are taught in two places.

414.

414.

Vedanā tīsu vīriyaṃ, sati ca caturāsikā;

Samādhi chasu paññā ca, sattaṭṭhānesu dīpitā.

Feeling is in three places; energy and mindfulness are in four groups; concentration is in six; and wisdom is explained in seven and eight places.

415.

415.

Ekavīsa paniccete, savibhattikanāmakā;

Sesā dvattiṃsati dhammā, sabbepi avibhattikāti.

These twenty-one are named 'divisible'; the remaining thirty-two factors are all 'indivisible'.

Iti cetasikavibhāge rāsisarūpakathā niṭṭhitā.

Thus in the Analysis of Mental Factors, the discourse on the groups and their nature is concluded.

Ekādasamo paricchedo.

The Eleventh Chapter.

Dvādasamo paricchedo

The Twelfth Chapter.

12. Rāsivinicchayakathā

12. The Discourse on the Determination of the Groups.

416.

416.

Tattha viññāṇakāyā cha, satta viññāṇadhātuyo;

Phassā cakkhādisamphassā, chabbidhā sattadhāpi ca.

Therein are the six bodies of consciousness and the seven consciousness-elements. Contacts—eye-contact and so on—are also sixfold and sevenfold.

417.

417.

Cakkhusamphassajādīhi[M 0.0037][V 0.0041], bhedehi pana vedanā;

Saññā ca cetanā ceva, bhinnā chadhā ca sattadhā.

But by the divisions beginning with that born of eye-contact, feeling, perception, and volition are also divided sixfold and sevenfold.

418.

418.

Cittuppādesu dhammā ca, khandhāyatanadhātuyo;

Āhārā ca yathāyogaṃ, phassapañcakarāsiyaṃ.

The dhammas in the arisings of consciousness—the aggregates, sense bases, elements, and nutriments, as is appropriate—are in the group of the five with contact.

419.

419.

Sabbe saṅgahitā honti, tasmā nāmapariggaho;

Mūlarāsi ca so sabba-saṅgahoti pavuccati.

All are included; therefore, this is the comprehension of mentality. And that root-group is called the 'all-inclusive'.

420.

420.

Jhānarāsimhi pañceva, dhammā sattappabhedato;

Indriyāni ca bāvīsa, dhammato pana soḷasa.

In the jhāna-group are five factors with seven divisions. The faculties are twenty-two, but in terms of phenomena, they are sixteen.

421.

421.

Nava maggaṅgadhammā ca, bhinnā dvādasadhāpi te;

Chaḷeva hetuyo tattha, desitā kaṅkhituddhavā.

And the nine path factors, which are also divided into twelve; six roots are taught therein, along with doubt and restlessness.

422.

422.

Dasa kammapathā dhammā, chaḷeva pana desitā;

Sesāva dasadhammehi, samānā caturāsayo.

The ten courses of action are taught, but as six factors. The remaining four groups are similar to these ten factors.

423.

423.

Paññā dasavidhā tattha, vedanā navadhā ṭhitā;

Samādhi sattadhā hoti, vīriyaṃ pana pañcadhā.

Therein, wisdom is tenfold, feeling is established as ninefold; concentration is sevenfold, and energy is fivefold.

424.

424.

Sati bhinnā catudhāva, vitakko tividho mato;

Dvidhā cittādayo honti, dasapañceva sambhavā.

Mindfulness is divided fourfold, applied thought is considered threefold; consciousness and others are twofold, being fifteen in all.

425.

425.

Sesā dvattiṃsa sabbepi, dhammā ekekadhāpi ca;

Hitvā rūpindriyānete, vibhāgā aṭṭhadhā kathaṃ.

All the remaining thirty-two factors are each singlefold. Excluding these form-faculties, how is there an eightfold division?

426.

426.

Phasso ca cetanā saññā, vicāro pīti jīvitaṃ;

Niravajjā cha yugaḷā, sāvajjamohakaṅkhitā.

Contact, volition, perception, sustained thought, joy, and the life-faculty; the six blameless pairs; and the faulty ones—delusion and doubt.

427.

427.

Yevāpanakadhammā ca, viratuddhaccavajjitā;

Dvādasā ceti sabbepi, dvattiṃsakekadhā tathā.

And the adventitious factors, excluding the abstinences and restlessness—these are twelve in all. Thus they are counted among the thirty-two singlefold factors.

428.

428.

Cittaṃ manindriyaṃ cittaṃ, saddhā saddhindriyaṃ balaṃ;

Balesu lokiyā vuttā, lokiye ca dukadvaye.

Consciousness is the mind-faculty and consciousness; faith is the faith-faculty and a power. Among the powers, they are said to be mundane and are in the two worldly pairs.

429.

429.

Lobhālobhādikā [M 0.0038][V 0.0042] dve dve,

Cattāro heturāsiyaṃ;

Micchādiṭṭhi ca maggaṅge,

Pañcakammapathepi te.

The pairs beginning with greed and non-greed are four factors in the group of roots. And wrong view is in the path factors; these are also in the five courses of action.

430.

430.

Yevāpanakarāsimhi, desitā viratuddhavā;

Maggahetūsu ceveti, dvidhā pañcadasa ṭhitā.

In the group of adventitious factors, abstinence and restlessness are taught; and also in the path factors and roots. Thus fifteen factors are established as twofold.

431.

431.

Vitakko jhānamaggesu, tividhā navadhā pana;

Vedanā mūlarāsimhi, tathā jhānindriyesu ca.

Applied thought, in the jhāna and path factors, is threefold. But feeling is ninefold, in the root-group and also in the jhāna factors and faculties.

432.

432.

Indriyamaggarāsimhi, balapiṭṭhidukattike;

Catudhā sati tattheva, vīriyampi ca pañcadhā.

In the aggregate of faculties and paths, in the powers and the Piṭṭhiduka pairs; therein mindfulness is fourfold, and energy is also fivefold.

433.

433.

Samādhi sattadhā vutto, jhānaṅgesu ca tattha ca;

Tattheva dasadhā paññā, hetukammapathesu ca.

Concentration is said to be sevenfold, in the jhānic factors and in those aggregates; therein wisdom is tenfold, in the roots and in the paths of kamma.

434.

434.

Dasanavasattapañcacatutidvekadhā ṭhitā;

Chaḷekakā pañcadasa, dvattiṃsa ca yathākkamaṃ.

They are established as tenfold, ninefold, sevenfold, fivefold, fourfold, threefold, twofold, and onefold; and there are six single factors, fifteen, and thirty-two, respectively.

435.

435.

Aṭṭha vibhāgasaṅkhepā, padāni dasadhā siyuṃ;

Tepaññāseva dhammā ca, aṭṭhārasa ca rāsayo.

There are eight divisions in brief, and the terms are tenfold; there are fifty-three dhammas indeed, and eighteen aggregates.

436.

436.

Iti dhammavavatthāne, dhammasaṅgaṇiyaṃ pana;

Cittuppādaparicchede, uddesanayasaṅgaho.

Thus, in the analysis of phenomena in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, in the Chapter on the Arising of Consciousness, this is the summary of the expository method.

437.

437.

Padāni caturāsīti, desitāni sarūpato;

Yevāpanakanāmena, soḷaseva yathārahaṃ.

Eighty-four terms are taught according to their own nature; by the name of Yevāpanaka, there are sixteen as is fitting.

438.

438.

Tatthāniyatanāmāni, padānekādaseva tu;

Vuttānekūnanavuti, niyatāneva sambhavā.

Therein, the terms named 'indeterminate' are but eleven; eighty-nine are stated, which are the determinate ones that occur.

439.

439.

Asambhinnapadānettha, tepaññāseva sabbathā;

Cittacetasikānaṃ tu, vasena paridīpaye.

Here, the uncombined terms are fifty-three in all; one should explain them by way of mind and mental factors.

440.

440.

Vibhāgapadadhammānaṃ[M 0.0039][V 0.0043], vasenevaṃ pakāsito;

Cittacetasikānaṃ tu, kamato rāsinicchayoti.

Thus is explained, by way of the divisions of terms and states, the determination of the aggregates of mind and mental factors in their order.

Iti cetasikavibhāge rāsivinicchayakathā niṭṭhitā.

Thus ends the discourse on the determination of aggregates in the Division of Mental Factors.

Dvādasamo paricchedo.

The Twelfth Chapter.

Terasamo paricchedo

The Thirteenth Chapter.

13. Rāsiyogakathā

13. The Discourse on the Combination of Aggregates

441.

441.

Iti rāsivīthiṃ ñatvā, labbhamānavasā budho;

Tesamevātha yogampi, cittuppādesu dīpaye.

Thus, having known the process of the aggregates, the wise one should then also explain their combination in the arisings of consciousness, in accordance with what is obtainable.

442.

442.

Kāmāvacarakusalassa, paṭhamadvayamānase;

Sabbepi rāsayo honti, yathāsambhavato kathaṃ.

In the first two types of wholesome sense-sphere consciousness, all the aggregates are present according to their possibility of occurrence. How so?

443.

443.

Phassapañcakarāsī ca, jhānapañcakarāsi ca;

Indriyaṭṭhakarāsī ca, maggapañcakarāsi ca.

The aggregate of the contact-pentad, the aggregate of the jhāna-pentad, the aggregate of the faculty-octad, and the aggregate of the path-pentad.

444.

444.

Balasattakarāsī ca, hetukammapathattikā;

Dasāvasesā rāsī ca, lokapāladukādayo.

And the aggregate of the power-heptad, the triads of roots and paths of kamma, the ten remaining aggregates, the pair of world-protectors, and so on.

445.

445.

Yevāpanakanavakaṃ, niyatuddhaccavajjitā;

Appamaññādvayañceva, tisso viratiyoti ca.

The nonad of Yevāpanakas, excluding the determinate ones and restlessness; and the pair of illimitables and the three abstinences.

446.

446.

Iti sattarasevete, desitā ca sarūpato;

Yevāpanakarāsī ca, labbhantiṭṭhārasāpi ca.

Thus these seventeen are taught according to their own nature; and the Yevāpanaka aggregates, eighteen in number, are also obtained.

447.

447.

Chappaññāsa padānettha, desitāni sarūpato;

Dhammā pana samatiṃsa, tattha honti sarūpato.

Here, fifty-six terms are taught according to their own nature; but thirty dhammas are present there according to their own nature.

448.

448.

Tāni [V 0.0044] yevāpanakehi, pañcasaṭṭhi padāni ca;

Dhammā cekūnatālīsa, bhavanti pana sambhavā.

With the Yevāpanakas, these become sixty-five terms; and thirty-nine dhammas are found to occur.

449.

449.

Tattha dvādasa dhammā ca, desitā savibhattikā;

Avasesā tu sabbepi, avibhattikanāmakā.

Therein, twelve dhammas are taught with classification; but all the remaining ones are named without classification.

450.

450.

Ekadvi [M 0.0040] ca ticatukka-chasattaṭṭhānikā pana;

Sattavīsa ca satteko, dvekeko ca yathākkamaṃ.

But they are in positions of one, two, three, four, six, seven, and eight; and twenty-seven, seventy-one, two, and one, respectively.

451.

451.

Niyatā tu catuttiṃsa, dhammāva sahavuttito;

Yathāsambhavavuttito, pañcadhā niyatā kathā.

But thirty-four dhammas are determinate due to their co-arising; according to their stated possibility of occurrence, the discourse on the determinate is fivefold.

452.

452.

Tattha cāniyate sabbe, gahetvā ca pahāya ca;

Paccekañca gahetvāpi, sattadhā yojanakkamo.

Therein, with all the indeterminate ones, by taking and abandoning, and also by taking them individually, the procedure of combination is sevenfold.

453.

453.

Sakimekūnatālīsa, catuttiṃsa yathākkamaṃ;

Pañcakkhattuñca yojeyya, pañcatiṃsāti paṇḍito.

The wise one should combine them: once thirty-nine and thirty-four respectively; and five times, yielding thirty-five.

454.

454.

Rāsayo ca padānīdha, dhammantaravibhattiyo;

Sarūpayevāpanake, niyatāniyate yathā.

The aggregates and terms here; the classifications of the different dhammas; the own-nature and the Yevāpanakas; the determinate and the indeterminate, as they are.

455.

455.

Yojanānayabhedañca, gaṇanāsaṅgahaṭṭhiti;

Labbhamānānumānena, sallakkhento tahiṃ tahiṃ.

And the different methods of combination; the counting, the summary, and the fixed positions; by inference from what is obtainable, discerning in each particular case.

456.

456.

Ñāṇaṃ ñāṇaviyuttamhi, hitvā pītiṃ upekkhite;

Vedanā parivattento, kāmapuññe ca sesake.

In consciousness dissociated from knowledge, one abandons knowledge; in that accompanied by equanimity, one abandons joy, thus changing the feeling in the remaining types of sense-sphere merit.

457.

457.

Mahākriye ca yojeyya, pahāya viratittayaṃ;

Appamaññā ca hitvātha, mahāpāke ca yojaye.

One should apply this in the great functional consciousness, having abandoned the three abstinences; and then, having abandoned the illimitables, one should apply it in the great resultant consciousness.

458.

458.

Takkādiṃ kamato hitvā, sabbattha viratittayaṃ;

Pañcame appamaññāya, hitvā rūpe ca yojaye.

Having abandoned applied thought and so on in order, and everywhere the three abstinences; in the fifth jhāna, having abandoned the illimitables, one should apply this in the form-sphere jhānas.

459.

459.

Hitvāppamaññā yojaye, yathājhānamanuttare;

Lokuttarindriyañceva, gahetvā viratittayaṃ.

Having abandoned the illimitables, one should apply this according to the jhānas in the supramundane; and having taken up the supramundane faculty and the three abstinences.

460.

460.

Jhānāni [V 0.0045] catutālīsa, sukhayuttāni vattare;

Upekkhitāni tevīsa, pañcamajjhāne ca sabbathā.

Forty-four jhānas are said to be associated with happiness; twenty-three are accompanied by equanimity, and always so in the fifth jhāna.

461.

461.

Appamaññāviratiyo, kāmapuññesu labbhare;

Appamaññā rūpajjhāna-catukke ca mahākriye.

The illimitables and the abstinences are obtained in sense-sphere merit; the illimitables are also obtained in the tetrad of form-sphere jhānas and in the great functional consciousness.

462.

462.

Lokuttaresu sabbattha, sambhoti viratittayaṃ;

Natthidvayampi āruppe, mahāpāke ca pañcame.

The three abstinences arise in all supramundane states. Neither of the two is found in the formless sphere, in the great resultant consciousness, or in the fifth jhāna.

463.

463.

Vitakkādittayaṃ [M 0.0041] paññā, pañca cāniyatā calā;

Hānibuddhivasā sesā, na calanti kudācanaṃ.

The triad beginning with applied thought, wisdom, and the five indeterminate factors are unstable, being subject to decline and growth; the remaining ones never waver.

464.

464.

Bāvīsatividho cettha, saṅgaho anavajjake;

Dvayadvayavasā ceva, jhānapañcakatopi ca.

Here in the blameless states, the summary is twenty-twofold: by way of pairs and also from the jhāna-pentad.

465.

465.

Iti ñatvānavajjesu, rāsisaṅgaha sambhavaṃ;

Sāvajjesupi viññeyyā, viññunā rāsayo kathaṃ.

Thus, having known the arising of the summary of aggregates in the blameless states, the aggregates in the blameworthy states should also be understood by the wise one. How so?

466.

466.

Lobhamūlesu paṭhame, phassapañcakarāsi ca;

Jhānapañcakarāsī ca, tathevindriyapañcakaṃ.

In the first of the consciousnesses rooted in greed, there are the aggregate of the contact-pentad, the aggregate of the jhāna-pentad, and likewise the faculty-pentad.

467.

467.

Maggabalacatukkañca, hetukammapathadukā;

Lokanāsakarāsī ca, samatho samathaddukā.

And the tetrad of path and power, the pairs of roots and paths of kamma, the aggregate that destroys the world, serenity, and the pair related to serenity.

468.

468.

Tatramajjhattataṃ hitvā, yevāpanakanāmakā;

Cattāro ceti labbhanti, tatthekādasa rāsayo.

Excluding equanimity here, those called 'inclusive' are four. Herein, eleven aggregates are obtained.

469.

469.

Dvattiṃseva padānettha, desitāni sarūpato;

Tāni yevāpanakehi, chattiṃseva bhavanti ca.

Thirty-two terms are taught here according to their nature. With the inclusive factors, they become thirty-six.

470.

470.

Asambhinnapadānettha, samavīsati sambhavā;

Savibhattikanāmā ca, nava dhammā pakāsitā.

Here, twenty phenomena arise with unmixed terms. And nine phenomena are explained with their distinctions.

471.

471.

Ekadvayaticatukka-chaṭṭhānaniyatā pana;

Ekādasa chaḷekā ca, kameneko punekako.

Fixed in positions of one, two, three, four, and six are, respectively: eleven, six, one, one, and again one.

472.

472.

Natthevāniyatā [V 0.0046] hettha, yevāpanakanāmakā;

Yojanānayabhedo ca, tasmā tattha na vijjati.

Herein, the indeterminate factors, those named 'inclusive', do not exist; therefore, the distinction of application and method is not found there.

473.

473.

Māno ca thinamiddhañca, issā macchariyaṃ tathā;

Kukkuccamiti sāvajje, chaḷevāniyatā matā.

Conceit, sloth and torpor, envy, and likewise avarice, and remorse—thus, these six are considered the indeterminate factors among the blameworthy.

474.

474.

Māno diṭṭhiviyuttesu, sasaṅkhāresu pañcasu;

Thinamiddhaṃ tayo sesā, paṭighadvayayogino.

Conceit is in the states dissociated from wrong view; sloth and torpor are in the five prompted states; the remaining three are associated with the two states of aversion.

475.

475.

Iccevamaṭṭha [M 0.0042] sāvajjā, anavajjaṭṭhavīsati;

Chattiṃsa mānasā sabbe, hontāniyatayogino.

Thus, eight are blameworthy and twenty-eight are blameless. All thirty-six mental factors are associated with the indeterminate.

476.

476.

Tehi yuttā yathāyogaṃ, ekadvittayapañcahi;

Dve dvāvīsaṃ tayo ceva, nava cātha yathākkamaṃ.

Connected with these, as is appropriate, by one, two, three, and five, are two, twenty-two, three, and then nine, respectively.

477.

477.

Iti vuttānusārena, labbhamānavasā pana;

Tadaññesupi yojeyya, sāvajjesu yathākkamaṃ.

Thus, in accordance with what has been stated and according to what is obtainable, one should apply this to the other blameworthy factors as well, in due order.

478.

478.

Lobhamūlesu lobhañca, dosañca paṭighadvaye;

Mohamūle kaṅkhuddhaccaṃ, gahetvā heturāsiyaṃ.

Greed in the greed-rooted states, hatred in the two states of aversion, and doubt and restlessness in the delusion-rooted states are to be taken in the aggregate of roots.

479.

479.

Diṭṭhiṃ diṭṭhiviyuttamhi, hitvā pītimupekkhite;

Vedanaṃ parivattento, dosamūle ca paṇḍito.

The wise one, having excluded wrong view in the states dissociated from wrong view, and joy in the states accompanied by equanimity, and by substituting the feeling in the aversion-rooted states, should apply the analysis.

480.

480.

Tathā kammapathaṃ diṭṭhiṃ,

Pītiṃ chandañca momuhe;

Kaṅkhite adhimokkhañca,

Hitvā yojeyya rāsayo.

Likewise, having excluded the course of action, wrong view, joy, and desire in the delusion-rooted states, and resolution in the doubt-accompanied state, one should apply the aggregates.

481.

481.

Cittassa ṭhitiṃ pattāsu, cittassekaggatā pana;

Kaṅkhite parihīnāva, indriyādīsu pañcasu.

However, in the doubt-accompanied state, stability of mind and one-pointedness of mind are indeed deficient, as are the five groups beginning with the faculties.

482.

482.

Iti dvādasadhā ñatvā, sāvajjesupi saṅgahaṃ;

Ahetukepi viññeyyā, yathāsambhavato kathaṃ.

Thus, having known the grouping in twelve ways in the blameworthy states, the exposition concerning the rootless states should also be understood according to their possible occurrence.

483.

483.

Aṭṭhārasāhetukesu[V 0.0047], pañcaviññāṇamānase;

Phassapañcakarāsī ca, jhānaṭṭhānadukaṃ tathā.

In the eighteen rootless states, in the five sense-consciousnesses and the mind-element, there are the aggregate of the contact-pentad and likewise the dyad of jhāna-foundations.

484.

484.

Indriyattikarāsī ca, yevāpanakanāmako;

Eko manasikāroti, cattāro rāsayo siyuṃ.

The aggregate of the faculty-triad, and that which is named 'inclusive'; and the single factor of attention—thus there are four aggregates.

485.

485.

Asambhinnā panaṭṭheva, dve tattha savibhattikā;

Ekadvayatikaṭṭhānā, chaḷeko ca punekako.

Indeed, eight are unmixed, and two there are with distinctions. Fixed in one, two, and three positions are six, one, and again one.

486.

486.

Manodhātuttikāhetu-paṭisandhiyuge pana;

Vitakko ca vicāro ca, adhikā jhānarāsiyaṃ.

However, in the mind-element triad and the rootless rebirth-linking pair, initial application and sustained application are additional in the jhāna aggregate.

487.

487.

Sukhasantīraṇe [M 0.0043] pīti, dutiyāvajjane pana;

Vīriyañca samādhiñca, labbhatindriyarāsiyaṃ.

Joy is obtained in the pleasurable investigating consciousness; however, in the mind-door adverting consciousness, energy and concentration are obtained in the faculty aggregate.

488.

488.

Adhikā hasite honti, pīti ca vīriyādayo;

Yevāpanādhimokkho ca, pañcaviññāṇavajjite.

Additional in the laughter-producing consciousness are joy, energy, and so forth; and the inclusive factor of resolution, except in the five sense-consciousnesses.

489.

489.

Iccānavajje bāvīsa,

Sāvajje dvādasāpare;

Yogā hetumhi pañcete,

Tālīsekūnakā kathāti.

Thus, there are twenty-two in the blameless, and twelve others in the blameworthy; these five connections are in the rooted states. Thus is the discourse on the thirty-nine.

Iti cetasikavibhāge rāsiyogakathā niṭṭhitā.

Thus, in the Analysis of Mental Factors, the Discourse on the Application of Aggregates is concluded.

Terasamo paricchedo.

The Thirteenth Chapter.

Cuddasamo paricchedo

The Fourteenth Chapter.

14. Rāsisambhavakathā

14. The Discourse on the Occurrence of Aggregates.

490.

490.

Naveva [V 0.0048] yevāpanakā, aṭṭhārasa ca rāsayo;

Navabhiṃsatisambhinnā, dasa dve savibhattikā.

There are indeed nine inclusive factors and eighteen aggregates. Twenty-nine are mixed, and twelve are with distinctions.

491.

491.

Ekadvayaticatuchasattaṭṭhānānavajjake;

Sattavīsati satteko, dvayameko punekako.

In the blameless, fixed in one, two, three, four, six, seven, and eight positions are, respectively: twenty-seven, seven, one, two, one, and again one.

492.

492.

Daseva yevāpanakā, ekādasa ca rāsayo;

Aṭṭhavīsatisambhinnā, daseva savibhattikā.

There are indeed ten inclusive factors and eleven aggregates. Twenty-eight are mixed, and indeed ten are with distinctions.

493.

493.

Ekadvayaticatukkachaṭṭhānaniyatā pana;

Aṭṭhārasa ca satteko, eko cekova pāpake.

In the unwholesome states, however, fixed in one, two, three, four, and six positions are eighteen, seven, one, and just one, respectively.

494.

494.

Dve yevāpanakā honti, rāsayo ca catubbidhā;

Terasettha asambhinnā, tayova savibhattikā.

There are two inclusive factors and four kinds of aggregates. Herein, thirteen are unmixed, and indeed three are with distinctions.

495.

495.

Ekadvayatikaṭṭhānā, dasa dveko ahetuke;

Iccānavajjā sāvajjā-hetuke yoganicchayo.

Fixed in one, two, and three positions in the rootless are ten, two, and one, respectively. Thus is the determination of connections in the blameless, blameworthy, and rootless states.

496.

496.

Sattāpi [M 0.0044] natthi sāvajje, niravajje pakāsako;

Ahetuke ca maggādirāsayo natthi cuddasa.

Seven factors are not found in the blameworthy, which is explained in the section on the blameless. And in the rootless states, the fourteen aggregates beginning with the path-aggregate are not found.

497.

497.

Anavajjā tu sāvajje, sāvajjakānavajjake;

Cittuppādamhi nattheva, natthobhayamahetuke.

The blameless are not found in a blameworthy consciousness, nor are the blameworthy in a blameless one. Indeed, in a rootless consciousness, neither is found.

498.

498.

Sāvajjā pana sāvajje, anavajjānavajjake;

Gahetabbā tu sabbattha, sādhāraṇā pakiṇṇakā.

The blameworthy factors are to be taken in the blameworthy consciousness, and the blameless in the blameless. But the common and miscellaneous factors should be taken everywhere.

499.

499.

Jhānapañcakacittesu, sattasaṭṭhisu niddise;

Jhānaṅgayogabhedena, rāsibhedaṃ tahiṃ tahiṃ.

In the sixty-seven consciousnesses of the fivefold jhāna system, one should indicate the division of groups in each case by the distinction in the combination of jhāna factors.

500.

500.

Catuchakkānavajjesu[V 0.0049], ñāṇapītikataṃ tathā;

Catuvīsa parittesu, catudhā bhedamuddise.

In the four sixes of blameless consciousness, the distinction is likewise made by knowledge and joy. In the twenty-four minor consciousnesses, one should indicate a fourfold division.

501.

501.

Sarāgavītarāgānaṃ, appamaññāpavattiyaṃ;

Karuṇāmuditā honti, kāmapuññamahākriye.

For beings with and without attachment, in the occurrence of the immeasurables, compassion and appreciative joy are present in the sense-sphere meritorious and great functional consciousnesses.

502.

502.

Upacārappanāpattā, sukhitā sattagocarā;

Tasmā na pañcamāruppe, mahāpāke anuttare.

Having attained access and absorption, they have happy beings as their object. Therefore, they are not found in the fifth formless attainment, in the great resultant consciousnesses, or in the supramundane consciousnesses.

503.

503.

Sotāpatitupekkhāsu, parikammādisambhave;

Jhānānaṃ tulyapākattā, tappākesu ca labbhare.

In the equanimity-accompanied consciousness of stream-entry, and in the arising of preliminary practice and so on, because of the corresponding result of the jhānas, they are obtained in their resultant consciousnesses as well.

504.

504.

Viratī ca sarāgānaṃ, vītikkamanasambhavā;

Sampatte ca samādāne, kāmapuññesu labbhare.

And for those with attachment, the abstinences, arising from the overcoming of transgression, are found in sense-sphere meritorious consciousnesses both on occasion and by undertaking.

505.

505.

Taṃtaṃdvārikadussilya-cetanucchedakiccato;

Magge ca tulyapākattā, phale ca niyatā siyuṃ.

In the path, because of their function of cutting off the volition for immoral conduct at the respective doors, and due to the corresponding result, they are also fixed in the fruition.

506.

506.

Pavattākāravisayabhinnā pañcāpi sambhavā;

Lokiye labbhamānāpi, visuṃ ceva siyuṃ na vā.

The five kinds of arising, distinguished by mode of occurrence and object, although found in the mundane sphere, may be separate or they may not be.

507.

507.

Pāpā labbhanti pāpesu, satta chakkekakā kamā;

Sarūpayevobhayakā, niyataṭṭha chaḷetare.

Unwholesome factors are found in unwholesome consciousnesses: seven, six, one, and one, respectively. Both are of the same nature; the other six have eight fixed factors.

508.

508.

Sādhāraṇā ca sabbattha, yathāvuttā pakiṇṇakā;

Tattha cekaggatā natthi, indriyādīsu kaṅkhite.

The miscellaneous factors, as stated, are common to all. Therein, one-pointedness is absent when there is doubt concerning the faculties and so on.

509.

509.

Chandādhimokkhā [M 0.0045] yevāpi, vīsekādasavajjite;

Uddhaccamekādasasu, majjhattamanavajjake.

Desire and decision are excluded from twenty and eleven consciousnesses respectively; restlessness is in eleven, and neutrality is in the blameless ones.

510.

510.

Sabbattha manasikāro, tidvekadvitikāpare;

Aṭṭhaṭṭhavīsacatūsu, pañcadvīsu yathākkamaṃ.

Attention is found everywhere. The other factors are found as three, two, and two in eight, twenty-eight, four, five, and two consciousnesses, respectively.

511.

511.

Samudāyavasenettha, uddhaccaviratittayaṃ;

Savibhattikamaññattha, avibhattikameva taṃ.

Here, by way of combination, are restlessness and the three abstinences. Elsewhere, they are taken with distinctions, or simply without distinction.

512.

512.

Cittuppādesu [V 0.0050] tenetaṃ, vibhattiavibhattikaṃ;

Iti sādhu sallakkheyya, sambhavāsambhavaṃ budhoti.

Therefore, in the arisings of consciousness, this is with and without distinction. Thus a wise person should well discern the possible and the impossible.

Iti cetasikavibhāge rāsisambhavakathā niṭṭhitā.

Thus ends the discussion on the occurrence of the groups in the Analysis of Mental Factors.

Cuddasamo paricchedo.

The Fourteenth Chapter.

Pannarasamo paricchedo

The Fifteenth Chapter.

15. Rāsisaṅgahakathā

15. The Discussion on the Summary of Groups.

513.

513.

Tettiṃsa ceva dvattiṃsa, ekatiṃsa ca tiṃsa ca;

Ekadvattiṃsahīnā ca, tiṃsa dhammānavajjake.

Thirty-three, thirty-two, thirty-one, thirty, thirty-one, and thirty are the factors in the faultless states.

514.

514.

Dasa dhammā tu sāvajje, chapañcacaturādhikā;

Ekādasa dasa nava, sattadhāhetuke pana.

But in the blameworthy states, there are ten factors increased by six, five, and four respectively. In the rootless states, however, there are eleven, ten, nine, and seven.

515.

515.

Itthaṃ cuddasadhā bhinnā, koṭṭhāsā tu sarūpato;

Vibhattā tehi yuttā ca, cittuppādā yathākkamaṃ.

Thus the portions are divided in fourteen ways according to their nature. The arisings of consciousness are classified accordingly and associated with them in sequence.

516.

516.

Tikaṭṭhakā pañcavīsa, dasa pañcādhikā nava;

Aṭṭhāraseti sattete, anavajjā tathetare.

Three, eight, twenty-five, ten, fifteen, nine, and eighteen. These seven are the faultless groups; likewise the others.

517.

517.

Dve cattāro chaḷekaṃ dve,

Pañcātha dasadhāpare;

Sāvajjāhetukā ceti,

Koṭṭhāsā honti cuddasa.

Two, four, six, one, two; then five and the other ten; and the blameworthy and the rootless: thus there are fourteen portions.

518.

518.

Nava [M 0.0046] cāpi cha cattāro, catupañcachasattakā;

Nava dve dve tatheko ca, yevāpanakasaṅgahā.

Nine, six, four; four, five, six, seven; nine, two, two, and also one: this is the summary of the sometimes-present factors.

519.

519.

Tehi [V 0.0051] yuttā panaṭṭhātha, vīsekatiṃsa mānasā;

Dve dve dve tīṇi cekaṃ dve, aṭṭha dasa yathākkamaṃ.

Then, associated with them are established the consciousnesses: eight, twenty, thirty-one; two, two, two, three; one, two; eight, and ten, in due order.

520.

520.

Sattatiṃsakato yāva, ekatiṃsānavajjake;

Tikaṭṭhakādike satta, ṭhitā niyatasaṅgahā.

From thirty-seven down to thirty-one factors are found in the faultless states. The seven groups beginning with the triads and octads are established as fixed combinations.

521.

521.

Pāpesu vīsa cekūna-vīsaṭṭhārasa soḷasa;

Catudhā dvīsu catūsu, catūsu dvīsu caṭṭhitā.

In the unwholesome states, there are twenty, nineteen, eighteen, and sixteen factors. They are established in four ways: in two, in four, in four, and in two consciousnesses.

522.

522.

Ekadvipañcadasasu, ca dvidhāhetukesu ca;

Tikadvekādhikā dhammā, dasaṭṭha ca yathākkamaṃ.

In one, two, five, and fifteen consciousnesses, and in the two kinds of rootless states, the factors are increased by three, two, and one; and are ten and eight, respectively.

523.

523.

Pañcadvekadvibhipañca, koṭṭhāsā niyatā ṭhitā;

Tehi yuttā panaṭṭhātha, vīsa dve dve tikekakā.

Five, two, two, and five portions are established as fixed. Associated with them are established: twenty, two, two, a triad, and a single one.

524.

524.

Pubbāparadvayāpuññe, kāmapāke ahetuke;

Pañcamānuttarāruppe, natthāniyatasambhavo.

In the former and latter pairs of unwholesome consciousness, in sense-sphere resultants, in the rootless, in the fifth jhāna, in the supramundane, and in the formless states, there is no occurrence of the unfixed factors.

525.

525.

Chattiṃsamānasesveva, labbhantāniyatā na vā;

Tepaññāsāvasesā tu, sabbe niyatayogino.

Only in the thirty-six consciousnesses are the unfixed factors found, sometimes present and sometimes not. But the other fifty-three are all associated only with fixed factors.

526.

526.

Niyatāniyate katvā, labbhantobhayathā tathā;

Sarūpayevobhayakā, tividhevaṃ tu saṅgahā.

Thus, being divided into fixed and unfixed, they are obtained in both ways. Both are of the same nature. In this way, the summary is threefold.

527.

527.

Ñeyyā vuttānusārena, tehi yuttāva mānasā;

Tato puna vibhāveyya, sabbasaṅgāhikaṃ nayaṃ.

The consciousnesses associated with them should be known according to the method stated. Then one should further analyze the all-inclusive method.

528.

528.

Ekūnatālīsakato, yāvekattiṃsakā ṭhitā;

Navadhā anavajjesu, tehi yuttā ca mānasā.

In nine ways, the factors in the faultless states are established, numbering from thirty-nine down to thirty-one, as are the consciousnesses associated with them.

529.

529.

Dve cattāro dasevātha, tikapañcādhikā dasa;

Tevīsa kamato satta, dve ca pañcadasāpare.

Two, four, and then ten; thirteen and fifteen; twenty-three and seven in sequence; and the other two and fifteen.

530.

530.

Dve ca dve tikadve dvekā, sāvajjesu ca soḷasa;

Ekūnavīsa vīsātha, vīsekadvitayādhikā.

Two and two, a triad, a pair, and a single one; and sixteen in the blameworthy states. Then nineteen and twenty, and twenty plus one, two, and three.

531.

531.

Ahetuke [M 0.0047][V 0.0052] panaṭṭhātha, dasekadvitayādhikā;

Dasapañca dvikekāti, bhavantekūnavīsati.

But then in the rootless states: eight; ten plus one, two, and three; ten, five, two, and one. Thus they become nineteen.

532.

532.

Labbhamānānusārena, dhammānaṃ pana saṅgaho;

Sakkā vuttanayeneva, viññātuṃ pana viññunāti.

The summary of factors, according to how they are obtained, can indeed be understood by the wise through the method already stated.

Iti cetasikavibhāge rāsisaṅgahakathā niṭṭhitā.

Thus ends the Discussion on the Summary of Groups in the Analysis of Mental Factors.

Pannarasamo paricchedo.

The Fifteenth Chapter.

Soḷasamo paricchedo

The Sixteenth Chapter.

16. Cittuppādakathā

16. The Discussion on the Arising of Consciousness.

533.

533.

Cittuppādesu dhammānaṃ, iti ñatvā vinicchayaṃ;

Cittuppādānamevātha, ñātabbo bhedasaṅgaho.

Having thus known the determination of factors in the arisings of consciousness, one should then understand the summary of the divisions of the arisings of consciousness themselves.

534.

534.

Vedanāhārato ceva, hetādhipatito tathā;

Jhānindriyamaggabalā, yevāpanapathādito.

From feeling and nutriment, and likewise from root and dominance; from jhāna, faculty, path, and power; and from the way of impulsion and so on.

535.

535.

Tattha sukhā ca dukkhā ca, adukkhamasukhāti ca;

Tisso ca vedanā vuttā, sambhogatthavisesato.

Therein, pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant—three feelings are spoken of, specifically with regard to the nature of experience.

536.

536.

Sukhaṃ dukkhaṃ somanassaṃ, domanassamathāparaṃ;

Upekkhindriyamiccevaṃ, pañcindriyavibhāgato.

Pleasure, pain, joy, displeasure, and the other, the faculty of equanimity—thus is the division into five faculties.

537.

537.

Kāyaviññāṇayugaḷe, sukhadukkhā hi vedanā;

Somanassaṃ domanassaṃ, iti nāmaṃ labhanti na.

In the pair of body-consciousness, feelings are indeed pleasure and pain; they do not obtain the names 'joy' and 'displeasure'.

538.

538.

Aññattha pana sabbattha, sukhā dukkhā ca vedanā;

Somanassaṃ domanassaṃ, iti nāmaṃ labhanti ca.

However, in all other cases, pleasant and painful feelings also acquire the names 'joy' and 'displeasure'.

539.

539.

Adukkhi [V 0.0053] asukhopekkhā, majjhattāti ca vedanā;

Pañcapaññāsacittesu, tadaññesu pakāsitā.

The feeling which is neither painful nor pleasant, that is, equanimity or neutrality, is declared in the other fifty-five types of consciousness.

540.

540.

Sukhadukkhindriyayuttaṃ, kāyaviññāṇakadvayaṃ;

Domanassindriyayuttaṃ, paṭighadvayamānasaṃ.

The pair of body-consciousnesses is associated with the faculties of pleasure and pain; the pair of consciousnesses accompanied by aversion is associated with the faculty of displeasure.

541.

541.

Aṭṭhārasa [M 0.0048] parittāni, catukkajjhānamādito;

Somanassindriyayuttā, dvāsaṭṭhividha mānasā.

Associated with the faculty of joy are sixty-two types of consciousness: eighteen sense-sphere ones, and those connected with the four jhānas.

542.

542.

Dvattiṃsa ca parittāni, tevīsa jhānapañcamā;

Hontipekkhindriyayuttā, pañcapaññāsa mānasā.

Thirty-two sense-sphere consciousnesses and twenty-three connected with the fifth jhāna; these fifty-five consciousnesses are associated with the faculty of equanimity.

543.

543.

Sukhayuttā tu tesaṭṭhi, dukkhayuttā tayo tahiṃ;

Adukkhamasukhayuttā, pañcapaññāsupekkhakā.

Sixty-three are associated with pleasure, and three therein with pain; fifty-five are associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, that is, with equanimity.

544.

544.

Ojaṭṭhamakarūpañca, vedanaṃ sandhimānasaṃ;

Nāmarūpañca kamato, āharantīti desitā.

Material form with nutritive essence as its eighth constituent, feeling, rebirth-linking consciousness, and name-and-form—these, in order, they nourish. Thus it has been taught.

545.

545.

Āhārā kabaḷīkāro, phasso sañcetanā tathā;

Viññāṇañceti cattāro, upatthambhā ca sambhavā.

The nutriments are edible food, contact, mental volition, and consciousness. These four are supporters and producers of existence.

546.

546.

Cittuppādesu sabbattha,

Āhārārūpino tayo;

Kabaḷīkāro āhāro,

Kāme kāyānupālako.

In all occurrences of consciousness, three nutriments are immaterial. The nutriment of edible food is the preserver of the body in the sense-sphere.

547.

547.

Alobho ca adoso ca,

Amoho ca tathāparo;

Lobho doso ca moho ca,

Hetū dhammā cha desitā.

Non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion, and likewise their opposites, greed, hatred, and delusion—these six things are taught as the root-conditions.

548.

548.

Kusalākusalā hetū, tayo abyākatāti ca;

Navadvādasadhā tattha, vipākakriyabhedato.

The roots are wholesome and unwholesome; three are also indeterminate. Therein, by the distinction between resultant and functional, they are of nine and twelve kinds.

549.

549.

Dasa [V 0.0054] pañcādhikā honti, bhūmibhedā tato tahiṃ;

Puññapākakriyābhedā, tālīsa catunūnakā.

Therein, by distinction of plane, there are fifteen kinds; by distinction of meritorious, resultant, and functional, there are thirty-six kinds.

550.

550.

Santīraṇamanodhātu-pañcaviññāṇamānase;

Voṭṭhabbane ca hasite, hetu nāma na vijjati.

In the investigating consciousness, the mind-element, the five sense-consciousnesses, the determining consciousness, and the smiling consciousness, no root is found.

551.

551.

Lobhamūlesu [M 0.0049] lobho ca,

Moho ca paṭighadvaye;

Doso moho ca labbhanti,

Moho ekova momuhe.

In the greed-rooted consciousnesses, greed and delusion are found; in the two rooted in aversion, hatred and delusion are found; in the delusion-rooted consciousnesses, only delusion is found.

552.

552.

Ñāṇena vippayuttesu,

Alobhādidvayaṃ bhave;

Tato sesesu sabbattha,

Alobhāditayopi ca.

In consciousnesses dissociated from knowledge, there is a pair of roots beginning with non-greed; in all the remaining cases, there is also the triad of roots beginning with non-greed.

553.

553.

Tihetukā sattacattā-līsa honti dvihetukā;

Bāvīsa dvekahetukā, aṭṭhārasa ahetukā.

Forty-seven are triple-rooted, twenty-two are double-rooted, two are single-rooted, and eighteen are rootless.

554.

554.

Chando cittañca vīriyaṃ, vīmaṃsāti catubbidhā;

Sahajātādhipā dhammā, vuttādhipatayo siyuṃ.

Intention, consciousness, energy, and investigation—these four are conditions of conascent dominance; they are said to be the dominants.

555.

555.

Yamālambaṃ garuṃ katvā, nāmadhammā pavattare;

Ārammaṇādhipanāmena, tadālambaṇamīritaṃ.

When mental phenomena proceed by taking an object as predominant, that object is called the condition of object-dominance.

556.

556.

Tihetukajavesveko, catūsupi yathārahaṃ;

Dvihetukesu sambhoti, vīmaṃsādhipatiṃ vinā.

In triple-rooted javanas, any one of the four dominants may arise, as is appropriate. In double-rooted javanas, any of the three may arise, but not the investigation-dominant.

557.

557.

Anuttare kāmapuññe, tihetukamahākriye;

Lobhamūle ca sāvajje, labbhatālambaṇādhipo.

Object-dominance is obtainable in supramundane consciousness, in sense-sphere meritorious consciousness, in triple-rooted great functional consciousness, and in blameworthy greed-rooted consciousness.

558.

558.

Tattha cāniyatā kāme, labbhamānāpi labbhare;

Mahaggatānuttaresu, niyatāva yathārahaṃ.

Therein, in the sense-sphere, the dominance is unfixed and arises only when the conditions are met. In the sublime and supramundane consciousnesses, it is fixed and arises as is appropriate.

559.

559.

Kriyādvihetupaṭighe[V 0.0055],

Natthevālambaṇādhipo;

Momūhāhetuke pāke,

Lokiye ca na kocipi.

There is no object-dominance in functional, double-rooted, and aversion-rooted consciousness; nor in delusion-rooted, rootless, and worldly resultant consciousness.

560.

560.

Ubhayādhipayuttā ca, sahajādhipayogino;

Ubhayāniyatādhippā, sahajāniyatādhipā.

Consciousnesses are classified in five ways: (1) those associated with both dominances; (2) those associated with conascent dominance; (3) those with both dominances unfixed; (4) those with conascent dominance unfixed;

561.

561.

Ubhayavippayuttā [M 0.0050] ca, pañcadhā tattha mānasā;

Aṭṭhaṭṭhārasa vīsaṃ cha, sattatiṃsa yathākkamaṃ.

(5) and those dissociated from both. The number of consciousnesses in these categories are, respectively: eight, eighteen, twenty, six, and thirty-seven.

562.

562.

Pañcādhipatiyogā ca, caturādhipayogino;

Tividhādhipayuttā ca, vimuttāpi ca sabbathā.

Another fourfold classification is: (1) those associated with five kinds of dominance; (2) those associated with four kinds of dominance; (3) those associated with three kinds of dominance; (4) and those wholly liberated from them.

563.

563.

Soḷasātha samattiṃsa, chaḷevātha yathākkamaṃ;

Sattatiṃsatividhāti, catudhevampi niddise.

The number of consciousnesses are, respectively: sixteen, thirty, six, and thirty-seven. Thus it is indicated in four ways.

564.

564.

Vīmaṃsādhipayuttā ca, sahajādhipayogino;

Ālambādhipayuttā ca, vippamuttāpi sabbathā.

A further fourfold classification is: (1) those associated with investigation-dominance; (2) those associated with conascent dominance; (3) those associated with object-dominance; (4) and those altogether liberated from them.

565.

565.

Catuttiṃsa dvipaññāsa, aṭṭhavīsa yathākkamaṃ;

Sattatiṃsati ceveti, catudhevampi niddise.

The numbers are, respectively: thirty-four, fifty-two, twenty-eight, and thirty-seven. Thus it is also indicated in four ways.

566.

566.

Sahajādhipaladdhā tu, dvepaññāseva sabbathā;

Ālambādhipaladdhā ca, ubhayādhipalābhino.

In all, fifty-two types of consciousness can have conascent dominance. Those that can have object dominance and those that can have both...

567.

567.

Aṭṭhavīseva sabbepi, dvepaññāseva sādhipā;

Sesā nirādhipā sabbe, sattatiṃsāpi sabbathā.

...are twenty-eight in all. Thus, fifty-two are with dominance. The remaining thirty-seven are all without dominance.

568.

568.

Vedanādivasenevaṃ, ñatvā bhedaṃ catubbidhaṃ;

Jhānindriyamaggabala-vasenāpi vibhāvaye.

Having thus known the fourfold distinction by way of feeling and so on, one should also analyze consciousness by way of the jhāna factors, faculties, path factors, and powers.

569.

569.

Vitakkaheṭṭhimaṃ jhānaṃ, manoparaṃ manindriyaṃ;

Hetuparañca maggaṅgaṃ, balaṃ vīriyapacchimaṃ.

The analysis of jhāna factors begins with initial application; the faculties considered are those up to the mind-faculty; path factors are absent in rootless consciousnesses; and powers are absent in those without energy.

570.

570.

Avitakke [V 0.0056] pakatiyā, tasmā jhānaṃ na vijjati;

Ahetuke ca maggaṅgaṃ, balañcāvīriye yathā.

Therefore, in consciousnesses naturally without initial application, jhāna factors are not found; and path factors are not found in the rootless, just as powers are not found in those without energy.

571.

571.

Aṭṭha rūpindriyānettha, agayhanteva sabbathā;

Maggindriyabalaṭṭhesu, samādhi ca na kaṅkhite.

Herein, the eight material faculties are not included at all. In the analysis of path factors, faculties, and powers, the inclusion of concentration is not in doubt.

572.

572.

Kāmapuññesvaniyatā, viratīpi anuddhatā;

Paññānuttaracittesu, indriyattayabhājitā.

The abstinences are unfixed in sense-sphere meritorious consciousness; in the supramundane consciousnesses, they are reckoned as a triad of faculties.

573.

573.

Sesā vuttānusārena, labbhamānajjhānādikā;

Tehi yuttā ca viññeyyā, cittuppādā yathākkamaṃ.

The remaining obtainable factors, such as the jhāna factors, should be understood according to what has been said, and the occurrences of consciousness should be known as associated with them, respectively.

574.

574.

Somanassayuttā [M 0.0051] kāme, lokuttaramahaggate;

Paṭhamajjhānacittā ca, pañcajhānaṅgikā matā.

The sense-sphere consciousnesses associated with joy, and the sublime and supramundane consciousnesses of the first jhāna, are considered to have five jhāna factors.

575.

575.

Dukkhupekkhāyuttā kāme, pañcaviññāṇavajjitā;

Dutiyajjhānacittā ca, catujhānaṅgikā siyuṃ.

The sense-sphere consciousnesses associated with pain and equanimity, excluding the five sense-consciousnesses, and the consciousnesses of the second jhāna, have four jhāna factors.

576.

576.

Jhānaṅgattayasaṃyuttā, tatiyajjhānamānasā;

Catutthapañcamāruppā, jhānaṅgadvayayogino.

The minds of the third jhāna are associated with three jhāna factors; the consciousnesses of the fourth and fifth jhānas and the formless sphere are associated with two jhāna factors.

577.

577.

Pañcaviññāṇayugaḷe, jhānaṅgaṃ natthi kiñcipi;

Itthaṃ jhānānaṃ bhedena, pañcadhā mānasā ṭhitā.

In the five pairs of sense-consciousness there is no jhāna factor at all. Thus, by the distinction of jhānas, minds are established in five ways.

578.

578.

Ekūnatiṃsati satta-tiṃsa cekādasāpare;

Catuttiṃsa dasevātha, gaṇikā tu yathākkamaṃ.

Twenty-nine, thirty-seven, and eleven others; then thirty-four and ten—such is the enumeration in respective order.

579.

579.

Lokuttaresu sabbesu, indriyāni navuccare;

Tihetukesu sabbesu, lokiyesu panaṭṭhadhā.

In all supramundane states, nine faculties are mentioned; but in all mundane triple-rooted states, there are eight.

580.

580.

Ñāṇena vippayuttesu, sattadhāva samuddhare;

Sitavoṭṭhabbanā puññe, pañcadhāva pakāsaye.

In those dissociated from knowledge, seven should be pointed out. In the smile-producing and determining consciousnesses, five should be proclaimed.

581.

581.

Vicikicchāsahagate, catudhāva viniddise;

Tīṇindriyāni vuttāni, sesāhetukamānase.

In the state accompanied by doubt, four should be pointed out. Three faculties are said to be in the remaining rootless minds.

582.

582.

Aṭṭha [V 0.0057] cekūnatālīsa, dvādasa vātha terasa;

Ekañca soḷasa ceti, chabbidhā tattha saṅgaho.

Eight, thirty-nine, twelve or thirteen, one, and sixteen—thus the summary there is sixfold.

583.

583.

Paṭhamānuttaraṃ jhānaṃ, aṭṭhamaggaṅgikaṃ mataṃ;

Sattamaggaṅgikaṃ nāma, sesaṃ jhānamanuttaraṃ.

The first supramundane jhāna is considered to have eight path factors; the remaining supramundane jhānas are said to have seven path factors.

584.

584.

Lokiyaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ, tathā kāme tihetukaṃ;

Pañcamaggaṅgikā nāma, cittuppādā pakāsitā.

The mundane first jhāna, and likewise the triple-rooted sense-sphere consciousnesses, are proclaimed as arisings of mind having five path factors.

585.

585.

Sesaṃ mahaggataṃ jhānaṃ, sampayuttā ca diṭṭhiyā;

Ñāṇena vippayuttā ca, catumaggaṅgikā matā.

The remaining sublime jhānas, consciousness associated with wrong view, and consciousness dissociated from knowledge are considered to have four path factors.

586.

586.

Dosamūladvayañceva, uddhaccasahitaṃ tathā;

Diṭṭhiyā vippayuttā ca, maggaṅgattayayogino.

The pair of consciousnesses rooted in hatred, that accompanied by restlessness, and those dissociated from wrong view are endowed with three path factors.

587.

587.

Vicikicchāsampayutto[M 0.0052], vutto maggo duvaṅgiko;

Amaggāhetuko ceti, sattadhā tattha saṅgaho.

That associated with doubt is said to have two path factors; the rootless consciousness is without path factors. Thus the summary there is sevenfold.

588.

588.

Aṭṭha dvattiṃsati ceva, dasa pañcādhikāpare;

Tālīsa kamato satta, ekañcaṭṭhadasāpare.

Eight, thirty-two, ten, fifteen, forty, seven, one, and eighteen.

589.

589.

Balāni pana satteva, sabbatthāpi tihetuke;

Ñāṇena vippayuttesu, cha balāni samuddise.

However, there are seven powers in all triple-rooted states; in those dissociated from knowledge, six powers should be pointed out.

590.

590.

Catudhākusale honti, tividhā kaṅkhite pana;

Dvibalaṃ sitavoṭṭhabbaṃ, abalaṃ sesamīritaṃ.

There are four powers in the unwholesome states, but three in the state of doubt. The smile-producing and determining consciousnesses have two powers; the remainder is said to be without powers.

591.

591.

Chabbidho saṅgaho tattha, sattatālīsathāpare;

Dvādasekādasekaṃ dve, soḷaseti yathākkamaṃ.

The summary there is sixfold: forty-seven, twelve, eleven, one, two, and sixteen, in respective order.

592.

592.

Itthaṃ pañca cha satta cha-koṭṭhāsā kamato ṭhitā;

Catuvīsati sabbepi, jhānaṅgādivasā kathā.

Thus, the sections are established in order as five, six, seven, and six. All twenty-four discussions are based on the jhāna factors and so forth.

Iti cetasikavibhāge cittuppādakathā niṭṭhitā.

Thus ends the Discussion on the Arising of Consciousness in the Analysis of Mental Factors.

Soḷasamo paricchedo.

The Sixteenth Chapter.

Sattarasamo paricchedo

The Seventeenth Chapter.

17. Diṭṭhisaṅgahakathā

17. The Discussion on the Compendium of Views.

593.

593.

Yevāpanakanāmena[V 0.0058], dhammā chandādayo tathā;

Khandhādayo ca koṭṭhāsā, uddiṭṭhā hi yathārahaṃ.

The phenomena beginning with desire, known as 'particulars' (yevāpanaka), and the divisions such as the aggregates, have been pointed out as appropriate.

594.

594.

Tattha chandādayo dhammā, vibhattāva yathārahaṃ;

Khandhādirāsayo vāpi, viññeyyā dāni sambhavā.

Therein, the phenomena beginning with desire have been analyzed appropriately; now the heaps, such as the aggregates, should be understood as they occur.

595.

595.

Vedanā vedanākkhandho, cakkhusamphassajādikā;

Saññā ca saññākkhandhoti, chabbidhāpi pakāsitā.

Feeling born of eye-contact and so on is the feeling aggregate; and perception is the perception aggregate. Both are declared to be sixfold.

596.

596.

Saṅkhārakkhandhanāmena, sesā cetasikā matā;

Vuttā viññāṇakāyā cha, viññāṇakkhandhanāmato.

The remaining mental factors are considered the formations aggregate; the six bodies of consciousness are called the consciousness aggregate.

597.

597.

Rūpakkhandho [M 0.0053] punekova, sampayuttāviyogino;

Arūpino ca cattāro, pañcakkhandhā pavuccare.

The form aggregate is one; the four immaterial aggregates are associated and inseparable. Thus the five aggregates are spoken of.

598.

598.

Manāyatananāmaṃ tu, cittameva tathāparā;

Cakkhuviññāṇadhātādisattaviññāṇadhātuyo.

The mind-base is simply consciousness; likewise the seven consciousness-elements, beginning with the eye-consciousness element.

599.

599.

Sabbe cetasikā dhammā, dhammāyatanasaṅgahā;

Dhammadhātūti ca vuttā, dvipaññāsāpi sabbathā.

All fifty-two mental factors are included in the dhamma-base and are also called the dhamma-element.

600.

600.

Sukhumāni ca rūpāni, nibbānañcettha gayhare;

Oḷārikāni rūpāni, dasāyatanadhātuyo.

Subtle forms and Nibbāna are also included here. Gross forms constitute ten bases and elements.

601.

601.

Cakkhusotaghānajivhā-kāyāyatananāmakā;

Rūpasaddagandharasa-phoṭṭhabbāyatanāni ca.

The bases named eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body, and the bases of forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles.

602.

602.

Dvādasāyatanā sabbe, hontaṭṭhārasadhātuyo;

Khandhā ṭhapetvā nibbānaṃ, natthi paṇṇatti tīsupi.

All twelve bases become the eighteen elements. Nibbāna is excluded from the aggregates, and concepts are not found in any of the three classifications.

603.

603.

Āhārādi [V 0.0059] ca koṭṭhāsā, pubbe vuttanayāva te;

Iti missakasaṅkhepo, viññātabbo vibhāvinā.

The sections beginning with nutriment are in the manner previously stated. Thus the miscellaneous compendium should be understood by the discerning one.

604.

604.

Dvādasākusalesveva, cuddasāpi vavatthitā;

Ye sāvajjāva tesampi, saṅgaho dāni niyyate.

The fourteen unwholesome mental factors are established only in the twelve unwholesome consciousnesses. Now the compendium of these blameworthy states is set forth.

605.

605.

Kāmāsavo bhavāsavo, diṭṭhāvijjāsavāti ca;

Cattāro āsavā vuttā, tayo dhammā sarūpato.

The canker of sensual pleasure, the canker of existence, the canker of views, and the canker of ignorance—these four cankers are spoken of. In essence, they are three phenomena.

606.

606.

Āsavā āsavaṭṭhena,

Oghā vuyhanato tathā;

Yojentīti ca yogāti,

Te cattāro ca desitā.

They are taints in the sense of flowing out, floods in the sense of sweeping away, and yokes in the sense of yoking. Thus these four have been taught.

607.

607.

Kāmabbhavo ca paṭigho, māno diṭṭhi ca saṃsayo;

Sīlabbataparāmāso, bhavarāgo tathāparo.

Sensual lust, aversion, conceit, wrong view, doubt, attachment to rites and vows, and likewise craving for existence,

608.

608.

Issā macchariyāvijjā, iti saṃyojanā dasa;

Aṭṭha dhammā sarūpena, abhidhamme pakāsitā.

Envy, stinginess, and ignorance—these are the ten fetters. As proclaimed in the Abhidhamma, in essence they are eight phenomena.

609.

609.

Issāmacchariyaṃ [M 0.0054] hitvā, katvā mānuddhavaṃ tahiṃ;

Bhinditvā bhavarāgañca, rūpārūpavasā dvidhā.

Omitting envy and stinginess, and adding conceit and restlessness; and splitting craving for existence in two according to the form and formless realms,

610.

610.

Pañcorambhāgiyā ceva, pañcuddhambhāgiyāti ca;

Dasa saṃyojanā vuttā, sutte satta sarūpato.

The five lower fetters and the five higher fetters—thus ten fetters are spoken of in the Suttas. In essence, they are seven phenomena.

611.

611.

Ganthā dhammā ca cattāro, tayo dhammā sarūpato;

Abhijjhākāyagantho ca, byāpādo ca pavuccati.

There are four ties, which are three states in essence; the bodily ties of covetousness and ill will are declared.

612.

612.

Sīlabbataparāmāso, kāyagantho tathāparo;

Idaṃsaccābhiniveso, iti diṭṭhi vibhedito.

Grasping at precepts and vows, likewise another bodily tie, and dogmatic adherence to 'this alone is truth'—thus is view distinguished.

613.

613.

Kāmacchando ca byāpādo, thinamiddhamathāparaṃ;

Tathā uddhaccakukkuccaṃ, kaṅkhāvijjāti aṭṭhime.

Sensual desire and ill will, then sloth and torpor; likewise restlessness and remorse, doubt, and ignorance—these are the eight.

614.

614.

Dhammā [V 0.0060] nivaraṇā nāma, chadhā ca pana desitā;

Micchādiṭṭhi panekāva, parāmāsoti vuccati.

The states called hindrances are taught as being sixfold; but wrong view is just one, and it is called 'grasping'.

615.

615.

Upādānāni cattāri, kāmupādādināmakā;

Diṭṭhisīlabbataṃ atta-vādupādānameva ca.

There are four kinds of clinging: clinging to sensual pleasures, clinging to views, clinging to precepts and vows, and clinging to the doctrine of self.

616.

616.

Lobhadiṭṭhivasā dveva, tividhā diṭṭhi desitā;

Diṭṭhi sīlabbatamatta-vādo ceti mahesinā.

Based on greed and view, the clingings are twofold. The view-based ones are taught as threefold by the Great Sage: clinging to views, to precepts and vows, and to the doctrine of self.

617.

617.

Lobho doso ca moho ca,

Māno diṭṭhi ca saṃsayo;

Thinamuddhaccamevātha,

Lokanāsayugaṃ tathā.

Greed, hatred, and delusion; conceit, wrong view, and doubt; sloth and restlessness; and likewise the pair that destroys the world: shamelessness and recklessness.

618.

618.

Itthaṃ kilesavatthūni, kilesāti pakāsitā;

Dasete tu samānāva, parato ca sarūpato.

Thus the bases of defilements are declared as defilements; these ten are similar both in their own nature and in relation to others.

619.

619.

Kāmarāgo ca paṭigho, māno diṭṭhi ca saṃsayo;

Bhavarāgo avijjāti, cha sattānusayā matā.

Lust for sensuality and aversion, conceit, view, and doubt; lust for becoming and ignorance—these seven are considered the latent tendencies.

620. Gāhā ca palibodhā ca, papañcā ceva maññanā.

620. Graspings and impediments, and also proliferations and conceivings.

Taṇhā māno ca diṭṭhi ca, diṭṭhi taṇhā ca nissayā.

Craving, conceit, and view; and view and craving are supports.

621.

621.

Parāmāsekako [M 0.0055] dveva, nissayā maññanā tayo;

Āsavoghayogaganthā, upādānā ca dubbidhā.

Grasping is single yet twofold; supports are twofold, conceivings are threefold; taints, floods, yokes, ties, and clingings are twofold.

622.

622.

Aṭṭha nīvaraṇā vuttā, sattadhānusayā kathā;

Saṃyojanā kilesā ca, daseva parato ṭhitā.

Eight hindrances are spoken of, the discourse is on the seven latent tendencies; fetters and defilements, too, are established as ten.

623.

623.

Ekadvitichasattaṭṭhadasakā tu yathārahaṃ;

Dhammā sarūpato honti, yathāvuttesu rāsisu.

In the aforesaid categories, the states in their essential nature number, as is appropriate, one, two, three, six, seven, eight, and ten.

624.

624.

Kāmarāgabhavarāgā, kāmāsavabhavāsavā;

Rūparāgārūparāga, iti lobho vibhedito.

Lust for sensuality and lust for becoming, the taint of sensuality and the taint of becoming, lust for form and lust for the formless—thus is greed analyzed.

625.

625.

Idaṃsaccābhiniveso[V 0.0061], diṭṭhi sīlabbataṃ tathā;

Attavādo parāmāso, iti diṭṭhi pavuccati.

Dogmatic adherence to 'this alone is truth,' view, precepts and vows, the doctrine of self, and grasping—thus is 'view' spoken of.

626.

626.

Diṭṭhi pañcadasavidhā, lobhaṭṭhārasadhā tahiṃ;

Sesā sapararāsīhi, samānā dvādasaṭṭhitā.

View is of fifteen kinds; therein, greed is of eighteen kinds. The remaining twelve are established as similar in the categories of self and others.

627.

627.

Ekādasasamuṭṭhāne, diṭṭhilobhā vavatthitā;

Avijjā sattasu vuttā, paṭigho pana pañcasu.

View and greed are established in eleven sources of arising; ignorance is said to be in seven, and aversion in five.

628.

628.

Māno ca vicikicchā ca, catuṭṭhānesu uddhaṭo;

Tīsu dvīsu ca thīnanti, aṭṭhete savibhattikā.

Conceit and doubt arise in four grounds; sloth in three and in two. These eight are with their classifications.

629.

629.

Issāmaccherakukkuccamiddhalokavināsakā;

Chāvibhattikadhammāti, asambhinnā catuddasa.

Envy, stinginess, remorse, torpor, and the world-destroying pair; these six are unclassified states, unmixed, fourteen in all.

630.

630.

Rūparāgārūparāga-kāmāsavabhavāsavā;

Honti diṭṭhiviyuttesu, pubbe vuttanayā pana.

Lust for form, lust for the formless, the taint of sensuality, and the taint of becoming: these exist in those dissociated from view, but according to the method previously stated.

631.

631.

Iti sāvajjasaṅkhepaṃ, ñatvā puna vicakkhaṇo;

Bodhipakkhiyadhammānaṃ, saṅgahampi vibhāvaye.

Thus, having known the summary of blameworthy states, the discerning one should then also clarify the compendium of the qualities pertaining to enlightenment.

632.

632.

Yesu saññācittadiṭṭhi-vipallāsā yathākkamaṃ;

Subhaṃ sukhaṃ niccamattā, iti dvādasadhā ṭhitā.

Wherein the distortions of perception, thought, and view occur sequentially, regarding things as beautiful, pleasant, permanent, and self—thus they are established in twelve ways.

633.

633.

Tattha kāye vedanāsu, citte dhammesu cakkamā;

Asubhaṃ dukkhamaniccamanattāti upaṭṭhitā.

Therein, regarding the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena respectively, mindfulness is established on them as foul, suffering, impermanent, and non-self.

634.

634.

Yathāvuttavipallāsapahānāya [M 0.0056] yathārahaṃ;

Bhinnā visayakiccānaṃ, vasena pana sambhavā.

For abandoning the aforesaid distortions as is appropriate, they arise, however, divided by way of their objects and functions.

635.

635.

Cattāro satipaṭṭhānā, kāyānupassanādayo;

Iti vuttā panekāva, sammāsati mahesinā.

The four foundations of mindfulness, beginning with contemplation of the body, are so called; but they are just one, spoken of by the Great Sage as Right Mindfulness.

636.

636.

Uppannānuppannapāpapahānānuppannāya ca;

Anuppannuppannehi vā, nibbatti abhivuddhiyā.

For the abandoning of arisen evil states and the non-arising of unarisen ones; and for the generation of unarisen wholesome states and the development of arisen ones.

637.

637.

Padahantassa [V 0.0062] vāyāmo, kiccābhogavibhāgato;

Sammappadhānā cattāro, iti vuttā mahesinā.

The striving of one who makes an effort, from the division of its function and application, is spoken of by the Great Sage as the four right strivings.

638.

638.

Chando ca vīriyaṃ cittaṃ, vīmaṃsāti ca tādinā;

Cattāro iddhipādāti, vibhattā caturādhipā.

Desire, energy, mind, and investigation—these are distinguished by the Such One as the four bases of spiritual power, the four dominant factors.

639.

639.

Saddhindriyañca vīriyaṃ, sati ceva samādhi ca;

Paññindriyañca pañceva, bodhipakkhiyasaṅgahe.

Faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom—these five are in the compendium of the qualities pertaining to enlightenment.

640.

640.

Indriyānindriyaṭṭhena, balaṭṭhena balāni ca;

Iti bhinnā vibhattā ca, duvidhāpi mahesinā.

As faculties by way of exercising control, and as powers by way of unshakable strength—thus they are differentiated and distinguished in two ways by the Great Sage.

641.

641.

Satī ca dhammavicayo, tathā vīriyapītiyo;

Passaddhi ca samādhi ca, upekkhāti ca tādinā.

Mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, as well as energy and rapture; tranquility, concentration, and equanimity—thus taught by the Such One.

642.

642.

Desitā satta bojjhaṅgā, bujjhantassa sabhāvato;

Kāyacittavasā bhinnaṃ, katvā passaddhimekakaṃ.

The seven enlightenment factors are taught, which by their nature lead to awakening. Though tranquility is divided by way of body and mind, it is counted as a single factor.

643.

643.

Sammādiṭṭhi ca saṅkappo, vāyāmo viratittayaṃ;

Sammāsati samādhī ca, maggo aṭṭhaṅgiko mato.

Right view and intention, effort, the three abstinences, right mindfulness, and concentration—this is considered the Eightfold Path.

644.

644.

Iti satteva saṅkhepā, sattatiṃsa pabhedato;

Ekaṃ katvāna passaddhiṃ, asambhinnā catuddasa.

Thus in summary there are seven groups, but thirty-seven factors by way of analysis. Making tranquility one, the distinct underlying states are fourteen.

645.

645.

Navadhā vīriyaṃ vuttaṃ, chasu rāsīsu pañcasu;

Aṭṭhadhā sati sesā tu, samānapadarāsikā.

Energy is said to be ninefold, in five of the six groups. Mindfulness is eightfold. The remaining factors have similar bases in the groups.

646.

646.

Pañcasveva tu paññā ca, samādhi caturāsiko;

Saddhā dvīsu vibhattāti, pañcete savibhattikā.

Wisdom is in five groups, and concentration is in four. Faith is distinguished as being in two. These five are thus classified.

647.

647.

Navā [M 0.0057] vibhattikā sesā, chando cittamathāparaṃ;

Pīti passaddhipekkhā ca, saṅkappo viratittayaṃ.

The remaining nine are classified: desire, mind, and then rapture, tranquility, equanimity, intention, and the three abstinences.

648.

648.

Iti vuttanayā sabbe, bodhipakkhiyasaṅgahā;

Lokuttaresu sambhonti, sabbathāpi yathārahaṃ.

Thus, according to the method explained, all the factors in the compendium of qualities pertaining to enlightenment arise in the supramundane states, in every way, as is appropriate.

649.

649.

Pubbabhāge [V 0.0063] yathāyogaṃ, lokiyesu ca labbhare;

Nibbedabhāvanākāle, chabbisuddhipavattiyaṃ.

In the preliminary stage, as is fitting, they are also found in mundane states; at the time of developing disenchantment, during the process of the six purifications.

650.

650.

Iti missakasāvajjā, bodhipakkhiyasaṅgahā;

Yevāpanakarāsimhi, yathāsambhavato ṭhitā.

Thus the mixed, the blameworthy, and the factors pertaining to enlightenment are established in the miscellaneous category according to their possibility of occurrence.

651.

651.

Kammapathā tu sambhonti, puññāpuññesu sabbathā;

Apathā ca sucaritā, tathā duccaritāpi ca.

Courses of action arise entirely in meritorious and demeritorious deeds; and also wrong paths, good conduct, and likewise bad conduct.

652.

652.

Tattha kammapathaṭṭhāne, anabhijjhādayo pana;

Upacārena vuccanti, vipākesu kriyesu vāti.

There, in the context of the courses of action, non-covetousness and the like are spoken of figuratively in relation to either their results or their functional states.

Iti cetasikavibhāge diṭṭhisaṅgahakathā niṭṭhitā.

Thus ends the discourse on the summary of views in the Analysis of Mental Factors.

Sattarasamo paricchedo.

The Seventeenth Chapter.

Niṭṭhito ca sabbathāpi cetasikavibhāgo.

And the Analysis of Mental Factors is now altogether complete.

Aṭṭhārasamo paricchedo

The Eighteenth Chapter.

3. Rūpavibhāgo

3. The Analysis of Matter.

18. Sarūpakathā

18. Discourse on Intrinsic Nature.

653.

653.

Tepaññāsa paniccevaṃ, nāmadhammā pakāsitā;

Aṭṭhavīsavidhaṃ dāni, rūpaṃ nāma kathīyati.

Thus fifty-three mental phenomena have been explained; now the twenty-eight kinds of what is called matter will be set forth.

654.

654.

Pathavāpo ca tejo ca, vāyo ceti catubbidho;

Cakkhusotaghānajivhā, kāyoti pana pañca ca.

Earth, water, fire, and air—thus the fourfold; and the five: eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body.

655.

655.

Rūpasaddagandharasā, cattāro ca athāparaṃ;

Itthipumbhāvayugaḷaṃ, jīvitaṃ hadayampi ca.

Furthermore, the four: visible form, sound, odor, and taste; the pair of femininity and masculinity, life, and also the heart-base.

656.

656.

Kāyaviññatti [M 0.0058][V 0.0064] cevātha, vacīviññatti ca dvayaṃ;

Ākāsadhātu rūpassa, lahutā mudutā tassa.

And then the pair: bodily intimation and verbal intimation; the space element, and its lightness and malleability of matter.

657.

657.

Kammaññatā upacayo, santati jaratā pana;

Aniccatā ca kabaḷīkārāhāroti sabbathā.

Wieldiness, production, continuity, and decay; and impermanence and edible food—thus all.

658.

658.

Aṭṭhavīsavidhaṃ hoti, rūpametaṃ sarūpato;

Tassa lakkhaṇabhedena, sabhāvañca vibhāvaye.

This matter is of twenty-eight kinds according to its intrinsic nature; one should clarify its essential nature by way of the distinctions in its characteristics.

659.

659.

Sandhāraṇaṃ tu pathavīdhātu kakkhaḷalakkhaṇā;

Ābandhanamāpodhātu, āpaggharaṇalakkhaṇā.

The earth element has the characteristic of hardness and the function of supporting; the water element has the characteristic of flowing and the function of binding.

660.

660.

Paripācanatā tejodhātu uṇhattalakkhaṇā;

Samudīraṇatā vāyodhātu vitthambhalakkhaṇā.

The fire element has the characteristic of heat and the function of maturing; the air element has the characteristic of distending and the function of impelling.

661.

661.

Sabbatthāvinibhuttāpi, asammissakalakkhaṇā;

Taṃtaṃbhāvasamussannasambhāresupalakkhitā.

Though inseparable everywhere, their individual characteristics are unmixed; they are discerned in composites where this or that element is predominant.

662.

662.

Aññamaññenupatthaddhā, sesarūpassa nissayā;

Catudhevaṃ kalāpesu, mahābhūtā pavattare.

Mutually supported and a basis for the other material phenomena, the great elements thus function in four ways within the material groups.

663.

663.

Cakkhu sambhāracakkhumhi, sattakkhipaṭalocite;

Kaṇhamaṇḍalamajjhamhi, pasādoti pavuccati.

The eye sensitivity is said to be the sensitive matter located in the composite eye, which consists of seven layers, in the middle of the black circle of the eye.

664.

664.

Yena cakkhupasādena, rūpāni anupassati;

Parittaṃ sukhumañcetaṃ, ūkāsirasamūpamaṃ.

It is by this eye-sensitivity that one sees forms; it is minute and subtle, comparable to the head of a louse.

665.

665.

Sotaṃ sotabilassanto,

Tambalomācite tathā;

Aṅgulivedhanākāre,

Pasādoti pakāsito.

The ear sensitivity is declared to be the sensitive matter inside the ear-hole, surrounded by fine copper-colored hairs, in the shape of a finger-ring.

666.

666.

Anto ajapadaṭṭhāne, ghānaṃ ghānabile ṭhitaṃ;

Jivhā jivhāya majjhamhi, uppalākārasannibhe.

The nose sensitivity is situated inside the nostril, at a place shaped like a goat’s hoof; the tongue sensitivity is in the middle of the tongue, resembling the tip of a lotus petal.

667.

667.

Iccevaṃ [V 0.0065] pana cattāro, taṃtaṃdesavavatthitā;

Kāyappasādopādinne, sabbaketi yathākkamaṃ.

Thus these four sensitivities are established in their respective locations; the body sensitivity, however, pervades the entire clung-to body. Thus they are described in due order.

668.

668.

Rūpādyābhighātārahabhūtānaṃ [M 0.0059] vā yathārahaṃ;

Daṭṭhukāmanidānādikammabhūtānameva vā.

Or they are, as appropriate, the material phenomena suitable for being impacted by visible form and so on; or they are what has been generated by kamma rooted in the desire to see and so on.

669.

669.

Pasādalakkhaṇā bhūtarūpānaṃ bhūtanissitā;

Kappāsapaṭalasnehasannibhāti ca vaṇṇitā.

They have the characteristic of sensitivity, are derived from and dependent on the great elements, and are described as resembling oil that has soaked a cotton cloth.

670.

670.

Pañcāpi jīvitārakkhā, rūpādiparivāritā;

Dhītarāva kumārāva, kalāpantaravuttino.

These five sensitivities, protected by the life faculty and surrounded by other material phenomena, exist within their respective material groups like a well-guarded daughter or son.

671.

671.

Rūpaṃ nibhāso bhūtānaṃ, saddo nigghosanaṃ tathā;

Gandho ca gandhanaṃ tattha, raso ca rasanīyatā.

Visible form is the radiance of the great elements; likewise, sound is resonance; odor is that which is smelled, and taste is that which is savored.

672.

672.

Bhūtattayañca phoṭṭhabbaṃ, āpodhātuvivajjitaṃ;

Saddo aniyato tattha, tadaññe sahavuttino.

The tangible object is the triad of great elements, excluding the water element. Among these, sound is variable, while the others are co-nascent.

673.

673.

Cakkhādipaṭihananalakkhaṇā tu yathākkamaṃ;

Pañceva pañcaviññāṇavīthiyā visayā matā.

They have the characteristic of impinging upon the eye and so on, respectively; they are considered the five sense objects in the five-door cognitive processes.

674.

674.

Itthindriyaṃ panitthittaṃ, itthibhāvoti desito;

Purisattaṃ tathābhāvo, purisindriya nāmako.

The female faculty is femininity, which is explained as the state of being female; likewise, masculinity is the state of being male, which is called the male faculty.

675.

675.

Taṃ dvayaṃ panupādinne, kāye sabbattha labbhati;

Kalāpantarabhinnañca, bhinnasantānavatti ca.

This pair is found everywhere in the clung-to body; they are distinct within the material groups and occur in separate continuities.

676.

676.

Rūpānaṃ kammajātānaṃ, anupālanalakkhaṇaṃ;

Jīvitindriyarūpanti, āyu nāma pavuccati.

That which has the characteristic of maintaining the material phenomena born of kamma is the material life faculty, which is also called life-span.

677.

677.

Manodhātuyā ca tathā, manoviññāṇadhātuyā;

Nissayalakkhaṇaṃ vatthurūpaṃ hadayanissitaṃ.

The physical base, which is dependent on the heart, has the characteristic of being a support for the mind-element and for the mind-consciousness-element.

678.

678.

Majjhe hadayakosamhi, aḍḍhappasatalohite;

Bhūtarūpamupādāya, cakkhādi viya vattati.

It is situated in the middle of the heart cavity, within half a handful of blood; depending on the great elements, it functions in a way similar to the eye sensitivity and so on.

679.

679.

Ākāsadhātu [V 0.0066] rūpānaṃ, paricchedakalakkhaṇā;

Taṃtaṃrūpakalāpānaṃ, pariyantoti vuccati.

The space element has the characteristic of delimiting material phenomena; it is said to be the boundary of the respective material groups.

680.

680.

Cittaṃ sahajarūpānaṃ, kāyassa gamanādisu;

Santhambhanasandhāraṇacalanassa tu paccayo.

Mind is a condition for its co-nascent material phenomena, and for the stiffening, supporting, and moving of the body in activities such as walking.

681.

681.

Vāyodhātuvikāroyaṃ[M 0.0060], kāyaviññattināmako;

Vāyodhātādhikānaṃ tu, bhūtānamiti kecanā.

This modification of the air element is called bodily intimation. Some, however, say it is a modification of the great elements in which the air element is predominant.

682.

682.

Tathā cittasamuṭṭhino, vacīghosappavattiyaṃ;

Upādinnarūpakāyaghaṭṭanassa tu paccayo.

Likewise, that which has arisen from mind is a condition for the friction within the clung-to material body that occurs in the production of the sound of speech.

683.

683.

Pathavīdhātuvikāroyaṃ, vacīviññattināmako;

Pathavīdhātādhikānaṃ tu, bhūtānamiti kecanā.

This modification of the earth element is called verbal intimation. Some, however, say it is a modification of the great elements in which the earth element is predominant.

684.

684.

Dvepi kāyavacīkammadvārabhūtā yathākkamaṃ;

Te pana ghaṭṭanāhetu-vikārākāralakkhaṇā.

Both of these, respectively, constitute the doors for bodily and verbal kamma. They have the characteristic of being a mode of alteration caused by impact.

685.

685.

Viññāpetīti kāyena, vācāya ca vicintitaṃ;

Sayañca viññāyatīti, viññattīti pakittitā.

It makes known by the body and by speech what is conceived, and is itself made known: thus it is called intimation.

686.

686.

Lahutā pana rūpānaṃ, adandhākāralakkhaṇā;

Mudutāpi ca rūpānaṃ, maddavākāralakkhaṇā.

Lightness of material form has the characteristic of non-sluggishness; softness of material form has the characteristic of pliancy.

687.

687.

Kammaññatā ca rūpānaṃ, yoggatākāralakkhaṇā;

Gāravathaddhatā yoggapaṭipakkhā yathākkamaṃ.

Wieldiness of material form has the characteristic of workableness; heaviness and rigidity are respectively opposed to them.

688.

688.

Sappāyamutumāhāraṃ, labhitvā cittasampadaṃ;

Lahū mudu ca kammaññaṃ, yadā rūpaṃ pavattati.

When material form occurs, having obtained suitable climate, food, and mental accomplishment, it is light, soft, and wieldy.

689.

689.

Tathāpavattarūpassa, pavattākārabheditaṃ;

Lahutādittayampetaṃ, sahavutti tadā bhave.

For material form that occurs thus, distinguished by its mode of occurrence, this triad beginning with lightness occurs simultaneously at that time.

690.

690.

Sappāyaṃ paṭivedhāya, paṭipattupakāritā;

Sākārā rūpasampatti, paññattāva mahesinā.

Suitability for penetration, helpfulness for practice, and the accomplishment of form with its aspects were declared by the Great Seer.

691.

691.

Rūpassopacayo [V 0.0067] nāma, rūpassācayalakkhaṇo;

Pavattilakkhaṇā rūpasantatīti pakāsitā.

The accumulation of material form, indeed, has the characteristic of the heaping up of material form; the continuity of material form is declared as having the characteristic of occurrence.

692.

692.

Rūpamācayarūpena, jāyaticcuparūpari;

Pekkhatopacayākārā, jāti gayhati yogino.

Material form arises by way of heaping up, successively, one upon another; by observing the mode of accumulation, birth is grasped by the yogi.

693.

693.

Anuppabandhākārena, jāyatīti sapekkhato;

Tadāyaṃ santatākārā, jāti gayhati tassa tu.

Observing that it arises in an uninterrupted manner, then for that one, birth is grasped in the mode of a continuity.

694.

694.

Evamābhogabhedena[M 0.0061], jātirūpaṃ dvidhā kataṃ;

Attūpaladdhibhāvena, jāyantaṃ vātha kevalaṃ.

Thus, by the distinction of apprehension, birth-form is made twofold: by way of the state of self-perception, or then as merely arising.

695.

695.

Rūpaṃ vivittokāsassa, pūrakaṭṭhena cīyati;

Abhāvā punabhāvāya, pavattaṃ santatīti ca.

Material form accumulates by its nature of filling an empty space; and from non-existence to renewed existence, it occurs as a continuity.

696.

696.

Evamākārabhedāva, sabbākāravarākaro;

Jātirūpaṃ dvidhākāsi, jātirūpavirocano.

Thus, by the distinction of modes, the illuminator of birth-form, the maker of the supreme mode, rendered birth-form twofold.

697.

697.

Jaratā navatāhāyā, rūpānaṃ pākalakkhaṇā;

Aniccatanti mappatti, paribhijjanalakkhaṇā.

Aging, the loss of newness, has the characteristic of the maturation of material forms; impermanence has the characteristic of breaking up.

698.

698.

Iti lakkhaṇarūpaṃ tu, tividhaṃ bhinnakālikaṃ;

Sabhāvarūpadhammesu, taṃtaṃkālopalakkhitaṃ.

Thus, characteristic form is threefold, differentiated by time; among the intrinsic phenomena of material form, it is distinguished by its respective time.

699.

699.

Yena lakkhīyati rūpaṃ, bhinnākāraṃ khaṇe khaṇe;

Vipassanānayatthāya, tamiccāha tathāgato.

That by which material form is characterized as having a different aspect from moment to moment, the Tathāgata has declared for the purpose of the method of insight.

700.

700.

Kabaḷīkāro āhāro,

Yāpetabbojalakkhaṇo;

Āhāro sendriyajāto,

Rūpakāyānupālako.

Edible food has the characteristic of nutritive essence for sustenance; food is the supporter of the material body that is born with sense faculties.

701.

701.

Iccevaṃ saparicchedā, savikārā salakkhaṇā;

Akiccapaṭivedhāya, dayāpannena tādinā.

Thus, with their delimitations, transformations, and characteristics, they were taught by the compassionate and Such-a-one for the penetration of what is unprofitable.

702.

702.

Tattha [V 0.0068] tattha yathāyogaṃ, desitāti pakāsitā;

Rūpadhammā sarūpena, aṭṭhavīsati sabbathā.

Here and there, as is appropriate, the material phenomena are taught and declared; by their intrinsic nature, they are twenty-eight in all respects.

703.

703.

Katvāna jātimekaṃ tu, tatthopacayasantatiṃ;

Sattavīsati rūpāni, bhavantīti viniddise.

However, having treated birth, accumulation, and continuity therein as one, one should specify that there are twenty-seven material phenomena.

704.

704.

Bhūtattayaṃ tu phoṭṭhabbaṃ, katvā chabbīsadhāpi ca;

Ubhayaṃ jātiphoṭṭhabbaṃ, gahetvā pañcavīsati.

And by treating the triad of primary elements and the tangible object as one, it is also twenty-sixfold; by taking both birth and the tangible object as one, it is twenty-five.

705.

705.

Rūpadhammānamiccevaṃ[M 0.0062], vibhāveyya visārado;

Sarūpaṃ nāmasaṅkhepaṃ, sabhāvañca salakkhaṇanti.
