Thus, a wise person should analyze the material phenomena: their intrinsic nature, a summary of their names, their own-being, and their characteristics.

Iti rūpavibhāge sarūpakathā niṭṭhitā.

Here ends the discourse on intrinsic nature in the Analysis of Material Form.

Aṭṭhārasamo paricchedo.

The Eighteenth Chapter.

Ekūnavīsatimo paricchedo

The Nineteenth Chapter.

19. Pabhedakathā

19. The Discourse on Distinctions.

706.

706.

Aṭṭhavīsavidhampetaṃ, rūpaṃ dāni yathārahaṃ;

Bhūtarūpādibhedehi, vibhajeyya vicakkhaṇo.

Now, a discerning one should analyze this twenty-eightfold material form as is appropriate, by way of distinctions such as primary material elements and so forth.

707.

707.

Pathavādikamidanti, bhūtarūpaṃ catubbidhaṃ;

Upādārūpamaññaṃ tu, catuvīsatividhaṃ bhave.

The primary material form, beginning with the earth element, is fourfold; the other, derived material form, however, is twenty-fourfold.

708.

708.

Pañcavidhampi cakkhādirūpamajjhattikaṃ mataṃ;

Tevīsatividhaṃ sesaṃ, bāhiranti pavuccati.

The fivefold material form beginning with the eye is considered internal; the remaining twenty-threefold is called external.

709.

709.

Rūpasaddagandharasaphoṭṭhabbā satta pañcadhā;

Pañcappasādavisayā, pañcārammaṇanāmakā.

Form, sound, odor, taste, and the tangible are the fivefold objects of the five sensitivities, named the five sense-objects.

710.

710.

Ekavīsatividhaṃ [V 0.0069] sesaṃ, dhammārammaṇasaṅgahaṃ;

Manoviññāṇaviññeyyaṃ, manodvārassa gocaraṃ.

The remaining twenty-onefold are included under the mind-object; they are cognizable by mind-consciousness and are the domain of the mind-door.

711.

711.

Pasādā visayā ceva, pañcakā dvepi sambhavā;

Dvādasāpi sarūpena, dasāyatanadhātuyo.

The five sensitivities and their objects, along with the two intimations, are twelve in all by their intrinsic nature; of these, ten are bases and elements.

712.

712.

Yadedaṃ pana sabbampi, rūpaṃ sappaṭighaṃ mataṃ;

Tadevoḷārikaṃ nāma, santiketi pavuccati.

However, all this material form that is considered to have impingement, that indeed is named 'gross' and is said to be 'near'.

713.

713.

Sesamappaṭighaṃ nāma, dhammāyatanadhātu ca;

Sukhumañceva rūpañca, rūpaṃ soḷasadhā ṭhitaṃ.

The remainder is named 'non-impinging,' and it is the mind-object base and element. It is also subtle material form; this material form is established as sixteenfold.

714.

714.

Chabbidhā vatthurūpaṃ tu, pasādahadayampi ca;

Avatthurūpaṃ sesaṃ tu, dvāvīsatividhaṃ bhave.

The base-form, however, is sixfold: the five sensitivities and the heart-base. The remaining non-base form, however, is twenty-twofold.

715.

715.

Pasādā [M 0.0063] ceva viññatti, dvārarūpaṃ tu sattadhā;

Sesaṃ advārarūpaṃ tu, ekavīsavidhampi ca.

The sense faculties and intimation, which are door-forms, are sevenfold; the remaining non-door forms, however, are twenty-onefold.

716.

716.

Pasādā bhāvayugaḷaṃ, jīvitañceti aṭṭhadhā;

Indriyarūpamaññaṃ tu, vīsadhānindriyaṃ siyā.

The sense faculties, the pair of sexes, and the life faculty—these eight are faculty-forms; the other, non-faculty form, however, is twentyfold.

717.

717.

Vaṇṇo gandho raso ojā, bhūtarūpanti aṭṭhadhā;

Avinibbhogamitaraṃ, vinibbhogaṃ tu vīsadhā.

Color, odor, taste, nutritive essence, and the primary elements are the eightfold inseparable forms; the other, separable forms, are twentyfold.

718.

718.

Avinibbhogarūpāni, saddavatthindriyāni ca;

Nipphannaṃ aṭṭhārasadhā, rūparūpanti veditaṃ.

The inseparable forms, sound, the heart-base, and the faculties—these eighteen kinds are produced, and are known as 'form as form'.

719.

719.

Paricchedo panākāso, viññattilahutādayo;

Vikārā lakkhaṇā ceva, rūpassupacayādayo.

The space element as limitation, intimation, lightness and so on, which are transformations, and the characteristics, namely, accumulation of form and so on.

720.

720.

Dasadhāpi anipphannaṃ, natthetaṃ paramatthato;

Rūpassetanti katvāna, rūpamicceva vuccati.

These ten are unproduced and do not exist in an ultimate sense; but having considered them as 'belonging to form,' they are simply called 'form.'

721.

721.

Rūpāyatanamevekaṃ, sanidassanamīritaṃ;

Anidassanamaññaṃ tu, sattavīsatividhampi ca.

The visual-form base alone is said to be visible; the other, however, which is invisible, is twenty-sevenfold.

722.

722.

Kammajaṃ [V 0.0070] panupādinnaṃ, anupādinnakāparaṃ;

Tividhaṃ cittajañceva, utujāhārajanti ca.

Kamma-born form is that which is clung to; the other, not clung to, is threefold: mind-born, temperature-born, and nutriment-born.

723.

723.

Cakkhusamphassavatthūti, cakkhudhātu pakittitā;

Na vatthu tassa sesaṃ tu, sattavīsatividhaṃ bhave.

The eye-element is declared as the basis for eye-contact; the remaining twenty-sevenfold, however, is not its basis.

724.

724.

Sotasamphassavatthādi-vasā ca duvidhā tathā;

Tividhā ca vibhāveyya, yathāsambhavato kathaṃ.

Likewise, by way of the ear-contact basis and so on, and the two sexes, one should analyze them threefold, according to how it is possible.

725.

725.

Sanidassanarūpañca, vaṇṇo sappaṭighampi ca;

Anidassanamaññaṃ tu, thūlaṃ sappaṭighaṃ bhave.

Visible form, that is, color, is also with impingement; the other invisible form, being gross, is also with impingement.

726.

726.

Anidassanarūpañca, sesamappaṭighampi ca;

Soḷasāti ca sabbampi, rūpaṃ tividhamuddise.

The remaining invisible form is also without impingement, and these are sixteen. Thus all form is declared as threefold.

727.

727.

Apattagāhakaṃ nāma, cakkhusotadvayaṃ pana;

Sampattagāhakaṃ nāma, ghānādittayamīritaṃ.

The pair, the eye and ear, are called 'that which grasps without contact'; the triad beginning with the nose is said to be 'that which grasps through contact'.

728.

728.

Agāhakamato [M 0.0064] sesaṃ, tevīsatividhaṃ bhave;

Kiñci sārammaṇaṃ nāma, na gayhatīti sabbathā.

The remaining twenty-three are non-apprehending; since no form apprehends an object at all, none is called 'with an object'.

729.

729.

Upādā ajjhattikaṃ rūpaṃ, upādā bāhiraṃ tathā;

Nopādā bāhirañceti, evampi tividhaṃ bhave.

Internal form that is clung to, likewise external form that is clung to, and external form that is not clung to—thus it is threefold.

730.

730.

Ajjhattikamupādinnaṃ, bāhirañca tathāparaṃ;

Anupādinnakañceti, evamādivasāpi ca.

Internal that is clung to, and the other, external, likewise; and that which is not clung to—also by way of such classifications.

731.

731.

Diṭṭhaṃ rūpaṃ sutaṃ saddo, gandhādi tividhaṃ mutaṃ;

Viññātamaññaviññeyyaṃ, manasāti catubbidhaṃ.

The seen is form; the heard is sound; the threefold beginning with odor is the sensed; the other, the cognizable, is that which is cognized by the mind. Thus it is fourfold.

732.

732.

Rūparūpaṃ paricchedo, vikāro lakkhaṇaṃ kamā;

Aṭṭhārasekakaṃ pañca, catukkanti ca taṃ tathā.

'Form as form', limitation, transformation, and characteristic, in sequence, are eighteen, one, five, and four respectively.

733.

733.

Dvārañca hoti vatthu ca, na vatthu dvārameva tu;

Na dvāraṃ vatthumevātha, nobhayanti ca niddise.

It is both door and basis; not a basis, but only a door; not a door, but only a basis; and neither—thus one should declare.

734.

734.

Upādā [V 0.0071] anupādinnaṃ, anupādinnakaṃ tathā;

Nopādā duvidhañceti, catuddhevampi desitaṃ.

Clung to and not clung to; likewise not clung to; and the two kinds that are not clung to—thus it is also taught in four ways.

735.

735.

Sappaṭigghamupādā ca, rūpamappaṭighaṃ tathā;

Nopādā duvidhañceti, catuddhā evamādito.

Form with impingement that is clung to; likewise, form without impingement; and the two kinds that are not clung to—thus, from the beginning, it is fourfold.

736.

736.

Ekādasekajarūpaṃ, hadayindriyanavakaṃ;

Kammajaṃ cittajañceva, tathā viññattikaṃ dvayaṃ.

The eleven forms born together; the nonad of the heart-basis and faculties; kamma-born and mind-born; and likewise the twofold intimation.

737.

737.

Saddo cittotujo tasmā, rūpamekaṃ dvijaṃ mataṃ;

Cittotāhārasambhūtaṃ, lahutādittayaṃ tijaṃ.

Sound is born of mind and temperature, therefore this one form is considered to be of dual origin; the triad beginning with lightness is born of mind, temperature, and nutriment, and is thus of triple origin.

738.

738.

Navākāsāvinibbhogā, kammādicatusambhavā;

Atha lakkhaṇarūpanti, rūpamevaṃ tu pañcadhā.

The nonad of inseparable forms and space is born from the four sources beginning with kamma; then there are the characteristic forms. Thus, form is fivefold.

739.

739.

Navākāsāvinibbhogā, nava vatthindriyāni ca;

Aṭṭhārasavidhaṃ rūpaṃ, kammajaṃ hoti piṇḍitaṃ.

The nonad of inseparable forms and space, and the nine forms of the heart-base and faculties; these eighteen kinds of form, taken together, are born of kamma.

740.

740.

Saddākāsāvinibbhogā, viññattilahutādayo;

Pañcadasavidhaṃ rūpaṃ, cittasambhavamuddise.

Sound, space, the inseparable forms, intimation, and the triad beginning with lightness; these fifteen kinds of form are declared as mind-produced.

741.

741.

Saddākāsāvinibbhogā[M 0.0065], lahutādittayanti ca;

Utusambhavamīrenti, rūpaṃ terasadhā ṭhitaṃ.

Sound, space, the inseparable forms, and the triad beginning with lightness; this form, produced by temperature, is said to be thirteenfold.

742.

742.

Paricchedāvinibbhogā, lahutādittayampi ca;

Evamāhārajaṃ nāma, rūpaṃ dvādasadhā ṭhitaṃ.

The limitation (space element), the inseparable forms, and the triad beginning with lightness; thus the form called nutriment-born stands as twelvefold.

743.

743.

Jāti jarā ca maraṇaṃ, na kutocipi jāyati;

Evampi pañcadhā hoti, rūpajātivibhāgato.

Birth, aging, and death do not arise from any cause. Thus form is fivefold, according to the classification of its origin.

744.

744.

Pañcavīsatividhaṃ kammaṃ, kāmarūpavavatthitaṃ;

Janeti kammajaṃ rūpaṃ, kāmarūpabhavadvaye.

Twenty-five kinds of kamma, established in the desire and form realms, generate kamma-born form in the two existences of desire and form.

745.

745.

Pañcaviññāṇamāruppa-vipākā sabbasandhiyo;

Cuti khīṇāsavasseti, soḷasete vivajjaye.

The ten sense-consciousnesses, the formless resultant consciousnesses, all rebirth-linking consciousnesses, and the death consciousness of an Arahant—these sixteen are to be excluded.

746.

746.

Pañcasattati [V 0.0072] sesāni, cittānimāni sambhavā;

Janenti cittajaṃ rūpaṃ, pañcavokārabhūmiyaṃ.

The remaining seventy-five consciousnesses, upon arising, generate mind-produced form in the five-aggregate realm.

747.

747.

Janebhi utujaṃ rūpaṃ, tejodhātu bhavadvaye;

Kāmabhūmiyamojā tu, janetāhārajaṃ tathā.

The heat element produces temperature-born form in the two realms of existence; and in the sense-sphere realm, nutritive essence likewise generates nutriment-born form.

748.

748.

Kammaṃ janeti rūpāni, attajāni khaṇe khaṇe;

Cittamuppādakālamhi, uppādānantaraṃ paraṃ.

Kamma generates its own resultant forms from moment to moment—at the time of a consciousness's arising, immediately after its arising, and thereafter.

749.

749.

Utusambhavamīrenti, rūpaṃ terasadhā ṭhitaṃ;

Paricchedāvinibbhogā, lahutādittayampi ca.

Temperature-born form is said to be of thirteen kinds, comprising space, the inseparable forms, and also the triad beginning with lightness.

750.

750.

Sandhiyampi kammajaṃ tu, pavattepi ca sambhavā;

Janeti rūpaṃ sesāni, pavatte, na tu sandhiyaṃ.

Kamma-born form arises both at rebirth-linking and in the course of existence; the remaining sources generate form in the course of existence, but not at rebirth-linking.

751.

751.

Indriyabaddhasantāne, kammādi tividhampi ca;

Janeti rūpaṃ matake, bāhire tu yathārahaṃ.

In a continuum bound with faculties, the three sources beginning with kamma also generate form; in a dead body and externally, however, this occurs only as is appropriate.

752.

752.

Iti kammādayo rūpaṃ, janenti ca yathāsakaṃ;

Sesānampi ca rūpānaṃ, paccayā honti sambhavā.

Thus, kamma and the other causes generate form, each according to its own function; and for the remaining forms as well, they are conditions for their arising.

753.

753.

Iti [M 0.0066] rūpavibhāgañca, jātibhedañca sambhavā;

Janakādippabhedañca, rūpānaṃ tattha dīpayeti.

Thus he elucidates there the classification of form, the variety of its arising, and the distinctions of its generating sources and so forth.

Iti rūpavibhāge pabhedakathā niṭṭhitā.

Thus ends the discussion of distinctions in the analysis of form.

Ekūnavīsatimo paricchedo.

The Nineteenth Chapter.

Vīsatimo paricchedo

The Twentieth Chapter.

20. Kalāpakathā

20. The Discourse on Groups

754.

754.

Iti [V 0.0073] vuttappakārena, sabbaṃ rūpampi piṇḍitaṃ;

Sahavuttiniyāmena, ekavīsavidhaṃ kathaṃ.

Thus, in the manner described, all form is collectively grouped; according to the principle of co-occurrence, how is it spoken of as twenty-onefold?

755.

755.

Kammaṃ cittotukāhārasamuṭṭhānā yathākkamaṃ;

Nava cha caturo dve ca, kalāpā ekavīsati.

From kamma, mind, temperature, and nutriment arise, respectively, nine, six, four, and two groups—twenty-one groups in total.

756.

756.

Jīvitañcāvinibbhoga-rūpāni ca yathākkamaṃ;

Cakkhādikehi yojetvā, dasakā aṭṭha dīpitā.

By combining the life faculty and the inseparable forms with the eye and the other bases in due order, the eight decades are explained.

757.

757.

Cakkhusotaghānajivhādasakā ca catubbidhā;

Kāyitthipumbhāvavatthudasakā ca tathāpare.

The eye, ear, nose, and tongue decades are fourfold; likewise, the others are the body, femininity, masculinity, and heart-base decades.

758.

758.

Jīvitenāvinibbhogarūpāni navakanti ca;

Navete kammajā nāma, kalāpā samudīritā.

And there is the life-nonad, composed of the inseparable forms with the life faculty. These nine groups are declared to be born of kamma.

759.

759.

Avinibbhogarūpāni, suddhaṭṭhakamathāparaṃ;

Kāyaviññattinavakaṃ, kāyaviññattiyā saha.

Next is the pure octad of inseparable forms, and the body-intimation nonad, which is the octad together with body-intimation.

760.

760.

Vacīviññattidasakaṃ, saddena sahavuttito;

Lahutādekādasakaṃ, tiṇṇannaṃ saha sambhavā.

The speech-intimation decad, due to its co-occurrence with sound; the undecad of lightness, etc., due to its arising together with the three.

761.

761.

Kāyaviññattilahutādīhi dvādasakaṃ bhave;

Vacīviññattilahutādīhi terasakaṃ tathā.

There is a duodecad with body-intimation and lightness, etc.; likewise, a tredecad with speech-intimation and lightness, etc.

762.

762.

Iti cittasamuṭṭhānā, kalāpā cha pakāsitā;

Rūpākāravikārampi, saṅgahetvā yathārahaṃ.

Thus, six groups originating from consciousness have been explained, including the modes and alterations of matter as is appropriate.

763.

763.

Suddhaṭṭhakaṃ [M 0.0067] tu paṭhamaṃ, saddena navakaṃ bhave;

Lahutādekādasakaṃ, lahutādīhi tīhipi.

The first is the pure octad; with sound, it becomes a nonad; and with the three properties beginning with lightness, it is an undecad.

764.

764.

Saddena [V 0.0074] lahutādīhi, tathā dvādasakanti ca;

Kalāpā utusambhūtā, catudhāva pakittitā.

And likewise, with sound and lightness, etc., it is a duodecad. The groups born of temperature are thus declared to be fourfold.

765.

765.

Suddhaṭṭhakañca paṭhamaṃ, āhārajamathāparaṃ;

Lahutādekādasakaṃ, iti dve ojajā matā.

The first nutriment-born group is the pure octad, and the other is the undecad with lightness, etc. Thus, these two are considered to be born of nutritive essence.

766.

766.

Kalāpānaṃ paricchedalakkhaṇattā vicakkhaṇā;

Na kalāpaṅgamiccāhu, ākāsaṃ lakkhaṇāni ca.

The wise say that space and the characteristics are not constituents of the groups, because their nature is to delimit and characterize the groups.

767.

767.

Tattha cekūnanavuti, tesaṭṭhi ca yathākkamaṃ;

Tālīsekūnavīsā ca, kalāpaṅgāni tāni ca.

Therein, the constituents of the groups are, respectively, eighty-nine, sixty-three, forty, and nineteen.

768.

768.

Lakkhaṇākāsarūpāni, kalāpesu tahiṃ tahiṃ;

Pañca pañceti rūpāni, tisataṃ soḷasādhikaṃ.

The forms of characteristics and space in the various groups—these five forms amount to three hundred and sixteen.

769.

769.

Agahītaggahaṇena, aṭṭhavīsavidhānipi;

Rūpakoṭṭhāsanāmena, pañcavīsati bhāvaye.

By the method of grasping the ungrasped, one should contemplate the twenty-eight kinds of material phenomena as twenty-five under the heading 'divisions of matter'.

770.

770.

Bhūtattayaṃ tu phoṭṭhabbaṃ, katvāpacayasantatiṃ;

Jātimekañca katvā vā, vinātha hadayaṃ tahiṃ.

This is done by omitting the heart-base, and then either by treating the three primary elements as the tangible, or by treating growth, continuity, and production as one.

771.

771.

Dhammasaṅgaṇiyaṃ hetaṃ, rūpakaṇḍe sarūpato;

Vatthurūpaṃ na niddiṭṭhaṃ, paṭṭhāne desitaṃ tu taṃ.

For in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, in its Section on Matter, the material basis is not specified in its own form; but it is taught in the Paṭṭhāna.

772.

772.

Dve saddanavakā ceva,

Tayo suddhaṭṭhakāpi ca;

Dve dve cittotusambhūtā,

Eko āhārajoti ca.

Two sound-nonads and also three pure octads; two are born of consciousness, two of temperature, and one is born of nutriment.

773.

773.

Tesamuṭṭhānikā pañca, kammajāni naveti ca;

Rūparūpavasenete, kalāpā cuddaseritā.

Five arising from the three origins and nine born of kamma; thus these material groups are declared to be fourteen.

774.

774.

Dasakesveva saṅgayha, jīvitanavakaṃ tahiṃ;

Bhāvaddasakamekaṃ vā, katvā vatthuṃ vinā tathā.

By including the life-nonad within the decads, or by treating the two sex-decads as one, and likewise omitting the heart-base.

775.

775.

Saddā [M 0.0068][V 0.0075] cittotujā dveva, tesamuṭṭhānikā tayo;

Suddhaṭṭhakā ca satteva, kammajā dasakāni ca.

There are only two sound groups, born of consciousness and temperature; three arising from the three origins; only seven pure octads; and the kamma-born decads.

776.

776.

Channavūtividhaṃ tattha, rūpaṃ bhāsanti paṇḍitā;

Agahītaggahaṇena, aṭṭhārasavidhaṃ bhave.

There the wise say that material form is of ninety-six kinds; by including what was not previously included, it becomes of eighteen kinds.

777.

777.

Tesameva kalāpānaṃ, sattakacchakkapañcakā;

Catukkā ca tikadvikā, ekakā ca yathārahaṃ.

Of those same groups, there are, as is appropriate, combinations of seven, six, five, four, three, two, and one.

778.

778.

Dve satta nava cha tayo, tayopi ca yathākkamaṃ;

Cattāroti catuttiṃsa, sahavuttikarāsayo.

Two, seven, nine, six, three, and also three, and four, in respective order; thus there are thirty-four heaps of co-existent phenomena.

779.

779.

Cakkhusotaghānajivhā-kāyavatthuvasā siyuṃ;

Itthipumbhāvadasakasahitā sattakā dvidhā.

The groups of seven are twofold, comprising the decads for the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and heart-base, along with either the femininity-decad or the masculinity-decad.

780.

780.

Cakkhusotaghānahīnā, paccekaṃ dve sabhāvakā;

Abhāvato bhāvahīno, itthaṃ chakkāpi sattadhā.

Lacking the eye, ear, and nose, each separately; two having their own nature; lacking the sex-faculty due to its absence. Thus the groups of six are sevenfold.

781.

781.

Cakkhusotavihīnā ca,

Cakkhughānavihīnakā;

Sotaghānavihīnā ca,

Sabhāvā dve tayo tayo.

Those lacking eye and ear; those lacking eye and nose; and those lacking ear and nose. With their own nature, these are two, three, and three respectively.

782.

782.

Cakkhādekekato hīnā,

Tividhāpi abhāvato;

Iccevaṃ pañcakā nāma,

Navakā rāsayo siyuṃ.

Lacking the eye and so on one by one, they are also threefold due to absence. Thus are named the groups of five; the collections are ninefold.

783.

783.

Cakkhādittayahīnāva, ekato dve sabhāvakā;

Cakkhādittayato dvīhi, tayo hīnā abhāvakā.

Lacking the triad of eye, etc., together, there are two with their own nature. Lacking two from this triad, there are three due to absence.

784.

784.

Rūpaloke cakkhusota-vatthujīvitanavakā;

Cattārova kalāpāti, catukkā cha yathārahaṃ.

In the Form Realm, there are the nonads of eye, ear, heart-base, and life—only these four groups. The groups of four are six, as is appropriate.

785.

785.

Jivhākāyavatthuvasā[M 0.0069][V 0.0076],

Abhāvo dve sabhāvakā;

Kāyabhāvavatthuvasā,

Iti honti tayo tikā.

Due to tongue, body, and heart-base; due to absence, two with their own nature; due to body, sex, and heart-base. Thus there are three groups of three.

786.

786.

Kāyavatthuvaseneko, dve ca cittotusambhavā;

Saddanavakaṭṭhakāti, dukā ca tividhā siyuṃ.

One due to body and heart-base; and two born of consciousness and temperature, namely the sound-nonad and the pure octad. Thus the groups of two are threefold.

787.

787.

Jīvitanavakañcekaṃ, tesamuṭṭhānikāni ca;

Suddhaṭṭhakāni tīṇīti, cattāro ekakā siyuṃ.

The one life-nonad, and the three pure octads arising from the three origins. Thus there are four single groups.

788.

788.

Catuttiṃsa paniccete, sandhiyañca pavattiyaṃ;

Rūparūpakalāpānaṃ, rāsayo honti sambhavā.

These indeed are the thirty-four possible heaps of material groups that arise at rebirth-linking and during the course of existence.

789.

789.

Sattati saṭṭhimiccevamādinā ca yathārahaṃ;

Kalāparāsirūpāni, tattha tattha vibhāvaye.

One should discern the material phenomena in the various heaps of groups, which amount to seventy, sixty, and so on, as is appropriate in each case.

790.

790.

Soḷasa pañcadasetiādibhedavasāpi ca;

Agahītaggahaṇena, tattha tattha viniddise.

And also by way of divisions such as sixteen, fifteen, and so on, one should specify them in each case by including what was not previously included.

791.

791.

Catucattālīsasataṃ, kalāpā honti piṇḍitā;

Chabbīsa tattha rūpāni, sahassañca catussataṃ.

One hundred and forty-four groups are collected. Therein are twenty-six material phenomena, and one thousand four hundred.

792.

792.

Iccāpāyacatukke ca, kāme sugatisattake;

Rūpe ca pañcadasake, asaññāpāyabhūmiyaṃ.

Thus in the four woeful planes, in the seven happy sense-sphere destinations, in the fifteen form realms, and in the plane of non-percipient beings.

793.

793.

Catukoṭṭhāsikesveva, sattavīsavidhesupi;

Jātiṭṭhānesu sattānaṃ, sandhiyañca pavattiyaṃ.

In the four divisions and in the twenty-seven kinds of beings' birth-places, both at rebirth-linking and during the course of existence.

794.

794.

Indriyabaddhasantāne, tathānindriyakamhi ca;

Bahisaṅkhārasantāne, matakāye ca sambhavā.

Arising in the continuity of a being with faculties, and likewise in that which is without faculties; in the continuity of external formations, and in a dead body.

795.

795.

Labbhamānakalāpā ca, kalāpānañca rāsayo;

Tattha vitthārasaṅkhepā, rūpānaṃ gaṇanāpi ca.

The obtainable groups and the heaps of groups, the analysis therein in detail and in brief, and also the enumeration of the material phenomena.

796.

796.

Ettha [M 0.0070][V 0.0077] rūpā avuttā hi, yathāvuttānusārato;

Vitthāretvāna viññeyyā, sabbathāpi ca viññunāti.

The material phenomena not detailed here should be understood by the wise by expanding upon what has been said, in all ways, in accordance with the stated method.

Iti rūpavibhāge kalāpakathā niṭṭhitā.

Thus concludes the discourse on groups in the Division of Form.

Vīsatimo paricchedo.

The Twentieth Chapter.

Ekavīsatimo paricchedo

The Twenty-First Chapter

21. Uppattikathā

21. The Discourse on Origination

797.

797.

Aṭṭhavīsati rūpāni, kalāpā cekavīsati;

Vuttā cettāvatā tesaṃ, uppādo dāni niyyate.

Twenty-eight material phenomena and twenty-one groups have thus far been stated; now their arising is to be explained.

798.

798.

Aṇḍajā jalābujā ca, saṃsedajopapātikā;

Iccuppattipabhedena, catasso yoniyo matā.

Egg-born, womb-born, moisture-born, and spontaneously arisen—these four kinds of birth are understood by way of the division of origination.

799.

799.

Bhummavajjesu devesu,

Pete nijjhāmataṇhike;

Nirayesu ca sambhoti,

Yonekāvopapātikā.

Among the deities, excluding the earth-dwelling ones, among the hungry ghosts consumed by craving, and in the hells, only the spontaneously arisen birth occurs.

800.

800.

Bhummadeve manussesu,

Tiracchānāsure tathā;

Petesu cāvasesesu,

Catassopi ca yoniyo.

Among earth-dwelling deities, humans, animals, and likewise among asuras, and among the remaining hungry ghosts, all four kinds of birth occur.

801.

801.

Tatthaṇḍajā jalābujā, gabbhaseyyasamuggamo;

Saṃsedajopapātikā, opapātikanāmakā.

Therein, the egg-born and womb-born are of womb-lying origination; the moisture-born and spontaneously arisen are called 'spontaneously arisen'.

802.

802.

Tattha [V 0.0078] sampuṇṇāyatano, gabbhaseyyasamuggamo;

Abhāvo dve sabhāvā ca, itthipumbhāvamissitā.

Therein, the womb-lying origination is with complete faculties; there is absence [of sex faculty], and the two states, female and male.

803.

803.

Paripuṇṇāparipuṇṇo, opapātikanāmako;

Abhāvo dve sabhāvā ca, caturāpāyabhūmiyaṃ.

The spontaneously arisen are with complete and incomplete faculties; in the four woeful planes, there is absence [of sex faculty] and the two states, female and male.

804.

804.

Sampuṇṇāyatanoveso[M 0.0071],

Kāme sugatiyaṃ pana;

Ādikappe abhāvo ca,

Dve sabhāvā tato paraṃ.

Those with complete faculties are in the happy destinations of the sense-sphere; there is absence [of sex faculty] at the beginning of the aeon, and the two states thereafter.

805.

805.

Aparipuṇṇāyatano, abhāvo ca mahaggate;

Iccevaṃ dasadhā honti, sabbā sandhisamuggamā.

In the exalted realms, there are those with incomplete faculties and absence [of sex faculty]; thus, all conjunctional originations are tenfold.

806.

806.

Tattheva dasadhā bhinne, attabhāvasamuggame;

Sandhiyañca pavatte ca, rūpuppattiṃ vibhāvaye.

Therein, in the tenfold division of the origination of individuality, one should discern the origination of form both at the moment of conjunction and in the course of existence.

807.

807.

Tatthābhāvakasattānaṃ, gabbhaseyyasamuggame;

Kāyavatthuvasā dveva, dasakā honti kammajā.

Therein, for beings without sex faculty, at the womb-lying origination, only two decads, the body-decad and the base-decad, are born of kamma.

808.

808.

Rūpasantatisīsāni, dve ca rūpāni vīsati;

Agahītaggahaṇena, tatthekādasa niddise.

The heads of the continuum of form are twenty-two material phenomena; by the inclusion of the unapprehended, eleven are designated there.

809.

809.

Tato paraṃ pavattimhi, vaḍḍhamānassa jantuno;

Cakkhudasakādayo ca, cattāro honti sambhavā.

Thereafter, in the course of existence of a growing being, the four [decads] beginning with the eye-decad also arise.

810.

810.

Iccābhāvakasattānaṃ, chaḷevuttamakoṭiyā;

Heṭṭhimakoṭiyā dveva, gabbhaseyyasamuggame.

Thus, for beings without sex faculty at the womb-lying origination, there are six [decads] in the highest category, and only two in the lowest category.

811.

811.

Cakkhusotaghānavasā, tattha tidvekahīnakā;

Eko tayo tayo ceva, siyuṃticatupañcakā.

Therein, with respect to eye, ear, and nose, [beings may be] deficient by three, two, or one. The combinations are one, three, and three respectively, so that there may be three, four, or five [decads].

812.

812.

Opapātikasaṅkhāte, abhāvakasamuggame;

Jivhākāyavatthuvasā, tayo heṭṭhimakoṭiyā.

In the spontaneously arisen, at the origination of beings without sex faculty, by way of tongue, body, and base, there are three [decads] in the lowest category.

813.

813.

Uttamakoṭiyā [V 0.0079] honti, chaḷevobhinnamantare;

Catukkapañcakā tattha, dvekahīnā tayo tayo.

In the highest category there are six [decads]. In between these two [extremes], there are groups of four and five. There, [beings are] deficient by two or one, in three ways each.

814.

814.

Chakkādayo abhāvānaṃ,

Iccevaṃ pañcasaṅgahā;

Eko tayo tayo ceko,

Ekoti ca yathākkamaṃ.

For those without sex faculty, the groups beginning with the six [decads] are thus summarized in five. In due order, they are: one, three, three, one, and one.

815.

815.

Sabhāvakānaṃ [M 0.0072] dvinnampi, duvidhā sattakādayo;

Bhāvādikā yathāvuttā, navadhā navadhā siyuṃ.

For both kinds of beings with sex faculty, the groups beginning with the seven [decads] are twofold; as previously stated, beginning with the sex-decad, they may be ninefold and ninefold.

816.

816.

Sattevuttamato heṭṭhā, ticatukkā tadantare;

Catukkapañcakacchakkā, pañcachakkāpi ca dvidhā.

From the highest category of seven [decads] downwards, there are groups of three or four in between; there are also groups of four, five, or six, and the groups of five or six are twofold.

817.

817.

Tiṇṇannampi vaseneva, sattakacchakkapañcakā;

Catukkatikadukkā ca, cha koṭṭhāsā yathārahaṃ.

By way of the three [types of beings], the sevenfold, sixfold, fivefold, fourfold, threefold, and twofold—these six divisions are appropriate.

818.

818.

Dve satta ca nava pañca, tayo ceko yathākkamaṃ;

Rūpasantatisīsānaṃ, rāsayo sattavīsati.

Two, seven, nine, five, three, and one, in due order; these are the twenty-seven aggregates of the heads of the continuum of form.

819.

819.

Kammajātā yathāyogaṃ, pavattanti khaṇe khaṇe;

Kāmāvacarasattānaṃ, paṭisandhipavattiyaṃ.

Kamma-born [forms], as appropriate, arise moment by moment for beings in the sense-sphere, at rebirth-linking and in the course of existence.

820.

820.

Tattha santatisīsāni, rūpāni ca yathārahaṃ;

Pubbe vuttanayeneva, sabbatthāpi viniddise.

Therein, the heads of the continuum of form and the material phenomena, as appropriate, should be distinguished everywhere, just as explained previously.

821.

821.

Sītuṇhotusamaññātā,

Tejodhātu ṭhitikkhaṇe;

Bhūtā sandhikkhaṇe rūpaṃ,

Janeti utujaṭṭhakaṃ.

The heat element, known as temperature, in the matter that has arisen at the moment of conjunction, generates the temperature-born octad at its moment of presence.

822.

822.

Paṭisandhimatikkamma, cittaṃ cittajamaṭṭhakaṃ;

Bhavaṅgādimupādāya, janetuppattiyaṃ pana.

Having passed beyond rebirth-linking, the mind, taking the life-continuum and so on as a basis, then generates the mind-originated octad at the moment of arising.

823.

823.

Bhuttāhāro [V 0.0080] ṭhitippatto, mātarā ca sayampi ca;

Sarīrānugato hutvā, janetāhārajaṭṭhakaṃ.

Consumed food, whether from the mother or from oneself, having reached stability and pervaded the body, generates the food-born octad.

824.

824.

Iti suddhaṭṭhakāni ca, tesamuṭṭhānikāpare;

Saddaviññattilahutā, sambhave sambhavanti ca.

Thus the pure octads, and others arising from them, such as sound, intimation, and lightness, arise at the time of their origin.

825.

825.

Itthaṃ catusamuṭṭhānā, kalāpā kāmabhūmiyaṃ;

Yāvajīvaṃ pavattanti, dīpajālāva santati.

Thus, these groups with four origins, in the sense-sphere, continue throughout life, as a continuum like the flame of a lamp.

826.

826.

Cakkhusotavatthuvasā, dasakā ca tayo paraṃ;

Jīvitanavakañceva, rūpāvacarabhūmiyaṃ.

In the form-sphere realms, by way of eye, ear, and base, there are three decads, and also the life-nonad.

827.

827.

Honti [M 0.0073] sandhipavattīsu, cattāro kammajā sadā;

Pubbe vuttanayeneva, pavatte utucittajā.

At the moment of rebirth-linking and during the course of existence, four kamma-born groups are always present; and as previously explained, during the course of existence, temperature-born and mind-born groups arise.

828.

828.

Jīvitanavakañcekaṃ, paṭisandhipavattiyaṃ;

Pavatte utujañceti, dvedhāsaññīnamuddise.

For the non-percipient beings, one should specify two kinds: the single life-nonad at rebirth-linking and during the course of existence, and the temperature-born group during the course of existence.

829.

829.

Iccuppattikamaṃ ñatvā, vibhāveyya tato paraṃ;

Kalāpānañca rūpānaṃ, sambhavāsambhavampi ca.

Having thus understood the sequence of origination, one should further analyze the arising and non-arising of groups and forms.

830.

830.

Indriyabaddhasantāne, sabbe sambhonti sambhavā;

Kalāpā ceva rūpāni, tathā santatirāsayo.

In a continuum bound by the faculties, all originations, groups, and forms, as well as the aggregates of continuity, arise.

831.

831.

Bahiddhā matakāye ca, nopalabbhanti kammajā;

Cittojajā kalāpā ca, utujā lahutādayo.

Externally and in a dead body, kamma-born groups are not found; nor are mind-born groups, nor temperature-born qualities such as lightness and so on.

832.

832.

Tathā suddhaṭṭhakasadda-navakañcotu sabbathā;

Kalāpā tattha labbhanti, dve ca rūpāni uddise.

Likewise, the pure octad and the sound-nonad, being temperature-born, are always found there as groups; and two kinds of material phenomena should be specified.

833.

833.

Tesamuṭṭhānikā sabbe, kalāpā natthi sandhiyaṃ;

Uppādakāle sabbattha, jaratāniccatāpi ca.

All groups originating from those other causes are not present at rebirth-linking. At the time of arising, everywhere, there are also decay and impermanence.

834.

834.

Kalāpā kammajā santi, jātirūpañca sandhiyaṃ;

Rūpāni ca kalāpā ca, sabbepi ca pavattiyaṃ.

Kamma-born material groups and nascent materiality exist at rebirth-linking; and all material forms and groups exist also during the course of existence.

835.

835.

Santi [V 0.0081] sabbāni rūpāni, kāmesu catusambhavā;

Jīvitanavakaṃ hitvā, kalāpā honti vīsati.

In the sense sphere, all material forms of fourfold origin exist. Excluding the life-nonad, there are twenty material groups.

836.

836.

Dasakesveva gahitaṃ, visuṃ kāme na labbhati;

Jīvitanavakaṃ nāma, rūpaloke visuṃ siyā.

It is included only in the decads; it is not found separately in the sense sphere. The so-called life-nonad may exist separately in the form realm.

837.

837.

Āhārajakalāpā ca, bhāvā dve cādikappike;

Ādikāle na labbhanti, pacchā labbhanti kecipi.

Nutriment-born groups, and for those at the beginning of an aeon the two sex faculties, are not found at the initial time; some are found later.

838.

838.

Ghānajivhākāyabhāva-dasakā rūpabhūmiyaṃ;

Āhārajakalāpā ca, na labbhanteva sabbathā.

The decads of nose, tongue, body, and sex, and nutriment-born groups, are not found at all in the form plane.

839.

839.

Cakkhusotavatthusaddā, kalāpā cittajāpi ca;

Asaññibhūmiyaṃ pubbe, vuttāpi ca na labbhare.

The groups of eye, ear, heart-basis, and sound, and also mind-born groups, and even those previously mentioned, are not found in the plane of non-percipient beings.

840.

840.

Kalāpā [M 0.0074] satta rūpāni, pañca rūpesvasaññisu;

Natthekādasa rūpāni, kalāpekūnavīsati.

In the form planes and among non-percipient beings, seven material groups and five material forms are found. Eleven material forms and nineteen groups are not present.

841.

841.

Tasmā tevīsa rūpāni, kalāpā pana cuddasa;

Tesamuṭṭhānikā santi, rūpāvacarabhūmiyaṃ.

Therefore, in the form-sphere plane, there are twenty-three material forms and fourteen groups, originating from their causes.

842.

842.

Sattaraseva rūpāni, kalāpā dve dvisambhavā;

Asaññīnaṃ tu sambhonti, natthārūpesu kiñcipi.

For non-percipient beings, just seventeen material forms and two groups from two origins arise; but in the formless realms, there is nothing whatsoever.

843.

843.

Uppattikkamamiccevaṃ, sambhavāsambhavampi ca;

Kalāpānañca rūpānaṃ, yathāyogaṃ vibhāvayeti.

Thus one should understand the sequence of arising, and the occurrence and non-occurrence of the material groups and forms, as is appropriate.

Iti rūpavibhāge uppattikathā niṭṭhitā.

Here ends the discourse on arising in the Analysis of Material Form.

Ekavīsatimo paricchedo.

The Twenty-First Chapter.

Dvāvīsatimo paricchedo

The Twenty-Second Chapter.

22. Pakiṇṇakakathā

22. Discourse on Miscellaneous Matters.

844.

844.

Itthaṃ [V 0.0082] rūpānamuppattiṃ, dīpetvā dāni vuccati;

Pavattikosallatthāya, tatthevetaṃ pakiṇṇakaṃ.

Having thus explained the arising of material forms, this miscellaneous section is now stated for the sake of skill in the course of existence.

845.

845.

Duvidhā sandhiyo tattha, missāmissavibhāgato;

Tividhāpi cekacatu-pañcavokārabhedato.

Therein, rebirth-linkings are twofold, by the division into mixed and unmixed; and also threefold, by the distinction of the one-, four-, and five-constituent planes.

846.

846.

Rūpamattā asaññīnaṃ, nāmābhāvā amissitā;

Nāmamattā arūpīnaṃ, rūpābhāvāti ca dvidhā.

For non-percipient beings, there is only materiality; it is unmixed due to the absence of mentality. For formless beings, there is only mentality, due to the absence of materiality. Thus, the unmixed are twofold.

847.

847.

Kāmāvacarikā ceva, rūpāvacarikāti ca;

Duvidhā missitā ceti, bhavanti ca catubbidhā.

The mixed linkings are twofold: those of the sense sphere and those of the form sphere. Thus, they are fourfold in total.

848.

848.

Ekaccatuvokārā ca, amissā pañca sandhiyo;

Chabbīsatividhā missā, pañcavokārasandhiyo.

The unmixed rebirth-linkings of the one- and four-constituent planes are five. The mixed rebirth-linkings of the five-constituent plane are of twenty-six kinds.

849.

849.

Itthaṃ bhūmippabhedena, ekatiṃsavidhāpi ca;

Santatirāsibhedena, siyuṃ tiṃsavidhā kathaṃ.

Thus, by the distinction of planes, they are of thirty-one kinds. By the distinction of the heaps of continuity, how can they be of thirty kinds?

850.

850.

Rūpasantatisīsānaṃ[M 0.0075],

Rāsayo sattavīsati;

Vuttā kāme vasā tesaṃ,

Sattakā kāmasandhiyo.

The heaps that are the headings of the material continuities are twenty-seven. It is said that on account of them, the sense-sphere linkings are of seven kinds.

851.

851.

Vedanāsaññāsaṅkhāra-viññāṇakkhandhasaṅgahā;

Sabbatthāpi catassova, nāmasantatiyo siyuṃ.

The collection of the aggregates of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness—everywhere there are just these four continuities of mentality.

852.

852.

Iccubhinnaṃ vasā honti, tatthekādasakādayo;

Santatirāsayo pubbe, vibhattā sattakādayo.

Thus, on account of both, there are continuities beginning with the elevenfold, and so on. The heaps of continuity, formerly undivided, are now divided into groups beginning with the sevenfold, and so on.

853.

853.

Ekādasakadasaka-navaṭṭhasattakā [V 0.0083] siyuṃ;

Chakkena saddhiṃ viññeyyā, tasmā tattha cha saṅgahā.

There may be groups of eleven, ten, nine, eight, and seven. They should be understood along with the group of six. Therefore, there are six collections there.

854.

854.

Aṭṭha santatiyo honti, rūpalokena missitā;

Aṭṭhako rāsi tattheko, tasmā santati vuccati.

There are eight continuities mixed with the form realm. Therein is one heap which is an octad; therefore, it is called a continuity.

855.

855.

Jīvitanavako tveko, asaññī paṭisandhiyaṃ;

Arūpīnaṃ catassopi, nāmasantatiyo siyuṃ.

The life-nonad is the one group for a non-percipient being at rebirth-linking. For formless beings, there may be the four continuities of mentality.

856.

856.

Iccekakacatukkānaṃ, vasena dve amissitā;

Aṭṭhavīsañca missāti, tiṃseva honti sandhiyo.

Thus, by way of the one-constituent and four-constituent planes, two are unmixed and twenty-eight are mixed; thus there are just thirty rebirth-linkings.

857.

857.

Ekuppādanirodhā ca, amissā tattha rāsayo;

Missitānaṃ vibhāgoyaṃ, yathāyogaṃ kathīyati.

The unmixed heaps there have a single arising and cessation. This division of the mixed ones is explained as is appropriate.

858.

858.

Uppādaṭṭhitibhaṅgānaṃ, vasā tīṇi khaṇānipi;

Samānāneva nāmānaṃ, ekacittakkhaṇaṃ mataṃ.

By way of arising, presence, and dissolution, there are three moments. For mentality, which has these same three, this is considered one mind-moment.

859.

859.

Tulyamuppādabhaṅgānaṃ, rūpānampi khaṇadvayaṃ;

Ekūnapaññāsamattaṃ, ṭhitikkhaṇamudīritaṃ.

For material form, the two moments of arising and dissolution are equal to those of mind. Its moment of presence is said to be a measure of forty-nine.

860.

860.

Nāmarūpānamuppādo, bhaṅgopi hi samo mato;

Dandhaṃ hi vattikaṃ rūpaṃ, nāmaṃ tu lahuvattikaṃ.

The arising and also the dissolution of mentality and materiality are considered equal. For materiality occurs slowly, but mentality occurs swiftly.

861.

861.

Tathā hi rūpe tiṭṭhante, cittuppādā tu soḷasa;

Uppajjitvā pavattitvā, bhijjanti ca lahuṃ lahuṃ.

For while a material form is present, sixteen arisings of consciousness, having arisen and occurred, dissolve in quick succession.

862.

862.

Tasmā [M 0.0076] hi ekapaññāsa-khaṇarūpakkhaṇaṃ tathā;

Sattarasacittakkhaṇaṃ, tikhaṇanti ca vuccati.

Therefore, one moment of material form, comprising fifty-one sub-moments, is equal to seventeen mind-moments; and this is also called the three moments.

863.

863.

Cittakkhaṇaṃ hi tiṇṇannaṃ, tattha viññattikadvayaṃ;

Lakkhaṇattayarūpaṃ tu, salakkhaṇavavatthitaṃ.

The two intimations exist for one mind-moment of three phases. But material form, having three characteristics, is established with its own characteristic duration.

864.

864.

Tasmā hitvā dvayañcetaṃ, bāvīsatividhampi ca;

Rūpaṃ nāma catukkañca, salakkhaṇaniyāmitaṃ.

Therefore, excluding this pair and also the twenty-two kinds, materiality and the mental quartet are determined by their own characteristics.

865.

865.

Ekuppādanirodhā [V 0.0084] ca, tattha tulyakkhaṇā matā;

Atulyakkhaṇadhammānaṃ, siyā bhedaṃ yathārahaṃ.

Those with a common arising and cessation are considered to have equal moments. For phenomena with unequal moments, a distinction should be made as is suitable.

866.

866.

Paṭisandhikkhaṇe jātaṃ, tasmā rūpaṃ tato paraṃ;

Sattarasamacittassa, bhaṅgena saha bhijjati.

Therefore, material form born at the moment of rebirth-linking perishes together with the dissolution of the seventeenth mind-moment thereafter.

867.

867.

Tassa ṭhitikkhaṇe jātaṃ, rūpampi ca tato paraṃ;

Aṭṭhārasamacittassa, uppāde pana bhijjati.

And material form born at the presence-moment of that mind perishes, however, at the arising of the eighteenth mind-moment thereafter.

868.

868.

Tassa bhaṅgakkhaṇe jātaṃ, rūpampi ca tato paraṃ;

Aṭṭhārasamacittassa, ṭhitikālesu bhijjati.

And material form born at the dissolution-moment of that mind perishes during the presence-phase of the eighteenth mind-moment thereafter.

869.

869.

Tathā dutiyacittassa, uppādamhi samuṭṭhitaṃ;

Aṭṭhārasamacittassa, bhaṅgena saha bhijjati.

Similarly, that which has arisen at the arising moment of the second consciousness perishes along with the dissolution of the eighteenth consciousness.

870.

870.

Iti vuttaniyāmena, sajātikkhaṇato paraṃ;

Ṭhatvā ekūnapaññāsa, khaṇāni puna bhijjati.

Thus, by the method stated, after its own arising-moment, having persisted for forty-nine moments, it then perishes.

871.

871.

Tasmā ekūnapaññāsa, kalāpā saha vattare;

Eko jāyati eko ca, bhijjatīti ca sabbathā.

Therefore, forty-nine groups are always present together; one arises and one perishes.

872.

872.

Ekasantatisambandhā, kalāpā saha kammajā;

Yathānupubbaghaṭitā, ekapaññāsa labbhare.

The groups born of kamma, connected by a single continuity and arranged in successive order, are obtained as fifty-one.

873.

873.

Sattavīsa paniccevaṃ, kāme dve rūpabhūmiyaṃ;

Rūpasantatisīsānaṃ, rāsayo sattakādayo.

Thus there are twenty-seven in the sense-sphere and two in the fine-material sphere. For the continuities of matter as the principal ones, the collections begin with the sevenfold one.

874.

874.

Ekūnatiṃsa sabbepi, kammajātā yathārahaṃ;

Ekapaññāsa ghaṭikā, pavattanti khaṇe khaṇe.

All twenty-nine kinds of kamma-born matter, as is appropriate, proceed moment by moment as fifty-one chains.

875.

875.

Tattha [M 0.0077] sandhikkhaṇe jātaṃ, sattarasamacetaso;

Uppāde bhijjaticcevaṃ, vutto aṭṭhakathānayo.

Therein, what is born at the moment of connection perishes at the arising of the seventeenth consciousness. Thus is the method of the commentaries stated.

876.

876.

Taṃ nayaṃ paṭibāhitvā, cittena saha bhijjati;

Cittena saha jātanti, vuttamācariyena hi.

Having rejected that method, it is held that it perishes together with the consciousness; for it has been said by the Teacher: 'It is born together with the consciousness.'

877.

877.

Ānāpānatakkacārā[V 0.0085], ekuppādanirodhakā;

Vuttā hi yamake kāyavacīsaṅkhāranāmakā.

In-and-out breathing and initial and sustained thought, having a single arising and ceasing, are called in the Yamaka the bodily and verbal formations.

878.

878.

Cittuppādakkhaṇe jātā, utu tassa ṭhitikkhaṇe;

Rūpaṃ janeti tatthāpi, utu bhaṅgakkhaṇepi ca.

The temperature born at the moment of consciousness-arising generates matter at its own presence-moment, and so too does the temperature at its dissolution-moment.

879.

879.

Anupubbakkamenevaṃ, jātaṃ rūpaṃ tathāparaṃ;

Aṭṭhārasamauppādaṭṭhitiādīsu bhijjati.

Thus in gradual succession matter is born, and likewise other matter. It perishes at the arising, presence, and so on, of the eighteenth consciousness.

880.

880.

Itthaṃ kalāpā ghaṭitā, utujāhārajāpi ca;

Ekasantatisambandhā, ekapaññāsa labbhare.

Thus the groups born of temperature and nutriment are also constituted. Connected by a single continuity, they are obtained as fifty-one.

881.

881.

Kalāpā cittajā yasmā, uppādakkhaṇasambhūtā;

Ghaṭikā saha labbhanti, tasmā sattaraseva te.

Since the mind-born groups arise at the arising-moment of consciousness, the chains obtained are therefore only seventeen.

882.

882.

Sabbepi rūpajanakā, cittuppāde yathāsakaṃ;

Janenti ṭhitibhaṅgesu, na janentīti kecanā.

All producers of matter generate it at the arising of consciousness according to their respective natures; but some say they do not generate it at the moments of presence and dissolution.

883.

883.

Kusalābyākatādīnaṃ, ekuppādanirodhatā;

Dhammānaṃ yamake vuttā, iti pāḷi vadanti ca.

And they quote the Pāli text, saying: 'It is stated in the Yamaka that wholesome, indeterminate, and other such states have a single arising and ceasing.'

884.

884.

Kusalādikasambandhā, tattha tattha hi desitā;

Iti vatvā pure vuttaṃ, icchantācariyā nayaṃ.

Having said, 'For the connection with the wholesome and so on has been taught in various places,' the teachers express their preference for the method stated before.

885.

885.

Iccevaṃ catusambhūtā, rūpasantatirāsayo;

Rūpāni ca kalāpā ca, ekābaddhā yathārahaṃ.

Thus the heaps of the continuity of matter, arisen from the four causes, and the material phenomena and groups, are bound together as one, as is appropriate.

886.

886.

Suttapavattamattānaṃ, sambuddhānampi pāṇinaṃ;

Yāva maraṇakālāpi, pavattanti nirantaraṃ.

For beings, even for the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, from the state of being asleep up to the time of death, these continuities proceed without interruption.

887.

887.

Āyukkhayā [M 0.0078] ca maraṇaṃ, tathā kammakkhayā siyā;

Ubhinnaṃ vā khayā cātha, upacchedakakammunā.

Death occurs by the exhaustion of the life-span, and likewise it may be by the exhaustion of kamma, or by the exhaustion of both, or by a destructive kamma.

888.

888.

Catudhāpi marantassa, tassevaṃ tu yathārahaṃ;

Sattarasacittakkhaṇamattasesamhi jīvite.

When, for one dying in any of these four ways, life has a remainder of only seventeen mind-moments,

889.

889.

Upariccuticittassa[V 0.0086], sattarasamacetaso;

Ṭhitikālamupādāya, na tu jāyati kammajaṃ.

From the presence-moment of the seventeenth consciousness counted backwards from the death-consciousness, kamma-born matter no longer arises.

890.

890.

Tassuppādakkhaṇe jātaṃ,

Rūpañca cutiyā saha;

Bhijjatīti mato nāma,

Tato hoti sa puggalo.

And the matter that arose at the arising-moment of the death-consciousness perishes along with it. Then that person is said to be 'dead'.

891.

891.

Cittajāhārajañcāpi, na jāyati tato paraṃ;

Utusambhavarūpaṃ tu, avasissati vā na vā.

Thereafter, mind-born and nutriment-born matter no longer arise; but matter produced by temperature may or may not remain.

892.

892.

Tato vuttanayeneva, matasatto yathārahaṃ;

Missāmissāhi sandhīhi, punadevopapajjati.

Then, by the method stated, the dead being is reborn again, as is appropriate, through mixed and unmixed connections.

893.

893.

Tato vuttanayeneva, ekūnatiṃsa kammajā;

Tesamuṭṭhānikā pañca, catuttiṃsa samissitā.

Then, by the method stated, there are twenty-nine kamma-born groups. Of these, five originate from other causes, and thirty-four are mixed.

894.

894.

Kalāpā rāsayo honti, sattavīsatibhūmisu;

Iti sabbapakārena, rūpadhammā pakāsitāti.

Groups are heaps in the twenty-seven planes. Thus in every way have material phenomena been explained.

Iti rūpavibhāge pakiṇṇakakathā niṭṭhitā.

Here ends the miscellaneous discussion in the Analysis of Matter.

Dvāvīsatimo paricchedo.

The Twenty-second Chapter.

Niṭṭhito ca sabbathāpi rūpavibhāgo.

And thus the Analysis of Matter is entirely completed.

Tevīsatimo paricchedo

The Twenty-third Chapter.

4. Nibbānavibhāgo

4. The Analysis of Nibbāna

23. Mūlavisuddhikathā

23. The Discourse on the Root Purification

895.

895.

Itthaṃ [M 0.0079][V 0.0087] cittaṃ cetasikaṃ, rūpañcevāti saṅkhatā;

Vuttā asaṅkhataṃ dāni, nibbānanti pavuccati.

Thus consciousness, mental factors, and matter have been called the conditioned. Now the unconditioned, called Nibbāna, will be spoken of.

896.

896.

Sīlavisuddhi ādimhi, tato cittavisuddhi ca;

Diṭṭhivisuddhināmā ca, kaṅkhāvitaraṇāpi ca.

In the beginning there is the purification of virtue, and then the purification of consciousness, the one named purification of view, and also the purification by overcoming doubt.

897.

897.

Tato paraṃ maggāmagga-ñāṇadassananāmikā;

Tathā paṭipadāñāṇa-dassanā ñāṇadassanaṃ.

After that come the purification named knowledge and vision of path and not-path, likewise the knowledge and vision of the way of practice, and the knowledge and vision.

898.

898.

Iccānukkamato vuttā, satta honti visuddhiyo;

Sattamānuttarā tattha, pubbabhāgā cha lokiyā.

Thus, spoken in sequence, there are seven purifications. Therein, the seventh is supramundane, while the six preceding ones are mundane.

899.

899.

Saṃvaro pātimokkho ca, tathevindriyasaṃvaro;

Ājīvapārisuddhi ca, sīlaṃ paccayanissitaṃ.

Restraint in accordance with the Pātimokkha, restraint of the sense faculties, purity of livelihood, and virtue concerning the requisites.

900.

900.

Iti sīlavisuddhīti, suddhametaṃ pavuccati;

Catupārisuddhisīlaṃ, dhutaṅgaparivāritaṃ.

This is called the purification of virtue, which is the fourfold purification of virtue, pure, and accompanied by the ascetic practices.

901.

901.

Kasiṇāni dasāsubhā, dasānussatiyo pana;

Appamaññā ca saññā ca, vavatthāruppakāti ca.

The ten kasiṇas, the ten foulnesses, and the ten recollections; the four illimitables, the one perception, the one analysis, and the four formless states.

902.

902.

Samathakkammaṭṭhānāni, tālīsaṭṭhakathānaye;

Pāḷiyaṃ tu vibhattāni, aṭṭhatiṃsāti vaṇṇitaṃ.

The serenity meditation subjects are forty in the commentarial method; but in the Pāli Canon they are divided and described as thirty-eight.

903.

903.

Pathavāpo ca tejo ca,

Vāyo nīlañca pītakaṃ;

Lohitodātamākāsaṃ[V 0.0088],

Ālokakasiṇanti ca.

Earth, water, fire, and air; blue, yellow, red, and white; space, and the light kasiṇa.

904.

904.

Kasiṇāni dasetāni, vuttānaṭṭhakathānaye;

Aṭṭheva pāḷiyaṃ hitvā, ante tu kasiṇadvayaṃ.

These ten kasiṇas are taught according to the method of the commentaries; but in the Pāli Canon, omitting eight, only the final two kasiṇas are given.

905.

905.

Uddhumātaṃ vinīlañca, vipubbakaṃ vikhāyitaṃ;

Vicchiddakañca vikkhittaṃ, hatavikkhittalohitaṃ.

The bloated and the livid, the festering and the gnawed; the cut-up and the scattered, the hacked-and-scattered, and the bloody.

906.

906.

Puḷavakaṃ [M 0.0080] aṭṭhikañceti, asubhā dasa desitā;

Rūpakāyavibhāgāya, dasakāyavipattiyā.

The worm-infested and the skeleton—thus the ten kinds of foulness are taught for the analysis of the material body and for the ten stages of bodily decay.

907.

907.

Buddhe dhamme ca saṅghe ca, sīle cāge ca attanā;

Devatopasamāyañca, sattānussatiyo kamā.

Recollection of the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha; of one's own virtue and generosity; and of deities and peace—these are the seven recollections in order.

908.

908.

Maraṇassati nāmekā, tathā kāyagatāsati;

Ānāpānassaticcevaṃ, dasānussatiyo matā.

Mindfulness of death is one, as is mindfulness directed to the body, and mindfulness of breathing; thus the ten recollections are considered.

909.

909.

Mettā karuṇā muditā, upekkhāti catubbidhā;

Vuttā brahmavihārā ca, appamaññāti tādinā.

Loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—these four are called the Brahmavihāras and the immeasurables by the Such One.

910.

910.

Ekāhāre paṭikkūla-saññā nāmekameva tu;

Catudhātuvavatthānaṃ, catudhātupariggaho.

One subject is the perception of repulsiveness in nutriment; the other is the analysis of the four elements, that is, the defining of the four elements.

911.

911.

Ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ, viññāṇañcamathāparaṃ;

Ākiñcaññaṃ tathā neva-saññānāsaññanāmakaṃ.

The base of infinite space, then the base of infinite consciousness; likewise, the base of nothingness, and the one named the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

912.

912.

Iccānukkamato vuttā, arūpajjhānikā pana;

Arūpakammaṭṭhānāni, cattāropi pakittitā.

Thus, in due order, have been spoken the formless jhānas; and the four formless meditation subjects have also been declared.

913.

913.

Kasiṇāsubhakoṭṭhāse, ānāpāne ca sabbathā;

Disvā sutvā phusitvā vā, parikammaṃ tu kubbato.

For one who in every way undertakes the preliminary work on the kasiṇas, the foulness meditations, the parts of the body, and mindfulness of breathing—whether having seen, heard, or touched the object—

914.

914.

Uggaho nāma sambhoti, nimittaṃ tattha yuñjato;

Paṭibhāgo tamārabbha, tattha vattati appanā.

for one applying themself to that object, the learning sign arises. Taking that as a basis, the counterpart sign appears, and in dependence on it, absorption occurs.

915.

915.

Sādhu [V 0.0089] sattā sukhī hontu, dukkhā muccantu pāṇino;

Aho sattā sukhappattā, hontu yadicchakāti ca.

‘May beings be happy! May living beings be freed from suffering! Oh, may beings not be parted from the happiness they have attained!’

916.

916.

Uddissa vā anodissa, yuñjato sattagocare;

Appamaññā panappenti, anupubbena vattikā.

For one who applies themself to the sphere of beings, whether in a specified or unspecified manner, the immeasurables are developed in due order.

917.

917.

Kasiṇugghāṭimākāse, paṭhamāruppamānase;

Tasseva natthibhāve ca, tatiyāruppaketi ca.

By removing the kasiṇa and attending to space, the mind reaches the first formless attainment; and by attending to the non-existence of that consciousness, it reaches the third formless attainment.

918.

918.

Yuñjantassa [M 0.0081] panetesu, gocaresu catūsupi;

Appenti anupubbena, āruppāpi catubbidhā.

And for one who applies themself to these four objects, the four kinds of formless states also arise in due order.

919.

919.

Ānāpānañca kasiṇaṃ, pañcakajjhānikaṃ tahiṃ;

Paṭhamajjhānikā vuttā, koṭṭhāsāsubhabhāvanā.

Mindfulness of breathing and the kasiṇas are subjects for the five-jhāna system. The development of the parts of the body and the foulness meditations are said to be subjects for the first jhāna only.

920.

920.

Sukhitajjhānikā tisso, appamaññā ca heṭṭhimā;

Upekkhāruppakā pañca, upekkhājhānikāti ca.

The three lower immeasurables are subjects for jhānas accompanied by happiness. The five subjects—equanimity and the formless attainments—are for jhānas of equanimity.

921.

921.

Ekā dasekā dasa ca, tayo pañceti sabbathā;

Parikammavasā tiṃsa, cha koṭṭhāsā yathākkamaṃ.

One ten, and another ten, three, and five in all; thirty by way of preliminary work, six sections in order.

922.

922.

Pañcakādisukhopekkhā, jhānabhedā catubbidhā;

Ekaccatupañcajhāna-vasena tividhā siyuṃ.

The distinctions of jhāna are fourfold: by the fivefold system and so forth, by happiness, and by equanimity. They are also threefold, according to whether they lead to one, four, or five jhānas.

923.

923.

Rūpārūpavasā dve ca, appanāto punekadhā;

Iccevamappanā kamma-ṭṭhānabhedā samissitā.

They are also twofold, by way of the form and formless spheres; and again onefold, from the standpoint of absorption. Thus are the absorption meditation subjects variously classified.

924.

924.

Dve ca saññāvavatthānā, aṭṭhānussatiyoti ca;

Sesā dasa pavuccanti, upacārasamādhikā.

The perception of repulsiveness in nutriment and the analysis of the four elements, along with the first eight recollections—these ten subjects are said to lead only to access concentration.

925.

925.

Parikammopacārānulomagotrabhuto paraṃ;

Pañcamaṃ vā catutthaṃ vā, javanaṃ hoti appanā.

After the moments of preparation, access, conformity, and change-of-lineage, the fifth or fourth impulsion is absorption.

926.

926.

Appanājavanaṃ sabbaṃ, lokuttaramahaggataṃ;

Tihetukaparittāni, purimāni yathārahaṃ.

All absorption impulsion is either supramundane or sublime. The preceding moments are, as appropriate, sense-sphere and accompanied by three wholesome roots.

927.

927.

Āvajjanā [V 0.0090] ca vasitā, taṃsamāpajjanā tathā;

Adhiṭṭhānā ca vuṭṭhānā, paccavekkhaṇa pañcamā.

Adverting, attaining, determining, emerging, and reviewing as the fifth—these are the five masteries.

928.

928.

Vasitāhi vasībhūtā, iti katvāna pañcahi;

Bhāventassa panappenti, uparūpari appanā.

Having become a master by means of these five masteries, for one who develops them, the absorptions arise one above the other.

929.

929.

Yuñjantassa tu vuṭṭhāya, kasiṇajjhānapañcamā;

Pañcābhiññā hi appenti, rūpasaddādigocare.

For one who applies themself after emerging from the fifth jhāna based on a kasiṇa, the five higher knowledges arise, having as their objects forms, sounds, and so on.

930.

930.

Lokuttarā panappenti, sabbe nibbānagocare;

Aniccadukkhānattāti, bhūmidhamme vipassato.

The supramundane states, all having Nibbāna as their object, arise for one who contemplates the phenomena of the planes of existence as impermanent, suffering, and non-self.

931.

931.

Tattha [M 0.0082] ca pādakajjhānaṃ, sammaṭṭhajjhānameva vā;

Ajjhāsayo ca vuṭṭhāna-gāminī ca vipassanā.

And therein, there are the basic jhāna, or the jhāna that has been contemplated, the meditator's inclination, and insight that leads to emergence.

932.

932.

Maggānaṃ jhānabhedāya, yathāyogaṃ niyāmatā;

Yathāsakaṃ phalānaṃ tu, maggā honti niyāmatā.

The jhānic character of the paths is determined by the corresponding basic jhāna. But for their respective fruits, the paths themselves are the determining factors.

933.

933.

Maggānantaramevātha, bhūmidhamme vipassato;

Phalasamāpattiyampi, appeti phalamānasaṃ.

Then, immediately after the path, the fruit-consciousness arises. For one who contemplates the phenomena of the planes, the fruit-consciousness also arises in the attainment of fruition.

934.

934.

Anupubbasamāpattiṃ, samāpajjissa vuṭṭhito;

Jhānadhamme vipassitvā, tattha tattheva paṇḍito.

The wise one, having entered into and emerged from the successive attainments, contemplates the jhāna factors right there in each attainment.

935.

935.

Catutthāruppamappetvā, ekadvijavanāparaṃ;

Nirodhaṃ nāma phusati, samāpattimacittakaṃ.

Having attained the fourth formless jhāna, after one or two impulsions of that jhāna, one touches the so-called attainment of cessation, the attainment without consciousness.

936.

936.

Arahā vā anāgāmī, pañcavokārabhūmiyaṃ;

Yathāsakaṃ phaluppādo, vuṭṭhānanti tato mato.

For an Arahant or a non-returner in the five-aggregate plane of existence, the arising of their respective fruit-consciousness is considered the emergence from that attainment.

937.

937.

Appanāpariyosāne, siyā sabbattha sambhavā;

Bhavaṅgapāto taṃ chetvā, jāyate paccavekkhaṇā.

At the conclusion of absorption, a lapse into the life-continuum may occur in every case. Cutting this off, the reviewing consciousness arises.

938.

938.

Iti vuttānusārena, appanānayasaṅgahaṃ;

Yathāyogaṃ vibhāveyya, tattha tattha vicakkhaṇo.

Thus, in accordance with what has been said, a discerning person should analyze this summary of the method of absorption, distinguishing each case as is suitable.

939.

939.

Cittavisuddhi [V 0.0091] nāmāyaṃ, cittasaṃklesasodhano;

Upacārappanābhedo, samatho pubbabhāgiyoti.

This is called Purification of Mind, the cleansing of the mind's defilements. Distinguished as access and absorption, it is serenity, which is the preliminary part.

Iti nibbānavibhāge mūlavisuddhikathā niṭṭhitā.

Thus in the Analysis of Nibbāna ends the discourse on the foundational purifications.

Tevīsatimo paricchedo.

The Twenty-Third Chapter.

Catuvīsatimo paricchedo

The Twenty-Fourth Chapter.

24. Pariggahavisuddhikathā

24. The Discourse on Purification by Comprehension.

940.

940.

Sīlacittavisuddhīhi, yathāvuttāhi maṇḍito;

Payogāsayasampanno, nibbānābhirato tato.

Adorned with the purifications of virtue and mind as described, endowed with proper application and disposition, one thereafter delights in Nibbāna.

941.

941.

Khandhāyatanadhātādippabhedehi [M 0.0083] yathārahaṃ;

Lakkhaṇapaccupaṭṭhāna-padaṭṭhānavibhāgato.

By way of the divisions of aggregates, bases, elements, and so on, as is fit; and by way of the distinction of characteristic, manifestation, and proximate cause.

942.

942.

Pariggahetvā saṅkhāre, nāmarūpaṃ yathākathaṃ;

Vavatthapento tatthevamanupassati paññavā.

Having comprehended the formations—that is, name-and-form as it is—the wise one determines and contemplates it right there.

943.

943.

Nāmarūpamidaṃ suddhaṃ, attabhāvoti vuccati;

Natthettha koci attā vā, satto jīvo ca puggalo.

This pure name-and-form is called an 'individual existence'; but here there is no self or being, no life-principle or person.

944.

944.

Yathāpi aṅgasambhārā, hoti saddo ratho iti;

Evaṃ khandhesu santesu, hoti sattoti sammuti.

Just as from an assemblage of parts the word 'chariot' arises, so too, when the aggregates are present, there is the convention 'a being.'

945.

945.

Khandhāyatanadhātūnaṃ, yathāyogamanukkamo;

Abbocchinno pavattanto, saṃsāroti pavuccati.

The uninterruptedly occurring succession of aggregates, bases, and elements, in their respective connections, is called saṃsāra.

946.

946.

Iti nānappakārena, tebhūmakapariggaho;

Bhūmidhammavavatthānaṃ, suddhasaṅkhāradassanaṃ.

Thus in various ways, this comprehension of the three planes, this determination of the phenomena of the planes, this seeing of bare formations,

947.

947.

Attadiṭṭhipahānena[V 0.0092], diṭṭhisaṃklesasodhanaṃ;

Diṭṭhivisuddhi nāmāti, ñāṇametaṃ pavuccati.

the cleansing of the defilement of view through the abandoning of self-view—this knowledge is called Purification of View.

948.

948.

Pariggahitasaṅkhāro, nāmarūpamapatthiyā;

Tato paraṃ yathāyogaṃ, pariggaṇhati paccaye.

Having comprehended the formations, not desiring name-and-form, one then, as is fit, comprehends their conditions.

949.

949.

Dukkhasamudayo tattha, taṇhā saṃsāranāyikā;

Samodhāneti saṅkhāre, tattha tatthupapattiyā.

Therein, the origin of suffering is craving, the leader through saṃsāra; it connects the formations for arising here and there.

950.

950.

Taṇhāsambhavamevetaṃ, tasmā dukkhaṃ pavuccati;

Tadappavatti nibbānaṃ, maggo taṃpāpakoti ca.

Since this arises from craving, it is called suffering; its non-occurrence is Nibbāna, and the path is the means for its attainment.

951.

951.

Catusaccavavatthāna-mukhenevampi paccaye;

Pariggaṇhanti ekacce, saṅkhārānamathāpare.

Some comprehend conditions by way of determining the Four Truths, while others comprehend those of the formations.

952.

952.

Ālokākāsavāyāpapathaviñcupanissayaṃ;

Bhavaṅgapariṇāmañca, labhitvāva yathārahaṃ.

Having duly obtained as support light, space, wind, water, and earth, and the transformation of the life-continuum,

953.

953.

Cha vatthūni ca nissāya, cha dvārārammaṇāni ca;

Paṭicca manasikāraṃ, pavattanti arūpino.

and depending on the six bases and the six sense objects, conditioned by attention, the immaterial phenomena proceed.

954.

954.

Yathāsakasamuṭṭhānaṃ[M 0.0084], vibhāgehi ca rūpino;

Pavattanti ekacceti, pariggaṇhanti paccaye.

Some comprehend conditions thus: that the material phenomena proceed according to their respective origins and divisions.

955.

955.

Avijjāpaccayā honti, saṅkhārā tu tato tathā;

Viññāṇaṃ nāmarūpañca, saḷāyatananāmakaṃ.

Conditioned by ignorance are the formations; then likewise consciousness, name-and-form, and what is called the sixfold sense base.

956.

956.

Phasso ca vedanā taṇhā, upādānaṃ bhavo tato;

Jāti jarā maraṇañca, pavattati yathārahaṃ.

And contact, feeling, craving, clinging, and then becoming; birth, aging, and death—all proceed accordingly.

957.

957.

Tato soko paridevo, dukkhañceva tathāparaṃ;

Domanassamupāyāso, sambhoti ca yathārahaṃ.

Thence sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise accordingly.

958.

958.

Etassa kevalassevaṃ, dukkhakkhandhassa sambhavo;

Paṭiccasamuppādova, natthañño koci kārako.

Thus is the origin of this entire mass of suffering. It is simply dependent origination; there is no other agent.

959.

959.

Tatthāvijjādayo [V 0.0093] dvepi, addhātīto anāgato;

Jātādayopare aṭṭha, paccuppannoti vaṇṇito.

Therein, the two beginning with ignorance are of the past time; [there is also] the future. The other eight beginning with birth are described as the present.

960.

960.

Puññāpuññāneñjavasā, saṅkhārā tividhā tathā;

Bhavekadeso kammañca, kammavaṭṭanti vuccati.

Formations are likewise threefold, by way of the meritorious, demeritorious, and imperturbable. These, and kamma which is a part of existence, are called the round of kamma.

961.

961.

Avijjātaṇhupādānā, klesavaṭṭamathāpare;

Vipākavaṭṭaṃ sattāpi, upapattibhavopi ca.

Ignorance, craving, and clinging are the round of defilements; the other seven links, along with rebirth-existence, are the round of results.

962.

962.

Avijjāsaṅkhārānaṃ tu, gahaṇe gahitāva te;

Taṇhupādānabhavāti, atīte pañca hetavo.

Indeed, when ignorance and formations are grasped, craving, clinging, and becoming are also grasped; these are the five causes in the past.

963.

963.

Taṇhupādānabhavānaṃ, gahaṇe gahitāva te;

Avijjā saṅkhārā ceti, paccuppannepi pañcake.

When craving, clinging, and becoming are grasped, ignorance and formations are also grasped; these are the five causes in the present.

964.

964.

Viññāṇādisarūpena, dassitaṃ phalapañcakaṃ;

Tathā tadeva jātādi-nāmenānāgatanti ca.

The pentad of results is shown in the form of consciousness and so on; and that same pentad is the future, under the names of birth and so on.

965.

965.

Atīte hetavo pañca, idāni phalapañcakaṃ;

Idāni hetavo pañca, āyatiṃ phalapañcakaṃ.

Five causes in the past, a pentad of results now; five causes now, a pentad of results in the future.

966.

966.

Hetuphalaṃ phalahetu, puna hetuphalāni ca;

Tisandhi catusaṅkhepaṃ, vīsatākāramabravuṃ.

Cause-and-result, result-and-cause, and again cause-and-result; three connections, four groups, and twenty modes have they taught.

967.

967.

Atthadhammapaṭivedha-desanānaṃ [M 0.0085] yathārahaṃ;

Gambhīrattā catunnampi, catugambhīratā matā.

Because of the profundity of these four—meaning, Dhamma, teaching, and penetration—this is known as the fourfold profundity.

968.

968.

Ekattanānattanayā, abyāpāranayoparo;

Tathevaṃdhammatā ceti, nayā vuttā catubbidhā.

The methods of unity and diversity, the method of non-agency, and that of specific conditionality—these four methods are declared.

969.

969.

Jarāmaraṇasokādi-pīḷitānamabhiṇhaso;

Āsavānaṃ samuppādā, avijjā ca pavattati.

For those constantly afflicted by aging, death, sorrow, and so on, ignorance proceeds from the arising of the taints.

970.

970.

Avijjāpaccayā honti, saṅkhārāpi yathā pure;

Baddhāvicchedamiccevaṃ, bhavacakkamanādikaṃ.

Conditioned by ignorance, formations arise as before; thus, bound and unbroken, the wheel of existence is without a beginning.

971.

971.

Taṇhāvijjānābhikaṃ [V 0.0094] taṃ, jarāmaraṇanemikaṃ;

Sesākārādighaṭikaṃ, tibhavārathayojitaṃ.

It has craving and ignorance as its hub, aging and death as its rim, and the remaining factors as its spokes, yoked to the chariot of the three planes of existence.

972.

972.

Tiaddhañca tivaṭṭañca, tisandhighaṭikaṃ tathā;

Catusaṅkhepagambhīranayamaṇḍitadesanaṃ.

An exposition of the three time periods, the three rounds, and joined by the three connections; adorned with the four groups and the profound methods.

973.

973.

Vīsatākāravibhāgaṃ, dvādasākārasaṅgahaṃ;

Dhammaṭṭhitīti dīpenti, idappaccayataṃ budhā.

The wise illuminate this specific conditionality, the stability of phenomena, which is divided into twenty modes and comprised of twelve factors.

974.

974.

Paṭiccasamuppādoyaṃ, paccayākāranāmato;

Saṅkhepato ca vitthārā, vividhākārabhedato.

This is dependent origination, also named the mode of conditionality, divided in brief and in detail according to its various aspects.

975.

975.

Janeti paccayuppanne, avijjādipavattiyā;

Avijjādinirodhena, nirodheti ca sabbathā.

Through the continuation of ignorance and so on, it generates conditioned phenomena; with the cessation of ignorance and so on, it ceases completely in every way.

976.

976.

Paccayappaccayuppanna-vaseneva pavattati;

Saṃsāroyanti ekacce, pariggaṇhanti paccaye.

Some comprehend conditions thus: 'Saṃsāra proceeds only by the force of conditions and conditioned phenomena.'

977.

977.

Samantapaṭṭhānamahāpakaraṇavibhāgato;

Ekacce pariggaṇhanti, catuvīsati paccaye.

Some comprehend the twenty-four conditions from the analysis in the Great Treatise, the Universal Paṭṭhāna.

978.

978.

Iti nānappakārena, paccayānaṃ pariggaho;

Sappaccayanāmarūpaṃ, vavatthānanti veditaṃ.

Thus, in various ways, is the comprehension of conditions; name-and-form together with its conditions is known as determination.

979.

979.

Idappaccayatāñāṇaṃ, paccayākāradassanaṃ;

Dhammaṭṭhiti yathābhūtañāṇadassananāmakaṃ.

This knowledge of specific conditionality, this seeing of the modes of conditions, is named knowledge of the stability of phenomena, knowledge and vision of things as they really are.

980.

980.

Kālattayavibhāgesu[M 0.0086], kaṅkhāsaṃklesasodhanaṃ;

Kaṅkhāvitaraṇā nāma, visuddhīti pavuccatīti.

The purification of the defilement of doubt concerning the divisions of the three periods of time is called the Purification by Overcoming Doubt.

Iti nibbānavibhāge pariggahavisuddhikathā niṭṭhitā.

Thus ends the discourse on the Purification by Comprehension in the Section on Nibbāna.

Catuvīsatimo paricchedo.

The Twenty-Fourth Chapter.

Pañcavīsatimo paricchedo

The Twenty-Fifth Chapter

25. Vipassanāvuddhikathā

25. Discourse on the Growth of Insight

981.

981.

Sīlacittadiṭṭhikaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhiyo[V 0.0095];

Patvā kalāpato tāva, sammaseyya tato paraṃ.

Having attained the purifications of virtue, consciousness, view, and overcoming doubt, one should first contemplate by way of groups, and then in greater detail.

982.

982.

Kalāpato sammasanaṃ, udayabbayadassanaṃ;

Bhaṅgañāṇaṃ bhayañāṇaṃ, tathādīnavanibbidā.

Contemplation by way of groups, discernment of arising and passing away, knowledge of dissolution, knowledge of fear, and likewise of danger and disenchantment.

983.

983.

Muccitukamyatāñāṇaṃ, paṭisaṅkhānupassanā;

Saṅkhārupekkhānulomamiccānukkamato ṭhitā.

Knowledge of the desire for deliverance, reflective contemplation, equanimity towards formations, and conformity knowledge—these stand in due sequence.

984.

984.

Vipassanāti cakkhātā, dasañāṇaparamparā;

Lakkhaṇattayamāhacca, saṅkhāresu pavattati.

This succession of ten knowledges, called insight, proceeds with regard to formations by comprehending the three characteristics.

985.

985.

Tasmā kalāpato tāva, sammaseyya tilakkhaṇaṃ;

Sammasitvā atītādikhandhāyatanadhātuyo.

Therefore, one should first contemplate the three characteristics by way of groups, after having contemplated the aggregates, sense bases, and elements of the past, etc.

986.

986.

Aniccā te khayaṭṭhena, khandhā dukkhā bhayaṭṭhato;

Anattā asārakaṭṭhena, iccābhiṇhaṃ vicintayaṃ.

One should reflect repeatedly thus: 'Those aggregates are impermanent in the sense of perishing, suffering in the sense of being fearful, and not-self in the sense of being without substance.'

987.

987.

Tassevaṃ sammasantassa, upaṭṭhāti tilakkhaṇaṃ;

Saṅkhāresu tato yogī, khaṇasantatiaddhato.

For one thus contemplating, the three characteristics become manifest. Then the yogi certainly sees the formations as a succession of moments.

988.

988.

Paccuppannāna dhammānaṃ, udayañca vayaṃ tathā;

Paññāsākārabhedehi, anupassati tattha hi.

For there one contemplates the arising and passing away of present phenomena through the fifty different aspects.

989.

989.

Avijjātaṇhākammānaṃ, udayā ca nirodhato;

Samudayā nirodhā ca, pañcannaṃ dassitā tathā.

From the arising and cessation of ignorance, craving, and kamma, the arising and cessation of the five aggregates are likewise shown.

990.

990.

Rūpassāhārato [M 0.0087] tiṇṇaṃ, phassato nāmarūpato;

Viññāṇasseti sabbepi, cattālīsa samissitā.

For the form aggregate from nutriment, for the three [mental aggregates] from contact, and for consciousness from name-and-form—thus all forty [aspects of arising] are included.

991.

991.

Nibbattilakkhaṇaṃ [V 0.0096] bhaṅga-

Lakkhaṇañcettha passato;

Khaṇatodayato ceti,

Samapaññāsa honti te.

For one who sees here the characteristic of production and the characteristic of dissolution, these aspects of momentary arising and passing away amount to fifty.

992.

992.

Iti khandhamukhenete, vibhattā udayabbayā;

Āyatannādibhedehi, yojetabbā yathārahaṃ.

Thus these arisings and passings away have been analyzed by way of the aggregates; they should be applied appropriately by way of the distinctions of the sense bases, etc.

993.

993.

Udayañca vayañcevaṃ, passato tassa yogino;

Vibhūtā honti saṅkhārā, samuṭṭhāti tilakkhaṇaṃ.

For that yogi who thus sees arising and passing away, the formations become distinct and the three characteristics arise.

994.

994.

Bodhipakkhiyadhammā ca,

Te passanti visesato;

Tato jāyantupaklesā,

Dasopaklesavatthukā.

They also see the factors of enlightenment with special clarity; then arise the corruptions of insight, which are founded on ten bases.

995.

995.

Obhāso pīti passaddhi, adhimokkho ca paggaho;

Sukhaṃ ñāṇamupaṭṭhānaṃ, upekkhā ca nikanti ca.

Illumination, rapture, tranquility, resolution, and exertion; happiness, knowledge, mindfulness, equanimity, and subtle craving.

996.

996.

Taṇhāmānadiṭṭhiggāhavasena tividhepi te;

Assādento unnamanto, mamāyanto kilissati.

By way of craving, conceit, and grasping at views, one becomes defiled concerning these in three ways: by savoring them, by exalting oneself, and by claiming them as 'mine'.

997.

997.

Maggaṃ phalañca nibbānaṃ, pattosmīti akovido;

Vekkhabujjhāti maññanto, pappoti adhimāniko.

Thinking, 'I have attained the path, the fruit, and Nibbāna,' the unskilled one, considering himself a clear perceiver, becomes arrogant.

998.

998.

Maggādayo na hontete,

Taṇhāgāhādivatthuto;

Taṇhāmānadiṭṭhiyo cupaklesā paripanthakā.

These are not the path and so on, for they are objects for craving and grasping. Craving, conceit, and views are corruptions and obstacles.

999.

999.

Porāṇameva khandhānaṃ, udayabbayadassanaṃ;

Tilakkhaṇārammaṇato, maggo nibbānapaccayo.

It is just the previous seeing of the arising and passing away of the aggregates, which takes the three characteristics as its object, that is the path, the condition for Nibbāna.

1000.

1000.

Iti [M 0.0088] maggaṃ amaggañca, visodhentassa sijjhati;

Visuddhi ca maggāmaggañāṇadassananāmikā.

Thus, for one who purifies the distinction between the path and the non-path, the purification named Knowledge and Vision of the Path and the Non-Path is accomplished.

1001.

1001.

Tathāparā [V 0.0097] visuddhīnaṃ, udayabbayadassanaṃ;

Ādiṃ katvā paṭipadāñāṇadassananāmikā.

Likewise, the next purification, named Knowledge and Vision of the Course of Practice, begins with the discernment of arising and passing away.

1002.

1002.

Pacchā saṃklesavikkhepavisuddhantaṃ yathā pure;

Paṭipajjati medhāvī, udayabbayadassanaṃ.

Afterwards, the wise one proceeds as before with the discernment of arising and passing away, until purified from the corruptions and distraction.

1003.

1003.

Iti khodayabbayānupassanāñāṇavīthiyaṃ;

Sikkhantassācireneva, paripakkā vipassanā.

Thus indeed, for one training in the way of the knowledge of contemplation of arising and passing away, insight matures before long.

1004.

1004.

Pahāyodayavohāraṃ, vayamevādhimuccato;

Uppādābhogamohāya, bhaṅgamevānutiṭṭhati.

Abandoning the concept of arising and focusing solely on passing away, not delighting in the appearance of arising, one abides observing only dissolution.

1005.

1005.

Tato nijjharadhārāva, gaṅgāvārodakaṃ viya;

Bhijjamānatiṇāniva, paṭipajjā sikhā viya.

Then, like the current of a waterfall, like the swift flow of a great river, like brittle stalks being snapped, like the flame of a lamp being extinguished.

1006.

1006.

Patante ca vayante ca, bhijjanticceva saṅkhate;

Passato tassa bhaṅgānupassanāñāṇamīritaṃ.

For one who sees conditioned things as just perishing, ceasing, and breaking apart, this knowledge is called the Contemplation of Dissolution.

1007.

1007.

Tato bhayānupassanā, sabhayāti vipassato;

Ādīnavānupassanā-ñāṇaṃ ādīnavāti ca.

Then, for one who sees all formations as fearful, there arises the Contemplation of Fear; and seeing them as dangerous, the Knowledge of Contemplation of Danger.

1008.

1008.

Nibbidānupassanā ca, nibbindantassa yogino;

Muccitukamyatāñāṇaṃ, tato muccitumicchato.

And for the yogi who is becoming disenchanted, there is the Contemplation of Disenchantment; then, for one who desires to be delivered, the Knowledge of the Desire for Deliverance.

1009.

1009.

Niccā ce na nirujjheyya, na bādheyya sukhā yadi;

Vase vatteyya attā ce, tadabhāvā na te tathā.

If they were permanent, they would not cease; if they were pleasant, they would not afflict; if they were self, they would be under one's control. Due to the absence of these, they are not so.

1010.

1010.

Suṭṭhu muccitumiccevaṃ, paṭipaccakkhato tato;

Paṭisaṅkhānupassanā-ñāṇaṃ jātanti vuccati.

Thus, for one truly desiring liberation and turning back from that, the knowledge of Contemplation of Reflection is said to arise.

1011.

1011.

Sādhukaṃ paṭisaṅkhāya, saṅkhāresu tilakkhaṇaṃ;

Supariññātasaṅkhāre, tatheva paṭipassati.

Having thoroughly reflected on the three characteristics in formations, and having fully understood the formations, one sees them just as they are.

1012.

1012.

Aniccā dukkhānattā ca, saṅkhārāva na cāparo;

Attā vā attanīyaṃ vā, nāhaṃ na tu mamāti ca.

Formations are just impermanent, suffering, and not-self, and there is nothing else; there is no self or what belongs to a self, not an 'I' nor a 'mine'.

1013.

1013.

Tatova [M 0.0089][V 0.0098] tattha majjhatto, nandirāgavinissaṭo;

Attattaniyabhāvena, saṅkhāresvajjhupekkhati.

Then, being impartial towards them and detached from delight and passion, one looks upon formations with equanimity, due to their being devoid of a self or what belongs to a self.

1014.

1014.

Saṅkhārupekkhāsaṅkhātaṃ, ñāṇaṃ tassa itīritaṃ;

Tato vuṭṭhānaghaṭitaṃ, anulomanti vuccati.

This is called the knowledge of equanimity towards formations, thus it is said; from that, the knowledge connected with emergence is called conformity knowledge.

1015.

1015.

Supariññātasaṅkhāre, susammaṭṭhatilakkhaṇe;

Upekkhantassa tasseva, sikhāpattā vipassanā.

Having fully comprehended formations and well discerned the three characteristics, for one who regards them with equanimity, insight attains its peak.

1016.

1016.

Saṅkhāradhamme ārabbha, tāva kālaṃ pavattati;
