Tīradassīva sakuṇo, yāva pāraṃ na passati.

Concerning the phenomena of formations, it proceeds for such a time, like a bird seeing the near shore, as long as it does not see the far shore.

1017.

1017.

Yadā passati nibbānaṃ, vuṭṭhānagahitā tadā;

Vuṭṭhānagāminī nāma, sānulomā pavuccati.

When it sees Nibbāna, then it is oriented towards emergence; it is called 'leading to emergence', together with conformity.

1018.

1018.

Iti dvīhi visuddhīhi, visuddhāya vipassato;

Vipassanāpaṭipadaṃ, pūretīti pavuccatīti.

Thus, for one who sees with insight purified by means of the two purifications, it is said that he fulfills the path of insight.

Iti nibbānavibhāge vipassanāvuddhikathā niṭṭhitā.

Thus, in the section on Nibbāna, the discussion on the development of insight is concluded.

Pañcavīsatimo paricchedo.

The Twenty-fifth Chapter.

Chabbisatimo paricchedo

The Twenty-sixth Chapter

26. Vuṭṭhānavisuddhikathā

26. The Discussion on the Purification of Emergence

1019.

1019.

Tassevaṃ paṭipannassa, sikhāpattā vipassanā;

Vuṭṭhānagāminī nāma, yadā hoti tadā pana.

For one thus practicing, when insight has attained its peak, it is then called 'leading to emergence'.

1020.

1020.

Parikammopacārānulomagotrabhuto paraṃ;

Maggo tato phalaṃ hoti, bhavaṅgā paccavekkhaṇā.

After preparation, access, conformity, and change-of-lineage, there is the path, then the fruit, a lapse into the life-continuum, and then reviewing.

1021.

1021.

Parikammopacārānulomasaṅkhātagocarā[V 0.0099];

Maggassāvajjanaṃ hutvā, nibbāne hoti gotrabhu.

Following the moments that have as their object what is designated as preparation, access, and conformity, the change-of-lineage consciousness arises, serving as the advertence to the path, with Nibbāna as its object.

1022.

1022.

Catutthaṃ pañcamaṃ vātha, chaṭṭhaṃ vāpi yathārahaṃ;

Appeti maggajavanaṃ, nibbāne sakimeva taṃ.

As the fourth, fifth, or sixth impulsion, as is appropriate, the path impulsion arises; it occurs only once, with Nibbāna as its object.

1023.

1023.

Tato [M 0.0090] phalāni tīṇi dve, ekaṃ vātha yathākkamaṃ;

Maggāvasesanirodhamaggavuṭṭhānavīthiyaṃ.

Then, in sequence, three, two, or one fruit moments arise in the cognitive process of the path, of cessation, and of emergence.

1024.

1024.

Tato bhavaṅgapātova,

Taṃ chetvā paccavekkhaṇā;

Tisso pañcavidhā honti,

Yathāyogaṃ tathā hi ca.

Then there is a lapse into the life-continuum; having cut that off, reviewing arises. These reviewing knowledges are threefold or fivefold, as is appropriate.

1025.

1025.

Maggaṃ phalañca nibbānaṃ, avassaṃ paccavekkhati;

Hīne kilese sese ca, paccavekkhati vā na vā.

One certainly reviews the path, the fruit, and Nibbāna; the defilements that have been abandoned and those that remain, one may or may not review.

1026.

1026.

Tato ca puna saṅkhāre, vipassanto yathā pure;

Appeti anupubbena, sesamaggaphalāni ca.

Then again, contemplating formations as before, one gradually attains the remaining paths and fruits.

1027.

1027.

Tattha vuccanti nibbāna-phalamaggavipassanā;

Suññatā cānimittā ca, tathāpaṇihitāni ca.

Herein are discussed Nibbāna, the fruit, the path, and insight, as well as emptiness, the signless, and the desireless.

1028.

1028.

Suññatāvipassanādināmena hi vipassati;

Vimokkhamukhabhūtāti, tividhā bhājitā tathā.

Indeed, one practices insight by way of what is named emptiness, and so on; as they are the gateways to liberation, they are thus classified as threefold.

1029.

1029.

Suññatādikanāmena, vimokkhā tividhā matā;

Nibbānaphalamaggā ca, samāpattisamādhayo.

By the names of emptiness and so on, the liberations are considered threefold: Nibbāna, the fruit, the path, and also attainments and concentrations.

1030.

1030.

Tattheva paṭhamabhūmiṃ, patto ariyapuggalo;

Sattakkhattuparamo so, sotāpannoti vuccati.

Having reached that very first stage, the noble person, who is destined for at most seven more rebirths, is called a stream-enterer.

1031.

1031.

Patto dutiyabhūmiñca, sakadāgāmināmako;

Sakimeva imaṃ lokaṃ, āgantvā hoti mānusaṃ.

Having reached the second stage, he is called a once-returner, for he returns to this world only once more to be reborn as a human.

1032.

1032.

Patto [V 0.0100] tatiyabhūmiñca, anāgāmīti vuccati;

Brahmalokā anāgantvā, idhakāmopapattiyā.

Having reached the third stage, he is called a non-returner, not returning from the Brahma world for rebirth here in the sensual realm.

1033.

1033.

Patto catutthabhūmiñca, arahā aggapuggalo;

Diṭṭheva dhamme dukkhaggiṃ, nibbāpetīti vuccati.

Having reached the fourth stage, the Arahant, the foremost person, is said to extinguish the fire of suffering in this very life.

1034.

1034.

Iti [M 0.0091] maggaphalaṭṭhānaṃ, vasā ariyapuggalā;

Dvidhāpi catudhā yuggā, aṭṭha honti vibhāgato.

Thus, according to their standing in path and fruit, the noble individuals are fourfold as pairs, and by way of division, they are eight.

1035.

1035.

Ubhatobhāgavimutta-

Vibhāgādivasā pana;

Vibhattā honti sattete,

Yathāyogaṃ tathā hi ca.

Moreover, by way of the classification beginning with the doubly-liberated one, these seven are distinguished, as is appropriate.

1036.

1036.

Saddhādhurassāniccato, vuṭṭhānaṃ dukkhatopi ca;

Paññādhurassānattato, iti dīpenti paṇḍitā.

For one whose faculty is faith, emergence is from impermanence and from suffering; for one whose faculty is wisdom, it is from non-self. Thus do the wise explain.

1037.

1037.

Saddhānusāri ādimhi, majjhe saddhāvimuttako;

Ante paññāvimuttova, tasmā saddhādhuro siyā.

The faith-follower at the beginning, the faith-liberated in the middle, and at the end the wisdom-liberated one; therefore, he is one whose faculty is faith.

1038.

1038.

Dhammānusāri ādimhi, diṭṭhippatto tatopari;

Ante paññāvimuttova, hoti paññādhuropi ca.

The Dhamma-follower at the beginning, the one attained to view thereafter, and at the end the wisdom-liberated one; he is also one whose faculty is wisdom.

1039.

1039.

Samathayānikā ceva, rūpānuttarapādakā;

Vipassanāyānikā ca, sabbe sukkhavipassakā.

There are those whose vehicle is serenity and those who use the form attainments as their basis; and there are those whose vehicle is insight, all of whom are dry-insight practitioners.

1040.

1040.

Dhuravuṭṭhānabhedena, honti pañceva sabbathā;

Āruppapādakā cāpi, ādimhi duvidhā tathā.

By the distinction of faculty and emergence, they are five in all respects; and those who have the formless attainments as their basis are likewise twofold at the beginning.

1041.

1041.

Chasu ṭhānesu majjhake, kāyasakkhīti bhājitā;

Ubhatobhāgavimutto, arahatte patiṭṭhito.

In the midst of the six stages of training, one is classified as a body-witness; the one liberated in both ways is established in Arahantship.

1042.

1042.

Itthaṃ vuttayānadhura-vuṭṭhānānaṃ vibhāgato;

Maggapphalabhūmiyo ca, sattaṭṭhāriyapuggalā.

Thus, by way of the classification of the vehicles, faculties, and emergences as stated, there are the stages of path and fruit, and the seven or eight noble individuals.

1043.

1043.

Tattha [V 0.0101] cānuttarañāṇaṃ, saccānaṃ paṭivedhakaṃ;

Samucchedappahānena, klesānusayasodhanaṃ.

Therein, the unsurpassed knowledge is the penetration of the truths, the purification of the underlying tendencies of the defilements by means of abandonment through eradication.

1044.

1044.

Catumaggavibhāgena, vuṭṭhānanti pakittitaṃ;

Ñāṇadassanavisuddhi, nāma hoti tathāpi ca.

By the fourfold division of the path, this is proclaimed as emergence; and it is also called the purification of knowledge and vision.

1045.

1045.

Maggo ca parijānāti, dukkhaṃ tebhūmakaṃ tathā;

Yathāyogaṃ pajahati, taṇhāsamudayampi ca.

And the path fully understands suffering, likewise that of the threefold realm; as is appropriate, it also abandons craving, the origin.

1046.

1046.

Nirodhaṃ [M 0.0092] sacchikaroti, maggasaccamanuttaraṃ;

Bhāvanāvīthimotiṇṇo, bhāvetīti pavuccati.

It realizes cessation; having entered the course of development, it develops the unsurpassed truth of the path, and thus is said to 'develop'.

1047.

1047.

Diṭṭhiggatavicikicchā-sīlabbatamasesato;

Apāyagamanīyañca, rāgadosādikattayaṃ.

Adherence to views, doubt, and grasping at rites and rituals, entirely; and the triad beginning with lust and hatred that leads to the lower realms.

1048.

1048.

Tadekaṭṭhe kilese ca, sahajātappahānato;

Pajahāti sotāpatti-maggo paṭhamabhūmiko.

The stream-entry path, the first stage, abandons the defilements associated with them by means of co-nascent abandonment.

1049.

1049.

Tadekaṭṭhe pajahati, rāgadosādikepi ca;

Thūle tu sakadāgāmi-maggo dutiyabhūmiko.

The once-returner path, the second stage, abandons the grosser forms of lust, hatred, and so on, and the defilements associated with them.

1050.

1050.

Pajahāti anāgāmi-maggo niravasesato;

Kāmarāgabyāpāde ca, tadekaṭṭhe ca sambhavā.

The path of the non-returner abandons without remainder sensual lust and ill will, and what arises from the same basis.

1051.

1051.

Rūpārūparāgamānu-ddhaccāvijjāti pañcakaṃ;

Aggamaggo pajahati, klese sese ca sabbathā.

Lust for form, lust for the formless, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance—this pentad the highest path abandons, and the remaining defilements entirely.

1052.

1052.

Iti saccapaṭivedhaṃ, klesakkhayaphalāvahaṃ;

Maggañāṇaṃ pakāsenti, visuddhiṃ sattamaṃ budhā.

Thus the wise declare the knowledge of the path—which is the penetration of the truths and brings the fruit of the destruction of the defilements—to be the seventh purification.

1053.

1053.

Chabbisuddhikamenevaṃ, sabbathāya visuddhiyā;

Sattamāyānupattabbaṃ, nibbānanti pavuccati.

Thus, by the procedure of the six purifications, for the sake of purity in every way, what is to be attained by the seventh is called Nibbāna.

1054.

1054.

Klesakkhayakaraṃ tāṇaṃ, saṃsārātikkamaṃ paraṃ;

Pārimaṃ tīramabhayaṃ, sabbasaṅkhāranissaṭaṃ.

That which brings the destruction of defilements, the refuge, the supreme transcendence of saṃsāra; the further shore, the fearless, the escape from all formations.

1055.

1055.

Tenammadanimmadanaṃ[V 0.0102], pipāsavinayādinā;

Klesasaṃsārasaṅkhāra-paṭipakkhanidassitaṃ.

Therefore, by its being the crushing of conceit, the removal of thirst, and so on, it is shown to be the opponent of the defilements, saṃsāra, and formations.

1056.

1056.

Ajarāmaramaccanta-manuppādamasaṅkhataṃ;

Anuttaramasaṅkhāraṃ, anantamatulañca taṃ.

Ageless, deathless, absolute, unoriginated, unconditioned; unsurpassed, uncompounded, endless, and incomparable is that.

1057.

1057.

Paramatthamanopammaṃ, santi appaṭimaṃ sukhaṃ;

Nirodhasacca nibbānaṃ, ekantaṃ amataṃ padaṃ.

The ultimate goal, the incomparable, peace, the matchless bliss; the truth of cessation, Nibbāna, the absolute, the deathless state.

1058.

1058.

Sopādisesanibbāna-dhātu [M 0.0093] ceva tathāparā;

Anupādisesā ceti, duvidhā pariyāyato.

By way of classification, it is twofold: the Nibbāna-element with residue remaining and, likewise, the other, the Nibbāna-element without residue remaining.

1059.

1059.

Suññataṃ cānimittañca, tathāpaṇihitanti ca;

Attādigāhābhāvena, tividhāpi ca bhājitaṃ.

As emptiness, the signless, and the undirected, it is also classified as threefold due to the absence of grasping at self and so on.

1060.

1060.

Klesasaṃsārasaṅkhāra-paccanīkavibhāgato;

Bhavakkhayādibhedehi, bahudhāpi pavuccati.

It is also spoken of in many ways: by its classification as the opponent of the defilements, saṃsāra, and formations; and by distinctions such as the destruction of being, and so forth.

1061.

1061.

Tadevamaccutaṃ dhammaṃ, lokuttaramakālikaṃ;

Vānābhāvā vānātīto, “nibbāna”nti pakittitaṃ.

Thus this permanent, supramundane, and timeless Dhamma is proclaimed 'Nibbāna' because, through the absence of craving (vāna), it has departed from craving.

Iti nibbānavibhāge vuṭṭhānavisuddhikathā niṭṭhitā.

Here ends the discourse on the purification of emergence in the Analysis of Nibbāna.

Chabbīsatimo paricchedo.

The Twenty-Sixth Chapter.

Niṭṭhito ca sabbathāpi nibbānavibhāgo.

And thus the Analysis of Nibbāna is entirely finished.

Sattavīsatimo paricchedo

The Twenty-Seventh Chapter.

5. Paññattivibhāgo

5. The Analysis of Concepts

27. Pabhedakathā

27. Discourse on the Divisions

1062.

1062.

Cittaṃ [V 0.0103] cetasikaṃ rūpaṃ, nibbānampi ca bhājitaṃ;

Tasmā dāni yathāyogaṃ, paññattipi pavuccati.

Mind, mental factors, matter, and Nibbāna have been analyzed; therefore now, as is appropriate, the concept, too, will be discussed.

1063.

1063.

Sā cāyaṃ atthapaññatti-nāmapaññattibhedato;

Duvidhā hoti paññatti, atthapaññatti tattha ca.

This concept is twofold, distinguished as meaning-concept and name-concept. Among these is the meaning-concept.

1064.

1064.

Sattasambhārasaṇṭhāna-saṅghāṭapariṇāmato;

Vikappupaṭṭhānākāravohārābhinivesato.

By way of a being, a collection, a shape, a combination, a transformation; by way of a mental construct, an appearance, a mode, a convention, and an adherence.

1065.

1065.

Tathā pavattasaṅketasiddhā atthā pakappitā;

Paññāpīyanti nāmāti, paññattīti pakittitā.

Likewise, constructed meanings, established by current convention, are made known by a name; this is declared to be 'concept'.

1066.

1066.

Atthā hi paramatthatthā, paññattatthāti ca dvidhā;

Tattha ca paramatthatthā, saccikaṭṭhā salakkhaṇā.

For meanings are twofold: ultimate meanings and conceptual meanings. Among these, ultimate meanings are real in the highest sense and possess their own intrinsic characteristics.

1067.

1067.

Paññattatthā [M 0.0094] saccikaṭṭhasalakkhaṇasabhāvato;

Aññathā gahitā taṃtamupādāya pakappitā.

Conceptual meanings are constructed by depending on this or that; they are grasped in a way different from the intrinsic nature of real entities that possess their own characteristics.

1068.

1068.

Tasmā upādāpaññatti, atthapaññattināmakā;

Paññapetabbanāmāva, paññattatthāva sabbathā.

Therefore, the derived concept called 'meaning-concept' is in every way the conceptual meaning of that which is to be designated by a name.

1069.

1069.

Paramatthā yathāvuttā, cittacetasikādayo;

Paññattā itthipurisamañcapīṭhapaṭādayo.

Ultimate realities, as stated, are mind, mental factors, and so on; concepts are 'woman,' 'man,' 'bed,' 'chair,' 'cloth,' and so on.

1070.

1070.

Yena vuccati taṃ nāmaṃ, paññapetīti vuccati;

Paññattīti ca sā nāmapaññattīti tato matā.

That by which something is expressed is a name; because it makes known, it is called a concept. Therefore, that is regarded as 'name-concept'.

1071.

1071.

Saṅkhā [V 0.0104] samaññā paññatti, vohāroti ca bhājitā;

Catudhā paññapetabbapaññattīti hi vaṇṇitā.

As term, convention, concept, and expression, the concept of the designatable is thus described as fourfold.

1072.

1072.

Tato nāmaṃ nāmakammaṃ, nāmadheyyaṃ athāparaṃ;

Nirutti byañjanamabhilāpoti pana bhājitā.

Then, it is distinguished as: name, the act of naming, appellation; and further, as language, expression, and utterance.

1073.

1073.

Nāmapaññatti nāmāti, paññatti duvidhā katā;

Sabbeva dhammā paññattipathāti pana bhājitā.

Name-concept is 'name'; thus concept is made twofold. However, all phenomena whatsoever are distinguished as being the range of concepts.

1074.

1074.

Paramatthapaññattatthā, duvidhā honti tattha ca;

Paññattipathāva honti, paramatthā salakkhaṇā.

Among them, there are two kinds: ultimate realities and conceptual meanings. Ultimate realities, possessing their own characteristics, are also within the range of concepts.

1075.

1075.

Paññattatthā paññatti ca, paññapetabbamattato;

Paññattipathā ca nāmapaññattipathabhāvato.

Conceptual meanings and concepts are merely what is to be designated; they are the range of concepts because they are the range for name-concepts.

1076.

1076.

Nāmampi paññāpetabbameva kiñcāpi kenaci;

Nāmamevampetaṃ tattha, paññatticceva vaṇṇitaṃ.

Although a name, too, is to be designated by some means, even such a name is, in that case, described simply as a concept.

1077.

1077.

Paññapetabbadhammā ca, tesaṃ paññāpitāpi ca;

Icchitabbāpi paññattipathā paññattinānatā.

The phenomena to be designated, their designations, and what is to be intended—this diversity of concepts should be understood as the range of concepts.

1078.

1078.

Iti vuttānusārena, vuttaṃ aṭṭhakathānaye;

Nayaṃ gahetvā etthāpi, paññatti duvidhā katā.

Thus, having adopted here the method stated in the commentaries, in accordance with what has been said, concept is made twofold.

1079.

1079.

Tasmimpi [M 0.0095] paramatthā ca, saccikaṭṭhasalakkhaṇā;

Atthā paññattimattā ca, atthapaññattināmakā.

In that system, too, there are ultimate realities, which are real and have their own characteristics; and there are meanings that are mere concepts, called 'meaning-concepts'.

1080.

1080.

Tesaṃ paññāpikā ceva, nāmapaññattināmikā;

Iccevaṃ vaṇṇanāmagge, ñeyyattā tividhā katā.

And their designator is called 'name-concept.' Thus, in this way of exposition, the knowable is made threefold.

1081.

1081.

Paramatthasaccaṃ nāma, paramatthāva tattha ca;

Saccikaṭṭhasabhāvattā, avisaṃvādakā hi te.

'Ultimate truth' refers to the ultimate realities themselves; for because their nature is to exist in the highest sense, they are non-deceptive.

1082.

1082.

Sammutisaccaṃ paññattidvayaṃ vohāravuttiyā;

Lokasamaññādhippāyāvisaṃvādakabhāvato.

Conventional truth is the pair of concepts, which serve for conventional expression; this is because they are non-deceptive with respect to the intention of worldly convention.

1083.

1083.

Iti [V 0.0105] saccadvayampetaṃ, akkhāsi purisuttamo;

Tenāpi nāmasaṃviññū, vohareyyubhayampi vā.

Thus the Supreme Person has declared this pair of truths. Therefore, one skilled in terms might make use of both.

Iti paññattivibhāge pabhedakathā niṭṭhitā.

Here ends the discussion of the distinctions in the analysis of concepts.

Sattavīsatimo paricchedo.

The Twenty-Seventh Chapter.

Aṭṭhavīsatimo paricchedo

The Twenty-Eighth Chapter

28. Atthapaññattikathā

28. The Discussion of Meaning-Concepts

1084.

1084.

Tattha ca pubbāpariya-pavattakkhandhasammatā;

Viññattindriyavipphāra-visesopanibandhanā.

There, considered as aggregates occurring in a series of prior and posterior, and bound by the specific conditions of expression, sense-faculty, and expansion—

1085.

1085.

Devayakkhamanussādi-nānābhedā salakkhikā;

Sattapaññatti nāmāyaṃ, svāyaṃ sattoti sammato.

—this is called the concept of a being, characterized by various distinctions such as gods, yakkhas, humans, and so on; this is reckoned as 'a being'.

1086.

1086.

Vaṭṭattayamupādāya,

Khandhāyatanavuttiyā;

Kārako vedako vāyaṃ,

Sandhāvati bhave bhave.

Based on the triple round, by the occurrence of aggregates and sense-bases, this doer, this experiencer, roams through existence after existence.

1087.

1087.

Tasmā saṃsāramāpanno, satto nāma sa puggalo;

Ahamattāparā itthī, purisoti ca kappito.

Therefore, that individual, having entered saṃsāra, is called a being; and 'I', 'self', 'other', 'woman', and 'man' are conceived.

1088.

1088.

Svāyaṃ [M 0.0096] khandhādito satto, aññoti ca na vuccati;

Khandhādivinimuttassa, sattasseva abhāvato.

This being is not said to be different from the aggregates and so forth, because a being apart from the aggregates and so forth does not exist.

1089.

1089.

Khandhā khandhānamevāyaṃ, sattoti ca na vuccati;

Khandhavohārato tassa, aññavohārasambhavā.

The aggregates are merely aggregates and are not called a being, because from the conventional usage regarding aggregates, another conventional usage arises in relation to them.

1090.

1090.

Iccevaṃ [V 0.0106] khandhanānatte-kattamuttopi atthato;

Tabbisesāvacarita-vohāro ca tu dissati.

Thus, though in reality it is free from being either different from or one with the aggregates, yet conventional speech operating with their distinctions is seen.

1091.

1091.

Tenāyaṃ puggalo satto, jāyatijjiyyatīti ca;

Mīyatīti ca tassāyaṃ, saṃsāroti pavuccati.

Therefore, this person, this being, is born, decays, and dies—this, for him, is called saṃsāra.

1092.

1092.

Mato jāto ca na sveva, khandhabhedopacārato;

Nāparo sveva santānabhedābhāvopacārato.

The one who has died and the one who is born are not the very same, due to the conventional usage based on the breakup of aggregates; nor are they another, due to the conventional usage based on the absence of a break in the continuity.

1093.

1093.

Nānattekattamiccevaṃ, puggalassopacārato;

Ucchedasassatattaṃ vā, tasmā nopeti puggalo.

Thus, due to the conventional usage regarding the individual, there is neither difference nor identity; therefore, the individual does not fall into annihilationism or eternalism.

1094.

1094.

Iccāyaṃ puggalo nāma, satto saṃsārakārako;

Khandhādikamupādāya, paññattoti pavuccati.

Thus, this individual called a being, the agent in saṃsāra, is said to be a concept dependent on the aggregates and so forth.

1095.

1095.

Tasmā puggalasaṅkhātā, saṃsāropanibandhanā;

Sattapaññatti nāmāti, viññātabbā vibhāvinā.

Therefore, that which is reckoned as an individual, connected with saṃsāra, is called the designation of a being—this should be understood by the discerning.

1096.

1096.

Ajjhattikā ca kesādikoṭṭhāsā bāhiresu ca;

Bhūmipabbatapāsāṇatiṇarukkhalatādikā.

And internal parts such as hair and so forth; and among external things, earth, mountains, rocks, grass, trees, vines, and so forth.

1097.

1097.

Bhūtasambhāranibbattivibhāgaparikappitā;

Tamupādāya sambhārapaññattīti pavuccati.

Conceptually constructed as the arising and distinction of elemental compositions, and taking that as its basis, it is called the designation of composition.

1098.

1098.

Bhūtasambhārasaṇṭhānavibhāgaparikappitā;

Saṇṭhānapaññatti nāma, thambhakumbhādikā matā.

Conceptually constructed as the arrangement and distinction of elemental compositions, this is called the designation of shape, considered as pillars, pots, and so forth.

1099.

1099.

Bhūtasambhārasaṅghātavisesaparikappitā;

Saṅghātapaññatti nāma, rathagehādikā matā.

Conceptually constructed as a specific combination of elemental compositions, this is called the designation of combination, considered as chariots, houses, and so forth.

1100.

1100.

Bhūtasambhāravisesapariṇāmapakappitā;

Pariṇāmapaññattīti, dadhibhattādikā matā.

Conceptually constructed as a specific transformation of elemental compositions, this is called the designation of transformation, considered as curdled milk, cooked rice, and so forth.

1101.

1101.

Itthamajjhattabahiddhā[M 0.0097], dhammā sambhārasambhūtā;

Santānavutti saṅketasiddhā paññatti pañcadhā.

Thus, internally and externally, phenomena arise from composition; the designation, established by convention through continuous occurrence, is fivefold.

1102.

1102.

Tathā [V 0.0107] tathā samuppannavikappābhogasammatā;

Vikappapaññatti nāma, kālākāsadisādikā.

Likewise, agreed upon through attention to various arisen conceptualizations, this is called the designation of conceptualization, such as time, space, direction, and so forth.

1103.

1103.

Taṃ taṃ nimittamāgamma, tatopaṭṭhānakappitā;

Upaṭṭhānapaññattīti, paṭibhāgādikā matā.

Based on various signs, and conceptually constructed from that presentation, this is called the designation of presentation, considered as the counterpart sign and so forth.

1104.

1104.

Visesākāramattāpi, atthantarapakappitā;

Ākārapaññatti nāma, viññattilahutādikā.

Even the mere mode of distinction, conceptually constructed as something else, is called the designation of manner, considered as intimation, lightness, and so forth.

1105.

1105.

Taṃ taṃ kāraṇamāgamma, tathā vohārakappitā;

Vohārapaññatti nāma, kathināpattiādikā.

Based on various causes, and thus conceptually constructed as conventional usage, this is called the designation of conventional usage, considered as the kathina ceremony, offenses, and so forth.

1106.

1106.

Bālo yo so ca me attā,

So bhavissāmi maṃ ca tu;

Nicco dhuvo sassatoti-

Ādikā pana sabbathā.

Furthermore, all such notions in every way, as 'the fool,' 'this is my self,' 'I will be,' 'me and you,' 'permanent, stable, eternal,' and so forth,

1107.

1107.

Tabbohāranimittānaṃ, abhāvepi pavattito;

Abhinivesapaññatti, nāma titthiyakappitā.

arising even in the absence of signs for their conventional usage, are called the designation of adherence, devised by sectarians.

1108.

1108.

Iccevaṃ lokasāsanatitthāyatanakappitā;

Santānamuttasaṅketasiddhā atthāpi pañcadhā.

Thus, conceptually constructed in the world, the Dispensation, and sectarian systems, meanings established by convention and free from continuity are also fivefold.

1109.

1109.

Saṅkānavuttisantānamuttabhedavasā dvidhā;

Atthapaññatti nāmāyaṃ, dasadhā paridīpitā.

By way of the twofold distinction—that based on continuity and that free from continuity—this designation of meaning is explained as tenfold.

1110.

1110.

Iti vuttappakāresu, paññattatthesu paṇḍitā;

Paññattimattaṃ sandhāya, voharanti yathākathaṃ.

Thus, regarding the meanings of designations explained in these ways, the wise speak conventionally, with reference to mere designation.

1111.

1111.

Tadaññe pana bālā ca, titthiyāpi akovidā;

Paññattimatidhāvitvā, gaṇhanti paramatthato.

But others—the foolish and unskilled sectarians—having run beyond mere designation, grasp them as ultimate reality.

1112.

1112.

Te tathā gahitākārā, aññāṇagahitā janā;

Micchattābhiniviṭṭhā ca, vaḍḍhanti bhavabandhanaṃ.

Those people, having grasped such modes, seized by ignorance and entrenched in wrong views, increase the bonds of existence.

1113.

1113.

Duvidhesupi [M 0.0098][V 0.0108] atthesu, tasmā paṇḍitajātiko;

Paramatthapaññattīsu, vibhāgamiti lakkhayeti.

Therefore, one who is wise, regarding both kinds of meanings, thus notes the distinction between the ultimate and designation.

Iti paññattivibhāge atthapaññattikathā niṭṭhitā.

Thus ends the discussion of meaning-designations in the Analysis of Designations.

Aṭṭhavīsatimo paricchedo.

The Twenty-Eighth Chapter.

Ekūnatiṃsatimo paricchedo

The Twenty-Ninth Chapter

29. Nāmapaññattikathā

29. The Discussion of Name-Designations

1114.

1114.

Nāmavohārasaṅketakāraṇopanibandhanā;

Yathāvuttatthasaddānaṃ, antarā cintanā gatā.

Bound by the causes of the conventional usage of names and signs, thought proceeds between the meanings and sounds as explained.

1115.

1115.

Nāmapaññatti nāmāyaṃ, atthasaddavinissaṭā;

Taṃdvayābaddhasaṅketañeyyākāropalakkhitā.

This is called the designation of name, which is devoid of meaning and sound, and is characterized by the knowable mode of convention bound to that pair.

1116.

1116.

Yā gayhati nāmaghosagocaruppannavīthiyā;

Pavattānantaruppanna-manodvārikavīthiyā.

It is grasped in the cognitive process arisen from the sphere of name and sound, and in the mind-door process arisen immediately subsequent to that.

1117.

1117.

Mañcapīṭhādisaddaṃ hi, sotaviññāṇavīthiyā;

Sutvā tameva cintetvā, manodvārikavīthiyā.

For, having heard the sound of 'bed,' 'chair,' and so forth through the ear-consciousness process, and having contemplated that very thing through the mind-door process,

1118.

1118.

Tato saṅketanipphannaṃ, nāmaṃ cintāya gayhati;

Nāmapaññattiatthā tu, tato gayhanti sambhavā.

from that, a name produced by convention is grasped through thought; but the meanings of name-designations are grasped from that as they arise.

1119.

1119.

Saddanāmatthapaññattiparamatthavasena hi;

Catudhā tividhā vātha, cintanā tattha icchitā.

Indeed, contemplation thereon is intended as fourfold or threefold: by way of sound, name, meaning-designation, and ultimate reality.

1120.

1120.

Itthamaṭṭhakathāmaggaṃ, vaṇṇentena hi dassito;

Nayo ācariyeneti, vibhāgoyaṃ pakāsito.

This division has thus been explained, for the method was shown by the Teacher, who describes the path of the commentaries.

1121.

1121.

Natthaññā [V 0.0109] kāci viññatti, vikārasahito pana;

Saddova nāmapaññatti, iccekaccehi vaṇṇitaṃ.

There is no other designation, but sound itself, accompanied by modification, is a name-designation—thus it is described by some.

1122.

1122.

Tadetaṃ nāmapaññattibhāvenekavidhampi ca;

Neruttikayādicchakavasā nāmaṃ dvidhā bhave.

This name, though of one kind by way of being a name-designation, becomes twofold by way of the etymological and the conventional.

1123.

1123.

Saññāsu dhāturūpāni, paccayañca tato paraṃ;

Katvā vaṇṇāgamādiñca, saddalakkhaṇasādhitaṃ.

Having established roots and forms, and then suffixes, in designations, and having made augmentations of letters and the like, it is accomplished by the characteristics of grammar.

1124.

1124.

Neruttikamudīrenti[M 0.0099], nāmaṃ yādicchakaṃ padaṃ;

Yadicchāya katamattaṃ, byañjanatthavivajjitaṃ.

They speak of the etymological name. A conventional word is merely made by choice, devoid of etymological meaning.

1125.

1125.

Tividhampi tadanvatthakādimañcopacārimaṃ;

Nibbacanatthasāpekkhaṃ, tatthānvatthamudīritaṃ.

That too is threefold: conforming to meaning, traditional, and figurative. Therein, that which conforms to meaning is stated with reference to its explanatory meaning.

1126.

1126.

Yadicchākatasaṅketaṃ, kādimañcopacārimaṃ;

Atambhūtassa tabbhāvavohāroti pavuccati.

The traditional and the figurative, which are designations made by choice, are said to be the usage of ascribing a nature to that which does not possess it.

1127.

1127.

Tathā sāmaññanāmañca, guṇanāmañca kittimaṃ;

Opapātikamiccevaṃ, nāmaṃ hoti catubbidhaṃ.

Likewise, names are fourfold: common names, attribute names, renowned names, and spontaneously arisen names.

1128.

1128.

Mahājanasammatañca, anvatthañceva tādisaṃ;

Tīṇi nāmāni candādināmaṃ tatthopapātikaṃ.

The name agreed upon by the great populace, and also the name conforming to meaning—these comprise three types of names. Therein, the name 'moon' and so forth is a spontaneously arisen name.

1129.

1129.

Yādicchakamāvatthikaṃ, nemittakamathāparaṃ;

Liṅgikaṃ ruḷhikañceti, nāmaṃ pañcavidhaṃ bhave.

Names are fivefold: arbitrary, occasional, indicative, symbolic, and traditional.

1130.

1130.

Yādicchakaṃ yathāvuḍḍhaṃ, vacchadammādikaṃ pana;

Āvatthikaṃ nemittakaṃ, sīlavāpaññavādikaṃ.

An arbitrary name is like 'Vuḍḍha'; 'calf', 'one to be tamed', and so forth are occasional names; an indicative name is like 'virtuous', 'wise', and so forth.

1131.

1131.

Liṅgikaṃ diṭṭhaliṅgaṃ tu, daṇḍīchattītiādikaṃ;

Ruḷhikaṃ lesamattena, ruḷhaṃ gomahiṃsādikaṃ.

A symbolic name refers to a visible mark, such as 'staff-bearer', 'umbrella-bearer', and so forth. A traditional name is established by a mere trace, like 'cow', 'buffalo', and so forth.

1132.

1132.

Vijjamānāvijjamāna-paññattobhayamissitā;

Vibhattā nāmapaññatti, chabbidhā hoti tattha hi.

Indeed, the name-designation is classified therein as sixfold, based on the existing, the non-existing, and a mixture of both.

1133.

1133.

Vijjamānapaññattīti[V 0.0110], vijjamānatthadīpitā;

Vuccati khandhāyatana-dhātupañcindriyādikā.

A designation of the existent, which indicates an existing object, is said to be the aggregates, sense-bases, elements, the five faculties, and so forth.

1134.

1134.

Avijjamānapaññatti-nāmikā paramatthato;

Avijjamānamañcādi, atthapaññattidīpitā.

That which is named a designation of the non-existent indicates a meaning-designation, such as 'bed' and so forth, which is non-existent from an ultimate perspective.

1135.

1135.

Vijjamānena avijja-mānapaññattināmikā;

Tevijjo chaḷabhiñño ca, sīlavā paññavāpi ca.

A designation of the non-existent by means of the existent is exemplified by 'one with threefold knowledge,' 'one with sixfold higher knowledge,' 'virtuous,' and 'wise.'

1136.

1136.

Avijjamānena vijja-mānapaññattināmikā;

Itthirūpaṃ itthisaddo, itthicittantiādikā.

A designation of the existent by means of the non-existent is exemplified by 'woman's form,' 'woman's sound,' 'woman's thought,' and so forth.

1137.

1137.

Vijjamānena [M 0.0100] tu vijja-mānapaññattināmikā;

Cakkhuviññāṇaṃ ca cakkhu-samphasso cevamādikā.

But a designation of the existent by means of the existent is exemplified by 'eye-consciousness,' 'eye-contact,' and so forth.

1138.

1138.

Avijjamānenāvijja-mānapaññattināmikā;

Khattiyaputto brāhmaṇa-putto iccevamādikā.

A designation of the non-existent by means of the non-existent is exemplified by 'son of a warrior,' 'son of a brahmin,' and so forth.

1139.

1139.

Iti vuttānusārena, nāmapaññattiyā budho;

Sarūpaṃ visayañceva, vibhāgañca vibhāvaye.

Thus, in accordance with what has been said, the wise one should discern the inherent nature, the object, and also the divisions of name-designations.

1140.

1140.

Iccevaṃ paramatthā ca, yathāvuttā catubbidhā;

Paññatti duvidhā ceti, ñeyyatthā chabbidhā matāti.

Thus, the ultimate realities are fourfold as stated, and designations are twofold—in this way, knowable objects are considered to be sixfold.

Iti paññattivibhāge nāmapaññattikathā niṭṭhitā.

Thus, in the Exposition of Designations, the discourse on name-designations is concluded.

Ekūnatiṃsatimo paricchedo.

The Twenty-ninth Chapter.

Niṭṭhito ca sabbathāpi paññattivibhāgo.

And thus the Exposition of Designations is concluded in its entirety.

Nigamanakathā

Concluding Discourse

1141.

1141.

Seṭṭhe [V 0.0111] kañcivare raṭṭhe, kāverinagare vare;

Kule sañjātabhūtena, bahussutena ñāṇinā.

By him who was born into a family in the excellent Kañcivara country, in the supreme city of Kāverī, who was learned and wise;

1142.

1142.

Anuruddhena therena, aniruddhayasassinā;

Tambaraṭṭhe vasantena, nagare tañjanāmake.

By the Elder Anuruddha, of unhindered fame, dwelling in the Tamba country, in the city named Tañjana.

1143.

1143.

Tattha saṅghavisiṭṭhena, yācitena anākulaṃ;

Mahāvihāravāsīnaṃ, vācanāmagganissitaṃ.

There, requested by one eminent in the Sangha, this unconfused work, based on the path of recitation of the dwellers of the Great Monastery,

1144.

1144.

Paramatthaṃ pakāsentaṃ, paramatthavinicchayaṃ;

Revealing the ultimate meaning, the Paramatthavinicchaya;

Pakaraṇaṃ kataṃ tena, paramatthatthavedināti.

This treatise was made by him, the one who knows the meaning of the ultimate realities.

Iti anuruddhācariyena racito

Thus, composed by the Teacher Anuruddha.

Paramatthavinicchayo niṭṭhito.

The Determination of the Ultimate Meaning is concluded.

Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Saccasaṅkhepo

The Summary of Truth

Ganthārambhakathā

Introduction to the Text

1.

1.

Namassitvā [M 0.0001][V 0.0001] tilokaggaṃ, ñeyyasāgarapāraguṃ;

Bhavābhāvakaraṃ dhammaṃ, gaṇañca guṇasāgaraṃ.

Having paid homage to the foremost in the three worlds, who has gone to the far shore of the ocean of the knowable; to the Dhamma, which brings about existence and non-existence; and to the Sangha, the ocean of virtues.

2.

2.

Nissāya pubbācariyamataṃ atthāvirodhinaṃ;

Vakkhāmi saccasaṅkhepaṃ, hitaṃ kārakayoginaṃ.

Relying on the doctrine of the ancient teachers, which does not contradict the meaning, I shall speak the Summary of Truth, beneficial for diligent practitioners.

1. Paṭhamo paricchedo

1. The First Chapter

Rūpasaṅkhepo

A Summary of Matter

3.

3.

Saccāni [V 0.0002] paramatthañca, sammutiñcāti dve tahiṃ;

Thaddhabhāvādinā ñeyyaṃ, saccaṃ taṃ paramatthakaṃ.

Herein, there are two truths: the ultimate and the conventional. That which is knowable through its intrinsic nature, such as hardness, is the ultimate truth.

4.

4.

Sannivesavisesādiñeyyaṃ sammuti taṃ dvayaṃ;

Bhāvasaṅketasiddhīnaṃ, tathattā saccamīritaṃ.

That which is knowable through distinctions of composition and so on is conventional truth. Because they are established by concept and convention, both are called 'truth' in the sense of being so.

5.

5.

Paramattho sanibbānapañcakkhandhettha rāsito;

Khandhattho ca samāsetvā, vuttotītādibhedanaṃ.

Herein, ultimate reality, taken as a group, consists of the five aggregates along with Nibbāna. The meaning of 'aggregate' is briefly stated as that which is differentiated into past, and so on.

6.

6.

Vedanādīsupekasmiṃ, khandhasaddo tu ruḷhiyā;

Samuddādekadese tu, samuddādiravo yathā.

However, the term 'aggregate' is applied by convention to a single constituent, such as feeling, just as the word 'ocean' is applied to a part of the ocean.

7.

7.

Tattha sītādiruppattā, rūpaṃ bhvāpānalānilaṃ;

Bhūtaṃ kathinadavatāpacanīraṇabhāvakaṃ.

Therein, it is called 'matter' because it is afflicted by such things as cold. It consists of earth, water, fire, and wind. The primary elements have the respective natures of hardness, fluidity, heat, and motion.

8.

8.

Cakkhu [M 0.0002] sotañca ghānañca, jivhā kāyo pabhā ravo;

Gandho rasojā itthī ca, pumā vatthu ca jīvitaṃ.

The eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body; visible form and sound; smell, taste, and nutritive essence; femininity, masculinity, the physical basis, and life.

9.

9.

Khaṃ jāti jaratā bhaṅgo, rūpassa lahutā tathā;

Mudukammaññatā kāyavacīviññatti bhūtikaṃ.

Space, generation, aging, and dissolution; also lightness, pliancy, and wieldiness of matter; bodily and verbal intimation, which are derived from the primary elements.

10.

10.

Cakkhādī daṭṭhukāmādihetukammajabhūtikā;

Pasādā rūpasaddādī, cakkhuñāṇādigocarā.

The eye and so on are material phenomena born of kamma that was caused by the desire to see, etc. The sensitive faculties, along with visible form, sound, and so on, are the respective objective fields for eye-consciousness and so on.

11.

11.

Ojā hi yāpanā itthipumaliṅgādihetukaṃ;

Bhāvadvayaṃ tu kāyaṃva, byāpi no sahavuttikaṃ.

Nutriment indeed serves for sustenance. Femininity and masculinity are the cause of the respective gender characteristics. This pair of faculties, like the body faculty, is pervasive throughout the body, but they are not co-existent.

12.

12.

Nissayaṃ vatthu dhātūnaṃ, dvinnaṃ kammajapālanaṃ;

Jīvitaṃ uppalādīnaṃ, udakaṃva ṭhitikkhaṇe.

The physical basis is the support for the two mind-elements. The life faculty preserves co-nascent kamma-born matter, like water sustains lotuses, during its moment of presence.

13.

13.

Khaṃ [V 0.0003] rūpānaṃ paricchedo, jātiādittayaṃ pana;

Rūpanibbatti pāko ca, bhedo ceva yathākkamaṃ.

Space is the delimiter of material phenomena. The triad of characteristics, beginning with generation, are respectively the production of matter, its maturation, and its dissolution.

14.

14.

Lahutādittayaṃ taṃ hi, rūpānaṃ kamato siyā;

Adandhathaddhatā cāpi, kāyakammānukūlatā.

Indeed, that triad of material qualities beginning with lightness consists, respectively, of non-sluggishness, non-rigidity, and suitability for bodily action.

15.

15.

Abhikkamādijanakacittajassānilassa hi;

Vikāro kāyaviññatti, rūpatthambhādikāraṇaṃ.

Bodily intimation is the alteration of the wind element born from consciousness that generates such movements as stepping forward; it is the cause of such states as the stiffening of the body.

16.

16.

Vacībhedakacittena, bhūtabhūmivikāratā;

Vacīviññattupādinnaghaṭṭanasseva kāraṇaṃ.

The alteration of the earth element, by a mind that intends to produce speech, is the cause of verbal intimation through the friction of material elements.

17.

17.

Rūpamabyākataṃ sabbaṃ, vippayuttamahetukaṃ;

Anālambaṃ parittādi, iti ekavidhaṃ naye.

All matter is morally indeterminate, dissociated from consciousness, rootless, without an object, and belonging to the sense-sphere, etc. Thus it may be classified in one way.

18.

18.

Ajjhattikāni cakkhādī, pañceteva pasādakā;

Vatthunā vatthu tāneva, dvārā viññattibhī saha.

The five sensitivities, the eye and so on, are internal. Those same five, together with the heart-basis, constitute the physical bases. Together with the two intimations, they are also doors.

19.

19.

Sesaṃ bāvīsati cekavīsa vīsati bāhiraṃ;

Appasādamavatthuṃ ca, advārañca yathākkamaṃ.

The remaining are, respectively: twenty-two external; twenty-one non-sensitive and not a physical base; and twenty not a door.

20.

20.

Pasādā pañca bhāvāyu, indriyanindriyetaraṃ;

Vināpaṃ ādito yāva, rasā thūlaṃ na cetaraṃ.

The five sensitivities, the two sex faculties, and the life faculty are faculties; the others are non-faculties. From visible form up to taste, along with the tangible object, are gross; the others are subtle.

21.

21.

Aṭṭhakaṃ [M 0.0003] avinibbhogaṃ, vaṇṇagandharasojakaṃ;

Bhūtaṃ taṃ tu vinibbhogamitaranti viniddise.

The inseparable octad consists of the four primary elements along with color, smell, taste, and nutritive essence. The other types of matter should be designated as separable.

22.

22.

Aṭṭhārasādito rūpā, nipphannaṃ tu na cetaraṃ;

Phoṭṭhabbamāpavajjaṃ tu, bhūtaṃ kāme na cetaraṃ.

The first eighteen types of matter are 'produced matter'; the others are not. The tangible object consists of the primary elements, excluding water; these exist in the desire realm, but not otherwise.

23.

23.

Sekkhasappaṭighāsekkhapaṭighaṃ dvayavajjitaṃ;

Vaṇṇaṃ taditaraṃ thūlaṃ, sukhumañceti taṃ tidhā.

Visible form, the other coarse matter, and subtle matter—thus it is threefold.

24.

24.

Kammajākammajaṃnevakammākammajato tidhā;

Cittojautujādīnaṃ, vasenāpi tidhā tathā.

It is threefold as: kamma-born, not kamma-born, and neither kamma-born nor not kamma-born. Likewise, it is also threefold by way of being born of mind, temperature, and nutriment.

25.

25.

Diṭṭhaṃ [V 0.0004] sutaṃ mutañcāpi, viññātaṃ vata cetasā;

Ekamekañca pañcāpi, vīsati ca kamā siyuṃ.

What is seen, heard, sensed, and cognized by the mind are, respectively, one, one, five, and twenty types of matter.

26.

26.

Hadayaṃ vatthu viññatti, dvāraṃ cakkhādipañcakaṃ;

Vatthu dvārañca sesāni, vatthu dvārañca no siyā.

The heart is a physical basis only. The two intimations are doors only. The pentad beginning with the eye are both physical bases and doors. The remaining material phenomena are neither a physical basis nor a door.

27.

27.

Nipphannaṃ rūparūpaṃ khaṃ, paricchedotha lakkhaṇaṃ;

Jātiādittayaṃ rūpaṃ, vikāro lahutādikaṃ.

'Matter-itself' is produced matter. Space is the delimiter. The triad beginning with generation is characteristic matter. Lightness and so on are alteration matter.

28.

28.

Yathā saṅkhatadhammānaṃ, lakkhaṇaṃ saṅkhataṃ tathā;

Paricchedādikaṃ rūpaṃ, tajjātimanatikkamā.

Just as the characteristics of conditioned phenomena are themselves conditioned, so too material phenomena such as the delimiter do not transcend their own conditioned nature.

29.

29.

Kammacittānalāhārapaccayānaṃ vasenidha;

Ñeyyā pavatti rūpassa, piṇḍānañca vasā kathaṃ.

Herein, the process of matter should be understood as occurring by way of its conditions—kamma, mind, temperature, and nutriment—and also how it occurs by way of material groups.

30.

30.

Kammajaṃ sendriyaṃ vatthu, viññatti cittajā ravo;

Cittaggijo lahutādittayaṃ cittānalannajaṃ.

The faculties and the physical basis are kamma-born. Intimation is mind-born. Sound is born of mind and temperature. The triad of lightness, etc., is born of mind, temperature, and nutriment.

31.

31.

Aṭṭhakaṃ jāti cākāso, catujā jaratā khayaṃ;

Kutoci neva jātaṃ tappākabhedaṃ hi taṃ dvayaṃ.

The inseparable octad, generation, and space are born from the four causes. Aging and dissolution, however, are not born from any cause, for that pair are simply maturation and breaking up.

32.

32.

Jātiyāpi na jātattaṃ, kutociṭṭhakathānayā;

Lakkhaṇābhāvato tassā, sati tasmiṃ na niṭṭhiti.

According to the method of the commentaries, even generation itself is not 'born' from any cause. Because it is itself a characteristic, it has no further characteristic, and being present, it has no duration.

33.

33.

Kammacittānalannehi, piṇḍā nava ca satta ca;

Cattāro dve ca viññeyyā, sajīve dve ajīvake.

The material groups originating from kamma, mind, temperature, and nutriment should be understood as nine, seven, four, and two, respectively.

34.

34.

Aṭṭhakaṃ [M 0.0004] jīvitenāyunavakaṃ bhāvavatthunā;

Cakkhādī pañca dasakā, kalāpā nava kammajā.

The nine kamma-born material groups are: the life-nonad, the decads of sex and the heart-base, and the five decads beginning with the eye.

35.

35.

Suddhaṭṭhaviññattiyuttanavakopi ca dasako;

Suddhasaddena navako, lahutādidasekako.

The mind-born groups are: the pure octad, the nonad with intimation, the decad with sound, and the undecad with the triad of lightness, etc.

36.

36.

Viññattilahutādīhi, puna dvādasa terasa;

Cittajā iti viññeyyā, kalāpā satta vā cha vā.

Again, with intimation and the triad of lightness, etc., there are groups of twelve and thirteen. Thus the mind-born material groups should be understood as six or seven in total.

37.

37.

Suddhaṭṭhaṃ [V 0.0005] saddanavakaṃ, lahutādidasekakaṃ;

Saddenalahutādīhi, caturotujakaṇṇikā.

The four temperature-born groups are: the pure octad, the sound-nonad, the undecad with the triad of lightness, etc., and the duodecad with sound and the triad of lightness, etc.

38.

38.

Suddhaṭṭhalahutādīhi, annajā dvetime nava;

Satta cattāri dve ceti, kalāpā vīsatī dvibhi.

The two nutriment-born groups are the pure octad and the undecad with the triad of lightness, etc. Thus, with nine, seven, four, and two groups from the respective causes, the total number of material groups is twenty-one.

39.

39.

Tayaṭṭhakā ca cattāro, navakā dasakā nava;

Tayo dveko ca ekena, dasa dvīhi ca tīhi ca.

Three octads and four; nine nonads and decads; three, two, and one by one; ten by two and by three.

40.

40.

Catunnampi ca dhātūnaṃ, adhikaṃsavasenidha;

Rūpabhedotha viññeyyo, kammacittānalannajo.

Herein, a distinction in matter born of kamma, mind, temperature, and nutriment should be understood as arising from the predominance of one of the four primary elements.

41.

41.

Kesādimatthaluṅgantā, pathavaṃsāti vīsati;

Pittādimuttakantā te, jalaṃsā dvādasīritā.

From head hair to brain matter, the earth element parts are twenty; from bile to urine, the water element parts are said to be twelve.

42.

42.

Yena santappanaṃ yena, jīraṇaṃ dahanaṃ tathā;

Yenasitādipākoti, caturaṃsānalādhikā.

That by which there is warming, that by which there is aging, and also that by which there is burning; that by which what is eaten, etc., is digested—thus the fire element has four parts.

43.

43.

Uddhādhogamakucchiṭṭhā, koṭṭhāseyyaṅgasāri ca;

Assāsoti ca viññeyyā, chaḷaṃsā vāyunissitā.

Upward-going, downward-going, that in the abdomen, that in the bowels, that coursing through the limbs, and the in-breath—these six should be known as dependent on the wind element.

44.

44.

Pubbamuttakarīsañcudariyaṃ caturotujā;

Kammā pācaggi cittamhā-ssāsoti chapi ekajā.

Pus, urine, feces, and intestinal contents—these four are born of temperature. The digestive fire is from kamma, the in-breath from mind; these six in total are single-born.

45.

45.

Sedasiṅghānikassu ca, kheḷo cittotusambhavā;

Dvijā dvattiṃsa koṭṭhāsā, sesā eva catubbhavā.

Sweat, nasal mucus, tears, and saliva are born of mind and temperature. The remaining thirty-two constituents are indeed born from four causes.

46.

46.

Ekajesvādicatūsu, utujā caturaṭṭhakā;

Jīvītanavako pācessāse cittabhavaṭṭhako.

Among the first four single-born constituents, there are four temperature-born octads. In the digestive fire there is the life-nonad, and in the in-breath, the mind-born octad.

47.

47.

Dvijesu [M 0.0005] manatejehi, dve dve honti panaṭṭhakā;

Sesatejānilaṃsesu, ekekamhi tayo tayo.

In the teeth, there are two octads each from mind and temperature. In each of the remaining parts of the fire and wind elements, there are three types of groups each.

48.

48.

Aṭṭhakojamanaggīhi, honti aṭṭhasu kammato;

Aṭṭhāyunavakā evaṃ, ime aṭṭha catubbhavā.

Octads from nutriment, mind, and temperature arise in the eight places originating from kamma. Thus, these eight places are born from four causes.

49.

49.

Catuvīsesu [V 0.0006] sesesu, catujesuṭṭhakā tayo;

Ekekamhi ca viññeyyā, piṇḍā cittānalannajā.

In the remaining twenty-four four-born constituents, three octads should be understood in each: the groups born of mind, temperature, and nutriment.

50.

50.

Kammajā kāyabhāvavhā, dasakāpi siyuṃ tahiṃ;

Catuvīsesu aṃsesu, ekekamhi duve duve.

Kamma-born body-decads and sex-decads may also exist there. In the twenty-four parts, there are two in each.

51.

51.

Pañcāpi cakkhusotādī, padesadasakā puna;

Navakā saddasaṅkhātā, dveticcevaṃ kalāpato.

Again, there are also the five place-decads of the eye, ear, and so on. The nonads are reckoned by sound. Thus, from the perspective of material groups, there are two or more.

52.

52.

Tepaññāsa dasekañca, navuttarasatāni ca;

Dasakā navakā ceva, aṭṭhakā ca siyuṃ kamā.

Fifty-three, eleven, and one hundred and nine—these are the decads, nonads, and octads, respectively.

53.

53.

Sekapañcasataṃ kāye, sahassaṃ taṃ pavattati;

Paripuṇṇindriye rūpaṃ, nipphannaṃ dhātubhedato.

Five hundred and one in the body; that thousand proceeds. In one with perfected faculties, produced form arises from the distinction of elements.

54.

54.

Cittuppāde siyuṃ rūpa-hetū kammādayo pana;

Ṭhiti na pāṭhe cittassa, na bhaṅge rūpasambhavo.

The causes of form, such as kamma and so on, exist at the arising of a thought. The arising of form does not occur at the duration phase of a thought, nor at its dissolution.

55.

55.

“Aññathattaṃ ṭhitassā”ti, vuttattāva ṭhitikkhaṇaṃ;

Atthīti ce pabandhena, ṭhiti tattha pavuccati.

Because it is said, 'alteration of that which endures,' the moment of duration exists. If so, duration is spoken of in that context by way of continuity.

56.

56.

Atha vā tikkhaṇe kammaṃ, cittamattudayakkhaṇe;

Utuojāttano ṭhāne, rūpahetū bhavanti hi.

Alternatively, kamma at the moment of arising, consciousness at the mere moment of its arising, and temperature and nutriment in their own respective places, are indeed the causes of material form.

57.

57.

Seyyassādikkhaṇe kāya-

Bhāvavatthuvasā tayo;

Dasakā hontibhāvissa,

Vinā bhāvaṃ duve siyuṃ.

At the first moment of conception, for one who will have a gender, three decads—dependent on body, gender, and the heart-base—arise. Without the gender [decad], there would be two.

58.

58.

Tato [M 0.0006] parañca kammaggicittajā te ca piṇḍikā;

Aṭṭhakā ca duve pubbe, vuttavuttakkhaṇe vade.

And after that, those groups born of kamma, temperature, and consciousness arise. And the octads and the two [decads] mentioned earlier, one should state that they arise at their respective, previously mentioned moments.

59.

59.

Kālenāhārajaṃ hoti, cakkhādidasakāni ca;

Catupaccayato rūpaṃ, sampiṇḍevaṃ pavattati.

In due time, the nutriment-born [kalāpa] arises, as do the eye-decad and the others. Thus, from the four causes, material form proceeds as a compacted mass.

60.

60.

Taṃ [V 0.0007] sattarasacittāyu, vinā viññattilakkhaṇaṃ;

Santatāmaraṇā rūpaṃ, jarādiphalamāvahaṃ.

That material form has a lifespan of seventeen consciousness-moments, with the exception of that which has the characteristic of communication. As a continuity until death, material form brings the fruit of aging and so forth.

61.

61.

Bhaṅgā sattarasuppāde, jāyate kammajaṃ na taṃ;

Taduddhaṃ jāyate tasmā, takkhayā maraṇaṃ bhave.

From the dissolution moment of the seventeenth consciousness [before death], that kamma-born matter is no longer produced. Thereafter it ceases to arise, and upon its exhaustion, death occurs.

62.

62.

Āyukammubhayesaṃ vā, khayena maraṇaṃ bhave;

Upakkamena vā kesañcupacchedakakammunā.

Death occurs through the exhaustion of the life-span, of kamma, or of both; or for some, through violent means or by a destructive kamma.

63.

63.

Opapātikabhāvissa, dasakā satta kammajā;

Kāme ādo bhavantaggijāhi pubbeva bhūyate.

For a being of spontaneous birth, there are seven kamma-born decads. In the sensual realm, at the outset they are born of kamma, and are later increased by those born of temperature.

64.

64.

Ādikappanarānañca, apāye andhakassa ca;

Badhirassāpi ādo cha, pubbevetarajā siyuṃ.

And for the humans of the first aeon, for the blind in the states of woe, and also for the deaf, six [decads] arise at the outset, before those born of other causes.

65.

65.

Tatthevandhabadhirassa, pañca honti abhāvino;

Yuttiyā idha viññeyyā, pañca vā caturopi vā.

Likewise, for one who is blind and deaf, there are five [decads]; for one without gender, there are four. Here, by reasoning, it should be understood that there are five or even four [decads].

66.

66.

Cakkhādittayahīnassa, caturova bhavantiti;

Vuttaṃ upaparikkhitvā, gahetabbaṃ vijānatā.

For one devoid of the three faculties beginning with the eye, it is said that only four exist. Having investigated what has been said, it should be grasped by the discerning.

67.

67.

Rūpe jīvitachakkañca, cakkhādisattakattayaṃ;

Pañca cha utucittehi, pañca chāsaññinaṃ bhave.

In the form-realm, there is the life-hexad and the three septads beginning with the eye. Five or six [types of kalāpas] arise from temperature and consciousness. For non-percipient beings, there may be five or six.

68.

68.

Pañcadhātvādiniyamā, pāṭhe gandharasojanaṃ;

Nuppatti tattha bhūtānaṃ, aphoṭṭhabbapavattinaṃ.

According to the textual principle concerning the primary elements and so on, there is no arising of scent, taste, or nutriment there, nor of the primary elements for those beings whose nature is the non-occurrence of the tangible.

69.

69.

Thaddhuṇhīraṇabhāvova, natthi dhātvādikiccato;

Aññaṃ gandhādīnaṃ tesaṃ, takkiccenopaladdhito.

The very nature of hardness, heat, and motion is nothing other than the function of the primary elements. Other qualities, such as scent, are likewise apprehended by their respective functions.

70.

70.

Rūpe sappaṭighattādi, tattha ruppanatā viya;

Ghaṭṭanañca ravuppādassaññatthasseva hetutā.

In material form, there is resistance and so on, just as there is the nature of being afflicted. And impact is indeed the cause for the arising of sound and for other things.

71.

71.

Icchitabbamimekantamevaṃ [M 0.0007] pāṭhāvirodhato;

Atha vā tehi viññeyyaṃ, dasakaṃ navakaṭṭhakaṃ.

This should be definitively accepted, in a way that does not contradict the text. Alternatively, by these [principles], the decad, nonad, and octad should be understood.

72.

72.

Sabbaṃ [V 0.0008] kāmabhave rūpaṃ, rūpe ekūnavīsati;

Asaññīnaṃ dasa gandharasojāhi ca brahmunaṃ.

All material form is found in the sensual realm; in the form-realm, nineteen types exist. For the non-percipient beings, there are ten, and for the brahmas, [their form is] without scent, taste, and nutriment.

Iti saccasaṅkhepe rūpasaṅkhepo nāma

Thus in the Compendium of Truths ends the Summary of Material Form.

Paṭhamo paricchedo.

The First Chapter.

2. Dutiyo paricchedo

2. The Second Chapter.

Khandhattayasaṅkhepo

The Summary of the Three Aggregates.

73.

73.

Vedanānubhavo tedhā, sukhadukkhamupekkhayā;

Iṭṭhāniṭṭhānubhavanamajjhānubhavalakkhaṇā.

The experience of feeling is threefold: pleasant, painful, and neutral. Its characteristic is the experience of the agreeable, the disagreeable, and the intermediate.

74.

74.

Kāyikaṃ mānasaṃ dukkhaṃ, sukhopekkhā ca vedanā;

Ekaṃ mānasameveti, pañcadhindriyabhedato.

Bodily and mental pain, and pleasant and neutral feeling: it is said that each is solely mental, according to the fivefold division of the faculties.

75.

75.

Yathā tathā vā saññāṇaṃ, saññā satinibandhanaṃ;

Chadhā chadvārasambhūtaphassajānaṃ vasena sā.

Perception is the act of cognizing in a particular way; perception is a basis for mindfulness. It is sixfold, according to its arising from contact born at the six doors.

76.

76.

Saṅkhārā cetanā phasso,

Manakkārāyu saṇṭhiti;

Takko cāro ca vāyāmo,

Pīti chandodhimokkhako.

Formations: volition, contact, attention, life faculty, stability, initial application, sustained application, effort, rapture, zeal, and determination.

77.

77.

Saddhā sati hirottappaṃ, cāgo mettā mati puna;

Majjhattatā ca passaddhī, kāyacittavasā duve.

Faith, mindfulness, conscience, and moral dread; generosity, loving-kindness, and wisdom; also equanimity and tranquility—this last being twofold, by way of body and of consciousness.

78.

78.

Lahutā mudukammaññapāguññamujutā tathā;

Dayā mudā micchāvācā, kammantājīvasaṃvaro.

Likewise, lightness, pliancy, wieldiness, proficiency, and uprightness; compassion, sympathetic joy, and the abstinences from wrong speech, wrong action, and wrong livelihood.

79.

79.

Lobho doso ca moho ca, diṭṭhi uddhaccameva ca;

Ahirīkaṃ anottappaṃ, vicikicchitameva ca.

Greed, hatred, and delusion; wrong view and restlessness; shamelessness and fearlessness of wrongdoing; and skeptical doubt as well.

80.

80.

Māno [M 0.0008][V 0.0009] issā ca maccheraṃ, kukkuccaṃ thinamiddhakaṃ;

Iti eteva paññāsa, saṅkhārakkhandhasaññitā.

Conceit, envy, and stinginess; remorse, sloth, and torpor. Thus, these fifty factors are designated as the aggregate of formations.

81.

81.

Byāpāro cetanā phasso, phusanaṃ saraṇaṃ tahiṃ;

Manakkāro pālanāyu, samādhi avisāratā.

Volition is engagement; contact is touching; mindfulness is recollection therein. Attention is directing the mind; the life faculty is maintenance; concentration is non-distraction.

82.

82.

Āropanānumajjaṭṭhā, takkacārā panīhanā;

Vīriyaṃ pīnanā pīti, chando tu kattukāmatā.

Placing upon, sustained examination, initial thought, sustained thought, striving; energy is invigoration, joy is rapture, and desire, indeed, is the wish to do.

83.

83.

Adhimokkho nicchayo saddhā,

Pasādo saraṇaṃ sati;

Hirī pāpajigucchā hi,

Ottappaṃ tassa bhīrutā.

Resolution is conviction; faith is serenity; mindfulness is recollection; conscience, indeed, is abhorrence of evil; moral dread is fear thereof.

84.

84.

Alaggo ca acaṇḍikkaṃ, cāgo mettā mati pana;

Yāthāvabodho majjhattaṃ, samavāhitalakkhaṇaṃ.

Non-attachment and non-fierceness, renunciation, loving-kindness, and wisdom; moreover, true understanding and equanimity, which has the characteristic of being well-composed.

85.

85.

Cha yugāni kāyacittadaragāravathaddhatā-

Akammaññattagelaññakuṭilānaṃ vinodanā.

The six pairs are for the dispelling of anxiety, heaviness, rigidity, unwieldiness, sickness, and crookedness of body and mind.

86.

86.

Tānuddhatādithinādidiṭṭhādīnaṃ yathākkamaṃ;

Sesakādiasaddhādimāyādīnaṃ vipakkhino.

These are, in due order, the opponents of those beginning with restlessness, sloth, and wrong view, and of the remaining ones beginning with lack of faith and deceit.

87.

87.

Dukkhāpanayanakāmā, dayā modā pamodanā;

Vacīduccaritādīnaṃ, virāmo viratittayaṃ.

Compassion is the desire to remove suffering; sympathetic joy is rejoicing; the threefold abstinence is abstinence from wrong conduct of speech and the like.

88.

88.

Lobho doso ca moho ca,

Gedhacaṇḍamanandhanā;

Kamena diṭṭhi duggāho,

Uddhaccaṃ bhantataṃ mataṃ.

Greed, hatred, and delusion are respectively craving, fierceness, and blinding of the mind; wrong view is a wrong grasp; restlessness is considered bewilderment.

89.

89.

Ahirīkamalajjattaṃ, anottappamatāsatā;

Saṃsayo vicikicchā hi, māno unnatilakkhaṇo.

Lack of conscience is shamelessness; lack of moral dread is heedlessness; doubt, indeed, is perplexity; conceit is characterized by elevation.

90.

90.

Parassakasampattīnaṃ[M 0.0009][V 0.0010],

Usūyā ca nigūhanā;

Issāmaccherakā tāpo,

Katākatassa socanā.

Jealousy of others' success and concealing one's own; envy and stinginess are anguish; remorse is sorrow for what is done and undone.

91.

91.

Thinaṃ cittassa saṅkoco, akammaññattatā pana;

Middhamiccevametesaṃ, lakkhaṇañca naye budho.

Sloth is the mind's contraction; torpor, moreover, is unwieldiness. A wise person should thus understand their characteristics.

92.

92.

Vedanādisamādhantā, satta sabbagasaññitā;

Takkādiadhimokkhantā, cha pakiṇṇakanāmakā.

The seven from feeling up to concentration are designated as universals; the six from initial thought up to resolution are named miscellaneous.

93.

93.

Saddhādayo viramantā, araṇā pañcavīsati;

Lobhādimiddhakantāni, saraṇāni catuddasa.

The twenty-five beginning with faith and ending with the abstinences are without defilement; the fourteen beginning with greed and ending with torpor are with defilement.

94.

94.

Issāmaccherakukkuccadosā kāme dayā mudā;

Kāme rūpe ca sesā cha-cattālīsa tidhātujā.

Envy, stinginess, remorse, and hatred are in the sensual realm, as are compassion and sympathetic joy. The remaining ones are in the sensual and form realms; forty-six are born of the three realms.

95.

95.

Chandanicchayamajjhattamanakkārā sauddhavā;

Dayādī pañca mānādī, cha yevāpana soḷasa.

Desire, resolution, equanimity, attention, with restlessness; compassion and the like are five; conceit and the like are six; indeed, these are sixteen.

96.

96.

Chandādī pañca niyatā, tatthekādasa netarā;

Ahirīkamanottappaṃ, lokanāsanakaṃ dvayaṃ.

The five beginning with desire are fixed; therein, eleven are not fixed. Lack of conscience and lack of moral dread are the pair that destroys the world.

97.

97.

Ete dve mohuddhaccāti, cattāro pāpasabbagā;

Lokapāladukaṃ vuttaṃ, hiriottappanāmakaṃ.

These two, with delusion and restlessness, are the four unwholesome universals. The pair named conscience and moral dread is said to be the world-guardians.

98.

98.

Ārammaṇūpanijjhānā, jhānaṅgā takkacārakā;

Pīti ekaggatā ceti, satta vittittayena ve.

The jhāna factors are for the close contemplation of the object: initial thought, sustained thought, joy, and one-pointedness. Thus, indeed, there are seven with a threefold variation.

99.

99.

Saddhā sati matekagga-dhiti lokavināsakā;

Pālakā nava cetāni, balāni avikampato.

Faith, mindfulness, wisdom, one-pointedness, and resolve are destroyers of the world. These nine protectors are powers, due to being unshaken.

100.

100.

Ettha saddhādipañcāyu, katvātra catudhā matiṃ;

Vedanāhi dvisattete, indriyānādhipaccato.

Here, the five beginning with faith, having made wisdom fourfold; with the feelings, these are twice seven, because of the dominance of the faculties.

101.

101.

Manarūpindriyehete[V 0.0011], sabbe indriyanāmakā;

Bāvīsati bhavantāyudvayaṃ katvekasaṅgahaṃ.

With the mind-faculty and the form-faculties, all these are named faculties. They become twenty-two, with the two life-faculties grouped as one.

102.

102.

Diṭṭhīhekaggatātakkasatīviratiyo [M 0.0010] pathā;

Aṭṭha niyyānato ādicaturo bhitvāna dvādasa.

View, one-pointedness, thought, mindfulness, and the abstinences are path factors. Eight are for leading out; the first four, by division, become twelve.

103.

103.

Phasso ca cetanā ceva,

Dvevetthāhāraṇattato;

Āhārā manavojāhi,

Bhavanti caturothavā.

Contact and volition, indeed, these two here are nutriments by way of appropriation. With mind and nutritive essence, the nutriments become four.

104.

104.

Hetu mūlaṭṭhato pāpe,

Lobhādittayamīritaṃ;

Kusalābyākate cāpi,

Alobhādittayaṃ tathā.

Causes are so called from their root-nature. In unwholesome states, the triad beginning with greed is declared; in wholesome and indeterminate states, likewise the triad beginning with non-greed.

105.

105.

Diṭṭhilobhadusā kammapathāpāyassa maggato;

Tabbipakkhā sugatiyā, tayoti cha pathīritā.

Wrong view, greed, and hatred are courses of action that are a path to states of woe. Their opposites are for a fortunate destiny. Thus six paths are declared.

106.

106.

Passaddhādiyugāni cha, vaggattā yugaḷāni tu;

Upakārā sati dhī ca, bahūpakārabhāvato.

The six beginning with tranquility are pairs, indeed, because they are grouped as such. Mindfulness and wisdom are helpers, because of their very helpful nature.

107.

107.

Oghāharaṇato yogā,

Yojanenābhavaggato;

Savanenāsavā diṭṭhi-

Mohejettha dudhā lubho.

Floods are so called because they carry one away; yokes, because they yoke one to the peak of existence. Taints are so called because they flow; they are wrong view and delusion, and here greed is twofold.

108.

108.

Daḷhaggāhena diṭṭhejā, upādānaṃ tidhā tahiṃ;

Diṭṭhi dosena te ganthā, ganthato diṭṭhiha dvidhā.

Clinging is so called from strong grasping; therein it is threefold, born of wrong view. The bodily knots are from wrong view and hatred, so called because they bind; here, wrong view is twofold.

109.

109.

Pañcāvaraṇato kāma-kaṅkhādosuddhavaṃ tapo;

Thinamiddhañca mohena, cha vā nīvaraṇānitha.

The hindrances are so called because they are five obstructions: sensual desire, doubt, hatred, restlessness, and remorse. With sloth-and-torpor and delusion, there are six hindrances here.

110.

110.

Katvā [V 0.0012] tāpuddhavaṃ ekaṃ, thinamiddhañca vuccati;

Kiccassāhārato ceva, vipakkhassa ca lesato.

Restlessness and remorse are treated as one, as are sloth and torpor. This is due to their function, their nutriment, and their common opponent.

111.

111.

Diṭṭhejuddhavadosandha-

Kaṅkhāthinuṇṇatī [M 0.0011] dasa;

Lokanāsayugenete,

Kilesā cittaklesato.

Wrong view, restlessness, hatred, delusion, doubt, sloth, and conceit—these, with the world-destroying pair, are the ten defilements, so called because they defile the mind.

112.

112.

Lobhadosamūhamāna-diṭṭhikaṅkhissamaccharā;

Saṃyojanāni diṭṭhejā, bhitvā bandhanato dudhā.

Greed, hatred, delusion, conceit, view, doubt, envy, and stinginess. The fetters are view and craving; having broken the bond, they are twofold.

113.

113.

Tāni mohuddhavaṃmānakaṅkhādosejadiṭṭhiyo;

Dudhādiṭṭhi tidhā lobhaṃ, bhitvā sutte dasīritā.

These are delusion, restlessness, conceit, doubt, hatred, craving, and views. View is twofold, greed is threefold; having broken them down, ten are declared in the suttas.

114.

114.

Diṭṭhilobhamūhamānadosakaṅkhā tahiṃ dudhā;

Katvā lobhamime sattānusayā samudīritā.

View, greed, delusion, conceit, hatred, and doubt—therein, having made greed twofold, these seven latent tendencies are declared.

115.

115.

Diṭṭhi eva parāmāso, ñeyyo evaṃ samāsato;

Attho saṅkhārakkhandhassa, vutto vuttānusārato.

View is indeed clinging, it should be known thus in brief. The meaning of the aggregate of formations is stated according to what was said.

Iti saccasaṅkhepe khandhattayasaṅkhepo nāma

Thus, in the Summary of the Truths, this is named the Summary of the Three Aggregates.

Dutiyo paricchedo.

The Second Chapter.

3. Tatiyo paricchedo

3. The Third Chapter.

Cittapavattiparidīpano

An Exposition on the Process of Consciousness.

116.

116.

Cittaṃ visayaggāhaṃ taṃ, pākāpākadato dudhā;

Kusalākusalaṃ pubbaṃ, paramabyākataṃ mataṃ.

That mind, which grasps an object, is twofold: resultant and non-resultant. The former is wholesome or unwholesome; the latter is considered indeterminate.

117.

117.

Kusalaṃ [V 0.0013] tattha kāmādibhūmito catudhā siyā;

Aṭṭha pañca cattāri ca, cattāri kamato kathaṃ.

Therein, wholesome consciousness, according to the planes beginning with the sense-sphere, may be fourfold. How are they eight, five, four, and four, in due order?

118.

118.

Somanassamatiyuttamasaṅkhāramanamekaṃ;

Sasaṅkhāramanañcekaṃ, tathā hīnamatidvayaṃ.

One mind is accompanied by joy, associated with wisdom, and unprompted; and one is prompted. Likewise, there is a pair inferior in wisdom.

119.

119.

Tathopekkhāmatiyuttaṃ, matihīnanti aṭṭhadhā;

Kāmāvacarapuññettha, bhijjate vedanādito.

Likewise, those accompanied by equanimity, associated with wisdom, and those devoid of wisdom—thus they are eightfold. Here, sense-sphere merit is distinguished by feeling and so on.

120.

120.

Dānaṃ [M 0.0012] sīlañca bhāvanā, pattidānānumodanā;

Veyyāvaccāpacāyañca, desanā suti diṭṭhiju.

Giving, virtue, and mental development; transfer of merit and rejoicing in it; service and reverence; teaching, listening, and straightening of view.

121.

121.

Etesvekamayaṃ hutvā, vatthuṃ nissāya vā na vā;

Dvārahīnādiyonīnaṃ, gatiyādippabhedavā.

Being one of these, whether depending on a basis or not, it possesses distinctions such as destination for those of origins lacking sense doors and so forth.

122.

122.

Tikālikaparittādigocaresvekamādiya;

Udeti kālamuttaṃ vā, matihīnaṃ vināmalaṃ.

It arises taking as its object one of the limited, related to the three times, etc., or a timeless object. For a consciousness devoid of wisdom, this occurs without the stainless one [Nibbāna as object].

123.

123.

Chagocaresu rūpādipañcakaṃ pañca gocarā;

Sesaṃ rūpamarūpañca, paññatti chaṭṭhagocaro.

Among the six fields of objects, the pentad beginning with form constitutes the five fields. The remainder—subtle form, the formless, and concepts—is the sixth field.

124.

124.

Ñāṇayuttavaraṃ tattha, datvā sandhiṃ tihetukaṃ;

Pacchā paccati pākānaṃ, pavatte aṭṭhake duve.

There, the excellent kamma associated with wisdom, having produced a three-rooted rebirth-linking, later ripens in the course of existence as two sets of eight resultants.

125.

125.

Tesuyeva nihīnaṃ tu, datvā sandhiṃ duhetukaṃ;

Deti dvādasa pāke ca, pavatte dhīyutaṃ vinā.

Among those, the inferior kamma, however, having produced a two-rooted rebirth-linking, gives twelve resultants in the course of existence, which are without wisdom.

126.

126.

Evaṃ dhīhīnamukkaṭṭhaṃ, sandhiyañca pavattiyaṃ;

Hīnaṃ panubhayatthāpi, hetuhīneva paccati.

Thus, the wisdom-less and the exalted kamma produce results both at rebirth-linking and in the course of existence. The inferior kamma, however, ripens in both instances only as rootless results.

127.

127.

Kāmasugatiyaṃyeva, bhavabhogadadaṃ idaṃ;

Rūpāpāye pavatteva, paccate anurūpato.

This gives enjoyment of existence only in the sense-sphere happy destinations. In the form realms and woeful states, it ripens accordingly only in the course of existence.

128.

128.

Vitakkacārapītīhi, sukhekaggayutaṃ manaṃ;

Ādi cārādipītādisukhādīhi paraṃ tayaṃ.

The mind endowed with applied thought, sustained thought, joy, happiness, and one-pointedness is the first. The subsequent three are formed by successively abandoning applied thought, sustained thought, and joy.

129.

129.

Upekkhekaggatāyantamāruppañcevamaṅgato[V 0.0014];

Pañcadhā rūpapuññaṃ tu, hotārammaṇato pana.

The final jhāna has equanimity and one-pointedness; the immaterial attainments are also thus by way of their factors. The form-sphere merit, however, is fivefold depending on the object of meditation.

130.

130.

Ādissāsubhamantassu-

Pekkhā mettādayo tayo;

Ādo catunnaṃ pañcannaṃ,

Sassāsakasiṇāni tu.

The ten foul objects are for the first jhāna; equanimity for the last. The three beginning with loving-kindness are for the first four. The in-and-out breaths and the kasiṇas are for all five.

131.

131.

Nabhatammanatassuññataccittacatugocare;

Kamenātikkamāruppapuññaṃ hoti catubbidhaṃ.

With the four objects—infinite space, infinite consciousness, nothingness, and the peak of consciousness—the fourfold immaterial wholesome consciousness arises in due order by transcendence.

132.

132.

Amalaṃ [M 0.0013] santimārabbha, hoti taṃ maggayogato;

Catudhā pādakajjhānabhedato puna vīsati.

That arises, having taken the stainless peace as its object, through application to the path. It is fourfold by path, and again twentyfold by the distinctions of the base jhānas.

133.

133.

Diṭṭhikaṅkhānudaṃ ādi, kāmadosatanūkaraṃ;

Paraṃ paraṃ taducchedī, antaṃ sesakanāsakaṃ.

The first path removes view and doubt; the next diminishes sensual desire and ill will. The one after that eradicates them, and the final one destroys what remains.

134.

134.

Evaṃ bhūmittayaṃ puññaṃ, bhāvanāmayamettha hi;

Paṭhamaṃ vatthuṃ nissāya, dutiyaṃ ubhayenapi.

Thus, wholesome consciousness is threefold by plane, here consisting of mental development. The first depends on a physical basis, the second on both or either.

135.

135.

Tatiye ādi nissāya,

Sesā nissāya vā na vā;

Honti ādidvayaṃ tattha,

Sādheti sakabhūbhavaṃ.

The third depends on the first type of support; the rest may or may not depend on a basis. There, the first two accomplish becoming in their own respective planes.

136.

136.

Sādhetānuttaraṃ santiṃ, abhiññā panidheva tu;

Jhānūdayaphalattā na, phaladānāpi sambhavā.

The supramundane paths accomplish the unsurpassed peace. Higher knowledge, however, arises only here. It is not a result of the arising of jhāna, nor is it produced from the giving of its fruit.

137.

137.

Nāññabhūphaladaṃ kammaṃ, rūpapākassa gocaro;

Sakammagocaroyeva, na caññoyamasambhavo.

Kamma does not give fruit in a different plane. The object of a form-resultant consciousness is only the object of its own kamma; another object is not possible.

138.

138.

Pāpaṃ kāmikamevekaṃ, hetuto taṃ dvidhā puna;

Mūlato tividhaṃ lobha-dosamohavasā siyā.

Unwholesome consciousness is of the sense-sphere only, one type. Again, by cause, it is twofold. By root, it may be threefold, due to greed, aversion, and delusion.

139.

139.

Somanassakudiṭṭhīhi[V 0.0015], yuttamekamasaṅkharaṃ;

Sasaṅkhāramanañcekaṃ, hīnadiṭṭhidvayaṃ tathā.

One is associated with joy and wrong view, unprompted; and another one is prompted. Likewise, two are dissociated from wrong view.

140.

140.

Upekkhādiṭṭhiyuttampi, tathā diṭṭhiviyuttakaṃ;

Vedanādiṭṭhiādīhi, lobhamūlevamaṭṭhadhā.

Also one associated with equanimity and wrong view, and likewise one dissociated from view. Thus, greed-rooted consciousness is eightfold, by way of feeling, view, and so forth.

141.

141.

Sadukkhadosāsaṅkhāraṃ, itaraṃ dosamūlakaṃ;

Mohamūlampi sopekkhaṃ, kaṅkhuddhaccayutaṃ dvidhā.

One aversion-rooted consciousness is unprompted, accompanied by displeasure; the other is prompted. The delusion-rooted consciousness is also twofold, accompanied by equanimity: one associated with doubt, the other with restlessness.

142.

142.

Tattha dosadvayaṃ vatthuṃ, nissāyevitare pana;

Nissāya vā na vā honti, vadhādisahitā kathaṃ.

Among them, the two aversion-rooted consciousnesses always depend on a physical basis; but the others may or may not depend on one. How do they arise accompanied by killing and so forth?

143.

143.

Pharussavadhabyāpādā, sadosena salobhato;

Kudiṭṭhimethunābhijjhā, sesā kammapathā dvibhi.

Harsh speech, killing, and ill will arise with aversion; wrong view, sexual misconduct, and covetousness arise with greed. The remaining courses of action arise from two roots.

144.

144.

Sandhiṃ [M 0.0014] catūsvapāyesu, deti sabbattha vuttiyaṃ;

Paccate gocaraṃ tassa, sakalaṃ amalaṃ vinā.

It gives rebirth-linking in the four woeful states and functioning everywhere. Its object is everything, with the exception of the stainless.

145.

145.

Abyākataṃ dvidhā pāka-kriyā tatthādi bhūmito;

Catudhā kāmapākettha, puññapākādito dudhā.

The indeterminate is twofold: resultant and functional. Therein, consciousness is fourfold according to plane. Here, sense-sphere resultant consciousness is twofold: wholesome-resultant and unwholesome-resultant.

146.

146.

Puññapākā dvidhāhetu-sahetūti dviraṭṭhakā;

Ahetū pañca ñāṇāni, gahaṇaṃ tīraṇā ubho.

Wholesome resultants are twofold, as rootless and with roots, thus two sets of eight. The rootless are the five sense-consciousnesses, receiving consciousness, and both investigating consciousnesses.

147.

147.

Kāyañāṇaṃ sukhī tattha, somanassādi tīraṇaṃ;

Sopekkhāni cha sesāni, sapuññaṃva sahetukaṃ.

Therein, body-consciousness is accompanied by pleasure; one investigating consciousness is with joy. The remaining six are with equanimity. The resultants with roots are like the wholesome consciousnesses.

148.

148.

Kevalaṃ sandhibhavaṅga-tadālambacutibbasā;

Jāyate sesametassa, pubbe vuttanayā naye.

It arises only with the functions of rebirth-linking, life-continuum, registering, and decease. The remainder of its functions should be understood in the manner previously stated.

149.

149.

Manussavinipātīnaṃ, sandhādi antatīraṇaṃ;

Hoti aññena kammena, sahetupi ahetunaṃ.

For humans born with defects, the functions from rebirth-linking to investigating occur by another kamma, whether it be with roots or rootless.

150.

150.

Pāpajā puññajāhetu-samā tīraṃ vinādikaṃ;

Sadukkhaṃ kāyaviññāṇaṃ, aniṭṭhārammaṇā ime.

The unwholesome-resultants are similar to the wholesome rootless resultants. Body-consciousness is accompanied by pain. These seven have undesirable objects.

151.

151.

Te [V 0.0016] sātagocarā tesu, dviṭṭhānaṃ āditīraṇaṃ;

Pañcaṭṭhānāparā dve te, parittavisayākhilā.

Among them, they have agreeable objects. The first investigating consciousness has two functions; the other two have five functions. All have limited objects.

152.

152.

Sampaṭicchadvipañcannaṃ, pañca rūpādayo tahiṃ;

Paccuppannāva sesānaṃ, pākānaṃ cha tikālikā.

For the two receiving consciousnesses and the five pairs of sense-consciousnesses, their objects are the five, form and so on, which must be present. For the remaining resultants, their six kinds of objects can be of the three times.

153.

153.

Rūpārūpavipākānaṃ, sabbaso sadisaṃ vade;

Sakapuññena sandhādi-sakiccattayataṃ vinā.

The resultants of the form and formless realms are said to be entirely like their corresponding wholesome consciousnesses, except that they perform only the threefold function beginning with rebirth-linking.

154.

154.

Samānuttarapākāpi, sakapuññena sabbaso;

Hitvā mokkhamukhaṃ taṃ hi, dvidhā magge tidhā phale.

Even the equal and unsurpassed resultants are entirely like their wholesome counterparts. Having left that door to liberation, it is indeed twofold in the path and threefold in the fruit.

155.

155.

Kriyā tidhāmalābhāvā,

Bhūmito tattha kāmikā;

Dvidhā hetusahetūti,

Tidhāhetu tahiṃ kathaṃ.

Functional consciousness, which is without stain, is threefold by plane. Therein, the sense-sphere functional is twofold: rootless and with roots. How are the rootless ones threefold there?

156.

156.

Āvajjahasitāvajjā[M 0.0015], sopekkhasukhupekkhavā;

Pañcachakāmāvacarā, sakalārammaṇā ca te.

The five-door adverting, mind-door adverting, and smile-producing consciousnesses are accompanied by equanimity or joy; these sense-sphere consciousnesses have all types of objects.

157.

157.

Saheturūparūpā ca, sakapaññaṃvārahato;

Vuttiyā na phale pupphaṃ, yathā chinnalatā phalaṃ.

The functional consciousness with roots, of the form and formless spheres, belonging to an Arahant, is like his wholesome consciousness. In its functioning, it is like a flower that bears no fruit, just as a severed vine bears no fruit.

158.

158.

Anāsevanayāvajja-dvayaṃ puthujjanassa hi;

Na phale vattamānampi, moghapupphaṃ phalaṃ yathā.

For a worldling, the two adverting consciousnesses, not being part of the impulsion process, bear no fruit even when they occur, just like a barren flower bears no fruit.

159.

159.

Tisatta dvicha chattiṃsa, catupañca yathākkamaṃ;

Puññaṃ pāpaṃ phalaṃ kriyā, ekūnanavutīvidhaṃ.

Twenty-one wholesome, twelve unwholesome, thirty-six resultant, and twenty functional: thus, respectively, there are eighty-nine types of consciousness.

160.

160.

Sandhi bhavaṅgamāvajjaṃ, dassanādikapañcakaṃ;

Gahatīraṇavoṭṭhabba-javataggocaraṃ cuti.

Rebirth-linking, life-continuum, adverting, the five functions beginning with seeing, receiving, investigating, determining, impulsion, registering, and decease.

161.

161.

Iti esaṃ dvisattannaṃ, kiccavuttivasādhunā;

Cittappavatti chadvāre, saṅkhepā vuccate kathaṃ.

Thus, now, by way of the performance of these fourteen functions, how is the process of mind at the six doors briefly explained?

162.

162.

Kāme [V 0.0017] sarāginaṃ kamma-nimittādi cutikkhaṇe;

Khāyate manasoyeva, sesānaṃ kammagocaro.

For those with passion in the sense-sphere, at the moment of death, kamma, the sign of kamma, or the sign of destiny appears to the mind-door only. For others, the object is kamma.

163.

163.

Upaṭṭhitaṃ tamārabbha, pañcavāraṃ javo bhave;
