Tadālambaṃ tato tamhā, cuti hoti javehi vā.

Taking that presented object, impulsion occurs five times. Thereafter, registering consciousness may arise, or death may occur immediately after the impulsions.

164.

164.

Avijjātaṇhāsaṅkhāra-sahajehi apāyinaṃ;

Visayādīnavacchādi-namanakkhipakehi tu.

For those bound for the lower realms, rebirth is caused by co-nascent ignorance, craving, and formations; but for others, by seeing the danger in sense objects, and by the forces of covering, bending, and projecting.

165.

165.

Appahīnehi sesānaṃ, chādanaṃ namanampi ca;

Khipakā pana saṅkhārā, kusalāva bhavantiha.

For others, covering and bending are due to unabandoned defilements; but here the projecting formations are only wholesome.

166.

166.

Kiccattaye kate evaṃ, kammadīpitagocare;

Tajjaṃ vatthuṃ sahuppannaṃ, nissāya vā na vā tahiṃ.

Thus, when the threefold function has been performed regarding the object illuminated by kamma, the corresponding physical basis arises simultaneously, whether depending on it or not.

167.

167.

Tajjā sandhi siyā hitvā, antarattaṃ bhavantare;

Antarattaṃ vinā dūre, paṭisandhi kathaṃ bhave.

The corresponding rebirth-linking may occur, having left the intermediate existence between lives. Without an intermediate existence, how could rebirth-linking occur at a distance?

168.

168.

Iheva kammataṇhādi-hetuto pubbacittato;

Cittaṃ dūre siyā dīpa-paṭighosādikaṃ yathā.

Right here, from the cause of craving for deeds and so forth, from a prior consciousness, the mind may be far away, like a lamp, an echo, and so forth.

169.

169.

Nāsaññā [M 0.0016] cavamānassa, nimittaṃ na cutī ca yaṃ;

Uddhaṃ sandhinimittaṃ kiṃ, paccayopi kanantaro.

For one passing away from the non-percipient realm, there is neither a sign nor the decease consciousness; what is the sign of rebirth-linking upwards, and what is the immediately proximate condition?

170.

170.

Pubbabhave cuti dāni, kāme jāyanasandhiyā;

Aññacittantarābhāvā, hotānantarakāraṇaṃ.

The decease in a previous existence is the immediately proximate cause for the birth-linking now in the sense-sphere, due to the absence of another intervening consciousness.

171.

171.

Bhavantarakataṃ kammaṃ, yamokāsaṃ labhe tato;

Hoti sā sandhi teneva, upaṭṭhāpitagocare.

When karma done in another existence obtains an opportunity, that rebirth-linking occurs precisely through that karma, in the object presented by it.

172.

172.

Yasmā cittavirāgattaṃ, kātuṃ nāsakkhi sabbaso;

Tasmā sānusayasseva, punuppatti siyā bhave.

Because he could not completely achieve dispassion of mind, therefore, for one with latent defilements, rebirth in existence may occur again.

173.

173.

Pañcadvāre siyā sandhi, vinā kammaṃ dvigocare;

Bhavasandhānato sandhi, bhavaṅgaṃ taṃ tadaṅgato.

Rebirth-linking may occur at the five doors with two kinds of objects, excluding kamma. Rebirth-linking is so-called from the linking of existences; from that, life-continuum arises as its factor.

174.

174.

Tamevante [V 0.0018] cuti tasmiṃ, gocare cavanena tu;

Ekasantatiyā evaṃ, uppattiṭṭhitibhedakā.

Decease is at the very end, by passing away in that same object. Thus, in a single continuity, there are the distinct moments of arising, duration, and dissolution.

175.

175.

Athaññārammaṇāpātha-gate cittantarassa hi;

Hetusaṅkhyaṃ bhavaṅgassa, dvikkhattuṃ calanaṃ bhave.

Then, when another object has come into range, indeed, as a condition for the subsequent consciousness, the life-continuum vibrates twice.

176.

176.

Ghaṭṭite aññavatthumhi, aññanissitakampanaṃ;

Ekābaddhena hotīti, sakkharopamayā vade.

When struck by another object, a vibration dependent on another occurs because they are bound together as one; this is explained by the simile of the pebble.

177.

177.

Manodhātukriyāvajjaṃ, tato hoti sakiṃ bhave;

Dassanādi sakadvāra-gocaro gahaṇaṃ tato.

Then, the functional adverting of the mind-element occurs once. Then, seeing and so forth, which takes the object of its own door; then, receiving.

178.

178.

Santīraṇaṃ tato tamhā, voṭṭhabbañca sakiṃ tato;

Sattakkhattuṃ javo kāme, tamhā tadanurūpato.

From that, investigating; and from that, determining, which occurs once. Then, impulsion seven times in the sense-sphere; from that, what is in accordance therewith.

179.

179.

Tadālambadvikaṃ tamhā, bhavaṅgaṃtimahantari;

Javā mahante voṭṭhabbā, paritte nitare manaṃ.

From that, two registering moments, followed by the life-continuum, in the case of a very great object. In a great object, it ends with impulsion; in a slight object, with determining; the mind does not proceed further.

180.

180.

Voṭṭhabbassa paritte tu, dvattikkhattuṃ javo viya;

Vadanti vuttiṃ taṃ pāṭhe, anāsevanato na hi.

But in the case of a slight object, the determining consciousness is said to be like impulsion occurring two or three times. They speak of this function in the text; indeed, it is not due to repetition.

181.

181.

Niyamopidha cittassa, kammādiniyamo viya;

Ñeyyo ambopamādīhi, dassetvā taṃ sudīpaye.

Here too, the fixed order of consciousness is like the fixed order of kamma and so forth; it should be known through the simile of the mango and others. Having shown it, one should illuminate it well.

182.

182.

Manodvāretarāvajjaṃ[M 0.0017], bhavaṅgamhā siyā tato;

Javokāme vibhūte tu, kāmavhe visaye tato.

Mind-door adverting may arise from the life-continuum. Then, when the sense-sphere object is clear, impulsion arises concerning that sense-sphere object.

183.

183.

Kāmīnaṃ tu tadālambaṃ, bhavaṅgaṃ tu tato siyā;

Avibhūte paritte ca, bhavaṅgaṃ javato bhave.

For sense-sphere beings, registering may arise, and from that, the life-continuum. But when the object is indistinct, the life-continuum may arise immediately after impulsion.

184.

184.

Avibhūte vibhūte ca, paritte aparittake;

Javāyeva bhavaṅgaṃ tu, brahmānaṃ catugocare.

Whether the object is indistinct or distinct, slight or not slight, for Brahmas, the life-continuum indeed arises immediately after impulsion in all four cases.

185.

185.

Mahaggataṃ panārabbha, javite dosasaṃyute;

Viruddhattā bhavaṅgaṃ na, kiṃ siyā sukhasandhino.

But having taken a sublime object, when an impulsion associated with aversion occurs, due to the opposition, does the life-continuum not arise for one whose rebirth-linking was pleasant?

186.

186.

Upekkhātīraṇaṃ [V 0.0019] hoti, parittenāvajjaṃ kathaṃ.

Niyamo na vināvajjaṃ, maggato phalasambhavā.

How does investigating with equanimity occur from a slight adverting? There is no fixed rule, for without adverting, fruit arises from the path.

187.

187.

Mahaggatāmalā sabbe, javā gotrabhuto siyuṃ;

Nirodhā ca phaluppatti, bhavaṅgaṃ javanādito.

All sublime and stainless impulsions, as well as change-of-lineage, may occur. From cessation, fruition attainment arises. The life-continuum arises after impulsion and so forth.

188.

188.

Sahetusāsavā pākā, tīraṇā dve cupekkhakā;

Ime sandhi bhavaṅgā ca, cuti cekūnavīsati.

The mundane resultants with root-causes, and the two investigating consciousnesses accompanied by equanimity: these nineteen perform the functions of rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and decease.

189.

189.

Dve dve āvajjanādīni, gahaṇantāni tīṇi tu;

Santīraṇāni ekaṃva, voṭṭhabbamitināmakaṃ.

Two are the advertings and so forth; three are those ending with receiving; one is investigating; and one is that named determining.

190.

190.

Aṭṭha kāmamahāpākā, tīṇi santīraṇāni ca;

Ekādasa bhavantete, tadārammaṇanāmakā.

The eight great sense-sphere resultants and the three investigating consciousnesses: these eleven are they that are named registering.

191.

191.

Kusalākusalaṃ sabbaṃ, kriyā cāvajjavajjitā;

Phalāni pañcapaññāsa, javanāni bhavantime.

All wholesome and unwholesome consciousnesses, functional consciousnesses excluding the advertings, and the supramundane fruit consciousnesses: these fifty-five become impulsions.

Iti saccasaṅkhepe cittapavattiparidīpano nāma

Thus, in the Compendium of Truths, the exposition named 'The Elucidation of the Process of Consciousness'.

Tatiyo paricchedo.

The Third Chapter.

4. Catuttho paricchedo

4. The Fourth Chapter.

Viññāṇakkhandhapakiṇṇakanayasaṅkhepo

A Summary of the Miscellaneous Method Concerning the Aggregate of Consciousness.

192.

192.

Ekadhādinayodāni[M 0.0018], paṭuvaḍḍhāya yoginaṃ;

Vuccate visayaggāhā, sabbamekavidhaṃ manaṃ.

Now the method beginning with the single-fold classification is declared, for the development of skill in yogis: in respect of grasping an object, all mind is of a single kind.

193.

193.

Ekāsīti tibhūmaṭṭhaṃ, lokiyaṃ suttarañca taṃ;

Sesaṃ lokuttaraṃ aṭṭha, anuttarañcitī dvidhā.

Eighty-one consciousnesses are mundane, located in the three planes, and are 'with a superior'. The remaining eight are supramundane and are 'unsurpassed'. Thus, the classification is twofold.

194.

194.

Lokapākakriyāhetū[V 0.0020], cekahetūti sattahi;

Tiṃsa nādhipati sādhi-pati sesātipī dvidhā.

By way of mundane, resultant, functional, rooted, one-rooted, two-rooted, and three-rooted—thus in seven ways. Thirty are without dominance, the rest with dominance; thus also twofold.

195.

195.

Chandacittīhavīmaṃsā-svekena matimā yutaṃ;

Vinā vīmaṃsamekena, ñāṇahīnamanaṃ yutaṃ.

When conjoined with one from among desire, consciousness, effort, and investigation, it is endowed with wisdom; without investigation, when conjoined with one of the others, it is a mind devoid of knowledge.

196.

196.

Parittānappamāṇāni, mahaggatamanāniti;

Tidhā chanava caṭṭha ca, tinavā ca yathākkamaṃ.

Limited, immeasurable, and exalted minds are thus threefold, numbering respectively: six and nine, eight, and three and nine.

197.

197.

Dvipañca cittaṃ viññāṇaṃ, tisso hi manodhātuyo;

Chasattati manoñāṇa-dhātūti tividhā puna.

The two sets of five sense-consciousnesses, and indeed three mind-elements; seventy-six are mind-consciousness-elements, thus threefold again.

198.

198.

Ekārammaṇacittāni, anabhiññaṃ mahaggataṃ;

Amalaṃ pañcaviññāṇaṃ, navapañca bhavantime.

Consciousnesses with a single object: the exalted without higher knowledge, the immaculate, and the five sense-consciousnesses. These are nine and five.

199.

199.

Pañcālambaṃ manodhātu, sābhiññaṃ kāmadhātujaṃ;

Sesaṃ chārammaṇaṃ taṃ hi, tecattālīsa saṅkhyato.

The mind-element has a fivefold object; so too the consciousness with higher knowledge and that born of the sense-sphere. The rest, which have a sixfold object, indeed number forty-three.

200.

200.

Kāmapākadusā cādi-maggo cādikriyā duve;

Rūpā sabbetirūpe na, tecattālīsa hontime.

Sense-sphere resultants, unwholesome consciousnesses, the initial path, and the two initial functional consciousnesses—all these, numbering forty-three, do not arise in the form sphere.

201.

201.

Vināva rūpenāruppa-vipākā caturo siyuṃ;

Dvecattālīsa sesāni, vattantubhayathāpi ca.

Indeed without form are the four immaterial resultants; the remaining forty-two also function in both ways.

202.

202.

Catudhāpi ahetvekadvihetukatihetuto;

Aṭṭhārasa dve bāvīsa, sattacattālisaṃ bhave.

Also fourfold by way of rootless, one-rooted, two-rooted, and three-rooted: there are eighteen, two, twenty-two, and forty-seven, respectively.

203.

203.

Kāme [M 0.0019] javā savoṭṭhabbā, abhiññādvayameva ca;

Rūpiriyāpathaviññattikarāme caturaṭṭhakā.

In the sense-sphere: impulsions and determinings, and indeed the two higher knowledges; in the form-sphere: those causing deportment and intimation. These are four groups of eight.

204.

204.

Chabbīsati javā sesā, karā rūpiriyāpathe;

Dvipañcamanavajjāni, kāmarūpaphalāni ca.

The remaining twenty-six impulsions perform the function of deportment in the form-sphere; excluded are the two sets of five sense-consciousnesses, the mind-element, and the sense-sphere and form-sphere results.

205.

205.

Ādikriyāti cekūna-vīsa rūpakarā ime;

Sesā cuddasa bhinnāvacuti sandhi na tīṇipi.

The initial functional consciousnesses are nineteen; these are form-functional. The remaining fourteen are separate; they do not perform the three functions of rebirth-linking, life-continuum, or decease.

206.

206.

Ekakiccādito [V 0.0021] pañca-vidhā tatthekakiccakā;

Dvipañcacittaṃ javanaṃ, manodhātuṭṭhasaṭṭhime.

Beginning with single-function, the classification is fivefold. Therein, those with a single function are: the two sets of five sense-consciousnesses, the impulsions, and the mind-element. These are sixty-eight.

207.

207.

Dvikiccādīni voṭṭhabbaṃ, sukhatīraṃ mahaggate;

Pākā kāmamahāpākā, sesā tīrā yathākkamaṃ.

Beginning with those of double function are: the determining consciousness; the exalted resultants; the great sense-sphere resultants; and the remaining investigating consciousnesses, respectively having two, three, four, and five functions.

208.

208.

Dassanaṃ savanaṃ diṭṭhaṃ, sutaṃ ghāyanakādikaṃ;

Tayaṃ mutaṃ manodhātuttayaṃ diṭṭhaṃ sutaṃ mutaṃ.

Seeing and hearing relate to the seen and the heard; smelling, tasting, and touching relate to the sensed. The objects of the three mind-elements are the seen, the heard, and the sensed.

209.

209.

Diṭṭhaṃ sutaṃ mutaṃ ñātaṃ, sābhiññaṃ sesakāmikaṃ;

Viññātārammaṇaṃ sesamevaṃ chabbidhamīraye.

The object is declared to be sixfold: seen, heard, sensed, and known. Consciousness with higher knowledge and the remaining sense-sphere consciousnesses have a cognized object, as do the rest.

210.

210.

Sattadhā sattaviññāṇadhātūnaṃ tu vasā bhave;

Vuccatedāni tasseva, anantaranayakkamo.

However, the classification may be sevenfold, according to the seven consciousness-elements. Now the method of their immediate succession will be stated.

211.

211.

Puññesvādidvayā kāme, rūpapuññamanantakaṃ;

Tappādakuttarānantaṃ, bhavaṅgañcāditīraṇaṃ.

From the first two wholesome sense-sphere consciousnesses, form-sphere wholesome consciousness is the immediate successor; that which produces the supramundane is succeeded by it, as are the life-continuum and the initial investigating consciousness.

212.

212.

Dutiyantadvayā tīraṃ, bhavaṅgaṃ tatiyadvayā;

Te anantāmalaṃ puññaṃ, majjhattañca mahaggataṃ.

From the last two, investigating consciousness [arises]; from the third pair, the life-continuum. Their immediate successors are the immaculate wholesome, the neutral, and the exalted.

213.

213.

Sabbavāre sayañceti, tepaññāsa tisatta ca;

Tettiṃsa ca bhavantete, rūpesu pana puññato.

In all instances, and from themselves, these are fifty-three, twenty-one, and thirty-three. In the form-sphere, however, from the wholesome...

214.

214.

Tappākā ca matiyutta-kāmapākā sayaṃ dasa;

Āruppapuññato te ca, sako pāko sayaṃ puna.

Its resultants, the ten knowledge-conjoined sense-sphere resultants, and from itself; and from immaterial wholesome, those same, its own resultant, and again from itself.

215.

215.

Adhopākā ca antamhā, tatiyañca phalantime;

Dasekadvitipañcāhi, maggā cekaṃ sakaṃ phalaṃ.

From the last, the lower resultants and the third fruit arise. From the ten, one, two, and five paths, one's own respective fruit arises.

216.

216.

Lobhamūlekahetūhi[M 0.0020], antakāmasubhā viya;

Satta dosadvayā kāma-bhavaṅgapekkhavā sayaṃ.

From the one-rooted greed-rooted consciousnesses, as from the final beautiful sense-sphere consciousnesses, seven arise. From the two hatred-rooted consciousnesses, the sense-sphere life-continuum arises, depending, and from itself.

217.

217.

Mahāpākatihetūhi, sāvajjā sabbasandhiyo;

Kāmaccutīhi sesāhi, sāvajjā kāmasandhiyo.

From the great three-rooted resultants, all faulty rebirth-linkings arise. From the remaining sense-sphere decease consciousnesses, the faulty sense-sphere rebirth-linkings arise.

218.

218.

Kāmaccuti [V 0.0022] ca voṭṭhabbaṃ, sayañca sukhatīrato;

Paṭicchā tīraṇāni dve, itarā sakatīraṇaṃ.

From the sense-sphere decease, determining arises, and from itself. From the joyful investigating consciousness, receiving and the two investigating consciousnesses arise; from the other, its own investigating consciousness.

219.

219.

Sakaṃ sakaṃ paṭicchaṃ tu, viññāṇehi dvipañcahi;

Rūpapākehi sāvajjā, sandhiyohetuvajjitā.

From each of the two sets of five sense-consciousnesses, its own respective receiving consciousness arises. From the form-sphere resultants, the faulty rebirth-linkings devoid of roots arise.

220.

220.

Arūpapākesvādimhā, kāmapākā tihetukā;

Antāvajjampi cāruppa-pākā ca nava hontime.

From the first of the immaterial resultants, the three-rooted sense-sphere resultants arise. The final, the adverting, and the immaterial resultants—these are nine.

221.

221.

Dutiyādīhi teyeva, adhopākaṃ vinā vinā;

Phalā tihetukā pākā, sayañceti catuddasa.

From the second and so on, those same arise, successively excluding the lower resultant. The fruits, the three-rooted resultants, and from itself—these are fourteen.

222.

222.

Dvipañcādikriyā hāsā, sayañcāruppavajjitā;

Ñāṇayuttabhavaṅgāti, dasa voṭṭhabbato pana.

From the functional consciousnesses beginning with the two sets of five, from laughter-producing, and from itself (excluding the immaterial), and from the knowledge-conjoined life-continuum—thus ten. From the determining consciousness, however...

223.

223.

Kāme javā bhavaṅgā ca, kāmarūpe sayampi vā;

Navapañca sahetādi-kiriyadvayato pana.

From the sense-sphere impulsions and life-continuum, or in the sense and form spheres, and from itself. Nine and five arise, however, from the two initial root-conjoined functional consciousnesses.

224.

224.

Sayaṃ bhavaṅgamatimā, rūpe sātakriyāpi ca;

Tappādakantimañceti, bāvīsa tatiyā pana.

The life-continuum itself, the consciousness endowed with knowledge, and the agreeable functional consciousness in the form-sphere, as well as that which is the basis for the final one—thus, the third group, however, comprises twenty-two.

225.

225.

Te ca pākā sayañcante, phalaṃ majjhā mahaggatā;

Kriyāti vīsati honti, sesadvīhi dukehi tu.

And those resultants, the final one itself, the middle fruits, the exalted ones, and the functional consciousnesses are twenty. The remaining, however, are by two pairs.

226.

226.

Vuttapākā sayañceti, cuddasevaṃ kriyājavā;

Tadārammaṇaṃ muñcitvā, paṭṭhānanayato naye.

The aforementioned resultants and itself, thus fourteen functional impulsions; excluding the registering consciousness, this should be understood according to the method of the Paṭṭhāna.

227.

227.

Atha sātakriyā sātaṃ, sesaṃ sesakriyāpi ca;

Tadālambaṃ yathāyogaṃ, vade aṭṭhakathānayā.

Then, the agreeable functional consciousness takes an agreeable object, and the remaining functional consciousnesses take the remaining objects. The registering consciousness should be stated as is appropriate, according to the method of the commentaries.

228.

228.

Mahaggatā kriyā sabbā, sakapuññasamā tahiṃ;

Antā phalantimaṃ hoti, ayameva visesatā.

Therein, all exalted functional consciousnesses are equal to their own wholesome counterparts. The final ones correspond to the final fruit; this indeed is the distinction.

229.

229.

Imassānantarā [M 0.0021] dhammā, ettakāti pakāsitā;

Imaṃ panettakehīti, vuccateyaṃ nayodhunā.

The states that are immediately subsequent have been declared to be this many. Now, however, this method is spoken of: 'This state is preceded by this many'.

230.

230.

Dvīhi [V 0.0023] kāmajavā tīhi, rūpārūpā catūhi tu;

Maggā chahi phalādi dve, sesā dve pana sattahi.

Sense-sphere impulsions are preceded by two; form and formless sphere impulsions by three; paths, however, by four; the first two fruits by six; the remaining two, however, by seven.

231.

231.

Ekamhā dasa pañcahi, paṭicchā sukhatīraṇaṃ;

Kāme dosakriyāhīna-javehi gahato sakā.

The pleasant investigating consciousness is from receiving; receiving is from the ten by way of five; the ten from one. In the sense-sphere, one's own grasping is from impulsions devoid of hate and functional consciousness.

232.

232.

Kāme javā kriyāhīnā, tadālambā savoṭṭhabbā;

Sagahañceti tettiṃsacittehi paratīraṇā.

The other investigating consciousness is preceded by thirty-three consciousnesses: in the sense-sphere, the impulsions devoid of functional consciousness, the registering consciousness, with the determining consciousness, and with grasping.

233.

233.

Kāmapuññasukhītīrakaṇhavoṭṭhabbato dvayaṃ;

Mahāpākantimaṃ hoti, anāruppacutīhi ca.

From the pair of sense-sphere wholesome and pleasant investigating, from unwholesome determining, and from death-consciousnesses outside the formless sphere, the final great resultant arises.

234.

234.

Sattatiṃsa panetāni, ettha hitvā dusadvayaṃ;

Etehi pañcatiṃsehi, jāyate dutiyadvayaṃ.

However, these are thirty-seven. Excluding from these the pair rooted in hate, the second pair arises from the remaining thirty-five.

235.

235.

Sukhatīrādi sattete, kriyato cāpi sambhavā;

Ñeyyā sesāni cattāri, bhavaṅgena ca labbhare.

These seven, beginning with the pleasant investigating consciousness, also arise from functional consciousness. It should be known that the remaining four are also obtained through the life-continuum.

236.

236.

Maggavajjā savoṭṭhabbasukhitīrajavākhilā;

Cutīti navakaṭṭhāhi, tatiyadvayamādise.

Excluding the paths, one should declare that the third pair arises from these nine states: all impulsions, with the determining consciousness, the pleasant investigating consciousness, and the death-consciousness.

237.

237.

Etehi dosavajjehi, sattatīhitaradvayaṃ;

Rūpapākā vināruppapākāhetuduhetuke.

The other pair arises from these seventy consciousnesses, which exclude the hate-rooted ones, the form-sphere resultants, the formless-sphere resultants, the rootless, and the two-rooted.

238.

238.

Tehevekūnasaṭṭhīhi, hontiruppādikaṃ vinā;

Hāsāvajje jave rūpe, aṭṭhachakkehi tehi tu.

By these very fifty-nine, excluding the formless and others, they arise. In the form-sphere, however, the impulsions, excluding the smile-producing one, arise from those eight groups of six.

239.

239.

Sādhopākehi teheva, dutiyādīni attanā;

Adhodhojavahīnehi, ekekūnehi jāyare.

By these same wholesome resultants, the second and following arise. They are generated by groups that are successively one less, as the lower and lower impulsions are excluded.

240.

240.

Sukhatīrabhavaṅgāni, sayañcāti tisattahi;

Antāvajjaṃ anāruppabhavaṅgehi panetaraṃ.

The pleasant investigating consciousness, the life-continuum, and itself—thus by twenty-one. The final faultless one, however, and the other, are by the life-continuums outside the formless sphere.

241.

241.

Vuttānantarasaṅkhāto, nayo dāni anekadhā;

Puggalādippabhedāpi, pavatti tassa vuccate.

The method called 'the enumeration of the immediately subsequent' has been explained. Now its occurrence is spoken of in various ways, with distinctions such as by person.

242.

242.

Puthujjanassa [M 0.0022][V 0.0024] jāyante, diṭṭhikaṅkhāyutāni ve;

Sekkhassevāmalā satta, anantānitarassa tu.

For the worldling, indeed, those associated with wrong view and doubt arise. For the trainee, seven are stainless. But for the other, they are the final ones.

243.

243.

Antāmalaṃ anāvajjakriyā cekūnavīsati;

Kusalākusalā sesā, honti sekkhaputhujjane.

The final stainless one and the nineteen functional consciousnesses that are not adverting are for the Arahant. The remaining wholesome and unwholesome ones exist for the trainee and the worldling.

244.

244.

Itarāni panāvajjadvayaṃ pākā ca sāsavā;

Tiṇṇannampi siyuṃ evaṃ, pañcadhā sattabhedato.

But the others—the two adverting consciousnesses and the resultants with taints—are for all three types of individuals. Thus, there are five groups according to the sevenfold division.

245.

245.

Kāme soḷasa ghānādittayaṃ dosamahāphalā;

Rūpārūpe sapākoti, pañcavīsati ekajā.

The twenty-five consciousnesses born in one plane are: sixteen in the sense-sphere—namely, the three pairs beginning with nose-consciousness, the two hate-rooted, and the great resultants; and the resultants of the form and formless spheres.

246.

246.

Kāmapākā ca sesādimaggo ādikriyā duve;

Rūpe javāti bāvīsa, dvijā sesā tidhātujā.

The twenty-two consciousnesses born in two planes are: the remaining sense-sphere resultants, the initial path, the two initial functional consciousnesses, and the form-sphere impulsions. The remaining are born in the three realms.

247.

247.

Vitthāropi ca bhūmīsu, ñeyyo kāmasubhāsubhaṃ;

Hāsavajjamahetuñca, apāye sattatiṃsime.

The detailed explanation in the planes should also be known. In the woeful states, these thirty-seven arise: the sense-sphere wholesome and unwholesome, excluding the smile-producing and the rootless.

248.

248.

Hitvā mahaggate pāke, asīti sesakāmisu;

Cakkhusotamanodhātu, tīraṇaṃ voṭṭhabbampi ca.

Excluding the exalted resultants, eighty consciousnesses arise in the remaining sense-sphere planes. These include the eye-element, ear-element, mind-element, as well as investigating and determining consciousness.

249.

249.

Dosahīnajavā so so, pāko rūpe anāriye;

Pañcasaṭṭhi chasaṭṭhī tu, parittābhādīsu tīsu.

In the form-sphere of non-ariyas, the impulsions devoid of hate and their respective resultants arise. Sixty-five types of consciousness arise there, but sixty-six in the three planes beginning with Parittābha.

250.

250.

Ādipañcāmalā kaṅkhādiṭṭhiyutte vinā tahiṃ;

Teyeva pañcapaññāsa, jāyare suddhabhūmisu.

Therein, excluding those associated with doubt and wrong view, the first five stainless ones arise. These very fifty-five arise in the Pure Abodes.

251.

251.

Ādimaggadusāhāsarūpahīnajavā sako;

Pāko voṭṭhabbanañcāti, titālīsaṃ siyuṃ nabhe.

Excluding the initial path, the two hate-rooted, the smile-producing, the form-sphere impulsions, their own resultants, and the determining consciousness—thus forty-three are in the formless sphere.

252.

252.

Adhodhomanavajjā te,

Pāko ceva sako sako;

Dutiyādīsu jāyante,

Dve dve ūnā tato tato.

In the second and subsequent planes, they arise, two by two fewer than the preceding. This is by excluding the lower and lower jhāna consciousnesses and each of their own resultants.

253.

253.

Arūpesvekamekasmiṃ[V 0.0025], rūpesvādittikepi ca;

Tike ca tatiye ekaṃ, dve honti dutiyattike.

In each of the formless spheres and also in the first triad of the form spheres, there is one. In the third triad, one; in the second triad, there are two.

254.

254.

Antimaṃ [M 0.0023] rūpapākaṃ tu, chasu vehapphalādisu;

Kāmasugatiyaṃyeva, mahāpākā pavattare.

The last form-sphere resultant, however, is in the six [planes] beginning with Vehapphala. In the happy destinations of the sense-sphere, only the great resultants occur.

255.

255.

Ghāyanādittayaṃ kāme, paṭighadvayameva ca;

Sattarasesu paṭhamaṃ, amalaṃ mānavādisu.

The three [consciousnesses] beginning with smelling in the sense-sphere, and also the two rooted in aversion; among the seventeen, the first; the pure [consciousnesses] in those beginning with conceit.

256.

256.

Ariyāpāyavajjesu, caturodipphalādikā;

Apāyāruppavajjesu, hāsarūpasubhakriyaṃ.

Excluding the [planes of] noble ones and the states of woe, the four [supramundane consciousnesses] beginning with the fruit; excluding the states of woe and the formless spheres, the laughter-producing, the form-sphere wholesome, and the functional [consciousnesses].

257.

257.

Apāyuddhattayaṃ hitvā, hotākāsasubhakriyaṃ;

Tathāpāyuddhadve hitvā, viññāṇakusalakriyaṃ.

Excluding the three [related to] states of woe and restlessness, the wholesome and functional [consciousnesses] of the sphere of infinite space arise; likewise, excluding the two [related to] states of woe and restlessness, the wholesome and functional [consciousnesses] of the sphere of infinite consciousness [arise].

258.

258.

Bhavaggāpāyavajjesu, ākiñcaññasubhakriyaṃ;

Diṭṭhikaṅkhāyutā suddhe, vinā sabbāsu bhūmisu.

Excluding the highest existence and the states of woe, the wholesome and functional [consciousnesses] of the sphere of nothingness [arise]. Those [consciousnesses] associated with wrong view and doubt [arise] in all planes, except for the pure [planes].

259.

259.

Amalāni ca tīṇante,

Bhavagge ca subhakriyā;

Mahākriyā ca hontete,

Terasevānapāyisu.

The three pure [fruits] at the end, the wholesome functional [consciousness] in the highest existence, and the great functional [consciousnesses]—these thirteen indeed arise in the planes that are not states of woe.

260.

260.

Anāruppe manodhātu, dassanaṃ savatīraṇaṃ;

Kāme aniṭṭhasaṃyoge, brahmānaṃ pāpajaṃ phalaṃ.

In the formless sphere, [there is no] mind-element, seeing, or investigating consciousness; for Brahmās, the fruit born of unwholesome deeds [does not arise] in the sense-sphere in connection with an undesirable object.

261.

261.

Voṭṭhabbaṃ kāmapuññañca, diṭṭhihīnaṃ sauddhavaṃ;

Cuddasetāni cittāni, jāyare tiṃsabhūmisu.

The determining consciousness, and the sense-sphere wholesome [consciousnesses] devoid of wrong view and pure; these fourteen consciousnesses arise in thirty planes.

262.

262.

Indriyāni duve antadvayavajjesvahetusu;

Tīṇi kaṅkhetarāhetupāpe cattāri terasa.

There are two faculties in the rootless [consciousnesses], excluding the two extremes; three in the doubt-accompanied; four in the other rootless unwholesome; and [in] thirteen [others].

263.

263.

Cha ñāṇahīne tabbantasāsave satta nimmale;

Cattālīse panaṭṭhevaṃ, ñeyyamindriyabhedato.

Six [faculties are] in those devoid of knowledge; seven in the tainted [consciousnesses with knowledge] and in the pure ones. Thus, for forty-eight [consciousnesses], the division by faculties is to be known.

264.

264.

Dve [V 0.0026] balāni ahetvantadvaye tīṇi tu saṃsaye;

Cattāritarapāpe cha, honti sesaduhetuke.

Two powers are in the two rootless extremes; three in doubt; four in the other unwholesome; six occur in the remaining two-rooted.

265.

265.

Ekūnāsīticittesu, matiyuttesu satta tu;

Abalāni hi sesāni, vīriyantaṃ balaṃ bhave.

Among the seventy-nine consciousnesses, seven [powers are] in those associated with wisdom; the remaining are indeed without powers, although energy can be a power.

266.

266.

Ajhānaṅgāni [M 0.0024] dvepañca, takkantā hi tadaṅgatā;

Jhāne pītiviratte ta-ppādake amale duve.

The jhāna factors are five, and two; those are indeed factors of that. In the [third] jhāna, detached from zest, and in the pure [fourth jhāna], its basis, there are two [factors].

267.

267.

Tatiye sāmale tīṇi, cattāri dutiye tathā;

Kāme nippītike cāpi, pañcaṅgāni hi sesake.

In the tainted third [jhāna], there are three [factors]; likewise, four in the second. And also in the sense-sphere [consciousnesses] without zest, and in the remaining, there are indeed five factors.

268.

268.

Maggā dve saṃsaye diṭṭhihīnasesāsubhe tayo;

Duhetuketare suddhajjhāne ca dutiyādike.

There are two path factors in the doubt-accompanied [consciousness]; three in the remaining unwholesome [consciousnesses] devoid of wrong view, in the other two-rooted [consciousnesses], and in the pure jhānas from the second onwards.

269.

269.

Cattāro pañca paṭhamajhānakāmatihetuke;

Sattāmale dutiyādi-jhānike aṭṭha sesake.

Four and five [path factors arise] in the first-jhāna and the sense-sphere three-rooted [consciousnesses]; seven in the pure jhānas from the second onwards; and eight in the remaining.

270.

270.

Hetvantato hi maggassa, amaggaṅgamahetukaṃ;

Chamaggaṅgayutaṃ natthi, balehipi ca pañcahi.

Indeed, from the cause of the path, [one reaches] the causeless, which is not a path factor. It is not associated with the six path factors, nor with the five powers.

271.

271.

Sukhitīratadālambaṃ, iṭṭhe puññajupekkhavā;

Iṭṭhamajjhetaraṃ hoti, tabbipakkhe tu gocare.

Pleasant investigating and registering consciousness arise with a desirable object after meritorious impulsions with equanimity. The object is desirable, neutral, or its opposite, in the contrary case.

272.

272.

Dosadvayā tadālambaṃ, na sukhikriyato pana;

Sabbaṃ subhāsubhe naṭṭhe, tadālambaṇavācato.

Registering consciousness does not arise after the two [consciousnesses rooted in] aversion, nor after the pleasant functional. When all beautiful and ugly [objects] are absent, [it does not arise], according to the teaching on registering.

273.

273.

Kriyato vā tadālambaṃ, sopekkhāya sukhī na hi;

Itarā itarañceti, idaṃ suṭṭhupalakkhaye.

Or registering consciousness [arises] from a functional one. Indeed, that which is accompanied by equanimity is not pleasant. As for 'the one and the other,' this should be well marked.

274.

274.

Sandhidāyakakammena, tadālambapavattiyaṃ;

Niyāmanaṃ javassāha, kammassevaññakammato.

By the kamma that gives rebirth-linking, in the occurrence of registering consciousness, he spoke of the determination of the impulsion, as of one kamma by another.

275.

275.

Citte cetasikā yasmiṃ,

Ye vuttā te samāsato;

Vuccare [V 0.0027] dāni dvepañce,

Sabbagā satta jāyare.

Which mental factors arise in which consciousness has been stated in brief. Now the fifty-two will be discussed. The seven universal mental factors arise [in all consciousnesses].

276.

276.

Takkacārādhimokkhehi, teyeva jāyare dasa;

Pañcaṭṭhānamanodhātu-pañcake sukhatīraṇe.

With initial thought, sustained thought, and decision, these ten [particular factors] arise; [they are absent] in the five sense-consciousnesses, the mind-element, and the pleasant investigating consciousness.

277.

277.

Ete pītādhikā hāse, vāyāmena ca dvādhikā;

Voṭṭhabbanepi eteva, dasekā pītivajjitā.

These, with joy in addition, are eleven in smiling consciousness. And with energy, they are twelve. In determining consciousness also, these same [arise], eleven without joy.

278.

278.

Pāpasādhāraṇā [M 0.0025] te ca, tipañcuddhaccasaññute;

Kaṅkhāyuttepi eteva, sakaṅkhā hīnanicchayā.

And those [factors] common to the unwholesome are connected with restlessness in all [unwholesome consciousnesses]. These same [factors arise] also in consciousness connected with doubt, which is accompanied by doubt and lacks decision.

279.

279.

Kaṅkhāvajjā paneteva, sadosacchandanicchayā;

Sattarasa duse honti, salobhantadvaye pana.

But these same [factors], excluding doubt, [arise] with aversion, desire, and decision. Seventeen [factors] are in the aversion-rooted [consciousnesses]. But in the last two greed-rooted [consciousnesses]...

280.

280.

Dosavajjā salobhā te,

Tatiyādidukesu te;

Diṭṭhipītidvayādhikā,

Dvinavekūnavīsati.

Those [factors] with greed, excluding aversion, [arise] in the third and subsequent pairs. With the addition of the pair, wrong view and joy, they are eighteen and nineteen respectively.

281.

281.

Pīticārappanāvajjā, ādito yāva tiṃsime;

Uppajjanti catutthādi-rūpārūpamanesu ve.

Excluding joy, sustained thought, and absorption, these thirty [beautiful factors] from the beginning arise indeed in the form and formless consciousnesses from the fourth [jhāna] onwards.

282.

282.

Pīticāravitakkesu,

Ekena dvititikkamā;

Tatiyādīsu teyeva,

Tiṃsekadvetayodhikā.

In regard to joy, sustained thought, and initial thought, by transcending one, two, and three [factors] respectively, in the third [jhāna] and so on, these same [factors] become thirty-one, thirty-two, and thirty-three.

283.

283.

Etevādidvaye kāme, dutiyādidukesu hi;

Matiṃ pītiṃ matippītiṃ, hitvā te kamato siyuṃ.

Indeed, in the first two sense-sphere [consciousnesses] and in the second and subsequent pairs, these same [factors arise], having abandoned wisdom, joy, and both wisdom and joy, respectively.

284.

284.

Jhāne vuttāva tajjhānikāmale viratādhikā;

Tatthetā niyatā vittiṃ, vade sabbattha sambhavā.

As stated, in the pure jhānic consciousnesses, they arise with the abstinences in addition. Therein, these are of fixed occurrence; one should say they arise all together.

285.

285.

Kāmapuññesu [V 0.0028] paccekaṃ,

Jayantāniyatesu hi;

Viratīyo dayāmodā,

Kāme sātasubhakriye.

Indeed, in the sense-sphere meritorious consciousnesses, the abstinences, compassion, and sympathetic joy arise individually and unfixedly; likewise in the sense-sphere's pleasant, beautiful, functional consciousnesses.

286.

286.

Majjhattepi vadanteke, sahetukasubhakriye;

Sukhajjhānepi paccekaṃ, hontiyeva dayāmudā.

Some say they also arise in the neutral, rooted, beautiful, functional consciousnesses. Even in the pleasant jhānas, compassion and sympathetic joy do indeed arise individually.

287.

287.

Thinamiddhaṃ sasaṅkhāre, diṭṭhihīnadvaye tahiṃ;

Mānena vā tayo sesadiṭṭhihīne vidhekako.

Sloth and torpor arise in the prompted consciousnesses, that is, in the pair devoid of wrong view. Or, with conceit, three factors arise in the remaining one devoid of wrong view.

288.

288.

Issāmaccherakukkuccā[M 0.0026], visuṃ dosayutadvaye;

Tatthantake siyuṃ thinamiddhakena tayopi vā.

Envy, stinginess, and worry arise separately in the two consciousnesses connected with hate. In the latter of these, one of them may occur with sloth and torpor, thus making three factors.

289.

289.

Ye vuttā ettakā ettha, iti cetasikākhilā;

Tatthettakesvidantevaṃ, vuccateyaṃ nayodhunā.

Thus, all the mental factors that have been spoken of herein are this many. Now this method is stated to determine which among them arise in which consciousnesses.

290.

290.

Tesaṭṭhiyā sukhaṃ dukkhaṃ, tīsupekkhāpi vedanā;

Pañcapaññāsacittesu, bhave indriyato pana.

Pleasure is in sixty-three consciousnesses, pain in three, and the feeling of equanimity in fifty-five. But from the standpoint of the faculties, it is otherwise.

291.

291.

Ekatthekattha ceva dvesaṭṭhiyā dvīsu pañcahi;

Paññāsāyāti viññeyyaṃ, sukhādindriyapañcakaṃ.

The pentad of faculties beginning with pleasure should be understood thus: pleasure in one, pain in one, joy in sixty-two, grief in two, and equanimity in fifty-five.

292.

292.

Dasuttarasate hoti, nicchayo vīriyaṃ tato;

Pañcahīne tatokūne, samādhindriyamādise.

Decision is in one hundred and ten consciousnesses; energy is in a number five less than that. One should point out the concentration faculty in a number less than that.

293.

293.

Chando ekasatekūnavīsa saddhādayo pana;

Ñāṇavajjā navahīnasate honti matī pana.

Desire-to-do is in one hundred and one consciousnesses. But faith and the others, excluding wisdom, are in ninety-one. Wisdom, however, is in seventy-nine.

294.

294.

Ekūnāsītiyā cāro, chasaṭṭhīsu panappanā;

Pañcapaññāsake pīti, ekapaññāsake siyā.

Sustained thought is in seventy-nine consciousnesses; but initial thought is in sixty-six. Joy is in fifty-five, but it may be in fifty-one.

295.

295.

Viratī chaṭṭhake vīse, karuṇāmuditātha vā;

Aṭṭhasopekkhacittena, aṭṭhavīsatiyā siyuṃ.

The abstinences are in twenty-six consciousnesses. Compassion and sympathetic joy, or these together with equanimity, are in twenty-eight.

296.

296.

Ahīrikamanottappamohuddhaccā [V 0.0029] dvādaseva;

Lobho aṭṭhasu cittesu, thinamiddhaṃ tu pañcasu.

Shamelessness, lack of moral dread, delusion, and restlessness are in all twelve unwholesome consciousnesses; greed is in eight consciousnesses; but sloth and torpor are in five.

297.

297.

Māno catūsu diṭṭhi ca, tathā dvīsu manesu hi;

Doso issā ca maccheraṃ, kukkuccañca bhavantime.

Conceit is in four consciousnesses, and wrong view is likewise in four. Indeed, hate, envy, stinginess, and worry are in two consciousnesses.

298.

298.

Ekasmiṃ vimatī hoti, evaṃ vuttānusārato;

Appavattinayo cāpi, sakkā ñātuṃ vijānatā.

Doubt is in one consciousness. According to what has been said, the method of non-occurrence can also be known by the wise.

299.

299.

Asmiṃ khandheva viññeyyo, vedanādīsvayaṃ nayo;

Ekadhādividho yutti-vasātenāviyogato.

This same method should be understood for this aggregate of consciousness and for the other aggregates of feeling and so on. They are treated as onefold or twofold by way of reasoning, due to their inseparability.

300.

300.

Upamā pheṇupiṇḍo ca, bubbuḷo migataṇhikā;

Kadalī māyā viññeyyā, khandhānaṃ tu yathākkamaṃ.

The aggregates should be understood in due order by the similes of a lump of foam, a bubble, a mirage, a plantain trunk, and a magical illusion.

301.

301.

Tesaṃ [M 0.0027] vimaddāsahanakhaṇasobhappalobhana-

Nisāravañcakattehi, samānattaṃ samāhaṭaṃ.

Their similarity is shown by their inability to withstand pressure, their momentary charm, their alluring nature, their corelessness, and their deceptiveness.

302.

302.

Te sāsavā upādānakkhandhā khandhāvanāsavā;

Tatthādī dukkhavatthuttā, dukkhā bhārā ca khādakā.

Those aggregates with taints are the clinging-aggregates; the other aggregates are taintless. Among them, the former, being a basis for suffering, are suffering, burdens, and devourers.

303.

303.

Khandhāniccādidhammā te, vadhakā sabhayā itī;

Asukhaddhammato cikkhā, ukkhittāsikarī yathā.

Those aggregates have the nature of impermanence and so on; thus they are murderers and are fraught with danger. They are declared as having the nature of suffering, like a person holding an upraised sword.

Iti saccasaṅkhepe viññāṇakkhandhapakiṇṇakanayasaṅkhepo nāma

Thus in the Saccasaṅkhepa ends the chapter named 'The Summary of the Miscellaneous Method concerning the Consciousness Aggregate'.

Catuttho paricchedo.

The Fourth Chapter.

5. Pañcamo paricchedo

5. The Fifth Chapter

Nibbānapaññattiparidīpano

The Exposition of the Designation of Nibbāna

304.

304.

Rāgādīnaṃ [V 0.0030] khayaṃ vuttaṃ, nibbānaṃ santilakkhaṇaṃ;

Saṃsāradukkhasantāpatattassālaṃ sametave.

The destruction of lust and so forth is declared to be Nibbāna, characterized by peace; it is sufficient to still the burning torment of the suffering of saṃsāra.

305.

305.

Khayamattaṃ na nibbānaṃ, sagambhīrādivācato;

Abhāvassa hi kummānaṃ, lomasseva na vācatā.

Mere destruction is not Nibbāna, on account of statements describing it as 'profound,' and so on; for indeed, of non-existence, like the hair of a tortoise, there is no such designation.

306.

306.

Khayoti vuccate maggo, tappāpattā idaṃ khayaṃ;

Arahattaṃ viyuppāda-vayābhāvā dhuvañca taṃ.

The path is called 'destruction'; by attaining it, this destruction is realized. Due to the absence of arising and passing away, it is permanent, like Arahantship.

307.

307.

Saṅkhataṃ sammutiñcāpi, ñāṇamālamba neva hi;

Chinde male tato vatthu, icchitabbamasaṅkhataṃ.

For knowledge does not take the conditioned and the conventional as its object. One should cut off the defilements; then the unconditioned reality is to be desired.

308.

308.

Pattukāmena taṃ santiṃ, chabbisuddhiṃ samādiya;

Ñāṇadassanasuddhī tu, sādhetabbā hitatthinā.

One who desires to attain that peace should undertake the six purities; then, the purity of knowledge and vision should be achieved by that one who seeks his welfare.

309.

309.

Cetanādividhā sīla-suddhi tattha catubbidhā;

Sopacārasamādhī tu, cittasuddhīti vuccate.

Therein, the purification of virtue is fourfold, with its divisions beginning with intention. Concentration, including both access and absorption, however, is called the purification of mind.

310.

310.

Sampādetvādidvesuddhiṃ, namanā nāmaṃ tu ruppa-

To rūpaṃ natthi attādivatthūti ca vavatthape.

Having accomplished the preliminary twofold purity, one should determine that 'name' is so-called because it inclines, and 'form' is so-called because it is afflicted, and that therein there is no self or other such entity.

311.

311.

Maṇindhanātape [M 0.0028] aggi, asantopi samāgame;

Yathā hoti tathā cittaṃ, vatthālambādisaṅgame.

Just as fire, though not pre-existing in their combination, arises from a sun-crystal, fuel, and the sun's heat, so too does the mind arise in the conjunction of a base, an object, and so forth.

312.

312.

Paṅgulandhā yathā gantuṃ, paccekamasamatthakā;

Yanti yuttā yathā evaṃ, nāmarūpavhayā kriyā.

Just as a lame man and a blind man, each unable to go by themselves, proceed when yoked together, so too do the activities called name and form.

313.

313.

Na nāmarūpato añño, attādi iti dassanaṃ;

Sodhanattā hi duddiṭṭhiṃ, diṭṭhisuddhīti vuccati.

The seeing that there is no self or the like apart from name and form, which serves to purify wrong view, is called the purification of view.

314.

314.

Avijjātaṇhupādāna-kammenādimhi [V 0.0031] taṃ dvayaṃ;

Rūpaṃ kammādito nāmaṃ, vatthādīhi pavattiyaṃ.

That duality has ignorance, craving, clinging, and kamma as its origin. In the course of existence, form arises from kamma and so forth, and name arises from the bases and so forth.

315.

315.

Sadā sabbattha sabbesaṃ, sadisaṃ na yato tato;

Nāhetunāñño attādiniccahetūti passati.

Because it is not always, everywhere, and for all beings the same, one therefore sees that it is not without a cause, nor is there another permanent cause such as a self or the like.

316.

316.

Evaṃ tīrayate kaṅkhā, yāya paññāya paccaye;

Diṭṭhattā suddhi sā kaṅkhātaraṇaṃ iti vuccati.

Thus, by that wisdom which discerns conditions, doubt is crossed over; because of this direct seeing, that purity is called the crossing over of doubt.

317.

317.

Pattaññātapariñño so, atraṭṭho yatateyati;

Tīraṇavhapariññāya, visuddhatthaṃ sadādaro.

He who has attained the full understanding of what is to be known, being established in this, the striver strives; for the sake of purification through the full understanding called 'discernment', he is ever diligent.

318.

318.

Tikālādivasā khandhe, samāsetvā kalāpato;

Aniccā dukkhānattāti, ādo evaṃ vipassati.

At the outset, having grouped the aggregates into bundles in terms of the three times and so forth, one thus contemplates them as impermanent, suffering, and not-self.

319.

319.

Khandhāniccā khayaṭṭhena, bhayaṭṭhena dukhāva te;

Anattāsārakaṭṭhena, iti passe punappunaṃ.

The aggregates are impermanent in the sense of decay; they are indeed suffering in the sense of fear; they are not-self in the sense of being without essence—thus one should see again and again.

320.

320.

Ākārehi aniccādicattālīsehi sammase;

Lakkhaṇānaṃ vibhūtatthaṃ, khandhānaṃ pana sabbaso.

One should thoroughly examine the aggregates in every way with the forty aspects of impermanence and so forth, for the sake of the manifestation of their characteristics.

321.

321.

Evañcāpi asijjhante, navadhā nisitindriyo;

Sattakadvayato sammā, rūpārūpe vipassaye.

And if one does not succeed in this way, with faculties sharpened ninefold, one should rightly contemplate form and formless phenomena in terms of the two sets of seven.

322.

322.

Rūpamādānanikkhepā, vayovuddhattagāmito;

Sammasevannajādīhi, dhammatārūpatopi ca.

One should examine form by its taking up and laying down, by its progression to aging and maturity, by its being produced from nutriment and so forth, and also by its nature as a mere phenomenon.

323.

323.

Nāmaṃ kalāpayamato, khaṇato kamatopi ca;

Diṭṭhimānanikantīnaṃ, passe ugghāṭanādito.

One should contemplate name by grouping it, by its momentary nature, by its sequential arising, and by the uprooting of views, conceit, and craving.

324.

324.

Avijjātaṇhākammanna-hetuto [M 0.0029] rūpaṃ ubbhave;

Vināhāraṃ saphassehi, vedanādittayaṃ bhave.

Form arises from the causes of ignorance, craving, kamma, and nutriment; the triad beginning with feeling arises from contact, without physical nutriment.

325.

325.

Tehiyeva vinā phassaṃ,

Nāmarūpādhikehi tu;

Cittaṃ [V 0.0032] hetukkhayā so so,

Veti ve tassa tassa tu.

Without those conditions, contact does not arise; it arises with name and form as the principal factors. Consciousness, however, upon the cessation of its respective cause, that very consciousness, indeed, ceases.

326.

326.

Hetutodayanāsevaṃ, khaṇodayavayenapi;

Iti paññāsākārehi, passe punūdayabbayaṃ.

Thus, by way of causal arising and cessation, and also by way of momentary arising and passing away, one should contemplate again the arising and passing away with its fifty aspects.

327.

327.

Yogissevaṃ samāraddhaudayabbayadassino;

Pātubhonti upaklesā, sabhāvā hetutopi ca.

For the yogi who has thus undertaken the seeing of arising and passing away, imperfections of insight appear, both from their own nature and from causes.

328.

328.

Te obhāsamatussāhapassaddhisukhupekkhanā;

Sati pītādhimokkho ca, nikanti ca dasīritā.

These ten are spoken of: illumination, wisdom, enthusiasm, tranquility, happiness, equanimity, mindfulness, rapture, resolve, and subtle craving.

329.

329.

Taṇhādiṭṭhunnatiggāhavatthuto tiṃsadhā te ca;

Taduppanne cale bālo, amagge maggadassako.

And these are thirtyfold, based on craving, view, conceit, and grasping. When they arise, the fool is shaken, seeing the non-path as the path.

330.

330.

Vipassanā pathokkantā, tadāsi matimādhunā;

Na maggo gāhavatthuttā, tesaṃ iti vipassati.

The wise one now sees thus: 'Insight has entered upon the path; but these phenomena are not the path, because they are objects for grasping.'

331.

331.

Upaklese aniccādi-vasage sodayabbaye;

Passato vīthinokkantadassanaṃ vuccate patho.

For one who sees the defilements as being subject to impermanence and so forth, with their arising and passing away, that vision which has entered upon the proper course is called the path.

332.

332.

Maggāmagge vavatthetvā, yā paññā evamuṭṭhitā;

Maggāmaggikkhasaṅkhātā, suddhi sā pañcamī bhave.

That wisdom which, having distinguished path from non-path, thus arises—that purity, known as the knowledge and vision of what is path and not-path, is the fifth.

333.

333.

Pahānavhapariññāya, ādito suddhisiddhiyā;

Tīraṇavhapariññāya, antago yatatedhunā.

For the achievement of purity from the outset through the full understanding called 'abandoning', he now strives to reach the end through the full understanding called 'discernment'.

334.

334.

Jāyate navañāṇī sā, visuddhi kamatodaya-

Bbayādī ghaṭamānassa, nava honti panettha hi.

That purity, comprising nine knowledges, arises; for one striving with arising and passing away and so forth in succession, there are indeed nine knowledges herein.

335.

335.

Santatīriyato ceva, ghanenāpi ca channato;

Lakkhaṇāni na khāyante, saṃkiliṭṭhā vipassanā.

When the characteristics do not appear, being obscured by continuity, by compactness, and by deportment, insight is defiled.

336.

336.

Tatotra [M 0.0030] sammase bhiyyo, punadevudayabbayaṃ;

Tenāniccādisampassaṃ, paṭutaṃ paramaṃ vaje.

Therefore, one should here examine more thoroughly, again and again, the arising and passing away. By that, seeing impermanence and so forth, one will attain supreme sharpness.

337.

337.

Āvaṭṭetvā [V 0.0033] yaduppādaṭṭhitiādīhi passato;

Bhaṅgeva tiṭṭhate ñāṇaṃ, tadā bhaṅgamatī siyā.

When, for one who sees by repeatedly adverting to arising, persistence, and so forth, knowledge becomes established on dissolution alone, then there is the knowledge of dissolution.

338.

338.

Evaṃ passayato bhaṅgaṃ, tibhavo khāyate yadā;

Sīhādiva bhayaṃ hutvā, siyā laddhā bhayikkhaṇā.

When, for one thus seeing dissolution, the triple existence appears as a terror; like a lion and so forth, it appears as fearful, and then the knowledge of fear is obtained.

339.

339.

Sādīnavā patiṭṭhante, khandhādittagharaṃ viya;

Yadā tadā siyā laddhā, ādīnavānupassanā.

When dangers become manifest, like the aggregates being a burning house, then the contemplation of danger is obtained.

340.

340.

Saṅkhārādīnavaṃ disvā, ramate na bhavādisu;

Mati yadā tadā laddhā, siyā nibbidapassanā.

Having seen the danger in formations, one does not delight in existences and the like; when wisdom is thus obtained, there arises insight into disenchantment.

341.

341.

Ñāṇaṃ muccitukāmaṃ te, sabbabhūsaṅkhate yadā;

Jālādīhi ca macchādī, tadā laddhā cajjamati.

When that knowledge desires to be freed from all conditioned things, like a fish from a net and the like, then the wisdom of relinquishment is obtained.

342.

342.

Saṅkhāre asubhāniccadukkhatonattato mati;

Passantī cattumussukkā, paṭisaṅkhānupassanā.

The mind, seeing formations as unattractive, impermanent, suffering, and not-self, becomes zealous to relinquish them; this is insight by reflection.

343.

343.

Vuttātra paṭubhāvāya, sabbañāṇapavattiyā;

Mīnasaññāya sappassa, gāhaluddasamopamā.

Here it is said, for the sake of readiness and for the arising of all knowledges, that there are similes: like the perception of a fish towards a snake, and like the capture by a hunter.

344.

344.

Attattaniyato suññaṃ, dvidhā “nāhaṃ kvacā”dinā;

Catudhā chabbidhā cāpi, bahudhā passato bhusaṃ.

Empty of self and what belongs to self, in two ways, by 'I am not anywhere' and so on; seeing intensely in four ways, six ways, and also in many ways.

345.

345.

Āvaṭṭatiggimāsajja,

Nhārūva mati saṅkhataṃ;

Cattabhariyo yathā dose,

Tathā taṃ samupekkhate.

Like a whirlpool, a firebrand, or a mirage, the mind regards the conditioned; as a man with four wives sees their faults, so one observes it with equanimity.

346.

346.

Tāva sādīnavānampi, lakkhaṇe tiṭṭhate mati;

Na passe yāva sā tīraṃ, sāmuddasakuṇī yathā.

The mind continues to stand upon the characteristic of danger, so long as it does not see the shore, just like a seabird.

347.

347.

Saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇāyaṃ, sikhāpattā vipassanā;

Vuṭṭhānagāminīti ca, sānulomāti vuccati.

This knowledge of equanimity towards formations is insight that has reached its peak; it is called 'leading to emergence' and is also termed 'conformity'.

348.

348.

Patvā [M 0.0031][V 0.0034] mokkhamukhaṃ satta, sādhetiriyapuggale;

Jhānaṅgādippabhede ca, pādakādivasena sā.

Having reached the entrance to liberation, it establishes the seven types of noble individuals; it does so by means of distinctions such as jhāna factors, and by way of the bases of psychic power and so forth.

349.

349.

Aniccato hi vuṭṭhānaṃ, yadi yassāsi yogino;

Sodhimokkhassa bāhullā, tikkhasaddhindriyo bhave.

If emergence from impermanence should occur for a yogi, then due to an abundance of conviction, he would become one with a keen faith faculty.

350.

350.

Dukkhatonattato tañce, siyā honti kamena te;

Passaddhivedabāhullā, tikkhekaggamatindriyā.

And if it should arise from suffering or not-self, then in sequence they become, due to an abundance of tranquility and joy, possessed of keen concentration and wisdom faculties.

351.

351.

Paññādhurattamuddiṭṭhaṃ, vuṭṭhānaṃ yadinattato;

Saddhādhurattaṃ sesehi, taṃ viyābhinivesato.

Emergence from not-self is declared to be wisdom-dominant; from the remaining two, it is faith-dominant, on account of a subtle adherence.

352.

352.

Dve tikkhasaddhasamathā, siyuṃ saddhānusārino;

Ādo majjhesu ṭhānesu, chasu saddhāvimuttakā.

Two types, those with keen faith and tranquility, would be faith-followers; at the initial and middle stages, in six instances, they are ones liberated by faith.

353.

353.

Itaro dhammānusārīdo, diṭṭhippatto anantake;

Paññāmuttobhayatthante, ajhānijhānikā ca te.

The other, at the initial stage, is a Dhamma-follower; in the subsequent stages, one who has attained the view; at the end, one liberated by wisdom or one liberated in both ways. And these may be either jhāna-attainers or non-jhāna-attainers.

354.

354.

Tikkhasaddhassa cantepi, saddhāmuttattamīritaṃ;

Visuddhimagge majjhassa, kāyasakkhittamaṭṭhasu.

Even for one with keen faith at the final stage, liberation by faith is spoken of; in the Visuddhimagga, for one with moderate faculties, the state of a body-witness is mentioned among the eight.

355.

355.

Vuttaṃ mokkhakathāyaṃ yaṃ, tikkhapaññārahassa tu;

Diṭṭhipattattaṃ hetañca, tañca natthābhidhammike.

But what was said in the discourse on liberation regarding one worthy of keen wisdom—namely, the state of having attained the view—that is not found in the Abhidhamma.

356.

356.

Te sabbe aṭṭhamokkhānaṃ, lābhī ce chasu majjhasu;

Kāyasakkhī siyuṃ ante, ubhatobhāgamuttakā.

If all of these are attainers of the eight liberations, then among the six intermediate types, they would be body-witnesses; at the end, they would be ones liberated in both ways.

357.

357.

Anulomāni cattāri, tīṇi dve vā bhavanti hi;

Maggassa vīthiyaṃ mandamajjhatikkhamatibbasā.

Indeed, in the path process, there are four, three, or two conformity moments, according to whether one's intelligence is slow, medium, or keen.

358.

358.

Visuddhimagge cattāri, paṭisiddhāni sabbathā;

Evamaṭṭhasāliniyā, vuttattā evamīritaṃ.

In the Visuddhimagga, the case of four conformity moments is entirely rejected; it is declared thus because it is so stated in the Aṭṭhasālinī.

359.

359.

Bhavaṅgāsannadosopi, nappanāya thirattato;

Suddhiṃ paṭipadāñāṇadassanevaṃ labhe yati.

A monk thus obtains the Purification of Knowledge and Vision of the Way; for even the fault of proximity to bhavaṅga, due to its stability, is not conducive to absorption.

360.

360.

Āvajjaṃ [M 0.0032][V 0.0035] viya maggassa, chaṭṭhasattamasuddhinaṃ;

Antarā santimārabbha, tehi gotrabhu jāyate.

Taking as its object the peace that lies between the sixth and seventh purifications, the change-of-lineage consciousness arises from them, like the adverting consciousness for the path.

361.

361.

Saṃyojanattayacchedī, maggo uppajjate tato;

Phalāni ekaṃ dve tīṇi, tato vuttamatikkamā.

Then the path that severs the three fetters arises; thereafter, one, two, or three fruit moments occur, according to the sequence described.

362.

362.

Tathā bhāvayato hoti, rāgadosatanūkaraṃ;

Dutiyo tapphalaṃ tamhā, sakadāgāmi tapphalī.

For one cultivating thus, there occurs the attenuation of passion and hatred; from that arises the second path and its fruit, and the bearer of that fruit is a once-returner.

363.

363.

Evaṃ bhāvayato rāgadosanāsakarubbhave;

Tatiyo tapphalaṃ tamhā, tapphalaṭṭhonāgāmiko.

For one cultivating in this way, there occurs the destruction of passion and hatred; from that arises the third path and its fruit, and one standing in that fruit is a non-returner.

364.

364.

Evaṃ bhāvayato sesadosanāsakarubbhave;

Catuttho tapphalaṃ tamhā, arahā tapphalaṭṭhako.

For one cultivating thus, there occurs the destruction of the remaining defilements; from that arises the fourth path and its fruit, and the Arahant is one who stands in that fruit.

365.

365.

Katakicco bhavacchedo, dakkhiṇeyyopadhikkhayā;

Nibbutiṃ yāti dīpova, sabbadukkhantasaññitaṃ.

His task is done, becoming is cut off; worthy of offerings through the destruction of the substrata, he attains Nibbāna—like an extinguished lamp—which is known as the end of all suffering.

366.

366.

Evaṃ siddhā siyā suddhi, ñāṇadassanasaññitā;

Vuttaṃ ettāvatā saccaṃ, paramatthaṃ samāsato.

Thus is accomplished the purification known as knowledge and vision. To this extent, the truth, the ultimate meaning, has been spoken in brief.

367.

367.

Saccaṃ sammuti sattādiavatthu vuccate yato;

Na labbhālātacakkaṃva, taṃ hi rūpādayo vinā.

That wherein beings and so on are spoken of, though they are not real things, is called conventional truth; for it is not found apart from form and so on, just like the circle made by a firebrand.

368.

368.

Tena tena pakārena, rūpādiṃ na vihāya tu;

Tathā tathābhidhānañca, gāhañca vattate tato.

In various ways, without abandoning form and so on, various designations and grasping proceed from that accordingly.

369.

369.

Labbhate parikappena, yato taṃ na musā tato;

Avuttālambamiccāhu, parittādīsvavācato.

Since it is apprehended through conception, it is therefore not false. They say its object is unexpressed, because in limited states of consciousness and so on, it is non-verbal.

370.

370.

Pāpakalyāṇamittoyaṃ, sattoti khandhasantati;

Ekattena gahetvāna, voharantīdha paṇḍitā.

This bad or good friend, this being, is a continuity of aggregates; the wise here, having grasped it as a unity, use it in conventional speech.

371.

371.

Pathavādi viyekopi, puggalo na yato tato;

Kudiṭṭhivatthubhāvena, puggalaggahaṇaṃ bhave.

Even when the earth element and so on are analyzed, a person is not found anywhere; because it is a basis for wrong view, the grasping of a 'person' occurs.

372.

372.

Etaṃ [V 0.0036] visayato katvā, saṅkhādīhi padehi tu;

Avijjamānapaññatti, iti taññūhi bhāsitā.

Having made this the object, with terms such as 'constituents' and so on, it is called 'a designation of what is non-existent'—thus it is said by those who know.

373.

373.

Paññatti [M 0.0033] vijjamānassa, rūpādivisayattato;

Kāyaṃ paññatti ce suṭṭhu, vadato suṇa saccato.

A designation is of what exists, because its object is form and so on. If one says, 'The body is a designation,' listen well to the truth from him who speaks.

374.

374.

Saviññattivikāro hi, saddo saccadvayassa tu;

Paññāpanattā paññatti, iti taññūhi bhāsitā.

Indeed, sound, a modification with intimation, pertains to the two truths; because it makes known, it is a designation—thus it is said by those who know.

375.

375.

Paccuppannādiālambaṃ, niruttipaṭisambhidā-

Ñāṇassāti idañcevaṃ, sati yujjati nāññathā.

That the knowledge of the analytical understanding of language has the present and so on as its object—this is fitting when it is so, and not otherwise.

376.

376.

Saddābhidheyyasaṅkhādi, iti ce sabbavatthunaṃ;

Paññāpetabbato hoti, paññattipadasaṅgaho.

If all things—sound, meaning, constituents, and so on—are to be designated, then they are included under the term 'designation' because they are designable.

377.

377.

“Sabbe paññattidhammā”ti, desetabbaṃ tathā sati;

Atha paññāpanassāpi, paññāpetabbavatthunaṃ.

If that were so, it should be taught that 'All phenomena are designations.' Then, regarding the act of designating and the objects to be designated...

378.

378.

Vibhāgaṃ ñāpanatthaṃ hi, tathuddeso katoti ce;

Na kattabbaṃ visuṃ tena, paññattipathasaṅgahaṃ.

If it is said that such an exposition is made for the purpose of making known the distinction, then for that reason one should not make a separate compilation of the ways of designation.

379.

379.

Paññāpiyattā catūhi, paññattādipadehi sā;

Parehi paññāpanattā, iti ācariyābravuṃ.

Because it is to be made known, and because it is made known by others, it is designated by the four terms beginning with 'designation'—thus said the teachers.

380.

380.

Rūpādayo upādāya, paññāpetabbato kira;

Avijjamānopādāyapaññatti paṭhamā tato.

Indeed, because it is to be designated by depending on form and so on, therefore the first is 'designation by way of what is non-existent'.

381.

381.

Sotaviññāṇasantānānantaraṃ pattajātinā;

Gahitapubbasaṅketamanodvārikacetasā.

By the mind-door consciousness—which arises immediately after the continuity of ear-consciousness and which has grasped the previously learned convention—

382.

382.

Paññāpenti gahitāya, yāya sattarathādayo;

Iti sā nāmapaññatti, dutiyāti ca kittitā.

by which they designate beings, chariots, and so on. Thus, that is called 'name-designation,' and it is proclaimed as the second.

383.

383.

Saddato aññanāmāvabodhenatthāvabodhanaṃ;

Kicchasādhanato pubbanayo eva pasaṃsiyo.

Because understanding the meaning by apprehending another name from the sound is difficult to accomplish, the former method is indeed to be praised.

384.

384.

Sā [V 0.0037] vijjamānapaññatti, tathā avijjamānatā;

Vijjamānena cāvijjamānā tabbiparītakā.

That designation is of what exists, and likewise of what does not exist; of what does not exist by means of what exists, and the reverse of that.

385.

385.

Avijjamānena vijjamānatabbiparītakā;

Iccetā chabbidhā tāsu, paṭhamā matiādikā.

Of what exists by means of what does not exist, and the reverse of that. Thus, these are of six kinds. Among them, the first is 'thought' and so on.

386.

386.

Satto [M 0.0034] saddho narussāho,

Seniyo manacetanā;

Iccevametā viññeyyā,

Kamato dutiyādikā.

A being, a faithful one, an energetic man, a soldier, mind, and volition—thus these should be understood in order as the second and so forth.

387.

387.

Evaṃ lakkhaṇato ñatvā,

Saccadvayamasaṅkaraṃ;

Kātabbo pana vohāro,

Viññūhi na yathā tathāti.

Having thus known the two truths by their characteristics without confusion, conventional usage should nevertheless be employed by the wise, and not haphazardly.

Iti saccasaṅkhepe nibbānapaññattiparidīpano nāma

Thus in the Synopsis of Truth ends the Elucidation of Nibbāna and Designation.

Pañcamo paricchedo.

The Fifth Chapter.

Saccasaṅkhepo niṭṭhito.

The Synopsis of Truth is concluded.
